How to use this guide

Read in order, once

Each chapter is cut into short parts that follow the slides in order. A part starts with the plain idea, shows a picture, and only then shows the formula or the code. If a word is new, it is explained where it first appears.

Click everything

Boxes marked Next step / Play run an algorithm one step at a time, with a sentence under the picture saying what just happened. Boxes with sliders and menus let you change the input and watch the answer change. The numbers come from the real algorithm, not from a drawing.

Guess, then reveal

Where a slide asks a question, the guide asks it too, then hides the answer behind a button. Each chapter ends with a one-page summary and a self-test.

Find your place in the slides

Small chips like slide 12 tell you which slide a section explains, so you can keep the deck open next to this page.

Picture it

Think of this guide as a patient study partner: nothing is assumed, and nobody laughs at a question.

Slips found in the slides

A few slides contain a small mistake or a loose wording. The guide points each one out where it appears, so you do not lose time wondering if you misread it.

Slides 1–40 · 01_recursion

Recursion from Scratch

Every idea in the slides, explained from zero, with pictures and step-by-step demos you can click through. If you can count a queue of people, you can do all of this.

Read it top to bottom once. Each part says which slides it covers, so you can also jump to the slide you are stuck on.

In this chapter

    Part 0 · Slide 1 is the title slide

    Start here: the words, and the one big idea

    Five words you need

    Everything later uses these five words. Skim them now, come back whenever a word feels fuzzy.

    WordPlain meaningExample
    functionA little machine. You put a number in, it gives an answer back.f(3) means: run the machine f with 3 put in.
    parameterThe thing you hand to the function. Some functions take two or three.In f(3) the parameter is 3.
    callUsing a function. A function can call other functions, even itself.“f(3) calls f(2)”
    arrayA row of numbered boxes, each holding one value.A[3] is the box at position 3.
    swapTwo boxes trade what they hold.Swapping A[1] and A[4] in a b c d gives d b c a.

    The one big idea, with a queue of people

    You are the last person in a line. You want to know how many people are in the line, counting you and everyone in front of you. You cannot see the front. What do you do?

    You tap the person in front and ask them the same question. They tap the next one and ask the same thing. This keeps going until the question reaches the person at the very front. That person looks ahead, sees nobody, and says “1” without asking anyone.

    Now the answers travel back. Person 2 hears “1”, adds themselves, and says “2”. Person 3 hears “2” and says “3”. You hear “3” and say “4”.

    The definition

    Recursion means solving a problem by asking the same question about a slightly smaller version of it, and stopping when the version is so small that the answer is obvious.

    Every recursive thing in these slides has exactly three ingredients. The queue shows all three.

    1. A base case. A situation so small that you know the answer without asking. The front person says 1.
    2. Progress. Every other case asks about something smaller, so the questions must eventually reach the base case. Each person asks the person one place closer to the front.
    3. Use the answer. When the smaller answer comes back, do a little bit of work to turn it into your answer. Add 1.

    Picture it

    If your head starts to hurt, you are probably trying to follow everyone at once. Do not. Follow just one person: ask the next one, wait, do my small bit. Trusting that the person in front will answer correctly is the whole skill.

    The story of all 40 slides in six sentences

    1. Some lists of numbers are easiest to describe with a rule that uses the previous number (part 1).
    2. Writing such a rule neatly gives a recurrence equation (part 2), and you get answers from it by unwrapping (part 3).
    3. A rule like that only works if it has a base case and makes progress (part 4).
    4. Mathematical induction is the proof method that fits this shape perfectly (part 5).
    5. Computer programs can be written the same way, called recursive functions (part 6). Two worked examples: reversing an array (part 7) and listing all permutations (part 8).
    6. To trust an algorithm you prove it correct and count its steps, and both jobs use the same tools (part 9). A trickier two-input example is in part 10, and the exercises are solved in part 11.

    Part 1 · Slides 2, 3 and 4

    Triangular numbers: a short rule beats a long list

    The puzzle slide 2

    The slide shows the first ten numbers of a sequence. A sequence is just a list of numbers in a fixed order. The row n says which place in the list, and the row T(n) says the number sitting there. Read T(n) as “T of n”, meaning “the n-th number”.

    n12345678910…
    T(n)13610152128364555

    The slide asks: how would you describe this sequence to a friend? Your friend wants to be able to work out the 11th, the 50th, the 1000th number, not just copy the ten they can already see.

    Why are they called triangular? extra picture

    Stack dots in rows: one dot in row 1, two in row 2, three in row 3, and so on. The total number of dots after n rows is T(n). The dots make a triangle, hence the name.

    Attempt 1: read the list out loud slide 3

    “The 1st number is 1. The 2nd number is 3. The 3rd number is 6, …”

    The slide calls this long yet incomplete. Long, because you need one sentence per number. Incomplete, because you can only ever list as many as you have patience for. Your friend learns nothing about the 11th number.

    Attempt 2: give a rule slide 4

    Two sentences are enough:

    1. The 1st number is 1. (a starting point)
    2. The n-th number, T(n), is the previous number T(n-1) plus n. (a way to get each next one)
    T(1) = 1the startT(n) = T(n−1) + nfor every n bigger than 1

    The slide says this is sufficient to reconstruct the whole sequence. Prove it to yourself by rebuilding the list, one step at a time:

    n12345678910
    previous, T(n−1)none136101521283645
    add nstart+ 2+ 3+ 4+ 5+ 6+ 7+ 8+ 9+ 10
    result, T(n)13610152128364555

    It matches the slide's table every time. Now the 11th number is easy: T(11) = T(10) + 11 = 55 + 11 = 66.

    Try it yourself

    n = 6

    Picture it

    Why do we need the starting sentence “the 1st number is 1”? Because the second sentence says “add n to the previous number”, and the very first number has no previous one. The starting sentence is the person at the front of the queue. In part 4 it gets its proper name: the base case.

    Two short sentences replaced an endless list. A description that gives each item in terms of an earlier item, plus a start, is called recursive. Part 2 writes it down in proper mathematical form.

    Part 2 · Slide 5

    Recurrence equations: a function that uses itself

    What the slide says slide 5

    “A mathematical function is recursive if it is defined in terms of itself.”

    Here is the slide's example. Do not panic at the curly brace. It only means “two rules, and which one you use depends on n”.

    f(n) =0n = 0f(n−1) + n2n > 0

    Reading it out loud

    RuleApplies whenIn plain words
    Rule An = 0The answer is 0. Nothing to work out. This is the front person, the base case.
    Rule Bn > 0The answer is the answer for one smaller number, f(n−1), plus n times n. This is a person asking the one in front, then adding their own bit.

    Notice Rule B has f on the left and on the right. That is what “defined in terms of itself” means. It is not a circle, because the right side uses a smaller n.

    Let us build the answers, smallest first

    Start from Rule A and climb with Rule B. Every row uses the row before it.

    n012345678
    howRule A0 + 1²1 + 45 + 914 + 1630 + 2555 + 3691 + 49140 + 64
    f(n)01514305591140204

    “Well defined for non-negative integers”

    Non-negative integers are 0, 1, 2, 3 and so on. The slide says the equation is well defined for them. That means: pick any of them, and the rules give exactly one answer, with no endless loop.

    Why does it work? Start at any n. Rule B sends you to n−1, then n−2, and so on, one step at a time, until you land on 0, where Rule A stops everything. For a negative number like −1, Rule B would send you to −2, then −3, and you would never reach 0. So the equation says nothing sensible there.

    Name to remember

    An equation like this, which defines a function using smaller values of itself plus starting values, is a recurrence equation. The triangular-number rule from part 1, T(n) = T(n−1) + n with T(1) = 1, is one too. The only differences are the extra squaring and that this one starts at 0.

    Part 3 · Slide 6

    Unwrapping: how to get an actual number out

    The idea slide 6

    A recurrence equation tells you how f(n) relates to f(n−1). Fine, but how do you get a real number like f(3)? The slide's answer: unwrap it until you reach a base case.

    Picture a present wrapped in a box, inside a box, inside a box. You open the big box and find a smaller one. You open that and find a smaller one. Finally you open the smallest box and there is the gift. The gift is the base case. Once you have it, you know everything.

    The slide's example, line by line

    We use the same f(n) = f(n−1) + n2 and f(0) = 0 from part 2, and want f(3). Blue is the part we still have to unwrap. Orange is the number we have already collected in our pocket.

    f(3) = f(2) + 3² = f(1) + 2² + 9 = f(0) + 1² + 13 = 14
    LineWhat happened
    f(3) = f(2) + 32Rule B with n = 3: f(3) is f(2) plus 3². The new unknown is f(2).
    = f(1) + 22 + 9Rule B again on f(2): it is f(1) plus 2². Meanwhile 3² was worked out as 9 and put in the pocket.
    = f(0) + 12 + 13Rule B on f(1): it is f(0) plus 1². The pocket grew: 2² is 4, and 4 + 9 = 13.
    = 14Now f(0) is the base case, Rule A says it is 0. So 0 + 1² + 13 = 0 + 1 + 13 = 14.

    So f(3) = 14. It matches the table you built in part 2 (0, 1, 5, 14). Two ways to get to the same answer.

    The slide keeps a running pocket while it goes down. The people wait until the answers come back up and add then. Both are the same calculation done in a different order, so use whichever one makes more sense to you.

    Try it yourself

    Part 4 · Slide 7

    The two rules every recursive definition must follow

    The slide slide 7

    Two important rules

    1. A base case. A case where the value is known directly, without using recursion.
    2. Progress. Every case that is solved recursively must call a case that is closer to a base case.

    Think of walking down a staircase. The base case is the floor: you stop there. Progress means every step you take goes down, never sideways and never up. Break either rule and you never arrive.

    Three broken recipes, tried out

    Here are real definitions that break the rules, and what happens when you try to unwrap them.

    DefinitionBroken ruleUnwrapping it
    g(n) = g(n−1) + n2 for every nno base caseg(2) = g(1)+4 = g(0)+1+4 = g(−1)+0+5 = g(−2) + … It walks past 0 and never stops.
    h(0) = 0 and h(n) = h(n+1) + n2no progress (wrong way)h(2) = h(3)+4 = h(4)+9+4 = h(5) + … The base case 0 is behind it, and it walks away.
    k(0) = 0 and k(n) = k(n) + 1no progress (standing still)k(2) = k(2) + 1 = (k(2)+1) + 1 = … It keeps asking itself the same question.

    In a real program each of these makes the computer call itself over and over until it runs out of memory and crashes. That is the price of breaking a rule.

    How to check progress

    Pick one number that measures how big the problem is. Call it the size. Then ask two questions:

    • Does every recursive call get a smaller size than the call that made it?
    • Is there a smallest size, and does the base case cover it?

    If both answers are yes, the chain of calls must end. For f(n) the size is n. For a queue of people it is the number of people ahead. In part 7 the size will be the number of boxes in an array, and in part 10 it will be a pair of numbers.

    Picture it

    Before you trust any recursive definition, ask the front-of-the-queue question: “Where does this stop, and does every call really get closer to there?” Two quick answers and you are safe.

    Part 5 · Slides 8 and 9

    Mathematical induction: knocking over infinitely many dominoes

    The problem it solves slide 8

    A statement S(n) is a claim about the number n. For example, S(n) could be “the n-th triangular number is n(n+1)/2”. For each n the claim is either true or false.

    Now you want to show it is true for every n from some starting value on. There are infinitely many n, so you cannot check them one by one. The slide's trick, mathematical induction (M.I.), lets you cover them all with just two checks. The starting value is called n0, read “n-zero”. The slide writes “for all n ≥ n0”, meaning every n from n0 upward.

    The two steps from the slide

    1. Basis. Prove S(n0), the statement for the smallest n. Push the first domino.
    2. Induction. Prove: if S(n0), …, S(k) are all true for some k ≥ n0, then S(k+1) is true too. Each domino, once the ones before it have fallen, knocks over the next one.

    The “if” part, S(n0) … S(k) are true, is called the induction hypothesis. You are allowed to assume it while proving S(k+1). You are not cheating: the basis already gave you the first domino, and the chain argument handles the rest.

    Try it yourself

    Pick a scenario, then watch the dominoes:

    Domino number n falling means “S(n) is true”. You need both steps. Without the basis nobody pushes the first domino, so nothing falls. Without a working induction step the chain stops at the first gap, and everything after it stays standing.

    Picture it

    Why does the slide say “S(n0), …, S(k) are true” and not just “S(k) is true”? Because both versions work. The slide's version gives you a bigger gift to use in the proof: all earlier cases, not only the last one. Most simple proofs, including the next one, only use the last.

    The slide's example slide 9

    The slide says “one can easily prove (by M.I.) that”:

    f(n) = n(n+1)(2n+1)6for every n ≥ 0

    Here f is the function from part 2, defined by f(0) = 0 and f(n) = f(n−1) + n2. So the claim is: the recipe that keeps adding squares gives the same numbers as this direct formula. First look at the numbers.

    n012345678
    recurrence f(n)01514305591140204
    n(n+1)(2n+1)/601514305591140204
    same?yesyesyesyesyesyesyesyesyes

    Nine matches is encouraging, but it is not a proof, because there are infinitely many n. Induction closes the gap.

    Step 1: the basis (n = 0)

    The recurrence's Rule A says f(0) = 0. The formula gives 0 · 1 · 1 / 6 = 0. They agree, so the first domino falls.

    Step 2: the induction

    Assume the formula is true for some k ≥ 0: f(k) = k(k+1)(2k+1)6. Show it is then true for k+1, meaning f(k+1) = (k+1)(k+2)(2k+3)6. (That is just the formula with n replaced by k+1.)

    What we writeWhy we may write it
    f(k+1) = f(k) + (k+1)2Rule B of the recurrence, valid because k+1 > 0.
    = k(k+1)(2k+1)6 + (k+1)2The assumption (induction hypothesis) replaces f(k).
    = (k+1)[k(2k+1) + 6(k+1)]6Pull out the common factor k+1, and write (k+1)² as 6(k+1)(k+1)/6 so everything is over 6.
    = (k+1)(2k2 + 7k + 6)6Multiply out: k(2k+1) = 2k² + k, and 6(k+1) = 6k + 6, so the sum is 2k² + 7k + 6.
    = (k+1)(k+2)(2k+3)6Factor: (k+2)(2k+3) = 2k² + 3k + 4k + 6 = 2k² + 7k + 6.

    The last line is exactly the claim for k+1. Both steps are proved, so the formula holds for every n ≥ 0.

    What induction cannot do

    Induction only checks a formula someone hands you. It does not tell you what the formula should be. Finding the formula is guessing, and the exercises in part 11 practise exactly that.

    Recursion and induction are twins

    Look at the proof. The line “f(k+1) = f(k) + (k+1)²” is just Rule B again. The base case of the recurrence became the basis of the proof. Same shape, opposite direction.

    Part 6 · Slides 10 and 11

    Recursion in code: a function that calls itself

    The same equation as a program slide 10

    The slide says: “similar to M.I. and recurrence equations, in a computer program a function can be recursive”. Here is the equation f(n) = f(n−1) + n2 turned into code. Read it right-hand column first.

    int f(n) { /* assume n >= 0 */

    Start of a function named f. It takes one input n and gives back a whole number (int). The note between /* */ is only for humans. It promises that n is never negative, because a negative n would never reach the base case.

    if (n == 0) return (0);

    Base case. If n is 0, hand back 0 straight away. (== asks “is it equal?”. A single = would mean “store this value”. The slide's font puts a gap between the two equals signs.)

    else return(f(n-1) + n*n);

    Recursive case. Call f again with the smaller number n-1. Wait for its answer. Add n*n, which is n times n. Hand the total back.

    }

    End of the function.

    In the equationIn the code
    Rule A f(0) = 0if (n == 0) return (0);
    Rule B f(n) = f(n−1) + n2else return(f(n-1) + n*n);

    The slide ends with a reminder: when you write a recursive function you must still obey the two rules, a base case and progress. Here the base case is n == 0 and the progress is n-1.

    What the computer does: a pile of unfinished calls

    When f(3) reaches f(2), it cannot finish yet, because it still has to add 3² to the answer. So the computer keeps a note: “when f(2) answers, add 9 and return”. Notes pile up like plates. The newest note is on top, and only the top one is running. This pile is called the call stack.

    Try it yourself

    Small problem solves big problem slide 11

    The slide's message: “in a sense, in recursive programming we use a solution of a smaller problem to solve a larger problem”. If you already know f(n-1), getting f(n) is easy: just add n². You do not need to know how f(n−1) got its answer. This is exactly what the people in the queue did.

    The leap of faith

    When you write a recursive function, pretend the function already works for smaller inputs. Then ask only one question: if I am handed the right answer for the smaller input, how do I turn it into the answer for mine? Do not try to follow every call in your head. The base case is what makes the faith justified.

    A recipe for writing any recursive function

    1. Choose the size. One number that says how big the problem is (n, the number of people, the number of boxes).
    2. Find the base case(s). The smallest sizes, where you simply know the answer.
    3. Find the step. How to build the answer for size n from the answer for something smaller.
    4. Check progress. Every recursive call must have a smaller size, and must end up at a base case.

    Parts 7 and 8 use exactly these four steps. The slides even ask the questions in this order.

    Part 7 · Slides 12 to 21

    Reversing an array, the recursive way

    The problem slide 12

    You are given an array A[1,n], a row of n boxes. Reverse it: the first box must end up holding what the last box held, the second box what the second-to-last held, and so on. The slide's example uses eight numbers.

    You could solve this with a plain loop. The slides want to show how to think recursively, using this friendly problem. So they ask the same two questions every time. Try each one before you open the answer.

    Question 1: what do we need? slides 13 and 14

    Your turn: if we want a recursive solution, what are the two issues we must deal with?

    We need some base cases, and a strategy for making progress. These are the two rules from part 4.

    Question 2: what is a base case here? slides 15 and 16

    Your turn: what counts as a base case for reversing an array?

    The slide's definition: a base case is one whose solution is readily known. There can be more than one. In this problem there are two:

    • The array is empty. There is nothing to flip, so do nothing.
    • The array has one element. A row of one looks the same flipped, so do nothing.

    Question 3: what does “smaller” mean? slides 17 and 18

    Recursion solves a big problem using a smaller one. So we need a way to say which problems are big and which are small. The slide calls it a measure of problem size.

    Your turn: what is a good measure of size for reversing an array?

    The slide suggests n, the number of elements. Fewer boxes means a smaller problem. An empty array has size 0, a single box has size 1.

    The key insight slides 19 and 20

    The slide's insight: if we know how to reverse an array with n−2 elements, we know how to reverse one with n elements.

    Why n−2 and not n−1? Because we fix two boxes at once. The first and last boxes just swap places. Whatever sits in the middle must also be flipped, and the middle is a smaller array with n−2 boxes.

    First, what exactly is a swap? Two boxes trade their contents.

    Now the slide's worked example, with six numbers. We trust the recursive call to reverse the middle four.

    From the idea to code slide 21

    There is a small problem. To reverse “the middle” we have to say which boxes are the middle. A function that only receives the array has no way to say it. So the slide generalises the problem: reverse just a part of the array, from box p to box q. The array whole is the special case p = 1, q = n.

    reverse(A,p,q) {

    A function that reverses the part of array A from box p to box q. It never touches boxes outside that part.

    if (p >= q) return; /* base cases */

    Base cases. If p and q have met (p = q, one box) or crossed (p > q, empty), there is nothing to flip. return means “stop here, do nothing more”. One test covers both base cases from question 2.

    swap(A[p],A[q]); /* swap the elements A[p] and A[q] */

    Trade the two ends of the part.

    reverse(A,p+1,q-1);

    Progress. Call the same function on the inside part: p moves one step right, q one step left. The part is now 2 boxes shorter.

    }

    End of the function.

    To reverse the whole array, call reverse(A,1,n);

    Recipe step (part 6)For reversing
    1 sizeThe number of boxes in the part, q − p + 1.
    2 base caseSize 0 or 1, which is the same as p >= q.
    3 stepSwap the two ends, then reverse the inside.
    4 progressEach call shrinks the size by 2, so it must end at size 1 or 0.

    Watch it run

    Here is the call-by-call trace for the slide-12 array. Orange boxes are p and q. Blue boxes are the part still to do. Green boxes are already in their final places.

    Try it yourself

    Things worth noticing

    • Even and odd lengths both work. With 8 boxes the fingers cross (p = 5, q = 4, empty). With 7 boxes they land on the same box (p = q = 4, one box). Both stop at p >= q.
    • The number of swaps is half the length, rounded down. 8 boxes need 4 swaps, 7 boxes need 3. Every swap fixes two boxes for good.
    • All the work happens on the way down. Each call swaps, then calls, and nothing is left to do after the inner call returns. Compare f(n) from part 6, which had to add n² after the answer came back.

    What if you forget the base case?

    Without if (p >= q) return; the fingers cross and keep going. The function would carry on swapping boxes, which actually undoes its own good work, until p and q fall off the ends of the array and the program crashes. The base case is not decoration. It is the brake.

    Part 8 · Slides 22 to 35

    All the permutations: the hardest example, taken slowly

    The problem slide 22

    You have n different characters stored in A[1..n]. Print every permutation of them. A permutation is one way of lining all the characters up in a row, using each exactly once. For [a,b,c] the slide lists six:

    [a,b,c] [a,c,b] [b,a,c] [b,c,a] [c,a,b] [c,b,a]

    How many are there in general? Three seats: 3 choices for the first, then 2 left for the second, then 1 for the last. So 3 × 2 × 1 = 6. For n characters it is n × (n−1) × … × 1, written n! and read “n factorial”. So 4! = 24, 5! = 120, and the number grows very fast.

    The same two questions slides 23 and 24

    The slide repeats the recipe: “if we want a recursive solution, we need one or more base cases, and a recursion strategy”.

    Your turn: can you think of a base case?

    One character. There is exactly one way to line up a single character: just itself. So the answer is known at once, and we only have to print it. (Zero characters also has exactly one arrangement, the empty one, but the algorithm on slide 29 only needs the one-character case.)

    The strategy: choose who stands last slides 25 to 28

    The slide's recursion strategy says: the permutations can be divided into n groups. All permutations in the i-th group end with the i-th character. Each group is formed by permuting the other n−1 characters and then adding the special one at the end.

    Think of seats: there are three seats in a row and three people, a, b and c. Ask first: who stands in the last seat? There are three choices. Once that is settled, the other two people must fill the first two seats, and that is the very same problem, only with 2 people instead of 3.

    The counting works out too: 3 groups, each holding 2 permutations (the arrangements of the other two letters), gives 3 × 2 = 6 permutations. Every permutation lands in exactly one group, so none is missed and none appears twice.

    The algorithm slide 29

    Here is the slide's code. It has three inputs: the array A, a number k, and the total length n. The idea is that perm(A,k,n) works on only the first k boxes and treats boxes k+1 to n as frozen. Read the right column slowly.

    perm(A,k,n) {

    Print all arrangements of the first k boxes of A. The boxes after k stay where they are.

    /* Characters stored in A[1..n]. Output all permutations of A[1..k] with A[k+1..n] appended. Chars in array A should be in the same order as it was before perm is called. Assume k >= 1. */

    These comments are the function's promises.

    1. Print every arrangement of boxes 1 to k, each one followed by the frozen boxes k+1 to n.

    2. When the function finishes, A must be in exactly the order it had before. Remember this one.

    3. k is at least 1.

    if (k==1) output A[1..n]

    Base case. The window has a single box, so there is only one arrangement. Print the whole array from box 1 to box n, which is that one arrangement followed by the frozen part.

    else for (i=1 to k) do {

    Try each box i in the window as the one that will stand last in the window. That is k choices, so the loop runs k times.

    swap(A[i],A[k]);

    Bring the chosen box to position k, the end of the window.

    perm(A, k-1, n);

    Progress. Now arrange the first k−1 boxes in every possible way. Position k holds the chosen one and is not touched again, so it counts as part of the frozen tail. The window is one box smaller.

    swap(A[i],A[k]);

    Undo the first swap, so the array is exactly as it was before this pass. Then the loop moves on to the next i. This keeps promise number 2.

    } }

    End of the loop and end of the function.

    One pass of the loop, as a picture slides 30 to 34

    Slides 30 to 34 build one pass of the loop as a picture. Here it is with actual letters: seven boxes, a window of k = 5, so the last two boxes are frozen.

    Slide 32 says “which is equivalent to…” and slide 33 says “append all these at the end of each permutation”, and slide 34 finishes with “which is equivalent to calling perm(A,k-1,n)”. That is the same statement in three steps: after the swap, printing “all arrangements of the rest, with the chosen box at the end” is exactly what a smaller call of perm does.

    A full run on a, b, c

    Now watch the whole recursion. We start with perm(A,3,3) on A = a b c. Each node is one call, with the array right after its swap. The edge label says which swap was done to get there.

    The printed order is bca, cba, cab, acb, bac, abc. It is not the order of slide 26, but it is the same six permutations, just discovered in a different sequence. Nobody promised alphabetical order.

    Try it yourself

    In the demo, striped boxes are the frozen tail. The orange box is the one chosen to stand last, and the blue box is where it came from. Every green flash is one permutation printed. Step through the n = 3 run once and watch the “undo” swaps. They are the part people find strange.

    Why the second swap matters

    The second swap(A[i],A[k]) looks pointless, since the work is done. It is not. Let us take it out and run the same input, a b c, to see what breaks. The outputs below come from running both versions.

    Version#1#2#3#4#5#6Different arrangements
    with the undo swapbcacbacabacbbacabc6 of 6, each once
    undo swap removedbcabcaabcabcbacbaconly 3, each twice. cba, cab and acb are missing.

    What goes wrong: after the first output bca, the array is left as b c a instead of being put back to c b a. The next pass of the loop starts from the wrong array, so the second output repeats bca where cba should be. The mistake then spreads through every later pass.

    Tidy-up rule

    If a recursive function borrows the array (here by swapping), it must put things back before it returns, so that its caller finds everything as it left it. Think of borrowing someone’s seat: give it back before the next person asks.

    Starting the whole thing slide 35

    To print all permutations of the entire array, call perm(A,n,n);. Here k = n, so the window is the whole array, and the frozen tail A[n+1..n] is empty, so nothing extra is appended.

    Recipe stepFor permutations
    1 sizek, the number of boxes in the window.
    2 base casek = 1: one box, one arrangement, print the array.
    3 stepFor each box i: swap it to the end of the window, solve the smaller window, swap back.
    4 progressThe window goes from k to k−1 every time, so it must reach 1.

    Picture it

    You do not need to hold the whole tree in your head to trust this code. Trust the three promises: “print all arrangements of the first k boxes”, “leave the array as you found it”, and “k is at least 1”. If perm(A,k-1,n) keeps those promises, then perm(A,k,n) keeps them too. That argument is exactly what part 9 turns into a proof.

    Part 9 · Slides 36 and 37

    Checking an algorithm: is it right, and how long does it take?

    Two jobs, two tools slide 36

    The slide says: to analyze an algorithm, we perform two tasks. The curved arrows on the slide connect each task to the tool from earlier in the chapter.

    The jobWhat it asksThe toolLearned in
    Prove its correctnessDoes it always do what it promises?Use M.I. (induction)part 5
    Estimate its running timeHow many steps does it take, as the input grows?Formulate it as a recursive function (a recurrence)parts 2 and 3

    Everything from the start of the chapter was preparation for these two jobs. We now do both for perm.

    Job 1: correctness by induction slide 37, first bullet

    The slide says: we can prove the correctness of perm(A,k,n) using M.I. The statement to prove is the function's promise from the comments in part 8.

    The statement S(k)

    For any array A and any n ≥ k: perm(A,k,n) prints every arrangement of A[1..k] followed by A[k+1..n], each exactly once, and leaves A exactly as it found it.

    Basis, k = 1. The function just prints A[1..n]. That is the only arrangement of one box, printed once, and nothing was swapped, so A is untouched. True.

    Induction, k ≥ 2. Assume S(k−1) is true. Look at pass number i of the loop.

    1. After swap(A[i],A[k]), the last box of the window holds the chosen value, and the first k−1 boxes hold the other k−1 values.
    2. By the assumption S(k−1), the call perm(A,k-1,n) prints every arrangement of those k−1 values, each followed by the chosen value and the frozen tail, once each. It also leaves the array unchanged.
    3. The second swap then puts the array back to what it was before the pass.

    So pass i prints exactly the arrangements whose last window item is the i-th value, each once. The k passes use k different last items, so together they print every arrangement, once each. The array is restored after every pass, so after the function ends it is as it started. S(k) is true. By induction, S(k) holds for all k ≥ 1. That is the argument from the “Picture it” note in part 8, made official.

    Job 2: counting the work slide 37, the rest

    Swaps are the work we count. The slide says perm(A,k,n) executes the swap statement f(k) times, where

    f(k) =0k = 12[k + k(k−1) + … + k(k−1)…2]k > 1

    and therefore, for k > 1,

    2(k!) ≤ f(k) ≤ 2e(k!)

    That looks scary, so let us build it from nothing, using the tools from parts 2 and 3.

    Step 1: write the recurrence

    Look at the code of perm. For k ≥ 2 the loop runs k times. Each pass does 2 swaps and one recursive call on k−1. That call itself costs f(k−1) swaps. So:

    f(1) = 0no swaps in the base casef(k) = 2k + k · f(k−1)k passes, each with 2 swaps and one smaller call

    Build the first values, smallest first, exactly as in part 2:

    k1234567
    howbase4 + 2·06 + 3·48 + 4·1810 + 5·8012 + 6·41014 + 7·2472
    f(k) swaps041880410247217318

    Check against part 8: for a, b, c the tree showed 3 passes at the top and 2 passes below each of the 3 children, so 9 passes of 2 swaps each, which is 18. It matches f(3) = 18. I also ran the real algorithm and counted its swaps for k up to 7, and they equal this table.

    Step 2: unwrap it

    Unwrap exactly like part 3. Replace f(k−1) using the same rule again and again:

    f(k) = 2k + k·f(k−1) = 2k + k·( 2(k−1) + (k−1)·f(k−2) ) = 2k + 2k(k−1) + k(k−1)·f(k−2) = … keep going until f(1) = 0 … = 2[ k + k(k−1) + … + k(k−1)…2 ]

    That is exactly the slide's formula. Test it with k = 4: 2[4 + 4·3 + 4·3·2] = 2[4 + 12 + 24] = 80. Correct.

    Step 3: squeeze it between two simple numbers

    Here is the trick that makes the bounds appear. Divide the recurrence by k!. Call g(k) = f(k) / k!, the number of swaps per arrangement:

    g(k) = g(k−1) + 2(k−1)!with g(1) = 0

    Why: f(k)/k! = 2k/k! + k·f(k−1)/k!, and k/k! is 1/(k−1)! while k·f(k−1)/k! is f(k−1)/(k−1)!. This is a much nicer recurrence, because each step only adds a small positive number. Unwrapping it gives

    g(k) = 2 ( 11! + 12! + 13! + … + 1(k−1)! )
    • Lower bound. Every term is positive, and g(2) = 2. So g(k) ≥ 2 for all k ≥ 2, which means f(k) ≥ 2·k!.
    • Upper bound. The famous series 1 + 1/1! + 1/2! + 1/3! + … adds up to the number e = 2.71828… (the slide's box: “e is the base of the natural log”). Without its leading 1 the series stays below e − 1, which is about 1.72. So g(k) is always below 2(e − 1), which is below 2e. Therefore f(k) ≤ 2e·k!.

    Step 4: how many times is “output” executed?

    The slide ends with this question. Count the base-case calls, since only they print. Let o(k) be the number of prints of perm(A,k,n). It is one print when k = 1. Otherwise the loop makes k calls to size k−1, each printing o(k−1) times:

    o(1) = 1base caseo(k) = k · o(k−1)k smaller calls

    Unwrap: o(k) = k · (k−1) · … · 1 = k!. So output runs k! times, once per permutation, as it should. In the full call perm(A,n,n) that is n! prints.

    k1234567
    output runs, k!126241207205040
    swaps, f(k)041880410247217318
    swaps ÷ k!02.003.003.333.423.433.44

    The takeaway: the work grows like k!, a number that explodes. For n = 10 there are 3,628,800 permutations to print. The slide's bound says the swaps never cost more than about 5.4 times the number of permutations (in truth about 3.4 times), so the algorithm spends its effort almost entirely on the thing it has to produce anyway.

    Picture it

    The pattern for analysing any recursive function: (1) look at the code and write “my cost = work I do myself + cost of my smaller calls”. (2) That is a recurrence equation. (3) Unwrap it, or build a table, or divide by something to tame it. The slides call this “formulate it as a recursive function”.

    Part 10 · Slide 38

    Two inputs at once: Ackermann's function

    The complication slide 38

    Everything so far had one input. The slide warns: there could be more than one variable in a recurrence equation or recursive function. Its example is Ackermann's function, which takes two numbers, m and n. It has three rules.

    RuleApplies whenSaysIn plain words
    1m = 0, any n ≥ 0A(0,n) = n+1Base case. If the first number is 0, just add 1 to the second.
    2m > 0, n = 0A(m,0) = A(m−1,1)If the second number is 0, call again with m one smaller and n set to 1.
    3m > 0, n > 0A(m,n) = A(m−1, A(m,n−1))First work out the inner call A(m,n−1). Then use its answer as the second input of an outer call with m one smaller.

    Progress with two numbers

    Part 4 said every call must get closer to a base case. With two numbers, closer means “smaller in dictionary order”: compare m first, and only if the ms are equal compare n.

    • Rule 2: m shrinks by 1. Smaller.
    • Rule 3, inner call A(m,n−1): m is the same, but n shrinks. Smaller.
    • Rule 3, outer call A(m−1, …): m shrinks. Smaller, even though the second input can be gigantic.

    Every call is smaller than the one that made it, and the smallest pairs have m = 0, where Rule 1 stops. So the rules obey both laws from part 4. It always finishes, though sometimes only after a very long time.

    One worked example: A(1,2)

    StepRule
    A(1,2) = A(0, A(1,1))Rule 3. We need the inner call A(1,1) first.
    A(1,1) = A(0, A(1,0))Rule 3 again. Inner call is A(1,0).
    A(1,0) = A(0,1) = 1 + 1 = 2Rule 2, then Rule 1.
    so A(1,1) = A(0,2) = 3Put 2 back into the outer call, Rule 1.
    so A(1,2) = A(0,3) = 4Put 3 back into the outer call, Rule 1.

    This is the same “down, then back up” as in part 3, only with a nested call. Here is a table of values, computed by running the three rules:

    A(m,n)n = 012345
    m = 0123456
    m = 1234567
    m = 235791113
    m = 35132961125253

    Spot the pattern: row 1 is n+2, row 2 is 2n+3, and row 3 is 2n+3 − 3 (for n = 5 that is 256 − 3 = 253). Each row grows far faster than the row above. The next row is hopeless to print: A(4,2) equals 265536 − 3, a number with 19,729 digits.

    It also takes a lot of calls. Computing A(2,2) = 7 needs 27 calls and A(2,3) = 9 needs 44, for tiny answers. That is why the slide uses it as a warning: a function with several inputs obeys the same two rules, but progress now takes more care to see.

    Part 11 · Slides 39 and 40

    The exercises, with hints first and answers folded away

    Try each one on paper first. Read the hint if you are stuck. Open the answer last.

    Exercise 1: a formula for T(n) slide 39

    “Based on the recurrence equation of the triangular numbers T(n), give a closed-form formula of T(n).”

    A closed-form formula gives T(n) straight from n, with no mention of T(n−1). It is the opposite of a recurrence: no unwrapping needed, you just plug in n.

    Hint

    Unwrap T(n) = T(n−1) + n like in part 3. You get T(n) = n + (n−1) + (n−2) + … + 2 + 1. Now find a quick way to add 1 to n. Try pairing the biggest with the smallest.

    Answer
    T(n) = n(n+1)2

    Why, with a picture. Take two copies of the triangle, turn one upside down, and fit them together. They make a rectangle with n rows and n+1 columns, so the two triangles hold n(n+1) dots in total, and one triangle holds half.

    Why, with pairing. In 1 + 2 + … + n, the first and last add to n+1, the second and second-to-last also add to n+1, and so on. There are n/2 such pairs, so the total is (n/2)(n+1).

    Why, with induction. Basis: T(1) = 1 = 1·2/2. Step: assume T(k) = k(k+1)/2. Then T(k+1) = T(k) + (k+1) = k(k+1)/2 + (k+1) = (k+1)(k+2)/2, which is the formula for k+1.

    Check: T(10) = 10·11/2 = 55, which matches slide 2.

    Exercise 2: lines cutting a plane slide 39

    “Let L(n) be the max number of regions formed by n lines in a plane. Give a recurrence equation of L(n). What is the relation between L(n) and T(n)?”

    Hint

    Draw 0, 1, 2 and 3 lines, and count the regions: 1, 2, 4, 7. Now ask what the newest line does. It crosses each older line once, and the crossing points chop it into pieces. Each piece splits one region in two.

    Answer
    L(0) = 1no lines, the whole planeL(n) = L(n−1) + nthe n-th line adds n regions

    Compare with T(n) = T(n−1) + n. The only difference is the starting value: L starts at 1 and T starts at 0 (with T(0) = 0). So L is T lifted up by one:

    L(n) = T(n) + 1 = n(n+1)2 + 1 = n2 + n + 22

    Values for n = 0, 1, 2, … are 1, 2, 4, 7, 11, 16, 22, 29. The pictures above show 2, 4 and 7.

    Exercise 3: guess the formula slide 40

    “You are given the following partial sequence. Guess a closed-form formula of f(n). Verify it against the following numbers in the sequence. Did you guess it right?”

    n12345678…
    f(n)512254469100137180

    The numbers to check against are 229, 284, 345, 412, 485, 564, 649 and 740, for n = 9 to 16.

    Hint

    Subtract each number from the next one to get a new row, the differences. If that row is still not constant, subtract again. When a row becomes constant, the number of subtractions tells you the shape of the formula: one subtraction means a straight line, two means a·n2 + b·n + c.

    Answer
    n12345678910…
    f(n)512254469100137180229284…
    1st difference71319253137434955…
    2nd difference66666666…

    The second differences are all 6, so the formula is a quadratic a·n2 + b·n + c, and the second difference of that is always 2a. So 2a = 6 and a = 3.

    Now use two known values. f(1) = 5 gives 3 + b + c = 5. f(2) = 12 gives 12 + 2b + c = 12. Subtract the first from the second: 9 + b = 7, so b = −2, and then c = 4.

    f(n) = 3n2 − 2n + 4

    Verify. n = 9: 3·81 − 18 + 4 = 229. n = 12: 3·144 − 24 + 4 = 412. n = 16: 3·256 − 32 + 4 = 740. All eight of the later numbers match, and so do the first eight we used. So yes, the guess was right.

    A caution in the spirit of part 5: matching sixteen numbers is strong evidence, but the slide only shows a partial sequence, so strictly it is a formula that fits everything given. To turn it into a proof you would need a rule for the sequence. The differences 7, 13, 19, … are 6n − 5, so the rule would be f(n) = f(n−1) + 6n − 5 with f(1) = 5, and the formula satisfies it: 3n2 − 2n − (3(n−1)2 − 2(n−1)) = 6n − 5.

    Part 12 · Revise from this

    Cheat sheet and self-test

    The whole chapter on one screen

    The recipe for any recursive thing

    1. Size. Pick one number that says how big the problem is.
    2. Base case. The smallest sizes, where the answer is obvious.
    3. Step. Assume the smaller problem is solved (leap of faith). Turn its answer into yours.
    4. Progress. Every call must have a smaller size and must reach a base case.
    solve(problem of size s) { if (s is tiny) /* base case */ return the obvious answer; smaller = solve(a problem of size less than s); /* progress */ return combine(smaller, my own small bit); /* use the answer */}

    Every term from the slides in one line

    TermMeaningWhere
    recurrence equationDefines a function using smaller values of itself, plus the starting values.part 2
    unwrappingReplacing f(n) by its rule again and again until a base case appears.part 3
    base caseA case with a directly known answer, no recursion needed. There may be several.part 4
    progressEach recursive call goes closer to a base case.part 4
    mathematical inductionProve S(n) for all n ≥ n₀ with a basis and an induction step.part 5
    induction hypothesisThe assumption that S is true up to k, used to prove S(k+1).part 5
    recursive functionA function in a program that calls itself, with a base case and progress.part 6
    call stackThe pile of unfinished calls. The newest is on top and the only one running.part 6
    measure of problem sizeOne number saying how big a problem is. It must shrink with each call.parts 4 and 7
    window and frozen tailIn perm: boxes 1..k still to arrange, and boxes k+1..n that stay put and are appended.part 8
    closed-form formulaA formula for T(n) from n alone, with no reference to earlier values.part 11

    Mistakes to avoid

    • No base case. The calls never stop. The program crashes.
    • No progress. The call asks the same question, or walks away from the base case.
    • Forgetting to put things back. If you borrow an array by swapping, swap back (perm's second swap).
    • Testing p == q instead of p >= q. On an even-length array p jumps past q and they are never equal.
    • Trying to follow every call in your head. Trust the smaller call and check only one level.
    • Treating a table of matches as a proof. Many checked cases suggest a formula, induction proves it.

    Self-test

    Answer each from memory, then open the answer.

    1. What are the two rules every recursive definition must follow?

      Answer

      A base case, where the value is known without recursion, and progress, meaning every recursive call goes to a case closer to a base case.

    2. With f(0) = 0 and f(n) = f(n−1) + n2, unwrap f(4).

      Answer

      f(4) = f(3) + 16 = f(2) + 9 + 16 = f(1) + 4 + 25 = f(0) + 1 + 29 = 30.

    3. What is wrong with defining k(n) = k(n) + 1?

      Answer

      No progress. It asks for k(n) in order to compute k(n), so it never gets closer to a base case, and there is no base case either.

    4. Name the two steps of induction, and say what each is in the domino picture.

      Answer

      The basis (prove S(n₀)) is pushing the first domino. The induction step (if S is true up to k then S(k+1) is true) is each domino knocking over the next. Both are needed.

    5. In reverse(A,p,q), why is the test p >= q and not p == q?

      Answer

      With an even number of boxes, p moves past q (for 8 boxes: p = 5, q = 4) and they are never equal, so p == q would never fire and the function would run off the array. p >= q covers both the empty part (p > q) and the one-box part (p = q).

    6. How many swaps does reverse(A,1,9) make on 9 boxes?

      Answer

      4. Each swap fixes two boxes, and the middle box needs no swap. That is half of 9, rounded down.

    7. Why does perm swap a second time after the recursive call?

      Answer

      To put the array back exactly as it was, so the next pass of the loop starts from the same array. Without it, outputs repeat and some permutations are never printed.

    8. How many times does output run in perm(A,5,5)?

      Answer

      5! = 120, once per permutation.

    9. What is A(1,1) in Ackermann's function?

      Answer

      3. A(1,1) = A(0, A(1,0)) = A(0, 2) = 3.

    10. Using L(n) = T(n) + 1, how many regions do 5 lines make at most?

      Answer

      T(5) = 15, so L(5) = 16.

    11. Which measure shows that reverse makes progress?

      Answer

      The number of boxes in the part, q − p + 1. It drops by 2 on every call, so it reaches 1 or 0, where the base case applies.

    Built from the 40 slides of “Induction, Recurrence Equations, and Recursive Calls”. The numbers, traces and counts in this guide were checked by running the slides' own definitions and algorithms.

    PreviousHomeNextChapter 2 · Algorithms

    Slides 1–94 · 02_algo

    Algorithms from Scratch

    What an algorithm is, how to say which one is better, why we count steps instead of seconds, and the big-O family of symbols. Towers of Hanoi and Fibonacci show it all in action.

    In this chapter

      Part 1 · Slides 1–9

      Programs, algorithms and a wallpaper

      Before any maths, let us get the words straight. Two of them sound the same and are not: program and algorithm.

      A program is for the machine slide 2

      A program is a list of instructions written in an exact language (C++, Java, Python). Every comma matters. The computer will do exactly what it says, nothing more. Before it runs, a compiler turns the text file into machine code, which is just long rows of 0s and 1s the chip can follow.

      An algorithm is for people slides 3–4

      An algorithm explains how to solve a problem, written so that a human can understand the idea. We skip the fine details (semicolons, variable types). The same algorithm can become a C++ program, a Java program or a Python program.

      The comparison to remember

      An algorithm is to a program what a plot is to a novel. The plot is the strategy. The novel is one particular telling of it, with every word chosen.

      Picture it

      Think of a cooking recipe. “Boil the pasta, then add the sauce” is the algorithm. Which pot, which stove and how many grams of salt is the program. A good recipe works in any kitchen.

      The slides give a more careful definition. An algorithm is a finite sequence of well-defined steps that stops after a finite amount of time. Three words matter: finite (not infinitely many steps), well-defined (no step says “do something clever”), and stops (it must finish).

      The usual workflow, from slide 4: given a problem, design an algorithm, turn it into a program, and, when you have several algorithms, analyse them to find the best one. This whole chapter is about that last step: how to compare algorithms.

      One problem, three attempts: the wallpaper slides 5–7

      Problem. Make a wallpaper pattern: a square of n × n pixels, each pixel either on (dark) or off (blank).

      1. Attempt 1 (just words): for every pixel, decide whether it should be on or off. This says nothing. How do we decide?
      2. Attempt 2 (an idea): for each pixel at position (x, y), compute a number c = f(x, y) and turn the pixel on if c is at least some threshold. Better, but what is f?
      3. Attempt 3 (a real algorithm): choose f concretely.
      for i = 1 to n for j = 1 to n { c = (i*i + j*j) mod 10; if c <= 3 plot(i, j); }
      for i = 1 to n

      walk down the rows, row 1, row 2, … row n.

      for j = 1 to n

      inside each row, walk across the columns.

      c = (i*i + j*j) mod 10

      square both coordinates, add, and keep only the last digit (that is what “mod 10” means: the remainder after dividing by 10). So c is always one of 0, 1, …, 9.

      if c <= 3

      only 4 of the 10 possible last digits (0, 1, 2, 3) turn the pixel on.

      plot(i, j)

      switch this pixel on.

      Try it. Change the size and the threshold. Press Next step to watch the double loop paint the picture one row at a time.

      Paint the wallpaper

      Why this example?

      Attempt 3 is a program in disguise: nothing is left to guess. Attempts 1 and 2 are only algorithm ideas. The slides use this problem again later, to count how many steps the algorithm takes (Part 6).

      Data structures: where the pixels live slides 8–9

      The algorithm handles data: n2 pixels, the number c, and so on. A data structure is a way to organise that data so the algorithm can reach it quickly. Here the natural choice is a 2-dimensional array, a grid of boxes where “pixel (i, j)” is directly reachable by its row and column.

      The sentence on slide 9

      Program = data structure + algorithm.

      The algorithm is the procedure (what to do). The data structure is the organisation (where things are kept). Most of this course is about choosing the right pair.

      Check yourself: which of these is an algorithm and which is a program?

      for (i=1; i<n; i++) { … } in C++ is a program (exact syntax for a specific language). “Add up the numbers one by one, keeping a running total” is an algorithm (language-free strategy).

      Part 2 · Slides 10–22

      Which algorithm is better?

      Usually a problem has many algorithms. To pick one we need a fair way to measure. Slide 10 says we must choose two things: a measure of problem size and a measure of resources (written as a function of that size).

      Problem size slide 11

      The size is whatever number tells you “how big is this job”. A bigger input should mean more work.

      ProblemSize
      Add up a set of n integersn, how many numbers
      Sort a list of n numbersn, number of entries
      Multiply two matricesthe dimensions of the matrices
      Multiply several matricesthe dimensions and how many matrices
      Solve a system of linear equationsthe number of unknowns

      The note on the slide: size may need more than one number (two matrix dimensions, plus how many matrices).

      Resources slide 12

      A resource is what the algorithm “spends”: running time, memory space, and so on. A good measure has three properties:

      1. It measures what we care about (time? memory?).
      2. It is a number, so two algorithms can be compared with “smaller is better”.
      3. It predicts: from the formula we can guess the cost on inputs we have not run.

      Why time? slide 13

      “We may buy space, but we may not buy time.” You can buy more memory chips. You cannot buy more hours in the day. So the main metric is running time.

      Two ways to compare speeds slides 14–15

      Method 1: stopwatch. Write both programs and time them.

      Easy. But the result is noisy: it depends on the programmer, language, compiler, operating system, machine and the input. You also cannot predict anything from one timing.

      Method 2: count operations. Find a formula in the problem size for how much work the algorithm must do, by counting some set of basic operations.

      This is the method of the course. It is the same on every machine and it does predict.

      Squaring a number three ways slides 16–22

      Problem: given a positive integer n, compute n2. Here are three silly but different algorithms.

      Alg 1: sum = n * n Alg 2: sum = 0; for i = 1 to n sum = sum + n; Alg 3: sum = 0; for i = 1 to n for j = 1 to n sum++;

      Algorithm 2 adds n to itself n times. Algorithm 3 adds 1 a total of n × n times. They all give n2.

      Count the operations. Alg 1 does 1 operation (one multiplication). Alg 2 does n additions. Alg 3 does n2 increments. By this count Alg 1 looks like the winner.

      But that is not fair (slide 19)

      An increment (sum++) is far cheaper for a computer than a multiplication. Counting all operations as equal is too crude.

      Let t1, t2, t3 be the time of an increment, an addition and a multiplication. Then the running times are:

      Alg 1: t3Alg 2: n × t2Alg 3: n2 × t1

      The slides pick numbers: a multiplication is 20 times an addition, which is 10 times an increment, so t3 = 20 t2 = 200 t1. In units of t1:

      Alg 1: 200Alg 2: 10nAlg 3: n2

      Which is best? Compare the three for small n. Alg 3 is smallest while n2 < 10n, that is n < 10. Alg 2 beats Alg 1 while 10n < 200, that is n < 20.

      nbest algorithm
      1 to 10Alg 3
      10 to 20Alg 2
      20 and upAlg 1

      The table is slide 22. At exactly n = 10 Algs 2 and 3 tie (both 100), and at exactly n = 20 Algs 1 and 2 tie (both 200). Play with the sliders below and watch the winner change.

      Which squaring algorithm wins?

      The big lesson of slide 22

      When n is large, the algorithm whose cost grows slowest wins (Alg 1 here, which does not grow at all). The ones that grow faster only win when the job is tiny. The rest of the chapter makes this idea precise.

      Check yourself: if a multiplication cost only 2 additions (and an addition cost 1 increment), who wins at n = 100?

      In units of an increment: Alg 1 costs t3 = 2 × 1 = 2, Alg 2 costs 100 × 1 = 100, Alg 3 costs 1002 = 10,000. Alg 1 still wins. Fast multiplication makes the winner even clearer; it takes an expensive multiplication and a tiny n to make Alg 3 win.

      Part 3 · Slides 23–25

      The plan for solving any problem

      The slides give a recipe for attacking a computational problem. Seven steps:

      1. Recognise the problem. It has to be of the kind a digital computer can solve.
      2. Build an abstract model: decide which operations are allowed. (For Hanoi: “move one disk”. For wallpaper: arithmetic and plot.)
      3. Design an algorithm that uses only the allowed operations.
      4. Analyse the algorithm: how much effort does it take? This gives an upper bound, a promise that the problem can be solved with at most this much work.
      5. Analyse the problem: if possible, work out how much effort is needed whatever algorithm you use. This gives a lower bound.
      6. Not satisfied? Look for a better algorithm and repeat.
      7. Build data structures that let the algorithm run efficiently. Sometimes steps 3 and 7 happen together: algorithm and data structure are designed as a pair.

      Upper bound and lower bound in one picture

      Upper bound = a ceiling. “I have an algorithm that does it in this much work, so the problem is no harder than this.”

      Lower bound = a floor. “Nobody can do it in less than this much work.” A lower bound is a statement about the problem, not about one algorithm.

      When the ceiling meets the floor, the algorithm is optimal: no better one can exist.

      Picture it

      You are told the river crossing takes at most 10 minutes (you have done it, that is your ceiling). A friend proves nobody can do it in less than 4 minutes (that is the floor). The truth lies between 4 and 10 minutes. When someone finds a 4-minute route, ceiling and floor meet and you can stop looking.

      Part 4 · Slides 26–47

      The Towers of Hanoi

      Hanoi is the textbook example of everything in the plan: a model, a recursive algorithm, an exact upper bound, a matching lower bound, and a nasty surprise about how fast things grow.

      The legend slides 26–27

      In a temple in Benares there are three diamond needles. At the creation of the world, 64 golden disks of different sizes were stacked on one needle, largest at the bottom. Priests move the disks, one at a time, day and night, from this needle to another. When all 64 have been moved, the world ends.

      The puzzle slide 28

      Three pegs, n disks of different sizes, stacked small-on-big on the origin peg. Move the whole stack to the destination peg. The third peg is the buffer (a parking spot). Three rules:

      1. Every disk is always on a peg.
      2. No disk is ever on top of a smaller disk.
      3. Only one disk at a time moves (the top one).

      Have a go. This is the real puzzle. Click a peg to pick up its top disk, then click another peg to drop it. Try 3 disks first. The best possible number of moves is shown.

      Play Towers of Hanoi

      The model (slide 29). The only operation is “move one disk from one peg to another”. We measure the cost as the number of moves, and the size is n, the number of disks.

      Think recursively slides 30–34

      Recursion needs a base case and a way to make progress. (If that sounds new, the recursion guide linked from the home page covers it from zero.)

      Base case. With one disk, just move it from origin to destination.

      Progress. Suppose I already know how to move n−1 disks. Can I move n? Yes, in three steps:

      1. Move the n−1 small disks to the buffer (this is the same puzzle, one disk smaller).
      2. Move the largest disk to the destination. It is free to go because the destination is empty.
      3. Move the n−1 small disks from the buffer onto the destination (again, one disk smaller).

      Picture it

      Do not try to follow every move in your head. Just trust: “if I can move a stack of n−1, I can use that as a tool”. Your job is only to write the three steps. The tower of two disks works exactly as the tower of one did, and so on down.

      Here it is as code. The function moves n disks from peg A to peg C, using peg B as the helper.

      Hanoi(A, B, C, n) { /* move n disks from peg A to peg C using peg B as an intermediate peg */ if (n = 1) move A's top disk to C; else { Hanoi(A, C, B, n-1); move A's top disk to C; Hanoi(B, A, C, n-1); }}
      Hanoi(A, B, C, n)

      The three pegs are just names given to the roles: A is where we take from, C is where we put, B is the helper.

      if (n = 1)

      The base case: one disk, one move.

      Hanoi(A, C, B, n-1)

      Step 1. Move the top n−1 disks from A to B. Now C is the helper (the roles are swapped).

      move A's top disk to C

      Step 2. A holds only the largest disk now. Move it to C.

      Hanoi(B, A, C, n-1)

      Step 3. Move the n−1 disks from B to C. Now A is the helper.

      Watch it run. Pick a number of disks and step through the moves. The move list at the bottom is the actual output of the algorithm.

      Watch the algorithm solve Hanoi

      Analysis: three questions slides 35–36

      1. Is the algorithm correct?

        Yes, by the same reasoning as above (a proof by induction). For n=1 it clearly works. If it works for n−1 disks, then in step 1 it parks them on B. The big disk can go to C because C is empty. In step 3 the small disks go back on top of the big one, which is allowed because they are all smaller. One thing to notice: while the small disks move, the big disk is just sitting there, but every smaller disk may rest on it, so it never gets in the way.

      2. How many moves does it use? (upper bound)

      3. What is the fewest moves any method could use? (lower bound)

      The upper bound: counting our moves slides 37–38

      Let f(n) be the number of moves our algorithm uses for n disks. One disk: 1 move. For n disks: two copies of the (n−1)-disk job, plus one move for the big disk.

      f(n) =1n = 12f(n−1) + 1n > 1

      That is a recurrence. Let us just compute the first few values (the “unwrapping by hand” trick):

      n1234567
      f(n)137153163127
      2n − 1137153163127

      The pattern is clear: f(n) = 2n − 1. To be sure, unwrap the recurrence by writing it out several times:

      f(n) = 2f(n−1) + 1f(n) = 2(2f(n−2) + 1) + 1 = 4f(n−2) + 3f(n) = 4(2f(n−3) + 1) + 3 = 8f(n−3) + 7f(n) = 2k f(n−k) + (2k − 1)

      Stop when we reach the base case, at k = n−1: f(n) = 2n−1 × 1 + 2n−1 − 1 = 2n − 1.

      Or prove it by induction. Base: f(1) = 1 = 21 − 1. Step: if f(n−1) = 2n−1 − 1 then f(n) = 2(2n−1 − 1) + 1 = 2n − 2 + 1 = 2n − 1. ✓

      Result

      Our algorithm takes exactly 2n − 1 moves. So 2n − 1 moves are enough: that is an upper bound for the problem.

      The lower bound: can anyone do better? slides 36, 39–45

      The lower bound is about the problem: it has to hold for every possible method that follows the rules, not only ours. The slides climb in four attempts, each better than the last:

      AttemptClaimReason
      0th (silly)at least 0 moves“It cannot take negative moves.” True, useless.
      1st (obvious)at least n movesEvery disk has to move at least once.
      2nd (better)at least 2n − 1 movesEvery disk except the largest has to move at least twice (it must get out of the way, then onto the largest), and the largest at least once: 2(n−1) + 1.
      3rd (best)at least 2n − 1 movesThe argument below.

      For the third attempt let g(n) be the smallest number of moves that any legal solution can use for n disks. (Careful: this is not f(n). f is what our algorithm uses; g is the best that is possible.)

      Look at the largest disk. It must move at least once. Consider the moment of its last move.

      1. Before it can move at all, the other n−1 disks must be stacked on a single other peg (otherwise they would sit on top of it or on its target). Getting the stack of n−1 there is the same problem with one disk fewer, so it costs at least g(n−1) moves.
      2. The big disk moves: at least 1 move.
      3. After its last move, the n−1 disks are stacked on the third peg and still have to travel to the destination, on top of the big disk. That is another copy of the problem: at least g(n−1) moves.
      g(n) =1n = 12g(n−1) + 1n > 1

      With “≥” instead of “=”: g(n) ≥ 2g(n−1) + 1 and g(1) ≥ 1. This is exactly the same recurrence as f, so exactly the same unwrapping gives g(n) ≥ 2n − 1.

      The ceiling meets the floor

      Our algorithm uses 2n − 1 moves (upper bound). No algorithm can use fewer (lower bound). So the algorithm is optimal: there is no cleverer way, so stop searching.

      Check yourself: what is the minimum number of moves for 5 disks, and how many for 10?

      25 − 1 = 31 and 210 − 1 = 1023. Each extra disk doubles the work (plus one).

      Should we fear the end of the world? slides 46–47

      The legend has 64 disks. If a superhuman monk moves one disk per second, non-stop, the job takes 264 − 1 seconds. Move the slider and see how fast it blows up.

      How long would the monks take?

      A slip on slide 46

      The slide says this is “385 billion years”. If you divide 18,446,744,073,709,551,615 seconds by the number of seconds in a year (about 31.6 million), you get about 585 billion years. The slide's number looks like a typo. It changes nothing important: both are far, far longer than the age of the universe (about 14 billion years).

      The real point (slide 47): the running time 2n − 1 is exponential in the problem size. Exponential algorithms become hopeless very quickly, as the next parts will show in numbers.

      Part 5 · Slides 48–57

      Trouble: inputs and operations

      Hanoi was a gift. For every size n there is only one puzzle, and only one kind of operation (“move”) to count. Slide 48 warns that real problems are messier. Two difficulties show up: different inputs of the same size, and different kinds of operations.

      Difficulty 1: the input changes the cost slides 49–53

      Problem: given an array A[1..n] of n ≥ 1 integers and a target x, say whether x is in the array. The obvious algorithm walks along the array until it finds x or runs out of boxes.

      array_search(A, x, n) { i = 1; while (x != A[i]) if (i == n) return ("not found"); else i++; return ("found");}
      i = 1;

      start at the first box.

      while (x != A[i])

      keep going as long as the box we are looking at is not the one we want. Each time we test this, that is one comparison. Comparisons are what we count.

      if (i == n) return "not found"

      we are on the last box and it is not x. Nothing left to check, so give up.

      else i++

      otherwise step to the next box.

      return "found"

      the while-test failed, which means x == A[i]. Found it.

      Try it with the three instances from slide 50. Notice how the same array size gives very different costs.

      Linear search, one comparison at a time

      ArrayFindComparisons
      1 3 2 4 5 611
      1 3 2 4 5 666
      1 3 2 4 5 76 (not there)6

      Slide 51 takes the pessimistic view. We usually measure the worst cost: the largest number of comparisons over all inputs of size n. For this algorithm the worst cost is exactly n comparisons. The algorithm itself is the proof that the problem can be solved with at most n comparisons, so that is an upper bound on the problem.

      Best, worst and average slides 52–53

      Best cost.

      The cheapest input. Here: 1 comparison. Not very telling: it says nothing about how hard the problem really is.

      Worst cost.

      The most expensive input. Here: n. A safe promise: “no input will ever cost more than this”.

      Average cost.

      The cost averaged over inputs, weighted by how likely each input I is: sum p(I) × cost(I).

      The average sounds fairer but is trickier. First you must know the probabilities p(I), and usually nobody does. Even when you do, the sum is usually harder to compute than the worst case. If you assume the target is present and each box is equally likely, the average is (1 + 2 + … + n)/n = (n+1)/2, about half the worst case.

      What the slides recommend

      Given an algorithm, find its worst cost first. Then, only if the problem is important enough, find its average cost.

      Difficulty 2: which operations count? slides 54–57

      For many problems there are several different operation types (add, multiply, compare…). Which should we count? Multiplying two 2 × 2 matrices shows the problem.

      Take two 2×2 matrices. Their product has four entries r, s, t, u:

      r = ae + bf  s = ag + bht = ce + df  u = cg + dh

      Algorithm 1 just computes those four lines: 8 multiplications and 4 additions.

      Algorithm 2 is a clever trick (it is a version of Strassen's method). It first computes seven products:

      p1 = a(g − h)  p2 = (a + b)hp3 = (c + d)e  p4 = d(f − e)p5 = (a + d)(e + h) p6 = (b − d)(f + h)p7 = (a − c)(e + g)

      and then builds the answer from them using only additions and subtractions:

      u = p5 + p1 − p3 − p7  r = p5 + p4 − p2 + p6s = p1 + p2  t = p3 + p4

      That is 7 multiplications and 18 additions/subtractions. One fewer multiplication, but 14 more additions. Is it better? It depends on how costly a multiplication is compared with an addition, and that depends on the machine. Try it.

      Matrix multiplication: which algorithm wins?

      The problem with counting exact operations

      The winner changes with the machine, so to compare algorithms we would always have to name a computer. That is not satisfying. Slide 57 says: this is not desirable. Hence the compromise in the next part.

      Part 6 · Slides 58–66

      A compromise: how fast does the cost grow?

      Slide 58 relaxes the question: do not count the exact number of each operation. Look only at the growth rate of the total as the size grows. It turns out that is enough to compare algorithms without naming a machine.

      Counting the wallpaper algorithm slides 59–60

      Here is the wallpaper algorithm again, with each statement given a (machine-dependent) cost per execution, c1, …, c5.

      for i = 1 to n /* c1 */ for j = 1 to n { /* c2 */ c = (i*i + j*j) mod 10 /* c3 */ if (c <= 3) /* c4 */ plot(i, j); /* c5 */ }

      How many times does each line run?

      StatementRunsWhy
      1: for inonce per row
      2: for jn2n rows × n columns
      3: c = …n2once per pixel
      4: ifn2once per pixel
      5: plotsomewhere from 0 to n2only the pixels that pass the test

      The exact costs c1 … c5 depend on the machine (how long does a mod take, a plot?), and the exact number of plots depends on the pattern. Slide 61 handles that by sandwiching the total time T(n) between two simple bounds.

      The sandwich slides 61–62

      Write the total as the sum of (runs × cost):

      T(n) = n c1 + n2 c2 + n2 c3 + n2 c4 + p × c5

      where p is the number of plots, 0 ≤ p ≤ n2.

      Upper bound: the most it can be is when every pixel is plotted, and n ≤ n2 (when n ≥ 1):

      T(n) ≤ n c1 + n2 (c2 + c3 + c4 + c5) ≤ (c1 + c2 + c3 + c4 + c5) n2

      Lower bound: the least it can be is when nothing is plotted; we may also throw away the n c1 term:

      T(n) ≥ (c2 + c3 + c4) n2

      So T(n) is squeezed between two constants times n2. Move n and see it.

      Order of growth

      We say T(n) grows like n2 and write T(n) = Θ(n2) (“theta of n squared”). This is called the order of growth, or the complexity. We forget the machine-dependent constants and keep only the shape.

      Why comparing only the growth is enough slides 63–65

      • To compare two algorithms we compare only their orders of growth. The slower the growth, the better.
      • For example, an algorithm with running time an2 + bn + c (any constants a, b, c) has complexity Θ(n2). It is more efficient than an algorithm of order Θ(n3), because n3 eventually grows much faster than n2.
      • Counting this way means we do not have to worry that different operations have different costs, as long as each takes a constant amount of time. We just count how many operations there are, up to an order like n2.
      Slide 65 asks: what is the complexity of the Hanoi algorithm?

      It makes f(n) = 2n − 1 moves, so the order of growth is Θ(2n). The −1 does not change the order, and each move takes constant time.

      Slide 66 then promises to study this “asymptotic efficiency” properly: how time grows as the input grows without limit. For all but very small inputs, the asymptotically better algorithm is the one to choose. The next part gives the exact symbols.

      Part 7 · Slides 66–79

      The asymptotic symbols: Θ, O, Ω, o, ω

      Asymptotic means “what happens when n gets enormous”. The five symbols below are the language we use to say it. They look scary and are not. Each one is simply a precise way of saying “grows like”, “grows no faster than” or “grows no slower than”.

      Θ (theta): grows exactly like slide 67

      Definition

      Θ(g(n)) is the set of all functions f(n) for which we can find three positive numbers c1, c2 and n0 such that

      0 ≤ c1 g(n) ≤ f(n) ≤ c2 g(n)  for every n ≥ n0

      If f(n) is in Θ(g(n)) we say g(n) is an asymptotically tight bound for f(n).

      In words: once n is past some starting point n0, f stays squeezed between two copies of g: one shrunk by c1 below it and one stretched by c2 above it. The constants are yours to choose; you only have to show that some choice works.

      The slide's example: f(n) = 2n2 + 4n − 1 is Θ(n2). Choose c1 = 2, c2 = 5, n0 = 1. Check both sides for every n ≥ 1:

      • 2n2 ≤ 2n2 + 4n − 1 because 4n − 1 > 0. ✓
      • 2n2 + 4n − 1 ≤ 5n2 is the same as 0 ≤ 3n2 − 4n + 1 = (3n−1)(n−1), true for all n ≥ 1. ✓

      Now do it yourself. Pick a function f, pick a guess g, and slide the constants. The page checks every n from n0 up to 200, shows where the inequality first breaks, and estimates the limit of f/g. The Suggest constants button finds good constants for you when they exist.

      Find the constants

      What this demo is and is not

      The check is numerical: it tests n up to 200. A real proof must work for every n ≥ n0, so use algebra for that (as in the example above). The demo is for building the feeling.

      Abusing the notation slides 68–70

      Formally Θ(g(n)) is a set of functions, so the correct statement is “f(n) ∈ Θ(g(n))”. Everybody writes f(n) = Θ(g(n)) instead. The equals sign here means “is some function in”, nothing more. It is one-way: you may not flip it around.

      More abuses, and what they mean:

      • 4n3 + Θ(n2) = Θ(n3) means: “4n3 plus some function of order n2 is some function of order n3.” The Θ(n2) stands for the stuff we do not care about.
      • 2n2 + 3n + 1 = 2n2 + Θ(n) means: the leftover 3n + 1 is of order n. This hides inessential detail.
      Slide 70 asks: what is Θ(1)?

      Any function that stays between two positive constants: 0 < c1 ≤ f(n) ≤ c2. In other words “a constant”, or in algorithm terms “constant time”.

      Observation

      With Θ we may throw away the lower-order terms and the coefficient of the leading term. 3n2 + 100n + 7 is simply Θ(n2).

      O (big oh): grows no faster than slide 71

      Definition

      O(g(n)) is the set of all f(n) for which there exist c > 0 and n0 > 0 with

      0 ≤ f(n) ≤ c g(n)  for every n ≥ n0

      Only the roof, no floor. It is an upper bound: “f grows no faster than g”. The slide's example, f(n) = 2n2 + 4n − 1:

      • is O(n2) ✓ (take c = 5)
      • is O(n3) ✓ (a roof can be far above; it is true but loose)
      • is not O(n) ✗ (no matter which c you pick, n2 eventually beats cn)

      Picture it

      “This hay bale weighs at most 50 kilos” is true if it weighs 20 kilos. It is just not a very helpful statement. Θ is the tight claim. O only promises a ceiling.

      Ω (big omega): grows no slower than slide 72

      Definition

      Ω(g(n)) is the set of f(n) for which there exist c > 0 and n0 > 0 with

      0 ≤ c g(n) ≤ f(n)  for every n ≥ n0

      Only the floor. It is a lower bound. And so: f(n) is Θ(g(n)) exactly when it is both O(g(n)) and Ω(g(n)).

      Using O to analyse algorithms slides 73–74

      Two handy facts. First, if f1(n) = O(g(n)) and f2(n) = O(g(n)), then f1(n) + f2(n) = O(g(n)) too (the constants just add). Second, O lets us describe the worst-case running time merely by inspecting the structure of the code.

      Wallpaper again: two nested loops, each running n times, with a constant-time body. The body runs n × n times and each run costs at most a constant, so the total is O(n2). No need to count every statement.

      o (little oh) and ω (little omega): strictly slower and strictly faster slides 75–77

      Big O allows the two functions to be equally fast (2n2 is O(n2)). Little o is strict: f grows strictly slower than g, whatever constant you multiply g by.

      Definitions

      o(g(n)): for every c > 0 there is an n0 such that 0 ≤ f(n) < c g(n) for all n ≥ n0.

      ω(g(n)): for every c > 0 there is an n0 such that 0 ≤ c g(n) < f(n) for all n ≥ n0.

      The important change from big O: it is “for every c”, not “there is some c”. You must beat any multiplier, even c = 0.0001.

      • 2n = o(n2) ✓, but 2n2 ≠ o(n2). (With c = 1 we would need 2n2 < n2, false.)
      • 2n2 = ω(n) ✓, but 2n2 ≠ ω(n2).

      The limit test is often the quickest way (slides 75 and 77):

      What f(n)/g(n) does as n → ∞Conclusion
      goes to 0f = o(g) (and so also f = O(g))
      settles at a positive constantf = Θ(g)
      grows without boundf = ω(g) (and so also f = Ω(g)), i.e. g = o(f)

      Slide 77 writes the third case as g/f → 0, which says the same thing. The middle line is a standard fact that follows from the definition of Θ.

      The five symbols as comparison signs slide 78

      SymbolCompares likeRead as
      O≤grows no faster than
      Ω≥grows no slower than
      Θ=grows at the same rate
      o<grows strictly slower
      ω>grows strictly faster

      Because they act like comparison signs, they obey familiar rules:

      • Transitivity (all five): if f = O(g) and g = O(h) then f = O(h). The same for Θ, Ω, o, ω.
      • Reflexivity (Θ, O, Ω): f = Θ(f). Everything grows as fast as itself.
      • Symmetry (only Θ): f = Θ(g) exactly when g = Θ(f).
      • Transpose symmetry: f = O(g) exactly when g = Ω(f); and f = o(g) exactly when g = ω(f). (Like a ≤ b ⇔ b ≥ a.)

      Rules for manipulating O slide 79

      RuleIn plain words
      nm = O(nm') when m ≤ m'A higher power always wins: n2 = O(n5).
      O(f) + O(g) = O(f + g)Adding two things with a ceiling gives a ceiling on the sum. (And f + g is dominated by the bigger of the two.)
      f = O(f)A function is a ceiling for itself.
      c · O(f) = O(f) for a constant cMultiplying by a fixed number changes nothing: 5 · O(n) = O(n).
      O(f) · O(g) = O(f · g)Loops inside loops multiply: O(n) · O(n) = O(n2).
      O(f · g) = f · O(g)You can pull an exact factor outside the O.
      Check yourself: is 3n log n + 5n O(n²)? Is it Θ(n²)?

      Yes it is O(n2): n log n grows slower than n2, so 3n log n + 5n ≤ 8 n2 for large n. It is not Θ(n2): the ratio (3n log n + 5n)/n2 goes to 0, so it is actually o(n2). Its true order is Θ(n log n).

      Part 8 · Slides 80–82

      Calculating running time from the code

      With O we can find the running time of a program by looking at its shape. The slides give four simple rules.

      Rule 1: loops.

      Cost of a loop ≤ (cost of the body, including the test) × (number of times it runs).

      Rule 2: one after another.
