          You cannot just copy each element to the same position, because the hash function depends on the table size: k mod 7 and k mod 17 are different functions. Every element must be hashed again with the new m and inserted into the new table. The new size is usually about twice the old one, and again a prime.

          The slide's example: the table has m = 7 slots, h(k) = k mod 7, linear probing, and we insert 13, 6, 15, 23, 24. Already 5 of 7 slots are full (α = 5/7 ≈ 0.71), too much. Rehash into m = 17 slots (the first prime after 2 × 7 = 14), taking the old elements in slot order 0, 1, …, 6.

          Rehashing from 7 slots to 17

          Cost

          Rehashing takes one pass over the old table and one insertion per element: O(n + m) time. That is expensive, but it only happens rarely: each time the table doubles, it takes as many new insertions again to fill it up to the same load. So the cost averages out to a small constant per insertion. (This is the same argument as for growing a dynamic array.) As a bonus, rehashing drops all the DELETED markers.

          Part 12 · Wrap-up

          Summary and self-test

          Chaining or open addressing?

          ChainingOpen addressing
          Where elements livein linked lists hanging off the slotsin the table itself
          Pointersyes, in every nodenone
          Load factor αcan be above 1must be below 1, keep below 0.5
          Search costO(1 + α)grows quickly as α → 1
          Deletejust unlink the nodeneeds a DELETED marker
          When fullchains simply get longermust rehash into a bigger table
          Clusteringnoneprimary (linear), secondary (quadratic)
          Probingh(k,i)ClusteringNeeds
          Linear(h1 + i) mod mprimary clusteringnothing special: visits every slot
          Quadratic(h1 + i2) mod msecondary clusteringm prime and α < ½ to be safe
          Double(h1 + i · h2) mod mlittleh2 ≠ 0 and coprime to m (e.g. m prime)

          The theme of the chapter

          Hashing makes the dictionary operations take constant time on average, but only if (1) the hash function spreads the keys, (2) the table is not too full, and (3) you have a sensible collision plan. Break any of the three and it can fall back to O(n).

          Test yourself

          1. Table of 300 slots, h(k) = k mod 300. Which slot does the university number 301234567 go to?

            Show the answer

            Take away the biggest multiple of 300 that fits: 300 × 1,004,115 = 301,234,500. What is left is 301,234,567 − 301,234,500 = 67. Slot 67.

          2. Hash “AB” (A = 65, B = 66) with radix 128 into m = 100 slots.

            Show the answer

            65 × 128 + 66 = 8320 + 66 = 8386, and 8386 mod 100 = 86. Slot 86.

          3. A chained table has m = 200 slots and stores n = 600 elements with simple uniform hashing. About how many elements does an unsuccessful search examine? A successful one?

            Show the answer

            α = 600/200 = 3. Unsuccessful: about α = 3 elements, plus the work of computing h: cost 1 + α = 4. Successful: about 1 + α/2 = 2.5.

          4. Why is h(k) = k mod 64 a poor choice if the keys are all multiples of 8?

            Show the answer

            64 = 26, so k mod 64 is just the last 6 bits of k. For multiples of 8 the last 3 bits are always 0, so only 64/8 = 8 of the 64 slots can ever be used. A prime such as 61 or 67 would use all of them.

          5. What goes wrong if delete simply puts NIL in the slot of an open-addressing table?

            Show the answer

            Search stops at the first NIL. Elements that were stored after the deleted one in the same probe sequence become unreachable: the search for them reports “not found” although they are in the table (Catherine in the demo). That is why we store DELETED.

          6. Insert 89, 18, 49, 58, 69 into a table of 10 slots with linear probing, h1(k) = k mod 10. Final table?

            Show the answer

            Slot 0: 49, slot 1: 58, slot 2: 69, slot 8: 18, slot 9: 89. The other slots are empty.

          7. What problem of linear probing does quadratic probing reduce, and what problem remains?

            Show the answer

            It reduces primary clustering (the jumps are no longer one slot at a time). But keys with the same starting slot still follow the same sequence: secondary clustering. And the sequence may not reach all slots unless m is prime and the table is under half full.

          8. For double hashing with m = 10 and h2(k) = 5, how many different slots can a key reach?

            Show the answer

            Only 2 (the start slot and the one 5 further on), because 5 and 10 share the factor 5. If m were 11, a jump of 5 would reach all 11 slots.

          9. An open-addressing table of 7 slots is 5/7 full. What should you do, and what is the new m for the slide's example?

            Show the answer

            Rehash: build a bigger table (about twice as big, preferably prime: 17) and re-insert every element with the new hash function k mod 17.

          10. Give one reason to prefer chaining and one to prefer open addressing.

            Show the answer

            Chaining: deletion is easy and the load factor can exceed 1, so it degrades gracefully. Open addressing: no pointers, so less memory per element and no allocation, which leaves room for a bigger table, but it must be kept well below full.

          PreviousChapter 3 · Data structuresNextChapter 5 · Trees

          Slides 1–25 · 05_tree

          Trees from Scratch

          What happens when a list is allowed to branch: the words used to talk about trees, how to store one in memory, the three ways to walk through one, and the special case of binary trees.

          In this chapter

            Part 1 · Slides 1–4

            From a list to a tree

            A list is one-dimensional slide 2

            In a linked list every element is followed by exactly one other element (except the last one, which is followed by nothing). You can only go in one direction, like a queue of people in a single line.

            A tree is multi-dimensional slide 3

            Now relax the rule: let an element be followed by several elements. The slide's example is a genealogy tree, a data structure that stores the descendants of a person called A:

            Picture it

            It is a family tree, but with a strict rule: everybody has exactly one parent, except the oldest ancestor at the very top, who has none. (Real families have two parents; our trees do not.) There is only one way to get from the top to anybody: follow the parents.

            Definition in one sentence slide 4

            We have moved from a one-dimensional linked list to a multi-dimensional structure. This is called a tree. A tree imposes a hierarchical structure on a collection of elements: some elements are “above” others.

            Trees are everywhere you see a hierarchy: folders inside folders on your computer, a company's organisation chart, the sections inside a book, the way a web page's elements nest inside each other. The slide uses them to search for a file in a directory, which we meet again in Part 4.

            Part 2 · Slides 5–13

            Tree words

            Trees come with a lot of words. They are all easy, but you must know them exactly, because the rest of the course uses them without explanation. Every word below is illustrated on the genealogy tree of Part 1.

            Nodes, root, edges slide 5

            A tree is a collection of nodes. One node is special and is called the root (A in our picture). Two nodes can be related by the parent-child relation; we draw it as a line called an edge, with the parent above and the child below. A is the parent of B; B is a child of A.

            A tree is defined by a tree slide 6

            The slide gives a recursive definition (Chapter 1 again!):

            1. Base: a single node is a tree. That node is its root.
            2. Step: take a node n and some trees T1, T2, …, Tk whose roots are n1, n2, …, nk. Make n the parent of n1, …, nk. The result is a tree with root n. The Ti are the subtrees of the root, and n1, …, nk are the children of n.

            Look how natural this is for recursion: every subtree of a tree is itself a tree, so any algorithm on trees can be written as “do something with the root, then handle each subtree the same way”. That is exactly what the traversals in Part 4 do.

            Two small questions slide 7

            The definition requires at least one node. We stretch it so that a set with no nodes is also a tree, called the null tree (this gives recursive code a base case: if (n == NULL) return;).

            Q: does every node have a parent?

            Show the answer

            No. The root has no parent. Every other node has exactly one.

            Q: does every node have children?

            Show the answer

            No. Many nodes have none; they are called leaves (see below).

            Paths slides 8–9

            A sequence of nodes ⟨n1, n2, …, nk⟩ in which each node is the parent of the next is an ancestor-descendant path from n1 down to nk. Its length is the number of links (edges) in it, which is k − 1. So a path of 5 nodes has length 4, and a path with a single node, ⟨n1⟩, has length 0.

            Ancestors and descendants slides 10–11

            If there is a path from a to b, then a is an ancestor of b, and b is a descendant of a.

            Q: can a node be an ancestor of itself?

            Show the answer

            Yes, according to the definition. The one-node sequence ⟨a⟩ is a path (of length 0), so a is an ancestor and a descendant of itself. That is why the next definition exists: if a ≠ b, we call a a proper ancestor (or descendant) of b.

            More words from slide 11:

            • A node with no children is a leaf (also an external node).
            • A node that is not a leaf is an internal node.
            • A subtree of a tree is a node together with all its descendants.
            • Two nodes with the same parent are siblings.

            Degree, depth, height, forests slide 12

            • The degree of x is the number of nodes adjacent to it, including its parent if it has one.
            • The depth of x is the length of the path from the root to x. (What is the depth of the root? 0: the path from the root to itself has no links.)
            • The height of a tree is the largest depth of any node.
            • A collection of trees is a forest. (Remove the root of a tree and what is left is a forest of its subtrees.)
            • The children of a node are ordered from left to right, so these two trees are different:

            A note about “degree”

            This slide's definition counts the parent as a neighbour. Many other books define the degree of a node as just its number of children. The two differ by one for every node except the root. If an exam asks for the degree, use the slide's definition: children + 1 (for the parent), except the root.

            How many edges? slide 13

            Q: how many edges does a tree with n nodes have? n − 1.

            Why? Show the argument

            Every node except the root has exactly one parent, and every edge joins a node to its parent. So there is one edge for each non-root node: n − 1 edges. Check on the genealogy tree: 16 nodes, 15 edges.

            Click around a tree slides 5–13

            Pick a tree and a node, and the demo answers every question above about that node: parent, children, siblings, ancestors, descendants, degree, depth, height.

            The vocabulary lab

            Cheat sheet

            WordMeaningOn the genealogy tree
            rootthe one node with no parentA
            parent / childjoined by an edge, parent aboveE is the parent of I and J
            siblingssame parentI and J
            leaf (external)no childrenB, C, H, I, K, L, M, N, P, Q
            internalat least one childA, D, E, F, G, J
            path lengthnumber of linksA → E → J → P has length 3
            ancestor of Pon the path from the rootJ, E, A (proper); also P itself
            subtree of JJ with all its descendantsJ, P, Q
            depth of Plinks from the root3 (the root has depth 0)
            height of the treelargest depth3 (P and Q)
            degree of E (slide's)neighbours, including the parent3 (A, I, J)

            Part 3 · Slides 14–17

            Storing a tree in memory

            So far a tree is only a drawing. A computer has no drawings, just boxes of memory and pointers (Chapter 3). So how do we store the genealogy tree? The slides try three times, and the first two fail on purpose.

            Attempt 1: a small array of child pointers slide 14

            struct tree_node { element ele; tree_node *child[4];}

            Each node holds its own data ele and an array of 4 pointers, one per child. Q: problem?

            Show the answer

            Some nodes have more than 4 children. In our tree, A has 6 (B, C, D, E, F, G), so the array is too short. And most of the other nodes have 0 or 1 child, so most of the 4 boxes sit empty.

            Attempt 2: make the array huge slide 15

            struct tree_node { element ele; tree_node *child[40];} /* assume nobody on this earth can ever have more than 40 children */

            Problem? We do not know ahead of time how many children a node will have. A guess that is big enough wastes a gigantic amount of memory: our 16-node tree would reserve 16 × 40 = 640 pointers, while the tree only has 15 real parent-child links. The other 625 pointers are NULL. (And somebody with 41 children still breaks it.)

            Q: what data structure stores a collection of elements when we do not know in advance how big the collection is?

            Show the answer

            A linked list (Chapter 3). It grows one node at a time and wastes nothing. So give each node a linked list of its children.

            Attempt 3: a linked list of children slide 16

            For each node, keep a linked list of its child nodes. The node itself stores only one pointer: to the first element of that list. This is called the leftmost-child, right-sibling representation. Every node has two pointers:

            • lc, the leftmost-child pointer: points to my first (leftmost) child.
            • rs, the right-sibling pointer: points to the next node in my parent's list, the sibling just to my right.

            The type of a node (slide 17) is now small and the same for every node, whether it has 0 or 100 children:

            struct tree_node { element ele; tree_node *lc; /* leftmost child */ tree_node *rs; /* right sibling */}

            Q (slide 17): what is the right sibling of the root?

            Show the answer

            NULL. The root has no parent, so it is not in anybody’s list of children, so it has no siblings.

            Picture it

            Think of a family queue at the cinema. The parent only remembers the first child. Each child holds the hand of the next child. To find child number 5, the parent grabs child 1 and walks along the chain: four hands later, there you are.

            Try it: count the pointers

            Choose a tree and drag the array size K. See how many pointers the array version wastes (and which nodes do not even fit), against the always-the-same 2 pointers per node of lc/rs. Then ask for the k-th child of a node and watch the pointers being followed.

            Array of children versus lc / rs

            Where do the n + 1 NULL pointers come from?

            With n nodes there are 2n pointers (an lc and an rs in each). Every node except the root is pointed to by exactly one pointer (its parent’s lc if it is the first child, otherwise its left sibling’s rs). That uses up n − 1 pointers. The remaining 2n − (n − 1) = n + 1 are NULL.

            The price you pay

            The array version reaches child number k in one step (child[k-1]). With lc/rs you must walk the sibling list: k steps. The two-pointer form saves memory and handles any number of children, but loses direct access to a child. (Nothing in the slides needs direct access, so the lists win.)

            Part 4 · Slides 18–22

            Visiting every node: traversals

            Why walk through a tree? slide 18

            Sometimes we want to visit all the nodes of a tree, one after another, in some order. The slide’s example: searching for a file in a directory. Folders contain folders, which contain files: a tree. To find a file you must look at every item until you meet it. “Visit” just means “do the job on this node” (print it, compare it with the key, add its size to a total). The question is only: in what order?

            Three popular orders slide 19

            The orders differ in when the node itself is visited compared with its subtrees:

            OrderRecipeMemory trick
            Preorderthe node, then each subtree left to right“pre” = before its subtrees
            Postordereach subtree left to right, then the node“post” = after its subtrees
            Inorder (binary trees only)left subtree, the node, right subtree“in” = in between the two

            All three are recursive, exactly as the tree definition is. Here is preorder from the slide:

            PREORDER (n) {

            a procedure that is handed a node n, the root of some (sub)tree.

            if (n == NULL) return;

            the null tree: nothing to do, so stop. This is the base case of the recursion.

            visit n;

            do the job on this node first.

            for i = 1 to k

            suppose n has k subtrees T₁, T₂, …, T_k, ordered from left to right.

            PREORDER (T_i);

            run the very same procedure on each subtree, left to right.

            slide 20 shows the walk on a ten-node tree: a dashed line goes round the tree, and the numbers are the nodes. The visiting order is 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 9, 6, 10, 4, 7: root first, then the whole subtree of its first child (just 2), then the whole subtree of the second child (3, 5, 8, 9, 6, 10), then the whole subtree of the third child (4, 7). The demo below starts with this very tree.

            Postorder and inorder slide 21

            Postorder moves the “visit” line to the end, inorder puts it between the left and the right subtree:

            POSTORDER (n) {

            same procedure, different order.

            if (n == NULL) return;

            base case.

            for i = 1 to k

            first all the subtrees…

            POSTORDER (T_i);

            …run on each of them, left to right.

            visit n;

            …and only then the node itself, last.

            INORDER (n) {

            for binary trees only: every node has a left and a right side.

            if (n == NULL) return;

            base case (a missing child is NULL).

            INORDER(left subtree);

            first the whole left side,

            visit n;

            then the node itself, in the middle,

            INORDER(right subtree);

            then the whole right side.

            Why inorder is only for binary trees

            “In between” only makes sense with exactly two sides. A node with six children has five gaps between them, so nobody knows where the node itself should go. For a binary tree there is exactly one gap: between left and right.

            A walk around the tree

            The slide’s dashed line is a nice way to remember all three. Walk around the outside of a binary tree, keeping it on your left, and you pass each node three times: on its left side, from below, and on its right side. The first time is its preorder turn, the second time its inorder turn, and the last time its postorder turn.

            Watch the recursion run

            Step through any of the traversals. Every step is one call, one visit or one return. The blue chips list the calls that are still waiting for their turn to finish (this is what the computer keeps on its call stack). Start with the tree of slide 20 and preorder, then switch to postorder and compare. For the binary trees you can also choose inorder, and you can show the quick calls on NULL.

            Preorder, postorder and inorder, call by call

            The three orders on our trees

            TreePreorderPostorderInorder
            slide 201 2 3 5 8 9 6 10 4 72 8 9 5 10 6 3 7 4 1(not binary)
            genealogyA B C D H E I J P Q F K L M G NB C H D I P Q J E K L M F N G A(not binary)
            binary treeA B D E G C F H ID G E B H I F C AD B G E A C H F I
            (3 + 4) × (5 − 2)× + 3 4 − 5 23 4 + 5 2 − ×3 + 4 × 5 − 2

            Bonus: why three orders exist

            On the expression tree, the three orders write the same formula in the three classic notations: inorder is the usual way we write it (but the brackets get lost: 3 + 4 × 5 − 2 is a different sum!), postorder is the “operands first, operator last” form that a stack evaluates (Chapter 3), and preorder puts the operator first. This is not on the slides; it is only here to show that the order really matters.

            Folders: preorder to search, postorder to add up

            Back to the slide’s own example, a directory. The two orders suit two different jobs. To find a file you look at each folder when you first arrive (preorder), and you can stop the moment you find it. To add up the size of a folder you must first know the sizes of everything inside it, so you visit the folder last (postorder). In this toy example a folder itself counts as 1 and each file has the size shown.

            Searching a directory and adding up sizes

            How long does a traversal take? slide 22

            Q: what is the complexity of the traversal algorithms? A: O(n), where n is the number of nodes.

            Why? Show the argument

            The procedure is called once for every node (each node has exactly one parent, and the parent calls it exactly once), and each call does a constant amount of work apart from its recursive calls: one visit and a loop over its children. So the total work is a constant times n. In a binary tree there are also quick calls on NULL (one for every missing child): n + 1 of them, so 2n + 1 calls in all, which is still proportional to n. You can see both numbers in the demo above by switching on show NULL calls.

            You cannot do better: to visit n nodes you have to spend at least one step on each. So a traversal is Θ(n).

            Part 5 · Slides 23–25

            Binary trees

            Definition slide 23

            A binary tree is a tree in which no node has more than 2 children. A node can have a left child, a right child, both, or none. Left and right are different things: a node with only a left child and a node with only a right child are different trees.

            If no node has a single child (every node has 0 or 2 children), the binary tree is called a full binary tree.

            Complete binary tree slide 24

            A complete binary tree of height h is a full binary tree in which all leaves are at the same depth (h). Nothing is missing: every level is packed. The third tree above is complete, with h = 2.

            Careful with the word “complete”

            In this course “complete” means “full, and every leaf at the same depth”. Many other books call that a perfect binary tree and use “complete” for something looser (all levels full except possibly the last, which is filled from the left). If you read another book, check which meaning it uses. For the exam, use the slide’s.

            Q (slide 24): how many nodes does a complete binary tree of height h have?

            Count level by level. The root level has 1 node. Every node has exactly two children, so each level has twice as many nodes as the one above: depth 0 has 20 = 1, depth 1 has 21 = 2, depth 2 has 22 = 4, and so on until depth h, which has 2h. Add them up:

            1 + 2 + 4 + … + 2h = 2h+1 − 1
            Why does the sum come out as 2^(h+1) − 1?

            Call the sum S. Doubling it gives 2S = 2 + 4 + 8 + … + 2h+1. Now subtract the original: almost everything cancels and what is left is 2S − S = 2h+1 − 1, so S = 2h+1 − 1. Another way to see it: the last level has 2h nodes, and all the levels above it together have one fewer than that (2h − 1).

            Try it: slide h from 0 to 5. The three numbers you want to remember: nodes 2h+1 − 1, leaves 2h, internal nodes 2h − 1.

            Count the nodes of a complete binary tree

            Height and number of nodes

            Turn the formula round: a binary tree of height h has at most 2h+1 − 1 nodes. So n nodes need a height of at least about log2 n. At the other extreme, a chain (the fourth tree) has height n − 1. So for n nodes, the height of a binary tree is somewhere between log2 (n+1) − 1 and n − 1. Remember this: the next chapters measure tree operations in terms of the height.

            Quick check. A binary tree has 1000 nodes. What are the smallest and the largest possible heights?

            Show the answer

            Largest: a chain, height 999. Smallest: we need 2h+1 − 1 ≥ 1000, so 2h+1 ≥ 1001. Since 210 = 1024 ≥ 1001 but 29 = 512 < 1001, we need h + 1 = 10, so the smallest height is 9. Same 1000 nodes: height 9 or height 999.

            Binary tree implementation slide 25

            Every node has at most two children, so no sibling lists are needed: just give each node two pointers, one per side.

            struct tree_node { element ele; tree_node *left; tree_node *right;}

            Does it look familiar? It is the same shape as the lc / rs node of Part 3, just with the names changed. That is the reason the lc/rs picture in Part 3 turned any tree into a binary tree. And the pointer counting is the same, too: a binary tree with n nodes has 2n pointers, n − 1 of them point to a child, and n + 1 are NULL. Those are exactly the NULL calls that INORDER, PREORDER and POSTORDER make in Part 4.

            Part 6 · Wrap-up

            Summary and self-test

            The chapter on one page

            IdeaIn one line
            Treenodes joined by parent-child edges; one root; every other node has one parent; n nodes have n − 1 edges
            Recursive definitiona node on top of some trees (its subtrees); a single node is a tree; the null tree is a tree too
            Measurespath length = links; depth of a node = links from the root; height of the tree = largest depth; degree = neighbours (children + parent)
            Storing itarrays of child pointers waste memory or do not fit; use lc (leftmost child) and rs (right sibling): 2 pointers per node, n + 1 of them NULL
            Traversalspreorder: node, then subtrees. Postorder: subtrees, then node. Inorder (binary only): left, node, right. All O(n)
            Binary treeat most 2 children (left, right); full: 0 or 2 children; complete: full with all leaves at depth h, so 2h+1 − 1 nodes

            The theme of the chapter

            Trees are lists that are allowed to branch, and everything about them is recursive: the definition, the traversals, and (soon) the way we count their nodes and measure their height. When you meet a tree problem, ask: “what do I do with the root, and what do I let the same procedure do on each subtree?”

            Test yourself

            1. How many edges does a tree with 100 nodes have? What is the depth of the root, and what is the height of a tree that has a single node?

              Show the answer

              99 edges (one for every node except the root). The root has depth 0, and a one-node tree has height 0.

            2. In the genealogy tree, list the proper ancestors of Q, its depth, and the siblings of I.

              Show the answer

              Q is a child of J, J of E, E of A: the proper ancestors are J, E, A. The path A → E → J → Q has 3 links, so the depth is 3. I and J are both children of E, so I’s only sibling is J.

            3. What is the degree of E, and of A, using the definition on slide 12?

              Show the answer

              Degree counts all neighbours, parent included. E has parent A and children I and J: 3. A is the root: it has no parent but 6 children: 6.

            4. Write the preorder and the postorder of the tree on slide 20 (root 1; its children, left to right, are 2, 3, 4; node 3 has children 5 and 6; 5 has children 8 and 9; 6 has child 10; 4 has child 7).

              Show the answer

              Preorder (node first): 1 2 3 5 8 9 6 10 4 7. Postorder (node last): 2 8 9 5 10 6 3 7 4 1. Check that 1 is first in the one and last in the other.

            5. Why is child[4] a bad way to store the genealogy tree, and why is child[40] not much better?

              Show the answer

              child[4] cannot hold A’s 6 children. child[40] holds them, but reserves 40 pointers for every one of the 16 nodes (640 in all) when only 15 are ever used, and it still breaks for a node with 41 children.

            6. A tree with 50 nodes is stored with lc and rs pointers. How many pointers exist, how many of them are NULL?

              Show the answer

              2 × 50 = 100 pointers. Each non-root node is pointed to once, so 49 pointers are in use and 100 − 49 = 51 = n + 1 are NULL.

            7. You have the lc/rs form of a tree and want the 4th child of a node. What do you do, and how many pointers do you follow?

              Show the answer

              Follow lc once to the 1st child, then rs three times: 4 pointers. (A child[] array would take 1 step, which is the price of lc/rs.)

            8. A binary tree has 9 nodes. If INORDER also counts the calls made on NULL, how many calls does a full traversal make?

              Show the answer

              One call per node (9) plus one NULL call per missing child. There are 2 × 9 = 18 child slots, of which 9 − 1 = 8 are filled, so 10 are NULL: 9 + 10 = 19 = 2n + 1 calls in all.

            9. What is the inorder of the binary tree whose root A has left child B and right child C, where B has left child D and right child E?

              Show the answer

              Left subtree of A first: that is D, then B, then E. Then A. Then the right subtree: C. Result: D B E A C.

            10. Is every full binary tree complete? How many nodes does a complete binary tree of height 4 have, and how many of them are leaves?

              Show the answer

              No: a root with two children, one of which has two leaf children, is full (every node has 0 or 2 children) but its leaves are at depths 1 and 2, so it is not complete. Height 4: 25 − 1 = 31 nodes, of which 24 = 16 are leaves.

            Slides 1–27 · 06_Search

            Searching from Scratch

            How to find one thing among many without opening every box: why an unsorted pile needs n looks, how a sorted list lets one look rule out many boxes, jump search, binary search, interpolation search, a puzzle about eggs, and when to use which.

            In this chapter

              Part 1 · Slides 2–4

              The problem: finding one thing among many

              What are we trying to do? slide 2

              You have a collection of n things, and every thing carries a key: a name, a student number, a price, whatever you look things up by. Somebody gives you one key and asks: is there a thing with this key in the collection, and if so, hand it over. That is searching.

              Picture it

              Picture n sealed envelopes on a table, each with a name written on the back. “Is there an envelope for Hannah?” The only way to learn what is inside is to turn one over. Each turn costs you effort, so the whole chapter is about how few envelopes you need to turn over.

              So far the course has shown two ways to search: linear search (look at the first, then the second, then the third…) and hashing (Chapter 4: compute from the key where the thing must be, and look just there).

              How good are those two? slide 3

              MethodAverage caseWorst case
              Linear searchO(n)O(n)
              Hashing, chainingO(1 + α)O(n)
              Hashing, open addressingO(11 − α)O(n)

              Here α is the load factor of the hash table from Chapter 4 (how full it is). Hashing is brilliant on average, but both methods have a worst case of O(n): in the worst case you really do turn over every envelope. This chapter looks at several searching strategies that have a better worst case.

              The model: what do we count? slide 4

              The setting is always the same. We have a list L of n elements, and one more element X (identified by a key k). We want to decide whether X is in L, and if it is, retrieve it.

              To compare algorithms fairly we need one number to count. The slide chooses: assume the running time is dominated by (or proportional to) the number of element–element comparisons, that is, the number of times we ask “is this element equal to / smaller than X?”. Everything else the algorithm does (moving an index, adding 1 to a counter) happens a constant number of times per comparison, so it never changes the order of growth.

              Rule of the game

              From now on cost = the number of comparisons of X with an element of L. We do not count comparisons between two elements of L, and we do not count the work to build the list in the first place.

              The slide then asks the question that drives the next part:

              Q: Must the worst case for any search algorithm take at least n comparisons?

              Make your guess first

              Think about it for a moment: to be sure that X is not in the list, don’t you have to look at everything? Part 2 shows that the answer is “yes” for a list in no particular order, and then shows exactly where the argument stops working.

              Part 2 · Slides 5–7

              Is n the worst case? The adversary argument

              The argument slides 5–6

              Claim: a search algorithm that works on any list (the numbers in no particular order) needs at least n comparisons in the worst case.

              Proof by contradiction. Suppose some correct algorithm always makes at most n − 1 comparisons of X with elements of L. There are n elements, but at most n − 1 comparisons, so on this input there is at least one element, say L[i], that the algorithm never compares with X.

              Now build a new instance (the picture on the slide): copy L, but deliberately put X into slot L[i].

              The algorithm cannot tell the difference. It never looked at box i, and every box it did look at holds the same number as before, so it makes exactly the same comparisons and gives exactly the same answer as before: “X is not in L”. But X is in the new list. So the algorithm is incorrect. That is a contradiction. Hence no correct search algorithm takes fewer than n comparisons (in the worst case).

              Picture it

              Think of a mean opponent, the adversary, who does not pick X until the very end. Every time you open a box he says “not equal”. He keeps this up until just one box is left unopened, and then he decides that X was in that box all along. Nothing he said was a lie, and you could not have known. The only way to beat him is to open all n boxes. Play against him below.

              Beat the adversary

              Why this is a nice kind of proof

              We did not analyse a particular algorithm. We showed something about all algorithms at once, including ones nobody has invented yet. This is called a lower bound: a floor that no algorithm can dig below. (In Chapter 2 you met the same idea for the Towers of Hanoi.)

              What the argument secretly needs slide 7

              The proof works only because of two assumptions:

              1. (1) the algorithm skips some L[i] on some input (it makes fewer than n comparisons);
              2. (2) if the algorithm skips L[i], it cannot gain any information about L[i] from the other comparisons.

              Assumption (2) is the weak spot. The slide hints at it with “c.f., sorted list”: if the list is sorted, then comparing X with one box does tell you something about many other boxes. If L[6] is smaller than X, then L[1], L[2], …, L[5] are smaller than X too, and you never had to open them. The adversary can no longer hide X in a box you skipped, because the boxes you skipped are already ruled out.

              So the conclusion on the slide is: if the data has some ordering structure (such as being sorted), the argument breaks, and we may be able to beat the O(n) worst case. Switch the demo above to Sorted list and try again: you can decide in a handful of comparisons.

              Hashing escapes in its own way

              Hashing also “gains information about boxes it never opened”: the hash function says where X would have to be, so every other box can be ignored. But the information is only as good as the table: if many keys collide, the worst case is still O(n) (slide 3). Sorting gives a guarantee that hashing cannot.

              Part 3 · Slides 8–10

              A sorted list: one look rules out many boxes

              A smarter first look slide 8

              With linear search we examine the first element of L, then the 2nd, the 3rd… Now suppose L is sorted in increasing order of keys. Try this instead: look at the 5th element first. There are three possible outcomes:

              OutcomeWhat we learn
              L[5] = XWe are done.
              L[5] > XGood news: the list is sorted, so L[6], L[7], … are even bigger. We only have to consider L[1], L[2], L[3], L[4].
              L[5] < XX is bigger than L[5], and L[1], …, L[4] are smaller than L[5]. So X is bigger than all of L[1], L[2], L[3], L[4] as well.

              The slide ends with: “in any case, this strategy seems to be better than linear search! (Why?)”

              Why is it better?

              With linear search, one comparison rules out exactly one box (the one you just opened). With a sorted list, one comparison rules out several boxes you never opened: if we are lucky, everything from L[5] to the end; if we are unlucky, the first five boxes. The ordering of the list is information, and the comparison turns that information into saved work.

              Nothing is special about 5. Whichever box you choose, the same three outcomes appear, and the choice only decides how many boxes each outcome rules out. The rest of the chapter is about choosing well.

              Jump search slide 10

              The first systematic strategy: jump along the list in steps of k, like a person reading house numbers on a long street who only checks every k-th house, and walks house by house only when they are close.

              1. Choose a number k < n.
              2. Interrogate L[k], L[2k], L[3k], … one after another, until you reach the first i with X ≤ L[ik].
              3. If X = L[ik], we are done.
              4. Otherwise X is bigger than L[(i−1)k] and smaller than L[ik]. If it is in the list at all, it is in the short stretch between them, so search that sub-list linearly: L[(i−1)k + 1], …, L[ik − 1].
              5. If no such i exists (the jumps run off the end of the list), search the leftover tail linearly: L[⌊n/k⌋k + 1], …, L[n].

              The symbol ⌊n/k⌋k in the last step is simply “the last multiple of k that still fits inside n”. (The slide text lost its ≤ sign in step 2; the picture’s labels, “(i−1)k < X” and “ik ≥ X”, show what is meant.)

              Run it yourself. Pick a list size, a jump size k and a number to look for, then step through. Watch how a big part of the list is crossed out after every jump.

              Jump search, step by step

              Two special cases to remember

              k = 1: every “jump” is one box, so jump search is linear search. k = n: you look at L[n] once and then scan everything before it: again about n comparisons. The good values of k are somewhere in between. How do we choose?

              Part 4 · Slides 11–14

              How big should the jump be? Square-root search

              Counting the comparisons slide 11

              Q: how many comparisons f(n,k) does jump search do in the worst case?

              Suppose mk ≤ n < (m+1)k. In words: m is how many whole jumps of size k fit inside the list, so m = ⌊n/k⌋.

              1. To find the right stretch we need at most m comparisons (L[k], L[2k], …, L[mk]).
              2. To scan inside one stretch we need at most k − 1 comparisons.
              3. So in the worst case we need m + k − 1 comparisons.
              f(n,k) = ⌊nk⌋ + k − 1
              Why k − 1 and not k?

              A stretch runs from the box just after one jump to the box just before the next jump: L[(i−1)k + 1] to L[ik − 1]. That is k − 1 boxes. The box L[ik] itself was already compared when we jumped onto it. The leftover tail at the end of the list is never longer than that either, because it has fewer than k boxes.

              Example from the previous part: n = 24, k = 4 gives ⌊24/4⌋ + 4 − 1 = 6 + 3 = 9 comparisons at worst, against 24 for linear search.

              What is the best k? slide 12

              Take n = 1000 and try some values:

              kjumps at most ⌊1000/k⌋then scan at most k − 1f(1000, k)
              33332335
              101009109
              30332962
              50204969
              3003299302

              (These five rows are slide 12’s table.) A tiny k means a huge number of jumps; a huge k means a long stretch to walk. The total is smallest in the middle, near k = 30. Slide the jump size around in the chart below and watch the valley.

              The valley of f(n, k)

              Finding the bottom of the valley slide 13

              We want (approximately) the minimum of nk + k − 1. We dropped the floor brackets, since they change the value by less than 1.

              The calculus way (the slide’s way). Treat k as a real number. The slope is −nk2 + 1, and the bottom of the valley is where the slope is 0:

              −nk2 + 1 = 0  ⟹  k2 = n  ⟹  k = √n

              The no-calculus way. The two parts nk and k multiply to the fixed number n. Two numbers with a fixed product have the smallest sum when they are equal (a rectangle with a fixed area has the smallest perimeter when it is a square). So nk = k, which again gives k = √n.

              Prove it with one line of algebra

              A square is never negative: (√k − √(n/k))2 ≥ 0. Expand it: k − 2√n + nk ≥ 0, so nk + k ≥ 2√n, with equality exactly when k = n/k, that is k = √n. No k can beat 2√n.

              Square-root search slide 14

              Jump search with k ≈ √n is called square-root search. Its worst case is

              f(n, √n) = ⌊n√n⌋ + √n − 1 ≈ 2√n − 1 = O(√n)
              nlinear searchk = √n2√n − 1
              10010010 + 9 = 1919
              10,00010,000100 + 99 = 199199
              1,000,0001,000,0001000 + 999 = 1,9991,999

              A real improvement

              A list a million long needs at most about 2000 comparisons instead of a million. O(√n) is already far better than O(n). But a sorted list can do much better still. Wait for the next part.

              Part 5 · Slides 15–20

              Binary search: always look in the middle

              Lucky and unlucky slide 15

              Look again at what one jump of size k achieves. We examine L[k] and compare it with X.

              Notice that luck decides how much we gain. Both outcomes give us a shorter list, but one gives us a much shorter list than the other.

              Which k protects us from bad luck? slides 16–17

              Q: if we want to eliminate the largest segment even if we are always unlucky (the worst case), what value of k shall we use?

              In the worst case we are always unlucky, so each comparison removes only the smaller of the two parts, min(k, n − k) boxes. Take n = 100:

              klucky: removes n − kunlucky: removes kguaranteed to remove
              10901010
              30703030
              50505050
              70307030
              90109010

              The guaranteed amount is largest when the two parts are equal, k = n/2. A: pick the middle element. In one comparison we eliminate half of the list, no matter what. Then repeat the same trick on the half that is left, until either X is found or the segment is reduced to one element. This is binary search.

              Picture it

              It is the game “guess my number between 1 and 100”. You never say “1? 2? 3?” (that is linear search). You say “50?”, hear “higher”, say “75?”, hear “lower”, and in a handful of guesses you have it. Or you look up a word in a dictionary: open in the middle, see which half the word is in, throw the other half away, repeat.

              The algorithm slide 18

              BinarySearch (L, low, high, X) {

              searches the segment L[low…high] for X. The first call is BinarySearch(L, 1, n, X): the whole list.

              while (high >= low) {

              keep going as long as at least one box is still in play. (If high < low the segment is empty.)

              mid = floor((low + high) / 2)

              the middle box, rounded down. With 7 boxes (1…7) that is box 4; with 4 boxes (1…4) it is box 2.

              case L[mid] {

              compare the middle element with X. There are three cases:

              < X: low = mid + 1;

              the middle is smaller than X, so X is to its right. Cross out everything up to mid.

              = X: return(mid);

              found. Report the position.

              > X: high = mid - 1;

              the middle is bigger than X, so X is to its left. Cross out everything from mid on.

              }

              the end of the case.

              }

              the end of the while. This brace is missing on the slide.

              return("not found!");

              we only get here when the segment ran empty: X is not in the list.

              }

              the end of the procedure (also missing on the slide).

              Each pass around the loop makes one comparison and cuts the segment low…high roughly in half. Step through it. With n = 15 the list shrinks 15 → 7 → 3 → 1.

              Binary search, step by step

              How many comparisons at worst? slide 19

              Q: what is the worst-case complexity of binary search? Let f(n) be the worst-case number of elements examined. One comparison, and then we continue with the larger of the two remaining halves, which has ⌊n/2⌋ boxes:

              f(n) =1n = 1f(⌊n/2⌋) + 1n > 1

              The same unwrapping trick as in Chapter 2: replace f on the right-hand side by its own definition, again and again.

              f(n) = f(⌊n/2⌋) + 1
              = f(⌊⌊n/2⌋/2⌋) + 2 = f(⌊n/4⌋) + 2
              = f(⌊n/2i⌋) + i

              The slide uses ⌊⌊n/2⌋/2⌋ = ⌊n/4⌋ and asks: “Can you show that?”

              Can you show that ⌊⌊n/2⌋/2⌋ = ⌊n/4⌋?

              Divide n by 4 with a remainder: n = 4q + r with 0 ≤ r ≤ 3. Then ⌊n/4⌋ = q. On the other side, ⌊n/2⌋ = 2q + ⌊r/2⌋, and ⌊r/2⌋ is 0 or 1. Halving again gives q + ⌊⌊r/2⌋/2⌋ = q + 0 = q. Both sides equal q. ∎ (The same idea, applied i times, gives ⌊n/2i⌋.)

              We stop unwrapping when the segment has one box: ⌊n/2i⌋ = 1. That happens exactly when 2i ≤ n < 2i+1, that is i = ⌊lg n⌋. Since f(1) = 1:

              f(n) = ⌊lg n⌋ + 1
              list size nlinear searchbinary search ⌊lg n⌋ + 1
              15154
              1,0001,00010
              1,000,0001,000,00020
              1,000,000,0001,000,000,00030

              Why this is spectacular

              Doubling the size of the list adds just one comparison. A billion sorted numbers can be searched with 30 comparisons. The worst case is O(lg n), which is far better than linear search’s O(n) and the square-root search’s O(√n).

              The average case slide 20

              Q: what is the average-case complexity of binary search? The slide’s answers:

              • Unsuccessful search (X is not in the list): same as the worst case. To prove that X is missing you must shrink the segment all the way to nothing.
              • Successful search (X is in the list): O(lg n).

              Count every possible search for a list of your chosen size, and see for yourself:

              Counting every possible search

              Why is a successful search close to the worst case too?

              Look at the tree picture above: the nodes at depth 0, 1, 2, 3 number 1, 2, 4, 8. Half of all the nodes are at the very bottom level, and a search for any of them needs the maximum number of comparisons. More than three quarters (12 of the 15) are on the bottom two levels. So a typical successful search is only about one comparison shorter than the worst one: still O(lg n).

              Part 6 · Slides 21–22

              Interpolation search: guess where X should be

              Why look in the middle? slide 21

              Binary search is pessimistic: it always opens the middle box, whatever X is. But you do not look up “Zebra” in a dictionary by opening it in the middle. You open it near the end, because you know roughly where Z lives.

              The slide gives the idea. Suppose L is a sorted list of n numbers. If L uniformly partitions the set of numbers (they are spread out evenly between the smallest and the largest), then X should be near L[pn], where p is the portion of the elements that are smaller than X. So, roughly, L[pn] is the element most likely to be near X.

              Picture it

              The numbers 10, 20, 30, …, 100 are spread evenly. Where is X = 70? It is two thirds of the way from 10 up to 100, so it should be about two thirds of the way along the list: around box 7. And it is: L[7] = 70.

              The rule slide 22

              With interpolation search, instead of always interrogating the middle element of a segment, we guess where in the segment X is likely to be. If L[low … high] is the segment to consider, we inspect box

              pos = low + ⌊p × (high − low)⌋   where   p = X − L[low]L[high] − L[low]

              Read p as “how far along, from 0 to 1, X sits between the smallest and the biggest number still in play”. If p = 0 we look at the first box; if p = 1, the last; if p = 0.5, exactly in the middle, just like binary search. After the probe we do what binary search does: smaller means low = pos + 1, bigger means high = pos - 1, and we repeat with the new segment.

              The slide states that the “average case” complexity of interpolation search is O(lg lg n). For a list of a million numbers, lg n is about 20 but lg lg n is only about 4.3.

              Step through it. The first list is spread evenly, so it finds things in one or two probes where binary search needs four or five. Then switch to the other lists and watch the guesses go wrong.

              Interpolation search, step by step

              Where does lg lg n come from? (not on the slides)

              Here is the usual intuition. On evenly spread numbers a probe lands close to X: a segment of m boxes shrinks to about √m boxes in one probe. Taking square roots again and again (1,000,000 → 1,000 → 32 → 6 → 2 → 1) needs only lg lg n rounds, because every square root halves the number of digits in binary: lg √m = 12 lg m. Binary search only halves the length of the segment, which is the slower lg n.

              The fine print: the evenly-spread assumption

              The promise on slide 22 is about the average case, and it only holds when the numbers are spread out roughly evenly. If they are bunched up, the guess p is a poor guide, and the algorithm can be much worse than binary search, even creeping toward O(n). The experiment below searches for 400 random numbers in three lists of the same length that are spread out in three different ways:

              Even and uneven numbers: the experiment

              Which one should you trust?

              Binary search makes no assumption about the numbers: its ⌊lg n⌋ + 1 is a guarantee, whatever the data. Interpolation search is a bet on the data: it can win big (4 probes instead of 19) or lose big. Use it when you know the numbers are nearly uniform (say, student numbers handed out in order); use binary search when you do not.

              Part 7 · Slide 23

              A practical problem: the egg puzzle

              The puzzle slide 23

              You wish to determine the critical height, which is the minimum floor of a building from which an egg breaks if tossed out of a window on that floor. You have a building with 500 floors and a supply of 10 eggs. You are only allowed one operation: toss an egg out of a window. If the egg does not break, you can use it again; if it breaks, it is gone.

              Q: how would you determine the critical height?

              It is a search problem in disguise

              Line up the floors 1, 2, 3, …, 500. If an egg breaks from floor f it also breaks from every higher floor, so the outcomes of tossing along the building look like a sorted list:

              survives, survives, survives, …, survives, BREAKS, breaks, breaks, …

              We are looking for the first “breaks”: the critical floor c. A toss is a comparison: it answers “is c at or below this floor (breaks) or above it (survives)?”. (We assume an egg tossed from floor 500 does break, so c is one of the floors 1 to 500, and that all eggs are alike.)

              So every search strategy of this chapter applies, but with a twist: a comparison that answers “breaks” costs you an egg. You have two things to economise, tosses and eggs.

              StrategyHowTosses (worst)Eggs it may break
              Linearfloor 1, 2, 3, … until it breaks4991
              Jump, k = 22floors 22, 44, 66, … until it breaks, then walk up the last stretch432
              Binarytoss from the middle, halve the range each time9up to 9

              (Linear search needs 499 tosses, not 500: if the egg survives floors 1 to 499, we know it breaks on floor 500 without throwing it.)

              With 10 eggs we can afford binary search, which is the fastest: at most 9 tosses (⌊lg 500⌋ + 1 = 9). Try all three strategies below, and then take eggs away.

              Dropping eggs from the 500-floor building

              Why 9 can’t be beaten

              Every toss has only two outcomes (breaks, survives), so t tosses can tell apart at most 2t different situations. There are 500 possible answers for the critical floor, and 28 = 256 < 500 ≤ 512 = 29. So no strategy can be sure after fewer than 9 tosses, and binary search reaches that limit. This is the same “one question, two answers” idea that makes the worst case of binary search lg n.

              Bonus (not on the slide): only 2 eggs

              With just two eggs, k = 22 gives 43 tosses, the best jump search can do. But a cleverer plan makes the jumps shorter and shorter: first toss from floor 32; if it breaks, walk up 1–31 (at most 32 tosses in all). If it survives, jump only 31 more floors (to 63): now a break costs 2 tosses so far plus at most 30 more, again 32 in all; then 30 more floors, and so on. Since 32 + 31 + 30 + … + 1 = 528 ≥ 500, 32 tosses always suffice, and no plan with two eggs can do better.

              Part 8 · Slides 24–27

              Linear vs binary vs hashing: which one to use?

              The price of being sorted slide 24

              Binary search is wonderful, but the slide adds a warning: in order for binary search to be possible, the array has to be sorted. If elements get inserted and deleted frequently, maintaining a sorted array could be expensive: insertion and deletion take O(n) time, although the worst-case search time is O(lg n).

              (Appending to an unsorted list takes constant time: just put the new element at the end. Sorting is paid for somewhere, either at insertion time or once up front.)

              Linear or binary? slide 25

              • If n is small, or if search is done rarely, linear search is better. The list does not need to be sorted.
              • Binary search is better if search is done very often, there is a lot of data, and the data is relatively static (does not change much).

              Flip the three questions below and see which advice applies:

              Which search should I use?

              The numbers slide 26

              The slide compares the worst-case number of comparisons of the three methods for n = 15, 255, 4095, 65535 and 1,048,575. (These are 24 − 1, 28 − 1, …, 220 − 1, so binary search needs exactly 4, 8, 12, 16 and 20.) The chart uses a log scale on both sides, because the values range from 4 to a million.

              Linear, square-root and binary search compared

              On the log chart, a straight line that rises steeply is linear search; square-root search rises at half that steepness; and binary search is almost flat: it grows by one comparison every time n doubles.

              What about hashing? slide 27

              Hashing is more difficult to design (choose a table size, a hash function, a way to resolve collisions) but in general gives the best “average” search time: O(1 + α). The slide lists two drawbacks:

              1. It uses more memory. A hash table must stay only partly full (a small load factor α) to stay fast, and chaining adds pointers.
              2. It does not support range search efficiently. A range search asks for all keys between two values, such as “every student number from 30 to 62”. A sorted array finds the first key by halving and then just reads along. A hash table put the keys in unrelated slots on purpose, so it has to look everywhere.

              Range search: sorted array against hash table

              So which one?

              If you only ever ask “is this exact key here?”, hashing is hard to beat. If you also need order (ranges, smallest, next bigger) then you want a sorted structure, and if the data keeps changing you want one that stays sorted cheaply. That is exactly what the next chapter, search trees, is for.

              Part 9 · Wrap-up

              Summary and self-test

              The chapter on one page

              IdeaIn one line
              The modelcost = number of comparisons of X with elements of the list
              Unsorted listany correct algorithm needs n comparisons in the worst case (adversary argument: it could hide X in any box you skipped)
              Sorted listone comparison can rule out many boxes you never opened, so we can beat O(n)
              Jump searchcheck L[k], L[2k], …, then scan one stretch: f(n,k) = ⌊n/k⌋ + k − 1
              Square-root searchjump search with k ≈ √n: about 2√n − 1, so O(√n)
              Binary searchalways look in the middle; worst case ⌊lg n⌋ + 1 comparisons, so O(lg n); the same for a failed search, O(lg n) on average for a successful one
              Interpolation searchlook where X should be if the numbers are spread evenly: average O(lg lg n) on such data, but can be worse than binary search on uneven data
              Egg problemtosses are comparisons, but a break also costs an egg; binary search needs 9 tosses for 500 floors
              Which to usesmall or rarely searched: linear. Large, searched often, rarely changed: binary on a sorted array. Exact lookups only: hashing (but no range queries)

              The theme of the chapter

              You can only beat “look at everything” if the data has structure that one comparison can exploit. Sorting is structure. The more a comparison tells you about the boxes you did not open, the fewer boxes you must open.

              Test yourself

              1. Why can no algorithm search an unsorted list of n numbers with fewer than n comparisons in the worst case? Which assumption of the argument fails when the list is sorted?

                Show the answer

                If an algorithm compared X with fewer than n elements, some box L[i] was never compared; put X in that box and the algorithm (which cannot see inside) gives the same, now wrong, answer. For a sorted list the assumption “skipping a box gives no information about it” fails: comparing with L[6] also tells you how X relates to L[1]…L[5].

              2. Jump search on n = 100 with k = 10: what is the worst-case number of comparisons? What about k = 1 and k = 100?

                Show the answer

                f(100, 10) = ⌊100/10⌋ + 10 − 1 = 10 + 9 = 19. For k = 1: 100 + 1 − 1 = 100 (plain linear search). For k = 100: 1 + 100 − 1 = 100 (look at L[100], then scan everything before it).

              3. Roughly which jump size is best, and what does it give for a list of a million numbers?

                Show the answer

                k ≈ √n, because nk and k have a fixed product and their sum is smallest when they are equal. For n = 1,000,000 that is k = 1000 and 1000 + 999 = 1999 comparisons.

              4. Run binary search by hand on L = [3, 8, 11, 15, 19, 22, 25] for X = 22. Which boxes are compared, and how many comparisons are used?

                Show the answer

                low = 1, high = 7: mid = 4, L[4] = 15 < 22, so low = 5. Then mid = ⌊(5+7)/2⌋ = 6, L[6] = 22 = X: found at position 6. 2 comparisons (boxes 4 and 6).

              5. How many comparisons does binary search need at most on 1000 numbers? Why does doubling the list add only one?

                Show the answer

                ⌊lg 1000⌋ + 1 = 9 + 1 = 10 (because 29 = 512 ≤ 1000 < 1024 = 210). After one comparison half of the list is gone, so a list twice as long needs just one extra comparison to get back down to the old size.

              6. Prove that ⌊⌊n/2⌋/2⌋ = ⌊n/4⌋, and say where this step is used.

                Show the answer

                Write n = 4q + r, 0 ≤ r ≤ 3. Then ⌊n/4⌋ = q, and ⌊n/2⌋ = 2q + ⌊r/2⌋ with ⌊r/2⌋ ∈ 0, 1, so ⌊⌊n/2⌋/2⌋ = q too. It is used when unwrapping f(n) = f(⌊n/2⌋) + 1 twice, to get f(⌊n/4⌋) + 2, and then generally f(⌊n/2i⌋) + i.

              7. Which is bigger for a successful search on a list of 1000 numbers, the worst case or the average case of binary search? Which for an unsuccessful search?

                Show the answer

                The worst case (10) is at least the average for a successful search (about 9, since most boxes are deep in the tree but not all of them). For an unsuccessful search the average is about the same as the worst case, since you always have to shrink the segment to nothing.

              8. Interpolation search on L = [10, 20, 30, …, 100] with X = 70: which box is probed first?

                Show the answer

                p = 70 − 10100 − 10 = 6090 ≈ 0.667, so pos = 1 + ⌊0.667 × (10 − 1)⌋ = 1 + 6 = 7. L[7] = 70: found with 1 comparison (binary search would need 4: boxes 5, 8, 6, 7).

              9. You have 500 floors and 10 eggs. What is the fewest tosses that can always find the critical floor, and with what strategy? What if you only had 2 eggs?

                Show the answer

                9 tosses: binary search on the floors. No strategy can do it in 8, because 8 tosses distinguish at most 28 = 256 < 500 cases. Binary search breaks at most 9 eggs, so 10 are enough. With only 2 eggs you must not break more than one before the last: jump search with k ≈ 22 uses at most 43 tosses (and shrinking jumps can get it down to 32).

              10. A sorted array is searched a million times a day and changes once a week. Another list receives 10 new items for every search. Which search method would you use for each, and why? What can a hash table not do that a sorted array can?

                Show the answer

                The first: binary search on a sorted array (many searches, lots of data, static). The second: linear search on an unsorted list, since inserting at the end is cheap while keeping an array sorted costs O(n) per insertion (or look at hashing or a search tree). A hash table cannot do range searches (all keys between two values) efficiently, because it scatters nearby keys over unrelated slots.

              PreviousChapter 5 · TreesNextChapter 7 · Binary search trees

              Slides 1–31 · 07_SEARTREE

              Binary Search Trees from Scratch

              How to keep a collection in sorted order and still add and remove things quickly. Binary search turned into a tree: search, smallest, successor, insert, delete, why the height is everything, and what goes wrong when the tree leans.

              In this chapter

                Part 1 · Slides 2–4

                From a sorted list to a tree

                Binary search, once more slide 2

                Chapter 6 gave us binary search: look at the middle element, and its answer throws half of the list away. It is fast (O(lg n)), but it has a catch you may have noticed: it needs a sorted array, because it must jump straight to the middle box.

                Now the slide asks: can we do binary search on a linked list? A linked list has no “box number 500”. To reach the middle you must walk there, one pointer at a time, which costs O(n) and ruins the whole idea.

                Picture it

                An array is a street where every house has a number, so you can drive straight to number 500. A linked list is a treasure hunt: each house only tells you where the next one is. To find the house in the middle you must follow the clues from the start.

                The slide’s fix: keep a pointer to the middle element. Then the first step of binary search is instant. But after the first step you are searching one half of the list, and that half needs a pointer to its middle too…

                Pointers to every middle slide 3

                Keep going: the whole list needs a pointer to d; the left half needs one to b; the right half one to f; the four single boxes a, c, e, g are their own middle. That is a lot of pointers. But look at what they form: d points to b and f; b points to a and c; f points to e and g. Why not store the pointers inside the nodes, and forget the list links altogether?

                That is a tree slide 4

                If we apply the idea of binary search to the sub-lists recursively, we get a tree: the root is the middle element, its left child is the middle of the left half, its right child the middle of the right half, and so on. The slide gives it a name: a binary search tree. Build one yourself:

                Turn a sorted list into a tree by taking middles

                What you just saw

                A search in this tree is binary search: start at the root (the middle), and at every node go left (smaller) or right (bigger). Each step discards about half of what is left. And unlike the array, the tree is made of pointers, so we can add and remove nodes without shifting anything. That is the whole attraction of this chapter.

                Part 2 · Slides 5–7

                What a binary search tree is

                What it can do, and what a node looks like slide 5

                A binary search tree supports these operations: search, minimum, maximum, predecessor, successor, insert and delete. The slide promises that all of them take O(lg n) time in the worst case if the tree is kept balanced. (That “if” matters a lot: it is the subject of the second half of this chapter and the whole of the next.)

                The slides assume that each node has four fields: the key (the thing we sort by), a pointer left to the left child, a pointer right to the right child, and a pointer parent to the node above (NULL for the root; a missing child is also a NULL pointer).

                The binary search tree property slide 6

                What makes it a search tree is one rule about where the keys sit. For simplicity the slides assume that all keys are different.

                The binary search tree property

                If x is a node, then x’s key is bigger than every key in x’s left subtree and smaller than every key in x’s right subtree.

                Here is the example tree of the next slide. Click a node and see its two subtrees:

                The property, node by node

                That the rule is about whole subtrees is the number-one trap with this chapter. It will come back in Example Question 1 at the end.

                Sorted order for free slide 7

                Q: Suppose I want to list the elements in increasing order of key values. Which tree traversal order shall I use?

                Think back to Chapter 5, then check

                Inorder: left subtree, then the node, then the right subtree. Everything in the left subtree is smaller than the node, and everything in the right subtree is bigger, so writing “left, node, right” produces the keys in increasing order. Try the other two orders in the box and see them fail.

                Which walk sorts the keys?

                So a binary search tree stores the keys sorted, and an inorder walk reads them out in O(n) time. Keep that in mind: it is the reason the tree can answer “what comes next?” questions.

                Part 3 · Slides 8–9

                Minimum, maximum and search

                The smallest key slide 8

                Where is the smallest key? Anything smaller than a node lives in its left subtree, so we keep going left until there is no left child. The last node is the minimum. The code assumes the tree is not empty and T points to its root:

                Tree_Minimum(T) {

                T is a pointer to the root. The tree must not be empty.

                x = T;

                start at the root.

                while (x->left != NULL)

                as long as x has a left child...

                x = x->left;

                ...step to it, because smaller keys are on the left.

                return(x);

                no left child left: nothing is smaller, so x holds the minimum.

                }

                the end of the procedure.

                The cost is the number of steps, at most the height h of the tree, so Tree_Minimum takes O(h) time. Tree_Maximum is the mirror image: keep going right.

                Searching slide 9

                Searching is binary search written on the tree. Compare the key we want with the key at x: equal means done, smaller means go left, bigger means go right. If we walk off the bottom (a NULL pointer), the key is not there.

                Tree_Search (T,k) {

                look for a node with key k in the tree whose root is T.

                x = T;

                start at the root.

                while (x != NULL) {

                keep going until we fall off the tree.

                case x->key {

                compare the key at x with k (three possible answers):

                > k : x = x->left;

                x’s key is bigger than k, so k, if it exists, is in the left subtree.

                = k: return (x);

                found it: return the node.

                < k: x = x->right;

                x’s key is smaller than k, so k can only be in the right subtree.

                }

                end of the case.

                }

                end of the while.

                return("not found!");

                we fell off the tree: the key is not in it.

                }

                end of the procedure.

                Run it, and the two siblings, Tree_Minimum and Tree_Maximum, on any tree you like (type your own keys: they are inserted from left to right):

                Search, minimum and maximum, step by step

                What does a search cost?

                Every step goes one level down, and the tree has h + 1 levels, so a search examines at most h + 1 nodes: it costs O(h). In a nicely balanced tree h is about lg n; in a badly shaped tree h can be as big as n − 1. The height is the only thing that matters, and Part 8 is about exactly that.

                Part 4 · Slide 10

                A theorem about subtrees

                What the slide says slide 10

                Let r be the root of the tree and x any node. Let T(x) be the subtree rooted at x (the node x and everything below it). The theorem on the slide reads:

                The theorem

                For every node m that is in the whole tree T(r) but not in T(x), and for every node y in T(x): either x and y are both smaller than m, or x and y are both bigger than m.

                In plain words: a key outside a subtree can never sit between two keys of that subtree. It is either below all of them or above all of them. Put differently, the keys of a subtree form one unbroken block in the sorted order. See it:

                A subtree is one block of the sorted order

                Why it is true slide 10

                Take an outside node m and look at the two paths from the root: one to m, one to x. They run together for a while and then split at some node a (or m is itself an ancestor of x). Only two things can happen:

                1. The paths split at a. One of them goes into a’s left subtree and the other into its right subtree. By the binary search property, everything in the left subtree is smaller than everything in the right subtree. So m is smaller than all of T(x) (if m went left), or bigger than all of it (if m went right). Done.
                2. m is an ancestor of x. Then T(x) lies completely inside one subtree of m, the left or the right. By the binary search property, that whole subtree is on one side of m. Done.

                Picture it

                Think of a shelf of books sorted by title. All the books in one section (a subtree) sit side by side. A book from another section cannot be wedged in the middle of this section, or the shelf would not be sorted.

                Why does the slide care? Because the next part uses it to prove that the rule for the successor gives the right answer: nothing can hide between a node and the key we pick.

                Part 5 · Slides 11–13

                Successor and predecessor

                What is a successor? slide 11

                The successor of a node x is the node with the smallest key that is bigger than x’s key: the next key in sorted order. (The predecessor is the previous one.) With a sorted array you would simply step to the next box. In a tree, “the next one” may be far away in the picture, so we need a rule.

                Q: which is x’s successor? If x has a right subtree TR, everything in it is bigger than x, and everything else bigger than x lies outside the subtree of x and is bigger than all of it. So the closest bigger key is the minimum of TR: step right once, then go left as far as you can.

                Q: what if TR is NULL? Then no bigger key is below x, so the successor must be an ancestor.

                Climbing up slide 12

                The rule on the slide: go up from x until you reach an ancestor a that is a left child. The successor of x is a’s parent. The slide shows it for 13 (its successor is 15): 7 is an ancestor of 13 but it is a right child, so we keep climbing; 6 is the first ancestor that is a left child, and its parent is 15.

                Why does that work? (The slide asks.)

                1. While we climb from a right child to its parent, the parent is smaller than what we came from. So none of those parents can be the answer, and x is the largest key in the subtree of the node a where we stop.
                2. a is a left child of its parent p. So all of a’s subtree, including x, is smaller than p. That makes p a bigger key.
                3. Could another key m sit between x and p? It is not in a’s subtree (x is the biggest there) and not in p’s right subtree (those keys exceed p). So m is outside the subtree of p, and by the theorem of slide 10 it is either below all of it or above all of it. But m < p, so below all of it, so m < x: a contradiction. Nothing sits between, and p is the successor.

                If we reach the root without ever coming from a left child, there is no parent left (y becomes NULL): x was the biggest key in the whole tree, and it has no successor.

                The code slide 13

                Tree_Successor(x) {

                find the node with the next bigger key after x.

                if (x->right != NULL)

                case 1: x has a right subtree.

                return(Tree_Minimum(x->right));

                the answer is the minimum of that subtree.

                y = x->parent;

                case 2: no right subtree. Look at the parent.

                while ((y!= NULL) &&

                keep climbing while there is a parent...

                (x == y->right)) {

                ...and we came up from its right child.

                x = y;

                move up one level.

                y = y->parent;

                and look at the next parent.

                }

                end of the loop.

                return(y);

                we stopped because we came from a left child (then y is the successor), or because y is NULL (no successor).

                }

                end of the procedure.

                Successor (and predecessor) of a node

                Costs so far

                Search, minimum, maximum and successor are all O(h) (slide 13): each one goes down the tree once or up the tree once, and never visits more than one node per level. The predecessor is the same algorithm with left and right swapped (switch the box above to “Predecessor”).

                Part 6 · Slides 14–15

                Insertion

                Pretend it is already there slide 14

                To insert a new node z, the slide gives a lovely trick: pretend that z is already in the tree, and “look for it”. The search follows the usual left/right decisions down the tree. Sooner or later it runs into a NULL pointer: that is exactly the place where z would have been, so we replace the NULL by a pointer to z.

                The slide inserts 13 into a tree with 12 at the root: 13 ≥ 12, go right to 18; 13 < 18, go left to 15; 13 < 15, go left: NULL. Here is where 13 hangs.

                The code slide 15

                Tree_Insert(T,z) {

                insert the new node z (its key is already filled in) into the tree with root T.

                y = NULL; /* y, if non-null, is the parent of x */

                y will always be one step behind x: the parent of the place we are looking at.

                x = T;

                start at the root.

                while (x != NULL) {

                walk down, exactly as in a search for z->key:

                y = x;

                remember where we are,

                if (z->key < x->key) x = x->left;

                smaller: go left,

                else x= x->right;

                otherwise go right.

                }

                now x is NULL: we found the empty place. Its parent is y.

                z->parent = y;

                z hangs below y...

                z->left = z->right = NULL;

                ...as a leaf: no children yet.

                if (y == NULL) T = z;
