                y is still NULL, so the tree was empty: z becomes the root. (In C, T is passed by reference, so that this assignment changes the caller’s own root pointer.)

                else if (z->key < y->key)

                otherwise decide on which side of y z belongs:

                y->left = z;

                smaller than y: the left slot...

                else

                ...

                y->right = z;

                ...bigger: the right slot.

                }

                end of the procedure.

                Insert a key, step by step

                Two facts to remember

                A new node is always a leaf: insertion never moves an existing node, so the sorted order of the old keys is untouched. The cost is one walk down: at most h + 1 comparisons, so insertion is O(h) too. And since all keys are assumed different, the else branch only meets keys that are strictly bigger.

                Part 7 · Slides 16–19

                Deletion

                Three cases slide 16

                Deleting is harder than inserting, because the node we remove may have children that must not be lost. The slide splits the job into three cases, by the number of children of the node z being deleted:

                1. Case 1: z has no children. Just remove it: set the pointer that led to z to NULL.
                2. Case 2: z has one child. “Splice out” z: link z’s parent directly to z’s child, skipping z (like removing one link from a chain).
                3. Case 3: z has two children. We cannot simply cut z out (two children, one parent slot). Instead replace z by its immediate successor y: copy y’s key into z, then splice out y.

                The pictures slide 17

                Slide 17 shows the three cases on one tree (the red node is the one removed from the picture):

                Why the successor? It is the one key we can put in z’s place without breaking the search tree property. It is bigger than everything in z’s left subtree, and smaller than everything else in z’s right subtree (it is the minimum of it). And by being a minimum, it has no left child, so it is easy to cut out. (The predecessor would work just as well, as the mirror image.)

                The code slides 18–19

                Careful reading: the variable y is the node that is really cut out of the tree. In cases 1 and 2 that is z itself; in case 3 it is the successor.

                Tree_Delete(T,z) {

                delete node z from the tree with root T.

                if ((z->left == NULL) ||

                if z has no left child...

                (z->right == NULL))

                ...or no right child, it has at most one child (cases 1 and 2):

                y = z; /* y is the node to be spliced out */

                z itself is cut out.

                else {

                z has two children (case 3):

                y = Tree_Minimum(z->right);

                y is z’s successor...

                z->key = y->key; /* copy other fields too */

                ...whose key (and any other data) is copied into z. Now y is the node to cut out.

                }

                end of the else.

                /* y must have a NULL left, or a NULL right. Why? */

                the slide asks why. Answer: in cases 1 and 2, because that is how we got here; in case 3, because y is a minimum, so it has no left child.

                if (y->left != NULL)

                first find the child of y that must survive, and call it x...

                x = y->left;

                ...the left one if there is one,

                else

                ...

                x = y->right;

                ...otherwise the right one (it may be NULL if y is a leaf).

                if (x != NULL) x->parent = y->parent;

                not on the slide (it is in the book): the surviving child must now point to its new parent.

                if (y->parent == NULL)

                does y have a parent?

                T = x;

                no: y was the root, so x becomes the root.

                else {

                yes: put x where y was, on the correct side.

                if (y->parent->left == y)

                was y a left child?

                y->parent->left = x;

                then x becomes that left child,

                else

                ...

                y->parent->right = x;

                otherwise the right child.

                }

                end of the else.

                /* return y, or free y, .... */

                the node y is now out of the tree; return it or free its memory.

                }

                end of the procedure.

                A slip on slides 18 and 19

                The code on the slides never sets x->parent. After splicing, the surviving child x would still believe its parent is the deleted node y. The slides’ Tree_Successor climbs parent pointers, so a later call could go wrong. The one extra line in the box above (which the book has) repairs it, and the demo below uses it.

                Delete a node, case by case

                Try the three cases on the slide-17 tree: delete 13 (case 1), 16 (case 2), 5 (case 3), and then the root 15. Switch the last box to “predecessor” to see the mirror-image version. The cost: the walk to find z, plus the walk down to y, plus a constant amount of pointer changes: O(h).

                Part 8 · Slides 20–22

                How tall can the tree get?

                Everything costs O(h) slides 20–21

                Every operation you have seen (search, minimum, maximum, successor, insert, delete) goes down or up the tree once. So the cost of all of them is O(h), where h is the height of the tree. The slide asks: what are the best, worst and average values of h?

                • Best case: h = ⌊lg n⌋. This happens for a well-balanced tree (the slide’s example: remove the leaves and what is left is a complete binary tree). No binary tree with n nodes is shorter, because a tree of height h has at most 2h+1 − 1 nodes (Chapter 5).
                • Worst case: h = n − 1. The tree has “degenerated into a list”: every node has one child. Then every operation is as slow as walking down a linked list: O(n).

                The same keys, different shapes slide 22

                The slide’s key observation: the height of a binary search tree depends on the sequence of insertions (and deletions), not only on which keys it holds. Insert the keys 1 to 15 in increasing order and every new key is the biggest so far, so it goes to the right of the last one: a list of height 14. Insert them in the order 8, 4, 12, 2, 6, … (the middle first) and you get a perfect tree of height 3. Try it:

                The same keys, inserted in different orders

                Picture it

                Building a search tree from a sorted list by inserting one key after another is the worst thing you can do: it gives a stick, not a tree. Sorted data is the unluckiest input of all for a plain binary search tree.

                The slide then asks about the average height. That needs a model of “average”, and the next part supplies one. (The slide adds that once random deletions are allowed the analysis is difficult, so it first sticks to random insertions only.)

                Part 9 · Slides 23–25

                Randomly built trees

                What does “average” mean here? slide 23

                The worst case is a list and the best case is a perfect tree. Which one should we expect? The slide defines a model: a randomly built binary search tree on n keys is the tree you get by inserting the n keys in a random order into an empty tree.

                The slide’s question: how many different sequences of insertions are there? Any of the n keys can come first, then any of the remaining n − 1, and so on: n!, and each is equally likely. The key fact is that different orders can build the very same tree. For example, 2, 1, 3 and 2, 3, 1 both give the tree with 2 on top. So the n! orders share out among far fewer trees, and some trees are far more popular than others. Count them:

                Build the tree for every possible order

                What you should notice

                For 5 keys: 120 orders but only 42 different trees (that is the Catalan number of Chapter 5). The “list” shape appears for only 2n−1 orders (for 5 keys, 16 of 120 orders), while the middle heights hold most of the orders. A “bad” tree is easy to describe but rare to draw by chance.

                The average height is O(lg n) slides 24–25

                Slide 24 states the result: the average height of a randomly built binary search tree with n nodes is O(lg n), so all the operations (search, insert, delete, …) have average cost O(lg n) on such trees. The slide does not prove it, and neither will we. (The proof is a known result about the shape of random trees; it uses the same idea as quicksort: the first key is a random pivot that splits the others into a left and a right part.) Slide 25 shows a graph of experiments, so let us run the experiment ourselves:

                Random trees: how tall do they grow?

                Two numbers are worth remembering. The average depth of a node in a random tree (which is what the cost of a successful search measures) is exactly 2(n+1)Hn/n − 4, where Hn = 1 + 12 + 13 + … + 1n is the harmonic number. That is about 2 ln n ≈ 1.39 lg n, only 39% more than the perfect tree. The height (the deepest node) is larger, roughly twice lg n for the sizes in the demo (and a little more for bigger n), but it still grows like lg n: ten times more keys add only a few levels.

                Picture it

                “On average” applies only if the insertion order is random. If your data arrives sorted (names in order, ids counting up, timestamps) your tree is a list, however good the theory sounds. That is why the next chapter makes the tree repair itself.

                Part 10 · Slides 26–27

                Deletion makes the tree lean

                The catch slide 26

                The “random tree” result only covers insertions. The slide warns: once deletions are included, the average cost may no longer be O(lg n). Our deletion algorithm “favors making the left subtrees deeper than the right”. The slide asks: why?

                Answer. Look at case 3 of the delete code again. A node with two children is always replaced by its successor, and the successor is taken from the right subtree. So deletions keep removing nodes from right subtrees, while insertions put new nodes on both sides at random. Over a long mixed run of deletions and insertions the right subtrees become smaller and shallower than the left ones, and the whole tree leans to the left (slide 27 shows such a lopsided tree).

                Watch it happen slide 27

                The demo builds a random tree, then repeats: delete a random key, then insert a brand-new random key. The tree always has the same number of keys. It tries three delete rules and averages six runs of each:

                Many deletions and insertions

                How to repair it slide 26

                The slide also asks: how would you modify delete to make the tree “more balanced”?

                1. Be fair between the two sides. Use the successor sometimes and the predecessor sometimes: alternate, or toss a coin each time. Now both subtrees lose nodes at the same rate and the lean goes away (compare the second and third cards in the demo).
                2. Choose the larger side. Take the replacement from whichever subtree of z is taller or has more nodes. That needs the heights or sizes stored in each node.
                3. Stop relying on luck. No delete rule can protect against a sorted insertion order, and the fair rules above are only observed to work on random data. A tree that guarantees its height is the cure, which is the subject of the next chapter: the AVL tree rotates nodes after every insertion or deletion so that the height stays O(lg n) whatever the order of the operations.

                Be careful what you conclude

                The demo uses small trees and short runs. It shows that the plain rule leans and that the fair rules help here. It does not prove that the fair rules stay good forever (long-run behaviour of search trees under updates is a subtle research topic). The only fully safe answer is a tree that rebalances itself.

                Part 11 · Slides 28–30

                Three example questions

                The deck ends with three questions that are typical exam material. Each has a short, elegant answer. For each one: first try yourself, then read.

                Question 1: is this binary tree a search tree? slide 28

                Given a binary tree, give an algorithm to check whether it is a binary search tree.

                The tempting wrong answer: “at every node, check that the left child is smaller and the right child is bigger”. It is wrong, because the rule is about whole subtrees, not just children. A tree where a node deep in the left subtree of 10 holds the key 12 passes the child-by-child test everywhere, yet it is not a search tree (the search for 12 would never look there).

                The right answer, idea 1: pass down an allowed range. The root may hold any key. Going left from a node with key k, every key must be below k (and still above the old lower limit); going right, every key must be above k. The code is short:

                bool IsBST(Node *x, int lo, int hi) {

                is the subtree at x a search tree whose keys all lie strictly between lo and hi?

                if (x == NULL) return true;

                an empty tree is fine.

                if (x->key <= lo || x->key >= hi)

                the key is outside the allowed range...

                return false;

                ...so the tree is not a search tree.

                return IsBST(x->left, lo, x->key) &&

                everything on the left must be below x->key (the lower limit is unchanged)...

                IsBST(x->right, x->key, hi);

                ...and everything on the right must be above x->key.

                }

                end.

                /* first call: IsBST(T, -INF, +INF) */

                at the start there is no limit at all.

                The right answer, idea 2: do an in-order traversal and check that the keys come out in strictly increasing order (keep the previous key in a variable). This works because of the central fact of the chapter (slide 6): the in-order walk of a search tree is sorted. Both ways take O(n) time: every node is looked at once.

                Spot the fake search tree

                Question 2: from a sorted array to a balanced tree slide 29

                Given an array A[0..n−1] of elements in sorted order, convert it to a balanced binary search tree.

                This is exactly the “binary search” picture of the start of the chapter, run in reverse. Make the middle element the root. The elements on its left in the array make the left subtree, the elements on its right make the right subtree, each built the same way, by recursion:

                Node* ArrayToBST(int A[], int lo, int hi) {

                build a balanced tree from the part A[lo..hi].

                if (lo > hi) return NULL;

                nothing left: an empty tree.

                int mid = (lo + hi) / 2;

                the middle box (rounded down).

                Node *x = NewNode(A[mid]);

                it becomes the root of this subtree.

                x->left = ArrayToBST(A, lo, mid - 1);

                everything to its left becomes the left subtree...

                x->right = ArrayToBST(A, mid + 1, hi);

                ...everything to its right becomes the right subtree.

                return x;

                hand back the root.

                }

                end.

                /* call: ArrayToBST(A, 0, n - 1) */

                the whole array.

                Every element is used exactly once, so the time is O(n). The two halves differ in size by at most 1 element, so the height is ⌊lg n⌋, the best possible. Press “play” in this demo (it is the first demo of the chapter again) to watch the tree grow from the middle outwards.

                Sorted array to balanced tree

                Question 3: from a sorted linked list to a balanced tree slide 30

                Given a linked list of elements in sorted order, convert it to a balanced binary search tree. Try to use as little extra space as possible.

                Now we cannot jump to the middle: finding the middle of a list means walking there. That is the problem the chapter started with (slides 2–3). There are three ways, and they trade time against space:

                MethodIdeaTimeExtra space
                A. Copy to an arraycopy the list into an array (O(n)), then use ArrayToBSTO(n)O(n) for the array
                B. Find the middle each timewalk to the middle of the list (slow and fast pointers), make it the root, repeat on each halfO(n lg n) (about n/2 steps per level, lg n levels)O(lg n) (the recursion)
                C. Build in list order (in-order simulation)build the left subtree first, then take the next list element as the root, then build the right subtree: the list is consumed from front to back, exactly as an in-order walk would visit itO(n)O(lg n) (the recursion)

                Method C is the best on both counts. It works because of the same fact as before: in-order = sorted order = the list. We know the size of the tree to build, so we know how many nodes belong to the left subtree; we build that many, and the list pointer has moved to exactly the root’s element.

                Node *head; /* the next list element to use */

                a global (or shared) pointer into the list; at the start it points at the first node.

                Node* Build(int n) {

                build a balanced tree from the next n elements of the list.

                if (n <= 0) return NULL;

                nothing to build.

                Node *left = Build(n / 2);

                the first n/2 elements make the left subtree. This uses them up, so head moves forward.

                Node *root = NewNode(head->key);

                now head is exactly the middle element: it is the root.

                head = head->next;

                consume it.

                root->left = left;

                attach the left subtree...

                root->right = Build(n - n / 2 - 1);

                ...and build the right subtree from all the elements that are left.

                return root;

                done.

                }

                end.

                /* call: T = Build(length_of_list); */

                we need the length once: one pass, O(n), no extra space.

                Sorted list to tree, using the list once

                Why the extra space is only lg n

                Method C uses no array and no copies: the only memory besides the new tree nodes is the call stack of Build, which is as deep as the tree is high, ⌊lg n⌋ + 1 calls. The tree nodes themselves are the answer, not “extra” space.

                Part 12 · Slide 31

                Summary and self-test

                The chapter on one page slide 31

                The conclusion slide says: a binary search tree stores ordered elements, with O(lg n) time if balanced. The “if” is the whole story of the next chapter.

                IdeaIn one line
                Why a treebinary search needs a pointer to the middle; a tree is the middle pointers, drawn as a structure (left < node < right)
                The ruleat every node: all keys in the left subtree are smaller, all keys in the right subtree are bigger (whole subtrees, not just children)
                In-order walkvisits the keys in sorted order, O(n); this is the property to use
                Search / min / maxgo left or right by comparing; min = keep going left, max = keep going right; O(h)
                Successorright subtree non-empty: its minimum. Otherwise climb until you come up from a left child: that parent. O(h)
                Insertsearch for the key; the NULL where the search ends is where the new leaf goes; O(h)
                Delete0 children: remove; 1 child: splice out; 2 children: copy the successor’s key into z and splice the successor out; O(h)
                Heightbest ⌊lg n⌋, worst n − 1 (a list, e.g. sorted insertion), depends on the order of operations
                Random treesn! orders, average height O(lg n); but always taking the successor makes the tree lean left after many deletions
                Check for BSTpass down a (lo, hi) range, or check that the in-order keys increase; O(n)
                Sorted data to treearray: middle is the root, recurse, O(n). List: build the left part, take the next element as root, build the right part: O(n) time, O(lg n) space

                The theme of the chapter

                A binary search tree turns “sorted order” into shape. Every operation follows one path from the root, so it costs the height. Everything depends on keeping the height small, and a plain search tree has no way to guarantee it.

                Test yourself

                1. Insert the keys 8, 3, 10, 1, 6, 14, 4, 7, 13 (in that order) into an empty search tree. What is the height? What does the in-order traversal print?

                  Show the answer

                  8 is the root; 3 left, 10 right; 1 left of 3, 6 right of 3, 14 right of 10; 4 goes left of 6, 7 right of 6, 13 left of 14. The deepest keys (4, 7, 13) are at depth 3, so the height is 3. In-order: 1 3 4 6 7 8 10 13 14 (sorted, of course).

                2. In the tree built on slide 7 (insert 15, 6, 18, 3, 7, 17, 20, 2, 4, 13, 9 in that order) find the successor of 13 and the predecessor of 15.

                  Show the answer

                  13 has no right child (its only child is 9, on the left), so climb: 13 is the right child of 7, 7 is the right child of 6, 6 is the left child of 15. The first left-child step ends at the parent 15, which is the successor of 13. The predecessor of 15 is the maximum of its left subtree: 6, then right to 7, then right to 13: 13.

                3. Delete the root 15 from the same tree with the slide’s algorithm. Which key is the new root, and which node is really cut out?

                  Show the answer

                  The root has two children, so we find its successor: the minimum of the right subtree. From 18 go left to 17, which has no left child: 17 is the successor. Its key is copied into the root, so the new root is 17. The node that is cut out is the old node of 17, a leaf, so the left pointer of 18 becomes NULL.

                4. Why can the node y that Tree_Delete cuts out never have two children?

                  Show the answer

                  If z has at most one child, y is z. If z has two children, y is the minimum of z’s right subtree, and a minimum has no left child (otherwise that left child would be smaller). In both cases y has at most one child, and splicing it out is easy.

                5. Why must a search tree be checked with whole subtrees (a range), not just parent and child?

                  Show the answer

                  The search property is about every key in a subtree, not only the nearest ones. Example: root 10, left child 5, and 5’s right child 12. Every parent-child pair is fine (5 < 10, 12 > 5), yet 12 sits in the left subtree of 10, so a search for 12 starts at 10, goes right and never finds it.

                6. You insert 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7 in this order. What is the height? In what order should you insert them to get the shortest possible tree?

                  Show the answer

                  Each key is the biggest so far and goes to the right of the previous one: a list of height 6 (= n − 1). For the best tree (height 2) insert the middle first, then the middle of each half: for example 4, 2, 6, 1, 3, 5, 7.

                7. How many different insertion orders are there for 5 keys, and how many different trees do they make?

                  Show the answer

                  5! = 120 orders, which produce only 42 different trees (the Catalan number C5), because different orders can build the same tree. For example, in 2, 1, 3 and 2, 3, 1 the root is always 2.

                8. What are the best and worst heights of a search tree with 1000 keys? Which operations get slow in the worst case?

                  Show the answer

                  Best: ⌊lg 1000⌋ = 9. Worst: 1000 − 1 = 999. Search, minimum, maximum, successor, insertion and deletion all cost O(h), so all of them go from about 10 steps to about 1000.

                9. Why does the deletion algorithm of the slides make the tree lean to the left after many updates? Name two fixes.

                  Show the answer

                  A node with two children is always replaced by its successor, which comes from the right subtree, so right subtrees keep losing nodes while insertions add to both sides. Fixes: alternate (or randomly choose) between successor and predecessor; or use a tree that rebalances itself (AVL, next chapter).

                10. Turn the sorted array [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7] into a balanced search tree with ArrayToBST. Which key is the root, and what is the shape of the tree? Why is converting a sorted linked list harder, and how can it still be done in O(n) time and O(lg n) extra space?

                  Show the answer

                  The middle A[3] = 4 is the root; the left half [1, 2, 3] gives root 2 with children 1 and 3; the right half [5, 6, 7] gives root 6 with children 5 and 7: a perfect tree of height 2. In a list you cannot jump to the middle (you must walk), so repeated “find the middle” costs O(n lg n). Instead build the tree in in-order: build the left subtree, take the next list element as the root, then build the right subtree. The list is read once from front to back, and only the recursion stack (⌊lg n⌋ + 1 deep) is extra.

                PreviousChapter 6 · SearchingNextChapter 8 · Balanced trees

                Slides 1–37 · 08_BALTREE

                Balanced Trees from Scratch

                How to make a search tree repair itself so it can never become a stick: the AVL rule, why it keeps the height near lg n, the rotation that fixes one broken node, the double rotation for the tricky case, and insertion and deletion in O(lg n).

                In this chapter

                  Part 1 · Slide 2

                  Why balance a tree?

                  The problem we left open slide 2

                  Chapter 7 ended with an uncomfortable fact. A binary search tree is fast only if it is balanced. With random insertions and no deletions the average search time is O(lg n), but the worst case is still O(n): insert sorted data and the tree becomes a list.

                  The slide states the cure in two lines. To get a better worst case, limit the height. Make the tree as balanced as possible. Everything in this chapter is one idea: after every insertion or deletion, check whether the tree has become too lopsided, and repair it right away, before the damage can pile up.

                  Picture it

                  Think of a shopkeeper who sorts the shelf as items arrive. The plain search tree is a shopkeeper who dumps everything on the nearest free spot and hopes for the best. The AVL tree is one who re-tidies a few items each time. It costs a little work per item, and the shop never turns into one long corridor.

                  What we will need

                  1. A precise rule for “balanced enough” that is cheap to check (the AVL rule, slide 3).
                  2. A proof that the rule really keeps the height small, about 1.44 lg n at worst (slides 4–7).
                  3. A repair move that does not break the search tree property: the rotation (slides 8–11), plus its double version (slides 17–24).
                  4. Insertion and deletion that use the repair move on the way back up (slides 25–36), in O(lg n) time.

                  Part 2 · Slide 3

                  The AVL rule

                  Definition slide 3

                  AVL tree

                  An AVL tree is a binary search tree in which, for every node, the heights of its left and right subtrees differ by at most 1. The height of a null (empty) tree is −1.

                  (AVL stands for the two people who invented it, Adelson-Velsky and Landis, in 1962.) Two things to notice:

                  • “For every node”. Not only the root. A tree whose root is balanced but whose bottom is a stick is not an AVL tree. (It is the same lesson as the search tree property of Chapter 7: the rule must hold everywhere.)
                  • The empty tree has height −1, so that a node with one child (height 0) and one empty side (height −1) is fine: they differ by 1. But a node whose only child has children of its own breaks the rule: that side has height 1, the empty side −1, a difference of 2.

                  Each node gets a balance: (height of left subtree) − (height of right subtree). The AVL rule says every balance must be −1, 0 or +1. The slide asks which of its two trees is an AVL tree. Try it, and then try your own:

                  Is this an AVL tree?

                  Answer to slide 3

                  The first tree is an AVL tree (every balance is −1, 0 or +1). The second is not: the root 6 has a left subtree of height 2 (under 2) and a right subtree of height 0 (just 9), a difference of 2. Notice that this second tree is almost fine; one node breaks the rule, and that is the node we will repair with a rotation.

                  Part 3 · Slides 4–7

                  How tall can an AVL tree be?

                  The claim slide 4

                  The AVL rule is only useful if it forces the height to be small. The slide gives the answer: the maximum height of an AVL tree with n nodes is about 1.44 lg(n+1) − 1.283, which is O(lg n). For example, with n = 2000 nodes the height is at most 14. (“For your interest”: in practice the average height is smaller, about lg(n+1) + 0.25, that is 11 or 12 for 2000 nodes. We measure this in Part 10.)

                  So an AVL tree is never more than about 44% taller than a perfect tree. Compare the plain search tree, which can reach height n − 1 = 1999. Now we prove it.

                  The idea of the proof slide 5

                  Instead of asking “how tall can a tree with n nodes be?”, turn the question around: how few nodes can an AVL tree of height h have? If even the thinnest AVL tree of height h needs many nodes, then with only n nodes you cannot reach a big h.

                  The thinnest AVL tree of height h has a root with one subtree of height h − 1 (to make the height h) and, to save nodes, the shortest allowed other subtree: height h − 2. And each of those subtrees is again the thinnest possible. Here they are for h = 0 to 4 (root orange, the taller subtree blue, the shorter green):

                  Let F(h) be the fewest nodes in an AVL tree of height h. The pictures show that

                  F(0) = 1, F(1) = 2, F(h) = 1 + F(h−1) + F(h−2) for h ≥ 2.

                  (The slide writes “≥” instead of “=”, because it proves a lower bound for every AVL tree, not just the thinnest one.) This looks like the Fibonacci numbers (1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, … each the sum of the two before it), and that is no accident. Try some values of n:

                  How tall can an AVL tree with n nodes be?

                  Proof of (a): at least F(h) nodes slide 6

                  Claim: every AVL tree of height h has at least F(h) nodes. Proof by induction on h.

                  1. Two facts about any AVL tree T. (1) Both subtrees of the root, TL and TR, are themselves AVL trees (the rule holds at every node, so it holds inside them). (2) If T has height h, then one subtree has height h − 1 and the other has height h − 1 or h − 2 (the root adds 1 to the taller one, and the rule limits the difference to 1).
                  2. Base cases. h = 0: the tree is a single node, F(0) = 1. h = 1: at least a root and one child, F(1) = 2.
                  3. Induction step. Let T have height h ≥ 2. By fact (2) say TL has height h − 1 and TR has height at least h − 2. By fact (1) and the induction hypothesis, TL has at least F(h − 1) nodes and TR at least F(h − 2). Adding the root: T has at least 1 + F(h − 1) + F(h − 2) nodes. That is F(h). ■

                  Proof of (b): F(h) is at least φh slide 7

                  Let φ = 1 + √52 ≈ 1.618, the golden ratio. The key property of φ is φ2 = φ + 1 (check: 1.618² = 2.618). Claim: F(h) ≥ φh. Induction:

                  • Base: F(0) = 1 = φ0 and F(1) = 2 ≥ 1.618 = φ1.
                  • Step: F(h) ≥ F(h−1) + F(h−2) ≥ φh−1 + φh−2 = φh−2(φ + 1) = φh−2 φ2 = φh.

                  Putting it together slide 7

                  If an AVL tree of height h has n nodes, then by (a) and (b)

                  n ≥ F(h) ≥ φh so lg n ≥ h lg φ so h ≤ lg nlg φ ≈ 1.44 lg n.

                  (lg φ ≈ 0.694 and 1 / 0.694 ≈ 1.44, which is where the slide’s 1.44 comes from.) So h = O(lg n). The slide also shows a looser but simpler bound that avoids φ altogether: n ≥ F(h) ≥ 2F(h−2) ≥ 4F(h−4) ≥ … ≥ 2h/2 (because F is increasing, F(h) > 2F(h − 2)), which gives h ≤ 2 lg n. Both say the same thing: the height is logarithmic.

                  A footnote on slide 4

                  The slide quotes the exact bound as 1.44 lg(n+1) − 1.283. That is a rounded version of the true expression: the exact maximum height is the largest h with F(h) ≤ n (the demo above computes it). For n = 2 the slide’s formula gives 0.999 while the true maximum height is 1, so the constants are rounded. Nothing else depends on the exact constants: what matters is O(lg n).

                  Part 4 · Slides 8–11

                  Rotations

                  Searching is easy, inserting is the problem slide 8

                  Since the height is O(lg n), searching an AVL tree takes O(lg n) time even in the worst case: it is the ordinary search of Chapter 7. The trouble is that insert and delete must be modified so that the AVL rule keeps holding.

                  The slide shows an example. Take the AVL tree 6 → (2 → (1, 4 → 3), 9) and insert 7. The key goes 6 → 9 → (left) 8 → (left) 7. Now node 9 has a left subtree of height 1 (8 with its child 7) and an empty right subtree (height −1): a difference of 2, so the rule is broken at 9. The fix on the slide is “right rotate at 9”: 8 becomes the parent, with 7 and 9 as its children. What is a rotation?

                  What a rotation is slides 9–11

                  A rotation on two nodes k2 and k1 (parent and child) reverses their parent-child relation. It changes the shape of the tree, but the search tree property is preserved. Here is the general picture (the triangles X, Y, Z are whole subtrees, of any size):

                  1. Right rotation (slide 10). k2’s left child k1 becomes the parent; k2 becomes k1’s right child. The subtree Y (which sat between them) is handed from k1 to k2. The left side gets shorter (X goes up one level), the right side taller (Z goes down one level).
                  2. Left rotation (slide 11). The mirror image: the right child comes up, the left side gets taller, the right side shorter.

                  Why is the search tree property preserved? Read the keys left to right: in both pictures the order is X, k1, Y, k2, Z. A rotation only changes how the tree is bracketed, never the sorted order, and the sorted order (the in-order list) is exactly what the search tree property says. Check it yourself: rotate any node in the demo and watch that the sorted strip does not change.

                  Rotate a node

                  Why rotations are useful

                  A rotation takes constant time: only a handful of pointers change (slides 32–33). And it moves one whole subtree up and another down, which changes heights, so it is exactly the tool to make a lopsided tree more balanced.

                  Which rotation? slide 12

                  The slide asks: which rotation do you do if the left subtree is taller than the right? Answer: a right rotation. It brings the (taller) left child up and sends the (shorter) right side down, evening things out. For a right subtree that is too tall, use a left rotation.

                  Part 5 · Slides 13–16

                  The simple cases

                  Three nodes slide 13

                  Start with the smallest trees that can break the rule: three keys. Insert 3, then 2, then 1: every new key goes to the left of the previous one, so we get a chain 3 → 2 → 1 (a stick). The root 3 has left height 1 and right height −1: broken. A right rotation at 3 brings 2 to the top with 1 and 3 as children: perfectly balanced.

                  Now insert 3, then 1, then 2. The root 3 has left child 1, which has a right child 2. Again the rule is broken at 3, so try the same cure, a right rotation at 3. The slide’s picture ends with “Oops!”: the result is 1 → (empty, 3 → (2, empty)): still a stick. The simple cure works on one shape and fails on the other. We will see why in Part 6.

                  Example 1: insertion into a bigger tree slide 14

                  The slide uses the tree 8 → (5 → (3, –), 60 → (45, 70)).

                  • Insert 7. 7 goes under 5 (to its right). Every node still satisfies the rule: “Still an AVL tree, so no rebalancing is needed.”
                  • Insert 1 (into the original tree). 1 goes under 3. Now node 5 has a left subtree of height 1 (3 with its child 1) and an empty right subtree (height −1): the slide writes these two numbers, 1 and −1, next to the node. They differ by 2, so the rule breaks at 5. A right rotation at 5 brings 3 to the top: 3 now has children 1 and 5. Note (the slide’s remarks): the parent-child relation of 3 and 5 is reversed and the search tree property is preserved.

                  More examples slides 15–16

                  Slide 15 repeats the lesson with 25 → 20 → 15 (a stick, cured by a right rotation at 25) and then shows 25 → 20 → 22 where the same cure fails: the 22 just moves from one side to the other. A bigger version of the same trouble is also shown. Slide 16 is the mirror image: 25 → 30 → 35 (a stick to the right, cured by a left rotation) and 25 → 30 → 27 (where it fails).

                  Shape of the 3 nodesWhich side is too tallWhere is the long branchCure
                  25 → 20 → 15leftstraight down the left (outside)one right rotation at 25
                  25 → 30 → 35rightstraight down the right (outside)one left rotation at 25
                  25 → 20 → 22leftleft, then right (a bend, inside)single rotation fails (slide 15)
                  25 → 30 → 27rightright, then left (a bend, inside)single rotation fails (slide 16)

                  So there are four ways for a node to become too tall, and two of them (the straight ones) are easy. The other two (the bends) are the subject of the next part.

                  Part 6 · Slides 17–24

                  When one rotation is not enough

                  Why a single rotation fails slides 17–18

                  Suppose the tree below k2 has its left subtree more than one level taller than its right one. Slides 17 and 18 find the core of the problem: the subtree Y, whose keys lie between the two nodes under rotation (k1 and k2), is taller than its sibling X. A rotation can only raise X and lower Z. It hands Y over to the other node but cannot lift it. If Y is the tall one, the problem simply moves:

                  The fix: rotate twice slide 19

                  The slide’s idea: use a rotation to solve the problem. First do a rotation that makes Y an outside subtree. Rotate the tree at k1 upon k1 and the root of Y (a left rotation at k1). Now the tall branch runs straight down the left side, which is the easy case, and a right rotation at k2 finishes the job. Two rotations in a row: a double rotation.

                  Slide 20 does it on the smallest example: 3 → 1 → 2. Left rotation at 1 gives the stick 3 → 2 → 1, right rotation at 3 gives 2 with children 1 and 3. Slide 21 names it the left-right double rotation (left rotation at the child, then right rotation at the parent) and shows the mirror image, the right-left double rotation (slide 22): 25 → 30 → 27, right rotation at 30, left rotation at 25, giving 27 with children 25 and 30.

                  Single rotation versus double rotation

                  The demo contains the trees of slides 15, 16, 21 and 22 (the four trees under “Do you know how to balance the following cases?”). Pick one, watch the single rotation fail on the bent cases, and then the double rotation succeed. Answers for slide 22, left to right: left-right (23 inside), left-right (21 inside), right-left (29 inside), right-left (33 inside). In each case the final subtree root is the middle one of the three nodes: 22, 22, 30 and 30.

                  The general form slides 23–24

                  Slides 23 and 24 draw the double rotation with whole subtrees. The nodes are labelled so that A is the middle key of the three (the one that ends up on top), and T1 to T4 are the subtrees in sorted order. Left-right: C is out of balance, its left child B leans to the right, to A.

                  The four cases, in one sentence each

                  Look at the taller child of the broken node, and at which of its two subtrees is taller. Outside heavy (left-left or right-right): one rotation at the broken node. Inside heavy (left-right or right-left): two rotations, first at the child (to make it an outside case) and then at the broken node.

                  Part 7 · Slides 25–30

                  Insertion, the whole algorithm

                  Which nodes can break? slides 25–26

                  Before the insertion the tree was an AVL tree. A new node only changes the height of the nodes on the way from it up to the root: nothing else sees it. So only the ancestors of the newly inserted node can have their balance condition violated (slide 26), and we only have to look at them.

                  The algorithm slide 27

                  1. Insert as in an ordinary search tree (Chapter 7): follow the search path, hang the new node as a leaf.
                  2. Go from the inserted node up to the root through the parent pointers, updating the height of every node on the way: height = 1 + max(height of left, height of right).
                  3. If a node on the path violates the AVL rule, perform a rotation (single or double) to restore balance, and keep going up.

                  The four cases slides 28–30

                  The summary slides sort every case by which side is too tall and where the new node went:

                  Unbalanced node is too tall on the…New node went into the…NameFix
                  left(a) left subtree of the left childleft-leftright rotation
                  left(b) right subtree of the left childleft-rightleft-right double rotation
                  right(a) right subtree of the right childright-rightleft rotation
                  right(b) left subtree of the right childright-leftright-left double rotation

                  Slide 28 (case 1a). The tree has 60 on top, with 50 as its left child (children 40 and 55; 40 has children 30 and 45), and a subtree on the right of 60. Insert 32: it goes 60 → 50 → 40 → 30 and hangs to the right of 30. Walk up: node 30 has height 1 now, node 40 has a left subtree of height 1 and a right subtree (45) of height 0: still fine. But node 50 has a left subtree (rooted at 40) of height 2 and a right subtree (just 55) of height 0: broken at 50. The new node is in the left subtree of the left child, so use a right rotation at 50: 40 becomes the parent, with 30 (and its child 32) on the left and 50 (children 45 and 55) on the right. The slide asks about inserting 25 instead of 32. 25 goes to the left of 30: the same case (left-left) and the same fix.

                  Slide 29 (case 1b). Same tree, insert 47: it goes under 45, to its right. Now 50 is broken again (left subtree rooted at 40 has height 2: 40, 45, 47), but the new node is in the right subtree of the left child: the inside. Use a left-right double rotation: left rotation at 40 (45 above 40), then right rotation at 50: the subtree is now 45 on top, with 40 (child 30) and 50 (children 47 and 55). Slide 30 says cases 2(a) and 2(b) are the mirror images (left rotation; right-left double rotation).

                  The demo runs the whole algorithm on these trees and lets you type any list of keys. Try the exercise on slide 30: insert 100, 56, 3, 8, 10, 30, 40, 50, 25, 46 one by one into an empty tree (it is the default in the “empty tree” choice).

                  AVL insertion, step by step

                  The answer to the exercise on slide 30

                  Six of the ten insertions break the rule, and each needs exactly one rebalancing: inserting 3 breaks 100 (right rotation at 100); 10 breaks 3 (left rotation at 3); 30 breaks 56 (left-right double rotation); 50 breaks 30 (left rotation); 25 breaks 56 (right rotation); 46 breaks 10 (left rotation). The final tree has 40 at the root, 10 as its left child (children 8 and 30, with 3 under 8 and 25 under 30) and 56 as its right child (children 50 and 100, with 46 under 50). Its height is 3. The same keys inserted into a plain search tree give height 8.

                  At most one rebalancing per insertion

                  In an AVL insertion the rebalancing needed is at most one single or double rotation. After it, the subtree has the same height it had before the insertion, so no ancestor above sees any change. (The slides keep walking to the root, updating heights, and that is harmless.) Deletion is different, as we will see.

                  Part 8 · Slides 31–33

                  Implementation

                  The node slide 31

                  Each node has three pointers (left, right, parent) and, new in this chapter, one integer: the height of the subtree rooted at the node. Storing the height lets us check the balance of a node in constant time, by looking at the heights of its two children, instead of measuring the subtrees every time.

                  struct tree_node {

                  a node of an AVL tree.

                  int key;

                  the element stored in the node.

                  tree_node *left;

                  left child (or NULL).

                  tree_node *right;

                  right child (or NULL).

                  tree_node *parent;

                  parent (NULL at the root): needed to walk up after an insertion.

                  int height;

                  height of the subtree rooted here: 0 for a leaf. An empty subtree counts as −1.

                  }

                  end of the struct.

                  Right rotation slides 32–33

                  Slide 32 explains which pointers change when B (x) is rotated with its left child A (y), with subtrees T1 (A’s left), T2 (A’s right) and T3 (B’s right): A’s parent and right child change; B’s parent and left child change; B’s original parent must now point to A instead of B (on its left or its right, depending on which child B was); and the root of T2 gets a new parent, B. The code is:

                  Right_Rotate(T, x) {

                  rotate x (B) with its left child.

                  y = x->left;

                  y points to A, the left child that will come up.

                  if (x->parent == NULL)

                  is B the root?

                  { T = y; y->parent = NULL; }

                  then A is the new root.

                  else {

                  otherwise A takes B’s place below B’s old parent:

                  y->parent = x->parent;

                  A’s parent = B’s old parent,

                  if (x == x->parent->left)

                  and if B was a left child...

                  x->parent->left = y;

                  ...A becomes that parent’s left child,

                  else

                  ...

                  x->parent->right = y;

                  ...otherwise its right child.

                  }

                  end of the else.

                  x->left = y->right;

                  A’s right subtree T2 becomes B’s left subtree.

                  if (y->right != NULL)

                  if T2 is not empty...

                  y->right->parent = x;

                  ...its root now has parent B.

                  y->right = x;

                  B becomes A’s right child.

                  x->parent = y;

                  and A is B’s parent.

                  UpdateHeight(x); UpdateHeight(y);

                  the slide asks “How?”: recompute B first (it is now the lower one) then A, each as 1 + max(height of left, height of right). O(1), since the children’s heights are stored.

                  }

                  end: O(1) time (slide 33).

                  A formatting slip on slide 33

                  On the slide the statement else y->p = x->p; is followed by the if (x == x->p->left) block at a deeper indentation, but no braces. Read literally the if would run even when x is the root and has no parent. The indentation shows the intention, which the braces in the version above make explicit.

                  The rest, which the slide asks you to write slide 33

                  Slide 33 ends with a challenge: can you write the algorithms for Left_Rotate, the two double rotations and insertion? What is the time complexity? Here they are (the code is not on the slides; it follows from them).

                  Left_Rotate(T, x) {

                  the mirror image: x (k1) comes down to the left, its right child y comes up.

                  y = x->right;

                  the right child that will come up.

                  if (x->parent == NULL) { T = y; y->parent = NULL; }

                  root case, as before.

                  else { y->parent = x->parent;

                  otherwise y takes x’s place...

                  if (x == x->parent->left) x->parent->left = y;

                  ...on the same side...

                  else x->parent->right = y; }

                  ...as x had.

                  x->right = y->left;

                  y’s left subtree becomes x’s right subtree.

                  if (y->left != NULL) y->left->parent = x;

                  fix that subtree’s parent pointer.

                  y->left = x; x->parent = y;

                  x becomes y’s left child.

                  UpdateHeight(x); UpdateHeight(y);

                  x first, then y.

                  }

                  O(1).

                  LeftRight_Rotate(T, x) {

                  left-right double rotation at the broken node x.

                  Left_Rotate(T, x->left);

                  first, a left rotation at x’s left child (the inside becomes an outside)...

                  Right_Rotate(T, x);

                  ...then a right rotation at x.

                  }

                  O(1). RightLeft_Rotate is the mirror: Right_Rotate(T, x->right); Left_Rotate(T, x);.

                  AVL_Insert(T, z) {

                  insert the node z and keep the tree an AVL tree.

                  Tree_Insert(T, z);

                  the ordinary insertion of Chapter 7 (z is a new leaf with height = 0).

                  x = z->parent;

                  start with the new node’s parent...

                  while (x != NULL) {

                  ...and climb to the root:

                  UpdateHeight(x);

                  recompute this node’s height from its children.

                  if (Height(x->left) - Height(x->right) == 2) {

                  the left side is 2 too tall:

                  if (Height(x->left->left) >= Height(x->left->right))

                  the extra height is on the outside...

                  Right_Rotate(T, x);

                  ...one right rotation,

                  else LeftRight_Rotate(T, x);

                  ...otherwise (inside) a left-right double rotation.

                  } else if (Height(x->right) - Height(x->left) == 2) {

                  the right side is 2 too tall: the mirror image:

                  if (Height(x->right->right) >= Height(x->right->left))

                  outside...

                  Left_Rotate(T, x);

                  ...one left rotation,

                  else RightLeft_Rotate(T, x);

                  ...inside: a right-left double rotation.

                  }

                  end of the checks.

                  x = x->parent;

                  go up. (After a rotation x sits below the new subtree root, so this just revisits the new root, which is balanced.)

                  }

                  end of the loop.

                  }

                  Height(NULL) is −1.

                  Time complexity slide 33

                  The ordinary insertion costs O(h). The climb visits at most h + 1 ancestors, and at each one the height update and the check cost O(1) and a rotation costs O(1). Total: O(h), and since h = O(lg n) for an AVL tree, insertion is O(lg n) in the worst case.

                  Part 9 · Slides 34–36

                  Deletion

                  The procedure slides 34–35

                  Deletion works the same way as insertion, upside down:

                  1. Delete the node as in an ordinary binary search tree (Chapter 7: 0, 1 or 2 children; with 2 children, copy the successor and cut out the successor’s node).
                  2. Go up to the root along the path from the parent of the node that was actually cut out.
                  3. For each node on that path: update its height, and rotate if it now violates the AVL rule.

                  The slide uses this tree and asks to delete 60, then 33, then 24 (each time, think of the original tree):

                  • Delete 60: a leaf. Its parent 50 becomes a leaf, 40 has two children of height 0, and so on: no rotation is needed, only a few heights shrink.
                  • Delete 33: it has one child (31), which takes its place. Now 35 has a left subtree of height 0 (just 31) and a right subtree (under 40) of height 2: broken at 35. 35’s right child is 40, whose own right side is the taller one (outside), so one left rotation at 35 brings 40 to the top of that subtree.
                  • Delete 24: a leaf (right child of 22). Now 22, 25 and 27 are fine, but 25’s height has dropped to 1, so at the root 30 the left subtree has height 1 while the right subtree (under 35) has height 3: broken at 30, far from the deleted node. 35’s taller side is its right (outside), so one left rotation at 30, and 35 becomes the root of the whole tree.

                  AVL deletion, step by step

                  Deletion is not as gentle as insertion

                  The slides do not spell out the cases for deletion, but there is one difference to know about. When a node is out of balance after a deletion, its taller child can have two subtrees of equal height (that cannot happen after an insertion). In that case a single rotation is right, and it is the case the demo’s rule (“if the outside is at least as tall as the inside, one rotation”) handles. Also, one rotation does not end the story: after the rotation, the subtree can be one level shorter than before the deletion, so ancestors higher up may break in turn. That is why the climb goes all the way to the root, and a deletion can use up to about lg n rotations (one per level), where an insertion uses at most one.

                  Complexity slide 36

                  The slide: since a rotation takes constant time, fixing the balance and updating the heights along one path takes O(lg n). Insert and delete therefore take O(lg n) time. The accounting is the same for both: finding the place costs O(h), the climb visits at most h + 1 nodes, and each visit costs O(1) (update a height, compare two numbers, maybe rotate). With h = O(lg n) from Part 3, all three operations (search, insert, delete) are O(lg n) in the worst case, whatever the order of the operations. This is what the plain search tree of Chapter 7 could not promise.

                  The slide also leaves you an exercise: write down the algorithm for deletion and analyze its time complexity. In pseudocode: Tree_Delete as in Chapter 7, remembering x = y->parent (the parent of the spliced-out node) before returning; then the same while (x != NULL) loop as in AVL_Insert, using >= to choose between a single and a double rotation. Time O(h) + O(h)·O(1) = O(lg n).

                  Part 10 · Slides 4, 36

                  How well does it work in practice?

                  The experiment slide 4

                  The height bound says the AVL tree is never worse than about 1.44 lg n. Slide 4 adds, “for your interest”, that on average it is much better: about lg(n+1) + 0.25, so for n = 2000 the height is 11 or 12 rather than 14. Let us check, and also run the case that destroyed the plain search tree: sorted insertions.

                  AVL trees versus plain search trees

                  What you should see

                  Random order: the AVL height is within one or two levels of the perfect ⌊lg n⌋, while the plain tree is roughly twice as tall. Sorted order: the plain tree is a list of height n − 1, and the AVL tree is as good as a perfect tree (insert 1, 2, 3, …, 15 in order and you get a perfect tree of height 3). And rebalancing is cheap: well under one rotation per insertion on average.

                  The bill slide 36

                  Plain search tree (Ch. 7)AVL tree (Ch. 8)
                  SearchO(h), worst O(n)O(lg n) always
                  InsertO(h), worst O(n)O(lg n) always, at most 1 rebalancing
                  DeleteO(h), worst O(n)O(lg n) always, up to O(lg n) rotations
                  Min, max, successorO(h)O(lg n)
                  Extra memorynoneone integer (the height) per node
                  Codeshortlonger: rotations and four cases

                  The price is a bit more memory and code. The reward is a guarantee: no input sequence, however nasty, can slow an AVL tree below O(lg n).

                  Part 11 · Slide 37

                  Summary and self-test

                  The chapter on one page slide 37

                  The conclusion slide has two phrases: a dynamic binary search tree that stays nearly balanced.

                  IdeaIn one line
                  The problema plain search tree can become a list: worst case O(n)
                  AVL ruleat every node the subtree heights differ by at most 1 (empty tree: height −1)
                  Height boundn ≥ F(h) ≥ φh with F(h) = 1 + F(h−1) + F(h−2), so h ≤ 1.44 lg n: O(lg n)
                  Rotationswap a parent with a child; keeps the in-order list; O(1)
                  Outside-heavy (LL, RR)one rotation at the broken node
                  Inside-heavy (LR, RL)double rotation: at the child, then at the broken node
                  Insertionordinary insert, climb up updating heights, fix the first broken ancestor; at most one rebalancing; O(lg n)
                  Deletionordinary delete, climb up from the parent of the cut-out node, fix every broken node; up to O(lg n) rotations; O(lg n) time
                  Nodekey, left, right, parent and height

                  The theme of the chapter

                  Do not hope for balance; enforce it. A cheap local test (compare two stored heights) and a cheap local repair (a rotation) are enough to keep the whole tree shallow, whatever order the keys arrive in.

                  Test yourself

                  1. A node has a left subtree of height 3 and a right subtree of height 1. What is its balance, and does it break the AVL rule? What if the right subtree were empty and the left subtree a single leaf?

                    Show the answer

                    Balance = 3 − 1 = +2: the rule is broken (it allows only −1, 0, +1). If the right subtree is empty (height −1) and the left is a single leaf (height 0): 0 − (−1) = +1, which is fine.

                  2. Why is it enough to prove “an AVL tree of height h has at least F(h) nodes” to bound the height? Compute F(5) and the tallest AVL tree that fits in 100 nodes.

                    Show the answer

                    If the thinnest tree of height h already needs F(h) nodes, a tree with only n nodes cannot have a height for which F(h) > n. F: 1, 2, 4, 7, 12, 20, 33, 54, 88, 143, … so F(5) = 20. For n = 100: F(8) = 88 ≤ 100 < F(9) = 143, so the tallest is height 8. (A perfect tree would be 6.)

                  3. Insert 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7 in this order into an empty AVL tree. Which rotations happen, and what is the final tree?

                    Show the answer

                    After 1, 2, 3 the root is out of balance (right-right): a left rotation makes 2 the root. 4 needs nothing. 5 breaks node 3 (right-right): left rotation, giving 2 → (1, 4 → (3, 5)). 6 breaks the root 2 (right-right): left rotation, 4 becomes the root. 7 breaks node 5: left rotation. In total 4 left rotations; the final tree is the perfect tree with root 4, children 2 and 6, leaves 1, 3, 5, 7, height 2. A plain search tree would have height 6.

                  4. Node x has left subtree height 4 and right subtree height 2. Its left child has a left subtree of height 2 and a right subtree of height 3. Which fix?

                    Show the answer

                    The left side is 2 taller, so x is broken. The taller subtree of the left child is its right one (3 > 2): the extra height is on the inside, the left-right case: double rotation, a left rotation at the left child and then a right rotation at x. A single right rotation would leave a node broken (slides 17–18).

                  5. Why does a single rotation not help when the subtree Y between k1 and k2 is the tall one?

                    Show the answer

                    A right rotation at k2 raises X by one level and lowers Z by one level, but only passes Y over from k1 to k2, keeping its height. With heights X = Z = h and Y = h+1, k1 ends up with subtree heights h and h+2 and is itself broken. The double rotation first turns Y’s root into the new parent, splitting Y over both sides.

                  6. After inserting a key, why do we only need to examine its ancestors?

                    Show the answer

                    The heights of nodes that are not ancestors of the new node do not change, because the new node is not in their subtree. A node that is not an ancestor therefore keeps the same two subtree heights it had before, and the tree was an AVL tree before.

                  7. In the tree of slide 28, which node breaks when 32 is inserted, which rotation fixes it, and what changes if 47 is inserted instead?

                    Show the answer

                    Inserting 32 breaks node 50 (left subtree of height 2, right subtree of height 0), and the new node is in the left subtree of the left child (40): right rotation at 50, which puts 40 on top of 30 (with 32) and 50. Inserting 47 also breaks 50, but the new node ends up in the right subtree of the left child: left-right double rotation (left at 40, right at 50), giving 45 on top of 40 and 50.

                  8. Delete 33 from the tree of slide 35. Which node breaks, and how is it fixed?

                    Show the answer

                    The node 33 has one child, 31, which takes its place. Node 35 now has a left subtree of height 0 and a right subtree (at 40) of height 2: broken. 40’s taller subtree is on its right (outside), so one left rotation at 35: 40 becomes the parent of 35 (children 31 and 38) and 50. Nothing above needs fixing.

                  9. How many rebalancing steps can one insertion need? One deletion? Why the difference?

                    Show the answer

                    Insertion: at most one (a single or double rotation): afterwards the subtree is as tall as it was before the insertion, so no ancestor notices. Deletion: possibly one per level, up to about lg n: a rotation may leave the subtree one level shorter than before the deletion, which can break the next ancestor. Both stay O(lg n) in total.

                  10. Why does every node store its height? What would happen without it?

                    Show the answer

                    The check at each ancestor needs the heights of two subtrees. If they are stored, the check is O(1). Without them, computing a height means walking the whole subtree, up to O(n) per check, and AVL insertion would cost O(n) or worse. Storing one integer per node and updating it during the climb keeps everything O(lg n).

                  PreviousChapter 7 · Binary search treesNextChapter 9 · Sorting I

                  Slides 1–58 · 09_sort1

                  Sorting I from Scratch

                  How to put a list in order. Three simple methods that swap neighbours (bubble, insertion, selection), why all of them need about n² steps, and then a smarter one: heap sort, which keeps the biggest number on top of a tree, and its cousin the priority queue.

                  In this chapter

                    Part 1 · Slides 1–3

                    The sorting problem

                    What we want slide 2

                    You are given a list A of n numbers in any order, for example 34 8 64 51 32 21. Your job is to rearrange them in increasing order: 8 21 32 34 51 64. That is all. The chapter is about how, and how many steps it costs.

                    The sorting problem

                    Given a list A of n numbers. Arrange the elements of A in increasing order of value.

                    As in the other chapters, the slides number the boxes of an array from 1: A[1] is the first number and A[n] the last.

                    Why sort at all? slide 2

                    The slide gives two reasons.

                    • It makes searching fast. In Chapter 6 you saw that binary search finds a number in about lg n looks, but only if the list is sorted. An unsorted pile needs n looks. Sorting costs something once, then every later search is cheap.
                    • It makes duplicates easy to find. In a sorted list two equal numbers stand next to each other, so one walk along the list, comparing each number with its neighbour, finds every duplicate: about n−1 comparisons. In an unsorted list you would have to compare every number with every other: n(n−1)/2 comparisons. For a million numbers that is a million against five hundred billion.

                    The question about the oranges slide 2

                    The slide asks: how would you sort 1 million oranges by size? Think about it for a moment before reading on.

                    Almost nobody would pick up two oranges, compare them, put them down, and repeat. The comparing method needs roughly 20 million comparisons for a million oranges (this chapter and the next explain why that is the best any comparing method can do). A real fruit packer does something cleverer: oranges roll along a belt over a sieve with holes of growing size, and each orange simply falls into the right bin. One look per orange, no comparing at all.

                    That trick works because we are allowed to look at the size directly. It is not available when the only thing we can do is ask “which of these two is bigger?”. Chapter 10 comes back to it (counting sort and radix sort). First, the comparing methods.

                    The rule of the game slide 3

                    The model

                    We can derive order information only by comparing elements. A sorting method in this model never looks inside a number; it just asks “is A[i] bigger than A[j]?” and moves numbers around according to the answers.

                    Every algorithm of this chapter and most of the next obey this rule. It makes the cost easy to measure: we count comparisons (and, where it matters, swaps), exactly as Chapter 2 taught us to count steps instead of seconds.

                    What is coming

                    SortMain ideaCost
                    Bubble sortscan again and again, swapping neighbours that are in the wrong orderΘ(n2)
                    Insertion sortkeep a sorted part on the left; slide each new number into placeΘ(n2) on average, Θ(n) if already sorted
                    Selection sortfind the biggest number and put it at the end; repeatΘ(n2)
                    Heap sortfind the biggest quickly by keeping the numbers in a heap (a tree)O(n lg n)

                    The first three are easy to understand and slow. The fourth is the first fast sorting algorithm of the course, and as a free gift it gives the priority queue, one of the most useful structures in computing.

                    Part 2 · Slides 4–11

                    Bubble sort

                    The idea slide 4

                    Imagine the list standing upright, big numbers heavy and small numbers light. Bubble sort walks along the list from the left, looking at two neighbours at a time. If the left one is bigger, it swaps them. Then it takes one step to the right and looks at the next pair. Heavy numbers get carried to the right (or, turned the other way up, light ones “bubble” up), and walking once through the whole list is called a pass. After a pass you start again, until the list is in order.

                    Bubble sort

                    Keep scanning the list, swapping neighbouring elements that are out of order, until the whole list is in order.

                    The first pass, by hand slides 4–9

                    The slides use 34 8 64 51 32 21. Here is the first pass, one comparison per line:

                    1. Compare 34 and 8: 34 is bigger, so swap. The list is 8 34 64 51 32 21.
                    2. Compare 34 and 64: in order, no swap.
                    3. Compare 64 and 51: swap. 8 34 51 64 32 21.
                    4. Compare 64 and 32: swap. 8 34 51 32 64 21.
                    5. Compare 64 and 21: swap. 8 34 51 32 21 64.

                    Look at what happened to 64, the biggest number: it was swapped again and again and was carried all the way to the end. That is the whole point of a pass: the biggest number of the part we scanned always ends up at the right end. It is now in its final place.

                    All the passes slide 10

                    Slide 10 shows the list at the end of each pass. Pass 2 does the same on the first five numbers only (64 is already home), and carries 51 to the end of those; and so on:

                    afterthe list
                    the start34 8 64 51 32 21
                    pass 18 34 51 32 21 64
                    pass 28 34 32 21 51 64
                    pass 38 32 21 34 51 64
                    pass 48 21 32 34 51 64

                    (After pass 4, the numbers 8 21 are the only ones not marked, and they are already in order; the code of slide 11 still makes a fifth pass to be sure.) Now run it yourself, one comparison at a time. Try your own numbers, a sorted list, and a reversed list.

                    Bubble sort, one comparison at a time

                    The code slide 11

                    BubbleSort (A) {

                    the list is in A[1…n].

                    /* elements in A[1..n] */

                    (a comment on the slide).

                    for (i=n; i>=2; i--) {

                    one pass for each i, from n down to 2. Positions after i already hold their final numbers.

                    for (j=1; j<=i-1; j++) {

                    j walks from the left up to just before i: every neighbouring pair (A[j], A[j+1]) in the part still in play.

                    if (A[j]>A[j+1]) swap(A[j],A[j+1]);

                    one comparison; if the left number is bigger, one swap.

                    } } }

                    end of the inner loop, the outer loop and the procedure.

                    Two things to see in the code

                    The inner loop is shorter every time. Pass i only goes up to i-1, because everything to the right of i is already final. The code never stops early. Even if the list becomes sorted after pass 2, it still does all the passes; so the number of comparisons does not depend on the input at all. The next part counts them.

                    Part 3 · Slides 12–18

                    Bubble sort: counting

                    What a pass guarantees slide 12

                    Observation (slide 12)

                    After the k-th iteration of the i loop, the biggest k elements are at the end of the list, in order: A[n] > A[n-1] > … > A[n-k+1], and all of them are bigger than everything in A[1…n-k].

                    That is exactly what you saw in the table of part 2: after pass 1 the biggest number is last; after pass 2 the two biggest are last, in order; and so on. This is why the algorithm is correct: after n−1 passes, n−1 numbers are in their final places, so the last one must be too.

                    How many comparisons? slide 12

                    The slide asks: how many element-element comparisons does bubble sort take? Count them pass by pass. Pass i compares the pairs j = 1, 2, …, i-1, that is i−1 comparisons. The passes use i = n, n−1, …, 2, so the total is (n−1) + (n−2) + … + 1:

                    Σi=1n−1 i = (n−1) n2 = Θ(n2)

                    For the six numbers of the example that is 5 + 4 + 3 + 2 + 1 = 15 comparisons (the demo counted 15), and for 1000 numbers it is 499,500. It is always that many, whatever the list.

                    How many swaps? slides 13–15

                    Comparisons are the same for every list, but swaps depend on the list. A sorted list needs none. A list in reverse order swaps at every comparison. The slide asks for the average number of swaps and gives the answer (n choose 2) / 2, that is n(n−1)/4. Here is the idea behind it, which is the most beautiful argument of the chapter.

                    Inversions slide 14

                    Inversion

                    Given an element x in the list, an element y is an inversion of x if y < x and y is on the right of x. In other words, an inversion is a pair of numbers that stand in the wrong order: the bigger one on the left.

                    The slide uses the list 2 4 3 1 5. For 2 the only smaller number on its right is 1. For 4 they are 3 and 1. For 3 it is 1. For 1 and 5 there are none. Total 1 + 2 + 1 = 4 inversions: the pairs (2,1), (4,3), (4,1), (3,1).

                    Inversions measure how unsorted a list is: a sorted list has none, and a reverse-sorted list of n numbers has every pair out of order, n(n−1)/2 of them. Count them on your own lists:

                    Count the inversions

                    The four questions of slide 15

                    1. How many inversions are there in a sorted list?

                      Show the answer

                      None. In a sorted list the bigger number is always on the right.

                    2. How many inversions does a swap of adjacent elements eliminate?

                      Show the answer

                      Exactly one (if the two were out of order). Swapping neighbours a b to b a fixes the order of that one pair, and changes nothing else: every other number is still on the same side of both of them, so its pairs with a and b are unchanged.

                    3. How many swaps does bubble sort take?

                      Show the answer

                      Exactly as many as the list has inversions. Bubble sort only swaps neighbours that are out of order, so every swap removes one inversion, and it ends with none. (The demos check this: the number of swaps equals the number of inversions.)

                    4. How many possible initial inputs (of n different numbers) are there?

                      Show the answer

                      n! (n factorial): n choices for the first place, n−1 for the second, and so on. For 5 numbers, 120 orders.

                    The average number of inversions slides 16–18

                    Slide 16 asks: let S be the set of all inputs of n elements. How would you compute the average number of inversions?

                    The direct way is to list all n! inputs, count the inversions of each, add them up and divide by n!. For n = 5 that is 120 lists; for n = 20 it is more than 2 × 1018. We need a trick, and the slides give it: pair each input with its reverse.

                    • The observation (slide 17). For any two numbers i and j: if (i, j) is an inversion in I, it cannot be one in Ir, and the other way round. So each pair contributes exactly one inversion to the two lists together.
                    • The count (slide 18). There are n choose 2 = n(n−1)/2 pairs, so I and Ir together have n(n−1)/2 inversions, and on average each has n(n−1)/4.
                    • All inputs. Every input I in S has its reverse Ir in S, so S splits into such pairs, and the argument applies to every pair. The average over all inputs is therefore also n(n−1)/4.

                    Test it on real data. This demo lists every order of 1…n (up to 40,320 of them), counts the inversions of each, and compares the exact average with the formula. The bar chart is symmetric, which is the reverse-pairing seen from another side: a list with k inversions has a reverse with n(n−1)/2 − k.

                    Every order, every inversion

                    What this proves about bubble sort

                    Bubble sort makes as many swaps as there are inversions, n(n−1)/4 on average, and n(n−1)/2 comparisons always. So its average case, like its worst case, is Θ(n2) (slide 18).

                    Part 4 · Slides 19–33

                    Insertion sort

                    The idea slide 19

                    Think of sorting playing cards in your hand. You pick up one card at a time and slide it left into the right place among the cards you already hold. The cards in your hand are always sorted, and every new card is inserted where it belongs.

                    Insertion sort

                    Maintain a sorted list (it starts with only the first element). At each step take the next number of the input and insert it into the sorted list in its proper place.

                    The example slides 19–29

                    The slides use 34 8 64 51 32 21. The sorted part is shown first, and each line below is the list after one insertion:

                    stepthe list (sorted part first)what happened
                    start34 | 8 64 51 32 21the sorted part is just 34
                    insert 88 34 | 64 51 32 218 < 34: one swap
                    insert 648 34 64 | 51 32 2134 < 64: stays, no swap
                    insert 518 34 51 64 | 32 2151 < 64: one swap, then 34 < 51: stop
                    insert 328 32 34 51 64 | 21swaps past 64, 51, 34; stops at 8
                    insert 218 21 32 34 51 64swaps past 64, 51, 34, 32; stops at 8

                    Run it, one comparison at a time. The blue boxes are the sorted part; the orange x is the number being slid into place.

                    Insertion sort, one comparison at a time
