                    The code slide 30

                    InsertionSort(A) {

                    the list is in A[1…n].

                    for (i=2; i<=n; i++) {

                    the sorted part is A[1…i-1]; A[i] is the next number to insert.

                    j = i-1;

                    j points at the left neighbour of the number we are sliding (which is at j+1).

                    while ((j>=1) && (A[j]>A[j+1])) {

                    keep going while there is a left neighbour and it is bigger. (If j reaches 0 the number has reached the front.)

                    Swap(A[j], A[j+1]);

                    move the number one place to the left.

                    j--;

                    and look at its new left neighbour.

                    }}}

                    end of the while loop, the for loop, and the procedure.

                    Each swap in the loop moves the number one place to the left, past a bigger neighbour, so it removes exactly one inversion. That is the key to the analysis.

                    How fast? slide 31

                    Inserting the i-th number may need up to i−1 swaps (if it is smaller than everything before it), and on average half of that, because it is equally likely to land anywhere in the sorted part.

                    • Worst case (the list is in reverse order): Σi=1n−1 i = (n−1) n2 = Θ(n2).
                    • Average case: Σi=1n−1 i2 = (n−1) n4 = Θ(n2). (This agrees with the inversion argument of part 3: swaps = inversions, and the average number of inversions is n(n−1)/4.)
                    • Best case (the list is already sorted): each number is compared once with its left neighbour and stays. That is n−1 comparisons and no swaps: Θ(n).

                    The best case is what makes insertion sort special among the three simple sorts: bubble sort and selection sort always do n(n−1)/2 comparisons, even on a sorted list. Insertion sort profits from a list that is already nearly sorted: its cost is about n plus the number of inversions. Select “Already in order” in the demo above and compare.

                    A limit for every neighbour-swapping sort slides 32–33

                    Slide 32

                    Bubble sort and insertion sort both swap only adjacent elements. By the inversion argument, the average list has n(n−1)/4 inversions, and each adjacent swap removes at most one. So they must make at least n(n−1)/4 swaps on average. In fact any sorting algorithm that only swaps adjacent elements has average case Ω(n2).

                    That is a strong statement: it does not matter how clever the program is. If it only ever swaps neighbours, it is stuck at n2. To be faster, a sorting algorithm must swap elements that are far apart, so that one swap removes many inversions (slide 33):

                    Selection sort (next) does swap far-apart elements, but, as you will see, it still needs n2 comparisons. Only heap sort (and the algorithms of Chapter 10) break the barrier.

                    Part 5 · Slides 34–37

                    Selection sort

                    The idea slide 34

                    Selection sort is like bubble sort, but it does the swapping only once per round, at the end. In each round, pick the biggest number of the part still unsorted and put it in the last place of that part. Then pick the second biggest and put it in the second last place, and so on.

                    Selection sort

                    Pick the largest element and put it in A[n]; pick the second largest and put it in A[n-1]; … Each round selects the maximum of what remains.

                    The example slide 34

                    List: 34 8 64 51 32 21. Round 1 looks at all six numbers and finds 64 (position 3). It swaps 64 with the last box (21): 34 8 21 51 32 64. Round 2 looks at the first five, finds 51, swaps it with the fifth box (32): 34 8 21 32 51 64. And so on:

                    afterthe list
                    the start34 8 64 51 32 21
                    round 134 8 21 51 32 64
                    round 234 8 21 32 51 64
                    round 332 8 21 34 51 64
                    round 421 8 32 34 51 64
                    round 58 21 32 34 51 64

                    Selection sort, one comparison at a time

                    The code slide 35

                    SelectionSort(A) {

                    the list is in A[1…n].

                    for (i=n; i>=2; i--) {

                    round i fills position i; positions after i are final.

                    max = i;

                    start by assuming that the number at position i is the biggest.

                    for (j=1; j<=i-1; j++) {

                    look at all the other numbers of the part still in play.

                    if (A[j] > A[max])

                    one comparison: is this number bigger than the biggest seen so far?

                    max = j;

                    then remember where it is.

                    }

                    end of the scan: max is the position of the biggest.

                    swap(A[i], A[max]);

                    one swap: the biggest goes to position i, its final place.

                    }}

                    end of the for loop and of the procedure.

                    How fast? slide 36

                    Round i compares A[j] with A[max] for j = 1, …, i−1, which is i−1 comparisons. Adding up the rounds gives, once more:

                    Σk=1n−1 k = (n−1) n2 = Θ(n2)

                    As with bubble sort, this number does not depend on the input: selection sort always makes n(n−1)/2 comparisons, even if the list is sorted already. But it makes at most n−1 swaps (one per round), far fewer than bubble sort’s up to n(n−1)/2. If swapping is expensive (big records to move), that matters.

                    A detail about the swap

                    If the biggest number is already at position i, then max = i and swap(A[i], A[max]) swaps a box with itself: nothing happens. The demo does not count those as moves, so you will see fewer than n−1 moves on some lists (and none at all on a sorted list).

                    Insertion sort versus selection sort slide 37

                    Selection sortInsertion sort
                    When is a number final?As soon as it is placed. Once we have found a position for an element, that position is final: it will not be moved again.Not until the very end: a later, smaller number can still push it to the right.
                    Already-sorted inputno help: still n(n−1)/2 comparisonsBenefits from partially ordered input: sorted input takes O(n)
                    Needs all the data first?yes: it must see the whole list to find the biggestNo: it can be done on-line. You do not need all the elements before you start sorting; each new one is inserted into the sorted part as it arrives.
                    Swapsat most n−1equal to the number of inversions

                    “On-line” is the idea of a card player who is dealt cards one by one and keeps the hand sorted at every moment: insertion sort can accept a new number at any time and the sorted part stays valid.

                    Part 6 · Slides 38–44

                    Heaps and the idea of heap sort

                    What is slow in selection sort? slide 38

                    Selection sort has one expensive step: picking the maximum of the numbers still unsorted. It scans all of them, every round: that is where the n2 comes from. The slide says: if we can perform the “pick maximum” step efficiently, we can reduce the time needed to run selection sort.

                    So we want a way of storing numbers where the biggest one is always easy to find, and where removing it does not cost much. The answer is the heap.

                    Heap and heap property

                    A heap is a binary tree in which the value of any node is at least as large as the values of its children (the heap property).

                    Which node contains the largest element? (the slide’s question). Follow the rule upwards: every node is at least as big as its children, so every parent is at least as big as everything below it, so the root is at least as big as all the nodes. The largest number is at the root: finding it takes one step.

                    A heap is not a search tree

                    Do not confuse it with Chapter 7. In a binary search tree left < parent < right. In a heap there is no order between the two children, only parent ≥ both children. The 10 may be left or right of the 12: nobody cares. That weaker rule is exactly why a heap is so cheap to maintain.

                    The idea of heap sort slide 39

                    Selection sort says: pick the maximum, put it at the end, repeat. Heap sort says the same thing but keeps the numbers in a heap so that picking the maximum is instant:

                    1. Build a heap from the numbers of A.
                    2. Remove the largest (it is at the root) and put it in A[n], its final place.
                    3. Fix the heap, which now has one number fewer, so that the maximum of the rest is at the root again.
                    4. Repeat steps 2–3 for A[n-1], A[n-2], … until nothing is left.
                    HeapSort(A) {

                    the slide’s outline (not yet real code).

                    build_heap(A);

                    step 1: arrange the numbers into a heap.

                    for (i=1; i<=n; i++) {

                    n rounds.

                    put largest element in A[n-i+1];

                    step 2: the root goes to the next free place from the right.

                    rebuild heap;

                    step 3: restore the heap property for the numbers that are left.

                    }}

                    end.

                    Two things need to be explained: how to fix the heap (steps 2–3) and how to build it (step 1). We start with the fixing.

                    Fixing a heap slides 40–41

                    The root has been taken away, and there is a hole at the top. To fix the heap, the slide picks a leaf x (the last one), puts it at the root, and then pushes x down the tree: swap x with its larger child, again and again, until the heap property is no longer violated.

                    Why the larger child? If x were swapped with the smaller one, the smaller child would become the parent of the larger one and break the rule. Swapping with the larger child keeps both children below a node at least as big as they are. Run slide 41 (the heap 18 10 12 5 4 6 3: remove 18, put the last leaf 3 on top, push it down):

                    Remove the maximum and fix the heap

                    How much does fixing cost? slide 42

                    The push-down never increases the height of the tree: x only ever moves down one level at a time. So if the heap has height m, one push-down takes at most m steps: O(m). The for loop of heap sort does n of them: total O(n m).

                    What is the smallest height m we can get, and how? (the slide’s question.) We have shown (Chapter 7, the best case for the height of a tree) that the shortest possible binary tree with n nodes has height ⌊lg n⌋, and a complete binary tree achieves that minimum. So if we keep the heap as compact as possible, m = about lg n, and the loop costs O(n lg n).

                    Left-complete trees slide 43

                    Left-complete binary tree

                    A left-complete binary tree is a complete binary tree with zero or more of its rightmost leaves deleted. In words: every level is completely full, except possibly the last, which is filled from the left with no gaps.

                    The goal, says the slide, is to build a left-complete binary tree for an array A of n elements without using extra memory on pointers. Normal trees need a pointer for every child. A left-complete tree has such a regular shape that we can store it in the array itself, with no pointers at all. Here is how.

                    A tree in an array slide 44

                    Number the nodes of a left-complete tree starting from the root, left to right, top to bottom: the root is 1, its children are 2 and 3, the next level is 4, 5, 6, 7, and so on. Then:

                    • the value of node number i is stored in A[i];
                    • the children of node i (if they exist) are A[2i] and A[2i+1];
                    • so the parent of node j is A[⌊j/2⌋] (the floor, because 2i and 2i+1 both divide down to i).

                    Check on the slide’s tree (12 10 6 5 4 3): node 1 holds 12 and its children are nodes 2 and 3, holding 10 and 6. Node 2 holds 10 and its children are nodes 4 and 5 (5 and 4). Node 3 holds 6 and has one child, node 6 (3), because node 7 does not exist (there are only 6 nodes). Move the selector and watch the formulas on any heap; or type numbers that are not a heap and see which parent is too small.

                    Heap as a tree and as an array

                    Why this is lovely

                    Going down is multiplying by 2 (and maybe adding 1); going up is dividing by 2. A computer does that in one step, and the whole tree is just the array A[1…n]. No pointers, no memory wasted, and the nodes of one level are next to each other. Chapter 5 stored trees with pointers to children; here the regular shape (no gaps, so no wasted boxes) lets the position in the array do the job of the pointers.

                    Part 7 · Slides 45–51

                    Heapify and BuildHeap

                    Heapify: the push-down in code slides 45–46

                    Heapify(A, i, n) takes the number at A[i] and pushes it down a heap whose last position is n, exactly as in the demo. It assumes that the two subtrees below i already are heaps; only A[i] itself may be too small. Here is the code of the slides, with the braces arranged as the comments show they were meant:

                    Heapify(A,i,n) {

                    push A[i] down the heap A[1…n] to maintain the heap property.

                    r = i;

                    r is the position where the number currently sits.

                    while (r <= floor(n/2)) {

                    as long as r has children (the positions after ⌊n/2⌋ are leaves).

                    if (2r == n) {

                    r has only one child, A[2r] (it is the last position).

                    if (A[r] < A[2r])

                    is the child bigger?

                    swap(A[r], A[2r]);

                    then swap.

                    break;

                    in either case we are done: there is nothing below the last position.

                    } else {

                    r has two children: compare A[r], A[2r] and A[2r+1].

                    if ((A[r] < A[2r]) && (A[2r] > A[2r+1])) {

                    the left child is bigger than r and bigger than its sibling: it is the largest of the three.

                    swap(A[r],A[2r]);

                    the left child comes up...

                    r = 2r;

                    ...and the number we are pushing is now at 2r.

                    }

                    end of the left case.

                    else if ((A[r] < A[2r+1]) && (A[2r+1] > A[2r])) {

                    otherwise, the right child is the largest of the three.

                    swap(A[r],A[2r+1]);

                    the right child comes up...

                    r = 2r+1;

                    ...and we continue from 2r+1.

                    }

                    end of the right case.

                    else break;

                    A[r] is the largest of the three: stop.

                    }}}

                    end of the else, the while loop and the procedure.

                    Two slips on slides 45–46

                    1. The braces. On slide 45 the else { /* r has 2 children */ comes right after break;}, so, read literally, it pairs with the inner if (A[r] < A[2r]). The comments make the intention clear: the else belongs to if (2r == n), as written above. 2. Equal numbers. The tests use strict >, so if the two children are equal and both bigger than A[r] (for example 1 with children 5 and 5), neither test is true and the loop breaks without fixing anything. The slides assume all numbers are different, and with different numbers the code is correct. The demos in this guide use the usual version, “swap with the larger child if it is bigger”, which also works with equal numbers.

                    Cost. Each trip round the loop goes one level down, so Heapify costs at most the height of A[i]: O(height of A[i]) (slide 50).

                    Building a heap slide 47

                    We have an unsorted array and want a heap. The slide builds it incrementally, from the bottom up:

                    BuildHeap(A) {

                    turn A[1…n] into a heap.

                    for (i=n/2; i>=1; i--) {

                    from the last node that has a child (position ⌊n/2⌋) back to the root.

                    Heapify(A,i,n);

                    push A[i] down; its two subtrees are heaps already.

                    }}

                    end.

                    The invariant (what is true after each trip round the loop): after the iteration for i, the subarray A[i, i+1, …, n] obeys the heap property. Going from bottom to top is what makes Heapify legal: by the time we reach node i, everything below it has already been made into heaps.

                    Why start at n/2? slide 48

                    The last element is A[n], whose parent is A[⌊n/2⌋]. So all the nodes A[⌊n/2⌋+1], …, A[n] are leaves. A leaf has no children, so it cannot violate the heap property. We skip them: about half of all the nodes need no work at all.

                    The example slide 49

                    The slide builds a heap from 4 1 3 2 16 9 10 14 8 7 (ten numbers; leaves are positions 6–10; the loop starts at i = 5). Watch the green region grow from the right and bottom until it covers everything:

                    BuildHeap, node by node

                    The result is 16 14 10 8 7 9 3 2 4 1, after 7 swaps. That is the heap used in the heap-sort example of slide 53.

                    How much does BuildHeap cost? slides 50–51

                    There are about n/2 calls of Heapify, each costing up to lg n. The crude answer would be n/2 × lg n = O(n lg n). That is a valid upper bound, but it is too pessimistic: most calls are on nodes near the bottom, which cannot be pushed down far. The slide counts properly.

                    Few nodes are high (and costly), many are low (and cheap). Adding up, with i = the height and 2h−i = the number of nodes of that height (slide 51):

                    O( Σi=1h i 2h−i ) = O(2h) = O(n)

                    Why is that sum only about 2h? Write it as 2h × (1/2 + 2/4 + 3/8 + 4/16 + …). The bracket is a famous series that adds up to 2 however many terms you take (it never reaches 2, it creeps towards it). So the sum is less than 2 · 2h, and 2h ≤ n (since h = ⌊lg n⌋). BuildHeap is O(n): linear, not n lg n. For a perfect tree the sum is exactly 2h+1 − h − 2, which is always less than n = 2h+1 − 1.

                    How many swaps does BuildHeap really make?

                    Part 8 · Slides 52–53

                    HeapSort

                    The finished algorithm slide 52

                    Now we have both pieces: BuildHeap to make the heap, and Heapify to repair it. In the outline of slide 39, “put the largest in A[n-i+1]” becomes a swap of the root with the last number of the heap, and “rebuild heap” becomes a call of Heapify on the root, with the heap now one number smaller:

                    HeapSort (A) {

                    sorts A[1…n] in increasing order.

                    BuildHeap(A);

                    step 1: make A a heap. O(n).

                    for (i=n; i>1; i--) {

                    n−1 rounds; i is the last place of the heap.

                    swap(A[i],A[1]);

                    the biggest number (at the root) goes to place i, its final position, and the number that was there goes to the root.

                    Heapify(A,1,i-1);

                    the heap is now A[1…i-1] (place i is left out for good). Push the new root down. O(lg n).

                    }}

                    end.

                    The array does two jobs at once: the left part A[1…i] is the heap, and the right part A[i+1…n] is the sorted tail of the biggest numbers, in final order. The sorted tail grows by one each round, the heap shrinks by one. No extra memory is needed.

                    Watch it work slide 53

                    Slide 53 starts from the heap 16 14 10 8 7 9 3 2 4 1 (the result of BuildHeap on slide 49) and repeats: swap the root to the end, shrink the heap, push down. In the demo the green boxes of the array are the final tail. The second preset runs BuildHeap first.

                    Heap sort, step by step

                    Look at the first round of slide 53: the root 16 swaps with the last number, 1. Now 16 is in its final place, and 1 sits at the root of a 9-number heap, where it is pushed down three levels: swapped with 14, then with 8, then with 4, ending at a leaf. The heap is 14 8 10 4 7 9 3 2 1, and 14 is on top, ready to be taken next.

                    How fast? slide 52

                    • BuildHeap: O(n) (part 7).
                    • The loop: n−1 rounds. Each does one swap and one Heapify that goes down at most the height of the heap, ⌊lg n⌋ levels: O(lg n).
                    • Total: O(n) + (n−1) × O(lg n) = O(n lg n).

                    The complexity of HeapSort (slide 52)

                    O(n lg n), for every input: sorted, reversed or random. For a million numbers that is about 20 million steps, instead of 500 billion for the n2 sorts. Heap sort also sorts in place (it uses only the array and a few variables). The next demo, at the end of the chapter, lets you measure it.

                    How can heap sort beat the neighbour-swapping limit of part 4? Look at what a swap does here: the root is swapped with the last number, which may be a hundred places away, so one swap can remove many inversions at once. That is the “swap elements that are far apart” of slide 33, made systematic by the tree.

                    Part 9 · Slides 54–58

                    Priority queues

                    What a priority queue is slide 54

                    The heap is useful for much more than sorting. The slide shows the main use: the priority queue.

                    Priority queue

                    A priority queue is a set ADT (abstract data type, Chapter 3) that supports three operations:
                    INSERT(S, x): insert x into the set S.
                    MAXIMUM(S): return the largest element of S.
                    DELETE_MAX(S): remove the largest element of S.

                    It is a queue, but the one that leaves first is not the one that arrived first (as in the queue of Chapter 3) and not the one that arrived last (as in the stack): it is the one with the highest priority, that is, the biggest number.

                    Scheduling jobs slide 55

                    The slide gives the classic example: a computer has many jobs waiting, each with a priority. When a job J arrives, we call INSERT(S, J). When the processor is free, we call MAXIMUM(S) to see the most urgent job and DELETE_MAX(S) to take it off the queue. Hospital emergency rooms work the same way: the sickest patient is seen first, not the one who came first.

                    The implementation slide 56

                    Store the set as a heap in the array A, with n the number of elements. Then the operations are almost free:

                    MAXIMUM(S) {

                    the biggest element.

                    /* suppose the elements are stored in array A */

                    the heap array.

                    return(A[1]);}

                    it is the root. O(1).

                    DELETE_MAX(S) {

                    remove the biggest element.

                    /* let n = size of heap */

                    the number of elements now.

                    if (n<1) return ("Heap underflow");

                    nothing to delete: report an error.

                    swap(A[1],A[n]);

                    the biggest goes to the last place, the last element goes to the root.

                    n--;

                    the heap forgets its last place. (The removed maximum is still sitting there, in A[n+1], if the caller wants it.)

                    Heapify(A,1,n);}

                    push the new root down, exactly as in heap sort. O(lg n).

                    DELETE_MAX is the “fix the heap” of part 6. Insertion needs the reverse.

                    Insertion: push up slides 57–58

                    To insert x into a heap, we put x at the end of the array (the first free place, which keeps the tree left-complete), and then “do a reverse of Heapify”: push x up the tree. Compare it with its parent; if the parent is smaller, swap and repeat; otherwise stop. Because a parent only has to be at least as big as its children, the only possible violation is between x and its parent, and moving x up repairs it level by level.

                    INSERT(S,x) {

                    add x to the heap.

                    n++;

                    one more element.

                    A[n] = x; i=n;

                    put it in the first free place; i is where it sits.

                    while ((i>1) && (A[floor(i/2)]<A[i])) {

                    while there is a parent and it is smaller than x...

                    swap (A[i],A[floor(i/2)]);

                    ...swap them,

                    i = floor(i/2);

                    ...and look at the next parent up.

                    } }

                    end of the loop and of the procedure.

                    Complexity: O(lg n), because x climbs at most the height of the tree, ⌊lg n⌋ levels. Slide 57 inserts 15 into the heap 16 14 10 8 7 9 3 2 4 1: 15 is put in position 11 (below 7) and climbs two levels: it swaps with 7, then with 14, and stops under 16.

                    INSERT: push the new number up

                    Now play with a complete priority queue: insert numbers, ask for the maximum, delete it. Notice that Delete max always returns the numbers from the biggest to the smallest: a priority queue used this way is heap sort (insert everything, then delete the maximum n times).

                    A priority queue made of a heap

                    OperationHowTime
                    MAXIMUMreturn A[1]O(1)
                    INSERTput at the end, push upO(lg n)
                    DELETE_MAXswap root with last, shrink, push the root down (Heapify)O(lg n)

                    Part 10 · All the slides

                    The four sorts side by side

                    A race

                    Now that all four algorithms are on the table, run them on the same lists. The demo counts element-to-element comparisons, as the slides do (and shows swaps in the table). Start with n = 50 random numbers, then try the other inputs, then grow n and keep an eye on the bars.

                    Bubble, insertion, selection and heap sort on the same lists

                    Things to look for:

                    • Random lists, growing n. From 100 to 1000 numbers (ten times more), the three simple sorts need about a hundred times more comparisons (n2 grows with the square), while heap sort needs about thirteen times more (n lg n).
                    • Already sorted. Insertion sort collapses to n−1 comparisons. Bubble and selection sort do not notice.
                    • Reverse order. The worst case for bubble and insertion sort: every pair is an inversion, so n(n−1)/2 swaps. Selection sort needs only about n/2 moves.

                    The table

                    SortComparisonsSwapsBest inputRemarks
                    Bubblen(n−1)/2 always= inversions; average n(n−1)/4, worst n(n−1)/2none: the code does all passessimplest; swaps only neighbours, so Ω(n2) on average
                    Insertionbetween n−1 and n(n−1)/2; about inversions + n−1= inversionssorted: Θ(n)on-line; good for nearly sorted data; swaps only neighbours
                    Selectionn(n−1)/2 alwaysat most n−1none for comparisonsfewest moves; each number is placed once and for all
                    HeapO(n lg n) (about 2 n lg n)O(n lg n)all inputs alikefast and in place; also gives the priority queue

                    All four sort in place: they use the array itself and only a few extra variables.

                    Which one would you pick?

                    • A handful of numbers, or numbers that are almost in order, or numbers that arrive one by one: insertion sort. Its simplicity and its good behaviour on nearly sorted data beat clever methods on small inputs.
                    • Moving a record is very expensive and comparing is cheap: selection sort makes the fewest moves.
                    • Many numbers and a guarantee: heap sort, O(n lg n) whatever the input and no extra memory. Chapter 10 adds merge sort and quicksort, and proves that no comparison-based sort can do better than about n lg n.
                    • You need “the biggest, now” again and again, with new items arriving: not a sort at all but a priority queue (part 9).
                    • Bubble sort: it is in the course because it is the easiest to analyse (inversions!). In practice, nobody chooses it.

                    Part 11 · The chapter on one page

                    Summary and self-test

                    The chapter on one page

                    IdeaIn one line
                    The modelwe learn about the order only by comparing two elements; we count comparisons and swaps
                    Inversiona pair out of order (bigger on the left); a sorted list has 0, a reversed one n(n−1)/2, an average one n(n−1)/4 (pair every list with its reverse)
                    Adjacent swapremoves exactly one inversion, so neighbour-swapping sorts are Ω(n2) on average
                    Bubble sortscan, swap neighbours; after pass k the k biggest are at the end; n(n−1)/2 comparisons; Θ(n2)
                    Insertion sortslide each number into the sorted part; swaps = inversions; Θ(n2) average and worst, Θ(n) if sorted; on-line
                    Selection sortfind the maximum, swap it into place; always n(n−1)/2 comparisons, at most n−1 swaps
                    Heapleft-complete binary tree stored in an array; parent ≥ children; node i has children 2i, 2i+1 and parent ⌊i/2⌋; the maximum is A[1]
                    Heapifypush a number down, swapping with the larger child; cost = height, O(lg n)
                    BuildHeapHeapify for i = ⌊n/2⌋ down to 1; leaves are skipped; total O(n) (sum of heights)
                    HeapSortBuildHeap, then repeat: swap root with last, shrink, Heapify the root; O(n lg n), in place
                    Priority queueMAXIMUM O(1); INSERT (push up) and DELETE_MAX (swap, Heapify) O(lg n)

                    The theme of the chapter

                    To beat n2 you must stop swapping neighbours and find the next number fast. A heap finds the maximum in one step and repairs itself in lg n steps, so selecting the maximum n times costs n lg n instead of n2.

                    Test yourself

                    1. How many comparisons does the bubble sort of slide 11 make on 8 numbers, whatever they are? How many swaps does it make on 3 2 1?

                      Show the answer

                      Comparisons: 7 + 6 + 5 + 4 + 3 + 2 + 1 = 8 × 7 / 2 = 28. For 3 2 1: pass 1 compares (3,2) swap, (3,1) swap: 2 1 3; pass 2 compares (2,1) swap: 1 2 3. 3 swaps, which is the number of inversions (3 pairs, all out of order).

                    2. How many inversions does 3 1 4 2 have? How many swaps does insertion sort make on it?

                      Show the answer

                      The pairs out of order: (3,1), (3,2), (4,2): 3 inversions. Insertion sort makes exactly one swap per inversion: 3 swaps. (Check: insert 1: swap with 3 → 1 3 4 2; insert 4: none; insert 2: swap with 4, swap with 3 → 1 2 3 4. Three swaps.)

                    3. Why does insertion sort take only O(n) time on a sorted list, while selection sort still takes n2?

                      Show the answer

                      Insertion sort compares each new number with its left neighbour, finds it is not smaller, and stops: one comparison per number, n−1 in all, no swaps. Selection sort has to look at every remaining number in every round to be sure it has found the maximum; it cannot tell that the list was sorted, so it always makes n(n−1)/2 comparisons.

                    4. Explain in a few lines why any sorting algorithm that only swaps neighbours needs about n2/4 swaps on average.

                      Show the answer

                      A list of n different numbers has n(n−1)/4 inversions on average (pair each list with its reverse: together they have all n(n−1)/2 pairs). A sorted list has none, so every inversion must be removed. A swap of two neighbours removes at most one inversion. So at least n(n−1)/4 swaps are needed on average, which is Ω(n2).

                    5. Run selection sort on 5 3 1 4 2. How many comparisons, and how many real moves?

                      Show the answer

                      Round 1 (i = 5): the maximum, 5, is at position 1; swap with position 5: 2 3 1 4 5. Round 2 (i = 4): the maximum of the first four is 4, already at position 4: no move. Round 3 (i = 3): the maximum of 2 3 1 is 3 at position 2; swap with position 3: 2 1 3 4 5. Round 4 (i = 2): the maximum of 2 1 is 2; swap: 1 2 3 4 5. Comparisons 4 + 3 + 2 + 1 = 10; real moves 3 (rounds 1, 3 and 4).

                    6. Is 20 15 18 9 16 7 3 a heap? If not, which node is the problem and how is it fixed?

                      Show the answer

                      Node 2 (15) has children at 4 and 5: 9 and 16. The child 16 is bigger than its parent 15: not a heap. Fix: Heapify(A, 2, 7): swap 15 with its larger child 16, giving 20 16 18 9 15 7 3, which is a heap (15 now has the child 9 and the child positions 10, 11 do not exist).

                    7. In a heap stored in an array, where are the children and the parent of the element at position 13?

                      Show the answer

                      Children at 26 and 27 (if the heap has that many elements); parent at ⌊13/2⌋ = 6.

                    8. Build a heap from 5 3 8 1 9 2 with BuildHeap, showing each step.

                      Show the answer

                      n = 6, so the loop runs for i = 3, 2, 1. i = 3: 8 has one child (A[6] = 2), which is smaller: nothing. i = 2: 3 has children 1 and 9: swap with 9, giving 5 9 8 1 3 2. i = 1: 5 has children 9 and 8: swap with 9, giving 9 5 8 1 3 2; then 5 (now at position 2) has children 1 and 3, both smaller: stop. The heap is 9 5 8 1 3 2, after 2 swaps.

                    9. Why is BuildHeap O(n) and not O(n lg n), although each Heapify can cost lg n?

                      Show the answer

                      A call of Heapify costs at most the height of its node, and most nodes are near the bottom: about half of them are leaves (skipped), a quarter have height 1, an eighth height 2, and so on. The total is the sum of the heights of all nodes, Σ i 2h−i = O(2h) = O(n), because the series 1/2 + 2/4 + 3/8 + … adds up to 2. Only the few nodes near the root can cost about lg n.

                    10. Insert 12 into the heap 16 14 10 8 7 9 3, and then delete the maximum. Show the array each time.

                      Show the answer

                      Insert 12: put it at position 8 (16 14 10 8 7 9 3 12); its parent is position 4 (8 < 12): swap, 16 14 10 12 7 9 3 8; the new parent is position 2 (14 ≥ 12): stop. One swap. Delete max: swap the root with the last, 8 14 10 12 7 9 3 | 16, and forget 16; push 8 down: swap with 14 (the larger child), swap with 12; it reaches position 4, which has no children among positions 1…7. The heap is 14 12 10 8 7 9 3, and 16 was returned.

                    PreviousChapter 8 · Balanced treesNextChapter 10 · Sorting II

                    Slides 1–39 · 10_sort2

                    Sorting II from Scratch

                    Two faster ways to sort: merge sort (cut in half, sort the halves, merge) and quicksort (split by a pivot, sort the parts). Then the surprise: a proof that no method based on comparing can beat about n lg n, and two clever methods, counting sort and radix sort, that escape the proof by not comparing at all.

                    In this chapter

                      Part 1 · Slides 2–3

                      Merge sort

                      The idea: divide, sort, merge slide 2

                      Chapter 9 ended with sorts that need about n2 steps (bubble, insertion, selection) and one that needs n lg n (heap sort). Merge sort is a second way to reach n lg n, and its idea is one you have already met in Chapter 1: solve a big problem by solving smaller copies of it. Sorting a list of 8 numbers is hard. Sorting a list of 1 number is trivial. So:

                      1. Divide the list into two roughly equal halves.
                      2. Sort each half on its own. (How? By the very same method: each half is cut in two, and so on.)
                      3. Merge the two sorted halves into one sorted list.

                      Divide and conquer

                      This pattern has a name: divide and conquer. Cut the problem into smaller problems of the same kind, solve them (by calling yourself), and combine the answers. The slide notes say merge sort “uses the divide and conquer paradigm”.

                      The only new piece: merging slide 2

                      The clever part is step 3. Merging looks like a lot of work, but it is easy because the two halves are already sorted. Imagine two queues of people, each lined up from the shortest to the tallest, and you must make one queue. You only ever need to compare the two people at the front: the shorter of the two is the shortest of everybody who is left, so he goes next. Repeat. The slide shows exactly this with the lists 1 13 24 26 and 2 15 27 28: first 1 (against 2), then 2 (against 13), then 13 (against 15), and so on, taking away the front of one list each time.

                      Merging two sorted lists, one front number at a time

                      Every comparison puts one number into its final place in the output, so merging n numbers in all takes at most n−1 comparisons, and the walk along the two lists costs O(n) time. The last numbers of one list are copied without any comparison when the other list is used up.

                      The code slide 3

                      MergeSort (A, low, high)

                      sort the part A[low…high] of the list.

                      /* sort the subarray A[low..high] */

                      (a comment on the slide).

                      if (high > low) {

                      more than one number? If high = low there is one number, which is already sorted: do nothing. This is the base case that stops the recursion.

                      mid = floor ((low+high)/2);

                      the middle position: the cut.

                      MergeSort(A,low,mid);

                      sort the left half (a smaller copy of the same problem).

                      MergeSort(A,mid+1,high);

                      sort the right half.

                      Merge(A, low, mid, high);

                      combine: A[low…mid] and A[mid+1…high] are both sorted, merge them into a sorted A[low…high].

                      } }

                      end of the if and of the procedure.

                      To sort the whole list, call MergeSort(A, 1, n). Compare with Chapter 1: this is a recursive function with a base case and two recursive calls, and the work happens when the calls return, on the way back up.

                      The slide asks two questions. Think first, then reveal.

                      1. What is the complexity of Merge()?

                        Show the answer

                        O(n) for n = high − low + 1 numbers: one walk along the two halves, each comparison puts one number in place (previous demo).

                      2. What is the complexity of MergeSort()?

                        Show the answer

                        O(n lg n). The next sections show why. (The notes of slide 3 write the recurrence T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n): two calls on half the list, plus the merge.)

                      Watching it run slides 2–3

                      This demo draws every call of MergeSort as a box, one row per level of cutting, with the whole list on top. Watch three things: the list is cut again and again down to single numbers (the recursion going down); then boxes turn green from the bottom up as merges happen (the recursion coming back); and the left half is always finished completely before the right half is started.

                      MergeSort, call by call

                      Why n lg n? slide 3 notes

                      Count the work level by level. At the top level one merge handles all n numbers: about n comparisons. At the next level two merges each handle n/2 numbers: together again about n. At the next, four merges of n/4: again about n. Every level costs about n. How many levels are there? Each level halves the pieces, from n numbers down to 1, which takes lg n halvings. So the total is about n times lg n.

                      The cost of each level of merging

                      The same thing as an equation. Write T(n) for the time to sort n numbers, and say the merge costs c n. Then T(n) = 2T(n/2) + c n. Replace T(n/2) by the same formula, again and again:

                      T(n) = 2T(n/2) + cn = 4T(n/4) + 2cn = 8T(n/8) + 3cn = … = nT(1) + c n lg n

                      After k rounds the formula has 2k pieces of size n/2k and has paid k c n for the merges. It stops when the pieces have size 1, that is when 2k = n, k = lg n. So T(n) = O(n lg n), and unlike quicksort (next parts) this holds whatever the input: merge sort always cuts exactly in the middle.

                      The price: extra memory

                      Merge cannot work inside the list itself without overwriting numbers it still needs, so it copies the two halves into temporary space. As the slide notes say: if the input is an array, merge sort needs O(n) extra space. The other sorts of Chapter 9 (and quicksort, next) work in place.

                      Part 2 · Slides 4–7

                      Quick sort: split by a pivot

                      The idea slide 4

                      Merge sort does its hard work at the end, in the merge. Quick sort keeps the divide-and-conquer idea but moves the hard work to the beginning, so that nothing has to be merged afterwards. How? Before cutting the list in two, rearrange it so that every number in the left part is at most every number in the right part. Then sort the two parts separately: the left part's numbers all belong before the right part's numbers anyway, so once each part is sorted, the whole list is sorted. No merge.

                      The slide notes add: quicksort is very fast in practice, and it needs no second array (the numbers are rearranged inside the list). It does use a little stack space for the recursive calls, which we come back to in part 4.

                      The key phase: partitioning slide 5

                      The rearranging step is called partitioning, and the plan is:

                      1. Pick any number from the list. It is called the pivot, v.
                      2. Move every number that is smaller than v to the left of it.
                      3. Move every number that is bigger than v to the right of it.
                      4. Numbers equal to v may go on either side.

                      Which number should be the pivot? For now, the slides take the first element. (Part 5 shows why this is a risky choice.) The notes say: “the pivot is like the root of a binary search tree”: just as the root of a BST splits the other keys into smaller on the left and bigger on the right (Chapter 7), the pivot splits the list. And just as with a BST, the choice of the root (here, the pivot) decides how well balanced everything is.

                      The code of PARTITION slide 6

                      The slide gives a neat way to do it with two fingers, i on the left and j on the right, walking toward each other. Here is the code, then a line-by-line reading:

                      PARTITION (A, p, r) {

                      partition the part A[p…r] of the list.

                      v = A[p]

                      the pivot is the first number of the part.

                      i=p-1; j=r+1

                      two fingers start just outside the part: i one place before it, j one place after.

                      while (TRUE) {

                      repeat until the return inside ends it.

                      do j--; while (A[j] > v);

                      move j left (first step, then test). Keep moving while A[j] is bigger than v: such a number is already on the right side. Stop at a number ≤ v.

                      do i++; while (A[i] < v);

                      move i right. Keep moving while A[i] is smaller than v. Stop at a number ≥ v.

                      if (i<j)

                      both fingers stopped, and i is still to the left of j: the number at i is on the wrong (left) side, the number at j is on the wrong (right) side...

                      swap(A[i],A[j]);

                      ...so swap them. Now both are on the correct side. Go round again.

                      else return(j)

                      the fingers have met or crossed: everything left of them is ≤ v, everything right of them is ≥ v. Return j, the place where the cut is.

                      } }

                      end of the loop and of the procedure (the slide leaves out the semicolons after the first while; C would need them).

                      A do … while loop does the step first and tests afterwards. That is why the fingers start outside the part: the first j-- moves j onto A[r], the first i++ moves i onto A[p].

                      The loop invariant (slide 6 notes)

                      At every moment: the numbers in A[p…i−1] are at most v; the numbers in A[j+1…r] are at least v; the numbers between the fingers, A[i…j], still need to be looked at. When the fingers meet, nothing is left to look at, so A[p…j] ≤ v ≤ A[j+1…r].

                      An example, by hand slide 7

                      The slide partitions 5 3 2 6 4 1 3 7. The pivot is v = 5.

                      1. j moves left from outside: 7 is bigger than 5, keep going; 3 is not bigger, stop (position 7). i moves right: the first number is 5, not smaller than 5, stop (position 1). i < j: swap 5 and 3. The list is 3 3 2 6 4 1 5 7.
                      2. j moves on: 1 is not bigger than 5, stop (position 6). i moves on: 3 and 2 are smaller than 5, keep going; 6 is not, stop (position 4). i < j: swap 6 and 1. The list is 3 3 2 1 4 6 5 7.
                      3. j moves on: 4 is not bigger than 5, stop (position 5). i moves on: 4 is smaller than 5, keep going; 6 is not, stop (position 6). Now i = 6 ≥ j = 5: the fingers have crossed. Return j = 5.

                      The result, as in picture (e) of the slide: 3 3 2 1 4 | 6 5 7. Everything left of the bar is at most 5, everything right of it is at least 5. Notice that the pivot 5 itself is not necessarily at the cut: it moved to position 7 in the first swap. Only the two parts matter. Now run it yourself; try the sorted, reversed and all-equal lists too.

                      PARTITION, one comparison at a time

                      Why the returned j is always inside the part slide 6 notes

                      The slide notes say PARTITION is called only when p < r (at least two numbers), and that j-- is executed at least twice because A[p] = v. Here is why that matters. The first scan of j certainly stops at p at the latest, because A[p] = v is not bigger than v. So j never falls off the left end, and the returned j is at least p. And the returned j is strictly less than r: either the first scan already stopped before r, or it stopped at r, in which case i = p < j = r, a swap happens and j moves left at least once more. The consequence: both parts, A[p…j] and A[j+1…r], always contain at least one number. That is what stops the recursion in the next part from going round in circles.

                      Each number is looked at about once by one of the two fingers, so PARTITION on a part of s numbers costs about s comparisons (the demo shows s + 1 or s + 2: the two fingers each look at one number too many when they cross), and at most about s/2 swaps, because each swap fixes two numbers at once.

                      Part 3 · Slide 8

                      Quick sort: the recursion

                      The code slide 8

                      With PARTITION in hand, quicksort is short:

                      QuickSort (A,p,r) {

                      sort the part A[p…r].

                      if (p<r) {

                      two or more numbers? If p = r there is one number: nothing to do (the base case).

                      q = PARTITION(A,p,r);

                      rearrange so that A[p…q] ≤ A[q+1…r] and get the cut q.

                      QuickSort(A,p,q);

                      sort the left part.

                      QuickSort(A,q+1,r);

                      sort the right part.

                      } }

                      end of the if and of the procedure.

                      To sort the whole array: QuickSort(A,1,n). Compare with MergeSort of part 1: same shape, two recursive calls on the two parts. The difference is where the work is: MergeSort works after the calls return (merging), QuickSort works before the calls (partitioning), and afterwards there is nothing left to do.

                      The slide asks: can we guarantee q < r? Think about why that matters first. If q could equal r, the call QuickSort(A,p,q) would be the very same call as the one we are in, and the program would repeat itself forever.

                      1. Can we guarantee q < r?

                        Show the answer

                        Yes. Part 2 showed that the j returned by PARTITION is always strictly less than r (and at least p), when p < r. So both calls get a part with at least one number fewer than A[p…r], and the recursion has to stop.

                      Watching it run slide 8

                      As with merge sort, each call is a box and each row is one level of the recursion. A bar after a number marks where PARTITION cut the box in two. A call’s children appear only after PARTITION has run. Try the sorted list, then change the Pivot menu to middle number or median of three and run the same list again: the picture becomes much shallower. That is the whole story of the next two parts.

                      QuickSort, call by call

                      Notice

                      Unlike merge sort, the pieces are not always halves. The shape of the tree of calls depends on the numbers: it is chosen by the pivots. A good pivot cuts the part near the middle, a bad pivot cuts off one or two numbers. How fast quicksort is depends entirely on how even the cuts are.

                      Part 4 · Slides 9–15

                      Quick sort: how fast?

                      What decides the speed slide 9

                      One PARTITION of a part with n numbers costs about n comparisons and at most about n/2 swaps. After that, the two parts are sorted by recursive calls. If the cut gives a left part of k numbers and a right part of n−k, then:

                      T(n) = T(k) + T(n−k) + O(n)

                      The cost of the partition, O(n), is the same for every k. What changes is the size of the two sub-problems, so the efficiency depends on how even the two parts are.

                      The worst case: the list is already sorted slide 10

                      Take the sorted list 1 2 3 … n. The pivot is the first number, 1: the smallest of all. Nothing is smaller than the pivot, so the left part has just the pivot, and the right part has everything else. The next call has n−1 sorted numbers and meets the same fate. The picture of the slide:

                      • 1 2 3 … n: cost about n, and it only puts one number in place.
                      • 2 3 … n: cost about n−1.
                      • …
                      • n−1 n: cost about 2.

                      The total is the sum of a staircase:

                      Σi=2n i = (n+2)(n−1)2 = Θ(n2)

                      That is as slow as bubble sort: quicksort’s worst case is O(n2). (The same happens if the list is in reverse order, or nearly sorted.) See it as a table: every row is one PARTITION call. With the first pivot the splits are always 1 + (size−1). Change Pivot to middle number to see the sorted list cut in halves instead.

                      Every PARTITION call of one run, in a table

                      Counting precisely

                      The slide says the cost of a partition is “about n”; the program of slide 6 actually looks at n + 1 or n + 2 numbers (the fingers overshoot by one each). Over the whole sorted list that adds about n in all, which changes nothing about the n2 growth.

                      The best case: even cuts slide 11

                      The best case is when every partition cuts its part into two roughly equal halves. Then, with T(n) the number of comparisons for n numbers:

                      T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n = 4T(n/4) + 2n = 8T(n/8) + 3n = … = nT(1) + n lg n

                      This is exactly the merge-sort equation of part 1: the same n per level and lg n levels. The slide ends with T(n) = n ⌈lg n⌉, using T(1) = 0 (one number needs no comparison), and concludes: the best case is O(n lg n) (slide 12).

                      The average case slides 12–15

                      The worst case is terrible, the best case is good. What happens on a typical list? The slides answer by averaging. Assume the numbers are all different and arrive in random order. Then the pivot (the first number) is equally likely to be the 1st, 2nd, …, nth smallest, each with probability 1/n. If the pivot is the kth smallest, the cut gives parts of about k and n−k numbers (slide 13 lists them: the pivot being the smallest or second smallest both give T(1) and T(n−1), then T(2) and T(n−2), and so on). Averaging over the n equally likely pivots:

                      T(n) = 1n ( T(1) + T(n−1) + Σq=1n−1 [ T(q) + T(n−q) ] ) + n

                      The first term, the sum over q, is the average of the costs of the sub-problems; the extra n is the cost of the partition. Slide 14 rewrites it (using T(1) = 0 and that T(n−1) is at most c′n2 for some constant c′, which folds the two special terms into the constant c), and the sum of T(q) + T(n−q) over all q counts every T(q) twice:

                      T(n) ≤ 2n Σq=1n−1 T(q) + cn

                      The slide solves this recurrence by induction (the notes say so) and obtains T(n) = O(n lg n) on average (slide 15). We will not redo the induction; the experiment below does the job of convincing: on random lists the comparison count is close to n lg n times a small constant (about 1.5 in our counting).

                      Why the average is so much better than the worst case

                      You do not need perfect halves. Even if every cut were as lopsided as 10% / 90%, the bigger piece shrinks to nine tenths of its size each time, so there are only about 6.6 lg n levels, each costing at most n: still O(n lg n). Only really lopsided cuts, again and again, are fatal, and on a random list they are very unlikely.

                      Quicksort in practice slide 15

                      The slide says: QuickSort is the fastest known sorting algorithm in practice (if programmed right). Although it is O(n lg n), same as heap sort, it has a smaller constant factor. “Same big-O” does not mean “same speed”: big-O hides the constant in front. Quicksort does little work per number: it scans the list sequentially from both ends and swaps, with no tree to climb (heap sort) and no copying into a second array (merge sort).

                      Stack space

                      Quicksort needs no second array, which is why the slide notes say O(1) extra space. Strictly, the recursive calls use stack space for the pending right parts: about lg n levels when the cuts are even, but up to n levels in the worst case. A common trick (not in the slides) is to recurse into the smaller part first and loop on the larger one, which keeps the stack at O(lg n) always.

                      Part 5 · Slide 16

                      Picking the pivot

                      The pivot is the whole game slide 16

                      Everything in quicksort hangs on the pivot: it should cut the list near the middle. The best possible pivot is the median, the middle number in sorted order, because then both parts have half of the numbers. Slide 16 lists the ideas.

                      • The first element (what our code does). It is quick to get, but bad if the list is mostly sorted: then the first element is nearly the smallest, and the cuts are lopsided. We saw the worst case on a completely sorted list. Lists in real programs are very often partly sorted, so this is a real danger.
                      • The median itself. Ideal, but “picking the median is expensive”. The notes add that it is possible to find the median in O(n) time, but the constant hidden in the big-O is large, so in practice it is not worth it.
                      • A random element. “Randomly” pick an element of the list instead of the first: choose a random position, swap that number with the first one, and then run the same PARTITION as before. Now no particular input is bad: the unlucky pivots are random and are very unlikely to happen again and again. The average-case analysis of part 4 then applies to any input, not just to random lists.
                      • The median of three. Pick three elements (for example the first, the middle and the last), find the median of those three, and use it as the pivot. Three numbers are cheap to compare, and the median of three is rarely the extreme of the list. For a sorted list, the middle element is exactly the median.

                      Why the code can stay the same

                      All of these rules only decide which number is moved to position p before PARTITION runs. The partition code itself, which assumes the pivot is A[p], does not change.

                      Compare the rules slides 13–16

                      This experiment runs quicksort with four pivot rules, and merge sort and heap sort for reference, on the same lists, and counts comparisons. Start with the random lists, then try already sorted and reverse order (the first-number rule explodes), then nearly sorted, then all numbers equal. Grow n and watch the first-number bars.

                      Four pivot rules, merge sort and heap sort

                      Two things to notice. First, on the random lists the four rules are all close to each other, as the average-case analysis predicts: the pivot rule only matters for inputs with structure. Second, the all-equal list does not hurt quicksort here, thanks to a design detail of the partition: both fingers stop on numbers equal to the pivot and swap them, which cuts a list of equal numbers into halves. (A partition that never swapped equal numbers would treat them all as “smaller” and cut off one number at a time.) This is why the slide says “elements that equal v can be put either left or right”.

                      Part 6 · Slides 17–20

                      How fast can sorting be? The detective game

                      The question slide 17

                      Merge sort and heap sort take O(n lg n) time, on average and in the worst case. Quicksort reaches it on average. A natural question: could there be a method that is even faster? How much time is necessary? The slides show that for all methods of a certain kind the answer is: n lg n, no less. The notes say what the kind is: merge sort and heap sort are comparison based. Their only way of learning about the numbers is to compare two of them (the model of Chapter 9, slide 3: the boxes are closed; compare two, or swap two).

                      To prove such a thing we need a way to talk about every possible algorithm of that kind at once. The slides do it with a game.

                      A detective game slide 18

                      There are ten suspects, numbered 1 to 10. One of them is the murderer. You may ask questions that have only yes or no as an answer (“is it a man?”), and your goal is to find the murderer with as few questions as possible. What would you ask?

                      The silly plan is to ask “Is it No. 1? Is it No. 2? …”: up to 9 questions. A clever plan asks questions that split the suspects in two: “is it a man?” (suspects 1–5 versus 6–10), then something that splits the remaining five, and so on.

                      The decision tree slides 19–20

                      Decision tree

                      A decision tree is a binary tree. Each node represents the set of possible events that are consistent with the information obtained so far. Each question is a node with two children: one for the answer yes, one for the answer no.

                      The tree of slide 20 is drawn below, and you can choose the murderer. The root knows nothing: all ten suspects are possible. After “is it a man?” only five are left on each side, and so on, until one suspect is left (a box at the bottom).

                      The decision tree of the detective game

                      Two facts to take with you:

                      • Every possible murderer must have a box of his own, a leaf of the tree, otherwise the plan could not tell him apart from someone else. So there are at least 10 leaves.
                      • A tree of height h (the longest path from the top has h questions) has at most 2h leaves, because every question at most doubles the number of branches. To have 10 leaves you need 2h ≥ 10, so h ≥ 4. No plan, however clever, can always find the murderer in fewer than 4 questions. The tree of the slide uses 3 questions for some suspects and 4 for others, 4 at most: it is optimal in the worst case.

                      Now, sorting is also a game of 20 questions. The “suspects” are the possible orders of the input, and the “questions” are the comparisons.

                      Part 7 · Slides 21–24

                      Sorting as a decision tree

                      How many orders are there? slide 21

                      Given n unsorted numbers A[1…n], the list can be in any of n! possible orders (n choices for the smallest’s position, then n−1, …). The slide lists the six orders of three elements, written as <1,2,3> meaning “A[1] is the smallest, then A[2], then A[3]”:

                      if the list satisfiesthe answer to give
                      A[1] < A[2] < A[3]<1,2,3>
                      A[1] < A[3] < A[2]<1,3,2>
                      A[2] < A[1] < A[3]<2,1,3>
                      A[2] < A[3] < A[1]<2,3,1>
                      A[3] < A[1] < A[2]<3,1,2>
                      A[3] < A[2] < A[1]<3,2,1>

                      The notes say: “to sort an array correctly means that the relative order of the elements in the input is known by the algorithm at the end.” Sorting is the detective game with n! suspects: the unknown is which of the n! orders the input is in.

                      Every comparison sort is a decision tree slides 22–23

                      If element-to-element comparisons are the only operations allowed, then whatever algorithm sorts the list can be described by a binary decision tree:

                      • every round node is one comparison, written ai:aj (“which of the ith and jth input numbers is smaller?”);
                      • it has two children, one for each answer, < and > (we look at distinct numbers; the notes say “each comparison can produce only 2 possible answers”);
                      • every leaf is a verdict: the order the algorithm has concluded, such as <2,3,1>.

                      Slide 23 draws the tree of insertion sort on 3 elements. Choose your own three numbers below and follow the highlighted path. You can also try the trees of other algorithms, and 4 elements (24 leaves). For bubble sort and selection sort some boxes are dashed: those algorithms ask a question whose answer they already know from earlier answers. Such comparisons never help, and the tree gets taller than necessary.

                      The decision tree of a sorting algorithm

                      The tree measures the cost slide 24

                      Running the algorithm on one particular input means walking one path from the root to a leaf. The number of comparisons used is the length of that path, i.e. the depth of the leaf. So:

                      • the worst-case number of comparisons is the depth of the deepest leaf: the height of the tree;
                      • the average number of comparisons is the average depth of the leaves (if all orders are equally likely).

                      The whole question of how fast a comparison sort can be has become a question about trees: in order to get the lower bound of sorting for the comparison-based model, we need to find the minimal height of a binary decision tree with n! leaves.

                      1. Why n! leaves?

                        Show the answer

                        The tree must be able to answer correctly for every possible input, and different input orders need different answers (different sorted arrangements of the original positions). So each of the n! possible orders ends at a leaf of its own. (If two different orders ended in the same leaf, the algorithm would give both the same answer, and it would be wrong for one of them.) The tree may have more leaves than n! if the algorithm is wasteful, but never fewer.

                      Part 8 · Slides 25–28

                      The lower bound: n lg n

                      Step 1: a tree of height h has few leaves slide 25

                      Lemma 1

                      A binary tree of height h has at most 2h leaves.

                      Why: the root level has one node. Every node has at most two children, so each level has at most twice as many nodes as the one above. At depth h there are at most 2h nodes, and every leaf is at depth at most h (and can be thought of as extended down to it).

                      Step 2: put the two facts together slide 25

                      The decision tree for sorting n elements has height h and at least n! leaves (part 7). The lemma says it has at most 2h leaves. Therefore:

                      2h ≥ n! ⇒ h ≥ lg(n!)

                      The height is at least lg(n!). So how big is lg(n!)? The next steps show it is about n lg n.

                      Step 3: an upper estimate for n! slide 25

                      n! = 1·2·3·…·n is a product of n numbers, each at most n, so

                      n! = 1 × 2 × 3 × … × n ≤ n × n × n × … × n = nn

                      and therefore lg(n!) ≤ n lg n. That is the easy side. We need the other side: n! cannot be much smaller than nn.

                      Step 4: a lower estimate, by pairing slides 25–26

                      First a little fact. For every k from 0 to n−1:

                      (k+1)(n−k) = k(n−k) + (n−k) ≥ k + (n−k) = n

                      (In the middle step, k(n−k) ≥ k because n−k ≥ 1.) So the product of the number k+1 counted from the beginning and the number n−k counted from the end is always at least n. Now write n! twice, once forwards, once backwards, and multiply place by place:

                      (n!)2 = [n (n−1) … 2 × 1] × [1 × 2 … (n−1) n] = Πk=0n−1 (k+1)(n−k) ≥ n × n × … × n = nn

                      So (n!)2 ≥ nn, and taking the square root, n! ≥ nn/2. Try different n in the table: every pair is at least n.

                      Every pair (k+1)(n−k) is at least n

                      Step 5: the conclusion slide 27

                      Putting the two estimates together:

                      nn/2 ≤ n! ≤ nn ⇒ n2 lg n ≤ lg(n!) ≤ n lg n ⇒ lg(n!) = Θ(n lg n)

                      Since the height h of the decision tree is at least lg(n!), h is Ω(n lg n). This is the theorem:

                      Theorem (slide 27)

                      Any sorting algorithm that uses only comparisons between elements takes Ω(n lg n) time in the worst case.

                      See the numbers for small n and check that nothing is hidden: for n = 5, lg 120 ≈ 6.9, so every comparison sort needs at least 7 comparisons for some input of five numbers (merge sort uses 8 at worst, insertion sort 10).

                      lg(n!) against (n/2) lg n and n lg n

                      What this tells us about the sorts you know: merge sort and heap sort (and quicksort on average) are as fast as a comparison sort can be, up to a constant factor. The simple sorts of Chapter 9, at n2, are not.

                      For your interest slide 28

                      The proof above is about the worst case. The slide adds that the same bound holds on average: the average depth of a leaf in a binary tree with n! leaves is also Ω(n lg n) (the notes say this can be proved by induction), so even on average, a comparison sort cannot beat n lg n. This is beyond what you need to prove in this course.

                      Part 9 · Slides 29–34

                      Counting sort: sorting without comparing

                      A way out of the theorem slide 29

                      The theorem of part 8 has a condition: only comparisons between elements. If we know something extra about the numbers, we need not obey it. Suppose every input number is a whole number in the range 1 to k, for some “small” k (ages, exam marks 1 to 10, the digits 0 to 9, …). Then we can sort in less than O(n lg n) time.

                      The idea: for each number x, count how many numbers are smaller than x. If 7 numbers are smaller than x, then x belongs in position 8. Counting tells us the final position of every number directly, without ever asking “is this bigger than that?” for two input numbers.

                      A first example slide 30

                      The slide takes 34 8 64 51 32 21 (all different) and counts, for each number, how many of the others are smaller:

                      number34864513221
                      smaller ones305421
                      goes to position416532

                      Writing each number in its position gives 8 21 32 34 51 64. The notes point out that in this example all keys are different. Real data has repeated keys, and then the idea needs more care, which is what the actual algorithm provides.

                      The algorithm: three arrays slide 31

                      • A[1…n] is the input.
                      • B[1…n] is the output.
                      • C[1…k] is the counting array: one counter for every possible key. At the end of the first steps, C[i] is the number of elements in A that are at most i.

                      The notes make the key observation: the last occurrence of key k must occupy position C[k] of the final array. (All the C[k] numbers at most k fill the places 1 to C[k], and the ones equal to k come last among them.) The extra space is O(n + k).

                      The code slide 32

                      CountingSort(A,k) {

                      A is the input with n numbers, each between 1 and k.

                      1) for (i=1;i<=k;i++) C[i] = 0;

                      start every counter at 0. k steps.

                      2) for (j=1; j<=n; j++) C[A[j]]++;

                      for every input number, add 1 to its own counter. Now C[m] = the number of elements equal to m. n steps.

                      3) for (i=2; i<=k; i++) C[i] = C[i] + C[i-1];

                      running total: add the counter before. Now C[m] = the number of elements at most m. k steps.

                      4) for (j=n; j>=1; j--) {

                      go through the input from the back, one number at a time. n steps.

                      B[C[A[j]]] = A[j];

                      C[A[j]] is the position where the last remaining number with this key must go. Put the number there.

                      C[A[j]]--;

                      the next number with the same key goes one place further left.

                      } }

                      end of the loop and of the procedure.

                      Follow it on the example of slide 33: 3 6 4 1 3 4 1 4, with k = 6. Look at the small labels under B: they show which input box each number came from.

                      Counting sort, one step at a time

                      Stable: why line 4 runs backwards slide 32 notes

                      Line 4 scans the input backwards. This makes the sort stable: if two input numbers have the same key, their relative order is the same in the output. Look at the key 4 in the demo: it occurs at A[3], A[6] and A[8]. The last one, A[8], is handled first and takes the last place for key 4; A[6] takes the place before it, and A[3] the one before that. So they stay in the same left-to-right order.

                      Why care, if equal numbers look the same? Because in real data each key carries something else with it (a student’s mark with the student’s name). The notes say it explicitly: we cannot just count how many copies of each key there are and write that many copies of the key, because we must output the pair together. And stability will be essential for radix sort in the next part.

                      How long does it take? slide 34

                      Count the four loops: line 1 takes k steps, line 2 takes n, line 3 takes k, line 4 takes n. Total O(n + k). If k is small, say k ≤ n (or k = O(n)), the time is O(n): linear.

                      1. Did we just prove that any sorting algorithm must take Ω(n lg n) time? In that case, how can counting sort take O(n)?

                        Show the answer

                        No contradiction. The theorem of part 8 is about algorithms that only compare elements. Counting sort never compares two input numbers: it uses a number as an address (C[A[j]]). It gets around the bound by using a special property of the input: the keys are whole numbers in 1…k. The price is that it works only for such keys, and it needs O(n + k) extra space (and if k is huge, say 109 possible keys for 100 numbers, the array C alone is far too big).

                      Part 10 · Slides 35–38

                      Radix sort: one digit at a time

                      Sorting numbers digit by digit slide 35

                      Counting sort needs the keys to be small whole numbers. What if the numbers are big, like 6-digit student numbers? A table with a million counters is too much. Radix sort (the notes call it “an extension of counting sort”) keeps the trick but looks at one digit at a time, and a digit is always small.

                      The slide: suppose we have n integers, each with d digits (shorter numbers are padded with zeros in front), and each digit is in the range 0 to k−1. (k is the radix, or base: 10 for ordinary decimal numbers.) If the numbers are known to lie in a range, we can sort them in “linear time” (the slide puts the words in quotation marks: we will see in what sense).

                      The idea and the code slide 36

                      The idea is to sort by the least significant digit first, and by the most significant digit last. This sounds backwards (we usually look at the biggest digit first, like in a dictionary), but it works, as the demo and the proof below show.

                      RadixSort(A,d) {

                      A is a list of n numbers with d digits each.

                      for (i=1; i<=d; i++) {

                      one pass for each digit, from the rightmost (i = 1) to the leftmost (i = d).

                      prepare k buckets: B[0..k-1];

                      one empty list (bucket) for each possible digit.

                      /* distribution */

                      first half of the pass.

                      scan A from head to tail,

                      go through the list in its current order...

                      for each element x, let m = x's i_th rightmost digit,

                      ...look at the digit of x that this pass is about...

                      append x to the end of bucket B[m];

                      ...and put x at the end of the bucket named by that digit.

                      /* concatenation */

                      second half of the pass.

                      concatenate the bucket lists.

                      join the buckets in the order 0, 1, …, k−1 into one list. This list is the input of the next pass.

                      } }

                      end of the loop and of the procedure.

                      The notes stress: in each pass, the use of lists (appending at the end, reading from the head) makes the pass stable, i.e. numbers with the same digit stay in the order they had before. Alternatively one can use counting sort for each pass, which is also stable.

                      The example of slide 37 slide 37

                      The slide sorts 413 213 313 111 242 412 301, whose digits are all between 0 and 4, so there are k = 5 buckets, 0 to 4, and d = 3 passes.

                      1. Pass 1, rightmost digit. 413 → bucket 3; 213 → 3; 313 → 3; 111 → 1; 242 → 2; 412 → 2; 301 → 1. Bucket 1 holds 111 301, bucket 2 holds 242 412, bucket 3 holds 413 213 313. Concatenate: 111 301 242 412 413 213 313. The list is now ordered by the last digit only.
                      2. Pass 2, middle digit. 111 → 1; 301 → 0; 242 → 4; 412 → 1; 413 → 1; 213 → 1; 313 → 1. Bucket 0: 301; bucket 1: 111 412 413 213 313; bucket 4: 242. Concatenate: 301 111 412 413 213 313 242. Ordered by the last two digits (01, 11, 12, 13, 13, 13, 42).
                      3. Pass 3, leftmost digit. 301 → 3; 111 → 1; 412 → 4; 413 → 4; 213 → 2; 313 → 3; 242 → 2. Bucket 1: 111; 2: 213 242; 3: 301 313; 4: 412 413. Concatenate: 111 213 242 301 313 412 413. Sorted.

                      Run it yourself. The digit a pass looks at is in orange. Try the ordinary decimal list, the binary numbers, and a list with numbers of different lengths (the short ones are padded with zeros in front, so 5 is treated as 0005).

                      Radix sort: distribution and concatenation

                      Why does it work? slide 38

                      The slide states a lemma and asks you to prove it by induction:

                      Lemma

                      After the i-th pass of RadixSort, the n numbers are sorted according to their i rightmost digits.
