                      The proof, in plain words. First pass (i = 1): the buckets are ordered by the rightmost digit, so after concatenating, the list is sorted by that digit. From pass i−1 to pass i: assume the list is sorted by the i−1 rightmost digits. Take two numbers x and y and look at digit i.

                      • If their digits i are different, the one with the smaller digit goes into an earlier bucket, so it comes first: right, because digit i is more important than all the digits to its right.
                      • If their digits i are the same, they go into the same bucket, in the order of scanning, which is the order they had in the list, sorted by the i−1 rightmost digits by assumption. Since digit i is equal, that is also the correct order by the i rightmost digits. This is where stability is needed: if the bucket could shuffle equal-digit numbers, the work of the earlier passes would be destroyed.

                      After pass d the list is sorted by all d digits, which is sorted.

                      How long does it take? slide 38

                      One pass distributes n numbers and collects k buckets: O(n + k). There are d passes:

                      T = O((n + k) d)

                      If the radix k is a constant (or at most n), this is O(nd). For ordinary 6-digit decimal numbers, d = 6 and k = 10: that is about 6 · (n + 10), linear in n. That is the sense of the quotation marks on slide 35: it is linear in n if the number of digits d is fixed.

                      The notes give the general view. If the keys are whole numbers in the range 0 to N−1 and we write them in base k, the number of digits is about d = log N / log k. In particular, if N = kd, we may choose k = n (one bucket per number), and the running time becomes O(n log N / log n). For example, to sort n numbers below n3, use base n and 3 passes: O(3n) = O(n), linear, even though a comparison sort needs n lg n.

                      Again no contradiction with the lower bound

                      Like counting sort, radix sort never compares two numbers with each other: it uses their digits as bucket addresses. It beats n lg n only because it knows more about the input (a limited number of digits, each of limited size).

                      Part 11 · Slide 39 and the whole of sorting

                      All the sorts together

                      Conclusion of the chapter slide 39

                      The last slide lists the two take-aways of this chapter:

                      • Lower bound for comparison-based sorting: a sort that only compares elements needs Ω(n lg n) comparisons (parts 6–8).
                      • Other models of sorting to achieve linear time: if the keys are special (small whole numbers, or numbers with few digits), counting sort and radix sort take O(n) (parts 9–10).

                      The race: seven comparison methods Chapters 9–10

                      Here are the comparison sorts of both chapters on the same lists. Try random lists of growing size, then sorted, reversed and nearly sorted lists. Notice the families: the three simple sorts (blue) grow like n2; heap sort, merge sort and quicksort (green) grow like n lg n; and on special inputs the winners change places.

                      Bubble, insertion, selection, heap, merge and quick sort

                      The big table

                      SortWorst caseAverageBest caseExtra spaceStable?
                      BubbleΘ(n2)Θ(n2)Θ(n2) (the slide code never stops early)O(1)yes
                      InsertionΘ(n2)Θ(n2)Θ(n) (sorted)O(1)yes
                      SelectionΘ(n2)Θ(n2)Θ(n2)O(1)no
                      HeapO(n lg n)O(n lg n)O(n lg n)O(1)no
                      MergeO(n lg n)O(n lg n)O(n lg n)O(n) extra arrayyes
                      QuickO(n2) (bad pivots)O(n lg n)O(n lg n)O(1) plus the recursion stackno
                      CountingO(n + k)O(n + k)O(n + k)O(n + k)yes
                      RadixO((n + k) d)O((n + k) d)O((n + k) d)O(n + k)yes (if each pass is)

                      The first six rows are comparison sorts, so none of them can beat n lg n in the worst case (the theorem), and heap sort and merge sort reach that. The last two are not comparison sorts and need special input. (The “stable?” column is not on the slides except for counting and radix sort; it is true for the versions of the code shown in these chapters, and it matters when records with equal keys must keep their order.)

                      Which one would you use?

                      • A general list, speed matters most: quicksort (with a random or median-of-three pivot), the fastest in practice.
                      • You must have a guarantee, whatever the input: merge sort or heap sort, both O(n lg n) in the worst case. Heap sort needs no extra memory; merge sort needs an extra array but is stable.
                      • Small lists, or lists that are almost in order: insertion sort.
                      • Keys are small whole numbers: counting sort. Numbers with a fixed number of digits: radix sort.

                      Part 12 · The chapter on one page

                      Summary and self-test

                      The chapter on one page

                      IdeaIn one line
                      Merge sortcut in half, sort each half (same method), merge the two sorted halves by comparing the fronts; T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n) = O(n lg n) always; O(n) extra space
                      PARTITIONpivot v = A[p]; finger i from the left stops at a number ≥ v, finger j from the right stops at a number ≤ v; swap; stop when they meet and return j; about n comparisons
                      Quick sortPARTITION, then QuickSort the two parts; no merge, no extra array; best and average O(n lg n), worst O(n2) (sorted list, first-element pivot)
                      Pivot choicefirst (risky), random (swap it to the front), median of three; the median itself is too expensive
                      Decision treea comparison sort is a binary tree: node = comparison, leaf = a possible order; worst case = height
                      Lower boundat least n! leaves, at most 2h, so h ≥ lg(n!) ≥ (n/2) lg n: every comparison sort needs Ω(n lg n) comparisons
                      Counting sortkeys in 1…k: count, running total, place from the back (stable); O(n + k)
                      Radix sortd digits in base k: distribute into buckets and concatenate, rightmost digit first, stably; O((n + k) d)

                      The theme of the chapter

                      Faster than n2 comes from divide and conquer: halving the problem lg n times, with linear work per level. n lg n is the limit for sorting by comparing. To go below it, stop comparing and use the structure of the keys.

                      Test yourself

                      1. Merge the sorted lists 2 5 9 and 1 3 4 10. Show the order in which numbers are taken, and count the comparisons.

                        Show the answer

                        Compare the fronts each time: 2 vs 1 → take 1; 2 vs 3 → 2; 5 vs 3 → 3; 5 vs 4 → 4; 5 vs 10 → 5; 9 vs 10 → 9. The left list is now used up, so 10 is copied without a comparison. Result 1 2 3 4 5 9 10, after 6 comparisons (7 numbers: at most 6).

                      2. How many levels of merging does merge sort need for 8 numbers, and what is the largest number of comparisons it can ever use for 8 numbers?

                        Show the answer

                        lg 8 = 3 levels (pairs of 1, pairs of 2, pairs of 4). The merges at the three levels use at most 4·1 + 2·3 + 1·7 = 4 + 6 + 7 = 17 comparisons: that is n lg n − n + 1 = 24 − 8 + 1 = 17.

                      3. Run PARTITION on 5 3 8 1 9 2 (pivot 5). What is the list afterwards, and what does it return?

                        Show the answer

                        j stops at 2 (position 6), i at 5 (position 1): swap, 2 3 8 1 9 5. Next j passes 9 and stops at 1 (position 4); i passes 3 and stops at 8 (position 3): swap, 2 3 1 8 9 5. Next j stops at 1 (position 3) and i at 8 (position 4): i ≥ j, so it returns j = 3. The parts are 2 3 1 (all ≤ 5) and 8 9 5 (all ≥ 5). 8 comparisons, 2 swaps.

                      4. Quick sort with the first element as pivot is run on the sorted list 1 2 3 4 5 6. What are the sizes of the two parts of each partition, and roughly how many comparisons are made in total?

                        Show the answer

                        The pivot is always the smallest number, so each partition cuts off a part of 1 number and leaves size − 1 numbers for the next call: sizes 6, 5, 4, 3, 2. The costs are about 6, 5, 4, 3, 2 (the slide’s count: (n+2)(n−1)/2 = 20; the program of slide 6 makes one or two more per call, 25 in all). In general about n2/2: Θ(n2).

                      5. Name two ways to avoid this bad behaviour on sorted lists.

                        Show the answer

                        Pick a random element as pivot (swap it with the first, then run the same PARTITION), or take the median of three elements (for example the first, middle and last). For a sorted list the middle element is the median, so both parts are halves. (Picking the true median is possible in O(n) time but with a large constant.)

                      6. You must find one murderer among 100 suspects using yes/no questions. What is the smallest number of questions that always suffices, and why can no plan do better?

                        Show the answer

                        7. Every question has two answers, so q questions can tell apart at most 2q suspects: 26 = 64 < 100 is too few, 27 = 128 ≥ 100 is enough (always ask a question that splits the remaining suspects as evenly as possible). In other words ⌈lg 100⌉ = 7: the decision tree needs 100 leaves and a tree of height h has at most 2h.

                      7. What is the smallest number of comparisons that could possibly be enough to sort 4 numbers in the worst case? How does merge sort compare?

                        Show the answer

                        There are 4! = 24 possible orders, so the decision tree needs 24 leaves, so its height h satisfies 2h ≥ 24, h ≥ ⌈lg 24⌉ = ⌈4.58⌉ = 5. Merge sort needs at most 4·2 − 4 + 1 = 5 comparisons for 4 numbers: it is optimal there. (For 5 numbers the bound is 7 and merge sort needs up to 8.)

                      8. Show that (4!)2 ≥ 44 with the pairing argument of slide 26, and say what it proves about lg(n!).

                        Show the answer

                        The pairs (k+1)(4−k) for k = 0, 1, 2, 3 are 1·4 = 4, 2·3 = 6, 3·2 = 6, 4·1 = 4, each at least 4. Their product is (4!)2 = 576 ≥ 4·4·4·4 = 256 = 44. In general (n!)2 ≥ nn, so n! ≥ nn/2 and lg(n!) ≥ (n/2) lg n: the height of a decision tree for sorting is Ω(n lg n).

                      9. Run counting sort on 2 3 1 3 2 1 2 (k = 3). Give C after line 2 and after line 3, and the output B. Which input boxes does each number of B come from?

                        Show the answer

                        After line 2: C = [2, 3, 2] (two 1s, three 2s, two 3s). After line 3: C = [2, 5, 7]. Line 4 scans A from the back: A[7] = 2 goes to B[5]; A[6] = 1 to B[2]; A[5] = 2 to B[4]; A[4] = 3 to B[7]; A[3] = 1 to B[1]; A[2] = 3 to B[6]; A[1] = 2 to B[3]. Output B = 1 1 2 2 2 3 3, coming from A[3], A[6], A[1], A[5], A[7], A[2], A[4]: equal numbers appear in input order, so the sort is stable. Total steps k + n + k + n = 3 + 7 + 3 + 7.

                      10. Radix sort the numbers 45 12 76 19 41 (base 10). Why must the passes start from the rightmost digit, and why must each pass be stable?

                        Show the answer

                        Pass 1 (units digit): 41 12 45 76 19. Pass 2 (tens digit): bucket 1 gets 12 and 19 (in the order they were in), bucket 4 gets 41 and 45, bucket 7 gets 76: 12 19 41 45 76. Why rightmost first: the last pass decides the final order of numbers with different leading digits, and numbers with the same leading digit must then be in the order given by the digits to their right, which the earlier passes have arranged. Why stable: within a bucket, numbers share the current digit; only the order from the earlier passes can tell them apart, so the pass must not shuffle them (12 stays before 19 in pass 2 because it was before it after pass 1).

                      PreviousChapter 9 · Sorting INextChapter 11 · Huffman coding

                      Slides 1–14 · 11_Huffman_Coding

                      Huffman Coding from Scratch

                      How to write a message with fewer bits. Give common symbols short codewords and rare symbols long ones, but in a way the receiver can still read back, and then find the best such code with a greedy method that uses a heap.

                      In this chapter

                        Part 1 · Slides 2 and 3

                        Codes: turning symbols into bits

                        A computer can only store 0s and 1s, so every letter, colour or command has to be written as a string of bits. A code is the rule that says which string of bits stands for which symbol. The string for one symbol is its codeword.

                        The slide lists three jobs for a code: conversion (changing one form into another, like letters into bits), encryption (hiding the message from people who should not read it) and compression (making the message shorter). This whole chapter is about the third job. The question is: how can the same message be written with fewer bits?

                        Binary coding: every symbol gets the same length slide 2

                        The slide shows a table for the symbols A to F with empty boxes to fill in. Let us fill it in. There are 6 symbols. One bit can name 2 things (0 and 1). Two bits can name 4 things (00, 01, 10, 11). Three bits can name 8 things. So 6 symbols need 3 bits each:

                        symbolABCDEF
                        codeword000001010011100101

                        This is a fixed-length code. It is the first of the three examples on the slide. Reading it back is easy: cut the incoming bits into groups of 3. The price is that A and F cost the same 3 bits, even if A turns up all the time and F almost never.

                        Variable-length coding: short codes for common symbols slide 2

                        You already do this when you text. You write “lol”, not “laughing out loud”, because you use it all the time. Morse code does the same: the most common English letter, E, is a single dot, and rare letters get long patterns. A variable-length code gives codewords of different lengths, short for frequent symbols and long for rare ones.

                        The slide gives two more codes for A to F, both of this kind:

                        symbolABCDEF
                        code 2101001000100001000001
                        code 30001001110011101

                        Which code is best depends on how often each symbol is used. Suppose a message has 100 symbols: A appears 45 times, B 13 times, C 12, D 16, E 9 and F 5. The fixed-length code needs 100 × 3 = 300 bits. Now give A the one-bit codeword 0 and the others 101, 100, 111, 1101, 1100 (B to F). The cost is 45·1 + 13·3 + 12·3 + 16·3 + 9·4 + 5·4 = 45 + 39 + 36 + 48 + 36 + 20 = 224 bits. That saves a quarter of the space, only by choosing codeword lengths to match how often symbols occur.

                        The idea of the chapter

                        Frequent symbol → short codeword. Rare symbol → long codeword. The art is to do it so that the receiver can still tell where each codeword ends.

                        The catch: the receiver sees no gaps slide 3

                        With a fixed-length code the receiver knows every codeword has 3 bits. With a variable-length code the bits arrive in one long stream, like 11010010010101011, with no spaces. Where does one codeword stop and the next begin?

                        Slide 3 shows two codes for the letters E, T, N, I, S and asks you to decode a bit string with each of them.

                        symbolETNISbits to decode
                        first code0111001010101111010010010101011
                        second code01010001111010100100101010

                        With the first code there is only one way to cut the bits: 11 · 0 · 100 · 100 · 1010 · 1011, which is T E N N I S, the word TENNIS. With the second code, the slide writes the word Ambiguous. The same bits can be read in many ways, as you can check yourself below. Try it, and press Enter after changing a box.

                        How many ways can these bits be read?

                        Ambiguous

                        A code is ambiguous if two different messages can produce the same bits. A receiver cannot decode such a code, however clever it is. The second code on slide 3 has 12 different readings of one 12-bit string. The next part says what goes wrong and how to avoid it.

                        Part 2 · Slide 4

                        Prefix codes: no codeword starts another

                        The rule slide 4

                        Prefix code

                        A code is a prefix code if no codeword is the beginning (the prefix) of another codeword.

                        “Beginning” means the first few characters, just as “pre” is the beginning of “prefix”. So 10 is a prefix of 101 and of 1000, but not of 011 or of 1. The name is slightly confusing: a prefix code is a code without such clashes (some books say “prefix-free”).

                        Why this makes reading easy

                        Read the bits one at a time. The moment the bits you have read spell a codeword, stop: that is the symbol. In a prefix code that codeword cannot be the beginning of a longer one (that is the whole rule), so you never have a choice and never have to look ahead. Write down the symbol, forget the bits, and start again. That is exactly how the first code on slide 3 gave TENNIS.

                        Now see why the second code of slide 3 fails. There T = 10 is the beginning of N = 100 and of S = 1010, and E = 0 is the beginning of I = 0111. After reading 10 you cannot know: is it a T, or the first two bits of an N or an S? Both could be true, so both readings survive, and the number of readings multiplies.

                        Which of these codes are prefix codes? slide 4

                        Slide 4 gives three codes for A to F, and the words “prefix code” and “uniquely decodable”. Check each one by asking, for every codeword, “does another codeword start with this?”.

                        codeABCDEFprefix code?
                        10001001110011101yes: no codeword starts another
                        2101001000100001000001yes: every codeword ends at its first 1, which acts as a full stop
                        3001011000111000101no: 00 starts 0001, 10 starts 101, 11 starts 11000

                        Type your own codes into the box below (write each as symbol=bits) and the picture shows at once whether it is a prefix code. The tree is explained in the next part; for now, red nodes mean a clash.

                        Is it a prefix code?

                        Prefix versus uniquely decodable

                        Slide 4 puts the words “prefix code” and “uniquely decodable” side by side. Every prefix code is uniquely decodable, as shown above. The other direction is false: the code 0, 01 is not a prefix code, yet 001 can only be read as 0 · 01. But such a code forces the receiver to look ahead, which makes decoding messier. Beyond the slides, and not examined: it is a known fact that you lose nothing by sticking to prefix codes, because every uniquely decodable code can be replaced by a prefix code with the same codeword lengths.

                        Part 3 · Slides 5 and 6

                        Prefix codes are binary trees

                        Draw the code as a tree slide 5

                        Every prefix code can be drawn as a binary tree (the trees of Chapter 5). The drawing rule is: start at the root, and let each bit tell you which way to go. 0 means go left, 1 means go right. A codeword is the list of turns from the root down to the symbol. Slide 5 draws the code A = 00, B = 010, C = 0110, D = 0111, E = 10, F = 11:

                        Look at where the symbols sit: all at the bottom, at leaves. That is no accident. It is the prefix rule seen as a picture. If a symbol sat on an inner node, the path down to the symbols below it would pass through that node, so the symbol’s codeword would be the beginning of their codewords.

                        Prefix code, as a picture

                        A code is a prefix code exactly when every symbol is at a leaf of its tree. The codeword length of a symbol is the depth of its leaf (the number of edges from the root).

                        Decoding is walking down the tree

                        The tree also gives the decoding method, with no table lookup at all. Start at the root. Read a bit, step left or right. If you land on a leaf, write down its symbol and jump back to the root. If you land on an inner node, read the next bit. Use Next step to watch the bits of TENNIS being read, and try the other codes.

                        Decode by walking the tree

                        The exercise on slide 6: build the tree from the code slide 6

                        The slide gives E = 0, T = 11, N = 100, I = 1010, S = 1011 and asks you to construct the tree. Do it one codeword at a time, always starting from the root:

                        1. E = 0. One step left from the root. Put E there.
                        2. T = 11. Right, then right. Put T there. (The node reached after the first 1 is now an inner node.)
                        3. N = 100. Right, then left (that creates the inner node 10), then left again. Put N there.
                        4. I = 1010. Right, left, right (a new inner node 101), then left. Put I there.
                        5. S = 1011. The same path, but the last step is right. Put S there.

                        The picture below is that tree. You can also type any code into the box, and it draws the tree and tells you whether the code is a prefix code.

                        Code in, tree out

                        Why the best trees have no half-empty inner nodes

                        Look for dashed circles when you try codes: they mark a branch that no codeword uses. If some inner node had only one child, you could delete that node and pull everything below it up by one level. Every codeword below it would become one bit shorter, and there would still be no clashes. So in a best-possible code every inner node has two children (the tree is full). The trees of slides 5, 6 and 8 are all full.

                        Part 4 · Slides 7 and 8

                        How good is a code? The average cost

                        Weights and depths slide 7

                        To compare two codes we have to know how often each symbol is used. Give symbol i a weight wi. The weight can be a count (“A appears 45 times”), a percentage or a probability, and it is just a measure of how common the symbol is. Its codeword has a length di, which is the depth of its leaf in the tree.

                        Sending symbol i once costs di bits. It is sent about wi times (if wi is a count). So the whole message costs wi × di bits for this symbol, and the total over all symbols is:

                        C(T) = Σ wi × di

                        The slide gives this one number several names: the average cost (bits per symbol, when the weights are probabilities that add up to 1), the average leaf depth (the depth of a leaf, averaged with each leaf counted according to its weight) and the weighted path length C(T). They are the same idea. A Huffman tree is a tree whose C(T) is as small as possible.

                        Why “weighted”

                        A leaf near the root with a big weight is cheap; the same leaf deep down is expensive. The weight says how much the depth matters. That is why the cheapest trees put the heavy leaves high and the light leaves low.

                        The worked example on slide 8 slide 8

                        The slide gives five symbols with their codewords and probabilities: A = 00 with 14, B = 010 with 18, C = 0110 with 116, D = 0111 with 116 and E = 1 with 12. Compute the average leaf depth by multiplying each length by its probability:

                        14 × 2 + 18 × 3 + 116 × 4 + 116 × 4 + 12 × 1= 12 + 38 + 14 + 14 + 12 = 158 = 1.875

                        So this code uses 1.875 bits per symbol on average. A fixed-length code for 5 symbols needs 3 bits (because 22 = 4 is too few and 23 = 8 is enough). The saving is (3 − 1.875) / 3 = 37.5%.

                        A common slip

                        Do not just average the depths: (2 + 3 + 4 + 4 + 1) / 5 = 2.8. That treats the rare C and D as if they were as important as E, which is sent half the time. Always multiply each depth by its weight.

                        Now play with it. Pick a preset or type your own table (symbol=bits:weight). Notice what happens with the third preset: the same tree shape, but with the symbols put in the wrong places, so the common symbols get long codewords and the cost goes up.

                        Cost of a code

                        Part 5 · Slides 9 to 11

                        Huffman's algorithm

                        We want the prefix code with the smallest C(T) for given weights. Trying every tree is hopeless for many symbols. David Huffman found a short method that builds the best tree directly. The slides first derive the idea (slide 9), then give the algorithm (slide 10) and an exercise (slide 11).

                        Two facts about the best code slide 9

                        Fact 1: the two rarest symbols get the longest codewords. Suppose a rare symbol r had a shorter codeword than a common symbol c. Swap the two codewords. The rare symbol now pays the long length, which hurts only a little because it is rare, and the common symbol gets the short length, which helps a lot because it is common. Written out, the change in cost is (wr − wc)(dc − dr), which is negative when wr < wc and dr < dc. So in a best code, rarer symbols never have shorter codewords than commoner ones.

                        Fact 2: the two rarest can be neighbours that differ only in the last bit. The longest codeword belongs to a deepest leaf. In a best tree every inner node has two children (part 3), so that deepest leaf has a sibling, also a leaf, at the same depth. Their codewords are the parent’s codeword followed by 0 for one and by 1 for the other: they differ only in the last bit. Put the two rarest symbols in those two places.

                        The idea: merge the two rarest into one slide 9

                        Call the weights w1, w2, …, wk and let wk−1 and wk be the two smallest. By the facts above they will be twin leaves. So pretend they are one single symbol of weight wk−1 + wk. That leaves k − 1 weights, a smaller problem of the same kind. Solve it (the same way), and then split the merged leaf into two leaves, adding a 0 to the codeword for one twin and a 1 for the other.

                        Doing this all the way down means you never have to solve anything: the recursion just says “merge the two smallest, again and again until one item is left”, and then the tree builds itself on the way back.

                        The algorithm slide 10

                        H = new Heap()for each w_i T = new Tree(w_i) H.Insert(T)while H.Size() > 1 T1 = H.DeleteMin() T2 = H.DeleteMin() T3 = Merge(T1, T2) H.Insert(T3)
                        H = new Heap()

                        an empty priority queue (Chapter 9, priority queues): a structure that gives you the smallest item quickly.

                        for each w_i

                        one pass over all the symbols.

                        T = new Tree(w_i)

                        a tree consisting of one single leaf with weight wi.

                        H.Insert(T)

                        put it in the queue. Trees are compared by the weight of their root.

                        while H.Size() > 1

                        keep going as long as at least two trees remain.

                        T1 = H.DeleteMin()

                        take out the lightest tree.

                        T2 = H.DeleteMin()

                        take out the next lightest.

                        T3 = Merge(T1, T2)

                        make a new root with T1 and T2 as its two children. Its weight is the weight of T1 plus the weight of T2.

                        H.Insert(T3)

                        put the combined tree back. It may now be among the smaller ones or a big one.

                        When the loop stops, the one tree left in the queue is the Huffman tree. Read the codewords off it: left edge 0, right edge 1.

                        Two small conventions

                        Which child goes left? It does not matter. Swapping the two children of a node flips one bit in every codeword below it, but all codeword lengths stay the same, so the cost is the same. Here the first tree taken out (the smaller) goes left. Ties: if several trees have the same weight, any choice gives a correct (best) tree. The demos take the older tree first, so the results are always the same.

                        The exercise on slide 11: weights 3, 5, 9, 14, 16, 35 slide 11

                        The slide asks for the Huffman tree and its internal weights. Follow the loop by hand. Each row shows the queue before the round, the two smallest, and the new node:

                        roundqueue (smallest first)takenew node
                        13 5 9 14 16 353 and 53 + 5 = 8
                        28 9 14 16 358 and 98 + 9 = 17
                        314 16 17 3514 and 1614 + 16 = 30
                        417 30 3517 and 3017 + 30 = 47
                        535 4735 and 4735 + 47 = 82

                        The internal weights are 8, 17, 30, 47 and 82 (the root). The leaves end up at these depths: 35 at depth 1; 9, 14 and 16 at depth 3; 3 and 5 at depth 4. The cost is 35·1 + (9 + 14 + 16)·3 + (3 + 5)·4 = 35 + 117 + 32 = 184. Run it yourself, step by step, and change the weights:

                        Build the Huffman tree

                        A shortcut for the cost

                        The total cost C(T) equals the sum of all the new node weights: 8 + 17 + 30 + 47 + 82 = 184. Why? A leaf of weight w at depth d has exactly d inner nodes above it, and each of them includes w in its weight. So w is counted d times in the sum of inner weights, which is exactly its contribution w × d to C(T). You can check this in the final step of the demo above, and in the demo of part 6.

                        How fast is it? slide 10

                        With n symbols there are n insertions at the start, and then n − 1 rounds, each doing two DeleteMins and one Insert. A heap does each operation in O(log n), so the total is O(n log n). (Building the first heap in one go takes only O(n), but the rounds still dominate.)

                        Try it on real text

                        The weights usually come from counting how often each character occurs in the text to be compressed. Type any message (up to 80 characters and 16 different characters). The demo counts, builds the Huffman tree, encodes the message, and then decodes it again to prove that nothing was lost.

                        Compress your own message

                        What the demo does not count

                        The receiver needs the tree (or the table of codes) to decode. A real compressed file has to store it, so for a very short message the table can cost more than the compression saves. For long texts, the table is tiny compared with the saving.

                        Part 6 · Slides 12 to 14

                        Why Huffman's code is the best

                        The algorithm looks reasonable, but does it really give the best possible code? We prove it. The slides use induction (Chapter 1, part 5) together with one helpful lemma.

                        What we must prove slide 12

                        Claim

                        For any weights, the tree built by Huffman’s algorithm has the smallest weighted path length C(T) among all binary trees with those leaf weights (that is, among all prefix codes).

                        The plan, as on slide 12, is induction on the number of codewords n:

                        1. Base case, n = 1. There is only one tree (a single leaf), so the algorithm is trivially best.
                        2. Induction hypothesis. Assume Huffman’s algorithm finds a best code for any n weights.
                        3. Step. Take n + 1 weights. Show that Huffman’s tree for them is also best. The slide stops at the dots here, because the missing piece is the key lemma on the next slide.

                        The key lemma slide 13

                        Key lemma

                        Given any tree T, there is a tree T′ in which the two lightest leaves are siblings, and C(T′) ≤ C(T).

                        Why it is true (the exchange argument). Look at the deepest leaves of T. Every deepest leaf has a sibling leaf at the same depth, so T has two sibling leaves b and c at the very bottom. Let a be a lightest leaf of T. If a is not already at the bottom, swap the weights of a and b. The tree shape does not change; only the two weights trade places. With depths da ≤ db and weights wa ≤ wb, the cost changes by:

                        new cost − old cost = (wa × db + wb × da) − (wa × da + wb × db) = (wa − wb)(db − da) ≤ 0

                        because the first bracket is at most 0 and the second is at least 0. So the cost cannot go up. Do the same for the second lightest leaf and c. Now the two lightest are siblings at the bottom, and the cost is not higher.

                        Putting it together slides 12 and 13

                        Take n + 1 weights; let w1 and w2 be the two smallest. Let T be any best tree for these weights.

                        1. Use the lemma. Change T into T′ in which the leaves w1 and w2 are siblings. Since T was best and C(T′) ≤ C(T), the tree T′ is also best.
                        2. Shrink it. Cut off the twins and let their parent become a single leaf of weight w1 + w2. This gives a tree S for n weights. The twins were one level deeper than their parent, so each of them was counted once more: C(T') = C(S) + w1 + w2.
                        3. What Huffman does. Its first step merges the same two weights, then it runs on the n weights, giving a tree HS, and finally splits the merged leaf. In the same way, C(H) = C(HS) + w1 + w2.
                        4. Induction hypothesis. HS is best for n weights, so C(HS) ≤ C(S).
                        C(H) = C(HS) + w1 + w2 ≤ C(S) + w1 + w2 = C(T') ≤ C(T)

                        But T was a best tree, so nothing can beat it, and therefore C(H) = C(T): Huffman’s tree is best too. That completes the induction. ∎

                        Empirical proof by brute force

                        You do not have to take the proof on trust. For a few weights you can list every possible tree shape (as a pattern of leaf depths), fill each with the best assignment of weights (heaviest to the shallowest leaves, as the lemma says), and see where Huffman’s cost lands in the list.

                        Every tree shape, ranked by cost

                        The exercise on slide 14: lower the weighted path length slide 14

                        The slide shows a tree with leaves 6, 4, 5, 5, 3, 6 and asks you to modify it to reduce the WPL. First compute where we start: the leaf depths are 2, 2, 4, 4, 3, 2 (in the order 6, 4, 5, 5, 3, 6), so C(T) = 6·2 + 4·2 + 5·4 + 5·4 + 3·3 + 6·2 = 12 + 8 + 20 + 20 + 9 + 12 = 81. (Check: the internal weights 29 + 10 + 19 + 13 + 10 also add up to 81.)

                        The key lemma tells us what to do. The two lightest leaves are 3 and 4, but they are not at the bottom: the bottom pair is 5 and 5. So swap 3 with a 5, then 4 with the other 5. The cost goes 81 → 79 → 77. That is a valid answer to the slide. But it is not the best possible: the best has C(T) = 75, and swapping weights can never reach it, because 75 needs a different shape. Huffman’s algorithm finds that shape. Click two leaves to swap them and see for yourself:

                        Slide 14: swap leaves

                        Part 7 · The chapter on one page

                        Summary and self-test

                        The chapter on one page

                        IdeaIn one line
                        Code, codeworda rule that writes each symbol as a string of bits; the string for one symbol is its codeword
                        Fixed vs variable lengthfixed: every codeword has the same length (easy to read); variable: frequent symbols get short codewords (saves space, but must be readable)
                        Ambiguoustwo different messages give the same bits, so the receiver cannot decode
                        Prefix codeno codeword is the beginning of another; read bits until they spell a codeword, then start again; never ambiguous
                        Code as a tree0 = left, 1 = right; prefix code ⇔ all symbols at leaves; codeword length = leaf depth
                        Cost C(T)Σ wi × di: the weighted path length, the total bits (or, with probabilities, the average bits per symbol)
                        Huffman’s algorithmput one-leaf trees in a heap; repeat: take the two lightest, join them under a new node (weight = sum), put it back; O(n log n)
                        Why it worksthe two lightest leaves can be siblings at the bottom (exchange lemma); merge them, solve the smaller problem (induction), split again
                        Cost shortcutC(T) = sum of the weights of all inner nodes

                        Small things to know about the slides

                        WhereWhat to know
                        Slide 7The slide names the average cost, the average leaf depth and C(T) but the formulas are not printed. Use C(T) = Σ widi (total bits) and divide by the total weight (or use probabilities) for the average.
                        Slide 9“Two rarest items will have the longest codewords” is true for some best code. If weights tie, a best code can have another symbol equally long, so the safe statement is “in some best code”.
                        Slide 11There is no tie in 3, 5, 9, 14, 16, 35, but whether a child goes left or right is free. The tree can be drawn mirrored; the internal weights and the cost 184 are the same.
                        Slide 12In the base case n = 1 the single codeword would have length 0 (or 1 bit by convention). Start from n = 2 if that bothers you; the argument is the same.
                        Slide 14The slide says “reduce”, not “minimise”. Swapping leaves gets to 77; the true minimum is 75 and needs a new shape.

                        Test yourself

                        1. Decode 11010010010101011 using the first code of slide 3 (E = 0, T = 11, N = 100, I = 1010, S = 1011).

                          Show the answer

                          Read until the bits spell a codeword: 11 = T, 0 = E, 100 = N, 100 = N, 1010 = I, 1011 = S. The message is TENNIS. Because the code is a prefix code, there is never a choice.

                        2. Which of these are prefix codes? (a) 0, 10, 110, 111 (b) 0, 01, 11 (c) 00, 01, 1, 10

                          Show the answer

                          (a) Yes: no codeword begins another. (b) No: 0 is the beginning of 01. (c) No: 1 is the beginning of 10.

                        3. Draw the tree for A = 0, B = 10, C = 110, D = 111. If the probabilities are 12, 14, 18, 18, what is the average cost?

                          Show the answer

                          The tree is a “staircase”: from the root, A is the left child; the right child has B as its left child; its right child has C and D as children. Depths: 1, 2, 3, 3. Average cost = 12 × 1 + 14 × 2 + 18 × 3 + 18 × 3 = 1.75 bits per symbol, against 2 bits for a fixed code of 4 symbols.

                        4. On slide 8, what is the average number of bits per symbol, and what would a fixed-length code cost for the same five symbols?

                          Show the answer

                          14 × 2 + 18 × 3 + 116 × 4 + 116 × 4 + 12 × 1 = 1.875 bits. A fixed-length code for 5 symbols needs 3 bits (23 = 8 ≥ 5). The saving is 37.5%.

                        5. Build the Huffman tree for the weights 3, 5, 9, 14, 16, 35. Give the internal weights, the codewords and C(T).

                          Show the answer

                          Rounds: 3+5 = 8; 8+9 = 17; 14+16 = 30; 17+30 = 47; 35+47 = 82. With the smaller tree on the left: 35 = 0; 9 = 101; 14 = 110; 16 = 111; 3 = 1000; 5 = 1001. C(T) = 35 + 27 + 42 + 48 + 12 + 20 = 184 = 8 + 17 + 30 + 47 + 82.

                        6. For the weights 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8 (the Fibonacci numbers), what does Huffman’s tree look like and what is its cost?

                          Show the answer

                          1+1 = 2; 2+2 = 4 (the older 2 first); 3+4 = 7; 5+7 = 12; 8+12 = 20. Each round joins the new tree with the next single leaf, so the tree is a long chain: leaf depths 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 5 for the weights 8, 5, 3, 2, 1, 1. Cost = 8 + 10 + 9 + 8 + 5 + 5 = 45 = 2 + 4 + 7 + 12 + 20.

                        7. You have 8 symbols that are all equally common. What does Huffman’s tree look like?

                          Show the answer

                          Equal weights never favour any symbol, so the best tree is the perfectly balanced one: every leaf at depth 3, every codeword 3 bits. This is the fixed-length code. (Try 8 equal weights in the demo of part 5.) Huffman only helps when the weights are uneven.

                        8. Slide 14: starting from the tree with leaf weights 6, 4, 5, 5, 3, 6 and cost 81, what does the key lemma suggest, and what is the final best cost?

                          Show the answer

                          The lightest leaves 3 and 4 should be siblings at the bottom. Swap 3 with a 5 (cost 79) and 4 with the other 5 (cost 77). The best possible is 75, which needs the shape Huffman builds: 3+4 = 7, 5+5 = 10, 6+6 = 12, 7+10 = 17, 12+17 = 29; the sum of the new weights 7 + 10 + 12 + 17 + 29 = 75.

                        9. Why does Huffman’s algorithm run in O(n log n) time?

                          Show the answer

                          The heap starts with n trees. Each of the n − 1 rounds does two DeleteMins and one Insert, and each heap operation costs O(log n). So the loop is O(n log n), and so is the setup. Total O(n log n).

                        10. Is the Huffman code for a given set of weights unique?

                          Show the answer

                          No. You may put the lighter tree on the left or on the right, and ties between equal weights can be broken in different ways. These give different codewords (and sometimes different tree shapes), but they all have the same cost, which is the minimum.

                        What to remember

                        The best code gives the rarest symbols the longest codewords, as twins at the bottom. Huffman’s algorithm builds it bottom-up: merge the two rarest, again and again. It works because of the exchange argument (swap a light leaf with a deeper heavy one and the cost never rises).

                        PreviousChapter 10 · Sorting IINextTutorial 1 · Problem solving

                        Tutorial 1 · Problem-solving strategy (Chapters 1–2) · 34 slides

                        Tutorial 1 Step by Step

                        How to design a recursive algorithm in three steps, how to time it with a recurrence, how to prove it right by induction, and two tips for finding the smaller problems. Two full worked examples (5ⁿ in O(log n) time, and the maximum subarray in O(n log n) time), then space complexity and study tips.

                        In this chapter

                          Part 1 · Slides 3–5

                          The three-step recipe

                          This tutorial is a how-to. Chapters 1 and 2 taught you what recursion and running time are. This one teaches you what to do when an exam question says “design an algorithm”. If any word below is new, the Chapter 1 and Chapter 2 guides explain it from scratch.

                          What is a recursive algorithm? slide 3

                          A recursive algorithm uses itself to solve one or more smaller, identical problems. The key question the slide asks is:

                          The key insight

                          Can I solve a big problem by (1) solving some identical but smaller problems (and pretending I already know their answers), then (2) combining those answers into the final result?

                          The slide shows a big blue square. Solving it “as a whole”, by brute force, is hard. But the square can be cut into four smaller squares (the red ones). Each red square is the same kind of problem, only smaller. Solve the four, combine their answers, done.

                          Picture it

                          Imagine counting every carrot in a long line of baskets. Brute force: walk along the whole line. Recursive: count the first basket, tell the helper behind you “count the rest and tell me the number”, then add. You never think about how that helper does it. You just trust the answer will arrive. That trust is step 1 of the recipe.

                          The recipe, with Factorial as the guinea pig slides 4–5

                          The tutorial uses the simplest recursive algorithm there is, Factorial(n), which computes n! = n × (n−1) × … × 2 × 1 (and 0! = 1). Here is its pseudocode, with the three steps marked:

                          if (n == 0) then

                          Step 3 – the base case (slide 5). The smallest problem, 0!, is answered directly, with no recursion. It is the place where the chain of calls stops.

                          return 1

                          The known answer: 0! = 1.

                          prev = Factorial(n - 1)

                          Step 1 – solve a smaller problem of the same kind (slide 4). We do not compute (n−1)! ourselves. We assume the function can do it, and ask it.

                          current = n * prev

                          Step 2 – combine. Knowing (n−1)!, the answer is n × (n−1)!.

                          return current

                          Hand the answer to whoever asked.

                          1. 1st step: smaller sub-problems. Evaluate some smaller sub-problem(s) of the original problem, solvable by the same procedure. For factorial: Factorial(n-1).
                          2. 2nd step: combine. Integrate the sub-problem answer(s) into the final answer. For factorial: multiply by n.
                          3. 3rd step: base case. Find the smallest sub-problem(s) and answer them directly, so the recursion has a place to stop. For factorial: n == 0.

                          Order of thinking is not order of writing

                          You design in the order 1, 2, 3 (what is the smaller problem, how do I combine, where does it stop). But in the code the base case comes first, because the function must check it before it calls itself. A missing or wrong base case means the function calls itself forever.

                          Watch the calls pile up and unwind

                          Press Next step. First the calls go down, each one waiting (blue) for the one below it, until the base case is reached. Then the answers come back up, and every waiting call finishes (green) by doing the multiplication on line 8. The stack on the right is the list of calls that are waiting right now.

                          Factorial(n): down to the base case, then back up

                          Why this matters later

                          This picture gives you both complexities for free. The number of calls (and multiplications) tells you the time; the height of the stack tells you the space the waiting calls occupy (Part 8).

                          Part 2 · Slide 6

                          How long does it take? The recurrence

                          Once the algorithm exists, the next question is its time complexity: how does the running time grow with n? For a recursive algorithm the slide gives a two-step method:

                          1. Set up a recurrence relation: an equation that says “the time for size n equals the time for the smaller call(s) plus the extra work in this call”.
                          2. Find its asymptotic bound: solve the recurrence (or unroll it) and read off the big-O.

                          Step 1: write the recurrence slide 6

                          Look at one call of Factorial(n) in the slide’s picture. It is a box that contains three things: a little bit of work (O(1): the if test), the smaller call T(n−1), and a little more work (O(1): the multiplication). So:

                          T(n) =c1if n = 0T(n−1) + c2if n > 0
                          • c1 is the base-case cost: the time when n = 0 (the test and return 1). It is a constant.
                          • c2 is the cost of everything in a call except the recursive call itself (the test, the multiplication, the return). Also a constant.
                          • T(n−1) is the time for the smaller call. We do not know it yet. We only say it is the same function T at a smaller input.

                          Picture it

                          The constants c1 and c2 are the price tags of “one bit of simple work”. We do not care whether that is 3 nanoseconds or 30. Big-O ignores them in the end, but writing them as letters lets us see where they end up.

                          Step 2: solve it by unrolling slide 6

                          Unrolling means: use the recurrence on itself again and again until the base case appears. The slide does it like this:

                          T(n) = T(n−1) + c2= T(n−2) + 2c2= …= T(n−k) + k c2= T(0) + n c2 (take k = n)= c1 + c2 n

                          Read the lines top to bottom. Each time we replace the leftmost T(·) using the recurrence, a new c2 appears, so after k replacements there are k copies of c2. We keep going until the argument reaches 0 (k = n), where T(0) = c1 is known. The result c1 + c2 n is a straight line in n, so T(n) = O(n).

                          Try it. Every line is the same number, just written differently. That is the whole trick.

                          Unroll T(n) = T(n−1) + c₂ line by line

                          A shortcut to remember

                          Most recursion times are (number of levels) × (work per level). For factorial: n levels of constant work give O(n). Parts 5 to 7 reuse this view on halving recursions, where the number of levels is only about lg n.

                          Part 3 · Slides 7–8

                          Is it correct? Proof by induction

                          “Prove the algorithm correct” means: show that for every valid input the algorithm gives the right output. Testing a few inputs is not a proof, because there are infinitely many more. The slide lists several proof styles (direct proof, contradiction, induction, and others). For recursive algorithms, induction is the natural one, because recursion is induction written as code:

                          In the algorithmIn the proof
                          the base case (if n == 0 ... return 1)the base case of the induction
                          trusting that Factorial(n-1) is rightthe induction hypothesis: assume P(smaller) is true
                          the combine step (n * prev)the inductive step: show P(n) follows

                          Why induction works: dominoes

                          Induction needs two things. Remove either and the proof is worthless. Try all three versions: the full proof (every domino falls), a proof with no base case (nothing ever falls) and a proof whose step is broken at one place (the chain stops there).

                          Why both the base case and the step are needed

                          The proof for Factorial slide 8

                          Let P(n) be the statement: “Factorial(n) returns n! for every non-negative integer n.”

                          Base case. When n = 0, Factorial(0) returns 1 (line 4), and 0! = 1. So P(0) is true.

                          Inductive step. Assume P(k) is true for every k < n (the induction hypothesis); in particular Factorial(n-1) returns (n−1)!. Now consider P(n) for n ≥ 1. Line 8 computes current = n × Factorial(n-1) = n × (n−1)! = n!. Line 10 returns it. So P(n) is true.

                          Conclusion. By mathematical induction, P(n) is true for all non-negative integers n.

                          A slip on the slide

                          Slide 8 ends its base case with “Therefore P(1) is true”, but the base case it just checked is n = 0. It should say P(0). (Check your own proofs for the same mistake: the base case you prove must be the one you state.)

                          Which kind of induction?

                          The slide assumes P(k) for all k < n, written “k = 0, 1, 2, ..., n−1”. That is strong induction (“assume everything smaller”). For factorial you only use k = n−1, so ordinary induction would do. But for algorithms that call a much smaller input (like power(n/2) in Part 6) strong induction is exactly what you need: the hypothesis must cover whatever size the recursive call uses.

                          Template for any recursive-algorithm proof

                          1. State P(n): “the algorithm returns the correct answer for every valid input of size n.”
                          2. Base case: check the input(s) that hit the base-case lines.
                          3. Hypothesis: assume P(k) for all smaller k the recursion might use.
                          4. Step: take the recursive answer(s) as correct, follow the combine lines, and show the result is correct for size n.
                          5. Conclude: by induction, P(n) holds for all n.

                          Part 4 · Slides 9–13

                          Tip 1: three ways to cut a problem

                          The slide says it plainly: the hardest part of designing a recursive algorithm is the first question, “how can I break the big problem into smaller problems that are identical to it?” (Slide 10 is the lecturer joking that designing recursive algorithms is “easy”; you can skip it.) The good news: there are only a few common ways to cut. If the input has size n, the slides list three.

                          Approach 1: ONE sub-problem of size n − k slide 11

                          Peel off one (or two) elements, solve the rest recursively, then fix things up with the peeled element(s). Typical sizes are n−1 or n−2.

                          • Calculating n! (our factorial): T(n−1), then multiply by n.
                          • Palindrome detection: compare the first and the last character; if equal, ask the same question on the inside (size n−2). The slide points to PP1 Chapter 2 Q11 (it is part (b); see Practice Problems 1).

                          Approach 2: ONE sub-problem of size n / k slide 12

                          You know the answer lives in one part (or can be built from one part), so you solve only that part, of size n/2 (or n/k), and throw the rest away or reuse the result. Because the size is divided, not just reduced by one, the recursion is very shallow.

                          • Calculating 5n: get 5n/2 once, then square it (Part 6; slide 12 points to PP1 Ch.2 Q12).
                          • Binary search (Chapter 6) is the same shape: look at one half only.

                          Approach 3: ALL sub-problems of size n / k slide 13

                          The answer could be in any part, so you solve every part (typically both halves) and combine. This is classic divide and conquer.

                          • Finding the maximum subarray: best in the left half, best in the right half, or one that crosses the middle (Part 7; slide 13 points to PP1 Ch.2 Q14).
                          • Merge sort (Chapter 10) and walking a whole binary tree (Chapter 5) have this shape as well.

                          Which approach? A quick decision guide

                          Ask yourselfIf yesTypical recurrence
                          Can I peel off one element and reduce the rest to the same problem?Approach 1T(n) = T(n−1) + O(1) or + O(n)
                          Can I throw half the input away (or does one half decide everything)?Approach 2T(n) = T(n/2) + O(1)
                          Could the answer be in either half, so I must look at both?Approach 3T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n) (or + O(1))

                          1. Which approach finds the largest number in a list by comparing the first element with the largest of the rest?

                            Show the answer

                            Approach 1: one sub-problem of size n−1 (the rest of the list), plus one comparison to combine. T(n) = T(n−1) + O(1), so O(n).

                          2. Which approach is binary search in a sorted list?

                            Show the answer

                            Approach 2: compare with the middle, keep only the half that can still contain the target. T(n) = T(n/2) + O(1), so O(log n).

                          3. Which approach counts the nodes of a binary tree?

                            Show the answer

                            Approach 3 (every sub-tree must be visited): count the left sub-tree, count the right sub-tree, add 1. Each sub-tree is a smaller copy of the same problem, but it is not always half the size, since a tree can be lopsided.

                          Part 5 · Slide 14

                          Tip 2: let the time limit hint at the design

                          Exam questions often say things like “design an algorithm faster than O(n)”. Do not read that as only a restriction. Read it as a hint: it tells you which recurrence you are allowed to aim for, and therefore which approach to use.

                          The five common recurrences slide 14

                          ApproachRecurrenceBig-OExample algorithm
                          1T(n) = T(n−1) + O(n)O(n2)Selection sort (Chapter 9)
                          1T(n) = T(n−1) + O(1)O(n)Linear search (Chapter 6)
                          2T(n) = T(n/2) + O(1)O(log n)Binary search (Chapter 6)
                          3T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(1)O(n)Binary tree traversal (slide: “Ch.7”)
                          3T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n)O(n log n)Merge sort (slide: “Ch.9”)

                          Chapter numbers on the slide

                          The slide’s chapter labels for the last two rows differ from the course’s own numbering used in this guide: tree traversal is in Chapter 5 (the tree chapter; Chapter 7 is search trees), and merge sort is in Chapter 10 (Chapter 9 has the simple sorts and heap sort). The recurrences and bounds themselves are right.

                          How to use the table

                          1. Need O(log n)? Only one thing gives a logarithm: halving with constant work around it, T(n/2) + O(1). Approach 2.
                          2. Need O(n log n)? Split in two, solve both, and spend linear time combining: 2T(n/2) + O(n). Approach 3 with an O(n) merge or scan.
                          3. Need better than O(n2)? Peeling one element and doing a linear scan each time is exactly T(n−1) + O(n) = O(n2). You must cut by a fraction instead.

                          See where the totals come from

                          Pick a recurrence and a size. The table lists the levels of the recursion: how many calls there are on each level, how big they are, and how much work the level costs. Add the last column to get the total, and compare it with the bound in the title.

                          The levels of five recursion trees

                          Picture it

                          Look at the merge-sort-shaped one: every level costs about n (twice as many calls, each half as big), and there are about lg n levels. Levels × cost per level is n lg n. For T(n/2) + O(1) each level costs 1 and there are lg n levels: just lg n.

                          Part 6 · Slides 15–20 · PP1 Chapter 2 Q12

                          Worked example 1: 5ⁿ in less than O(n) time

                          The question slide 15

                          Given a positive integer n, design an algorithm power(n) that calculates 5n faster than O(n) time.

                          Your answer should include: (1) pseudocode of power(n); (2) a verbal explanation of how it works; (3) the worst-case time complexity; (4) a correctness proof by mathematical induction.

                          Notice that the question already lists what a full answer contains. When you write an exam answer, tick these four boxes in order.

                          Insight: start with the brute force, then look for what to skip slide 16

                          Brute force: multiply 5 by itself n times, 5 × 5 × 5 × … × 5. That is O(n) multiplications, which the question forbids. The hint “faster than linear” points to Approach 2 (cut to n/2):

                          1. First find the answer to a sub-problem of half the size: 5n/2.
                          2. Then square it: 5n/2 × 5n/2 = 5n.

                          The slide’s picture shows the row of n fives with only half of it computed. The other half is the part “we can skip the multiplications in”: instead of doing it again, we reuse the first half’s answer.

                          Picture it

                          If you already own a stack of 8 carrots and want 16, you do not fetch 16 new ones. You copy the stack of 8 and push the two stacks together. Doubling is cheaper than counting.

                          The algorithm slides 17–18

                          if (n == 1) then

                          3rd step, base case. The smallest sub-problem is n = 1, where 51 is simply 5.

                          return 5

                          the known answer for n = 1.

                          x = power(floor(n / 2))

                          1st step, smaller sub-problem. Ask for 5⌊n/2⌋, once, and keep it in x. (⌊ ⌋ rounds down, which matters for odd n.)

                          if (n % 2 == 0) then

                          2nd step, combine. If n is even, then n/2 is a whole number and x = 5n/2.

                          return x * x

                          square it: 5n/2 · 5n/2 = 5n.

                          else

                          otherwise n is odd, ⌊n/2⌋ = (n−1)/2 and x = 5(n−1)/2.

                          return x * x * 5

                          squaring gives 5n−1, one factor of 5 short, so multiply by 5.

                          Press Next step with n = 13: the sizes go 13 → 6 → 3 → 1, only four calls. Try other values (also very odd and very even ones such as 16).

                          power(n): halve on the way down, square on the way up

                          Call it ONCE

                          The whole saving depends on line 7 being a single call whose answer is stored in x. If you wrote power(n/2) * power(n/2) you would make two calls on every level: T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(1) = O(n), no better than brute force. Remember: Approach 2 means one sub-problem.

                          Time complexity slide 19

                          T(n) =c1if n = 1T(n/2) + c2if n > 1
                          • The recursion has at most O(log n) levels (halve until you reach 1).
                          • Each level does O(1) work: one test and one or two multiplications.
                          • Overall: T(n) = O(log n).

                          To see it by unrolling, use n = 2m so every halving is exact. After k halvings the size is n/2k and there are k copies of c2; the size reaches 1 at k = lg n:

                          T(n) = T(n/2) + c2 = T(n/4) + 2c2 = … = T(1) + c2 lg n = c1 + c2 lg n

                          Unroll T(n) = T(n/2) + c₂

                          Beyond the slide

                          The slide counts each multiplication as O(1). That is the standard assumption for the course. (In real life 5n has about 2.3n binary digits, so for large n a multiplication is not constant time; but then the brute-force method would also cost more than n steps.)

                          Proof of correctness slide 20

                          Let P(n) be: “power(n) returns 5n for every positive integer n.” Because the recursive call uses ⌊n/2⌋, not n−1, we need strong induction.

                          Base case. n = 1: power(1) returns 5, which is 51. So P(1) is true.

                          Inductive step. Assume P(k) for all positive integers k < n; i.e. power(k) returns 5k for k = 1, 2, ..., n−1. Take n > 1. Line 7 sets x = power(⌊n/2⌋), and ⌊n/2⌋ is between 1 and n−1, so the hypothesis applies.

                          • n even. x = power(n/2) = 5n/2, so the function returns x · x = 5n/2 · 5n/2 = 5n.
                          • n odd. x = power((n−1)/2) = 5(n−1)/2, so the function returns x · x · 5 = 5(n−1)/2 · 5(n−1)/2 · 5 = 5n−1 · 5 = 5n.

                          Either way P(n) is true. Conclusion. By strong induction, P(n) holds for every positive integer n.

                          Why n > 1 in the step

                          The step only covers n > 1, because n = 1 is handled entirely by the base case. If the step also ran for n = 1 it would ask for power(0), which the algorithm is not defined for.

                          Part 7 · Slides 21–25 · PP1 Chapter 2 Q14(a)

                          Worked example 2: the maximum subarray

                          The question slide 21

                          Given an array of integers S[1..n], find the largest positive sub-array sum and return it. If no such sub-array exists, return 0.

                          (a) There is a divide-and-conquer method with four steps: (1) the largest sum in the left half; (2) the largest sum in the right half; (3) the largest sum containing the middle elements; (4) compare the results of (1), (2), (3) and take the largest. Write the pseudocode and analyse the time complexity.

                          A sub-array is a block of consecutive elements. The slide’s example is −2 4 −3 2 3 −1 2 −4 −3 5 and the output is 7, from the green block 4 −3 2 3 −1 2: 4 − 3 + 2 + 3 − 1 + 2 = 7.

                          Insight: brute force, then divide slide 22

                          Brute force. For every starting element, scan to the right and track the best sum seen. That is n scans of up to n elements: O(n2).

                          To scan fewer elements, the slide uses Approach 3 (all sub-problems of size n/2). Every sub-array lies in exactly one of three places:

                          • Direction 1: completely inside the left half. Solve this smaller problem recursively: maxSumL.
                          • Direction 2: completely inside the right half. Recursively: maxSumR.
                          • Direction 3: crossing the middle: it contains the last element of the left half and the first element of the right half. These are not covered by any smaller call, so we compute them directly by scanning outward from the middle. The best one is maxBorderSumL + maxBorderSumR.

                          Picture it

                          Cut a long line of baskets in the middle. A bunch of neighbouring baskets is either left of the cut, right of the cut, or straddling the cut. The first two are the same problem on a shorter line. Only the straddling bunch needs special care, and it is easy: take the best stretch ending at the cut on the left, and the best stretch starting at the cut on the right, and join them.

                          The algorithm slides 23–24

                          function MaxArray1(S, left, right)

                          find the best sum inside S[left..right]. The first call is MaxArray1(S, 1, n).

                          if (left == right) then

                          3rd step, base case: a single element.

                          return Max(S[left], 0)

                          the best sum of one element is the element itself, but we may also choose “nothing” (0) if it is negative.

                          middle = Floor((left + right) / 2)

                          the cut. The left half is left..middle, the right half middle+1..right.

                          maxSumL = MaxArray1(S, left, middle)

                          1st step (directions 1 and 2): solve both halves recursively. This is Approach 3, so there are two calls.

                          maxSumR = MaxArray1(S, middle + 1, right)

                          (the second of the two sub-problems)

                          maxBorderSumL = 0; borderSumL = 0

                          2nd step (direction 3): set up the left border scan. The best starts at 0, i.e. “take nothing”.

                          maxBorderSumR = 0; borderSumR = 0

                          the same for the right.

                          for (i = middle to left) do

                          walk outward to the left, starting at the middle element.

                          borderSumL = borderSumL + S[i]

                          the sum of the stretch from i up to the middle.

                          maxBorderSumL = Max(maxBorderSumL, borderSumL)

                          remember the largest such stretch.

                          for (i = middle + 1 to right) do

                          the mirror image, walking outward to the right.

                          borderSumR = borderSumR + S[i]

                          the sum of the stretch from the middle+1 up to i.

                          maxBorderSumR = Max(maxBorderSumR, borderSumR)

                          remember the largest.

                          return Max(maxSumL, maxSumR, maxBorderSumL + maxBorderSumR)

                          the best of the three directions.

                          Why starting the border sums at 0 is safe

                          The border scans may “take nothing” on one side, so the crossing candidate might really be just a stretch on one side. That is harmless: such a stretch is a valid sub-array, so it can never beat the true best (and the problem lets the answer be 0 when everything is negative). The test array in the demo below with all-negative numbers shows the answer 0.

                          Run it. Each step finishes one call (the calls finish in the order left half, right half, combine, bottom up). Blue boxes are the part of the array the call looked at, green boxes are the best crossing stretch, l and r mark the ends and mid the cut.

                          MaxArray1 on your own array

                          Time complexity slide 25

                          T(n) =c1if n = 1T(⌊n/2⌋) + T(⌈n/2⌉) + c2 nif n > 1

                          The O(1) base case matches the first line. In the second line the two T terms are the two recursive calls (halves of size ⌊n/2⌋ and ⌈n/2⌉), and c2 n is the work of the two border for loops, which together touch every element of the current part once: O(n).

                          • Both recursions together have at most O(log n) levels.
                          • Each level scans (parts of) the array once in total: O(n) per level.
                          • Overall: T(n) = O(n log n), better than the brute-force O(n2).

                          Unrolling for n = 2m shows the same, and also why: each level has twice as many calls but half-size ones, so every level costs the same c2 n:

                          T(n) = 2T(n/2) + c2 n = 4T(n/4) + 2c2 n = … = n T(1) + c2 n lg n = c1 n + c2 n lg n

                          Unroll T(n) = 2T(n/2) + c₂n

                          Pattern to remember

                          Two halves + a linear scan = n log n, whether the scan is merging (merge sort), counting inversions, or this border scan. If the scan were constant time, the same shape would give only O(n) (the tree-traversal row of Tip 2).

                          Part 8 · Slides 26–29

                          Space complexity

                          Time asks “how many steps?”. Space asks “how much memory?”. Same idea: count how the memory grows with the input size n.

                          The definition slide 27

                          The space complexity of an algorithm is the total space it uses, as a function of the input size. It is the sum of two parts:

                          • Space occupied by the input variables (the things you were given), and
                          • Space occupied by temporary variables, called the extra space (what the algorithm creates itself while working).
                          func(n, m) { r = 5 + m; k = Array(n); return r;}

                          In the slide’s little function, n and m are inputs (one number each: O(1) apiece). r is a temporary number: O(1). k = Array(n) is a temporary array of n boxes: O(n). So the extra space is O(n) and the overall space is O(n) too.

                          The cost of common building blocks slide 28

                          DataSpace
                          A simple value (int, double, char)O(1)
                          A pointerO(1)
                          An array, linked list, stack or queue of n elementsO(n)

                          Picture it

                          Memory is a row of boxes. One carrot-count takes one box. A list of n counts takes n boxes. Space complexity just counts boxes that grow with n.

                          A full example slide 29

                          function F(A, b, c) sum = 0 for (p = 1 to b) do if (A[p] > c) then sum = sum + 2 * A[p] end if end for return sumend function
                          VariableKindSpace
                          Ainput (array of n numbers)O(n)
                          b, cinputs (single numbers)O(1) each
                          sum, ptemporary (extra)O(1) each

                          Read the two answers

                          Overall space complexity: O(n) (dominated by the input array A). Extra space complexity: O(1) (just two numbers, no matter how big n is). When a question says “in place” or asks for “O(1) extra space”, it means this second number.

                          Beyond the slides: recursion uses space too

                          The slides count variables. A recursive algorithm also uses memory for its waiting calls, the stack you watched in the demos. Each waiting call holds its own copy of the local variables, so the extra space is about (depth of the stack) × (space per call).

                          AlgorithmStack depthExtra space (stack only)
                          Factorial(n)n + 1 callsO(n)
                          power(n)about lg n + 1 callsO(log n)
                          MaxArray1about lg n + 1 callsO(log n)

                          (The slides do not state these; they follow from the stack pictures. In an exam, if the question says “analyse the space complexity” of a recursive algorithm, mention the stack.)

                          1. An algorithm receives an array A of n numbers and builds a sorted copy in a new array before returning the median. What are its overall and extra space complexities?

                            Show the answer

                            Input A: O(n). The new array is temporary: extra O(n). Overall = input + extra = O(n) + O(n) = O(n).

                          2. The same algorithm, but it sorts A in place and then reads the middle box. Extra space?

                            Show the answer

                            O(1) if the sorting method itself needs only a few temporary variables (like insertion sort or heap sort). The overall space is still O(n) because of the input.

                          Part 9 · Slides 30–33

                          Study tips

                          The last slides are advice from the tutor. Here they are, in order.

                          General study tips slides 31–32

                          • Follow the lecture progress. Do not learn everything hours before the final examination.
                          • For every algorithm or data structure, use this checklist:
                            1. Run it on a numerical example to see how it works.
                            2. Grasp the intuition / key insight: how does it solve the problem elegantly, or faster?
                            3. Understand the key implementation details (but do not drill too deep).
                            4. Know its time complexity: average, worst and best case.
                            5. Compare it with other algorithms in the same category: similarities and differences.
                          • Practice is the key. By doing exercises and understanding their solutions you build your own problem-solving strategy for unknown problems. Do all the assignments yourself; do all the exercises in the Practice Problem Set (see the three practice-problem sets in this guide); do exercises on GeeksforGeeks (the slide gives a “top 100 DSA interview questions, topic-wise” list); do past papers on ExamBase.
                          • Ask immediately. Consult the lecturers and TAs as soon as you hit a difficulty. Do not let problems stack up.

                          Is LeetCode useful for COMP2119? slide 33

                          The tutor’s own stance: 50 / 50, and a coding interview is different from an exam on theoretical topics.

                          ProsCons
                          Some problems are traditional algorithm-design problems.Problem quality: many look tedious or are more about syntax grinding.
                          You can check immediately whether your solution is correct.Implementation vs. idea: you may focus too much on code, when algorithm design is about the big picture of the strategy.
                          Solution quality: many published answers are specific to one language’s syntax.

                          Picture it

                          The exam asks for ideas, recurrences, bounds and proofs, as in Parts 1 to 8 above. Use online coding practice as a check for your ideas, not as a replacement for writing them out on paper.

                          The whole tutorial in one table

                          TaskWhat to doWorked example
