                          Self-test

                          1. What are the three steps of the recursive recipe, and which one stops the recursion?

                            Show the answer

                            (1) Solve smaller identical sub-problem(s), assuming they work; (2) combine their answers into the final answer; (3) find the smallest sub-problem(s) as the base case. The base case stops the recursion.

                          2. What are c1 and c2 in T(n) = T(n−1) + c2, with T(0) = c1?

                            Show the answer

                            c1 is the (constant) cost of the base case; c2 is the (constant) cost of everything in one call except the recursive call.

                          3. Why is x = power(n/2) stored in a variable, and what would go wrong if you called power(n/2) twice?

                            Show the answer

                            One call gives the recurrence T(n/2) + O(1) = O(log n). Two calls give 2T(n/2) + O(1) = O(n), which is no faster than the brute-force loop.

                          4. Why do we need the base case and the inductive step in an induction proof?

                            Show the answer

                            The step alone says only “if one domino falls, the next falls”; without a base case nobody pushes the first domino. The base case alone proves just one value.

                          5. The max-subarray algorithm splits the array in two halves and also scans from the middle. Why is the scan needed?

                            Show the answer

                            A best sub-array may cross the middle. It lies in neither half, so neither recursive call can find it. The border scan finds the best crossing sum in O(n) time.

                          6. Overall vs. extra space of a function that receives an array of n numbers and uses only three temporary numbers?

                            Show the answer

                            Overall O(n) (the input array); extra O(1).

                          Tutorial 2 · Graph search (Chapter 3) · 60 slides

                          Tutorial 2 Step by Step

                          Two ways to search a graph. Depth-first search (DFS) dives as far as it can and backs up when stuck; Dijkstra’s algorithm finds the shortest route when the edges have lengths. Step-by-step demos of both, a maze where DFS and BFS give very different answers, the cost of Dijkstra, why it breaks on negative edges, and both exercises worked out.

                          In this chapter

                            Part 1 · Slides 2–5

                            Why search a graph?

                            Tutorial 2 is about graphs, the dots-and-lines pictures of Chapter 3. A vertex (plural vertices) is a dot, an edge is a line joining two dots, and two vertices joined by an edge are neighbours (or adjacent). Sometimes each edge has a number on it, its weight or length, like a distance in kilometres or a travel time.

                            Graphs are everywhere slides 2–4

                            The first three slides are motivation, but each one hides a real question that a graph search answers:

                            SlideReal-life graphVertices → edgesA question it can answer
                            2Social networkpeople → friendshipsIs there a chain of friends from me to this stranger?
                            2Plane routesairports → flightsHow many flights do I need to get there?
                            3Railway map (HKU, Tai Wai, …)stations → track sections (with travel times)Fastest trip from HKU to Tai Wai? Shortest trip that avoids a certain station? Which two stations are the farthest apart?
                            4“Who likes what” databasepeople and foods → “likes” linksWho does a person like? Which food does their friend like? How many friends like sushi?

                            Picture it

                            Picture a valley of grazing spots joined by paths. “Can I get to the clover field at all?” and “What is the shortest walk to the clover field?” are exactly the two kinds of question in this tutorial. The first needs a search that visits every reachable place (DFS or BFS). The second, when paths have different lengths, needs Dijkstra.

                            The plan slides 5, 29, 50

                            1. Depth-first search (DFS) with an explicit stack, and how it differs from BFS (Parts 2–6).
                            2. Dijkstra’s algorithm for shortest paths in a weighted graph (Parts 7–9).
                            3. Two take-home exercises (Part 10), then a summary and self-test (Part 11).

                            Two words that sound alike

                            Search here means “visit vertices in some systematic order”. It is not the searching of a sorted array or a search tree from Chapters 6–7. A graph search starts at one vertex and spreads out along the edges.

                            Part 2 · Slides 6–7

                            DFS: the idea

                            Depth-first search (DFS) travels through a graph in a depthward motion: from where you stand, step to a neighbour you have not seen yet, then to its unseen neighbour, and so on as deep as possible. When you reach a dead end (every neighbour is already visited), you back up one step and try again from there. A stack remembers the way back.

                            Picture it

                            Picture exploring a cave with a ball of string. You always take the first unexplored tunnel you see and keep going. At a dead end you walk back along the string to the last fork that still has an unexplored tunnel. The ball of string is the stack: the most recent fork is always on top.

                            The three rules slide 7

                            1. Rule 1: go forward. Visit an adjacent unvisited vertex. Mark it visited, display it, and push it onto the stack.
                            2. Rule 2: back up. If there is no adjacent unvisited vertex, pop a vertex off the stack. (That pops every vertex that has no unvisited neighbours, one after another, until it reaches one that has.)
                            3. Rule 3: repeat rules 1 and 2 until the stack is empty.

                            What is on the stack

                            The stack always holds the path from the start vertex to where you are now. The top is your current vertex; the one below it is the vertex you came from, and so on down to the start. Popping means “step back one edge”.

                            Two different DFS codes in this course

                            Chapter 3 (its DFS part) wrote DFS differently: pop a vertex, mark it, then push all its unvisited neighbours. This tutorial’s version is the “peek the top, advance to one unvisited neighbour, pop only when stuck” style. Both are DFS and both visit every reachable vertex, but because they treat the neighbours in a different order they can visit the vertices in a different order. On the graph of Part 3, the version here (neighbours in alphabetical order) visits S, A, D, B, C; the Chapter 3 version pushes A, B, C and pops C first, so it would visit S, C, D, B, A. In an exam, use the version the question shows, and follow its rule for which neighbour comes first.

                            Mark when you push, here

                            In this version a vertex is marked visited at the moment it is pushed (line 12 of the code in Part 4), so it can never be on the stack twice. In the Chapter 3 version a vertex is marked when it is popped, so it may be pushed several times.

                            Part 3 · Slides 8–15

                            DFS step by step

                            The slides use a small diamond-shaped graph with five vertices S, A, B, C, D. S is joined to A, B and C; each of A, B and C is joined to D. The search starts at S and always chooses the neighbour that comes first alphabetically. Here is what each slide says, in plain words:

                            SlideWhat happensStack afterwards (bottom → top)

                            9Mark S visited, push it. Look for an unvisited neighbour of S, alphabetically: A, B, C are all unvisited, so A comes first.S
                            10Mark A visited, push it. A’s neighbours are S (visited) and D. Only D counts.S A
                            11Mark D visited, push it. D’s neighbours are A (visited), B and C (both unvisited). Alphabetical order: B.S A D
                            12B is on top. Its neighbours S and D are both visited, so B is a dead end: pop B.S A D B → S A D

                            DFS visit order: S, A, D, B, C. Press Next step below to watch it happen. The number under each vertex is the order in which it was first reached.

                            DFS with a live stack

                            Things to try

                            Switch to BFS (queue) on the same graph and compare: BFS visits S, A, B, C, D, all the vertices at distance 1 before the one at distance 2. Switch “Try neighbours” to largest first and watch the DFS order change to S, C, D, B, A: the order depends on which neighbour you favour, but every vertex is still visited exactly once. The third graph in the menu is Exercise 1; try it now if you like.

                            DFS dives, BFS spreads

                            In the demo, DFS reaches the deepest vertex D at step 3, before it has looked at B or C. BFS visits all neighbours of S first. That is the whole difference between a stack and a queue.

                            Part 4 · Slide 16

                            The DFS pseudocode

                            Slide 16 turns the three rules into code. v is the start vertex; n is the number of vertices. (The slide’s comments are not closed with */; they are closed below.)

                            DFS(G, v) {

                            G is the graph; v is the vertex where the search starts.

                            Stack S; /* start with an empty stack */

                            An empty stack. It will always hold the current path from v.

                            bool visited[n]; /* a bit per vertex */

                            visited[x] says whether x has been reached. Every entry starts as 0.

                            S.push(v);

                            Rule 1 for the start vertex: push it …

                            visited[v] = 1;

                            … and mark it visited.

                            while (S is not empty) do

                            Rule 3: keep going until the stack is empty.

                            u = S.top(); /* not popped */

                            Look at the vertex on top without removing it. It is where we currently stand.

                            bool advanced = false;

                            A flag remembering whether we managed to move deeper this time round.

                            for each unvisited neighbour w of u

                            Look at the neighbours of u in the agreed order (e.g. alphabetical, or smallest number first).

                            S.push(w);

                            Rule 1: go forward to the first unvisited neighbour …

                            visited[w] = 1;

                            … mark it …

                            advanced = true;

                            … note that we advanced …

                            break; /* go deeper first */

                            … and stop looking at the other neighbours. We dive into w first. The other neighbours will be looked at later, when we come back to u.

                            end for

                            End of the neighbour loop.

                            if (advanced == false) then S.pop() /* all neighbours are visited */

                            Rule 2: we could not advance, so u is a dead end. Pop it: step back one edge.

                            end while

                            The stack is empty: every vertex reachable from v has been visited.

                            }

                            Done.

                            Why the break matters

                            Without the break the loop would push all unvisited neighbours of u in one go and wander off in a different order: it would no longer be a depth-first search. The break says “take exactly one step, then re-examine the top of the stack”. And because the loop is re-entered from the top every time, when we return to u its earlier neighbours are now visited and the for automatically picks the next one.

                            Why it costs O(|V| + |E|) slide 18

                            Every vertex is pushed once and popped once (that is the |V| part). Each time we look at the top vertex u we scan its neighbour list; with an adjacency list the total length of all lists is 2|E| for an undirected graph (that is the |E| part). Careful: the version above rescans u’s list from the start every time u is on top, which can repeat work. A real implementation keeps a pointer per vertex saying “I have already looked at the first k neighbours”, so each edge is examined a constant number of times. The slide quotes the usual bound O(|V| + |E|), for both DFS and BFS.

                            Part 5 · Slides 17–18

                            DFS versus BFS

                            You already met breadth-first search (BFS) in Chapter 3. The two searches are the same program with one thing swapped: the container that holds “vertices to visit next”.

                            BFSDFS
                            PrincipleWalk through all vertices on the same level before moving to the next level. (Level = number of edges from the start.)Go as far as possible along one path, until you reach a vertex with no unvisited neighbour; then back up.
                            Data structureA queue: first in, first out. The oldest waiting vertex is next.A stack: last in, first out. The newest vertex is next.
                            TimeO(|V| + |E|)O(|V| + |E|)
                            Suitable forFinding paths when the start is near the destination.Finding paths when the start is far from the destination.

                            Picture it

                            Ripples in a pond (BFS): the wave spreads out evenly in all directions, touching everything at distance 1, then distance 2, and so on. Someone in a labyrinth (DFS): they commit to one corridor and follow it to the end before trying another.

                            What BFS gives you that DFS does not

                            BFS reaches every vertex by a path with the fewest edges, because it finishes level k before starting level k+1. So the first time BFS meets the destination, the route it followed is a shortest one (in number of edges). DFS gives no such promise: it finds a path, which may wander a long way round. The next part shows a maze where the difference is dramatic.

                            A heuristic, not a theorem

                            The slide’s “suitable for” row (BFS if the destination is near, DFS if it is far) is rule-of-thumb advice about speed, not a guarantee. A lucky DFS can reach a near target at once, and BFS must read a whole level before it moves on, so for a far target on a wide graph it holds a huge queue. The solid facts are the two rows above it: the data structure, and the equal worst-case time. What is guaranteed is that BFS finds a path with the fewest edges and DFS may not.

                            Part 6 · Slides 19–28

                            Example: a maze

                            Slides 19–28 put both searches in an 8×8 maze. B (at the bottom-left corner) is the beginning, D is the destination, blue squares are walls, grey squares are walkable. You may move to the four neighbouring squares (up, down, left, right), never diagonally. The destination D is only three steps from B: right, right, up. The slides show how DFS and BFS go about finding it.

                            To talk about squares, the demo names columns a–h from the left and rows 1–8 from the bottom (like chess), so B is a1 and D is c2.

                            What the slides show slides 20–28

                            • Slide 20, “DFS Path 1”: DFS gets lucky. It goes right, right, then up into D: 3 steps.
                            • Slide 21, “DFS Path 2”: DFS takes a different turn and finds a long route: up the left column to the sixth row, right along it, down the fifth column, left two squares, then down into D. That is 15 steps, five times as long.
                            • Slides 22–28, “BFS Path 1 & 2”: BFS grows a blob outwards from B one layer at a time. Whichever way you break ties, it reaches D by the same 3-step route (right, right, up).

                            So the message of the slides: what DFS finds depends on which neighbour it tries first (it can be short or long), while BFS always finds a shortest route. The demo lets you try all 24 possible orders of the four directions (Up, Right, Down, Left).

                            Maze: BFS (queue) versus DFS (stack)

                            What happens with all 24 orders

                            I ran every order in this maze, stopping as soon as the search reaches D. BFS always needs just 7 marked squares and returns a 3-step path, whatever the order. DFS marks between 28 and 38 squares and returns a path of 27 or 33 steps, depending on the order (for example Up–Right–Down–Left gives 27 steps and Right–Up–Down–Left gives 33). Same maze, same destination, a route 9 to 11 times longer. With any fixed order, DFS here goes a long way round before it reaches D.

                            Why this is the point of the example

                            The example shows the one thing BFS has that DFS lacks: BFS finds a path with the fewest steps. DFS finds a path, and in a maze it might be an awful one. In exchange, DFS keeps only the current path in memory (the stack), which can be much smaller than BFS’s queue of a whole level.

                            Both drawn DFS paths are illustrations

                            Neither drawn DFS path comes from a fixed direction order. Path 1 needs “Right before Up” at the start but “Up before Right” one square later; Path 2 needs the opposite pair of choices. They show two things DFS might do. The demo’s numbers are for the algorithm exactly as coded on slide 16 with one fixed order, stopping the moment D is marked; with a fixed order DFS here finds a 27-step or a 33-step route, never the lucky 3-step one.

                            Part 7 · Slides 30–35

                            Dijkstra: the problem and the idea

                            Why BFS and DFS are not enough slide 30

                            BFS and DFS treat every edge as the same size, so they suit unweighted graphs. BFS minimises the number of edges. But if the edges have different lengths (five short hops can be shorter than one long road) then “fewest edges” is not “shortest”. Dijkstra’s algorithm is the popular answer for weighted graphs.

                            The exact problem slide 31

                            Single-source shortest paths

                            Given a graph G = (V, E) with non-negative edge weights and a distinguished source vertex s ∈ V, find the shortest distance from s to every vertex in the graph.

                            The length of a path is the sum of the weights of its edges. The shortest distance to x is the smallest length over all paths from s to x. Notice “non-negative”: weights may be 0 or positive, never negative. Part 9 shows why that is essential.

                            The big idea: grow a Shortest Path Graph slides 32–35

                            The algorithm builds, step by step, a shortest path graph (SPG): the vertices and edges that make up shortest routes from s. It does so by growing:

                            1. Start tiny. The smallest sub-graph of the SPG contains just the source s (distance 0).
                            2. Attach one “correct” vertex at a time (with the edge that leads to it), so that the bigger graph is still part of the SPG: every vertex in it already has its true shortest distance.
                            3. Which vertex is the correct one? Among the vertices not yet in the SPG, pick the one with the smallest distance from s through the SPG so far (slides 34–35: the “closest” one). Add it and repeat until every vertex is in.

                            Picture it

                            You want to know how long it takes to reach every barn from the farmhouse. First mark the farmhouse “0 minutes”. Then ask: of all barns not yet marked, which can I reach soonest using the places I have already marked? That barn’s time is now certain, because any other route to it would have to leave the marked area through some other, no-nearer barn, so it can only be longer. Mark it, and repeat.

                            Why the closest one is certain

                            Suppose x is the nearest unmarked vertex, reached at distance d through the marked area. Any other route to x must first step out of the marked area to some other unmarked vertex y, whose distance is at least d (x was the nearest), and then travel on with non-negative weights, so the route is at least d long in total. Nothing beats d. This argument uses non-negative weights, and it fails if an edge can be negative.

                            Part 8 · Slides 36–46

                            Dijkstra step by step

                            The slides run Dijkstra on a directed graph with six vertices s, a, b, c, d, e and these edges (the arrow shows the direction you may travel):

                            s→a 9   s→d 14   s→e 15   a→b 23   a→d 2   d→b 18   d→c 30   d→e 5   e→c 20

                            The source is s. The slide uses three kinds of numbers, and so does the demo:

                            • Highlighted number (slides 37+): the final shortest distance of a vertex that is already in T. In the demo: the green label.
                            • Shaded number (slide 38+): the current best guess of a vertex not yet in T. In the demo: the plain label under a blue vertex.
                            • ∞: nothing found yet.

                            T is the set of vertices whose distance is final. It starts empty and grows by one vertex at a time.

                            The slides in a table slides 36–46

                            SlideT after itWhat happensGuesses for (a, b, c, d, e)
                            36{ }Start: the empty graph, nothing known.∞, ∞, ∞, ∞, ∞
                            37{s}s is at distance 0, the closest possible. Add it.∞, ∞, ∞, ∞, ∞
                            38{s}Look at the edges leaving s: a = 0+9, d = 0+14, e = 0+15.9, ∞, ∞, 14, 15
                            39{s, a}Smallest guess outside T is a with 9. Final. Add it.—
                            40{s, a}Edges leaving a: b = 9+23 = 32 (was ∞); d = 9+2 = 11, better than 14, so update.9, 32, ∞, 11, 15
                            41{s, a, d}Smallest outside T: d with 11. Add it.—
                            42{s, a, d}Edges leaving d: b = 11+18 = 29 (beats 32); c = 11+30 = 41; e = 11+5 = 16, not better than 15, keep 15.9, 29, 41, 11, 15

                            Final distances from s: a = 9, d = 11, e = 15, b = 29, c = 35. The shortest paths follow the green “came from” edges: s→a→d (11) is shorter than the direct s→d (14); b is reached by s→a→d→b, not by the tempting s→a→b (32).

                            Now run it yourself. Each Next step alternates between add (move the closest vertex into T) and relax (look at its outgoing edges and improve guesses). “Relax” is the standard word for “replace a distance by a smaller one”.

                            Dijkstra: add the closest vertex, then relax its edges

                            One-line summary of every round

                            Pick the closest outside vertex, declare its distance final, then for each edge out of it test dist(v) + length < dist(x) and, if true, lower dist(x).

                            A detail the slide pseudocode glosses over

                            The demo, like the slides’ pictures, treats a vertex already in T as finished: its distance is never changed again. The pseudocode of the next part loops over all edges out of v, including ones that lead back into T. With non-negative weights such an edge can never improve a final distance, so the two readings give the same answers. (With a negative edge they would not, and neither version is correct. See Part 9.)

                            Part 9 · Slides 47–49

                            Dijkstra's code, its cost and its limit

                            The pseudocode slide 47

                            Dijkstra(G, s) {

                            s is the source vertex.

                            /* dist(x) = shortest distance found so far from s to x */

                            The array of guesses. (The slide closes this comment with /* by mistake; it should be */.)

                            dist(s) = 0; dist(x) = ∞ for every other vertex x;

                            Source at 0, everything else “not reached yet”. Costs O(|V|): one assignment per vertex.

                            T = { };

                            The set of vertices whose distance is final starts empty.

                            while T ≠ V do

                            Repeat until every vertex is in T. (The slide writes T ≠ G; it means all vertices, V.) This loop runs |V| times.

                            pick the vertex v ∉ T with the smallest dist(v);

                            Find the closest outside vertex. With a plain array this means scanning all of it: O(|V|) per round, so O(|V|²) over the whole run.

                            add v to T;

                            Its distance is now final. O(1) each, O(|V|) in total.

                            for all edges (v, x) ∈ E

                            Look at every edge leaving v.

                            if dist(x) > dist(v) + Length(v, x)

                            Is going through v a shorter way to x?

                            dist(x) = dist(v) + Length(v, x);

                            Yes: lower the guess (“relax”). Each edge is looked at once in the whole run, because each vertex v is added to T only once: O(|E|) in total.

                            }

                            End.

                            Totals, not per round

                            The red braces on the slide, O(|V|), O(|V|²), O(|V|) and O(|E|), are the costs of those lines added up over the entire run, not per loop round. Adding them: O(|V| + |V|² + |V| + |E|) = O(|V|²), since |E| is at most about |V|².

                            Making it faster: a priority queue slide 48

                            The expensive line is the “pick the smallest”, because an array is not sorted by distance. A priority queue (usually built as a heap, see Chapter 9) always hands you its smallest element quickly. It takes O(log |V|) to extract the minimum and O(log |V|) to lower a distance. So:

                            • picking the minimum, |V| times: O(|V| log |V|);
                            • lowering a distance, at most once per edge: O(|E| log |V|).

                            Total: O((|E| + |V|) log |V|), as on the slide. Which implementation wins depends on how many edges the graph has:

                            Array versus priority queue

                            Sparse or dense?

                            A sparse graph has about as many edges as vertices (a road map: each junction has 3 or 4 roads), so the priority queue wins hugely. A dense graph has about |V|² edges, and there the plain array version, with no heap overhead, is the better choice.

                            The limitation: no negative edges slide 49

                            Dijkstra’s algorithm assumes that adding an edge to a path never makes it shorter. That is true when weights are non-negative and false otherwise. Slide 49 takes the same graph as before but replaces the edge a→d (2) by d→a with weight −100:

                            • At step 1 Dijkstra adds a and asserts dist(a) = 9, the edge s→a.
                            • But there is a path s→d→a of length 14 + (−100) = −86, much shorter.

                            The “closest vertex is certain” argument of Part 7 broke: the route through d looked longer at the moment of the decision, but a negative edge later pays it back. Run it and see how the mistake spreads:

                            Dijkstra on the slide-49 graph (negative edge)

                            Not just one wrong number

                            Dijkstra’s b = 32 is also wrong (the true distance is −63, via s→d→a→b). Only c happens to come out right here. For graphs with negative edges you need a different algorithm (the Bellman–Ford algorithm is the classic one; it is outside this course). A negative cycle is worse: no shortest distance exists, because you can go round and round to make the length as small as you like.

                            Part 10 · Slides 51–59

                            Take-home exercises

                            Exercise 1Easy

                            BFS and DFS orders

                            Starting from node 1, give the BFS and DFS traversal order of the graph below. Always visit the smallest neighbouring node first.

                            The graph (slide 51): node 1 is joined to 2, 3, 4 and 5. Node 2 and node 3 are both joined to 6. Node 4 and node 5 are both joined to 7. Nodes 6 and 7 are both joined to 8.

                            Think first

                            Neighbour lists in increasing order: 1: 2 3 4 5  |  2: 1 6  |  3: 1 6  |  4: 1 7  |  5: 1 7  |  6: 2 3 8  |  7: 4 5 8  |  8: 6 7. For BFS keep a queue (front first); for DFS keep the stack and take one step at a time.

                            BFS (queue). Start: queue [1].

                            1. Take 1; its unseen neighbours 2, 3, 4, 5 join the queue. Visited so far: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5.
                            2. Take 2: neighbour 6 is new, so 6 joins. Take 3: its neighbour 6 is already seen. Take 4: neighbour 7 is new, so 7 joins. Take 5: 7 is already seen.
                            3. Take 6: neighbour 8 is new, so 8 joins. Take 7: 8 is already seen. Take 8: nothing new.

                            BFS order: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8 (level by level: 1; then 2–5; then 6, 7; then 8).

                            StepTop of stack and what it doesStack after

                            Exercise 2Medium

                            Dijkstra with two goals

                            G1 and G2 are goal nodes, and A is the start node. Find the shortest distance and shortest path from A to G1 or G2.

                            The graph (slide 53), undirected: A–B 1, A–G1 5, A–G2 7, B–C 1, B–G2 3, C–G2 3.

                            Think first

                            Run Dijkstra from A and keep the vertex order A, B, C, G1, G2 for your table of distances. Stop when both goals are in T, or earlier if you can already tell which goal is closer.

                            2{A}A is closest (0): add it. Relax: B = 0+1 = 1, G1 = 0+5 = 5, G2 = 0+7 = 7.(0, 1, ∞, 5, 7)
                            3{A, B}Closest outside: B (1). Add. Relax: C = 1+1 = 2; G2 = 1+3 = 4 beats 7. (The edge back to A leads into T.)(0, 1, 2, 5, 4)
                            4{A, B, C}Closest outside: C (2). Add. Relax: G2 = 2+3 = 5 is not better than 4, so keep 4.(0, 1, 2, 5, 4)
                            5{A, B, C, G2}Closest outside: G2 (4). Add. Distance to G2: 4. Path: A → B → G2.(0, 1, 2, 5, 4)
                            6{A, B, C, G2, G1}Last: G1 (5). Distance to G1: 5. Path: A → G1.(0, 1, 2, 5, 4)

                            Answer: the nearest goal is G2, at distance 4, along A → B → G2. The other goal, G1, is at distance 5 along A → G1. The tempting direct edge A–G2 (7) loses to the 3-edge detour through B (1 + 3).

                            Exercise 2 in the demo

                            Which goal?

                            The question asks for the shortest distance to G1 or G2, i.e. to whichever goal is closer. Since G2 enters T before G1, you could stop as soon as the first goal is added (step 5), because that vertex has the smallest distance of all vertices not yet in T.

                            Part 11 · Summary

                            Summary, self-test and slips

                            The whole tutorial in one table

                            DFSBFSDijkstra
                            SolvesVisit everything reachable; find a path.Visit everything reachable; find a path with the fewest edges.Shortest distance (smallest total weight) from one source to every vertex.
                            EdgesUnweightedUnweightedWeighted, non-negative
                            ToolStackQueueArray of guesses, or a priority queue
                            Next vertexThe newest: dive deeper.The oldest: finish the level.The closest one not yet in T.

                            Self-test

                            1. In the slide-16 DFS, what does the stack contain at any moment?

                              Show the answer

                              The path from the start vertex to the vertex you are currently at (the top). Popping steps back one edge.

                            2. Why does the inner loop of the DFS code have a break?

                              Show the answer

                              So that it takes exactly one step deeper and then re-examines the top of the stack. Without it, all unvisited neighbours would be pushed at once and the search would no longer be depth-first.

                            3. Run DFS from 1, smallest neighbour first, on the graph 1–2, 1–3, 2–4, 3–4. What is the visit order, and the BFS order?

                              Show the answer

                              DFS: 1, 2, 4, 3 (from 1 to 2; from 2 to 4; 4’s neighbours are 2 and 3, so push 3). BFS: 1, 2, 3, 4.

                            4. Which finds a path with the fewest edges, BFS or DFS? What did the maze show?

                              Show the answer

                              BFS. In the maze BFS always found the 3-step route; DFS found a 27- or 33-step route (for any of the 24 neighbour orders of the demo).

                            5. In Dijkstra, why can the distance of the closest outside vertex be declared final?

                              Show the answer

                              Any other route to it must leave the finished area through a vertex that is at least as far, and then add edges of non-negative weight, so it cannot be shorter.

                            6. Dijkstra with an array costs O(|V|²). Where does the |V|² come from, and how does a priority queue help?

                              Show the answer

                              Each of the |V| rounds scans the whole array for the minimum: |V| × |V|. A priority queue finds the minimum in O(log |V|), giving O((|E| + |V|) log |V|), better for sparse graphs.

                            7. The graph has edges s→a (2), s→b (3), b→a (−5). What does Dijkstra say for dist(a), and what is the truth?

                              Show the answer

                              Dijkstra adds a first (2) and declares it final. The true shortest distance is 3 + (−5) = −2, through b. Negative edges break Dijkstra.

                            Tutorial 3 · Stacks, queues and linked lists (Chapter 3) · 48 slides

                            Tutorial 3 Step by Step

                            Stacks and queues are promises about the order in which items come out; arrays and linked lists are ways of keeping that promise. This tutorial builds one from the other, solves two classic puzzles with them (the next lower day, and the Josephus circle), compares the costs of the four kinds of linked list, and ends with feedback on Written Assignment 1.

                            In this chapter

                              Part 1 · Slides 2 to 7

                              Stacks and queues, built from each other

                              A stack and a queue are not pieces of memory. They are promises about which item comes out next. This part states the two promises, then shows that a promise can be kept in more than one way: one structure can imitate another, and one array can hold two stacks. (The structures themselves are from Chapter 3.)

                              The two promises slide 3

                              StackQueue
                              RuleLIFO: last in, first outFIFO: first in, first out
                              OperationsPUSH(x), POP(), TOP(), EMPTY(): all on one endENQUEUE(x) at the back; DEQUEUE(), FRONT() at the front
                              CostWith an array or a linked list, every one of these boundary operations is O(1).
                              Think of it asa pile of plates: you can only touch the top one. The newest unresolved candidate.a line at a ticket counter. Arrival order, or going round a circle.

                              Picture it

                              A stack remembers “what I was in the middle of”: the thing I started last must be finished first. A queue remembers “who has been waiting longest”. Whenever a problem says “the most recent …” or “the nearest …”, think stack. Whenever it says “in order of arrival” or “taking turns”, think queue.

                              A queue from two stacks slide 4 · CLRS 10.1-6

                              The puzzle. You only own two stacks. Make something that behaves like a queue. The slide’s solution:

                              1. ENQUEUE(x): push x on the stack IN.
                              2. DEQUEUE(): pop from the stack OUT.
                              3. If OUT is empty when you need to dequeue, first move all items from IN to OUT, one at a time (pop from IN, push onto OUT). Only then pop from OUT.

                              Why does that give first-in-first-out? IN holds items with the newest on top. Emptying IN into OUT reverses the order, so the oldest item lands on top of OUT, ready to be popped first. Items that arrive while OUT is still full wait in IN; they are all newer than anything in OUT, so they can wait.

                              A queue made of two stacks

                              The cost. ENQUEUE is one push: O(1). A single DEQUEUE that triggers a move costs O(n) in the worst case. But look at one item’s whole life: it is pushed onto IN, popped from IN, pushed onto OUT and popped from OUT, at most four stack operations, and it is moved across only once. So n operations cost at most 4n in total, and the amortized cost of each operation is O(1). (Amortized means “averaged over a whole sequence of operations, in the worst sequence”; no luck or randomness involved.)

                              A common mistake

                              Do not move items back from OUT to IN after a dequeue. The point is that once an item has crossed to OUT it is already in the right order. Moving things back and forth would make every operation O(n) and wreck the amortized bound.

                              A stack from two queues slide 5 · CLRS 10.1-7

                              The reverse puzzle. Two queues, make a stack. A queue never lets the newest item jump the line, so some operation has to do rearranging, and one of the two operations must pay O(n). The slide keeps the logical top of the stack at the front of the active queue:

                              • PUSH(x) O(n): enqueue x into the empty second queue, then move every old item behind it, then swap the queues’ roles. Now x is at the front.
                              • POP() O(1): dequeue the front.

                              The slide also mentions the mirror image: make PUSH O(1) (just enqueue at the back) and POP O(n) (move all but the last item to the other queue, dequeue the last, swap roles). Try both:

                              A stack made of two queues

                              Why the asymmetry?

                              Two stacks can build a queue with amortized O(1) per operation, because reversing twice restores the order. Two queues cannot build a stack that cheaply: moving a queue to another queue keeps the order, so nothing is ever reversed, and each rearrangement really does cost n moves. (The slide only asks for a correct design with the costs stated.)

                              Two stacks in one array slide 6 · CLRS 10.1-2

                              The puzzle. You have one array A[1..n]. Fit two stacks into it, each with O(1) operations, so that overflow happens only when all n cells are in use. The naive plan, “give each stack half”, fails: the left stack could overflow at n/2 items while the right one is empty and half the array is wasted.

                              The trick: make the stacks grow towards each other.

                              • The left stack starts at A[1] and grows to the right; topL is the index of its top (0 when empty).
                              • The right stack starts at A[n] and grows to the left; topR is the index of its top (n+1 when empty).
                              • Each PUSH or POP changes one of the two numbers by 1: O(1).
                              • The free cells are exactly those strictly between topL and topR. The array is full exactly when topL + 1 = topR. The two stacks share the free space, so neither wastes any.

                              Two stacks, one array

                              What these exercises reveal slide 7

                              • The order of access is a contract. Arrays, stacks and queues can all be used to implement it, in many ways.
                              • Reversing, rotating and wrapping change where the next item appears.
                              • State the representation invariant first, in one sentence (for example “the top is at the front of the active queue”), then count operations.
                              • Worst-case and amortized costs can differ: the two-stack queue has a worst case of O(n) for one DEQUEUE but an amortized cost of O(1).

                              Part 2 · Slides 8 to 15

                              The monotone stack: the next lower day

                              This is the tutorial’s big idea: a stack that throws away candidates that can never be the answer. It turns a slow double loop into one pass. The problem is Practice Problems 2, Chapter 3, Question 6.

                              The problem and an example slide 8

                              Day i has rainfall A[i]. For every day i, find the first later day j with A[j] < A[i] (strictly less), and report B[i] = j − i, the number of days you wait. If there is no such day, B[i] = −1.

                              Example from the slide: A = [4, 2, 5, 7, 6, 1] gives B = [1, 4, 3, 1, 1, −1].

                              day i123456
                              A[i]425761
                              next lower day j26656–
                              B[i] = j − i14311−1

                              Your turn. For A = [3, 4, 5, 2, 8, 9, 4], work out B before reading on (the slide asks the same).

                              1. What is B for A = [3, 4, 5, 2, 8, 9, 4]?

                                Show the answer

                                Day 1 (3): the first lower day is day 4 (rainfall 2), so 3. Day 2 (4): day 4, so 2. Day 3 (5): day 4, so 1. Day 4 (2): nothing later is lower, so −1. Day 5 (8): day 7 (4), so 2. Day 6 (9): day 7, so 1. Day 7: −1.
                                B = [3, 2, 1, −1, 2, 1, −1]. You can check it in the demo below.

                              The slow way slide 9

                              For each day i, scan j = i+1, i+2, … and stop at the first A[j] < A[i]. Stopping early keeps it correct, but not fast. If the rainfall never goes down (1, 2, 3, …), no day has an answer, so every scan runs to the end: (n−1) + (n−2) + … + 1 comparisons, which is Θ(n²). The waste: each scan forgets everything the earlier scans learned about the same days.

                              The key insight: dominance slide 10

                              Process the days from right to left, so the part to the right of the current day (the suffix) is already summarized. Now think about two later days i < j with A[i] ≤ A[j]:

                              Dominance

                              If i < j and A[i] ≤ A[j], then day j can never be the answer for any day to the left of i.

                              Why? Take any earlier day d < i for which j would be lower: A[j] < A[d]. Then also A[i] ≤ A[j] < A[d], so i is lower than d too, and nearer. Day j is always beaten by i. So once we meet i, we can delete j forever. A stack is the perfect store for this: the newest candidate is on top, and cleanup happens at the top.

                              Picture it

                              Think of people standing in a row, and you want to know the nearest person to your right who is shorter than you. A taller person standing behind a shorter-or-equal person is hidden: anyone looking from the left would stop at the shorter one first. So hidden people are simply sent home.

                              The invariant slide 11

                              • The stack holds candidate day numbers from the days already processed (the suffix).
                              • From top to bottom the day numbers increase and the rainfall strictly decreases.
                              • At day i: pop while A[TOP] ≥ A[i]. Afterwards the top, if any, is the nearest later day with lower rainfall.

                              The algorithm slide 12

                              S = empty stackfor i = n down to 1: while not EMPTY(S) and A[TOP(S)] >= A[i]: POP(S) if EMPTY(S): B[i] = -1 else: B[i] = TOP(S) - i PUSH(S, i)return B
                              S = empty stack

                              the stack of candidate days (indices).

                              for i = n down to 1:

                              right to left, so everything to the right has been processed.

                              while not EMPTY(S) and A[TOP(S)] >= A[i]:

                              the top day is not lower than day i, so it is dominated.

                              POP(S)

                              delete it forever.

                              if EMPTY(S): B[i] = -1

                              nobody to the right is lower.

                              else: B[i] = TOP(S) - i

                              the nearest lower day, as a distance.

                              PUSH(S, i)

                              day i becomes a candidate for the days to its left. Record the answer before pushing, or you would find day i itself.

                              Three details the slide stresses: store indices, not rainfall values, because the output is a distance; the test is ≥, not >, because equal rainfall does not make the traveller happier (the answer needs strictly lower); and the stack needs only PUSH, POP, TOP, EMPTY.

                              Next lower day, step by step

                              The trace on the slide slide 13

                              For A = [4, 2, 5, 7, 6, 1], scanning from day 6 down to day 1 (each entry is day:rainfall, top first):

                              after processing daystack, top firstwhat happened
                              66:1empty stack, so B[6] = −1; push.
                              55:6, 6:1top is 1, not ≥ 6, so B[5] = 6−5 = 1; push.
                              44:7, 5:6, 6:1top is 6, not ≥ 7, so B[4] = 1; push.
                              33:5, 6:1pops days 4 and 5 (7 ≥ 5, 6 ≥ 5); top is day 6, so B[3] = 3; push.
                              22:2, 6:1pops day 3 (5 ≥ 2); top is day 6, so B[2] = 4; push.
                              11:4, 2:2, 6:1top is 2, not ≥ 4, so B[1] = 1; push.

                              Why it is correct, and why it is O(n) slide 14

                              • Correct. A popped day j is dominated by a nearer day with rainfall ≤ A[j] (the day that made us pop it), so it could never be a correct answer for any day further left. The first survivor on the stack is therefore the earliest later day with rainfall strictly below A[i].
                              • Fast. Every index is pushed once and popped at most once. The while loop looks like a nested loop, but its total number of iterations over the whole run is at most the number of pops, which is at most n. So the whole algorithm is O(n), even though a single day may pop many entries.
                              • Space. B and the stack each use O(n).

                              The usual “nested loop” trap

                              “A loop inside a loop is O(n²)” is only a guess. Count the total work the inner loop does over the whole run (here, at most n pops in all), not the worst case of one visit multiplied by n. This is amortized analysis by counting pushes and pops.

                              When is a monotone stack a good idea? slide 15

                              • The question asks for the nearest later (or earlier) item meeting an inequality.
                              • A closer item can make a farther candidate permanently irrelevant (dominance).
                              • The newest surviving candidate is the one to test first.
                              • Always prove the dominance claim and count each push and pop once before you say O(n).

                              Part 3 · Slides 16 to 22

                              The Josephus circle: a queue, then a formula

                              A second classic from Practice Problems 2 (Chapter 3, Question 7). This time the right tool is a queue, because people stand in a circle and take turns. We will solve it by simulation first, and then see how a simple formula skips the simulation completely.

                              The problem slide 16

                              People 0, 1, …, n−1 stand in a circle. Starting from person 0, count around the circle; every k-th person leaves. After someone leaves, counting resumes with the next survivor. Who is the last person standing?

                              • n = 5, k = 2: people leave in the order 1, 3, 0, 4; the survivor is 2.
                              • n = 6, k = 3: people leave in the order 2, 5, 3, 1, 4; the survivor is 0.

                              Why a queue matches a circle slide 17

                              A circle has no beginning or end; a queue has a front and a back. But a queue where the front person goes to the back is a circle going round:

                              • The front of the queue is the next person to be counted.
                              • To count one person without removing them, dequeue and enqueue them again: they move to the back and the cyclic order is unchanged.
                              • To remove the k-th person, move k−1 people from the front to the back, then dequeue once more and do not put that person back.
                              • The new front is exactly the next person, which is where counting must resume.

                              The algorithm slide 18

                              Q = empty queuefor i = 0..n-1: ENQUEUE(Q, i)remaining = nwhile remaining > 1: repeat k-1 times: x = DEQUEUE(Q) ENQUEUE(Q, x) DEQUEUE(Q) remaining--return DEQUEUE(Q)
                              Q = empty queue

                              the circle, front = the person counted next.

                              for i = 0..n-1: ENQUEUE(Q, i)

                              in label order, so person 0 is at the front.

                              while remaining > 1:

                              rotate only while at least two people remain; the last one is the survivor.

                              repeat k-1 times: x = DEQUEUE(Q); ENQUEUE(Q, x)

                              count k−1 safe people: they go to the back, in the same cyclic order.

                              DEQUEUE(Q)

                              the k-th person leaves and is not put back.

                              return DEQUEUE(Q)

                              only one person is left.

                              Josephus with a queue

                              The trace on the slide slide 19

                              For n = 6, k = 3 the queue starts as [0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5]. Rotate 0 and 1 to the back, remove 2: the queue is [3, 4, 5, 0, 1]. Rotate 3 and 4, remove 5: [0, 1, 3, 4]. Then 3, 1 and 4 leave in the next rounds and [0] remains. Removed in order: 2, 5, 3, 1, 4.

                              Correctness and cost slide 20

                              • Invariant: the front of Q is the next person to be counted, and Q keeps the cyclic order of the people still in the game.
                              • Rotation keeps both properties (it only moves the front to the back), and removal deletes exactly the k-th person, leaving the next person at the front.
                              • There are n−1 removals and each round makes k queue steps (k−1 rotations and one removal): O(kn) time. The queue holds at most n people: O(n) space.

                              When only the survivor matters: a recurrence slide 21

                              If we only want the last person, simulating everyone is wasteful. Let F(n, k) be the survivor’s label (people numbered from 0). Look at what happens right after the first removal:

                              1. The first person to leave is number k−1 (people 0, 1, …, k−1 are counted).
                              2. Counting resumes at person k. Relabel the people so that person k becomes 0, person k+1 becomes 1, and so on around the circle. Now there are n−1 people, and the game is exactly the same game with n−1 people.
                              3. Its survivor has the new label F(n−1, k). To get back to the old label, undo the shift: add k and wrap around the circle of n people.
                              F(1, k) = 0F(n, k) = (F(n − 1, k) + k) mod n

                              Compute F(2), F(3), …, F(N) in turn, keeping only the previous value: O(N) time and O(1) extra space. Check with n = 5, k = 2: F(1) = 0, F(2) = (0+2) mod 2 = 0, F(3) = (0+2) mod 3 = 2, F(4) = (2+2) mod 4 = 0, F(5) = (0+2) mod 5 = 2. The demo above prints this table under the finished simulation, for any n and k.

                              Queue or recurrence? slide 22

                              • Choose the queue when every intermediate removal or rotation matters (for example you must print the order in which people leave).
                              • Choose the recurrence when only the final survivor is required.
                              • First model the state faithfully; then ask whether it can be compressed. The input and output requirements decide which data structure is useful.

                              Part 4 · Slide 23

                              Stacks, queues, DFS and BFS

                              You have already met depth-first and breadth-first search in Chapter 3 and Tutorial 2. Slide 23 states the relationship in one sentence each: the two searches are the same loop with a different waiting room.

                              • DFS uses a stack (an explicit one, or the recursion stack): the newest frontier vertex is next. It dives deep before it comes back.
                              • BFS uses a queue: the oldest frontier vertex is next. It finishes the whole level before going deeper, which is why it visits vertices in level order.
                              • With adjacency lists, both take O(V+E) time.
                              • BFS gives the shortest path length (number of edges) in an unweighted graph.

                              The slide’s graph has S joined to A and B, A joined to C and D, and B joined to E, and neighbours are read from left to right. BFS visits S, A, B, C, D, E; DFS visits S, A, C, D, B, E. Run both and watch the waiting room change:

                              One loop, two waiting rooms

                              Try the second graph

                              Choose “plus an edge D–E”. BFS is unchanged, but DFS now reaches E through D, so it visits E before B. The stack remembers B for later, but by then E is already done. The two orders can differ a lot, and that is why the choice between them matters in Tutorial 2’s maze.

                              Part 5 · Slides 24 to 30

                              Linked lists: four forms, seven operations

                              A linked list can be singly or doubly linked, and sorted or unsorted. That makes four kinds. Which one is best depends on what you do with it. This part works out, for each kind, the worst-case cost of seven operations. It is a classic exercise (CLRS Problem 10-1), and the table at the end is worth knowing by heart because you can re-derive it.

                              The pieces slide 24

                              • A node stores a key and NEXT. A doubly linked node also stores PREV.
                              • HEAD points to the first node. TAIL may point to the last.
                              • Splicing (inserting or removing) at a place you already hold a pointer to is O(1): change a couple of pointers.
                              • But searching for a key, or finding a missing predecessor, can cost O(n): a list has no index to jump to; you can only walk.

                              The rules of the exercise (slide 25): the seven operations are SEARCH, INSERT, DELETE, SUCCESSOR, PREDECESSOR, MINIMUM, MAXIMUM. We store both HEAD and TAIL, and for DELETE and the successor/predecessor operations x is a node we already hold a pointer to (if you are given only a key, you first pay for a SEARCH). Costs are worst case.

                              SEARCH and INSERT slide 26

                              • SEARCH(k): O(n) in all four forms. Sorted order may let an unsuccessful search stop early, but the worst case is unchanged.
                              • INSERT(x): unsorted lists (singly or doubly): O(1), just put the node at HEAD. Sorted lists: O(n) to find where it belongs.

                              DELETE slide 27

                              • Given the node x in a singly linked list, you must change the previous node’s NEXT, but nothing tells you who the previous node is: walk from HEAD, O(n). Sortedness does not give a PREV pointer, so sorted singly is O(n) too.
                              • Given x in a doubly linked list: x.prev.next = x.next and x.next.prev = x.prev. O(1).
                              • If you are given only a key, every form first pays O(n) for SEARCH.

                              SUCCESSOR and PREDECESSOR slide 28

                              These mean the next larger and next smaller key (not the next node).

                              • Unsorted: the neighbour in key order could be anywhere, so scan: O(n).
                              • Sorted singly: SUCCESSOR(x) = x.next, O(1). PREDECESSOR(x) has no back pointer, so O(n).
                              • Sorted doubly: both are one pointer away, O(1).

                              MINIMUM and MAXIMUM slide 29

                              • Unsorted (singly or doubly): scan, O(n) for either.
                              • Sorted ascending: MINIMUM is HEAD, O(1). With a maintained TAIL, MAXIMUM is also O(1).
                              • Without TAIL, MAXIMUM on a sorted singly linked list reverts to O(n): you must walk to the end.

                              Pick any cell below and see the reason; the toggle shows the effect of the TAIL pointer.

                              Four list forms, seven operations

                              The trade-off slide 30

                              • Sorting makes neighbour queries (successor, predecessor) and extreme queries (minimum, maximum) cheap.
                              • Doubly linked nodes make deletion and backward movement cheap.
                              • Both choices cost something: sorting makes insertion slow (O(n) to find the spot), and doubly linked nodes need extra memory per node and extra pointer updates.
                              • So choose the representation from the operations you need most. A log you only append to and sometimes scan? Unsorted singly. A structure with frequent deletes by pointer? Doubly linked.

                              Part 6 · Slides 31 to 34

                              Stack, queue and UNION with a singly linked list

                              An array can overflow, and growing it costs time. A linked list never overflows (until memory runs out) and keeps every operation at the boundary O(1). This part shows how to run a stack and a queue on a singly linked list, and then how to join two sets in constant time.

                              A stack in a singly linked list slide 31 · CLRS 10.2-2

                              Let TOP = HEAD. The newest item is the first node, so both stack operations work at the front of the list, which a singly linked list handles perfectly:

                              • PUSH(x): create a new node, set new.next = HEAD, then HEAD = new.
                              • POP(): if the list is empty, report underflow; otherwise save HEAD’s key and set HEAD = HEAD.next.

                              No traversal, so O(1) each. (The slide’s picture: HEAD→9→4→2; PUSH(7) gives 7→9→4→2; POP moves HEAD to the 9 again.)

                              A queue in a singly linked list slide 32 · CLRS 10.2-3

                              A queue works at both ends, so keep two pointers: HEAD (the front, for DEQUEUE) and TAIL (the back, for ENQUEUE).

                              • ENQUEUE(x): make a new node; if the queue is empty, set both HEAD and TAIL to it; otherwise TAIL.next = new and TAIL = new.
                              • DEQUEUE(): take HEAD’s key and set HEAD = HEAD.next. If that removed the last node, also set TAIL = NIL. Forgetting this leaves TAIL pointing at a deleted node, and the next ENQUEUE would attach to garbage.

                              Why not use TAIL for removal? Because a singly linked list cannot step backwards: removing the last node needs its predecessor. That is why the front is HEAD, where removal is easy, and the back is TAIL, where insertion is easy.

                              A stack or a queue on a singly linked list

                              Constant-time UNION slides 33–34 · CLRS 10.2-6

                              The problem. Two disjoint sets S1 and S2 are stored as singly linked lists. Produce their union in O(1) time. The input lists may be destroyed.

                              The trick is that a union of unordered, disjoint sets is just one list stuck on the end of the other. With a HEAD and a TAIL pointer for each set:

                              UNION(S1, S2): if S1.head == NIL: return S2 if S2.head == NIL: return S1 S1.tail.next = S2.head S1.tail = S2.tail invalidate the S2 record return S1
                              if S1.head == NIL: return S2

                              nothing to join: the answer is the other list.

                              if S2.head == NIL: return S1

                              same, the other way round.

                              S1.tail.next = S2.head

                              one link: the last node of S1 now points to the first node of S2.

                              S1.tail = S2.tail

                              one update: the new last node is the old last node of S2.

                              invalidate the S2 record

                              its nodes now belong to S1, so S2 must not be used again.

                              return S1

                              the result keeps S1.head and takes S2.tail.

                              UNION in a constant number of steps

                              Cost: O(1) time and space: two pointer changes whatever the sizes. This only works because of the assumptions: the sets are disjoint (no duplicates to remove), the records may be destroyed (the nodes are reused, not copied), and a TAIL pointer exists. Take any one of them away and the cost changes, as the next part shows.

                              Part 7 · Slides 35 to 40

                              Mergeable heaps built from lists

                              A mergeable heap is a priority queue that can also be merged with another one. The slides ask which linked-list representation makes which operation cheap, and the answer is a lovely lesson in trade-offs.

                              The definition slide 35

                              • A min-heap (as an abstract data type) stores keys and exposes the smallest one.
                              • MINIMUM returns that key; EXTRACT-MIN removes it; MAKE-HEAP creates an empty heap; INSERT adds a key.
                              • A mergeable heap also supports UNION(H1, H2).
                              • The ADT does not say “binary tree”. A heap is whatever answers these operations; the array-based tree of Chapter 9 is just one way.

                              The exercise slide 36

                              Implement MAKE-HEAP, INSERT, MINIMUM, EXTRACT-MIN and UNION using linked lists, in three situations: (a) sorted lists, (b) unsorted lists, (c) unsorted lists where the two heaps hold disjoint sets of keys. The two heaps have sizes m and n; N = m + n. Assume INSERT receives a fresh key (one not already in the heap), and that we maintain HEAD, TAIL and a MIN pointer.

                              (a) Sorted lists slide 37

                              • MAKE-HEAP: O(1). MINIMUM and EXTRACT-MIN: O(1), the minimum is at HEAD.
                              • INSERT: O(n), you must search the sorted list for the position.
                              • UNION: O(m+n), a merge of two sorted chains (as in merge sort), skipping a key that appears in both.
                              • Sorted order pays for fast minimum queries with slower updates.

                              (b) Unsorted lists that may overlap slide 38

                              • MAKE-HEAP and (fresh-key) INSERT: O(1). MINIMUM: O(1) through the MIN pointer.
                              • EXTRACT-MIN: O(n). Unlink the minimum, then scan the whole list to find the new minimum for the MIN pointer.
                              • UNION must remove duplicate keys, so pointer splicing alone is not enough.
                              • Checking every pair costs O(mn). Better: sort the combined list with a linked-list merge sort and delete adjacent duplicates, O(N log N).

                              (c) Disjoint unsorted sets slide 39

                              • MAKE-HEAP, INSERT and MINIMUM are still O(1).
                              • EXTRACT-MIN is still O(n): after removing the minimum, nobody knows who is next.
                              • UNION is O(1): splice the TAIL of one list to the HEAD of the other (exactly as in the previous part), and update the result’s MIN pointer with one comparison between the two MIN pointers.

                              Mergeable heaps from lists

                              operation(a) sorted(b) unsorted, overlapping(c) unsorted, disjoint
                              MAKE-HEAPO(1)O(1)O(1)
                              INSERT (fresh key)O(n)O(1)O(1)
                              MINIMUMO(1)O(1)O(1)
                              EXTRACT-MINO(1)O(n)O(n)
                              UNIONO(m+n)O(N log N) (or O(mn))O(1)

                              The strategy slide 40

                              • Write down the operation mix first (how often each operation happens), then choose singly or doubly, sorted or unsorted.
                              • Track which node pointers the algorithm already owns. “Given a node x” and “given a key” are very different problems.
                              • Use HEAD, TAIL or MIN metadata only when its update cost is accounted for. (A MIN pointer is free to read, but EXTRACT-MIN must pay to find the next one.)
                              • Exploit disjointness and destructive UNION when the problem grants them; they turn a hard merge into one splice.

                              Picture it

                              Think of two piles of exam papers. If each pile is sorted, merging them is a careful zip. If they are unsorted but you know no student appears in both piles, you just put one pile on top of the other. If they might share students, you must first find and remove the duplicates, and that costs real work.

                              Part 8 · Slides 41 to 48

                              Feedback on Written Assignment 1

                              The last slides of the tutorial give feedback on Written Assignment 1 (Recursion and algorithm analysis). The complete assignment, with every solution explained step by step and checked with demos, is a separate view: Written Assignment 1 →. Here are the eight lessons of the feedback slides, each with a pointer to the full explanation.

                              SlideThe lessonFull explanation
                              41What a proof must contain. To show f = O(g) you must exhibit constants c > 0 and n0 with |f(n)| ≤ c|g(n)| for every n ≥ n0. For Θ you also need a positive lower-bound constant. “The biggest term wins” or “it worked for n = 10, 100, 1000” is not a proof.WA1 Q1(b)
                              42A complete two-sided bound. For (n/2 − √n + 5 log n)²: when n ≥ 16, √n ≤ n/4, so the bracket is at least n/4; and log n ≤ n makes it at most 6n. Hence n²/16 ≤ h(n) ≤ 36n² for all n ≥ 16.WA1 Q1(b)(i)
                              43Closed form plus induction, both required (6 proof marks each). For T(2)=4, T(n)=4T(n−1)+3 the closed form is 5·4n−2 − 1. For the 10-power recurrence, induct on r where n = 10r.WA1 Q2(a)
                              44Enough base cases. Tilings with tiles of length 1 and 3: T(1)=1, T(2)=1, T(3)=2, recurrence from n=4. Strings avoiding abb: T(1)=2, T(2)=4, recurrence from n=3.WA1 Q2(b)
                              45Derive the recurrence by classes that are disjoint and exhaustive: strings ending in a (from any valid string of length n−1), strings ending in ab (from any valid string of length n−2), and the single all-b string. So T(n) = T(n−1) + T(n−2) + 1.WA1 Q2(b)(ii)
                              46Spot the overcount. T(1)=2, T(2)=4, T(3)=7 and T(4)=12. The tempting T(n−1)+T(n−2)+T(n−3) predicts 13: the third class is one string, not T(n−3) of them. The official 2T(n−1) − T(n−3) is equivalent for n ≥ 4.WA1 Q2(b)(ii)
                              47Explain the runtime. FindSmallest loops i = 1 to m: exactly m iterations of O(1) work, so Θ(m). Best allowed m = 1 gives Θ(1); worst m = n gives Θ(n). Where the smallest value sits does not change the count.WA1 Q3
                              48Complete binary-search pseudocode. In a sorted array of distinct integers find i with A[i]=i in o(n): declare mid with floor division, return it if A[mid]=mid, go left if A[mid]>mid, right if A[mid]<mid. Each call halves the range: O(log n).WA1 Q4

                              Slips and loose wording

                              On slide 48 the pseudocode returns NIL when lo > hi and uses mid−1 / mid+1. The official solution instead keeps mid in the left half and returns NULL when low = high; both are correct (see the WA1 view). Slide 44 gives the shorter recurrence T(n)=T(n−1)+T(n−2)+1 for the strings, which needs only two base cases, fewer than the three of the official T(n)=2T(n−1)−T(n−3). The question asked for the least number of base cases, so the shorter one is the better answer.

                              Part 9 · The tutorial on one page

                              Summary and self-test

                              The tutorial on one page

                              IdeaIn one line
                              Stack / queueLIFO / FIFO; every boundary operation is O(1) on an array or a linked list.
                              Queue from two stacksENQUEUE pushes on IN; DEQUEUE pops OUT and refills it from IN only when empty. Worst case O(n), amortized O(1) (at most 4 stack operations per item).
                              Stack from two queuesEither PUSH or POP must move n items: O(n) for one, O(1) for the other.
                              Two stacks, one arrayGrow from the two ends; full exactly when topL + 1 = topR.
                              Monotone stackNearest later lower item: scan right to left, pop while A[TOP] ≥ A[i], answer = top, push. Each index pushed and popped once: O(n).
                              JosephusA queue that rotates simulates the circle in O(kn); F(1)=0, F(n)=(F(n−1)+k) mod n gives the survivor in O(n).
                              DFS / BFSThe same loop; DFS uses a stack (newest first), BFS a queue (oldest first, level order). Both O(V+E).
                              Four list formsDoubly linked makes DELETE(x) and PREDECESSOR cheap; sorted makes SUCCESSOR, MIN and MAX cheap and INSERT slow. SEARCH is O(n) always.
                              Stack and queue on a listStack at HEAD; queue with HEAD to remove and TAIL to add (set TAIL = NIL when it empties). All O(1).
                              UNIONDisjoint sets with HEAD/TAIL: splice in O(1). Overlapping sets must remove duplicates: much more work.

                              Two wording notes

                              I found no mistakes in the tutorial slides. Two small things can confuse a first reading: the Josephus picture on slide 16 writes the counting positions (“1st”, “2nd”, …) next to the people’s numbers, so read the big number as the person and the small ordinal as the count; and slide 29’s “sorted ascending” matters: in a list sorted descending the roles of MINIMUM and MAXIMUM swap.

                              Test yourself

                              1. Using a queue built from two stacks IN and OUT, you run: ENQUEUE 1, 2, 3; DEQUEUE; ENQUEUE 4; DEQUEUE; DEQUEUE. What do the three dequeues return?

                                Show the answer

                                1, 2, 3. After the three enqueues IN = [1, 2, 3]. The first DEQUEUE finds OUT empty and moves everything: OUT now has 1 on top; it pops 1. The 4 goes onto IN. The next two DEQUEUEs pop 2 and 3 from OUT; the 4 is still waiting in IN.

                              2. What is the worst-case cost of one DEQUEUE in that design, and what is the amortized cost over n operations?

                                Show the answer

                                Worst case O(n), when OUT is empty and all n items sit in IN. Amortized O(1): each item crosses from IN to OUT at most once, so across n operations there are at most 4n stack operations.

                              3. The array A[1..10] holds two stacks with topL = 4 and topR = 8. How many more items can be pushed in total before overflow?

                                Show the answer

                                3. The free cells are those strictly between the tops: 5, 6 and 7. Overflow happens exactly when topL + 1 = topR, here after three more pushes in any mix of the two stacks.

                              4. For A = [5, 3, 8, 6, 2, 7] compute B (distance to the next strictly lower day, or −1).

                                Show the answer

                                B = [1, 3, 1, 1, −1, −1]. Day 1 (5): day 2 is lower, 1 day. Day 2 (3): the first lower is day 5 (2), 3 days. Day 3 (8): day 4 (6), 1 day. Day 4 (6): day 5, 1 day. Day 5 (2): nothing later is lower. Day 6: last day. Paste it into the demo of part 2 to see the stack do it.

                              5. Josephus with n = 7 and k = 3: who leaves, in what order, and who survives? Check with the recurrence.

                                Show the answer

                                The queue gives the order 2, 5, 1, 6, 4, 0 and the survivor 3. The recurrence: F(1)=0; F(2)=(0+3) mod 2=1; F(3)=(1+3) mod 3=1; F(4)=(1+3) mod 4=0; F(5)=(0+3) mod 5=3; F(6)=(3+3) mod 6=0; F(7)=(0+3) mod 7=3. Same survivor.

                              6. In a singly linked queue with HEAD and TAIL, why must DEQUEUE set TAIL = NIL when it removes the last node?

                                Show the answer

                                Otherwise TAIL still points at the node that was just removed. The next ENQUEUE would link the new node after that dead node, and the new item would be unreachable from HEAD. With HEAD = TAIL = NIL the next ENQUEUE correctly takes the “empty queue” branch.

                              7. Given a pointer to a node x, what do DELETE(x) and PREDECESSOR(x) cost in (a) a singly linked list and (b) a sorted doubly linked list?

                                Show the answer

                                (a) Both O(n): you must walk from HEAD to find the node before x. (b) Both O(1): x.prev and x.next are right there.

                              8. Why is UNION O(1) for disjoint unsorted lists, but not O(1) if the heaps may share keys?

                                Show the answer

                                With disjoint sets there are no duplicates to find, so one link and one TAIL update are enough. If keys may be shared, a key in both heaps must appear only once in the result, so you must detect it: that needs O(mn) pair checks, or an O(N log N) sort-and-dedupe.

                              9. The same loop runs DFS and BFS. What one change turns one into the other?

                                Show the answer

                                The waiting room: take the next vertex from a stack (newest first) for DFS, or from a queue (oldest first) for BFS.

                              What to remember

                              A stack or queue is a promise about order, and any structure that keeps the promise will do. To make a design work, state the invariant first, then count. And a loop inside a loop is not automatically quadratic: count the total pushes and pops.
