                              Practice Problems 1 Step by Step

                              Every problem of the set, with the full solution explained from the first line: writing and solving recurrences, mathematical induction, big-O / Omega / Theta, counting what an algorithm does, and designing recursive algorithms. Try each one first, then open the solution. Demos let you check the answers with your own numbers.

                              In this chapter

                                Part 1 · Chapter 1 Part 1 · Q1

                                Writing a recurrence

                                This set has two chapters. Chapter 1 is recursion (recurrence relations and induction; see Chapter 2 of this guide for the theory and Tutorial 1 for the recipe). Chapter 2 is algorithm analysis (see the same chapter). Each problem below is marked Easy, Medium or Hard exactly as in the set.

                                How to use this page

                                Read the problem, try it on paper, then press Show the worked solution. Where the question asks for numbers, a demo lets you change the input and see the answer recomputed. The problems are numbered as in the PDF: “Ch.1 Q4” is Chapter 1, problem 4.

                                What a recurrence relation is

                                A recurrence relation describes a quantity T(n) in terms of the same quantity for smaller inputs, plus the starting values (the base cases). To write one, ask: “If I already knew the answer for smaller sizes, how would I get the answer for size n?” That is exactly step 1 and step 2 of the recursion recipe from Tutorial 1.

                                Ch.1 · Q1Easy

                                Write a recurrence relation for each quantity

                                For each problem below, write a recurrence relation for T(n), where n is an integer. You do not need to solve it.

                                1. T(n) = the sum of the first n positive integers.
                                2. T(n) = the sum of the first n odd integers.
                                3. T(n) = n factorial.
                                4. T(n) = the n-th Fibonacci number.
                                5. T(n) = the value of $10,000 after n years in a bank paying 10% interest compounded annually.
                                6. T(n) = the number of ways to climb n stairs if you take one, two or three stairs at a time.
                                7. T(n) = the number of ways to deposit n dollars in a vending machine using $1 coins, $1 bills and $5 coins only, where the order of deposits matters.

                                Think first

                                For each one, imagine you already have T(n−1) (or T(n−2), …). What is the last thing that happens, and how does it change the answer? Do not forget the starting values.

                                Show the worked solution
                                PartRecurrenceWhy
                                (a)T(1) = 1; T(n) = T(n−1) + n for n > 1The sum 1+2+…+n is the sum 1+…+(n−1) plus the last number n.
                                (b)T(1) = 1; T(n) = T(n−1) + 2n − 1 for n > 1The odd numbers are 1, 3, 5, …; the n-th one is 2n−1.
                                (c)T(0) = T(1) = 1; T(n) = n · T(n−1) for n > 1n! = n × (n−1)!. Both 0! and 1! equal 1.
                                (d)T(1) = 0, T(2) = 1; T(n) = T(n−1) + T(n−2) for n > 2Each Fibonacci number is the sum of the previous two. (Here the sequence is counted 0, 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, …, so the 1st is 0; two starting values are needed because the rule looks back two steps.)
                                (e)T(0) = 10000; T(n) = 1.1 · T(n−1) for n ≥ 1Adding 10% means multiplying by 1.1.
                                (f)T(n) = 0 for n < 0; T(0) = T(1) = 1; T(n) = T(n−1) + T(n−2) + T(n−3) for n > 1Classify the climbs by their last step (1, 2 or 3 stairs). “T(n) = 0 for n < 0” is a handy convention: you cannot climb a negative number of stairs, so a step of 3 from n = 2 contributes nothing.
                                (g)T(n) = 0 for n < 0; T(0) = 1, T(1) = 2; T(n) = 2T(n−1) + T(n−5) for n > 1Classify by the last item deposited: a $1 coin or a $1 bill (2 choices, leaving n−1) or a $5 coin (1 choice, leaving n−5). The slide’s starting values are T(0) = 1 (do nothing) and T(1) = 2 (coin or bill).

                                Why order matters

                                When the order of deposits matters, putting in a coin then a bill is a different way from a bill then a coin. So you are counting sequences, and the “last item” method counts each sequence exactly once.

                                Check each recurrence against a direct count

                                Part 2 · Chapter 1 Part 1 · Q2 and Q3

                                Solving recurrences by telescoping

                                The method: telescope (unroll) until the base case

                                To solve a recurrence means to find a closed form: a formula for T(n) that does not mention T on the right-hand side. The method of these problems is telescoping (unrolling):

                                1. Substitute the recurrence into itself a few times and look for the pattern after k unrollings: T(n) = T(n−k) + (something that depends on k).
                                2. Choose k so that the argument hits the base case (for T(n−1) that is k = n−1 or n, depending on the base; for T(n/3) it is k = log3 n).
                                3. Plug in the base value, add up the “something” using a known sum, and simplify.
                                4. State the Θ bound: keep the fastest-growing term and drop constants.

                                Sums you will need

                                Arithmetic: 1+2+…+n = n(n+1)/2. Geometric: 1+r+…+rn−1 = (rn−1)/(r−1). Squares: 1²+…+n² = n(n+1)(2n+1)/6. Cubes: 1³+…+n³ = n²(n+1)²/4. (The set prints these as a hint for Q3.)

                                Ch.1 · Q2Easy

                                Solve and state the Θ bound

                                Solve each recurrence by deriving a closed form, and state its Θ bound.

                                1. T(1) = 3,   T(n) = T(n−1) + 3 for n > 1
                                2. T(0) = 1,   T(n) = T(n−1) + 2 for n > 0
                                3. T(0) = 0,   T(n) = T(n−3) + 5 for n > 0  (n a multiple of 3)
                                4. T(1) = 3,   T(n) = T(n/3) + 3 for n > 1  (n a power of 3)
                                5. T(1) = 5,   T(n) = T(n/2) + 1 for n > 1  (n a power of 2)
                                Show the worked solution

                                (a) Each unrolling adds one more 3:

                                T(n) = T(n−1) + 3T(n) = [T(n−2) + 3] + 3 = T(n−2) + 3·2T(n) = T(n−k) + 3k

                                The base case is T(1), so set n−k = 1, i.e. k = n−1: T(n) = T(1) + 3(n−1) = 3 + 3n − 3 = 3n. So T(n) = 3n, which is Θ(n).

                                (b) Same, but the base is T(0), so k = n: T(n) = T(0) + 2n = 2n + 1. Θ(n).

                                (c) This one steps down by 3: after k unrollings T(n) = T(n−3k) + 5k. To reach T(0) we need 3k = n, so k = n/3 (that is why n must be a multiple of 3): T(n) = T(0) + 5·n/3 = 5n/3. Θ(n).

                                (d) The argument now gets divided by 3 each time, so after k unrollings it is n/3k, and the added amount is 3k:

                                T(n) = T(n/3) + 3T(n) = [T(n/9) + 3] + 3 = T(n/32) + 3·2T(n) = T(n/3k) + 3k

                                n/3k = 1 when k = log3 n. So T(n) = T(1) + 3 log3 n = 3 + 3 log3 n, which is Θ(log n) (the base of a logarithm only changes a constant factor).

                                (e) Likewise with halving: T(n) = T(n/2k) + k, k = log2 n, so T(n) = 5 + log2 n. Θ(log n).

                                Rule of thumb

                                Subtracting a constant each time (n−1, n−3) gives about n levels. Dividing by a constant each time (n/2, n/3) gives about log n levels. The answer is (number of levels) × (work per level), unless the work per level changes.

                                Ch.1 · Q3Medium

                                Solve the harder recurrences

                                Solve each recurrence (closed form) and state its Θ bound.

                                1. T(1) = 1,   T(n) = T(n−1) + n
                                2. T(0) = 1,   T(n) = 2T(n−1) + 3
                                3. T(1) = 0,   T(n) = 3T(n−1) + 1
                                4. T(0) = 1,   T(n) = T(n−1) + 3n2
                                5. T(1) = 1,   T(n) = 5T(n/5) + 3  (n a power of 5)
                                6. T(1) = 1,   T(n) = T(n/8) + n  (n a power of 8)
                                7. T(1) = 0,   T(n) = 5T(n/5) + n/5  (n a power of 5)
                                Show the worked solution

                                (a) The thing added changes each time (n, then n−1, then n−2, …):

                                T(n) = T(n−1) + nT(n) = [T(n−2) + (n−1)] + nT(n) = T(1) + [2 + 3 + … + n]

                                The unrolling stops at T(1) after k = n−1 steps. Since T(1) = 1, we get 1 + 2 + 3 + … + n = n(n+1)/2, which is Θ(n²).

                                (b) Now there is a multiplier 2 at each step, so the earlier constants get doubled again and again:

                                T(n) = 2T(n−1) + 3T(n) = 2[2T(n−2) + 3] + 3 = 22 T(n−2) + (2·3 + 3)T(n) = 23 T(n−3) + (22·3 + 2·3 + 3)T(n) = 2k T(n−k) + 3(2k−1 + … + 2 + 1)

                                With k = n and T(0) = 1: T(n) = 2n + 3(2n − 1)/(2−1) = 4·2n − 3 = 2n+2 − 3. That is Θ(2n).

                                (c) The same idea with a multiplier 3: T(n) = 3k T(n−k) + (3k−1 + … + 3 + 1). Stop at T(1) = 0 with k = n−1: T(n) = 0 + (3n−1 − 1)/(3−1) = (3n−1 − 1)/2. Θ(3n).

                                (d) Add up squares: T(n) = T(0) + 3[12 + 22 + … + n2] = 1 + 3·n(n+1)(2n+1)/6. Multiply out: 1 + (2n3 + 3n2 + n)/2 = (2n3 + 3n2 + n + 2)/2. Θ(n3).

                                (e) Five sub-problems of size n/5, each level costing a constant 3 per call:

                                T(n) = 5T(n/5) + 3T(n) = 5[5T(n/25) + 3] + 3 = 52 T(n/52) + (5·3 + 3)T(n) = 5k T(n/5k) + 3(5k−1 + … + 5 + 1)

                                At k = log5 n, 5k = n and T(1) = 1: T(n) = n + 3(n−1)/4 = (7n − 3)/4. Θ(n). (Many cheap calls: the number of calls grows like n.)

                                (f) One sub-problem of size n/8, but each level adds the current size, which shrinks geometrically: T(n) = T(n/8k) + [n/8k−1 + … + n/8 + n]. That bracket is n(1 + 1/8 + 1/82 + …), a geometric sum, so T(n) = 1 + 8(n−1)/7 = (8n − 1)/7. Θ(n): the top level dominates.

                                (g) Five sub-problems of size n/5 plus n/5 of work in each call. At every level the work adds up to the same amount: level 1 has one call doing n/5; level 2 has five calls doing n/25 each = n/5 in total; and so on. So the total is (n/5) × (number of levels = log5 n):

                                T(n) = 5k T(n/5k) + k·(n/5)T(n) = 0 + (n/5) log5 n

                                Θ(n log n).

                                Where does each pattern come from?

                                Constant added each time (T(n−1)+constant) → n times that constant → Θ(n). Add n-ish each time (T(n−1)+n) → a sum 1+2+…+n → Θ(n2). Multiply by 2 or 3 each time (T(n−1)×2) → exponential. Halve and add a constant → log n. Split into b pieces → compare the work per level and the number of levels (the Master theorem of Chapter 1 automates this).

                                Closed form versus the recurrence, row by row

                                Part 3 · Chapter 1 Part 1 · Q4

                                Harder recurrences: the Θ bound without solving fully

                                Ch.1 · Q4Hard

                                State and explain the Θ bound

                                For each recurrence, state and explain the Θ bound. You need not telescope all the way to the base case.

                                1. T(1) = 0,   T(n) = 9T(n/9) + 9n + 9  (n a power of 9)
                                2. T(n) = 0 for n ≤ 2,   T(n) = T(√n) + 1 for n > 2  (n = 22k)
                                3. T(n) = 1 for n ≤ 1,   T(n) = T(⌊√n⌋) + log n for n > 1
                                4. T(n) = 0 for n ≤ 1,   T(n) = T(⌊2n/5⌋) + T(⌊3n/5⌋) + n
                                5. T(n) = 0 for n ≤ 1,   T(n) = T(⌊n/2⌋) + T(⌊n/3⌋) + T(⌊n/6⌋) + n

                                Think first

                                Ask two questions: how many levels does the recursion have, and how much work is done on each level in total? Multiply. If the level totals are not all equal, add them up (a geometric series is dominated by its biggest term).

                                Show the worked solution

                                (a) Θ(n log n). Look at level i (level 0 is the top). There are 9i calls, each of size n/9i, each doing 9·(n/9i) + 9 work. So the level costs 9n + 9i+1. There are log9 n levels (k = log9 n):

                                T(n) = 9k T(n/9k) + k·9n + 9(9k − 1)/8T(n) = 0 + 9n log9 n + 9(n − 1)/8T(n) = 9n log9 n + 9n/8 − 9/8

                                The term 9n log9 n beats the rest, so Θ(n log n). (The “+9” per call is a lower-order extra: it adds only about n in total.)

                                (b) Θ(log log n). Taking a square root halves the exponent: √(n) = n1/2. So T(n) = T(n1/2) + 1 = T(n1/4) + 2 = T(n1/2k) + k. With n = 22m the exponent n1/2k becomes 2 after k = log2 log2 n steps, where T(2) = 0. So T(n) = log2 log2 n exactly. Example: n = 16 → 4 → 2: two steps = log2 4 = lg lg 16.

                                (c) Θ(log n). Ignore the floor (it changes nothing important) and take n = 22k again. After each square root the log of the argument halves: log n, then ½ log n, then ¼ log n, … The total is T(n) = 1 + (1 + 1/2 + 1/4 + … + 1/2k−1) log n. The bracket is a geometric series that is always between 1 and 2, i.e. Θ(1), so T(n) = Θ(log n).

                                (d) Θ(n log n). Draw the recursion tree. The root has size n and splits into 2n/5 and 3n/5. The work done at a node is its size, and the two children’s sizes always add up to the parent’s size, so every level that is still full costs n in total (level 1: 2n/5 + 3n/5 = n; level 2: 4n/25 + 6n/25 + 6n/25 + 9n/25 = n; …).

                                The tree is lopsided: the shortest branch always takes the 2/5 child, so it ends after about log5/2 n levels; the longest branch always takes the 3/5 child and lasts log5/3 n levels. So

                                n · log5/2 n ≤ T(n) ≤ n · log5/3 n

                                (the left side counts only the levels that are completely full; the right side pretends all levels up to the longest branch are full). Both sides are constant multiples of n log n, so Θ(n log n).

                                (e) Θ(n log n). The same picture with three children of sizes n/2, n/3, n/6, and n/2 + n/3 + n/6 = n, so again every full level costs n. The shortest branch always takes the smallest child (n/6, dividing by 6 each time) and ends after log6 n levels; the longest branch always takes the biggest child (n/2) and lasts log2 n levels. So n log6 n ≤ T(n) ≤ n log2 n: Θ(n log n).

                                Lopsided trees: which branch is shortest?

                                The branch where the size shrinks the most per step reaches size 1 first. In (d) that is the 2/5 branch (length log5/2 n), in (e) the 1/6 branch (length log6 n). The branch that shrinks the least per step is the longest.

                                Is the ratio T(n) divided by the guess a constant?

                                Part 4 · Chapter 1 Part 2 · Q5 and Q6

                                Mathematical induction

                                The three boxes of every induction proof

                                Induction proves a statement P(n) for every whole number n from some start. It works like falling dominoes (see Tutorial 1, Part 3). You always write the same three boxes:

                                1. Base case. Check P for the first value (usually n = 1 or n = 0) by plain arithmetic.
                                2. Hypothesis. Assume P(k) is true for some k. (The set’s wording “where k < n” is the strong-induction form: it assumes the statement for the smaller values. For these problems P(k) alone is enough.)
                                3. Step. Starting from the left side of P(k+1), use the hypothesis to rewrite it, and finish at the right side of P(k+1). Then say “by M.I., P(n) is true for all n”.

                                Do not assume what you are proving

                                The hypothesis is about k. You must never start the step by writing the claim for k+1 and “simplifying both sides” until they match. Start from one side of the k+1 statement and transform it into the other.

                                Ch.1 · Q5Easy

                                Prove each statement by induction

                                Prove, by mathematical induction, for all positive integers n:

                                1. 1² + 3² + 5² + … + (2n−1)² = ⅓ n(2n−1)(2n+1)
                                2. 1²/(1·3) + 2²/(3·5) + 3²/(5·7) + … + n²/((2n−1)(2n+1)) = n(n+1) / (2(2n+1))
                                3. n! ≥ 2n−1
                                Show the worked solution

                                (a) The sum of the first n odd squares.

                                Base case. n = 1: the left side is 1² = 1. The right side is ⅓·1·(2−1)(2+1) = ⅓·1·1·3 = 1. They agree. (The printed solution writes the left side as “2(1) − 1” instead of [2(1)−1]²; the value 1 is the same.)

                                Hypothesis. Assume 1² + 3² + … + (2k−1)² = ⅓ k(2k−1)(2k+1).

                                Step. Look at n = k+1. The new sum is the old sum plus one more term, (2(k+1)−1)² = (2k+1)²:

                                LHS = [12 + 32 + … + (2k−1)2] + (2k+1)2LHS = (1/3)k(2k−1)(2k+1) + (2k+1)2LHS = (1/3)(2k+1)[k(2k−1) + 3(2k+1)]LHS = (1/3)(2k+1)(2k2 + 5k + 3)LHS = (1/3)(2k+1)(k+1)(2k+3)

                                (The second step uses the hypothesis; the third factors out the common (2k+1); and 2k2+5k+3 = (k+1)(2k+3).) The right side of P(k+1) is ⅓(k+1)(2(k+1)−1)(2(k+1)+1) = ⅓(k+1)(2k+1)(2k+3): the same. So P(k+1) holds, and by induction P(n) holds for all positive n. ■

                                (b) A sum of fractions.

                                Base case. n = 1: the left side is 1²/(1·3) = 1/3 and the right side is 1·2/(2·3) = 1/3.

                                Hypothesis. The sum up to the k-th term equals k(k+1)/(2(2k+1)).

                                Step. Add the (k+1)-th term, (k+1)²/((2k+1)(2k+3)):

                                LHS = k(k+1) / (2(2k+1)) + (k+1)2 / ((2k+1)(2k+3))LHS = (k+1)/(2k+1) · [ k/2 + (k+1)/(2k+3) ]LHS = (k+1)/(2k+1) · [ k(2k+3) + 2(k+1) ] / (2(2k+3))LHS = (k+1)/(2k+1) · (2k2 + 5k + 2) / (2(2k+3))LHS = (k+1)(k+2) / (2(2k+3))

                                (We used 2k2+5k+2 = (2k+1)(k+2), which cancels the (2k+1) in the denominator.) The right side of P(k+1) is (k+1)(k+2)/(2(2(k+1)+1)) = (k+1)(k+2)/(2(2k+3)). ■

                                (c) An inequality, not an equation.

                                Base case. n = 1: 1! = 1 ≥ 20 = 1.

                                Hypothesis. k! ≥ 2k−1.

                                Step. (k+1)! = (k+1) · k! ≥ (k+1) · 2k−1 ≥ 2 · 2k−1 = 2k. The first ≥ is the hypothesis (multiplying both sides by the positive number k+1); the second uses k+1 ≥ 2, true because k ≥ 1. ■

                                Ch.1 · Q6Medium

                                Solve the recurrence, then prove your answer

                                For each recurrence, derive a closed form and prove it by mathematical induction.

                                1. T(0) = 1,   T(n) = T(n−1) + 2 for n > 0
                                2. T(0) = 1,   T(n) = 2T(n−1) + 3 for n > 0
                                Show the worked solution

                                The closed forms come from Q2(b) and Q3(b): (a) T(n) = 2n + 1 and (b) T(n) = 2n+2 − 3. Now prove them. The new idea compared with Q5: the “left side” in the step is a value of T, and the recurrence tells you how to rewrite it.

                                (a) Base. n = 0: T(0) = 1 and 2·0 + 1 = 1. Hypothesis. T(k) = 2k + 1. Step.

                                T(k+1) = T(k) + 2T(k+1) = (2k + 1) + 2T(k+1) = 2(k+1) + 1

                                That is the formula for k+1. ■

                                (b) Base. n = 0: T(0) = 1 and 20+2 − 3 = 4 − 3 = 1. Hypothesis. T(k) = 2k+2 − 3. Step.

                                T(k+1) = 2T(k) + 3T(k+1) = 2(2k+2 − 3) + 3T(k+1) = 2k+3 − 6 + 3T(k+1) = 2(k+1)+2 − 3

                                That is the formula for k+1. ■

                                See the base case and the induction step with real numbers

                                Part 5 · Chapter 2 Part 1 · Q1 and Q2

                                Asymptotic notation: O, Omega, Theta

                                The three symbols in one picture

                                For two functions f(n) and g(n), look at the ratio f(n) / g(n) as n gets very large (the full definitions with constants c and n0 are in Chapter 2):

                                The ratio f/gf = O(g)f = Ω(g)f = Θ(g)
                                shrinks towards 0 (f is slower)TFF
                                settles near a positive constant (same growth)TTT
                                grows without bound (f is faster)FTF
                                keeps swinging (neither bounded above nor below)FFF

                                So O means “at most this fast”, Ω means “at least this fast”, Θ means “exactly this fast, up to constants”. Constants and lower-order terms never matter.

                                True or false for O, Ω, Θ

                                Show the worked solution
                                f(n)g(n)OΩΘWhy (look at f/g)
                                n²n³TFF1/n → 0
                                2n3nTFF(2/3)n → 0
                                log2 nlog10 nTTTconstant ratio log2 10 ≈ 3.32 (change of base)
                                2n²10000nFTFn/5000 → ∞
                                2n+12nTTTratio = 2
                                log √n√(log n)FTFlog √n = ½ log n; ½√(log n) → ∞
                                sin xcos xFFFthey trade places and one is 0 where the other is ±1
                                72n7nFTF7n → ∞
                                200 n log nn²TFF200 log n / n → 0
                                2n2n/2FTF2n/2 → ∞

                                Three traps in this table

                                (1) Different bases of the same exponential matter (2n vs 3n) but a constant added in the exponent does not (2n+1 = 2·2n). (2) Changing the base of a logarithm never matters; but log of a square root is only a constant times log, whereas a square root of a log is a different, slower function. (3) Dividing the exponent is not a constant factor: 2n/2n/2 = 2n/2 still grows without bound.

                                1116a constant, Θ(1)

                                Why a huge constant still ranks first

                                1116 is about 4.6 × 1016, a very large number, but it never changes, while log n eventually grows past any fixed number. That is why a constant, however large, is at the bottom of the ladder.

                                Part 6 · Chapter 2 Part 1 · Q3 and Q4

                                Proving bounds from the definition

                                The definitions you must use

                                StatementWhat you must exhibit
                                f(n) = O(g(n))constants c > 0 and n0 such that 0 ≤ f(n) ≤ c·g(n) for all n ≥ n0
                                f(n) = Ω(g(n))c > 0, n0 such that 0 ≤ c·g(n) ≤ f(n) for all n ≥ n0
                                f(n) = Θ(g(n))c1, c2 > 0 and n0 such that c1·g(n) ≤ f(n) ≤ c2·g(n) for all n ≥ n0

                                To prove: find witnesses. To disprove: show no witnesses can exist

                                To prove a bound you only have to find constants that work (they need not be the best). To disprove one you assume constants exist, then show that for a big enough n the inequality must fail (a contradiction). The standard tricks for finding constants: for an upper bound, replace every term by a bigger term of the target size (e.g. 4n ≤ 4n2); for a lower bound, drop positive terms or replace by smaller ones.

                                Ch.2 · Q3Medium

                                Prove or disprove by the definition

                                1. 5n + 4 = O(n²)
                                2. (n + 2√n + log n)5 = Θ(n5)
                                3. 0.00001n = O(1)
                                4. 3n5 − 2n2 + 4n + 2 = Θ(n5)
                                5. (n + 2 log n)3 = Ω(n3)
                                Show the worked solution

                                (a) True. For n ≥ 1 we have n ≤ n2 and 1 ≤ n2, so 5n + 4 ≤ 5n2 + 4n2 = 9n2. Witnesses: c = 9, n0 = 1.

                                (b) True. Lower bound: for n ≥ 1 the added terms 2√n and log n are non-negative, so the bracket is at least n and its fifth power at least n5: c1 = 1. Upper bound: for n ≥ 1, √n ≤ n and log n ≤ n, so the bracket is at most n + 2n + n = 4n, and (4n)5 = 1024n5: c2 = 1024. Witnesses: c1 = 1, c2 = 1024, n0 = 1.

                                (c) False. Suppose 0.00001n ≤ c for all n ≥ n0. But when n > c/0.00001, we get 0.00001n > c: a contradiction. A linear function, however flat, is never bounded by a constant.

                                (d) True. For n ≥ 2: lower bound: 3n5 − 2n2 + 4n + 2 ≥ 3n5 − 2n2 = n5 + 2(n5 − n2) ≥ n5, because n5 ≥ n2. Upper bound: dropping the negative term gives ≤ 3n5 + 4n + 2, and for n ≥ 2 we have 4n + 2 ≤ n5 (at n = 2: 10 ≤ 32), so the total is ≤ 4n5. Witnesses: c1 = 1, c2 = 4, n0 = 2.

                                (e) True. For n ≥ 1, log n ≥ 0, so n + 2 log n ≥ n and its cube is at least n3. Witnesses: c = 1, n0 = 1.

                                Test the witness constants (and break them)

                                Ch.2 · Q4Hard

                                Statements about sets of functions

                                Prove or disprove by the definition:

                                1. Θ(1) + Ω(1) = Ω(1)
                                2. O(n log n) + O(3n) = Θ(n)
                                3. If f(n) = O(g(n)), then f(n) + g(n) = Θ(g(n)).
                                4. Given g(n) ≥ 1 and f(n) ≥ 1: if f(n) = O(g(n)), then √(f(n)) = O(√(g(n))).
                                5. Given log g(n) ≥ 1 and f(n) ≥ 1 for all large n: if f(n) = O(g(n)), then log f(n) = O(log g(n)).

                                Think first

                                An expression like “O(n) + O(n)” means: any function in the first set plus any function in the second set. To disprove, you need just one pair of functions that breaks the claim. Remember that O allows the function to be much smaller (even 0).

                                Show the worked solution

                                (a) True. Take f in Θ(1): there are c1, c2, n1 with c1 ≤ f(n) ≤ c2 for n ≥ n1. Take g in Ω(1): c′ ≤ g(n) for n ≥ n2. For n ≥ max(n1, n2), f(n) + g(n) ≥ c1 + c′ > 0, a positive constant. That is the definition of Ω(1).

                                (b) False. O is only an upper bound, so it contains functions that are tiny. The function 0 belongs to O(n log n) and the function 3 belongs to O(3n) (both are ≤ the bound for n ≥ 1). Their sum is the constant 3. If 3 were Θ(n) there would be c1 > 0 with c1n ≤ 3 for all large n; but for n > 3/c1 that is false. So not every member of the sum is Θ(n).

                                (c) True. Since f = O(g) there are c and n0 with 0 ≤ f(n) ≤ c·g(n) for n ≥ n0. Then f + g ≥ 0 + g = g (lower bound with c1 = 1) and f + g ≤ c·g + g = (c+1)·g (upper bound with c2 = c+1). So f + g = Θ(g).

                                (d) True. From f ≤ c1·g (for n ≥ n0) take square roots: √f ≤ √c1 · √g ≤ (c1+1) · √g, using √c1 ≤ c1 + 1. So c = c1+1 works.

                                (e) True. From f ≤ c1·g (we may assume c1 ≥ 1, since enlarging c1 keeps the inequality true): log f ≤ log c1 + log g. Because log g ≥ 1 and log c1 ≥ 0, we have log c1 ≤ (log c1)(log g). Hence log f ≤ (log c1 + 1)(log g), and c = log c1 + 1 works for all n past the point where log g ≥ 1 and f ≥ 1. (The “≥ 1” conditions are what stop log f from being negative or log g from being too small to absorb the constant.)

                                Part 7 · Chapter 2 Part 2 · Q5 to Q10

                                Analysing algorithms: counting what they do

                                How to analyse an algorithm

                                1. Decide what to count: statements executed, or one kind of operation (additions, comparisons, multiplications).
                                2. Count how many times each line runs. A loop body runs once per round; a nested loop multiplies; two loops one after the other add. A recursive function’s cost satisfies a recurrence (Part 2).
                                3. Find the worst case and the best case: which inputs make the count biggest and smallest?
                                4. Summarise with a bound: O for an upper bound, Θ when the bound is tight.
                                Ch.2 · Q5Easy

                                Doubled sum: worst and best case

                                The algorithm F(A, b, c) takes an array A[1..n] and an integer b (1 ≤ b ≤ n) and sums, twice, the first b entries that are bigger than c:

                                1: function F(A, b, c)2: sum = 04: for (p = 1 to b) do5: if (A[p] > c) then6: sum = sum + 2 * A[p]7: end if8: end for10: return sum11: end function
                                1. Counting statements executed: which b and c give the worst case and the best case? How many statements run in each?
                                2. Counting arithmetic operations (+, −, ×, ÷): same question.
                                Show the worked solution

                                (a) Statements. The loop always runs b times, and line 6 runs only when A[p] > c.

                                • Worst case: b = n, and c smaller than every element of A. Then every pass through the loop also executes line 6. Line 2 runs once, line 4 runs n times (or n+1 if you also count the final failed loop test), line 5 runs n times, line 6 runs n times, line 10 once: 3n + 2 statements (or 3n + 3).
                                • Best case: b = 1, and c bigger than every element. Line 2 once, line 4 once (or twice), line 5 once, line 6 never, line 10 once: 4 statements (or 5).

                                (b) Arithmetic operations. Only line 6 does arithmetic: one multiplication (2 × A[p]) and one addition. (The loop counter’s +1 is not counted here.)

                                • Worst case (same input as before, b = n, c small): n additions + n multiplications = 2n.
                                • Best case (b = 1, c huge, so line 6 never runs): 0 operations.

                                Why two answers (3n+2 or 3n+3)?

                                Whether you count the loop test that ends the loop is a convention. Either is fine as long as you say which you use; both are Θ(n).

                                Ch.2 · Q6Easy

                                A mysterious algorithm

                                1: function F(A, B) ▷ A and B are positive integers2: P = 03: while (A > 0) do4: if (A mod 2 == 1) then5: P = P + B6: end if8: A = floor(A / 2)9: B = 2 * B10: end while12: return P13: end function
                                1. What is returned for A = 10, B = 6?   (b) For A = 13, B = 5?   (c) What does the algorithm do?   (d) Worst-case tight bound on the running time?   (e) Space complexity?
                                Show the worked solution

                                (a) A = 10 (binary 1010), B = 6. Rounds: (10, 6): even, skip → (5, 12): odd, P = 12 → (2, 24): even → (1, 48): odd, P = 12 + 48 = 60 → A becomes 0. Returns 60.

                                (b) A = 13 (1101), B = 5: (13, 5) odd, P = 5; (6, 10) even; (3, 20) odd, P = 25; (1, 40) odd, P = 65. Returns 65.

                                (c) It multiplies A by B (10 × 6 = 60, 13 × 5 = 65). The idea (“Russian peasant multiplication”): write A in binary, A = Σ (bit × power of two). Each round halves A (moving to the next bit) and doubles B (so B is B × 2round). When the current bit of A is 1 we add the current B, which is exactly B × (that bit’s power of two).

                                (d) Θ(log A). A is halved every round, so the loop runs ⌊log2 A⌋ + 1 times (the number of binary digits of A); each round costs constant time.

                                (e) O(1). Three integer variables (A, B, P), no arrays, no recursion.

                                Run the double-and-halve algorithm on your own numbers

                                Ch.2 · Q7Easy

                                Worst-case time of three loop programs

                                Algorithm1(n): for i = 1 to n: for j = n down to i: b = 1Algorithm2(n): for i = n/2 to n: j = 2; while (j ≤ n): j = 2*jAlgorithm3(n, m): for i = 1 to n: a = 1; then, separately, for j = 1 to m: b = 1

                                State and explain the worst-case time of each in big-O.

                                Show the worked solution

                                Algorithm 7.1: O(n²). For each i the inner loop runs from j = n down to i, that is n−i+1 times. Over i = 1..n the line b = 1 runs (n) + (n−1) + … + 1 = n(n+1)/2 times. The other lines run at most O(n) times. Total O(n²).

                                Algorithm 7.2: O(n log n). The outer loop runs about n/2 times. Inside, j doubles 2, 4, 8, … until it passes n, which takes at most log2 n rounds. Multiply: (n/2) × log n = O(n log n). Note that j is reset to 2 each time, so the inner cost does not shrink.

                                Algorithm 7.3: O(n + m). The loops are sequential, not nested: n steps then m steps. Two independent variables, so the answer keeps both.

Algorithm 2 does the same but combines in c1n time. Assume n is a power of 2 and the base case n = 1 costs c2. (a) Write the recurrences. (b) State and explain a Θ bound for each.

                                (a)

                                T1(n) =c2n = 12T1(n/2) + c1n > 1
                                T2(n) =c2n = 12T2(n/2) + c1 nn > 1

                                (b) Algorithm 1: Θ(n). Unroll: T(n) = 2T(n/2) + c1 = 4T(n/4) + (2c1 + c1) = … = 2k T(n/2k) + c1(2k−1 + … + 2 + 1). At k = log2 n: T(n) = c2 n + c1(n − 1). The number of calls doubles every level (1, 2, 4, …, n), each doing constant work, so the cost is proportional to n.

                                Algorithm 2: Θ(n log n). Now level i has 2i calls each doing c1(n/2i), which is c1n in total on every level: T(n) = 2k T(n/2k) + k c1 n, so T(n) = c2 n + c1 n log2 n.

                                The Master theorem shortcut

                                The set reminds you that if a question does not ask you to solve a recurrence you may quote the Master theorem: for T(n) = 2T(n/2) + f(n), a constant f gives Θ(n) (the leaves dominate) and f(n) = Θ(n) gives Θ(n log n) (every level costs the same). See Chapter 1 and Tutorial 1, Part 5.

                                Ch.2 · Q10Medium

                                DOODLE: lines on a coordinate plane

                                1: function DOODLE(n, m)3: if (n > 0) then4: DrawLine((n,n), (m,m))5: DrawLine((n,m), (m,n))6: DOODLE(n - 1, m)7: end if9: end function

                                Each “if” takes time c1; each DrawLine takes c2. (a) Write a recurrence for the running time T(n). (b) Solve it and give a tight bound.

                                Show the worked solution

                                (a) When n ≤ 0 only the if test runs: T(0) = c1. Otherwise the call does the test (c1), two DrawLines (2c2), and one recursive call:

                                T(n) =c1n = 0T(n−1) + c1 + 2c2n > 0

                                (b) Every call adds the same constant c1 + 2c2, and there are n such calls before the base case: T(n) = T(0) + n(c1 + 2c2) = c1 + c1 n + 2c2 n, which is Θ(n). (Note that m plays no role in the cost: the drawing takes constant time wherever the points are.)

                                Part 8 · Chapter 2 Part 3 · Q11 to Q13

                                Designing recursive algorithms (1)

                                The recipe for every design question

                                Part 3 of Chapter 2 only asks you to follow the three-step recipe from Tutorial 1 and to write the answer down clearly:

                                1. Base case: the smallest input whose answer you know without recursion.
                                2. Recursive step: shrink the input, trust the recursive call to solve the smaller problem (the “leap of faith”), then combine.
                                3. Analyse: write the recurrence, solve it (telescoping or levels), and give a bound. If asked, prove correctness by induction that follows the shape of the recursion.
                                Ch.2 · Q11Easy

                                Smallest element and palindrome check

                                Write recursive pseudocode, explain how it works and analyse its time complexity.

                                1. Given an array A[1..n], find the minimum. (Example: A = [3, −10, 10, −6, 2, 5] gives −10.)
                                2. Given a string S of length n, decide whether it is a palindrome. (abba gives True, abb gives False.)
                                Show the worked solution

                                (a) smallest(A, n).

                                function smallest(A, n) if (n == 1) then return A[1] min = smallest(A, n - 1) ▷ leap of faith: min of the first n-1 if (A[n] < min) then return A[n] else return minend function

                                How it works. A one-element array has itself as its minimum. Otherwise ask the recursion for the minimum of the first n−1 elements, then compare it with the last element A[n] and return the smaller.

                                Time. c1 is the cost of one comparison step and c2 the base case:

                                T(n) =c2n = 1T(n−1) + c1n > 1

                                Telescoping: T(n) = T(n−k) + k c1; stop at k = n−1 to get T(n) = c2 + (n−1)c1 = c1 n + c2 − c1, which is O(n) (in fact Θ(n)).

                                (b) ispalindrome(S, left, right), first called as ispalindrome(S, 1, S.length()).

                                function ispalindrome(S, left, right) if (left ≥ right) then return True ▷ 0 or 1 characters left if (S[left] != S[right]) then return False return ispalindrome(S, left + 1, right - 1)end function

                                How it works. Compare the outermost two characters. If they differ it cannot be a palindrome. If they match, the string is a palindrome exactly when the inside (without those two) is a palindrome, so recurse on the inside. When no more than one character remains the answer is True.

                                Time. Every call shrinks the length by 2:

                                T(n) =c20 ≤ n ≤ 1T(n−2) + c1n > 1

                                Telescoping: after k steps T(n) = T(n−2k) + k c1. For even n stop at k = n/2 (reaching T(0)): T(n) = c2 + c1 n/2. For odd n stop at k = (n−1)/2 (reaching T(1)): T(n) = c2 + c1 (n−1)/2. Both are O(n).

                                Worst case versus best case

                                The palindrome check can stop early at the first mismatch (best case constant time, e.g. “abcda” fails immediately). The bound O(n) is the worst case, which happens when the string is a palindrome.

                                Ch.2 · Q12Medium

                                Compute 5ⁿ faster than O(n)

                                Given a positive integer n, design power(n) that computes 5n in less than O(n) time. Give pseudocode and a verbal explanation, the worst-case time, and a proof of correctness by mathematical induction. Hint: 513 = (56)² · 5 and 56 = (53)².

                                Show the worked solution
                                function power(n) if (n == 1) then return 5 x = power(floor(n / 2)) if (n % 2 == 0) then return x * x else return x * x * 5end function

                                Idea. Instead of multiplying by 5 once per step (n steps), halve the exponent: 5n = (5⌊n/2⌋)² when n is even, and the same times 5 when n is odd. One recursive call on half the size, then one or two multiplications.

                                Time.

                                T(n) =c1n = 1T(floor(n/2)) + c2n > 1

                                The exponent is halved every call, so there are about log2 n levels, each doing constant work: O(log n). (Compare 51000000: about 20 calls instead of a million.)

                                Proof of correctness (strong induction). Let P(n) be: power(n) returns 5n.

                                • Base case n = 1: returns 5 = 51.
                                • Inductive step. Assume P(k) for every 1 ≤ k < n. Then x = power(⌊n/2⌋) = 5⌊n/2⌋, because ⌊n/2⌋ is smaller than n. If n is even, the result is x·x = 5n/2·5n/2 = 5n. If n is odd, the result is x·x·5 = 5(n−1)/2·5(n−1)/2·5 = 5n. So P(n) holds.

                                By strong induction P(n) is true for all positive integers n.

                                Try it live

                                Tutorial 1 has a stepper that unwinds power call by call: see Tutorial 1, Part 6.

                                Ch.2 · Q13Medium

                                Evaluating a polynomial with fewer multiplications

                                The algorithm below evaluates Q(x) = A[0] + A[1]·x + A[2]·x² + … + A[k−1]·xk−1 for an array of length k ≥ 1.

                                1: function evaluatePolynomial(A, x)2: Q = 04: for (i = 0 to k-1) do5: t_i = A[i]7: for (j = 1 to i) do8: t_i = t_i * x9: end for11: Q = Q + t_i12: end for14: return Q15: end function
                                1. How many multiplications (line 8) and additions (line 11) does it use, in terms of k?
                                2. Write a recursive algorithm using exactly k−1 multiplications.
                                3. (i) Prove it correct by induction. (ii) Show it uses exactly k−1 multiplications.
                                Show the worked solution

                                (a) Term i needs i multiplications (the inner loop runs i times), so the total is 0 + 1 + 2 + … + (k−1) = k(k−1)/2 multiplications. Line 11 runs once for each of the k terms: k additions.

                                (b) Idea: nest the polynomial (the Horner scheme). Factor out x again and again:

                                Q(x) = A[0] + x·(A[1] + x·(A[2] + … + x·A[k−1]))

                                The bracket is itself the same kind of polynomial, built from the array that starts one position later. Call evaluatePolynomial(A, x, 0):

                                function evaluatePolynomial(A, x, i) k = A.length if (i == k - 1) then return A[i] return A[i] + x * evaluatePolynomial(A, x, i + 1)end function

                                (c)(i) Correctness. For 0 ≤ i < k define Qi(x) = A[i] + A[i+1] x + A[i+2] x2 + … + A[k−1] xk−1−i. Let P(i): evaluatePolynomial(A, x, i) returns Qi(x). We prove it for i going down from k−1 to 0.

                                • Base case i = k−1: returns A[k−1] = Qk−1(x).
                                • Step. Assume P(r+1) for some 0 ≤ r < k−1. Then the call at r returns A[r] + x·Qr+1(x) = A[r] + x·(A[r+1] + A[r+2]x + … + A[k−1]xk−2−r) = A[r] + A[r+1]x + … + A[k−1]xk−1−r = Qr(x).

                                So P(i) holds for all 0 ≤ i < k, and in particular P(0) says the call returns the whole polynomial Q(x).

                                (c)(ii) Counting multiplications. The function is called for i = 0, 1, …, k−1: k calls in total. Every call except the base case does exactly one multiplication (x times the returned value), so there are k−1 multiplications. The cost falls from quadratic (k²/2) to linear.

                                Naive versus nested: same answer, far fewer multiplications

                                Part 9 · Chapter 2 Part 3 · Q14 to Q16

                                Designing recursive algorithms (2)

                                Ch.2 · Q14Hard

                                Largest sub-array sum, two ways

                                Given S[1..n] of integers, return the largest sum of any consecutive sub-array, or 0 if no sub-array has a positive sum. Example: S = [−2, 4, −3, 2, 3, −1, 2, −4, −3, 5] has best sub-array [4, −3, 2, 3, −1, 2] with sum 7.

                                1. Divide and conquer: (1) best sum in the left half, (2) best in the right half, (3) best that crosses the middle, (4) take the largest. Write the pseudocode and analyse it.
                                2. Design an O(n)-time, O(1)-extra-space algorithm, explain it and analyse it.
                                Show the worked solution

                                (a) MaxArray1(S, left, right), called as MaxArray1(S, 1, n).

                                function MaxArray1(S, left, right) if (left == right) then return Max(S[left], 0) middle = floor((left + right) / 2) maxSumL = MaxArray1(S, left, middle) ▷ case 1 maxSumR = MaxArray1(S, middle + 1, right) ▷ case 2 ▷ case 3: the best sum that crosses the middle maxBorderSumL = 0; borderSumL = 0 for (i = middle down to left): borderSumL += S[i]; maxBorderSumL = Max(maxBorderSumL, borderSumL) maxBorderSumR = 0; borderSumR = 0 for (i = middle + 1 to right): borderSumR += S[i]; maxBorderSumR = Max(maxBorderSumR, borderSumR) return Max(maxSumL, maxSumR, maxBorderSumL + maxBorderSumR)end function

                                A best sub-array lies completely in the left half, completely in the right half, or crosses the middle. A crossing one is a best “suffix of the left half” glued to a best “prefix of the right half”, each found by one scan outward from the middle (starting the maximum at 0 allows an empty side).

                                Time.

                                T(n) =c1n = 1T(floor(n/2)) + T(ceil(n/2)) + c2 nn > 1

                                There are about log2 n levels, and the crossing scans on one level touch every element about once, so each level costs O(n): O(n log n).

                                (b) MaxArray2(S, n)

                                function MaxArray2(S, n) tempSum = 0; maxSum = 0 for (i = 1 to n): tempSum = tempSum + S[i] tempSum = Max(0, tempSum) maxSum = Max(maxSum, tempSum) return maxSumend function

                                Why it works. Keep the best sum of a sub-array that ends at the current position (tempSum). If that running sum ever becomes negative, it can only hurt any longer sub-array, so throw it away and restart from 0. Remember the largest value ever seen (maxSum).

                                Time and space. One loop of n rounds with constant work in each: O(n) time; only two extra variables: O(1) extra space.

                                Watch both algorithms run

                                Tutorial 1 steps through exactly this problem on the same array: see Tutorial 1, Part 7. The linear algorithm is known as Kadane’s algorithm.

                                Ch.2 · Q15Hard

                                Find the missing integer

                                A[1..n] holds all of the n + 1 integers p, p+1, …, p+n except one.

                                1. Brute force: try every integer from p to p+n. Explain and analyse.
                                2. Compare the sum of A with the sum of p..p+n. Explain and analyse.
                                3. Analyse FindMissingRecursive, which splits the array into a lower and an upper half by swapping, decides which half lacks an element, and recurses on it. Assume n = 2k − 1.
                                Show the worked solution

                                (a) Brute force, O(n²).

                                function FindMissing(A, n, p) for (j = p to p + n): found = False for (i = 1 to n): if (A[i] == j) then found = True if (found == False) then return jend function

                                For each candidate number j scan the whole array to see whether it appears; the first one that never appears is the answer. Two nested loops of about n and n+1 rounds with constant work inside: O((n+1)n) = O(n²).

                                (b) Sum method, O(n).

                                function FindMissingBySum(A, n, p) sum = 0 for (i = 1 to n): sum = sum + A[i] full_sum = (n + 1) * (p + p + n) / 2 ▷ p + (p+1) + ... + (p+n) return full_sum - sumend function

                                The full list p..p+n has n+1 terms with average (2p+n)/2, so its sum is (n+1)(2p+n)/2. The array has everything except one number, so (full sum) − (array sum) is the missing number. One pass over the array: O(n).

                                (c) FindMissingRecursive, O(n). Each call scans the current part once (the swaps cost O(1) each) and then recurses on one half only. So the number of elements scanned is

                                n + n/2 + n/4 + … + 1 < 2n = O(n)

                                The exact count, with T(1) = 1 and T(n) = n + T(n/2) for n ≥ 2 (here n/2 stands for the next array length 2k−1 − 1): with n = 2k − 1,

                                T(2k − 1) = (2k − 1) + (2k−1 − 1) + … + (22 − 1) + T(1)

                                which sums to 2n − log2(n+1) = 2n − k, so O(n). This count includes one look at the last remaining element (the base case T(1) = 1). The demo below counts only the elements visited by the partitioning loops, which is one fewer: 2n − k − 1. Either way the order is O(n), far below brute force’s n(n+1).

                                Watch the halving search find the missing number

                                Ch.2 · Q16Hard

                                Towers of Hanoi with red and yellow disks

                                There are n disk sizes and 3 pegs. For each size there is one red and one yellow disk. All 2n disks start on one peg, ordered by size, and must be moved to another peg in the same order (including the colours) in as few moves as possible. The usual rule applies: a disk may not sit on a smaller disk; two disks of the same size may sit on each other in either order. Let P(n) be the number of moves.

                                1. Find P(1) and P(2). (b) Describe a recursive algorithm in words. (c) Form a recurrence for P(n). (d) Solve it. (e) Give a big-O bound.
                                Show the worked solution

                                (a) P(1) = 3, P(2) = 11.

                                For n = 1 (two disks of equal size) the colours would be reversed if we simply moved both across, so we use the spare peg to reverse them twice: 1) top disk to the spare peg, 2) bottom disk to the destination, 3) top disk from the spare peg onto the destination. 3 moves.

                                For n = 2: 1) move the two small disks to the destination peg (2 moves, any colour order); 2) move the two large disks to the spare peg (2 moves, their order is now reversed); 3) move the two small disks back to the original peg (2 moves); 4) move the two large disks from the spare peg to the destination (2 moves, now correct again); 5–7) move the two small disks with the 3-move trick of n = 1. Total 2 + 2 + 2 + 2 + 3 = 11 moves.

                                (b) The algorithm. Let Q(m) be the number of moves to shift the m smallest sizes (2m disks) to another peg ignoring colour order. To move all n sizes with the colours preserved:

                                1. Move the 2n−2 smaller disks from the original peg to the destination peg (Q(n−1) moves).
                                2. Move the two largest disks from the original peg to the spare peg (2 moves). Their order is now reversed.
                                3. Move the 2n−2 smaller disks from the destination peg back to the original peg (Q(n−1) moves).
                                4. Move the two largest disks from the spare peg to the destination (2 moves). Their order is now correct again.
                                5. Now the 2n−2 smaller disks, back in their original order on the original peg, are moved to the destination with the same algorithm, recursively (P(n−1) moves).

                                The base case n = 1 takes 3 moves.

                                (c) The recurrence. Ignoring colours, moving 2m disks of m pairs is just the ordinary Towers of Hanoi with every disk doubled, which costs twice the ordinary count: Q(m) = 2(2m − 1) = 2m+1 − 2. So

                                P(n) = Q(n−1) + 2 + Q(n−1) + 2 + P(n−1) = (2n − 2) + 2 + (2n − 2) + 2 + P(n−1) = 2n+1 + P(n−1)
                                P(n) =3n = 1P(n−1) + 2n+1n > 1

                                (d) Solving. Unroll: P(n) = 2n+1 + 2n + … + 23 + P(1). The powers 23, …, 2n+1 form a geometric series with sum 23(2n−1 − 1)/(2 − 1) = 2n+2 − 8. Hence

                                P(n) = 2n+2 − 8 + 3 = 2n+2 − 5 (n ≥ 1)

                                Check: P(1) = 8 − 5 = 3, P(2) = 16 − 5 = 11, P(3) = 32 − 5 = 27.

                                (e) P(n) = 4·2n − 5, so the algorithm takes O(2n) moves.

                                What the set does not prove

                                The set asks for an algorithm and its count, not a proof that no shorter solution exists. A breadth-first search over every legal configuration confirms that 3, 11 and 27 are the true minimum for n = 1, 2, 3 (so the formula is tight there), but the general lower-bound argument is not part of the official solution.

                                Step through the coloured Hanoi solution

                                Part 10 · Summary

                                Summary, self-test and slips

                                The whole set in one table

                                Question typeWhat to doAnswers in this set
                                Write a recurrenceBase case(s) plus “answer for n in terms of smaller answers”. Ask: what does the last step add or multiply?Ch.1 Q1: T(n−1)+n, T(n−1)+2n−1, n·T(n−1), Fibonacci, 1.1·T(n−1), tribonacci-type counts
                                Solve a recurrenceTelescope (substitute again and again until the base case) and write the closed form. Or count levels × work per level.Ch.1 Q2–Q4; Ch.2 Q9, Q10, Q11
                                Induction proofBase case, assume for k, show for k+1 (or strong induction on all smaller sizes), name where the hypothesis is used.Ch.1 Q5–Q6; Ch.2 Q12, Q13
                                Prove or disprove a boundProve: exhibit constants. Disprove: assume constants exist and contradict them for a huge n, or give one counter-example pair.Ch.2 Q1–Q4
                                Analyse codeCount the runs of each line (nested multiplies, sequential adds, halving gives log). Find the worst-case input.Ch.2 Q5–Q8
                                Design a recursive algorithmCut the problem (n−1, n/2, both halves), combine, base case. Then recurrence, bound and (if asked) induction proof.Ch.2 Q11–Q16

                                Self-test

                                1. What does telescoping a recurrence like T(n) = T(n−1) + c do, and when do you stop?

                                  Show the answer

                                  You substitute the recurrence into itself, T(n) = T(n−2) + 2c = T(n−3) + 3c …, spot the pattern T(n−k) + k·c, and stop when the argument reaches the base case (here k = n−1 or n).

                                2. Why does T(n) = 2T(n/2) + c give Θ(n) but 2T(n/2) + cn give Θ(n log n)?

                                  Show the answer

                                  Level i has 2i calls. With a constant combine cost the work per level doubles, so the bottom level (about n calls) dominates the total. With a linear combine cost each level costs the same cn in total, and there are log2 n levels.

                                3. To prove f(n) = Θ(g(n)) from the definition, what do you have to produce? To disprove it?

                                  Show the answer

                                  Prove: three constants c1, c2 > 0 and n0 with c1g ≤ f ≤ c2g for all n ≥ n0. Disprove: show that for any choice of constants the inequality fails for some large n (usually by contradiction).

                                4. Why is the double loop for i = 1 to n: for j = n down to i still O(n²) although the inner loop gets shorter?

                                  Show the answer

                                  The inner loop runs n, n−1, …, 1 times: the total is n(n+1)/2, which is half of n² plus a little. Constants are ignored, so it is O(n²).

                                5. What does the doubling-and-halving algorithm of Ch.2 Q6 compute, and why does it take Θ(log A) time?

                                  Show the answer

                                  It computes A·B. A is halved every round, so the loop ends after as many rounds as A has binary digits.

                                6. How does the nested (Horner) form save multiplications in Q13?

                                  Show the answer

                                  Every term A[i]xi shares its powers of x with the next one, so instead of recomputing xi for each term (k(k−1)/2 multiplications) we multiply once per level of the nesting (k−1).

                                7. Why does the max-subarray algorithm of Q14(b) reset its running sum to 0 when it goes negative?

                                  Show the answer

                                  A negative running sum can only make every longer sub-array worse, so the best sub-array that continues past this point is better off starting fresh at the next element.

                                8. In the red/yellow Hanoi problem, why do two disks of the same size need a trip via the third peg?

                                  Show the answer

                                  Moving a pair directly reverses its order (the red one ends above the yellow one). Moving it twice, first to the spare peg and then to the destination, swaps the order twice and restores it. That doubling explains why P(n) = 2n+1 + P(n−1).
