Chapter 5 is trees (Chapter 5). The problems are numbered exactly as in the PDF: “Ch.3 Q6” is problem 6 of the Chapter 3 section, and the graph problems are Ch.3 Q11 to Q16. Each is marked Easy, Medium or Hard as in the set.

                                  How to use this page

                                  Read the problem, try it on paper, then press Show the worked solution. A hint comes first when one helps. The set itself says these problems are for your own practice and need no submission, so the full solutions here are fair to read.

                                  Ch.3 · Q1Easy

                                  True or false: lists, stacks and queues

                                  For each statement, say whether it is True or False. For a False statement, correct the wrong part.

                                  1. A data type is defined as a set of values and a collection of operations on those values.
                                  2. The elements of a stack can be accessed randomly.
                                  3. Inserting an element at the head of an unsorted array-based list is an O(n) operation.
                                  4. Items come out of a stack in the same order they go in.
                                  5. A queue ADT works by inserting elements at one end and deleting from the same end.
                                  6. The worst case time complexity for searching an element inside a linked list is O(n).
                                  7. A linked list can have variable size of length.

                                  Think first

                                  Picture the thing: a stack is a pile of plates (you touch only the top plate), a queue is a line at a shop (join at the back, leave from the front), an array is a row of numbered boxes in a fixed block of memory.

                                  Show the worked solution
                                  PartVerdictWhy
                                  (a)TrueThat is the definition of a data type: values plus the operations allowed on them. (An integer is the set of whole numbers with +, −, ×, ….)
                                  (b)FalseA stack gives access to one element only: the most recently pushed one (the top). To reach the third plate you must remove the two above it. Correction: only the top element can be accessed.
                                  (c)TrueIn an array the elements sit in consecutive boxes. To put a new element in box 1, the existing n elements must each shift one box to the right: n moves, so O(n). (A linked list does this in O(1).)
                                  (d)FalseA stack is Last-In First-Out. Push 1, 2, 3 and the pops return 3, 2, 1: the reverse order. Correction: the most recently pushed item comes out first.
                                  (e)FalseA queue is First-In First-Out: people join at the back and leave from the front. Correction: insert at one end (the back) and delete at the opposite end (the front).
                                  (f)TrueThe only way to find a value in an unsorted linked list is to follow the arrows from the head. In the worst case the value is last or missing, so all n nodes are visited: O(n).
                                  (g)TrueEach node is created separately and joined by a pointer, so you can add or remove nodes whenever you like and the list grows and shrinks. (Contrast with a plain array, whose size is fixed when it is made.)

                                  The one-line memory aids

                                  Stack = pile of plates, LIFO. Queue = shop queue, FIFO. Array insert at the front = shift everything. Linked list search = walk the chain. See the List ADT, the Stack ADT and the Queue ADT for the full pictures.

                                  Ch.3 · Q2Easy

                                  Run the operations; what do they cost?

                                  1. An empty linked list L inserts at the head. Write the elements, from the head, after: insert(12), insert(3), insert(5), delete(5), search(3), insert(2), search(12), delete(2), delete(12), insert(85), insert(62).
                                  2. An empty stack S: push(12), push(3), push(5), pop(), push(26), push(2), pop(), pop(), push(85), pop(), pop(). Write the popped elements in order.
                                  3. An empty queue Q: enqueue(12), enqueue(3), enqueue(5), dequeue(), enqueue(26), enqueue(2), dequeue(), dequeue(), enqueue(85), dequeue(), dequeue(). Write the dequeued elements in order.
                                  4. List L with n elements, only the head pointer known. Give the time of Search(L, x), Insert(L, k, x), Delete(L, x) for a singly linked and a doubly linked list.
                                  5. Stack S with n elements: the time of Push(S, x) and Pop(S).

                                  Think first

                                  For (a)–(c), keep a little picture and update it after every operation. Which end is the “head”, the “top” and the “front”? Most mistakes are about that.

                                  Show the worked solution

                                  (a) Linked list, insert at the head. Each new element becomes the first one. Searching changes nothing.

                                  operationlist after it (head on the left)
                                  insert(12)12
                                  insert(3)3, 12
                                  insert(5)5, 3, 12
                                  delete(5)3, 12
                                  search(3)3, 12 (unchanged)
                                  insert(2)2, 3, 12
                                  search(12)2, 3, 12 (unchanged)
                                  delete(2)3, 12
                                  delete(12)3
                                  insert(85)85, 3
                                  insert(62)62, 85, 3

                                  (b) Stack. Push puts on the top; pop removes the top. The stack (bottom → top) changes like this: [12] → [12, 3] → [12, 3, 5] → pop gives 5 → [12, 3] → [12, 3, 26] → [12, 3, 26, 2] → pop gives 2 → pop gives 26 → [12, 3] → [12, 3, 85] → pop gives 85 → pop gives 3. Popped in order: 5, 2, 26, 85, 3 (the 12 is still in the stack).

                                  (c) Queue. Enqueue joins the back; dequeue removes the front. The queue (front → back): [12, 3, 5] → dequeue gives 12 → [3, 5] → [3, 5, 26, 2] → dequeue gives 3 → dequeue gives 5 → [26, 2] → [26, 2, 85] → dequeue gives 26 → dequeue gives 2. Dequeued in order: 12, 3, 5, 26, 2.

                                  Run any list of operations, one step at a time

                                  The same ten operations on a stack and on a queue give opposite-feeling results: the stack hands back the newest item (5, 2, 26, 85, 3) while the queue hands back the oldest (12, 3, 5, 26, 2). Switch the structure above and compare.

                                  (d) Costs of a list with n elements, knowing only the head.

                                  Search(L, x)Insert(L, k, x)Delete(L, x)
                                  singly linkedO(n)O(n)O(n)
                                  doubly linkedO(n)O(n)O(n)
                                  • Search: you must walk from the head, up to n steps.
                                  • Insert at position k: first walk k nodes along (up to n in the worst case), then relink in O(1). Insert at the very head would be O(1), but the question asks about a general position.
                                  • Delete the element with value x: first find it (O(n)); unlinking is O(1). A doubly linked list lets you unlink a node in O(1) if you already hold a pointer to that node, but here you only hold the head and a value, so the search still dominates. That is why the doubly linked list is no better in this table.

                                  (e) Stack. Push and pop only touch the top, so both take O(1) whatever the size n (with a linked list you change the head; with an array you change one index).

                                  Part 2 · Chapter 3 Part 2 · Q3

                                  Linked-list pointer tricks

                                  Question 3 asks for three algorithms on a singly linked list using only O(1) extra space: delete every node with a given value, reverse the list, and detect a cycle. All three are done by moving a few pointers along the list and rewiring next arrows. For the pictures behind linked lists, see Linked lists and Tutorial 3. The node is

                                  struct Node { int data; Node *next;};

                                  How to think about pointer problems

                                  Draw the boxes and arrows. For every line of code, redraw the arrows that change. Before you overwrite an arrow, ask: “Have I saved where it was pointing?” Almost every bug is a lost arrow.

                                  Watch all three work

                                  Delete all val, reverse, and detect a cycle: step by step

                                  Ch.3 · Q3(a)Medium

                                  Delete every node whose data equals val

                                  Given the head of a singly linked list (at least one node) and an integer val, design Delete(head, val) that removes all nodes whose data equals val. Example: 1→2→4→3→4→5 with val = 4 becomes 1→2→3→5. Give pseudocode, a verbal explanation, the worst-case time, and use only O(1) extra space.

                                  Think first

                                  To remove a node X you must change the next of the node before it. So stand on the node before the one you are testing. What if the very first node must be removed? Who is “before” it? Invent one.

                                  Show the worked solution
                                  function Delete(head, val) dummy = Node() dummy.next = head current = dummy while current.next != NULL do if current.next.data == val then current.next = current.next.next else current = current.next return dummy.next
                                  dummy = Node()

                                  a fake node placed in front of the list. Its data is never used.

                                  dummy.next = head

                                  the real list hangs behind the dummy.

                                  current = dummy

                                  current always points at the node before the one being tested.

                                  while current.next != NULL do

                                  stop when there is nothing left to test.

                                  if current.next.data == val then

                                  the next node must go.

                                  current.next = current.next.next

                                  skip over it: the arrow now jumps past the bad node. current does not move, because the node that is now next has not been tested yet (it might be a second 4 in a row).

                                  else current = current.next

                                  the next node is fine, so step forward.

                                  return dummy.next

                                  the new head. If the old head was deleted, this is different from head, which is why we do not return head.

                                  Why the dummy? Without it, deleting the first node would be a special case: there is no node before it to rewire, so you would need extra code to move head. With a dummy in front, every real node has a node before it, so one loop handles everything, even a list like 4→4→4 (the answer is the empty list: dummy.next becomes NULL).

                                  Trace for 1→2→4→3→4→5, val = 4:

                                  current is the node holdingcurrent.next holdsaction
                                  dummy1not 4, move on
                                  12not 4, move on
                                  24is 4: 2.next now points to 3. current stays at 2
                                  23not 4, move on
                                  34is 4: 3.next now points to 5. current stays at 3
                                  35not 4, move on
                                  5NULLloop ends; return dummy.next = 1→2→3→5

                                  Time: each iteration either advances current by one node or deletes one node, and nothing is ever revisited, so there are at most n iterations of O(1) work each: O(n). Space: three pointers: O(1).

                                  Ch.3 · Q3(b)Medium

                                  Reverse a linked list

                                  Design Reverse(head) that reverses the list by changing the links between nodes and returns the new head. Example: 1→2→3→4→5 becomes 5→4→3→2→1. Pseudocode, explanation, time, O(1) extra space.

                                  Think first

                                  Turn one arrow at a time. To turn the arrow of node X so that it points backwards, you need to know the node behind it, and you need to remember the node ahead before you destroy the arrow that leads there. Three pointers: previous, current, next.

                                  Show the worked solution
                                  function Reverse(head) curr = head prev = NULL after = NULL while curr != NULL do after = curr.next curr.next = prev prev = curr curr = after return prev
                                  prev = NULL

                                  the new list starts empty: the old first node will become its last node, pointing to NULL.

                                  after = curr.next

                                  save the way forward before the next line destroys it.

                                  curr.next = prev

                                  turn the arrow around.

                                  prev = curr

                                  the node just finished is now the one behind.

                                  curr = after

                                  move forward along the old list.

                                  return prev

                                  when curr falls off the end (NULL), prev is the old last node: the new head.

                                  Trace on 1→2→3 (three passes):

                                  passafter = curr.nextcurr.next = prevthen prev, curr =
                                  121 → NULL1, 2
                                  232 → 12, 3
                                  3NULL3 → 23, NULL (stop; return 3)

                                  The result 3→2→1→NULL. If you switched the first two lines (turning the arrow before saving after), you would lose the rest of the list. Try the reverse task in the demo above and watch the orange arrows.

                                  Time: each node is handled once with four O(1) assignments: O(n). Space: three pointers: O(1). (A recursive version would use O(n) call-stack space, which is not allowed here.)

                                  Ch.3 · Q3(c)Medium

                                  Detect a cycle

                                  A cycle occurs when a node’s next points back to an earlier node. Design Cycle(head) that returns True if there is a cycle, else False. Example: 1→2→3→4→2 gives True; 1→2→3→4→5 gives False. O(1) extra space.

                                  Think first

                                  Think of two runners on a track. If the track has a loop, a faster runner eventually laps the slower one. If the track ends, the fast runner just reaches the end. How can you make a list “run”?

                                  Show the worked solution
                                  function Cycle(head) slow = head fast = head while slow != NULL and fast != NULL and fast.next != NULL do slow = slow.next fast = fast.next.next if slow == fast then return TRUE return FALSE
                                  slow, fast

                                  the tortoise and the hare, both starting at the head.

                                  while ... fast.next != NULL

                                  both checks keep fast.next.next legal: if fast or fast.next is NULL we have reached an end, so there is no cycle. (Check fast.next before using fast.next.next.)

                                  slow = slow.next

                                  one step.

                                  fast = fast.next.next

                                  two steps.

                                  if slow == fast

                                  the two pointers stand on the same node: they have met inside a loop.

                                  return FALSE

                                  the hare fell off the end of the list: no loop.

                                  Why do they meet if there is a cycle? Once both are inside the loop (of length L), look at the gap from slow forward to fast. Each round the hare moves 2 and the tortoise 1, so the gap grows by exactly 1 (mod L). The gap can only take the values 0, 1, …, L−1, so within L rounds it hits 0, and then they stand on the same node. A hare can never jump over the tortoise, because the gap changes by one at a time.

                                  Why not meet if there is no cycle? The hare reaches NULL first, the loop ends, and the answer is False.

                                  Time: the tortoise needs at most n−L steps to get into the loop, and then at most L more rounds for the gap to close. The total is at most n rounds of O(1) work: O(n). Space: two pointers: O(1).

                                  The obvious solution that is not allowed

                                  You could store every visited node in a set and say True when you see one twice. That is correct and O(n) time, but it uses O(n) extra space, and the question says O(1). The two-pointer idea (Floyd’s tortoise and hare) removes the set.

                                  Check yourself

                                  1. Run Delete on 4→4→4 with val = 4. What is returned, and which line of the code made that work?

                                    Show the answer

                                    The empty list (NULL). The dummy’s next was rewired past all three nodes, and return dummy.next returns NULL. The dummy node is what lets the first node be deleted by the same code as any other.

                                  2. In Delete, why do we not move current forward right after removing a node?

                                    Show the answer

                                    The node that is now current.next has not been tested yet. In 1→4→4→2 the second 4 would be skipped if current jumped forward.

                                  3. In Reverse, what goes wrong if the lines after = curr.next and curr.next = prev are swapped?

                                    Show the answer

                                    The old forward arrow is overwritten before it is saved, so after becomes the previous node (or NULL) and the loop never reaches the rest of the list.

                                  Part 3 · Chapter 3 Part 2 · Q4 and Q5

                                  Algorithms with a stack or a queue

                                  These problems are about choosing the right tool. A stack (last in, first out) turns things around: whatever went in last comes out first. A queue (first in, first out) keeps the order of arrival and lets you serve the oldest item first. See the Stack ADT and the Queue ADT. The tool below replays the queue algorithms of Q4(b), Q4(d) and Q5 so you can watch the queue change.

                                  First non-repeating letter, binary numbers 1 to n, and the housing queue

                                  Ch.3 · Q4Medium

                                  Four string and number problems with a stack or a queue

                                  For each part, design an algorithm that uses a stack or a queue; give pseudocode, a verbal explanation and the worst-case time.

                                  1. Given a string r, return it reversed. (“abc” gives “cba”.)
                                  2. Given a string r, return the index of the first non-repeating character, or −1. (“lovecs” gives 1; “lovecslove” gives 5.)
                                  3. Decide whether r is a palindrome. (“abccba” is; “abccb” is not.)
                                  4. Given a positive integer n, print the binary representations of 1 to n. (n = 7 prints 1, 10, 11, 100, 101, 110, 111.)

                                  Think first

                                  (a) and (c): a stack hands things back in the opposite order. (b) and (d): you need to remember the order of arrival and look at the oldest first, which is a queue. For (d), look at how 100 and 101 are built from 10.

                                  Show the worked solution

                                  (a) Reverse a string: push everything, then pop everything

                                  function Reverse(r) result = String() S = Stack() for i = 1 to r.length do S.push(r[i]) while S.isEmpty() == FALSE do result = result + S.pop() return result

                                  Pushing a, b, c leaves c on top. Popping gives c, b, a. That is the reversal. Time: n pushes and n pops, each O(1): O(n).

                                  (b) First non-repeating character: a queue of letters in arrival order

                                  function Unique(r) count = array of zeros, one per possible character Q = Queue() for i = 1 to r.length do c = r[i] count[c] = count[c] + 1 Q.enqueue((c, i)) while Q.front() != NULL and count[Q.front().first] > 1 do Q.dequeue() if Q.front() == NULL then return -1 return Q.front().second
                                  count

                                  how many times each character has been seen so far.

                                  Q.enqueue((c, i))

                                  every character joins the back together with its position i, so the queue keeps the order of first appearance.

                                  while ... count[Q.front().first] > 1

                                  the oldest candidate has since been seen again, so it is not unique: remove it. Look only at the front.

                                  return Q.front().second

                                  after the whole string, the front is the oldest letter still seen only once: its position is the answer.

                                  Why only the front? A repeated letter in the middle of the queue is harmless: it will be thrown away later, when it reaches the front. Only the front decides the answer. Why correct: counts never decrease, so a removed letter really repeats; and everything ahead of the front was removed, so the front is the earliest survivor. Time: one pass; each letter is enqueued once and dequeued at most once: O(n) (with a fixed alphabet the count table is O(1) to access).

                                  (c) Palindrome: compare the string with its own reversal

                                  function isPalindrome(r) S = Stack() for i = 1 to r.length do S.push(r[i]) for i = 1 to r.length do if r[i] != S.pop() then return FALSE return TRUE

                                  The first pop gives the last letter, which must equal the first letter; the second pop gives the second-last, which must equal the second, and so on. Any mismatch means not a palindrome. Time: two passes of O(1) steps: O(n). (Comparing only the first half would also do.)

                                  (d) Binary numbers: grow each number by writing 0 or 1 after it

                                  function generateBinary(n) Q = Queue() Q.enqueue("1") while n >= 1 do r = Q.front() Q.dequeue() print(r) Q.enqueue(r + "0") Q.enqueue(r + "1") n = n - 1

                                  Notice 10 and 11 come from 1; 100 and 101 come from 10; 110 and 111 from 11. So the numbers can be produced from earlier numbers by appending 0 and 1. A queue serves the oldest first, so the output comes out in the order 1, 10, 11, 100, 101, … (shorter numbers before longer ones, and in increasing order within one length). Time: n rounds, each doing a constant number of queue operations: O(n) (each printed number has about log n digits, so the written output is longer; the question counts the loop).

                                  Ch.3 · Q5Medium

                                  Flats for the waiting list

                                  Residents queue for flats of type A or B. The flats are allocated in the given order: no flat is given out until all flats in front of it have gone. The resident at the front of the waiting list is shown the first available flat; if it matches the resident’s preference, he/she takes it and leaves; otherwise he/she goes to the back of the list. There are n residents (list R[1…n] of preferences) and m flats (list F[1…m] of types). Find the number of people who finally get no flat. Example: F = [A, A, B, A], R = [B, A, B] gives 2.

                                  (a) Write noFlat(F, R) using a stack or a queue and explain it. (b) Give its worst-case time.

                                  Think first

                                  “Goes to the back of the list” is exactly what a queue does. When does it stop? When the flat on offer is a type that nobody still waiting wants: every resident has been tried and refused, so nobody can ever move on.

                                  Show the worked solution
                                  function noFlat(F, R) resident = Queue() queueSize = R.length count = 0 flatIndex = 1 for i = 1 to R.length do resident.enqueue(R[i]) while resident.isEmpty() == FALSE and flatIndex <= F.length do currResident = resident.dequeue() if currResident != F[flatIndex] then resident.enqueue(currResident) count = count + 1 else count = 0 queueSize = queueSize - 1 flatIndex = flatIndex + 1 if count == queueSize then break return queueSize
                                  resident = Queue()

                                  the waiting list, front = first in line.

                                  queueSize

                                  how many people are still waiting (it goes down only when someone takes a flat).

                                  count

                                  how many people in a row have refused the current flat.

                                  currResident = resident.dequeue()

                                  the person at the front is shown the current flat F[flatIndex].

                                  if currResident != F[flatIndex]

                                  refusal: to the back of the line, and the refusal counter goes up.

                                  else count = 0 ... flatIndex + 1

                                  a match: the person leaves, the next flat is offered, and the refusal counter starts again from 0.

                                  if count == queueSize then break

                                  every person still waiting has refused this very flat in a row, so nobody wants it. Flats must go in order, so no later flat can be given either.

                                  return queueSize

                                  the people who never got a flat.

                                  Check it on the example. F = [A, A, B, A], R = [B, A, B]. Flat 1 (A): B refuses (count 1), A takes it (count 0, 2 people left: B, B), flat 2 (A): B refuses (count 1), B refuses (count 2 = queueSize): stop, answer 2. Run it in the tool above (“Q5 flats”) and step through.

                                  (b) Time. After each flat is given out, at most n refusals can happen before either a match or the stop. There are at most m flats. So the loop runs at most about m × n times with O(1) work each, plus O(n) to fill the queue: O(mn).

                                  A faster way (bonus; it is not asked)

                                  Because residents keep rotating, a person who wants type A will eventually be at the front when an A flat is offered, as long as somebody wanting A is still in the line. So only the counts matter: count how many residents want A and want B. For each flat in order, if the count for its type is 0 then stop; otherwise subtract 1. The answer is the number of people left. That is O(n + m). (I checked this against the queue version on thousands of random inputs; they always agree.)

                                  Part 4 · Chapter 3 Part 2 · Q6 and Q7

                                  Next lower day, and the Josephus circle

                                  Two Hard problems that Tutorial 3 explains at length. Here you get the full answers to this problem set with the key ideas; for the slow, step-by-step version see the monotone stack and the Josephus circle.

                                  Ch.3 · Q6Hard

                                  How long until Jeff is happier?

                                  Day i has rainfall A[i]. Starting from each day, how many days must Jeff wait for a day with strictly less rainfall? If there is none, the answer is −1. Return the array B. Example: A = [4, 2, 5, 7, 6, 1] gives B = [1, 4, 3, 1, 1, −1].

                                  1. Write the expected output for A = [3, 4, 5, 2, 8, 9, 4].
                                  2. HappyJeff1 (below) is the naive method. (i) Explain how it works. (ii) Give its worst-case time.
                                  3. (i) Write HappyJeff2(A, n) running in O(n) using a stack, and explain it. (ii) Analyze its time.
                                  function HappyJeff1(A, n) B = Array(n) for i = 1 to n do B[i] = -1 for i = 1 to n do for j = i+1 to n do if A[j] < A[i] then B[i] = j - i break return B

                                  Think first

                                  (c): scan from the right. Keep a stack of days that could still be someone’s answer. When a new day arrives, any day on the stack with rainfall at least as big can never be the answer for a day further left, because the new day is nearer and no bigger. Throw those away.

                                  Show the worked solution

                                  (a) Day 1 (3): the first lower day is day 4 (rainfall 2), wait 3. Day 2 (4): day 4, wait 2. Day 3 (5): day 4, wait 1. Day 4 (2): nothing later is lower, −1. Day 5 (8): day 7 (4), wait 2. Day 6 (9): day 7, wait 1. Day 7: −1. So B = [3, 2, 1, −1, 2, 1, −1].

                                  (b)(i) B starts as all −1 (“no happier day yet”). For every day i the inner loop looks at the following days j = i+1, i+2, … and stops at the first one with A[j] < A[i], recording the wait j − i. If the inner loop ends without finding one, the −1 stays.

                                  (b)(ii) The worst case is when no day has a lower day after it (for example the rainfall only goes up: 1, 2, 3, …, n). Then each day scans all the later days: (n−1) + (n−2) + … + 1 = n(n−1)/2 comparisons, so O(n²). The initialization costs only O(n).

                                  (c)(i)

                                  function HappyJeff2(A, n) B = Array(n) S = Stack() for i = n down to 1 do while S.isEmpty() == FALSE and A[i] <= A[S.top()] do S.pop() if S.isEmpty() == FALSE then B[i] = S.top() - i else B[i] = -1 S.push(i) return B
                                  for i = n down to 1

                                  right to left, so the days to the right are already summarized in the stack.

                                  while ... A[i] <= A[S.top()]

                                  the day on top is not lower than day i (equal rainfall does not count: Jeff needs strictly less), and it is farther than i, so for any day to the left of i it is beaten by day i. Delete it.

                                  B[i] = S.top() - i

                                  whatever is now on top is the nearest later day with strictly smaller rainfall.

                                  S.push(i)

                                  day i becomes a candidate for the days to its left (do this after recording the answer).

                                  Next lower day, step by step

                                  (c)(ii) Every day is pushed once and popped at most once, so the total number of stack operations over the whole run is at most 2n. The while loop looks like a nested loop, but its total number of iterations is at most the number of pops, which is at most n. With the O(n) setup, the whole algorithm is O(n) time and O(n) space.

                                  Ch.3 · Q7Hard

                                  The Josephus problem

                                  n prisoners stand in a circle, numbered 0 to n−1. Starting from prisoner 0, every k-th prisoner is removed, until one remains and is freed. Example: n = 5, k = 2: execution order 1, 3, 0, 4; survivor 2.

                                  1. Write the execution order and the survivor for n = 6, k = 3.
                                  2. With a queue, design an algorithm for the survivor in O(kn) time and explain it.
                                  3. Let A(n, k) be the survivor. (i) Find the relation between A(n, k) and A(n−1, k). (ii) Design an O(n) algorithm using it.

                                  Think first

                                  (b): a circle is a queue where the front person is sent to the back. Counting off k people means sending the first k−1 to the back and removing the k-th. (c): after the first person is removed you have the same game with one fewer person, but the people are renamed. Work out how to translate a name in the small game back to a name in the big game.

                                  Show the worked solution

                                  (a) Count 1, 2, 3 starting at prisoner 0: the third is prisoner 2, removed. Continue from 3: 3, 4, 5, so prisoner 5 is removed. From 0: 0, 1, 3 (2 and 5 are gone), so 3. From 4: 4, 0, 1, so 1. From 4: 4, 0, 4 (1,2,3,5 gone), so 4. Order: 2, 5, 3, 1, 4; survivor 0.

                                  (b) With a queue.

                                  function FindSurvivor1(n, k) Q = Queue() for i = 0 to n-1 do Q.enqueue(i) while n > 1 do for i = 1 to k-1 do x = Q.dequeue() Q.enqueue(x) Q.dequeue() n = n - 1 return Q.dequeue()

                                  The queue is the circle, with the front being the person where counting continues. The inner loop sends the first k−1 people to the back (they are safe this time); the k-th is then at the front and is removed. After n−1 such rounds one person is left. Time: n−1 rounds, each with k−1 rotations and one removal, all O(1) steps: about kn operations, so O(kn).

                                  (c)(i) The relation.

                                  Josephus recurrence

                                  A(1, k) = 0 and A(n, k) = ( A(n−1, k) + k ) mod n.

                                  Why. With n prisoners, the first one removed is prisoner (k−1) mod n. Counting then restarts at the next prisoner, whose number is k mod n. The circle now has n−1 people, and it plays exactly like a fresh game of size n−1 in which the restart person is called “0”, the next “1”, and so on. So a name j in the small game belongs to the person (j + k) mod n in the big game. If the small game’s survivor is called A(n−1, k), the survivor in the big game is that person’s big-game name.

                                  Check with n = 6, k = 3: the first removal is prisoner 2, and the game restarts at prisoner 3, so the new names are 3→0, 4→1, 5→2, 0→3, 1→4. The survivor of the 5-game is 3, and name 3 in the small game is prisoner (3+3) mod 6 = 0. Yes: survivor 0.

                                  n12345678
                                  A(n, 3)01103036

                                  (c)(ii) The algorithm.

                                  function FindSurvivor2(n, k) survivor = 0 for i = 2 to n do survivor = (survivor + k) mod i return survivor

                                  Start with the 1-person game (survivor 0) and grow it one person at a time using the relation. One pass of n−1 steps, no queue: O(n) time, O(1) space.

                                  Josephus circle: the queue way and the formula way

                                  Part 5 · Chapter 3 Parts 2 and 3 · Q8, Q9 and Q10

                                  Rooms, a queue from two stacks, and range queries

                                  Ch.3 · Q8Hard

                                  Which rooms can the player reach?

                                  n rooms in a row, numbered 0 to n−1, room i with competence value c[i] > 0. The player starts in one room and their competence is that room’s value. They can move between neighbouring rooms as long as their competence is not smaller than the room’s value. Let l[i] and r[i] be the leftmost and rightmost room reachable from room i.

                                  1. Each room has a treasure v[i] > 0, collected once. Let t[i] be the total collected starting in room i. Knowing only l, r, v, write pseudocode for t in O(n) time and O(n) extra space.
                                  2. Knowing only c, design an efficient algorithm for l[0…n−1]. State its time and space.

                                  Think first

                                  (a): the reachable rooms form one stretch from l[i] to r[i]. You need “the sum of a stretch” many times: precompute running totals. (b): what stops the player going left from room i? The first room on the left whose value is bigger than c[i]. That is a “nearest bigger to the left” problem: a monotone stack again.

                                  Show the worked solution

                                  (a) Prefix sums. Let ps[i] = v[0] + … + v[i], with ps[−1] = 0. Then the sum of the treasures from room l to room r is ps[r] − ps[l−1] (everything up to r minus everything before l).

                                  function treasureTime1(l, r, v, n) ps[-1] = 0 for i = 0 to n-1 do ps[i] = ps[i-1] + v[i] for i = 0 to n-1 do t[i] = ps[r[i]] - ps[l[i]-1] return t

                                  Two passes, each room visited once: O(n) time, and ps and t take O(n) space. Example: c = [3, 1, 2, 5, 2, 2, 4] has l = [0, 1, 1, 0, 4, 4, 4] and r = [2, 1, 2, 6, 5, 5, 6]. With v = [4, 1, 7, 2, 5, 3, 6] the prefix sums are 4, 5, 12, 14, 19, 22, 28 and t = [12, 1, 8, 28, 8, 8, 14]. For room 0: ps[2] − ps[−1] = 12 − 0 = 12 = 4 + 1 + 7.

                                  (b) l[i] by a stack. From room i the player walks left through rooms with c ≤ c[i] and is stopped by the first room j < i with c[j] > c[i]. So l[i] = j + 1, or 0 if there is no such room.

                                  function treasureTime2(c, n) S = Stack() l = Array(n) for i = 0 to n-1 do while S.isEmpty() == FALSE and c[S.top()] <= c[i] do S.pop() if S.isEmpty() == TRUE then l[i] = 0 else l[i] = S.top() + 1 S.push(i) return l
                                  while ... c[S.top()] <= c[i]

                                  the player from room i can walk through that room (its value is at most c[i]), and, for any later room, room i blocks at least as well, so the popped room is no longer needed.

                                  l[i] = S.top() + 1

                                  the room on top is the first one that is bigger than c[i]: it blocks, so we stop just after it.

                                  S.push(i)

                                  room i may block rooms further right.

                                  Computing l[i] with a stack, room by room

                                  Time: each room is pushed once and popped at most once, so the loop does at most 2n stack operations: O(n). Space: the stack and the array l hold up to n numbers each: O(n). The array r comes from the mirror image of the same pass, going right to left.

                                  Ch.3 · Q9Hard

                                  A queue built from two stacks

                                  Implement a queue using only two stacks S1 and S2 (operations isEmpty, push, pop, top).

                                  1. Write enqueue and dequeue.
                                  2. Start with two empty stacks and run (i) enqueue(1), enqueue(2), enqueue(3); (ii) dequeue(); (iii) enqueue(4), enqueue(5). Write both stacks, starting from the element that pops first.
                                  3. Explain step by step what the code does for the dequeue() in (ii).

                                  Think first

                                  A stack reverses order. Do the reversal twice and you get the original order back. Put newcomers in one stack; when you need the front, pour that stack into the other.

                                  Show the worked solution
                                  function enqueue(x) S1.push(x) function dequeue() if S2.isEmpty() == TRUE then while S1.isEmpty() == FALSE do S2.push(S1.pop()) if S2.isEmpty() then return NULL else return S2.pop()

                                  New elements always go on S1. Pouring S1 into S2 reverses the order, so the oldest element ends up on top of S2; that is the queue’s front.

                                  afterS1 (top first)S2 (top first)
                                  (i) enqueue 1, 2, 33, 2, 1empty
                                  (ii) dequeue()empty2, 3
                                  (iii) enqueue 4, 55, 42, 3

                                  (c) The dequeue in (ii) step by step. S2 is empty, so we must refill it. Pop 3 from S1 and push it on S2; pop 2 and push it; pop 1 and push it. Now S1 is empty and S2 holds 1, 2, 3 with 1 on top. Pop 1 from S2 and return it: the first element enqueued is the first out. Left: S2 = 2, 3 (top first).

                                  The next dequeue after (iii) returns 2 straight from S2 with no pouring; the elements 4 and 5 wait in S1 until S2 runs dry. A pour moves each element at most once, so over a long run every element is moved only twice (one push, one move), and the average cost per operation is O(1) even though one dequeue can cost O(n).

                                  A queue from two stacks, step by step

                                  Ch.3 · Q10Hard

                                  Range queries on keys with tags

                                  An item is a pair (k, t), a key and a tag. In a set S all tags differ but keys may repeat. A range query [x, y] returns the tags of all items whose key lies in [x, y]. Example: S = {(1, f), (5, d), (10, z), (10, w), (20, g)}; the query [5, 15] returns d, z, w.

                                  1. Describe a structure that supports the query with O(n) space (n = number of items).
                                  2. (i) Explain how the query runs in O(log m + k) time, where m is the number of distinct keys and k the number of tags reported. (ii) Analyze it.

                                  Think first

                                  Sort the distinct keys so you can binary-search the start of the range. Several items share a key, so hang their tags on a list under that key.

                                  Show the worked solution

                                  (a) Keep an array of the distinct keys, in ascending order. Next to each key store a linked list of all the tags that have this key. For the example:

                                  position1234
                                  distinct key151020
                                  tag listfdz → wg

                                  Space: m ≤ n keys plus n list nodes in total (each item appears in exactly one list): O(n).

                                  (b)(i) The query. (1) Binary-search the array for the first key that is at least x. (2) From there walk right through the array while the key is at most y. (3) For each key visited, walk its tag list and report every tag. For [5, 15]: the first key ≥ 5 is key 5 (position 2); walk on to key 10 (≤ 15), then key 20 is too big, so stop. Report d from key 5, then z and w from key 10.

                                  (b)(ii) Time. Step 1 is a binary search over m keys: O(log m). Let k′ be the number of distinct keys inside [x, y]: walking over them costs O(k′). Walking their tag lists costs O(k), the number of tags reported. Every key has at least one tag, so k′ ≤ k. Total O(log m + k′ + k) = O(log m + k).

                                  Where the idea comes from

                                  This is the “sorted array for fast search, lists for repeated keys” idea of Sorted lists. The output size k is unavoidable (you must at least write the answers), so a time of O(log m + k) is as good as such a query can be.

Where I could not see the exact picture, the graph drawn here is one that gives exactly the official answers, so every trace below is checked against the official result.                                   Ch.3 · Q11Easy

                                  Adjacency matrix against adjacency list

                                  A simple undirected graph G has n vertices, m edges, and maximum degree dmax.

                                  1. Use an example to show how an adjacency matrix and an adjacency list represent G.
                                  2. Give the worst-case time of each task for the matrix and for the list, in terms of m, n, dmax: (i) check whether u and v are joined by an edge; (ii) count the neighbours of u; (iii) count the vertices of degree 0.
                                  3. What change would make task (ii) faster in both structures?

                                  Think first

                                  Matrix: an n × n grid of 0/1, one row per vertex. List: one short list of neighbours per vertex. For each task ask: “Which part of the structure must I read, and how long is it?”

                                  Show the worked solution

                                  (a) An example. The set’s graph has 8 vertices 0 to 7 and the nine edges (0,7), (1,2), (2,3), (2,7), (3,6), (4,5), (4,6), (5,6), (6,7).

                                  Adjacency matrix: a 1 at row i, column j means the edge (i, j) exists. For an undirected graph it is symmetric.

                                  Adjacency list: for every vertex, the list of its neighbours.

                                  vertexneighbours
                                  07
                                  12
                                  21, 3, 7
                                  32, 6
                                  45, 6
                                  54, 6
                                  63, 4, 5, 7
                                  70, 2, 6

                                  (b) The costs.

                                  taskmatrixlistreason
                                  (i) is u–v an edge?O(1)O(dmax)matrix: read one cell. List: scan u’s list, which has at most dmax entries.
                                  (ii) number of neighbours of uO(n)O(dmax)matrix: count the 1s in row u, all n cells. List: count the entries of u’s list.
                                  (iii) number of degree-0 verticesO(n²)O(n)matrix: check every row (n cells each). List: check whether each of the n lists is empty.

                                  (c) Store an extra array neighborNum[1…n] with the degree of every vertex, and update it when an edge is added or removed. Then task (ii) is a single array read, O(1), for both structures.

                                  Common slip

                                  The cost of a list operation depends on the length of one list, not on the total number of edges. That is why dmax appears. Writing O(m) for the list in (i) or (ii) is too pessimistic.

                                  Ch.3 · Q12Easy

                                  BFS and DFS orders on a directed graph

                                  For the directed graph drawn in the set, list the visiting order of BFS and of DFS starting at A. Always visit the vertex with the smallest letter first.

                                  Think first

                                  BFS = a queue (serve the oldest discovered vertex). DFS = go as deep as possible along the smallest unvisited neighbour, and only back up when stuck. Write the out-neighbours of every vertex in alphabetical order first.

                                  Show the worked solution

                                  Out-neighbours, alphabetically: A: B, D · B: C, E, G · C: A · D: C · E: H · F: none · G: F · H: F, G.

                                  BFS (queue, first discovered is served first). A vertex is marked when it is discovered, not when it is served.

                                  servenewly discoveredqueue afterwards
                                  AB, DB, D
                                  BC, E, GD, C, E, G
                                  D(C is already known)C, E, G
                                  C(A is known)E, G
                                  EHG, H
                                  GFH, F
                                  H(F, G known)F
                                  F–empty

                                  BFS order: A, B, D, C, E, G, H, F.

                                  DFS (go deep, smallest first): A → B → C. C’s only neighbour A is visited, so back up to B. B’s next neighbour E → H → F (F has no out-edges), back to H; H’s next neighbour G (its neighbour F is visited), back up through H, E, B to A. A’s next neighbour D (its neighbour C is visited).

                                  DFS order: A, B, C, E, H, F, G, D.

                                  Compare the two

                                  BFS goes level by level (distance 0, then 1, then 2…). DFS dives. The same graph gives different orders, and both are valid; the only rule that matters is the tie-break (here: smallest letter).

                                  BFS and DFS side by side (from Chapter 3)

                                  Ch.3 · Q13Medium

                                  All possible DFS paths, and where could vertex 6 hang?

                                  1. A directed graph on nodes 1 to 7 is given by its adjacency matrix (a picture in the set). Give all possible DFS visiting orders starting at node 1.
                                  2. An undirected graph on 1–6 has known edges 1–2, 2–3, 3–4, 3–5; the edges at vertex 6 are unknown. Find every possible set of vertices from 1 to 5 that 6 could be joined to, so that BFS from vertex 1 (neighbours in ascending order) visits 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6.

                                  Think first

                                  (a): DFS is only ambiguous when a vertex has two or more unvisited out-neighbours. Find those choice points and try each order. (b): BFS visits in order of distance from vertex 1. Where may vertex 6 sit (what distance) so that it is found after 2, 3, 4 and 5?

                                  Show the worked solution

                                  (a) The matrix (1 = edge from the row to the column) that gives the official answer is below; written as lists it is 1→2; 2→3, 4; 3→6, 7; 4→7; 5→(none); 6→1, 5; 7→5.

                                  from \ to1234567
                                  10100000
                                  20011000
                                  30000011
                                  40000001
                                  50000000
                                  61000100
                                  70000100

                                  The choice points are node 2 (go to 3 or 4 first) and node 3 (go to 6 or 7 first). Node 1 has only one choice, and 4, 6, 7 have at most one unvisited neighbour when reached.

                                  • 2 goes to 3 first, and 3 goes to 6 first: 1, 2, 3, 6 (6→1 seen, so 6→5), 5, back to 3, then 7 (7→5 seen), back to 2, then 4. Order 1, 2, 3, 6, 5, 7, 4.
                                  • 2 goes to 3 first, and 3 goes to 7 first: 1, 2, 3, 7, 5 (7→5), back to 3, then 6 (its neighbours 1 and 5 are seen), back to 2, then 4. Order 1, 2, 3, 7, 5, 6, 4.
                                  • 2 goes to 4 first: 1, 2, 4, 7 (4→7), 5 (7→5), back up to 2, then 3. Now 3’s neighbour 7 is already visited, so only 6 remains: 6. Order 1, 2, 4, 7, 5, 3, 6 (here node 3 has no real choice, since 7 is already visited).

                                  So there are exactly three possible orders: 1→2→3→6→5→7→4, 1→2→3→7→5→6→4 and 1→2→4→7→5→3→6. (A brute-force check over every neighbour ordering confirms this.)

                                  (b) BFS lists vertices by distance from vertex 1. The distances of the known part are: 1 at 0, 2 at 1, 3 at 2, 4 and 5 at 3. The order 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 means vertex 6 must come after 4 and 5, so its distance must be 3 or 4:

                                  • If 6 were joined to 1 or 2, its distance would be 1 or 2, and BFS would find it before 3, 4 and 5. Not allowed.
                                  • If 6 is joined to 3, its distance is 3, and 3 lists its neighbours in ascending order 2, 4, 5, 6, so 6 comes after 4 and 5. Fine.
                                  • If 6 is joined to 4 or to 5 (and not 3), its distance is 4, so it comes after both. Fine.
                                  • Any combination of 3, 4, 5 works for the same reasons. The empty set does not: vertex 6 would never be reached.

                                  So the possible sets are {3}, {4}, {5}, {3, 4}, {3, 5}, {4, 5}, {3, 4, 5}: seven sets, namely every non-empty subset of {3, 4, 5}.

                                  Choose the neighbours of vertex 6 and run BFS

                                  Part 7 · Chapter 3, graphs · Q14 to Q16

                                  Modelling with graphs: access cards, cycles, the bridge

                                  These three problems do not ask you to run a known algorithm; they ask you to turn a story into a graph and name the graph problem hiding inside. The recipe is always: what is a vertex? what is an edge (and its weight)? what is the question in graph words?

                                  Ch.3 · Q14Medium

                                  James Bond and the access cards

                                  A facility has v rooms (1 to v) and m corridors, each joining two rooms. Room r needs access level ar > 0. James starts in room 1 with a level-b card that opens any room of level at most b. For every room, find the minimum number of rooms he must unlock to reach it, or −1 if impossible. Example: rooms 1–5, corridors 1–2, 1–5, 2–3, 2–5, 3–4, 3–5, 4–5, levels [1, 2, 2, 2, 6], card level 4: answer [0, 1, 2, 3, −1].

                                  1. Model it as a graph problem. (b) Write the algorithm, explain it, and give its worst-case time.

                                  Think first

                                  Rooms are vertices, corridors are edges. “Fewest rooms” = fewest edges on a path (unweighted shortest path = BFS). What do the access levels do to the graph? They make some vertices forbidden.

                                  Show the worked solution

                                  (a) The model. An unweighted undirected graph G = (V, E): each vertex is a room, each edge is a corridor, and the access level of room r is stored in an array A. The question becomes: find the shortest path (fewest edges) from vertex 1 to every other vertex, using only vertices whose level is at most b. Each step enters a new room, so the number of edges equals the number of rooms unlocked.

                                  (b) The algorithm. An ordinary BFS that refuses to enter forbidden rooms.

                                  function findDistance(G, A, b) Q = Queue() Q.enqueue(1) dist[1..v] = -1 dist[1] = 0 while Q.isEmpty() == FALSE do i = Q.dequeue() for each neighbour j of i do if dist[j] == -1 and A[j] <= b then dist[j] = dist[i] + 1 Q.enqueue(j) return dist
                                  dist[1..v] = -1

                                  −1 means “not reached yet”, which is also the right final answer for unreachable rooms.

                                  dist[j] == -1

                                  not discovered yet (so each room enters the queue at most once).

                                  A[j] <= b

                                  the card opens this room. If the level is too high, skip it: it is never queued, so no path can pass through it.

                                  dist[j] = dist[i] + 1

                                  BFS finds vertices in order of distance, so the first time we see j is its shortest distance.

                                  Rooms of level above b keep −1, and so do rooms that can only be reached through them. (Room 1 is where James starts; the question gives distance 0 to it regardless of its level.)

                                  BFS with an access card: change the level b

                                  Time: it is BFS, plus an O(1) level test per edge: O(|V| + |E|) = O(v + m).

                                  Ch.3 · Q15Hard

                                  The shortest cycle through a node

                                  In a directed graph G, a cycle <n1, n2, …, nk, n1> follows directed edges and returns to its start; its length is the number of edges. Example: in the set’s graph, the smallest cycle through node 4 is <1, 2, 3, 4, 1>, length 4.

                                  1. Describe a suitable data structure. (b)(i) Given a node x, write an algorithm for the length of the smallest cycle through x and explain it. (ii) Its complexity, with justification.

                                  Think first

                                  A cycle through x is a path that leaves x and comes back. Which part of it can you get from a BFS started at x? What is the very last edge of the cycle?

                                  Show the worked solution

                                  (a) Adjacency lists, in both directions. For every node u keep Adj[u]: the nodes v with an edge u→v. Also keep RevAdj[u]: the nodes v with an edge v→u (the edges coming into u). The second list lets us find the edges coming back to x instantly.

                                  (b)(i) The idea. Any cycle through x looks like: leave x, walk along a path to some node v, then use one edge v→x to return. The shortest such cycle uses the shortest path from x to v.

                                  1. Run BFS from x along Adj. This gives dist[v], the shortest number of edges from x to every reachable v.
                                  2. For every v in RevAdj[x] (the nodes with an edge back to x) that was reached, the cycle x → … → v → x has length dist[v] + 1.
                                  3. Answer the smallest of those lengths, or −1 if no such v was reached (no cycle through x).
                                  function SmallestCycle(x) dist[all] = -1; dist[x] = 0 Q = Queue(); Q.enqueue(x) while Q.isEmpty() == FALSE do u = Q.dequeue() for each v in Adj[u] do if dist[v] == -1 then dist[v] = dist[u] + 1 Q.enqueue(v) best = infinity for each v in RevAdj[x] do if dist[v] != -1 then best = min(best, dist[v] + 1) if best == infinity then return -1 return best

                                  An example (a graph I built so that the answer for node 4 is the one in the set):

                                  node x1234567
                                  smallest cycle through x4224433

                                  For x = 4: BFS from 4 reaches 1 at distance 1, 2 at 2, 3 and 6 at 3, 5 and 7 at 4. The nodes with an edge into 4 are 3 and 7: dist 3 and 4, so candidate lengths 4 and 5. The smallest is 4: the cycle 4→1→2→3→4. For x = 2, BFS reaches 3 at distance 1, and there is an edge 3→2 back, so the cycle 2→3→2 has length 2.

                                  (ii) Complexity. BFS visits each node and each edge once: O(|V| + |E|). The last loop looks at the nodes with an edge into x, at most |V| of them, each in O(1): O(|V|). The sum is O(|V| + |E|).

                                  Ch.3 · Q16Hard

                                  Four people, one torch, one narrow bridge

                                  Four people A to D come to a river at night. A narrow bridge holds at most two people at once, and there is one torch that must be carried on every crossing. A crosses in w minutes, B in x, C in y, D in z; two people together move at the slower person’s speed. Find the fastest way to get everybody across. Describe how to model this as a graph problem: the type of graph, what a vertex is, what an edge is, and the graph problem to solve.

                                  Think first

                                  Stop thinking about people walking; think about situations. A situation says who stands on which side and where the torch is. What moves you from one situation to another? How much does that cost?

                                  Show the worked solution
                                  • Graph type: a weighted directed graph.
                                  • Vertex: a state of the whole situation: which of the four people are on the left bank, which on the right, and on which side the torch is. The set writes the left bank, then R for the river, then the right bank, with T for the torch; so “ABCDTR” is the start (everyone and the torch on the left) and “RABCDT” is the goal (everyone and the torch on the right). “ABCRDT” means A, B, C on the left and D with the torch on the right.
                                  • Edge: one crossing. From a state there is an edge to every state reached by sending one person, or two people, from the torch’s side to the other side. Its weight is the time of that crossing: the time of the slower person.
                                  • Graph problem: a single-source shortest path problem. Find the path of minimum total weight from the start state ABCDTR to the goal state RABCDT. The weights are all positive, so Dijkstra’s algorithm solves it (see Dijkstra).

                                  How big is the graph? Each of the four people is on one of two sides, and the torch is on one of two sides: at most 25 = 32 vertices, with at most 10 outgoing edges each (4 single crossings + 6 pairs). Tiny, so Dijkstra is instant.

                                  Try the times 1, 2, 5, 10 below: the best total is 17 minutes (A and B cross, A returns, C and D cross, B returns, A and B cross again). Notice that the cleverest plan sends the two slowest people together.

                                  The fastest crossing, found as a shortest path in the state graph

                                  Part 8 · Chapter 4 Part 1 · Q1 to Q4

                                  Hash tables: inserting, sizing, true or false, probe sequences

                                  Chapter 4 is hashing. The ideas you need: a hash function sends a key to a slot; collisions (two keys, one slot) are handled by chaining (a list in each slot) or open addressing (probe other slots). Read Chaining, Open addressing, Probing, Load factor and clustering, Quadratic probing and double hashing and Performance and rehashing first if any word here is new.

                                  Ch.4 · Q1Easy

                                  Fill three hash tables

                                  Insert the keys 53, 62, 75, 18, 27, 33, 40, 98 in this order into each table, and draw the final table.

                                  1. Size 13, primary hash h′(k) = k mod 13, open addressing with linear probing step f(i) = 4i.
                                  2. Size 7, h′(k) = k mod 7, collisions handled by chaining.
                                  3. Size 13, double hashing: h(k, i) = (h1(k) + i·h2(k)) mod 13, with h1(k) = k mod 13 and h2(k) = 5 − (k mod 3).

                                  Think first

                                  Work one key at a time, in order. For every key: compute the first slot; if it is taken, compute the next probe (i = 1, 2, …) until you find an empty slot. Keep a table of which slots are taken.

                                  Show the worked solution

                                  (a) Linear probing with step 4. Probe i looks at slot (k mod 13 + 4i) mod 13.

                                  62101010

                                  1855 (taken), 99

                                  33777
                                  4011, 5, 9, 0 (all taken), 17 mod 13 = 44
                                  9877 (taken), 1111

                                  (b) Chaining, size 7. Each slot keeps a list; a key goes to slot k mod 7 (added at the end here).

                                  slotchain
                                  098
                                  1–
                                  2–
                                  3–
                                  453 → 18
                                  575 → 33 → 40
                                  662 → 27

                                  (53 mod 7 = 4, 62 mod 7 = 6, 75 mod 7 = 5, 18 mod 7 = 4, 27 mod 7 = 6, 33 mod 7 = 5, 40 mod 7 = 5, 98 mod 7 = 0.) The order inside a chain depends on whether you add at the head or the tail; both are accepted as long as you say which.

                                  (c) Double hashing. The step depends on the key: h2(k) = 5 − (k mod 3).

                                  keyh1h2slots triedstored at
                                  531311
                                  621031010
                                  7510510 (taken), 15 mod 13 = 22
                                  185555
