                                    Ch.6 · Q1Easy

                                    True or false: search algorithms

                                    For each statement, say whether it is True or False. For a False statement, make a correction.

                                    1. Binary search can be used on an unsorted array.
                                    2. Linear search can have better space complexity than hashing.
                                    3. For jump search, the optimal jump size for minimizing comparisons is the cube root of the list size.
                                    4. The average time complexity of binary search is significantly better than its worst case time complexity.
                                    5. Linear search can outperform binary search if the dataset is small.
                                    6. Interpolation search has O(log log n) worst case time complexity for any sorted array.
                                    7. The lower bound for successful searching in an unordered array is Ω(n) comparisons in the worst case.

                                    Think first

                                    For each one ask: “What does this algorithm need (sorted? uniform?), and what does it cost?” Binary search needs order. Jump search balances two kinds of steps. Interpolation search is fast only when the keys are spread evenly.

                                    Show the worked solution
                                    PartVerdictWhy
                                    (a)FalseBinary search throws away half the list by looking at the middle box and asking “is my target smaller or larger?”. That question only makes sense if the list is sorted. Correction: binary search needs a sorted list.
                                    (b)TrueLinear search needs no extra memory (O(1) besides the list). A hash table needs its own table, O(n) extra space.
                                    (c)FalseJump size k costs about n/k jumps plus up to k steps inside the block: n/k + k, smallest when k = √n (Chapter 6, square-root search). Correction: the square root, not the cube root.
                                    (d)FalseBoth cases are O(log n). On average you save about one comparison, not a whole order of growth. Correction: they have the same complexity, O(log n).
                                    (e)TrueFor a handful of items, scanning is so cheap that the setup of binary search (sorting, bookkeeping) is not worth it. Big-O hides constants; small n is where constants win.
                                    (f)FalseThe O(log log n) result needs an assumption: the keys are sorted and spread roughly evenly. For clumped keys interpolation search can degrade to O(n). Correction: only for uniformly distributed sorted data.
                                    (g)TrueIf the list is unordered, nothing tells you where the target is: in the worst case you must look at every item (the adversary argument).

                                    Jump search: try different step sizes (from Chapter 6)

                                    Ch.6 · Q2Easy

                                    Jump search in words

                                    Given a list L of n elements and a target X, we want to test whether X is in L.

                                    1. What property must L have before jump search can be applied?
                                    2. Explain the principle of jump search.
                                    3. State the worst-case and average-case complexities (Big-O, in element comparisons) of jump search. Explain the worst-case result.

                                    Think first

                                    Think of looking for a word in a printed dictionary by flipping several pages at a time until you pass it, then stepping back and reading page by page.

                                    Show the worked solution

                                    (a) L must be sorted. Without order, “I have passed the target” means nothing.

                                    (b) The principle. Choose a jump size k. Instead of looking at every box, look only at boxes k, 2k, 3k, … until you see an element that is greater than or equal to X. Now X, if it exists, is inside the block of k boxes you just jumped over, so do an ordinary linear search inside that one block.

                                    (c) The costs. With the best jump size k = √n:

                                    • Worst case: O(√n). The worst target sits at the very end of a block, just before the next jump point. You make about n/k = √n jumps to get to the right block, and then a linear scan through the whole block of k = √n boxes: √n + √n = 2√n, which is O(√n).
                                    • Average case: O(√n) as well: the target is typically halfway along, so you do about half of each part, and half of 2√n is still a constant times √n.

                                    Where jump search sits

                                    Linear search: O(n). Jump search: O(√n). Binary search: O(log n). Jump search is the middle child; it is useful when going backwards is expensive, because it only ever steps forward and backs up by at most one block.

                                    Total comparisons against the jump size (from Chapter 6)

                                    Ch.6 · Q3Medium

                                    Largest pair sum in O(n)

                                    Given an unsorted array A[1…n] of n distinct integers, n ≥ 2, write pseudocode for LargestSum(A) that finds the largest sum of two elements in O(n) time, and analyze its time. Example: for [12, 34, 10, 6, 40] the answer is 34 + 40 = 74.

                                    Think first

                                    The largest sum of a pair is simply the largest number plus the second largest number. You do not need to sort (that would cost O(n log n)). Carry two boxes, “first” and “second”, through one pass.

                                    Show the worked solution

                                    The idea. Keep the two biggest numbers seen so far, first ≥ second. Start with the first two elements in the right order. Then look at each remaining element once:

                                    • bigger than first: the old first becomes second, and the new element is the new first;
                                    • otherwise, if bigger than second: it is the new second;
                                    • otherwise: ignore it.
                                    function LargestSum(A) if A[1] > A[2] then first = A[1]; second = A[2] else first = A[2]; second = A[1] for i = 3 to n do if A[i] > first then second = first first = A[i] else if A[i] > second then second = A[i] return first + second

                                    Trace on [12, 34, 10, 6, 40].

                                    after readingfirstsecondwhat happened
                                    12, 34341234 > 12, so the order is swapped at the start
                                    10341210 is smaller than both: ignored
                                    63412ignored
                                    40403440 beats first: 34 slides down to second

                                    The answer is 40 + 34 = 74.

                                    Time. The first if costs O(1). The loop runs n − 2 times and each round does a constant number of comparisons and assignments, so O(n). Everything else is O(1). Total: O(n).

                                    Common slip

                                    Do not forget the else if branch. If you only compare with first, then for [5, 9, 7] the number 7 is ignored and you return 14 instead of 16.

                                    Part 2 · Chapter 6, search algorithms · Q4 to Q6

                                    A rotated pile, the phones, covering with segments

                                    These three problems use binary search on something that is not a plain sorted list. The skill being tested is recognising “I can keep throwing half of the possibilities away” (read Binary search and the egg puzzle again if needed).

                                    Ch.6 · Q4Medium

                                    How many scripts did Ben read?

                                    Jeff sorted n scripts in ascending order of UID (all different). Ben read k scripts from the top (1 ≤ k ≤ n) and put them back at the bottom without changing their order. The UIDs are in the list A[1…n], top script first. Example: A = [43, 60, 71, 3, 14, 23, 26] gives k = 4 (Ben read 3, 14, 23, 26).

                                    1. Jeff’s reOrder1(A, n) is below. Explain how it works and give its worst-case time.
                                      function reOrder1(A, n) for i = 1 to n - 1 do if A[i] > A[i + 1] then return n - i return n
                                    2. Write pseudocode for reOrder2(A, n) that is asymptotically faster; explain it and give its worst-case time.

                                    Think first

                                    The pile is two sorted runs glued together: the large UIDs first, then the small ones that Ben moved. There is exactly one place where the order drops. Part (b) asks you to find that place without walking along the whole list: compare the middle with the last element.

                                    Show the worked solution

                                    (a) How reOrder1 works. It walks from the top and stops at the first i with A[i] > A[i+1]: the point where the order drops, i.e. the boundary between the “originally last” scripts and the ones Ben moved. The scripts from position i + 1 to n are the ones Ben read, so k = n − i. If it never finds a drop, the pile is still fully sorted, which means Ben read all n scripts, so it returns n.

                                    Time: O(n). The loop runs at most n − 1 times, each round costs O(1).

                                    (b) Binary search for the drop.

                                    function reOrder2(A, n) left = 1; right = n while left < right do mid = floor((left + right) / 2) if A[mid] > A[right] then left = mid + 1 else right = mid return n - left + 1

                                    Why the comparison with A[right] works. Because of the rotation, the list looks like big run … big run | small run … small run. If A[mid] > A[right], then A[mid] is in the big run (a script in the small run can never be larger than the last script), so the smallest UID, where the small run begins, is to the right of mid: left = mid + 1. Otherwise A[mid] is in the small run (or the list is sorted), so the beginning of the small run is at mid or to its left: right = mid. The window shrinks until left = right: the position of the smallest UID. Ben read the scripts from there to the end: k = n − left + 1.

                                    Time: O(log n): every round halves the window, exactly like binary search.

                                    Find k with reOrder2, one round at a time

                                    Common slips

                                    (1) Comparing A[mid] with A[left] looks natural but fails when the list is already sorted (k = n): A[mid] is never smaller than A[left] there, so the window would move right and miss the smallest UID at position 1. Compare with A[right]. (2) The fully sorted case (k = n) works automatically: every round sets right = mid until left = right = 1 and the answer is n. Try k = n in the tool.

                                    Ch.6 · Q5Medium

                                    Testing the Nokia 3310 with 1, 2 or many phones

                                    You want to find the smallest height h (a positive integer) from which a phone breaks when thrown at or above that height. Each trial throws one phone from any height x. A phone that does not break can be reused; a broken one is gone. For each case, explain an efficient strategy and its worst-case number of trials in terms of h.

                                    1. You have 1 phone only.
                                    2. You have 2 phones only.
                                    3. You have an infinite number of phones.

                                    Think first

                                    With one phone you can never afford a break until you are sure, so you must climb one height at a time. With two you can afford one “risky” break to find a rough block. With unlimited phones you can afford to break many, so use the fastest search you know. (This is the egg puzzle of Chapter 6 with phones.)

                                    Show the worked solution

                                    (a) One phone: linear search. Throw at heights 1, 2, 3, … in turn. The first break is at h. You need h trials, so O(h). Skipping ahead is not safe: if the phone breaks at a height you jumped to, you have no phone left to test the heights you skipped.

                                    (b) Two phones: jump search. Throw the first phone at heights s, 2s, 3s, … until it breaks at some x·s. Then h is in the block ((x − 1)s, xs]. Use the second phone linearly inside that block, one height at a time. That costs about h/s + s trials. The official answer says O(h): for a fixed step s that is right, because the first term h/s still grows like h.

                                    Can you beat O(h) with two phones? Yes.

                                    If you let the steps grow (1, 2, 3, 4, …), the first phone lands on the triangular numbers 1, 3, 6, 10, 15, … Say it breaks at the j-th throw. The block it leaves has only j heights, so the second phone needs at most j − 1 more throws. Together about 2j trials, where j(j + 1)/2 ≥ h, i.e. O(√h) trials. Try it below. With a fixed step the first phone needs h/s throws: for s = 10 and h = 1,000,000 that is 100,000 throws. A fixed step only does well if you happen to know a bound H on the height and choose s ≈ √H. The growing-steps plan needs no such knowledge and uses about 2,400 throws for the same h (at most about 2,830 for any h up to a million).

                                    (c) Unlimited phones: double, then binary search. We do not know how tall the building is, so first find an upper bound: throw at heights 1, 2, 4, 8, … (doubling) until a phone breaks at 2i. That takes i + 1 ≤ log2 h + 2 throws. Now h is in (2i−1, 2i]. Run an ordinary binary search on that range: if the phone breaks, search the lower half, otherwise the upper half; about i − 1 more throws. Total O(log h).

                                    Throwing phones: compare the four plans

                                    Why not start binary search straight away in (c)?

                                    Binary search needs a known range [1, N]. Here h is only known to be “finite”, so the doubling phase creates the range. This trick, called exponential search, is also how you search an unbounded sorted list.

                                    Ch.6 · Q6Hard

                                    Cover the points with k segments, minimise the longest

                                    Given n distinct integer points on an axis, 0 ≤ ai ≤ w, sorted increasingly, we use k line segments to cover all of them. Let L be the length of the longest segment. Write pseudocode returning the smallest possible integer L, running in O(n log w) time. Example: {1, 2, 4, 6} with k = 2 gives L = 2.

                                    Think first

                                    Turn it into a yes/no question: “If every segment may have length x, can k segments cover all points?” That question is easy to answer greedily in O(n). And the answer is monotone: if length x works, any longer length works too. A yes/no question that is monotone in a number is a job for binary search on the answer, between 0 and w: log w rounds × O(n) each = O(n log w).

                                    Show the worked solution

                                    Step 1: the yes/no check CanCover(A, n, k, x). Greedy: put the left end of a segment on the leftmost uncovered point and stretch it as far as the length x allows (it covers every point up to start + x). Then start the next segment at the next uncovered point. Count segments; if you ever need more than k, the answer is “no”.

                                    Why greedy is right: moving the first segment further left never helps (nothing is to the left of its first point), so the best start for it is exactly the leftmost point, and by the same argument for every later segment.

                                    function CanCover(A, n, k, x) used = 0; i = 1 while i <= n do used = used + 1 if used > k then return False start = A[i] while i <= n AND A[i] <= start + x do i = i + 1 return True function FindMin(A, n, k, w) low = 0; high = w while low < high do mid = floor((low + high) / 2) if CanCover(A, n, k, mid) then high = mid // mid is long enough; maybe shorter works else low = mid + 1 // too short; the answer is bigger return low

                                    Step 2: binary search on L. The answer lies in [0, w]. Test the middle. “Yes” means mid is long enough, so the smallest working length is mid or smaller: high = mid (keep mid, it might be the answer). “No” means mid is too short: low = mid + 1.

                                    Time. CanCover: the inner and outer loops together move i forward over every point once: O(n). FindMin: the window [low, high] halves each round, starting from size w + 1, so about log2(w + 1) rounds. Total O(n log w).

                                    Binary search on the longest segment, step by step

                                    The pattern to remember

                                    “Find the smallest x such that a condition holds, where the condition is monotone” → binary search on x, with a fast check inside. You will meet it again as “binary search on the answer” in many contest and exam problems.

                                    Part 3 · Chapter 7, binary search trees · Q1 and Q2

                                    Binary search trees: statements and average cost

                                    Background for this part: What a binary search tree is, Insertion and Deletion in Chapter 7. The one rule to keep in your head: for every node, everything in its left subtree is smaller, everything in its right subtree is larger.

                                    Ch.7 · Q1Easy

                                    True or false: binary search trees

                                    For each statement, say whether it is True or False. For a False statement, point out the incorrectness.

                                    1. In a binary search tree, the left and right subtrees of a node are also binary search trees.
                                    2. A node in a binary search tree must have two children.
                                    3. Each node of a binary search tree has a parent.
                                    4. The in-order traversal of a binary search tree always outputs the data in non-decreasing order.
                                    5. The height of a binary search tree with n nodes is always less than √n.

                                    Think first

                                    For (e) look for a counter-example: which insertion order makes a tree as tall as possible?

                                    Show the worked solution
                                    PartVerdictWhy
                                    (a)TrueEvery node of the left subtree is smaller than the root and obeys the same rule towards its own descendants, so the left subtree is itself a binary search tree. Same for the right. This is what makes recursive algorithms on search trees work.
                                    (b)FalseA node may have 0, 1 or 2 children. Leaves have none; a tree built from 1, 2, 3 has nodes with one child. Correction: a node has between 0 and 2 children.
                                    (c)FalseThe root has no parent. Correction: every node except the root has a parent.
                                    (d)TrueIn-order = left subtree, node, right subtree, which lists the keys from smallest to largest (Chapter 7, from a sorted list to a tree). “Non-decreasing” because duplicates may be allowed.
                                    (e)FalseThe shape depends on the insertion order. Insert 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 into an empty tree: every key goes right of the previous one, a chain of height 5, which is bigger than √6 ≈ 2.45. In the worst case the height is n − 1. Correction: the height can be as large as n − 1 (and is at least log2(n + 1) − 1).

                                    The same keys, a very different height (from Chapter 7)

                                    Ch.7 · Q2Easy

                                    Linear search against a search tree, with probabilities

                                    A list of 12 keys is [5, 4, 8, 1, 9, 7, 6, 2, 12, 11, 10, 3]. The probability that each element (in the same order) is searched is [0.1, 0.05, 0.05, 0.1, 0.2, 0.05, 0.05, 0.1, 0.05, 0.1, 0.05, 0.1]. (For example key 9 is searched with probability 0.2.)

                                    1. For a linear search over the list, what is the average number of elements inspected in a successful search?
                                    2. Draw the binary search tree obtained by inserting the elements in the order listed.
                                    3. Calculate the average number of nodes inspected for a successful search in this tree.
                                    4. Draw the tree after deleting the element 8.

                                    Think first

                                    “Average number inspected” = sum over keys of (probability × number of elements/nodes looked at to find it). In a list, key number i costs i looks. In a tree, a node at depth d costs d + 1 looks (the root costs 1).

                                    Show the worked solution

                                    (a) Linear search. Key in position i needs i inspections:

                                    0.1·1 + 0.05·2 + 0.05·3 + 0.1·4 + 0.2·5 + 0.05·6 + 0.05·7 + 0.1·8 + 0.05·9 + 0.1·10 + 0.05·11 + 0.1·12 = 6.4

                                    (b) The tree. Insert one key at a time: compare with the root, go left if smaller, right if larger, until you fall off the tree.

                                    1. 5 is the root. 4 < 5: left child of 5. 8 > 5: right child of 5.
                                    2. 1: < 5, < 4: left child of 4. 9: > 5, > 8: right child of 8. 7: > 5, < 8: left child of 8.
                                    3. 6: > 5, < 8, < 7: left child of 7. 2: < 5, < 4, > 1: right child of 1.
                                    4. 12: > 5, > 8, > 9: right child of 9. 11: … > 9, < 12: left child of 12. 10: < 12, < 11: left child of 11.
                                    5. 3: < 5, < 4, > 1, > 2: right child of 2.

                                    (c) Average in the tree. Depth + 1 of each key: 5 → 1; 4, 8 → 2; 1, 9, 7 → 3; 6, 2, 12 → 4; 11, 3 → 5; 10 → 6.

                                    0.1·1 + 0.05·2 + 0.05·2 + 0.1·3 + 0.2·3 + 0.05·3 + 0.05·4 + 0.1·4 + 0.05·4 + 0.1·5 + 0.05·6 + 0.1·5 = 3.45

                                    The popular key 9 (probability 0.2) is 5th in the list but only the 3rd node in the tree.

                                    (d) Deleting 8. Node 8 has two children (7 and 9), so use the case-3 rule from Chapter 7: copy the successor, the smallest key of the right subtree (here 9, which has no left child), into 8’s place and cut the old node 9 out (its right child 12 moves up). The result: 9 is the right child of 5, 7 is the left child of 9. Using the predecessor 7 instead (replace 8 by 7, then 6 moves up) is equally valid; the set says so.

                                    The tree, the averages and the deletion (choose a key to delete)

                                    Why the tree wins

                                    The tree’s average depends on its shape. A balanced tree of 12 keys would need at most 4 inspections per search; this one needs 6 for key 10, yet the average still wins clearly because the frequently searched keys sit near the top. (Putting popular keys at the top is exactly what an “optimal” search tree does.)

                                    Part 4 · Chapter 7, binary search trees · Q3

                                    Four algorithms on a search tree

                                    Problem 3 asks for four small algorithms. For each: the pseudocode, why it works, and the worst-case time. Remember the three tools from Minimum, maximum and search: walking down one path costs O(h), visiting every node costs O(n), and an in-order walk visits the keys in sorted order.

                                    Ch.7 · Q3Medium / Hard

                                    Min, Sum, MaxRange and kthSmall

                                    Each node has data, left, right and parent. In these trees the key at a node is ≥ every key in its left subtree and ≤ every key in its right subtree (duplicates are allowed). The tree has at least one node and n nodes. For each part write pseudocode, explain it and analyse the worst-case time.

                                    1. Min(root): return the minimum key.
                                    2. Sum(root): return the sum of all keys.
                                    3. MaxRange(root, a, b): return a pointer to a node with the maximum key in the range [a, b]. If several nodes tie, return the one that appears latest in the in-order traversal. If there is none, return NULL.
                                    4. kthSmall(root, k): return the k-th smallest key in O(h + k) time, where h is the height and k is a constant, 1 ≤ k ≤ n.

                                    Think first

                                    (a) the smallest key is as far left as you can go. (b) you must touch every node, so any traversal works. (c) at each node, decide which side(s) can still contain an answer; when the node itself is in range, the biggest answers are on the right. (d) an in-order traversal, but stop after k nodes.

                                    Show the worked solution

                                    (a) Min. Keep going left until there is no left child.

                                    function Min(root) while root.left != NULL do root = root.left return root.data

                                    The smallest key is at the leftmost node, because “left” always leads to smaller keys. Each step goes one level down, so the time is O(h).

                                    A small wording slip in the official explanation

                                    The official text says the loop “walks left until reaching a leaf”. The code is right, the word is not: the leftmost node may have a right child, so it need not be a leaf. The stopping rule is “no left child”.

                                    (b) Sum. Recursion on the definition: the sum of a tree is its own key plus the sum of the left tree plus the sum of the right tree; the empty tree sums to 0.

                                    function Sum(root) if root == NULL then return 0 return root.data + Sum(root.left) + Sum(root.right)

                                    Every node is visited exactly once and does O(1) work: O(n). (No search-tree property is needed; it works on any binary tree.)

                                    (c) MaxRange. At a node with key v:

                                    • v > b: too big, and so is everything to its right. The answer can only be in the left subtree.
                                    • v < a: too small, and so is everything to its left. The answer can only be in the right subtree.
                                    • a ≤ v ≤ b: in range. Anything bigger that is still in range is in the right subtree, and so is any later duplicate in in-order. So ask the right subtree first. If it finds a node, that node is the answer; if it returns NULL, then v itself is the answer.
                                    function MaxRange(root, a, b) if root == NULL then return NULL if root.data > b then return MaxRange(root.left, a, b) if root.data < a then return MaxRange(root.right, a, b) max = MaxRange(root.right, a, b) if max != NULL then return max else return root

                                    Each call makes one recursive call (never both children), so the calls form one downward path: O(h). Not O(n): that would be the mistake of searching both sides.

                                    (d) kthSmall. The in-order traversal outputs keys in sorted order, so the k-th node visited is the k-th smallest. Do it with an explicit stack so that you can stop early: push the whole left path; pop a node (count it); then continue with its right child.

                                    function kthSmall(root, k) s = Stack(); p = root; count = 0 while p != NULL or not s.isEmpty() do while p != NULL do // go as far left as possible s.push(p) p = p.left p = s.pop() count = count + 1 if count == k then return p.data p = p.right

                                    Time. Count the pushes and the pops. At most k pops happen before the function returns. Every push is either matched by a later pop (so at most k of them) or the node is still on the stack at the end, and the stack never holds more than h + 1 nodes (it is one root-to-node path). So there are at most k + h + 1 pushes and k pops, each costing O(1): O(h + k).

                                    Run any of the four algorithms on your own tree

                                    Try this

                                    Pick (c) MaxRange with a = 26, b = 58 on the default tree: the answer is 50, found after visiting only the nodes along one path. Then set b = 100: the answer is 80. Finally choose an empty range, such as a = 71, b = 79, and see NULL come back.

                                    Part 5 · Chapter 7, binary search trees · Q4 and Q5

                                    Where does a new key hang? Cons cells

                                    Two proof-and-design problems. Q4 is a short proof about where an inserted key ends up (read Successor and predecessor and Insertion). Q5 asks you to build lists and trees from nothing but “cons cells”, the building block of languages like Lisp (read Chapter 3 for linked lists and Chapter 5 for trees).

                                    Ch.7 · Q4Hard

                                    The parent of a new key is its predecessor or its successor

                                    A strict BST stores distinct integers. A new key q (not stored) is inserted along the usual search path and placed at the first null pointer, with no rotations. Its predecessor p is the largest stored key smaller than q; its successor s is the smallest stored key larger than q. Depth = distance from the root in edges.

                                    1. Build T1 by inserting 20, 10, 50, 30, 40, 70 and T2 by inserting 20, 10, 50, 40, 30, 70. (i) For q = 32 find p, s and the parent of the new node in each tree. (ii) Does insertion always choose the numerically closer of p and s?
                                    2. Suppose both p and s exist. Prove that the insertion parent is either p or s. (Hint: track the last visited key smaller than q and the last visited key larger than q.)
                                    3. Assume both exist. (i) Prove that one of p, s is a proper ancestor of the other, by considering their lowest common ancestor. (ii) Deduce a rule that identifies the parent using only their depths.
                                    4. (i) What is the parent if only one of p, s exists? (ii) What happens if neither exists?

                                    Think first

                                    Walk the search path for q in your head. Every time you go right you pass a key smaller than q; every time you go left you pass a key larger than q. The last key you passed in each direction is the best candidate so far for p and for s.

                                    Show the worked solution

                                    (a)(i) The two trees. In both, the keys around 32 are p = 30 and s = 40. But the trees are shaped differently.

                                    • T1: the search path for 32 is 20 → 50 → 30 → 40, and 32 falls off the left of 40. Parent = 40 (s). Depths: 30 is at depth 2, 40 at depth 3.
                                    • T2: the path is 20 → 50 → 40 → 30, and 32 falls off the right of 30. Parent = 30 (p). Depths are reversed: 40 at depth 2, 30 at depth 3.

                                    (a)(ii) No. In both trees 30 is much closer to 32 than 40 is, but in T1 the parent is 40. Numerical distance does not decide; the shape does.

                                    Insert q into T1, T2 or your own tree and see p, s and the parent

                                    (b) The parent is p or s.

                                    • While searching for q, at a visited key v < q we go right and record v. The left subtree of v contains only keys smaller than v, so none of them can beat v as the largest key below q. Any better candidate must be in the right subtree we are about to search. When v > q we go left, discarding v and its right subtree (all bigger than v, hence not predecessors).
                                    • So when we reach the null pointer, the last recorded smaller key is exactly p. Symmetrically the last recorded larger key is exactly s.
                                    • The very last visited node updates one of these two records (it is either smaller or larger than q), and it is also the insertion parent. So the parent is p or s.

                                    (c)(i) One is an ancestor of the other. Suppose neither is an ancestor of the other. Let z be their lowest common ancestor. Then p is in z’s left subtree and s in its right subtree (they are on different sides, or one would be an ancestor), so p < z < s. Since q is not stored, z ≠ q. If z < q, then z is a stored key between p and q, contradicting that p is the largest key below q. If z > q, then z is a stored key between q and s, contradicting that s is the smallest key above q. Either way a contradiction, so one of p, s is a proper ancestor of the other.

                                    (c)(ii) The deeper one is the parent. Say p is the ancestor of s. Then s > p is in p’s right subtree, so p has a right child. The new key q > p must go right at p and therefore cannot stop there. By (b) the parent is p or s, so it is s, the deeper one. The mirror case (s the ancestor of p) gives p. The depths cannot tie, because one is a proper ancestor of the other. Rule: the parent is whichever of p, s has the greater depth.

                                    (d)(i) Only one exists. If only p exists, q is larger than every key, so it is inserted as the right child of the maximum key, which is p. If only s exists, q is smaller than all keys and becomes the left child of the minimum, which is s.

                                    (d)(ii) Neither exists. Then there are no stored keys at all: the tree is empty and the new node becomes the root.

                                    Ch.7 · Q5Hard

                                    Lists and trees out of cons cells

                                    A cons cell has two slots, CAR and CDR, each holding a value or a reference to another cons cell. A linked list stores a value in CAR and points CDR to the next cell; NIL ends the list. For example (1, 3, 4, 2) is four cells in a chain. All variables are integers or references to cons cells. Available operations: cons(x, y) creates a cell; L → car and L → cdr access the slots. (The set also shows linear search, FindElement, and head insertion, HeadInsert(L, e) = cons(e, L).)

                                    1. Given a list L (possibly empty), reverse it and return it.
                                    2. Given a list L of size 2k, return the root of a complete binary tree with the values at the leaves only. Internal nodes are cons cells with CAR = left child and CDR = right child. For (1, 3, 4, 2): a root whose left child is the cell (1, 3) and right child is the cell (4, 2).
                                    3. Explain how to build a binary search tree out of cons cells that supports the Chapter 7 operations. Show how a node is stored.

                                    Think first

                                    Draw the cells as boxes with two slots. (a) reversing a list means turning every arrow around; you only need to remember three things while doing so: the cell behind you, the cell you are on, the cell ahead. (b) splitting a list of length 2k into two halves gives two lists of length 2k−1: recursion. (c) a node needs 4 fields but a cons cell only has 2 slots: chain cells.

                                    Show the worked solution

                                    (a) Reverse the list. The official answer turns the arrows around in place:

                                    function ReverseList(L) ptr = NIL // the part already reversed next = L // the cell we are on while next != NIL do nextnext = next -> cdr // remember what is ahead next -> cdr = ptr // turn this arrow around ptr = next // step forward next = nextnext return ptr

                                    Trace for (1, 3, 4, 2): ptr starts at NIL. Step 1: cell 1 now points to NIL, ptr = cell 1. Step 2: cell 3 points to cell 1, ptr = cell 3. Step 3: cell 4 points to cell 3. Step 4: cell 2 points to cell 4. At the end ptr = cell 2 and the list reads (2, 4, 3, 1). If L is empty, the loop is skipped and NIL is returned. Time O(n), extra space O(1).

                                    A note on the rules

                                    The table of allowed operations lists only reading a slot (L → car, L → cdr) and cons. The official answer writes to a slot (next → cdr = ptr), which is outside that table. A version that obeys the table to the letter builds a new list and never modifies a cell:

                                    function ReverseList(L) ptr = NIL cur = L while cur != NIL do ptr = cons(cur -> car, ptr) // HeadInsert of each element cur = cur -> cdr return ptr

                                    It is the same idea as pushing every element onto a stack and then reading the stack from the top: each element is head-inserted in turn, so the last one ends up first. Also O(n) time, but O(n) extra space for the new cells. In an exam, state which assumption you use.

                                    (b) List to complete binary tree. Official, top-down: if the list has one element, return that value (a leaf). Otherwise find the middle with two pointers (one moves two steps while the other moves one), cut the list there, convert both halves recursively, and return cons(left, right):

                                    function ListToTree(L) if L == NIL then return NIL else if L -> cdr == NIL then return L -> car // one element: a leaf len_ptr = L; half_ptr = L; prev_ptr = NIL while len_ptr != NIL do // half_ptr moves once per two steps of len_ptr len_ptr = len_ptr -> cdr prev_ptr = half_ptr half_ptr = half_ptr -> cdr if len_ptr != NIL then len_ptr = len_ptr -> cdr prev_ptr -> cdr = NIL // split the list into two halves left = ListToTree(L) right = ListToTree(half_ptr) prev_ptr -> cdr = half_ptr // optional: restore the list return cons(left, right)

                                    Time. Finding the middle of a list of length m costs about m/2 steps, and each level of the recursion handles n cells in total, so T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n) = O(n log n). (The set does not ask for the time.)

                                    A faster way that needs no pointer surgery

                                    Build the tree bottom-up: one pass joins neighbours, (a, b), (c, d), …, so a list of 2k items becomes a list of 2k−1 cells. Repeat until one cell remains. Each pass is a simple recursion with cons only:

                                    function Pass(L) // pair up neighbours if L == NIL then return NIL return cons( cons(L -> car, (L -> cdr) -> car), Pass((L -> cdr) -> cdr) ) function ListToTree(L) while L -> cdr != NIL do L = Pass(L) return L -> car

                                    The passes cost n + n/2 + n/4 + … < 2n, so O(n) in total, and the original list is never changed. Try it:

                                    Bottom-up pairing: watch the list collapse into a tree

                                    (c) A search-tree node. A BST node needs four fields (key, parent, left, right), but a cell has only two slots. Chain cells: use CAR of the first cell for the key and CDR to point to a second cell; in the second cell, CAR holds the parent and CDR points to a third cell whose CAR is the left child and CDR the right child.

                                    fieldhow to read it from a node N
                                    keyN → car
                                    parent(N → cdr) → car
                                    left child((N → cdr) → cdr) → car
                                    right child((N → cdr) → cdr) → cdr

                                    A reference to a node is a reference to its first cell, and NIL means “no child” or “no parent”. Every Chapter 7 operation (search, minimum, successor, insertion, deletion) uses only these four reads, plus assigning a slot when a pointer must change; each field is at most three steps from the node, so the running times stay the same as with ordinary nodes.

                                    Part 6 · Chapter 8, AVL trees · Q1 to Q3

                                    AVL trees: insertion and deletion sequences

                                    Chapter 8 starts with three “draw the tree after every operation” problems. The method never changes: (1) insert or delete exactly as in an ordinary search tree; (2) walk from that place up to the root, updating heights; (3) at the lowest node whose two subtrees differ in height by 2, rotate. Read The AVL rule, The simple cases, When one rotation is not enough, Insertion and Deletion first if any of this is new.

                                    Four cases, one table

                                    Look at the unbalanced node x (the one that is 2 too tall on one side), at its tall child c, and at which side of c is taller.

                                    shapenamefix
                                    x left-heavy, c left-heavy (or balanced)left-leftone right rotation at x
                                    x right-heavy, c right-heavy (or balanced)right-rightone left rotation at x
                                    x left-heavy, c right-heavyleft-rightleft rotation at c, then right rotation at x
                                    x right-heavy, c left-heavyright-leftright rotation at c, then left rotation at x

                                    Naming in the set's pictures

                                    In the PDF’s drawings for Q1, the arrow is labelled by the rotation: “LL Rotation” for the chain 21, 26, 30 (which is a right-right shape, fixed by one left rotation), “RR Rotation” for the chain 26, 21, 9 (a left-left shape, fixed by one right rotation), and “LR” / “RL” for the double rotations (the order in which the two rotations are done). This guide, like Chapter 8, names the shape first. The pictures and the slides agree on what the final tree looks like, which is all an answer needs.

The first node with ±2 is the one to fix; then look at its tall child to choose single or double rotation.

Height 3, and there were 6 re-balancings in all (one single left, one single right, one left-right and three right-left).

                                    Ch.8 · Q2Medium

                                    Insert 4, 7, 1, then delete 5 and 7

                                    Consider the AVL tree with root 8; 8’s children are 3 and 12; 3 has children 2 and 6; 6 has the left child 5; 12 has the left child 10.

                                    1. Perform insert(4), insert(7) and insert(1) with the necessary rotations. For each, draw the tree right before and right after re-balancing.
                                    2. From that tree, perform delete(5) and delete(7), with rotations. Draw before and after re-balancing for each.

                                    Follow the insertion and deletion algorithms of the Chapter 7 and 8 notes (for deletion of a node with two children, copy the successor).

                                    Think first

                                    Heights first. Which nodes are on the path from the new leaf to the root? Update bottom-up and stop at the first node that is off by 2. For deleting a node with two children, remember the Chapter 7 rule: copy in the successor (smallest key of the right subtree) and cut that node out; the repair starts from the parent of the node that was cut out.

                                    Show the worked solution

                                    (a) Insertions.

                                    • insert(4). Path 8, 3, 6, 5: 4 becomes the left child of 5. Node 6 is now left-heavy by 2 (its left subtree 5–4 has height 1, its right subtree is empty, height −1) and its child 5 is left-heavy: left-left, one right rotation at 6. Now 5 is the parent of 4 and 6.
                                    • insert(7). Path 8, 3, 5, 6: 7 becomes the right child of 6. Node 3 is right-heavy by 2 (left subtree: just 2; right subtree 5 → 6 → 7 has height 2) and its child 5 is right-heavy: right-right, one left rotation at 3. Now 5 sits above 3 (children 2, 4) and 6 (right child 7).
                                    • insert(1). Path 8, 5, 3, 2: 1 becomes the left child of 2. Node 8 is left-heavy by 2 (left subtree rooted at 5 has height 3, right subtree 12–10 has height 1) and its child 5 is left-heavy: left-left, one right rotation at 8. Now 5 is the root, with 8 (children 6 and 12) on the right.

                                    Tree after (a): root 5; left child 3 (children 2 and 4; 2 has the left child 1); right child 8 with children 6 (right child 7) and 12 (left child 10).

                                    (b) Deletions.

                                    • delete(5). The root has two children. Its successor is the smallest key in the right subtree: from 8, go left to 6, which has no left child: 6. Copy 6 into the root and cut the old node 6 out (its right child 7 takes its place). Check the heights from 8 upward: 8 now has the left child 7 (height 0) and the right child 12 (subtree height 1), so 8 has height 2; the root’s left subtree (3, 2, 1) also has height 2. Nothing is off by 2: no re-balancing needed.
                                    • delete(7). 7 is a leaf: cut it off. Walk up from its parent 8: left subtree empty (−1), right subtree 12–10 (height 1): node 8 is right-heavy by 2. Its right child 12 is left-heavy (child 10), so right-left: a right rotation at 12, then a left rotation at 8. Now 10 is the top of that subtree, with children 8 and 12.

                                    Final tree: root 6; left child 3 (children 2 and 4; 2 has the left child 1); right child 10 with children 8 and 12.

                                    Other correct answers

                                    For delete(5) you could also copy the predecessor (the largest key of the left subtree, here 4). The set says to follow the notes, which use the successor; with the predecessor the tree comes out differently but is also a valid AVL tree. Always state which rule you use.

                                    Ch.8 · Q3Medium

                                    Insert 38, 25, 12, 120, 57, 96, 98, 43; then delete 98 and 120

                                    1. Show the result of inserting 38, 25, 12, 120, 57, 96, 98, 43 (in that order) into an initially empty AVL tree. Show the final tree after each insertion.
                                    2. Show the result of deleting 98 and 120 from that tree. Show the tree after each deletion.

                                    Think first

                                    Only the shape right after each operation is asked for, but you still need the rotation logic to get it. Watch for 57 (a zig-zag under 38) and 98 (a zig-zag under 120).

                                    Show the worked solution

                                    Part 7 · Chapter 8, AVL trees · Q4 to Q6

                                    AVL facts, the thinnest AVL trees, pruning leaves

                                    Now the theory behind AVL trees: true/false statements, how few nodes a tree of a given height can have (read How tall can an AVL tree be?), and a proof-style problem about removing leaves round by round.

                                    Ch.8 · Q4Medium

                                    True or false: AVL trees

                                    For each statement say True or False. For a False statement, point out the incorrectness.

                                    1. The worst-case height of an AVL tree with n nodes is log2 n.
                                    2. If the left child’s left subtree becomes taller after an insertion, a simple right rotation is always sufficient to rebalance.
                                    3. The height of a null tree is considered to be 0 in AVL tree definitions.
                                    4. Only the descendants of the newly inserted or deleted node can have their balance factors violated after the operation.
                                    5. After deleting a node from an AVL tree, rebalancing can require O(log n) time in the worst case.

                                    Think first

                                    Remember what the AVL rule compares (heights of the two child subtrees) and which nodes’ heights can change when one leaf appears or disappears: only the nodes above it, on one path to the root.

                                    Show the worked solution
                                    PartVerdictWhy
                                    (a)Falselog2 n is roughly the height of a perfect tree, the best case. An AVL tree can be taller: the worst case is about 1.44 log2 n. Correction: the worst-case height is O(log n).
                                    (b)TrueThat is the left-left case: one right rotation at the unbalanced node restores the AVL rule.
                                    (c)FalseThe empty tree has height −1 (a single node has height 0). That convention makes the formula “height = 1 + max(heights of the children)” work for leaves.
                                    (d)FalseOnly the ancestors of the changed place can be violated: they are the only nodes whose subtrees changed.
                                    (e)TrueAfter a deletion, a rotation can shorten a subtree and so cause another violation higher up; in the worst case you rotate at every ancestor, up to O(log n) of them. (After an insertion, one rebalancing is always enough.)
                                    Ch.8 · Q5Medium

                                    The thinnest AVL trees and a recurrence

                                    1. For AVL trees of height 2 and of height 3, draw an example with the minimum number of nodes among AVL trees of that height.
                                    2. Write a recurrence for the minimum number of nodes in an AVL tree of height h.

                                    Think first

                                    To be as thin as possible at the top, one child subtree must be as tall as allowed (height h − 1) and the other as short as the AVL rule allows (height h − 2). Both of them should themselves be thinnest trees.

                                    Show the worked solution

                                    (b) The recurrence first. Let T(h) be the least number of nodes of an AVL tree of height h. The root needs a child subtree of height exactly h − 1 (otherwise the height would not be h). The other child may be shorter by 1 at most, so height h − 2, and the fewest nodes comes from making both thinnest:

                                    T(0) = 1,  T(1) = 2,  T(<i>h</i>) = T(<i>h</i> − 1) + T(<i>h</i> − 2) + 1 for <i>h</i> > 1

                                    So T: 1, 2, 4, 7, 12, 20, 33, … This is the Fibonacci recurrence plus 1: T(h) = F(h + 3) − 1 with F(1) = F(2) = 1. Fibonacci numbers grow like φh with φ ≈ 1.618, so n ≥ about φh, i.e. h ≤ about 1.44 log2 n: the O(log n) height of AVL trees.

                                    (a) The examples. Height 2: root with a thinnest height-1 subtree (a node with one child: 2 nodes) on one side and a single node (height 0) on the other: 4 nodes in all; for example 26 with children 21 and 30, and 21 has the left child 9. Height 3: root with a thinnest height-2 subtree (4 nodes) on one side and a thinnest height-1 subtree (2 nodes) on the other: 1 + 4 + 2 = 7 nodes; the set uses root 12, left child 8 (children 5 and 11; 5 has the left child 4) and right child 18 (the left child 17).

                                    How tall can an AVL tree with n nodes be? (from Chapter 8)

                                    Ch.8 · Q6Hard

                                    Pruning the leaves round by round

                                    An empty subtree has height −1 and a leaf has height 0. An AVL tree is a strict BST whose two child-subtree heights differ by at most 1 at every node. One pruning round removes all nodes that are leaves at the start of the round; nodes that become leaves wait for the next round. No rotations, no key changes; pruning an empty tree leaves it empty.

                                    1. The tree has root 4, left child 2, right child 5; node 2 has children 1 and 3. (i) Is it an AVL tree? (ii) Remove only leaf 5, without rebalancing: still AVL? (iii) Starting again, what remains after one complete round? Is it AVL?
                                    2. For any non-empty binary tree of height h, prove that one round leaves height h − 1. Include h = 0.
                                    3. (i) Prove or disprove: one round always turns an AVL tree into an AVL tree (possibly empty). (ii) Why is that consistent with the single-leaf deletion in (a)?
                                    4. (i) For an AVL tree of height 8: the height after three rounds, and after how many rounds is it first empty? (ii) A perfect BST with 127 nodes: after three rounds, how many nodes remain and what is the height?

                                    Think first

                                    For (b) think about where the deepest leaves are, and which node is their parent. For (c) a tiny function does all the work: a subtree of height a has height max(a − 1, −1) after a round. Ask how a difference of at most 1 behaves under that function.

                                    Show the worked solution

                                    (a)(i) Node 2 has height 1 (two leaf children), node 5 has height 0, so at the root the heights are 1 and 0: balanced. Nodes 1, 3, 5 are leaves, balanced. Yes, it is an AVL tree.

                                    (a)(ii) Remove only 5. The root now has a left subtree of height 1 and an empty right subtree (height −1): difference 2. Not an AVL tree.

                                    (a)(iii) A full round removes the leaves 1, 3 and 5 together. What remains is the root 4 with the single left child 2 (node 2 is not removed in this round: it only becomes a leaf). At the root the heights are 0 and −1: balanced. Yes, still AVL.

                                    (b) If h = 0 the tree is a single node, a leaf; it is removed and the empty tree has height −1 = h − 1. If h ≥ 1: every node at depth h is a leaf (nothing is deeper) and disappears, so the new height is at most h − 1. The parent of a deepest leaf, at depth h − 1, had a child so it was not a leaf: it survives, so the height is at least h − 1. Exactly h − 1.

                                    (c)(i) True. Pruning keeps the search-tree order (we only delete nodes). Let a subtree have height a ≥ −1. After a round its height is f(a) = max(a − 1, −1) (by part (b); an empty subtree stays empty). Take a surviving node whose child subtrees had heights a and b with |a − b| ≤ 1. Their new heights are f(a) and f(b), and f never changes a difference by more than it was: |f(a) − f(b)| ≤ |a − b| ≤ 1. Concretely: if both subtrees are non-empty, both heights drop by exactly 1 and the difference is unchanged. If one subtree is empty (height −1), the AVL rule forces the other to have height at most 0, i.e. to be a single leaf, and that leaf is removed too: both are empty and the node is balanced. If the original root was a leaf, the result is the empty tree, which is trivially valid.

                                    (c)(ii) The statement is about a complete round, where all leaves go at the same moment. In (a)(ii) we removed one leaf and left the other leaves (1 and 3) in place; such an intermediate tree can be unbalanced, and a real deletion would need a rotation. Compare (a)(ii) with (a)(iii): same tree, different outcome.

                                    (d)(i) Every round lowers the height by exactly 1, so after three rounds the height is 8 − 3 = 5. The empty tree has height −1, which is reached after 8 − (−1) = 9 rounds.

                                    (d)(ii) The perfect tree with 127 = 27 − 1 nodes has height 6. Three rounds remove the bottom three levels, leaving a perfect tree of height 3, which has 24 − 1 = 15 nodes, height 3.

                                    Part 8 · Chapter 8, AVL trees · Q7 and Q8

                                    Splaying, and the most valuable object in a price range

                                    Two “design something with trees” problems. In Q7 you compare two ways of keeping a search tree fast: balancing (AVL) against moving each searched key to the root. In Q8 you store extra information at the nodes of an AVL tree so that a range question can be answered in O(log m) time.

                                    Ch.8 · Q7Hard

                                    Move the popular key to the root

                                    Some keys are searched far more often than others, so we might move a popular key to the root. Let splay(x) turn a BST T into a BST T′ with the same keys and x at the root. Each node has key, parent, left, right.

                                    1. Design an algorithm for splay(x), using the rotations from the AVL chapter. (You need not keep the tree AVL.)
                                    2. On an initially empty BST do: insert 8, insert 1, search 1, insert 5, insert 6, search 5, search 6, insert 10, insert 12, insert 13, search 13, search 1, search 1. If splaying is not used but the tree is balanced as an AVL tree, count the key matchings of the searches.
                                    3. Repeat on an initially empty, unbalanced BST, applying splaying after every operation. Count the key matchings of the searches.

                                    Think first

                                    (a) A rotation moves a node one level up and keeps the search-tree order. So: while x has a parent, rotate x above it. The direction depends on whether x is a left or a right child. (b), (c) A “key matching” is one comparison of the searched key with a node: the number of nodes on the path from the root to the key, including both ends.

                                    Show the worked solution

                                    (a) The algorithm.

                                    function TreeSplay(T, x) while x.parent != NIL do y = x.parent if y.left == x then right_rotate(T, y) // x is a left child: rotate the parent right else left_rotate(T, y) // x is a right child: rotate the parent left

                                    Each pass of the loop lifts x by one level, so after depth(x) passes it is the root. A right rotation at y promotes y’s left child (which is x) above y; a left rotation promotes the right child.

                                    Careful: this is not the textbook splay tree

                                    The official algorithm rotates x up one step at a time. Real splay trees look at two levels at once (“zig-zig” and “zig-zag” steps) and that is what gives them their O(log n) amortized guarantee. With single rotations only, a bad sequence stays bad: insert 1, 2, …, 64 and then search 1, 2, …, 64 twice, and the move-to-root tree needs 4,286 key matchings against only 656 for an AVL tree (try it in the tool below with fewer keys). The question only asks you to follow the stated algorithm, so do that, but know the difference.

                                    (b) AVL, no splaying. Draw the tree after each operation:

                                    • insert 8, 1 gives 8 with the left child 1. search 1: compare with 8, then 1: 2 matches.
                                    • insert 5 goes right of 1: node 8 is left-heavy by 2 with a right-heavy child: left-right double rotation. Tree 5 → (1, 8). insert 6: left of 8.
                                    • search 5: the root: 1. search 6: 5, 8, 6: 3.
                                    • insert 10 (right of 8). insert 12: right of 10, so the root 5 becomes right-heavy by 2 with a right-heavy child: left rotation at 5. Tree: 8 → (5 → (1, 6), 10 → (–, 12)). insert 13: right of 12: node 10 is right-heavy by 2: left rotation. Tree: 8 → (5 → (1, 6), 12 → (10, 13)).
                                    • search 13: 8, 12, 13: 3. search 1: 8, 5, 1: 3, and again 3 (the AVL tree does not change on a search).
                                    search1561311total
                                    matches21333315

                                    A label slip in the official table

                                    In the set’s solution the first row of both tables is headed “insert”; the row lists the searched keys, so it should read “search”.

                                    (c) Splaying after every operation (no balancing). After each insert or search, the touched key is rotated to the root.

                                    • insert 8, insert 1 (then splay: 1 is the root, 8 its right child). search 1: it is the root: 1.
                                    • insert 5: path 1, 8, left of 8, then splayed to the root: 5 → (1, 8). insert 6: path 5, 8, then splayed: 6 → (5 → (1, –), 8).
                                    • search 5: path 6, 5: 2; splay brings 5 up: 5 → (1, 6 → (–, 8)). search 6: path 5, 6: 2; splay: 6 → (5 → (1, –), 8).
                                    • insert 10, 12, 13: each is placed to the right and rotated to the root, so the tree becomes a left-leaning chain 13 → 12 → 10 → 6 → 5 (→ 1) with 8 below 6. search 13: it is the root: 1.

                                    Ch.8 · Q8Hard

                                    The most valuable object with price between x and y

                                    There are m objects, each with a distinct price pi and a value vi (positive integers). Design a data structure using O(m) space such that, given two prices x < y, it returns the value of the most valuable object whose price is strictly between x and y (x < pi < y) in O(log m) time. You may assume at least one such object exists and may use results from the lecture notes without proof. Give: the construction, the pseudocode of the query, and the explanation with its time.

                                    Think first

                                    A search tree can find “everything between x and y” as a handful of whole subtrees plus a few single nodes, if the tree is balanced (so there are only O(log m) of them). If every node already knows the best value inside its whole subtree, you never need to look inside a whole subtree.

                                    Show the worked solution

                                    The data structure: an AVL tree keyed by price, with extra fields. One node per object. Each node n stores price, value, left, right, and, for the subtree Sn rooted at n:

                                    • min_price: the smallest price in Sn,
                                    • max_price: the largest price in Sn,
                                    • max_value: the largest value in Sn.

                                    Each of these is computed from the two children in O(1): max_value = max(value, left.max_value, right.max_value), min_price = left.min_price (or the node’s own price if no left child), and so on. So they can be filled in by one post-order pass (O(m)), and if you keep inserting later, a rotation only changes two nodes whose fields are recomputed in O(1). Space: a constant number of fields per node, O(m). The AVL property gives height O(log m).

                                    The query: two walks down the tree. The picture to have in mind: the keys strictly between x and y form one “slice” of the sorted order. Walk down towards x (the left walk) and down towards y (the right walk). Along the left walk, whenever you step left (so the current node’s price is above x), the current node and its entire right subtree lie above x; if they are also below y they are completely inside the slice, and their stored max_value covers them in one step. The right walk does the mirror image with left subtrees.

                                    function findMostValuableObject(root, x, y) l_node = root; r_node = root; hv = 0 while l_node != NULL do // left walk: follow x if x <= l_node.price then if l_node.right != NULL and l_node.right.max_price < y and x < l_node.right.min_price then hv = max(hv, l_node.right.max_value) // whole right subtree is inside if x < l_node.price and l_node.price < y then hv = max(hv, l_node.value) // the node itself is inside l_node = l_node.left else l_node = l_node.right while r_node != NULL do // right walk: follow y if y >= r_node.price then if r_node.left != NULL and r_node.left.max_price < y and x < r_node.left.min_price then hv = max(hv, r_node.left.max_value) // whole left subtree is inside if x < r_node.price and r_node.price < y then hv = max(hv, r_node.value) r_node = r_node.right else r_node = r_node.left return hv

                                    Why the tests on max_price and min_price? Before the two walks separate, a subtree can stick out past y (or below x). Using its stored maximum would then be wrong, so we only use a stored value when the whole subtree is inside (x < min_price and max_price < y). The part that sticks out is not lost: the other walk goes down into it and handles it piece by piece. The tool below compares the answer with brute force on any data you type.

                                    Time. Each walk moves down one level per iteration, so at most h + 1 iterations each, with h = O(log m), and each iteration does O(1) work. Total at most 2(h + 1) iterations: O(log m).

                                    Two walks down the tree: which subtrees are used?

                                    A wording slip in the official explanation

                                    The official text speaks of the “right sibling” of the current node; the code (and the logic) use the current node’s right child (and, in the second loop, its left child). Also note the line hv = 0: it relies on all values being positive, which the problem states.
