                                    Written Assignment 1 · Recursion and algorithm analysis (Chapters 1–2) · due 30 Sept 2026

                                    Written Assignment 1 Step by Step

                                    The official solution, explained from the first line. Four questions: which function grows faster (the T/F table), proofs of asymptotic bounds, solving recurrences and proving them by induction, and designing a fast recursive search. Every claim has a demo so that you can check it with your own numbers.

                                    In this chapter

                                      Part 1 · Question 1(a)

                                      Question 1(a): which function grows faster?

                                      The question gives six pairs of functions (f(n), g(n)) and asks, for each pair, three yes/no questions: is f = O(g)? Is f = Ω(g)? Is f = Θ(g)? Write T or F. If the symbols are still fuzzy, read Chapter 2, part 7 first; here is the whole idea in three lines.

                                      The three symbols, in plain words

                                      SymbolPlain meaningThink of it as
                                      f = O(g)f grows no faster than g: from some point on, f ≤ (a constant) × g.≤
                                      f = Ω(g)f grows at least as fast as g: from some point on, f ≥ (a positive constant) × g.≥
                                      f = Θ(g)Both at once: f is squeezed between two constant multiples of g.=

                                      Picture it

                                      Look at the ratio f(n) / g(n) for huge n. If it sinks to 0, f is much smaller: only O is true. If it blows up to infinity, f is much bigger: only Ω is true. If it stays between two positive numbers, the functions are the same size up to a constant: all three are true (Θ).

                                      The answer table

                                      f(n)g(n)OΩΘWhy, in one line
                                      50n100nTTTThe example done for you: f/g is exactly 1/2 for every n.
                                      5√n3/nFTFf grows, g shrinks towards 0, so f/g = (5/3)n1.5 → ∞.
                                      n!nn/2FTFStirling: n! behaves like (n/e)n, which beats (√n)n once √n > e.
                                      50n + 200 log5 n5log2 nTFF5log2 n = nlog2 5 ≈ n2.32, much bigger than n.
                                      7 cos²n + 1002 sin n + 3TTTBoth wiggle, but both stay between two positive constants, so their ratio does too.
                                      n / (log10 log2 n)³(√7)2 log2 nTFF(√7)2 log2 n = 7log2 n = nlog2 7 ≈ n2.81, far above n.

                                      Row by row

                                      Row 2: a growing function against a shrinking one

                                      5√n goes up; 3/n goes down (3, 1.5, 1, 0.75, …). So f ends up above g by more and more: f = Ω(g) is true. But “f = O(g)” would need f to stay within a constant multiple of g, and the ratio (5/3)n1.5 has no ceiling. So O is false and Θ is false.

                                      Row 3: factorial against nn/2

                                      The problem gives you the hint: n! ≈ √(2πn)(n/e)n. Drop the harmless √(2πn) factor (it is bigger than 1), and rewrite n = n1/2·n1/2:

                                      n! > (n/e)n = (n(1/2))n × (n(1/2)/e)n = n(n/2) × (sqrt(n)/e)n

                                      Once √n > e (that is, n > e² ≈ 7.4), the bracket (√n/e) is bigger than 1, and a number bigger than 1 raised to the power n only grows. So n! > nn/2 from then on, and the ratio keeps exploding. That gives Ω true, O false, Θ false. (The official remark stops at n! > nn/2, which already proves Ω. To refute O you need the extra fact that the ratio is unbounded, which the factor (√n/e)n shows.)

                                      Rows 4 and 6: hiding a power inside an exponent

                                      Both rows use the same disguise. The identity is alogb n = nlogb a. Why: write a as blogb a, then alogb n = (blogb a)logb n = (blogb n)logb a = nlogb a. With it:

                                      • Row 4: 5log2 n = nlog2 5 ≈ n2.32. The left function is 50n + 200 log5 n, which is Θ(n) (the log term is much smaller than n). Linear against power 2.32: f/g → 0, so only O.
                                      • Row 6: (√7)2 log2 n = (71/2)2 log2 n = 7log2 n = nlog2 7 ≈ n2.81. The top function is n divided by a number that is at least 1 for large n (log10 log2 n ≥ 1 when n ≥ 210 = 1024), so f ≤ n for large n. Linear against power 2.81: only O.

                                      Row 5: two functions that never settle down

                                      cos²n lives between 0 and 1, so 7 cos²n + 100 lives between 100 and 107. And sin n lives between −1 and 1, so 2 sin n + 3 lives between 1 and 5. Neither function has a limit (they keep wiggling), so the “look at the limit” trick does not work, but we do not need it. The ratio f/g is at least 100/5 = 20 and at most 107/1 = 107, every single time. A ceiling and a positive floor: that is exactly Θ.

                                      A common mistake

                                      Do not decide by comparing a few values at small n. In row 4, at n = 10 the first function is the bigger one (about 786 against 210), yet f = O(g) is true: from n = 24 onwards g is bigger, and by n = 100 it is nearly eight times bigger (5572 against 44,041). Asymptotic means “from some n0 onwards”. Look at the shape of the functions, not at the first few values.

                                      Watch the ratio settle

                                      The demo shows f/g for n from 10 to 108. Pick a row and watch the trend: shrinking towards 0, exploding, or staying between two constants. (Some values are astronomically large; they are written as a power of ten.) A table is evidence about the trend; the sentences above are the proof.

                                      The ratio f(n) / g(n) for huge n

                                      Part 2 · Question 1(b)

                                      Question 1(b): prove or disprove, by definition

                                      “By definition” means you may not say “the biggest term wins”. You must go back to the definition and produce (or refute) the constants. Here are the two definitions you need, with the meaning of every letter.

                                      The definitions

                                      f(n) = O(g(n)) means: there exist constants c > 0 and n0 such that for all n ≥ n0: f(n) ≤ c·g(n).

                                      f(n) = Θ(g(n)) means: there exist c1 > 0, c2 > 0 and n0 such that for all n ≥ n0: c1·g(n) ≤ f(n) ≤ c2·g(n).

                                      So to prove a statement you choose the constants and show the inequality for every n from n0 on. To disprove it you show that no choice of constants can work. All logarithms in this course are base 2. Here is the picture to keep in mind for a Θ proof:

                                      Picture it

                                      Draw the curve h(n) and two copies of the reference curve n², one scaled down by c1 and one scaled up by c2. A Θ proof says: from n0 on, h stays inside the corridor between them. The corridor can be as wide as you like (here 1/16 to 36), as long as it is a fixed constant factor.

                                      (i) Is (n/2 − √n + 5 log n)² = Θ(n²)? — True

                                      Call the function h(n). The strategy: bound the bracket B(n) = n/2 − √n + 5 log n from below and above by easy multiples of n, then square.

                                      1. A lower bound for the bracket. Take n ≥ 16. Then √n ≤ n/4 (square both sides of 4√n ≤ n to get 16n ≤ n², which holds for n ≥ 16). Also 5 log n ≥ 0. So B(n) ≥ n/2 − n/4 + 0 = n/4. This number is positive, so squaring keeps the direction: h(n) ≥ (n/4)² = n²/16.
                                      2. An upper bound for the bracket. Throw away the minus term (that only makes the bracket bigger), and use log n ≤ n: B(n) ≤ n/2 + 5n = 5.5n ≤ 6n. So h(n) ≤ (6n)² = 36n². (The official solution writes the cruder n − 0 + 5n = 6n; same result.)
                                      3. Name the constants. c1 = 1/16, c2 = 36, n0 = 16. For every n ≥ 16: n²/16 ≤ h(n) ≤ 36n². This is the definition, so h(n) = Θ(n²). ∎

                                      Why 16?

                                      It is the first n where √n ≤ n/4 is guaranteed. Any bigger n0 also works, and so do other constants: the definition only asks that some constants exist. Choose them to make your own algebra easy.

                                      (ii) Is 4n2.5 + n = O(100n)? — False

                                      Plain words: a function with n2.5 in it cannot stay below a constant times a function that is only linear. To prove that, use proof by contradiction: assume it is true and show something impossible happens.

                                      1. Assume it is true. Then some c and n0 exist with 4n2.5 + n ≤ c·100n for all n ≥ n0.
                                      2. Divide by n (positive, so the direction stays): 4n1.5 + 1 ≤ 100c. Therefore 4n1.5 < 100c, i.e. n1.5 < 25c, i.e. n < (25c)2/3.
                                      3. Contradiction. The right side is one fixed number, but the claim was supposed to hold for all n ≥ n0, and there are arbitrarily large n. Take any n bigger than both n0 and (25c)2/3: the inequality fails. So no such c exists, and the statement is false. ∎

                                      (iii) If f(n) = n·g(n²) and g(n) = O(log n), is f(n) = O(n log n)? — True

                                      Here you do not know g exactly; you only know its definition-level fact. Start by unpacking what you are given, then use it.

                                      1. Unpack the hypothesis. g(n) = O(log n) means some c1 > 0 and n0 give g(n) ≤ c1 log n for all n ≥ n0.
                                      2. Plug in n² instead of n. This is allowed whenever n² is also past n0, which is true as soon as n ≥ n0 (and n ≥ 1). Then g(n²) ≤ c1 log(n²) = c1·2 log n. The key fact is that log(n²) = 2 log n: squaring the input only doubles the log.
                                      3. Multiply by n. f(n) = n·g(n²) ≤ n·2c1 log n = (2c1)·n log n.
                                      4. Name the constants. c2 = 2c1 and the same n0. So f(n) = O(n log n). ∎

                                      A common mistake

                                      Compare with what would happen if the hypothesis were g(n) = O(n). Then g(n²) could be as large as n², and the argument would give f = O(n³), not O(n). The statement is true because logs are so slow that squaring the input costs only a constant factor.

                                      Check the constants yourself

                                      Pick a statement and slide n. For (i) you see the function sandwiched between the two fences and a count of how many integer values were tested; for (ii) you see the constant c that would be needed grow without limit; for (iii) you see the worst allowed g still stay under 2c1 n log n.

                                      Constants, fences and the missing constant

                                      Part 3 · Question 2(a)

                                      Question 2(a): solve the recurrence, then prove it

                                      For each recurrence you must do two separate jobs, and each one earns its own marks:

                                      1. Solve it: unroll the recurrence until you hit the base case, add everything up, and get a closed form (a formula with no T on the right). Then state the Θ bound.
                                      2. Prove it: the closed form you found by unrolling is only a guess until you prove it by mathematical induction.

                                      Both techniques were taught in Chapter 1, part 3 (unwrapping) and part 5 (induction). If “unrolling” is a new word, the image is a staircase: every step of the recurrence takes you one stair down, and you collect a little bit of work at every stair.

                                      (i) T(2) = 4,  T(n) = 4T(n−1) + 3 for n > 2

                                      Solving it

                                      Unroll twice to see the pattern, and keep the brackets separate:

                                      T(n) = 4 T(n−1) + 3T(n) = 4 (4 T(n−2) + 3) + 3 = 42 T(n−2) + (4 × 3 + 3)T(n) = 43 T(n−3) + (42 × 3 + 4 × 3 + 3)

                                      After k unrollings there is a factor 4k in front of T(n−k), plus a leftover sum 3(4k−1 + … + 4 + 1). We want to land on the base case T(2), so we need n − k = 2, i.e. k = n − 2. The leftover sum is a geometric series (each term is 4 times the previous one): 1 + 4 + … + 4k−1 = (4k − 1)/(4 − 1). So:

                                      T(n) = 4(n−2) × T(2) + 3 × (4(n−2) − 1) / 3 = 4 × 4(n−2) + 4(n−2) − 1 = 5 × 4(n−2) − 1

                                      The closed form is T(n) = 5·4n−2 − 1. Sanity check with the recurrence: T(2) = 5·1 − 1 = 4 ✓; T(3) = 4·4 + 3 = 19 and 5·4 − 1 = 19 ✓. For the bound: 5·4n−2 = (5/16)·4n, and the −1 is negligible, so T(n) = Θ(4n).

                                      Proving it by induction

                                      Induction has a fixed shape. Write it in these labelled boxes and you will not forget a mark.

                                      1. State the proposition. Let P(n) be: “T(n) = 5·4n−2 − 1”. We prove it for all integers n ≥ 2 (the recurrence starts at 2).
                                      2. Base case n = 2. T(2) = 4 by definition, and 5·40 − 1 = 4. They match.
                                      3. Inductive step. Assume P(k) for some k ≥ 2: T(k) = 5·4k−2 − 1. Prove P(k+1). Start from the recurrence and use the assumption once:
                                      T(k+1) = 4 T(k) + 3 = 4 (5 × 4(k−2) − 1) + 3 = 5 × 4(k−1) − 4 + 3 = 5 × 4((k+1)−2) − 1

                                      That is exactly P(k+1). By induction, P(n) holds for every n ≥ 2. ∎

                                      (ii) T(1) = 0,  T(n) = T(n/10) + 10n² for n > 1, n a power of 10

                                      Solving it

                                      Now the argument shrinks by a factor 10 each time, so after k unrollings we are at T(n/10k). Reaching T(1) needs n/10k = 1, i.e. k = log10 n. The work collected on the way down:

                                      T(n) = 10 n2 + 10 (n/10)2 + 10 (n/100)2 + … + 10 (n/10(k−1))2 + T(1)

                                      Factor out 10n²: each term is the previous one divided by 100, so

                                      T(n) = 10 n2 (1 + 1/100 + 1/1002 + … + 1/100(k−1))T(n) = 10 n2 × (1 − (1/100)k) / (1 − 1/100)

                                      Because n = 10k, we have (1/100)k = 1/102k = 1/n². And 1/(1 − 1/100) = 100/99. So

                                      T(n) = 10 n2 × (100/99) × (1 − 1/n2) = 1000 (n2 − 1) / 99

                                      Closed form: T(n) = 1000(n² − 1)/99, so T(n) = Θ(n²). (Intuition: the very first term 10n² is already almost everything; the later terms form a series that shrinks 100-fold each time and together add only about 1% more.)

                                      Proving it by induction (on r, not on n)

                                      Here n takes only the values 1, 10, 100, 1000, …, so “n + 1” is not a legal next case. The trick is to count the powers: write n = 10r and induct on the exponent r = 0, 1, 2, …

                                      1. Proposition. P(r): T(10r) = 1000((10r)² − 1)/99, for every integer r ≥ 0.
                                      2. Base case r = 0. T(1) = 0, and 1000(1² − 1)/99 = 0. They match.
                                      3. Inductive step. Assume P(k). Prove P(k+1). The number 10k+1 divided by 10 is 10k, so the recurrence lets us use the assumption:
                                      T(10(k+1)) = T(10k) + 10 (10(k+1))2 = 1000 ((10k)2 − 1) / 99 + 10 (10(k+1))2

                                      Write everything over 99 and note that (10k+1)² = 100·(10k)², so 10(10k+1)² = 1000(10k)² = 99000(10k)²/99:

                                      T(10(k+1)) = [1000 (10k)2 − 1000 + 99000 (10k)2] / 99 = [100000 (10k)2 − 1000] / 99 = 1000 ((10(k+1))2 − 1) / 99

                                      (since 100·(10k)² = (10k+1)²). That is P(k+1). ∎

                                      Where marks are lost

                                      (1) Stopping after the unrolling and never proving the closed form. (2) In an induction, forgetting to say where the inductive hypothesis is used. (3) Proving the step by starting from the answer you want to reach and manipulating both sides until they look the same. Start from the recurrence side and arrive at the closed form, as above. (4) In part (ii), inducting on n even though n only takes powers of 10.

                                      Check both closed forms with real numbers

                                      The table recomputes T(n) the slow way, straight from the recurrence, with exact big integers, and compares it with the closed form. Every row should show a tick. This does not replace the induction (it only tests a few values), but it catches algebra slips.

                                      Recurrence versus closed form

                                      Part 4 · Question 2(b)

                                      Question 2(b): writing a recurrence for a counting problem

                                      This time nobody gives you the recurrence. You must invent it from a story: “how many ways can …?” You do not solve it. You must write the rule and the fewest base cases that make the rule complete.

                                      The method that always works

                                      Take any object you are counting, of size n. Ask “what does it look like at one end?” Sort all the objects into groups by that answer. The groups must be disjoint (nothing in two groups) and exhaustive (nothing left out). Peel off the end part, and what remains is a smaller object of the same kind. So the number of objects is the sum, over groups, of the number of smaller objects.

                                      (i) Tilings of a 1 × n board with tiles of length 1 and 3

                                      Look at the first tile. There are only two possibilities:

                                      • It is a 1-tile. It covers one cell, and the remaining 1 × (n−1) board can be tiled in T(n−1) ways.
                                      • It is a 3-tile (only possible if n ≥ 3). It covers three cells, and the remaining 1 × (n−3) board can be tiled in T(n−3) ways.

                                      Every tiling starts with exactly one of these, so T(n) = T(n−1) + T(n−3). The rule looks back as far as n−3, so for it to be legal we need n − 3 ≥ 1, i.e. n ≥ 4. That leaves n = 1, 2, 3 as base cases, and we can count them by hand:

                                      nThe tilingsT(n)
                                      111
                                      21 11
                                      31 1 1  and  32
                                      T(n) = 1 for n = 1, 2; T(3) = 2; T(n) = T(n−1) + T(n−3) for n ≥ 4

                                      Check one value: T(4) = T(3) + T(1) = 2 + 1 = 3, and the tilings of a 1 × 4 board are 1111, 31 and 13. ✓

                                      (ii) Strings of length n over {a, b} that do not contain “abb”

                                      The official solution takes a different route from the tilings: it adds one letter to the front, which doubles the strings, and then subtracts the bad ones. That gives:

                                      T(n) = 2 T(n−1) − T(n−3) for n ≥ 4, with T(1) = 2, T(2) = 4, T(3) = 7

                                      Why: put ‘a’ or ‘b’ in front of any valid string of length n−1, giving 2T(n−1) candidates. The only candidates that are bad are those where the new front letter creates the forbidden pattern “abb” at the very beginning: ‘a’ followed by a valid string starting “bb”, i.e. “abb” followed by any valid string of length n−3. There are T(n−3) of those. That is a correct answer, and it needs three base cases: T(1) = 2 (‘a’, ‘b’), T(2) = 4 (all four strings) and T(3) = 7 (all eight strings except ‘abb’).

                                      The question asked for the least number of base cases, and there is a slightly better answer with only two. Classify the valid strings by how they end (for n ≥ 3):

                                      The string ends in …What is in front of that endingHow many
                                      aany valid string of length n−1 (adding an ‘a’ at the end cannot create “abb”, which ends in b)T(n−1)
                                      abany valid string of length n−2 (adding “ab” at the end cannot make “abb”, which needs two b’s in a row at its end)T(n−2)
                                      bbnothing but b’s. The letter just before the final “bb” cannot be ‘a’ (that would spell “abb”), so it is a ‘b’ (or the string has ended). The same argument applies to that b, and so on back to the start. Every letter is b: the single string “bb…b”.exactly 1

                                      Those three groups are disjoint (different endings) and cover everything (a string ends in ‘a’, or in ‘b’; if it ends in b, it is ‘ab’ or ‘bb’). So:

                                      T(n) = T(n−1) + T(n−2) + 1 for n ≥ 3, with T(1) = 2, T(2) = 4

                                      This looks back only to n−2, so two base cases are enough: T(3) = 4 + 2 + 1 = 7 ✓, T(4) = 7 + 4 + 1 = 12. The official 2T(n−1) − T(n−3) gives the same numbers (2·7 − 2 = 12). The two recurrences are equal for all n ≥ 4; the difference is only in how many starting values they need.

                                      The tempting wrong answer

                                      “Ends in a, ends in ab, ends in abb, … so T(n−1) + T(n−2) + T(n−3)”. The third group is not “any valid string of length n−3” plus a tail: strings ending in bb are only the all-b string, which is one string. This wrong recurrence gives 7 + 4 + 2 = 13 for n = 4, but the true count is 12.

                                      A pleasant surprise

                                      Look at the numbers 2, 4, 7, 12, 20, 33, 54, 88, 143. Add 1 to each and you get 3, 5, 8, 13, 21, 34, 55, 89, 144: the Fibonacci numbers (Chapter 2, part 10). So T(n) = Fib(n+3) − 1, and the number of valid strings grows like (1.618…)n, noticeably slower than the 2n strings in total.

                                      List them all and check the recurrence

                                      Choose a problem and a size. The demo lists every tiling or valid string, counts them by brute force, and compares the count with the recurrences in a table. For the strings it shows the three groups by their endings and the wrong guess next to the right ones.

                                      Every tiling and every string, with the recurrence checked

                                      Part 5 · Question 3

                                      Question 3: the running time of FindSmallest

                                      The algorithm is short. Read it line by line, like a computer would.

                                      function FindSmallest(A, m) # A[1..n], 1 <= m <= n min = infinity for i = 1 to m: if A[i] < min: min = A[i] return min
                                      min = infinity

                                      a starting champion that every real number beats. One step.

                                      for i = 1 to m

                                      the loop looks only at the first m cells, not at all n.

                                      if A[i] < min: min = A[i]

                                      compare, and maybe replace the champion. Either way: one comparison and at most one assignment, so O(1).

                                      return min

                                      one step.

                                      The question is about cases: for the same array A, which values of m make the algorithm fastest (best case) and slowest (worst case)?

                                      The key observation

                                      Count the loop, not the array

                                      The loop runs exactly m times, whatever numbers are in the array. The if may or may not replace the champion, but both outcomes cost O(1). So the cost depends on m and on nothing else: the total is Θ(m).

                                      That already answers both parts. In the best case the loop is as short as possible, and in the worst case it is as long as possible.

                                      Which m?What happensTime
                                      (a) Best casem = 1The loop body runs once; the other lines are single steps. Constant work.O(1)
                                      (b) Worst casem = nThe loop body runs n times, each O(1), plus a few single steps: n·O(1) + O(1).O(n)

                                      Two common mistakes

                                      1. Writing “best case: the minimum is in the first cell”. That does not make this algorithm faster; it never stops early. (A search that stops when it finds the target would have that best case; this one does not.) 2. Saying “the time is O(n) in the best case too, because m could be n”. A case is a specific input: the best case is the input with the smallest cost, and that is m = 1.

                                      Watch the loop

                                      Type an array, pick m, and step through. The box labelled loop iterations used always ends at exactly m: change the numbers in the array and it does not move; change m and it does.

                                      FindSmallest: count the iterations

                                      Part 6 · Question 4

                                      Question 4: What a coincidence — finding A[i] = i fast

                                      The task. You are given a sorted array A[1..n] of distinct integers, in increasing order. Find an index i with A[i] = i (a “coincidence”), using a recursive algorithm asymptotically faster than O(n). You must give three things: (1) pseudocode with a verbal explanation, (2) the worst-case running time, (3) a proof of correctness by induction.

                                      “Faster than O(n)” with sorted data is a big hint: binary search (Chapter 6, part 5). But binary search normally looks for a value. Here the target is not a value but a relationship between the value and the position. Why can we still throw away half the array?

                                      The idea: look at the difference A[i] − i

                                      Imagine a second row under the array that stores d[i] = A[i] − i. A coincidence is a 0 in the second row. How does the second row behave when you step one cell to the right?

                                      • The integers are distinct and increasing, so A[i+1] ≥ A[i] + 1 (the next integer up is at least one more).
                                      • The position goes up by exactly 1.
                                      • So d[i+1] = A[i+1] − (i+1) ≥ A[i] + 1 − i − 1 = d[i]. The second row never goes down.

                                      Picture it

                                      A row of numbers that never decreases is sorted! So “find a 0 in the difference row” is just binary search in a sorted row. At the middle cell: if d > 0, everything to its right is also ≥ d > 0, so no zero hides on the right: go left. If d < 0, everything to its left is ≤ d < 0, so no zero on the left: go right. If d = 0, we found it.

                                      The algorithm never builds the second row. It just compares A[mid] with mid.

                                      The pseudocode (official solution)

                                      function Find(A, low, high): mid = floor((low + high) / 2) if A[mid] == mid: return mid else if low == high: return NULL if A[mid] > mid: return Find(A, low, mid) else: return Find(A, mid + 1, high)
                                      mid = floor((low + high) / 2)

                                      the middle cell of the current range. Use floor division so mid is a whole number.

                                      if A[mid] == mid: return mid

                                      a coincidence: done at once.

                                      else if low == high: return NULL

                                      the range has one cell and it is not a coincidence: there is none. This is the base case.

                                      if A[mid] > mid: return Find(A, low, mid)

                                      difference > 0: everything to the right has an even larger difference. Keep the left part, low..mid. (mid itself is not a coincidence, but keeping it is harmless and the range still shrinks.)

                                      else: return Find(A, mid + 1, high)

                                      difference < 0: everything to the left has an even smaller difference. Keep only the part right of mid.

                                      The first call is Find(A, 1, n). Try it on the examples; the toggle shows the other common version (from the tutorial slide), which drops mid when it moves (mid−1 / mid+1) and stops when the range is empty. Both are correct.

                                      Find: halving the range using A[mid] against mid

                                      Which version should I write?

                                      Either. In the official version the range [low, high] never becomes empty, which is why the base case is low == high. In the tutorial version the range can become empty (low > high), which is then the base case that returns NIL. Pick one and make the base case match your recursive calls: that is the most common bug here.

                                      (2) The worst-case running time

                                      Each call does a constant amount of work (c1: one division, one or two comparisons) and then makes at most one recursive call on a smaller range. How big is that range? If the current range has s = high − low + 1 cells, then with mid = ⌊(low + high)/2⌋:

                                      • the left part low..mid has ⌈s/2⌉ cells,
                                      • the right part mid+1..high has ⌊s/2⌋ cells.

                                      The worst case takes the bigger one, ⌈s/2⌉. With c2 for the single-cell base case:

                                      T(n) =c2n = 1T(ceil(n/2)) + c1n > 1

                                      Unroll it. Every unrolling halves the size (the ceiling is harmless) and adds one c1; the size reaches 1 after ⌈log n⌉ halvings:

                                      T(n) ≤ T(n/2) + c1 ≤ T(n/4) + 2 c1 ≤ … ≤ T(1) + c1 ceil(log n) ≤ c2 + c1 ceil(log n)

                                      So T(n) = O(log n), which is asymptotically faster than O(n). Try n = 1,000,000: a scan needs up to a million checks, this needs about twenty.

                                      (3) Correctness by induction

                                      We prove that Find works for every range size. This is strong induction: to prove the case of size r we assume all smaller sizes work, because the recursive call is on a range of any smaller size.

                                      1. Proposition P(r). For every range of r cells (1 ≤ r ≤ n), Find(A, low, high) returns an index i in the range with A[i] = i if one exists, and NULL if none exists.
                                      2. Base case r = 1. Then low = high = mid. If A[mid] = mid, the algorithm returns mid: correct. Otherwise the test low == high succeeds and it returns NULL: correct, because the only cell is not a coincidence.
                                      3. Inductive step. Take a range of r > 1 cells and assume P(k) for all 1 ≤ k < r. Three cases:
                                        • A[mid] = mid: the algorithm returns mid. Correct.
                                        • A[mid] > mid: for every j > mid, A[j] ≥ A[mid] + (j − mid) > mid + (j − mid) = j, so no coincidence exists to the right. Any coincidence in the range must lie in low..mid (indeed in low..mid−1). The algorithm searches low..mid, which has ⌈r/2⌉ < r cells (because r > 1). By the induction hypothesis the recursive call is right.
                                        • A[mid] < mid: symmetrically, for every j < mid, A[j] ≤ A[mid] − (mid − j) < mid − (mid − j) = j, so no coincidence on the left. The algorithm searches mid+1..high, which has ⌊r/2⌋ < r cells, and by the hypothesis it is right.
                                      4. Conclusion. P(r) holds for all r, in particular for r = n. ∎

                                      Why “distinct” matters

                                      The word “distinct” is what makes the difference row never decrease. Without it the algorithm can fail. Take A = [2, 2, 2, 2, 2] (sorted, but not distinct). Index 2 is a coincidence (A[2] = 2). But Find starts at mid = 3, sees A[3] = 2 < 3 and goes right, away from index 2, and ends with NULL. The proof above uses distinctness in the inequality A[j] ≥ A[mid] + (j − mid), which fails when values can repeat.

                                      More than one answer?

                                      If several coincidences exist, the question accepts “an index”, so any one is fine. Because the difference row never decreases and only has integer values, the zeros always form one block of consecutive cells. The preset examples show a single fixed point, the whole array (every cell is a coincidence) and no coincidence at all.

                                      Part 7 · The assignment on one page

                                      Summary, marking lessons and self-test

                                      The whole assignment in one table

                                      QuestionWhat was askedThe answer in one line
                                      1(a)T/F for O, Ω, Θ on six pairsCheck f/g at huge n: → 0 gives only O, → ∞ only Ω, trapped between positive constants gives all three. Rewrite alogb n as nlogb a.
                                      1(b)Prove or disprove three bounds by definition(i) true, fences n²/16 and 36n² for n ≥ 16; (ii) false, the needed c grows like n1.5; (iii) true, log(n²) = 2 log n.
                                      2(a)Solve two recurrences, prove by induction(i) 5·4n−2 − 1 = Θ(4n); (ii) 1000(n² − 1)/99 = Θ(n²), induct on r where n = 10r.
                                      2(b)Write counting recurrencesTilings: T(n) = T(n−1) + T(n−3), base 1, 1, 2. Strings avoiding abb: T(n) = T(n−1) + T(n−2) + 1, base 2, 4 (or the official 2T(n−1) − T(n−3), base 2, 4, 7).
                                      3Best and worst case of FindSmallestThe loop always runs m times: best m = 1, O(1); worst m = n, O(n).
                                      4Recursive search for A[i] = i faster than O(n)Binary search on the never-decreasing difference A[i] − i; T(n) ≤ T(⌈n/2⌉) + c, so O(log n); strong induction on the range size.

                                      What the marking was looking for

                                      • Constants, quantifiers and a conclusion. A bound proof names c and n0 and says “for all n ≥ n0”. A disproof assumes the bound and reaches a contradiction.
                                      • Two jobs for a recurrence. Solve (unroll and sum), then prove (induction). The proof starts from the recurrence and ends at the closed form.
                                      • The fewest base cases. A recurrence that refers back d steps needs the first d values. Look at how far back it reaches before you decide.
                                      • Cases are inputs. Best and worst case are particular inputs (here, particular m), not guesses about where the answer sits.
                                      • Pseudocode, not program code. The cover page says marks are deducted for C++/Python/Java in written assignments. Plain pseudocode with a sentence of explanation is what is wanted.

                                      Two small loose ends in the official solution

                                      • For 2(b)(ii) the official recurrence needs three base cases, while the two-base-case version T(n) = T(n−1) + T(n−2) + 1 meets the question’s “least number of base cases” more tightly. Both are correct recurrences for the same numbers.
                                      • For 1(a) row 3 the printed remark proves n! > nn/2, which gives Ω. To also see why O is false you need that the ratio is unbounded; the extra factor (√n/e)n in part 1 shows it.

                                      Test yourself

                                      1. Is n² + 10n = Θ(n²)? Give the constants.

                                        Show the answer

                                        Yes. For n ≥ 10: n² ≤ n² + 10n ≤ 2n² (because 10n ≤ n² when n ≥ 10). So c1 = 1, c2 = 2, n0 = 10.

                                      2. For f(n) = 2n and g(n) = 3n fill in O, Ω, Θ.

                                        Show the answer

                                        f/g = (2/3)n → 0. So O true, Ω false, Θ false. (Different bases are different growth rates, unlike different constants in front.)

                                      3. Solve T(1) = 1, T(n) = 2T(n−1) + 1. Closed form, Θ bound, and the base case of your induction.

                                        Show the answer

                                        Unroll: T(n) = 2n−1·1 + (2n−2 + … + 1) = 2n−1 + 2n−1 − 1 = 2n − 1, so Θ(2n). Induction base: n = 1 gives 2 − 1 = 1 ✓. Step: 2(2k − 1) + 1 = 2k+1 − 1 ✓.

                                      4. How many ways can a 1 × 6 board be tiled with tiles of length 1 and 3? And how many strings of length 5 over {a, b} avoid “abb”?

                                        Show the answer

                                        Tilings: T(4) = 3, T(5) = T(4) + T(2) = 4, T(6) = T(5) + T(3) = 4 + 2 = 6. Strings: 2, 4, 7, 12, then T(5) = 12 + 7 + 1 = 20.

                                      5. Why does FindSmallest take the same time on [1, 2, 3, 4, 5] and on [5, 4, 3, 2, 1] when m = 5?

                                        Show the answer

                                        The loop runs 5 iterations either way, and each iteration costs O(1) whether or not the if replaces the minimum. The data decides which assignments happen, not how many comparisons.

                                      6. Run Find (official version) on A = [−3, −1, 2, 4, 7, 9, 12]. What is returned and how many probes?

                                        Show the answer

                                        Range 1..7: mid = 4, A[4] = 4. A coincidence on the very first probe: returns 4, one probe. (Try the first preset in the demo, and step through the other presets to see the range shrink.)

                                      7. Why would the same algorithm fail if the array may contain repeated values?

                                        Show the answer

                                        The argument “if A[mid] > mid, every cell to the right also has A[j] > j” needs A[j] ≥ A[mid] + (j − mid), which holds only when the integers are distinct. With repeats, the difference A[i] − i can drop, and a coincidence can hide on the side we throw away (for example [2, 2, 2, 2, 2]).

                                      8. What is the recurrence for the running time of Find, and what does it solve to?

                                        Show the answer

                                        T(1) = c2, T(n) ≤ T(⌈n/2⌉) + c1. It solves to T(n) ≤ c2 + c1⌈log n⌉ = O(log n).

                                      What to remember

                                      Asymptotic statements are about ratios at huge n. A recurrence is solved by unrolling and then proved by induction. A counting recurrence is found by asking “what does the object look like at one end?” And a recursive search that discards half of the input each time costs O(log n).

                                      Written Assignment 2 · Data structures and hashing (Chapters 3–4) · due 21 Oct 2026 (passed)

                                      Written Assignment 2 Step by Step

                                      Where two singly linked lists join, the biggest poster on a fence, a stack that can be reversed in one step, and three hash tables filled by hand. The due date has passed, so every question is worked out fully here: use it to check your own submission and to practise the ideas.

                                      In this chapter

                                        Part 1 · Question 1

                                        Question 1: where do the two timelines join?

                                        Two lists of historical events start separately. At some node they merge, and from that node on they are one and the same chain. You are given the two head pointers A and B and must return a pointer to the node where they join. The rules: O(n) time, only O(1) extra space, and you may not change the lists.

                                        The picture, and three words to name its parts

                                        In the example of the assignment, list A is a → b → c → f → g → NULL and list B is d → e → f. The node f is the same node in both lists (the next pointer of e points to the very node that c points to). The shape is a letter Y turned on its side. Give the three pieces names:

                                        • a = the nodes that belong to list A only (here a, b, c: a = 3);
                                        • b = the nodes that belong to list B only (here d, e: b = 2);
                                        • c = the shared nodes, starting at the join (here f, g: c = 2).

                                        So the whole timeline has n = a + b + c nodes (here 7). The problem tells you each list has at least one node before the join (a ≥ 1, b ≥ 1) and that the join exists (c ≥ 1).

                                        Compare nodes, not events

                                        The test for “we are at the join” is p == q: do both pointers point at the same node in memory? Do not compare the event text. Two different nodes can store the same event string.

                                        Three ideas that do not satisfy the rules

                                        IdeaTimeExtra spaceProblem
                                        For each node of A, walk all of B looking for itO(n²)O(1)Too slow.
                                        Put every node of A into a hash table, then walk B until a node is found in the tableO(n)O(n)Uses linear extra space (it is a fine answer if the space limit is dropped).
                                        Walk A and set a visited flag in each node, then walk B until a flagged nodeO(n)O(1)Changes the nodes, which the remarks forbid.

                                        The two-pointer trick (the hint of the assignment)

                                        Here is the key worry. If both pointers start at their own heads and move one node per step, the pointer on the shorter list reaches the join earlier, so they are out of step. We need to cancel the difference in lengths without computing any length.

                                        Picture it

                                        Let p walk list A, and when it falls off the end (NULL), let it continue from the head of list B. Let q walk list B and then continue from the head of list A. Each pointer then walks “its own list plus the other list”, so both walk exactly the same total distance. The difference in the two lists cancels, and they arrive at the join at the same moment.

                                        function Join(A, B): p = A q = B while p != q: if p == NULL: p = B else: p = p.next if q == NULL: q = A else: q = q.next return p
                                        p = A; q = B

                                        two pointers, one at the head of each list. This is all the extra space we use.

                                        while p != q:

                                        keep going until both pointers are on the same node.

                                        if p == NULL: p = B else: p = p.next

                                        move p one node. If it has run off the end of its list, it restarts at the head of the other list.

                                        if q == NULL: q = A else: q = q.next

                                        the same for q, with the lists swapped.

                                        return p

                                        at this point p and q are the same node: the join.

                                        Why do they meet at the join?

                                        Count the moves of p (each move takes it off one position and onto the next, and NULL counts as a position):

                                        • a + c moves to get from the head of A to NULL (one move for each node of A it leaves);
                                        • 1 move to jump from NULL to the head of B;
                                        • b moves to walk along the private part of B and step onto the join node.
                                        moves of p = (a + c) + 1 + b = a + b + c + 1

                                        For q the same count with a and b swapped gives (b + c) + 1 + a: the same number. Both pointers are therefore on the join node after exactly a + b + c + 1 = n + 1 moves. Could they meet earlier on some other node? While they are on the private parts they stand on different nodes (private parts are different nodes). On the shared part they stand on the same node only if they have walked the same distance, and with equal distance they are at the join. If a = b they meet at the join already on the first pass, after a moves, without any jump.

                                        Two pointers that swap lists when they fall off the end

                                        The first setting of the demo is the example of the assignment (a = 3, b = 2, c = 2): p and q meet at f after 8 moves. Slide the numbers to see the meeting point never changes, only the number of moves.

                                        Another correct answer: use the lengths

                                        You may also solve it with three passes: (1) count the length of A, (2) count the length of B, (3) start one pointer on the longer list, move it ahead by the difference of the lengths, and then advance both pointers together until they are the same node. This is also O(n) time and O(1) space. Both are accepted; the hint of the assignment points to the first one because it is shorter and needs no length variables.

                                        (b) The running time

                                        Every loop iteration moves each pointer once and does a constant amount of other work: O(1). The loop ends once the two pointers meet, at the latest after a + b + c + 1 = n + 1 iterations (the worst case, when a ≠ b). So the worst-case time is (n + 1)·O(1) = O(n). The only extra storage is the two pointers p and q: O(1) space. Nothing is changed in the lists.

                                        What if there were no join?

                                        The assignment promises a join, but notice what happens otherwise: after |A| + |B| moves both pointers are NULL at the same time, so p == q and the function returns NULL. The same loop also answers “do these two lists merge?”.

                                        Part 2 · Question 2(a)

                                        Question 2(a): the naive poster algorithm and its bug

                                        The problem. A fence has n vertical planks, each 1 metre wide, with heights A[1..n]. You want to stick up a rectangular poster so that it is completely covered by wood: it may not stick out above any plank it covers. What is the largest possible area?

                                        In the example A = [2, 1, 5, 6, 2, 3] the best poster sits on planks 3 and 4: it can be 5 metres tall (the shorter of the two planks) and 2 metres wide, area 5 × 2 = 10.

                                        Picture it

                                        A poster that covers planks i to j is exactly as wide as the number of planks, j − i + 1, and as tall as the shortest of those planks, because a taller poster would stick out above that plank. So the whole problem is: over all ranges i..j, maximise (shortest plank in the range) × (number of planks in it).

                                        Reading Poster1

                                        function Poster1(A, n): width = 0 maxArea = 0 for i = 1 to n: height = +infinity for j = i to n: height = Min(height, A[j]) width = j - i maxArea = Max(maxArea, height * width) return maxArea
                                        for i = 1 to n

                                        try every plank i as the left end of the poster.

                                        height = +infinity

                                        nothing covered yet, so the poster could be as tall as we like.

                                        for j = i to n

                                        extend the right end one plank at a time: the poster now covers planks i..j.

                                        height = Min(height, A[j])

                                        the new plank may be shorter: the poster must shrink to the shortest plank so far. This keeps the shortest height without rescanning.

                                        width = j - i

                                        the width of the poster. This is the faulty line.

                                        maxArea = Max(maxArea, height * width)

                                        remember the best area seen.

                                        (i) Which line is wrong?

                                        The faulty line is line 11 of the printed pseudocode, width = j − i. A poster on planks i..j covers j − i + 1 planks, not j − i. (Check with a single plank: i = j gives width 0 and area 0, although one plank of height 5 holds a poster of area 5.) This is the classic “fence-post” slip: the gaps between plank i and plank j number j − i, while the planks number one more.

                                        (ii) The corrected line

                                        width = j − i + 1

                                        Everything else is fine. (For A = [2, 1, 5, 6, 2, 3] the version as printed returns 6 instead of 10; the demo below shows it.)

                                        (iii) The worst-case running time

                                        The inner loop does a constant amount of work (O(1): one Min, one subtraction, one multiplication, one Max). It runs n − i + 1 times when the outer loop is at i. Adding over all i:

                                        total iterations = n + (n−1) + … + 2 + 1 = n (n + 1) / 2

                                        That is n²/2 + n/2, so the time is Θ(n²). The loops do not depend on what the heights are, so the best, average and worst cases are all the same: worst-case O(n²) (and also Ω(n²)). For a fence of 100,000 planks that is about 5 billion iterations: too slow, which is why the next part uses a stack.

                                        Poster1: every range, with the printed bug and the fix

                                        Where marks are lost

                                        Do not answer “line 10” (the Min line is right) or “line 7”. And in (iii), say why it is quadratic by counting the inner iterations (n(n + 1)/2); “two nested loops, so n²” is true here but is not a count.

                                        Part 3 · Question 2(b)

                                        Question 2(b): the poster in O(n) with a stack

                                        The quadratic algorithm tries every range. We want O(n) with a stack. The idea is to ask the question from the point of view of one plank.

                                        Two solutions, one idea

                                        This part gives two correct solutions. Solution 1 (two passes, the version in the ChatGPT solution sheet) finds the nearest shorter plank on the left in one scan and on the right in a second scan, exactly like the nearest-smaller-item (“next lower day”) problems of Practice Problems 2 and Tutorial 3; it is the easier one to explain. Solution 2 (one pass with a sentinel) is shorter but folds both scans into one. Both are O(n). Write whichever you can explain best; the table at the end of this part compares them.

                                        The idea: fix the shortest plank

                                        In the best poster, some plank is the shortest one it covers (call it plank k, height h = A[k]). The poster has height h. To be as wide as possible it should reach left and right until it meets a plank shorter than h, because every plank in between is at least as tall as h and can therefore be covered. So for each plank k:

                                        • L(k) = the nearest plank to the left of k that is shorter than k (0 if none),
                                        • R(k) = the nearest plank to the right of k that is shorter than k (n + 1 if none),
                                        • best poster with height A[k] has area A[k] × (R(k) − L(k) − 1).

                                        The answer is the maximum of that over all k. Finding L and R for every plank by scanning outwards would again cost O(n²) (a decreasing fence makes every scan long). But “nearest shorter item” is exactly what a stack finds in one pass; it is the same trick as the “next lower day” problem of Tutorial 3, part 2. The two solutions differ only in how they use that trick.

                                        Solution 1: two passes (nearest shorter plank on each side)

                                        function Poster2(A, n): L = array of size n S = empty stack # plank numbers; heights strictly increase from bottom to top for i = 1 to n: # pass 1: left to right while S is not empty and A[TOP(S)] >= A[i]: POP(S) if S is empty: L[i] = 0 # no shorter plank on the left else: L[i] = TOP(S) PUSH(S, i) empty the stack S maxArea = 0 for i = n downto 1: # pass 2: right to left while S is not empty and A[TOP(S)] >= A[i]: POP(S) if S is empty: r = n + 1 # no shorter plank on the right else: r = TOP(S) width = r - L[i] - 1 maxArea = Max(maxArea, A[i] * width) PUSH(S, i) return maxArea
                                        L = array of size n

                                        L[i] will be the number of the nearest plank on the left of i that is shorter than plank i (0 if there is none).

                                        while S is not empty and A[TOP(S)] >= A[i]

                                        a plank on the stack that is not shorter than plank i can never be the nearest shorter plank for i, nor for any plank to the right of i (plank i is closer and no taller). So it is popped.

                                        if S is empty: L[i] = 0 else L[i] = TOP(S)

                                        what is left on top is shorter than plank i and is the closest such plank, because every plank between them was popped by a plank not taller than it.

                                        PUSH(S, i)

                                        plank i may be the answer for a later plank, so it goes on the stack. Heights on the stack now increase strictly from bottom to top.

                                        empty the stack S

                                        pass 2 starts from nothing.

                                        for i = n downto 1

                                        the same scan, mirrored: from the right. The top of the stack after the pops is the nearest shorter plank on the right, called r (n + 1 if none).

                                        width = r - L[i] - 1

                                        the planks strictly between L[i] and r: all of them are at least as tall as plank i.

                                        maxArea = Max(maxArea, A[i] * width)

                                        the best poster whose height is exactly A[i] and which contains plank i; keep the largest over all i.

                                        The explanation to write. The stack holds plank numbers in strictly increasing order of height. In the first pass we pop the planks that are at least as tall as plank i; the plank left on top is the nearest shorter plank on the left, stored in L[i] (0 if none). After emptying the stack, the same scan from the right gives the nearest shorter plank on the right, r (n + 1 if none). All planks from L[i] + 1 to r − 1 are at least as tall as plank i, so the biggest poster of height A[i] that contains plank i has area A[i] × (r − L[i] − 1). Every best poster has the height of its shortest plank, so the maximum of these areas is the answer. Equal heights are popped on purpose (“≥”): an equal plank does not stop the poster, so it must not limit the width.

                                        Watch Solution 1 run

                                        Pass 1 and pass 2 each step through the planks; the green-outlined bar is the nearest shorter plank just found, and the table fills in L and R. Then each plank’s own poster (dashed orange) is measured. Try A = [2, 1, 5, 6, 2, 3] (answer 10), then 4 4 4 4 to see equal heights not limiting the width.

                                        Poster2, two passes: L, R and the area of each plank

                                        Solution 2: one pass with a sentinel

                                        The same two quantities, found in one scan. A plank is popped at the moment its right-hand shorter neighbour arrives, and at that moment the plank underneath is its left edge.

                                        The pseudocode

                                        function Poster2(A, n): S = empty stack # holds plank numbers; heights never decrease from bottom to top maxArea = 0 A[n+1] = 0 # a sentinel: an extra plank of height 0 on the right for i = 1 to n+1: while S is not empty and A[TOP(S)] > A[i]: h = A[POP(S)] # this plank cannot extend any further right if S is empty: left = 0 else: left = TOP(S) # the plank under it is the left edge width = i - left - 1 maxArea = Max(maxArea, h * width) PUSH(S, i) return maxArea
                                        S = empty stack

                                        the stack remembers the planks whose right edge is not known yet.

                                        A[n+1] = 0

                                        a pretend plank of height 0 after the last real plank. It is shorter than every real plank, so it forces everything still on the stack to be popped at the end.

                                        for i = 1 to n+1

                                        read the planks from left to right, one at a time.

                                        while S is not empty and A[TOP(S)] > A[i]

                                        plank i is shorter than the plank on top. So the top plank’s poster cannot go any further right than i − 1: its right edge is now known.

                                        h = A[POP(S)]

                                        take the top plank off the stack; its height is the height of the poster we are about to measure.

                                        left = TOP(S) (or 0 if empty)

                                        after the pop, the new top is the nearest plank to the left that is not taller: the poster stops just to its right.

                                        width = i - left - 1

                                        the planks strictly between the new top and plank i.

                                        maxArea = Max(maxArea, h * width)

                                        remember the best poster.

                                        PUSH(S, i)

                                        plank i is not shorter than the new top, so it waits on the stack until a shorter plank arrives.

                                        Watch it run

                                        The picture shows the planks; the dashed orange rectangle is the poster being measured at a pop; the green outline is the best so far. The right-hand column is the stack. Use the default A = [2, 1, 5, 6, 2, 3] and check that it ends with 10 (planks 3 and 4, height 5).

                                        Poster2: the stack finds every poster in one pass

                                        Why it is correct (the stack invariant)

                                        At every moment the plank numbers on the stack have non-decreasing heights from bottom to top, and the plank directly under any stack entry is the nearest plank to its left that is not taller. Why: before pushing i we pop every plank that is taller than A[i], so what stays on top is not taller; and every plank between that top and i was taller and has just been popped (or was popped earlier). Hence when plank k is popped by plank i:

                                        • i is the first plank to the right of k that is shorter than k (anything between was at least as tall, or it would have popped k earlier);
                                        • the plank under k is the nearest on the left that is not taller.

                                        So h * width is the area of the widest poster of height A[k]. If the plank under k has exactly the same height, the width found is a little short, but that equal plank is popped immediately after (it is still taller than A[i]) and measures the full width. Every plank gets popped exactly once because of the sentinel, so every plank’s best poster is considered, and the maximum is the answer.

                                        (ii) The running time (both solutions)

                                        In both solutions a while loop sits inside a for loop, which looks like O(n²), but count the total work instead of the work per round. For Solution 2 (one pass):

                                        • Each plank number is pushed exactly once: n + 1 pushes in total (the sentinel included).
                                        • Each plank number is popped at most once, and only after it was pushed: at most n pops in total (the sentinel itself is pushed last and never popped).
                                        • The body of the while loop runs once per pop, so over the whole run it runs at most n times, and every pop is O(1).

                                        Total: at most 2n + 1 stack operations plus O(n) other work, so the worst-case time is O(n) (and the stack needs O(n) space). For Solution 1 the same count is done once per pass: in each pass every plank number is pushed exactly once and popped at most once (n pushes, at most n pops), emptying the stack between the passes pops at most n more, and everything else per plank (the assignment, the width, the Max) is O(1). So the total is at most about 4n stack operations plus O(n) work: worst case O(n), with the array L and the stack using O(n) extra space. A single round of the for loop may pop many planks, but the pops are paid for by the pushes that came earlier: that is called amortized analysis, as in Tutorial 3, part 1.

                                        Which one should you write?

                                        Solution 1: two passesSolution 2: one pass, sentinel
                                        Idea in one linenearest shorter plank on the left, then on the right, then A[i] × (r − L[i] − 1)a plank is measured when the plank that ends its poster arrives; the plank under it is the left edge
                                        Link to the courseliterally the nearest-smaller-element technique of PP2 and Tutorial 3, used twicesame technique, merged into one loop
                                        Invariant to stateheights on the stack strictly increase; what remains after popping is the nearest shorter plankheights do not decrease; the plank under an entry is the nearest not-taller one, and equal planks are fixed up by the next pop
                                        Equal heightspop with ≥; nothing more to sayneeds the extra remark that an equal plank is popped right after and measures the full width
                                        Extrasan array L, two scansa sentinel plank of height 0
                                        Time, spaceO(n), O(n)O(n), O(n)

                                        Both give 10 for A = [2, 1, 5, 6, 2, 3] and agree with the quadratic brute force on every fence tried. For a written answer, Solution 1 is the safer choice: its pieces are each one familiar technique, the correctness argument has no special case, and it is easier to explain in a few sentences. Solution 2 is a good one to know because it is the shortest code.

                                        Test it by brute force

                                        Both demos run the real algorithm and, at the end, compare it with the quadratic brute force on the same planks. Try planks that are all equal (4 4 4 4), strictly increasing (1 2 3 4 5), strictly decreasing (5 4 3 2 1) and a single plank. The result is correct every time.

                                        Part 4 · Question 3

                                        Question 3: the reversible stack

                                        Design a stack with Push, Pop and a new operation Reverse that turns the whole stack upside down (the bottom becomes the top). All three must take O(1) time, and the number of elements is not known in advance.

                                        The difficulty, and the trick

                                        A real reversal means moving every element, which costs O(n). To get O(1) we do not move anything. We only remember which end of the structure we are currently calling the top. After Reverse, the old bottom is simply the end we now treat as the top.

                                        Picture it

                                        A row of books on a shelf. A stack of books has its top at the right end. To “reverse” the stack, do not rearrange the books: just announce “from now on the top is the left end”. Pushing and popping now happen at the left end. Announcing takes one breath, however many books there are.

                                        For that to work, we must be able to add and remove at both ends of the structure in O(1).

                                        (a) The data structure: a doubly linked list

                                        Why this one?

                                        • Singly linked list: removing the last node needs the node before it, and finding it costs O(n). Not good once the top can be at the tail.
                                        • Array: adding at the front costs O(n) (shift everything), and the size is unknown in advance, so it would also need resizing.
                                        • Doubly linked list with pointers to both ends: every node has prev and next, so adding or removing at either end needs only a few pointer changes, and it grows by one node at a time. Exactly what we need.

                                        (b) The extra permanent variables

                                        • head: pointer to the first node of the list (NULL when empty);
                                        • tail: pointer to the last node (NULL when empty);
                                        • reversed: a boolean flag, initially false. When false the top of the stack is the tail of the list; when true the top is the head.

                                        (A size counter is optional; nothing here needs it.)

                                        (c) How each operation works

                                        The question asks for words, not pseudocode. Here is the answer in a few sentences per operation, with the table that sits behind it.

                                        OperationIf reversed = false (top = tail)If reversed = true (top = head)
                                        Push(x)Create a node for x and add it as the new last element (after tail); update tail (and head too if the list was empty).Create a node for x and add it as the new first element (before head); update head (and tail too if the list was empty).
                                        Pop()Remove the last node, move tail to its prev, and return the removed value.Remove the first node, move head to its next, and return the removed value.
                                        Reverse()Flip the flag: reversed becomes the opposite of what it was. Nothing else changes.

                                        The answer in prose: “Push: add the element at the end of the list that is currently the top (the tail if reversed is false, the head if it is true). Pop: remove the element from that same end and return it. Reverse: toggle the reversed flag. Each takes a constant number of pointer changes, independent of the stack size, so each is O(1).”

                                        Edge cases to handle

                                        Pushing onto an empty list: the new node is both head and tail. Popping the last remaining node: set both head and tail to NULL. Popping an empty stack: report an error. With the flag set, the “old tail” node is now at the bottom, and a Reverse followed by a Reverse puts everything back, at the cost of two flag flips.

                                        A worked example

                                        1. Push 1, Push 2, Push 3 with reversed = false: the list is 1 ↔ 2 ↔ 3, the top is the tail 3. Stack (top first): 3, 2, 1.
                                        2. Reverse: the flag becomes true; the list still reads 1 ↔ 2 ↔ 3 but now the top is the head 1. Stack (top first): 1, 2, 3. The bottom element (1) became the top, as required.
                                        3. Push 4: the top is the head, so 4 is added in front: 4 ↔ 1 ↔ 2 ↔ 3. Stack (top first): 4, 1, 2, 3.
                                        4. Pop returns 4 (removed from the head), and the next Pop returns 1.

                                        Try it yourself, and watch that the list in the picture is never rearranged; only the ▲top marker and the flag change.

                                        A stack that reverses in one step

                                        Part 5 · Question 4

                                        Question 4: three hash tables, filled by hand

                                        Insert the keys 15, 24, 30, 59, 46, 75, 44, 17, in that order, into three different hash tables, and draw each final table. The three schemes were explained in Chapter 4: chaining, open addressing with linear probing, and double hashing. Here is the procedure for each, then every insertion worked out.

                                        The method for every open-addressing table

                                        For each key, compute its home slot from the hash function. If the slot is free, store the key. If it is occupied (a collision), try the next slot in the probe sequence, and the next, until a free slot appears. Do the keys in the order given: the order decides who gets the home slot.

                                        (a) Size 13, h(k) = k mod 13, probing with f(i) = 2i

                                        The i-th slot tried for key k is (h(k) + 2i) mod 13, for i = 0, 1, 2, … So after a collision we skip a slot: the sequence goes h, h + 2, h + 4, … (wrapping around at 13).

                                        keyh(k)slots tried, in orderstored in
                                        1515 mod 13 = 2slot 2 (free)2
                                        2424 mod 13 = 11slot 11 (free)11
                                        3030 mod 13 = 4slot 4 (free)4
                                        5959 mod 13 = 7slot 7 (free)7
                                        4646 mod 13 = 7slot 7 (holds 59) → slot 9 (free)9
                                        7575 mod 13 = 10slot 10 (free)10
                                        4444 mod 13 = 5slot 5 (free)5
                                        1717 mod 13 = 4slot 4 (holds 30) → slot 6 (free)6

                                        Two collisions happened: 46 (home slot 7 is taken by 59, so it moves two slots on to 9) and 17 (home slot 4 is taken by 30, so it goes to 6). The final table:

                                        0123456789101112
                                        1530441759467524

                                        Why 2i is safe here

                                        The step 2 and the size 13 have no common factor (13 is prime), so the probe sequence visits all 13 slots before it repeats: an empty slot is always found while the table has room. With an even table size, stepping by 2 would only ever reach half of the slots.

                                        (b) Size 3, h(k) = k mod 3, chaining

                                        Each slot holds a chain (a linked list) of all keys that hash to it. There is no probing: a collision just adds to the chain. Following Chapter 4, a new key is inserted at the front of its chain (constant time).

                                        keyh(k)what happens
                                        1515 mod 3 = 0goes to the front of the chain in slot 0
                                        2424 mod 3 = 0goes to the front of the chain in slot 0
                                        3030 mod 3 = 0goes to the front of the chain in slot 0
                                        5959 mod 3 = 2goes to the front of the chain in slot 2
                                        4646 mod 3 = 1goes to the front of the chain in slot 1
                                        7575 mod 3 = 0goes to the front of the chain in slot 0
                                        4444 mod 3 = 2goes to the front of the chain in slot 2
                                        1717 mod 3 = 2goes to the front of the chain in slot 2

                                        The final table (the first element of each chain is on the left):

                                        slotchain (first element on the left)
                                        075 → 30 → 24 → 15 → NULL
                                        146 → NULL
                                        217 → 44 → 59 → NULL

                                        If you prefer to add new keys at the back of each chain, the chains read 15 → 24 → 30 → 75 (slot 0) and 59 → 44 → 17 (slot 2), with 46 alone in slot 1. The question does not fix the order within a chain, so either is accepted as long as you say which you used. Notice how uneven the chains are: slot 0 holds half of the keys. With a table of size 3 and 8 keys the load factor is 8/3 ≈ 2.7, which is why the chains are long.

                                        (c) Size 13, double hashing: h(k, i) = (h1(k) + i·h2(k)) mod 13

                                        Now the step size depends on the key: h1(k) = k mod 13 gives the home slot and h2(k) = (k mod 11) + (k mod 3) gives how far to jump after every collision. Two keys with the same home slot usually get different jumps, so they do not follow each other around.

                                        keyh1(k)h2(k)slots tried, in orderstored in
                                        1515 mod 13 = 2(15 mod 11) + (15 mod 3) = 4 + 0 = 4slot 2 (free)2
                                        2424 mod 13 = 11(24 mod 11) + (24 mod 3) = 2 + 0 = 2slot 11 (free)11
                                        3030 mod 13 = 4(30 mod 11) + (30 mod 3) = 8 + 0 = 8slot 4 (free)4
                                        5959 mod 13 = 7(59 mod 11) + (59 mod 3) = 4 + 2 = 6slot 7 (free)7
                                        4646 mod 13 = 7(46 mod 11) + (46 mod 3) = 2 + 1 = 3slot 7 (holds 59) → slot 10 (free)10
                                        7575 mod 13 = 10(75 mod 11) + (75 mod 3) = 9 + 0 = 9slot 10 (holds 46) → slot 6 (free)6
                                        4444 mod 13 = 5(44 mod 11) + (44 mod 3) = 0 + 2 = 2slot 5 (free)5
                                        1717 mod 13 = 4(17 mod 11) + (17 mod 3) = 6 + 2 = 8slot 4 (holds 30) → slot 12 (free)12

                                        Three collisions here: 46 (slot 7 is taken by 59; step 3, so slot 10), 75 (slot 10 is taken by 46; step 9, so (10 + 9) mod 13 = 6) and 17 (slot 4 is taken by 30; step 8, so (4 + 8) = 12). The final table:

                                        0123456789101112
                                        1530447559462417

                                        A trap in this h2

                                        A good second hash function must never be 0 (a step of 0 tries the same slot forever) and must not share a factor with the table size. Here h2 is at most 10 + 2 = 12, and 13 is prime, so any non-zero value works. But h2(k) = 0 for every multiple of 33 (for example 33 or 66): such a key that collides could never be placed. None of our eight keys is a multiple of 33, so the question is safe, but you should be able to say why the design is fragile.

                                        Check your drawings

                                        The demo below inserts the keys one at a time with all three schemes (and plain linear probing for comparison), showing every slot tried. Change the keys or the table size to experiment. The result for the three assignment tables is the one drawn above.
