                                        Part 6 · The assignment on one page

                                        Summary and self-test

                                        The whole assignment in one table

                                        QuestionThe ideaThe answer
                                        1 JoinTwo pointers; when one falls off the end it restarts at the head of the other list, so both walk the same total distance.O(n) time (at most n + 1 moves each), O(1) space, lists unchanged. Compare node pointers, not event text.
                                        2(a) Poster1Line 11, width = j − i, counts gaps, not planks.Fix: width = j − i + 1. Time Θ(n²): n(n + 1)/2 inner iterations.
                                        2(b) Poster2For each plank as the shortest one, find the nearest shorter plank on each side with a monotone stack: either two passes (left, then right) or one pass with a sentinel 0 that flushes the stack.O(n): each plank is pushed once and popped at most once.
                                        3 Reversible stackDo not move anything; remember which end is the top.Doubly linked list with head, tail and a boolean reversed. Push/Pop at the top end; Reverse flips the flag. All O(1).
                                        4 Hash tablesHome slot by the hash function, then follow the probe sequence, keys in the given order.(a) slots 2:15, 4:30, 5:44, 6:17, 7:59, 9:46, 10:75, 11:24. (b) 0: 75→30→24→15, 1: 46, 2: 17→44→59. (c) 2:15, 4:30, 5:44, 6:75, 7:59, 10:46, 11:24, 12:17.

                                        Test yourself

                                        1. Lists A and B have 4 and 6 private nodes and share 3 nodes. How many moves does each pointer make before Join stops?

                                          Show the answer

                                          a = 4, b = 6, c = 3, so a ≠ b and the pointers meet after a + b + c + 1 = 14 moves, on the join node. (If both lists had 5 private nodes, they would meet after only 5 moves.)

                                        2. Why is p == q the right test, and what would go wrong comparing the event strings?

                                          Show the answer

                                          The two timelines merge at one particular node. Two different nodes can hold the same text, so comparing strings might stop too early on a node that is not the join. Pointer equality is true only for the identical node.

                                        3. Run Poster1 as printed on A = [4, 4]. What does it return, and what should it return?

                                          Show the answer

                                          As printed: i = 1, j = 1: width 0; j = 2: height 4, width 1, area 4; i = 2: width 0. It returns 4. Correct: a poster across both planks is 4 × 2 = 8.

                                        4. How many times does the inner loop of Poster1 run for n = 10?

                                          Show the answer

                                          10 + 9 + … + 1 = 10·11/2 = 55.

                                        5. Run Poster2 (one-pass Solution 2) on A = [3, 1, 3]. List the pops and the answer.

                                          Show the answer

                                          Sentinel A[4] = 0. i=1: push 1. i=2 (height 1): pop plank 1 (height 3, the stack is then empty so left = 0, width = 2 − 0 − 1 = 1, area 3); push 2. i=3 (height 3): the top (height 1) is not taller, push 3. i=4 (height 0): pop plank 3 (height 3, left = 2, width = 4 − 2 − 1 = 1, area 3); pop plank 2 (height 1, empty stack so left = 0, width = 4 − 0 − 1 = 3, area 3); push 4. The answer is 3 (the planks 1–3 at height 1 also give 3). With the two-pass Solution 1 the same fence gives L = [0, 0, 2] and R = [2, 4, 4], so the widths are 1, 3, 1 and the areas 3, 3, 3: again 3.

                                        6. Why does Poster2 not take O(n²), although a while loop sits inside a for loop?

                                          Show the answer

                                          The pops cannot outnumber the pushes: each plank is pushed once and popped at most once, so the while-loop body runs at most n times in total across all rounds of the for loop. Total work is about 2n.

                                        7. After Push 1, Push 2, Reverse, Push 3, Pop, Pop on the reversible stack, what did the two pops return, and which end of the list is the top at the end?

                                          Show the answer

                                          After the two pushes the list is 1 ↔ 2 (top = tail). Reverse: flag true, top = head (1). Push 3: added at the head: 3 ↔ 1 ↔ 2. Pop returns 3, Pop returns 1. The flag is still true, so the top is the head (now the node 2).

                                        8. Where does key 38 go in table (a) if it were inserted last (after the eight keys)? And in table (c)?

                                          Show the answer

                                          38 mod 13 = 12, and slot 12 is free in table (a): it goes to slot 12. In table (c) slot 12 holds 17, so we jump by h2(38) = (38 mod 11) + (38 mod 3) = 5 + 2 = 7: (12 + 7) mod 13 = 6, which holds 75 (collision again); next (12 + 14) mod 13 = 0, free: slot 0.

                                        What to remember

                                        A second pointer that restarts on the other list cancels a difference in lengths. “Nearest smaller item” problems are a monotone stack, and a loop inside a loop is not automatically quadratic. An operation can be O(1) when you change a label instead of moving the data. And for hash tables, write down the probe sequence of each key: that is what the marker wants to see.

                                        Written Assignment 3 · Trees, AVL trees, searching and sorting (Chapters 5–10) · due 25 Nov 2026

                                        Written Assignment 3 Guide and solutions

                                        Four questions: rebuild a tree from its preorder, work a BST and an AVL tree through delete and insert, search a bitonic array in logarithmic time, and make QuickSort safe against bad pivots. Parts 2 to 5 are a guide to the ideas, with practice tools and a ladder of hints for every sub-question; Parts 6 to 9 are my own worked solutions to all four questions, written with the methods of the lectures and the practice sets. They are unofficial: the official solutions will follow when they are released.

                                        In this chapter

                                          Part 1 · Read this first

                                          Before you start: what is asked, and how to use this guide

                                          How this part of the app is organised

                                          Written Assignment 3 is due 25 Nov 2026, 7:00 pm. The cover page says “all answers must be your own work”, so use what follows to understand the methods and to check your own working, and write your own answer in your own words. Parts 2 to 5 explain every idea the questions rely on, give tools to practise on other examples, and give a ladder of hints for each sub-question. Parts 6 to 9 are my own worked solutions to Questions 1 to 4, with pictures, pseudocode in the style of the lectures, and demos; every number in them was also checked by a program. They are unofficial: when the official solutions come out, compare with them and tell me what differs.

                                          The four questions on one page

                                          QuestionMarksWhat it is aboutRead firstGuide partWorked solution

Find it, draw the tree, give the postorder and the height, then redraw it in the leftmost-child / right-sibling form and read off its inorder.tree words, storing a tree, traversalsPart 2Part 6
                                          Q2 BST and AVL25%One concrete AVL tree. Search path, successor, predecessor, height; delete a key with two children; insert a key without rebalancing, then find the unbalanced ancestor and fix it with rotations.search, successor, insertion, deletion, AVL rule, rotations, AVL insertionPart 3Part 7
                                          Q3 Bitonic array25%An array that rises and then falls. Find the peak in O(log n), then search for any value in O(log n), then state time and extra space.binary search, worst casesPart 4Part 8
                                          Q4 Robust QuickSort30%Why sorted input ruins QuickSort, why good partitions make it fast, what a weaker guarantee still gives, and how to write a QuickSort that falls back to HeapSort when partitions keep being bad.PARTITION, how fast?, pivots, HeapSortPart 5Part 9

                                          Q4 is worth the most and Q3 asks for pseudocode, so start with those two early; Q1 and Q2 are careful, mechanical work that rewards a clean drawing at each step. Try each question yourself first (Parts 2 to 5), then open the matching solution part.

                                          The rules printed on the cover page

                                          • Pseudocode, not program code. “Marks will be deducted if you submit program code (C++, Python, Java).” Pseudocode means plain statements such as “while lo < hi: let mid be the middle index”, with indentation for structure, plus a sentence of explanation. No semicolons, no int, no library calls.
                                          • Logarithms are to base 2 unless stated otherwise.
                                          • Heights. The height of a non-empty tree is the largest depth of any node, and depth counts edges from the root. So a leaf has height 0 and an empty (null) tree has height −1. Every height you write, in Q1(c) and all through Q2, uses this convention. (Some books count nodes instead, so a leaf has height 1; do not mix the two.)
                                          • One PDF to Moodle, readable. Hand-drawn trees are fine if the photo is clear; draw one picture per step rather than editing one picture.

                                          How to use the hint ladders

                                          Every sub-question below has folded hints numbered 1, 2, 3. The idea is to earn each hint by trying first: spend ten minutes on the question with pen and paper, open Hint 1 only if you are stuck, and keep going. Hint 1 names the idea, Hint 2 gives the method, Hint 3 usually tells you what to check at the end. The hints stop short of the final value on purpose; the finished answers are in Parts 6 to 9, so try the question before you look.

                                          How to write a justification (the “briefly justify” marks)

                                          Several parts say “briefly justify”, “explain” or “state why”. Marks for these go to a short chain of three pieces:

                                          1. The claim, stated plainly (“the missing value is …”, “the tree is not AVL”, “the running time is …”).
                                          2. The fact you used, named so that the marker can see it (a definition, or a property from the lectures: “in a tree on n nodes there are n − 1 edges” is the style of fact meant here).
                                          3. The step that connects them, with your actual numbers in it (“node 30 has left height 1 and right height −1, which differ by 2”).

                                          A bare answer earns little even when it is right; a short chain with a small mistake in the numbers usually keeps most of the marks.

                                          Where the tools are

                                          Each part has live tools that work on different examples from the assignment: a tree rebuilder (Part 2), the chapter’s search, deletion and AVL demos (Part 3), a find-the-peak game (Part 4), and a level-by-level QuickSort table plus a “is this partition good?” checker (Part 5). Part 10 has a set of fresh practice questions with answers, and a one-page summary.

                                          Part 2 · Question 1 (20 marks)

                                          Question 1: trees from a preorder list

                                          Question 1 gives you a tree without drawing it: only the order in which a preorder walk visits the nodes, and how many children each node has. The four parts are: (a) find a missing number, (b) draw the tree, (c) write the postorder and the height, (d) redraw the tree in the leftmost-child / right-sibling form and read off its inorder. If the words are shaky, read tree words, storing a tree and traversals first.

                                          Idea 1: preorder plus child counts says everything

                                          Preorder visits a node, then its first subtree (all of it, in preorder), then its second subtree, and so on. So right after a node in the list comes the whole first subtree below it. Suppose the list is X Y Z with child counts 2 0 0. X is the root and has two children. The next two entries are Y and Z, both with zero children, so they are the two leaves: X has children Y and Z, in that order. That is the whole trick, repeated.

                                          When a subtree is bigger than one node it takes up more of the list, and you must know where it ends. The child counts tell you: a subtree has ended when every node inside it has received all the children it was promised. Keeping track of that is easiest with a stack of nodes that still need children.

                                          Picture it

                                          Read the list from left to right. Keep a pile of “parents who are still waiting for children”, with the most recent parent on top. Each new node is the next child of the parent on top. If the new node has children of its own, it goes on top of the pile and the following nodes will hang below it. A parent leaves the pile when it has received all the children it asked for.

                                          Tool: rebuild a tree from preorder and child counts

                                          The tool is preloaded with an example that is not the assignment’s tree (nodes M to T). Step through it, and watch the pile on the right. Then change the lists: you can type your own node names and counts, including lists that cannot be a tree, and the tool will say what goes wrong and why.

                                          Rebuild a tree from its preorder and the number of children of each node

                                          Idea 2: counting the parent–child links

                                          Every node except the root has exactly one parent. So if you add up the “number of children” of all the nodes, you count each non-root node exactly once. A tree with n nodes therefore has the child counts adding up to a number you can predict. The tool shows that total in the green or red box. Whenever the total is wrong, the pile method either runs out of nodes (somebody is still waiting for children when the list ends) or has nodes left over (nobody is waiting, but the list goes on).

                                          (a) The missing number

                                          One entry in the list is a question mark and you must say what it is and justify it briefly. What the marker wants to see: the fact you used, and the numbers from this list put into it.

                                          Hint 1 · what to count

                                          How many nodes are there in the preorder list? A tree with that many nodes has how many parent–child links (edges)? Now, from the point of view of the child counts, what does each count measure?

                                          Hint 2 · the method

                                          Add up the child counts you do know. The full total must equal the number of links. The missing entry is whatever number makes that happen. Write the equation, with the actual numbers, as your justification.

                                          Hint 3 · how to check yourself

                                          Put your value into the tool above (use your own node names and the assignment’s list of counts). A correct value lets the pile method finish with every node placed and nobody waiting. A wrong value gives one of the two error messages. Also ask: could a leaf have been intended? Could the number be negative? (It is a count of children, so it is a whole number from 0 upward.)

                                          (b) Reconstruct and draw the tree

                                          “Ordered” means the left-to-right order of the children matters, so draw each node’s children left to right in the order they appear in the list. Mark the root at the top. A neat way to present the answer: a small table (node, number of children, its children in order) followed by the picture.

                                          Hint 1 · where to start

                                          The first node in preorder is the root. Take its child count: that is the number of subtrees that follow. Which node starts the first of them?

                                          Hint 2 · the pile method, in words

                                          Go through the list one node at a time. For each node write down who its parent is (the node on top of the pile), then update the pile: remove the parent if it now has all its children, and add the new node if it has children of its own. When the list ends, the pile must be empty.

                                          Hint 3 · how to check yourself

                                          Three quick checks: (i) the picture has exactly as many nodes as the list; (ii) every node has the number of children that the list says; (iii) reading your picture in preorder (root, then each subtree left to right) gives back the list in the same order.

                                          (c) Postorder and height

                                          Postorder is the mirror of preorder in one respect: visit all the subtrees (left to right, each in postorder) and visit the node last. The root therefore comes last. Height uses the cover-page convention: the number of edges on the longest path from the root down to a leaf; a single node has height 0. Both are a matter of reading your own drawing from part (b), so an error in (b) carries into (c) and (d); that is why it is worth the time to check the drawing.

                                          The chapter demo below shows the three traversals on a chapter tree, call by call. Use it to see how “visit” and “go down” interleave.

                                          Preorder, postorder and inorder, call by call

                                          Hint 1 · a trick for postorder

                                          Write the postorder recursively: post(node) = post(first child), post(second child), …, then the node itself. Work from the bottom: the first node printed is the leftmost leaf.

                                          Hint 2 · height without counting every path

                                          Height of a node = 0 if it is a leaf, otherwise 1 + the largest height among its children. Fill the heights in from the leaves up. The answer is the height of the root.

                                          Hint 3 · how to check yourself

                                          The postorder list has the same nodes as the preorder list, in a different order, and the root is the last entry. A leaf you can reach in the fewest steps is not the one that decides the height: look for the longest chain.

                                          (d) The leftmost-child / right-sibling representation

                                          This representation turns any ordered tree into a binary tree by giving every node exactly two pointers:

                                          • lc (leftmost child): the node’s first (leftmost) child, or null if it has no children;
                                          • rs (right sibling): the next child of the same parent, to its right, or null if it is the last child.

                                          The binary tree is drawn with lc as the left child and rs as the right child. The binary tree has the same nodes; only the edges are different. The chapter demo shows the construction for two trees: step between the two pictures until the rule feels automatic.

                                          Array of children versus lc / rs

                                          Then the last piece: the inorder of a binary tree is “left subtree, node, right subtree”. Apply that to your new binary tree, not to the original one.

                                          Hint 1 · build a table first

                                          Make a table with one row per node and two columns, lc and rs. For each node, ask two questions of your part (b) tree: “who is your first child?” and “who is the next child of your parent, to your right?” Only after the table is complete, draw the binary tree from it.

                                          Hint 2 · drawing

                                          Start with the root. Its lc goes down-left. Its rs is always null (the root has no siblings). Then follow each node’s lc down to the left and its rs to the right. A long run of siblings becomes a chain going down-right.

                                          Hint 3 · cross-checks before you trust the answer

                                          (i) The binary tree has the same number of nodes and every node appears once. (ii) Its preorder reads exactly like the original tree’s preorder. (iii) Once you have the inorder list, compare it with the lists you wrote in part (c). One of the original tree’s traversals looks the same. Try the same comparison on the example tree in the tool above (write down its postorder from the tool, and do the lc/rs picture by hand): why would “left subtree, node, right subtree” on a tree where left = children and right = later siblings give a familiar order? Using such a match to check your work is fine; the marks are for the drawing and the list you derive.

                                          Common slips in this question

                                          • Writing the children of the wrong node: if a node has 0 children, the very next entry in the list is not its child; it belongs to a node still waiting on the pile.
                                          • Mixing up “number of children” (what the list gives) with “number of descendants”.
                                          • Counting height in nodes. With the cover-page convention a single node has height 0 and a null tree −1.
                                          • Drawing siblings in the lc/rs picture as left children. Siblings are always the right child; the first child is the left child.
                                          • Taking the inorder of the original tree. An ordinary tree has no single “between the children” spot to put the node, which is why the question asks for it on the binary version.

                                          When you have your own answer

                                          Compare with my worked solution in Part 6 (unofficial; the official one will follow). Check the method first, then the numbers.

                                          Part 3 · Question 2 (25 marks)

                                          Question 2: a BST and an AVL tree, step by step

                                          Question 2 shows one AVL tree with eight keys, and asks five things about it. Parts (a), (b) and (c) each start from the original tree. Part (d) and (e) continue from the tree you get at the end of (c). That arrangement matters: if you carry a deletion from (b) into (c) you will answer a different question.

                                          The two definitions that everything uses

                                          BST property: for every node, all keys in its left subtree are smaller and all keys in its right subtree are larger. AVL property: it is a BST and, for every node, the heights of the left and right subtrees differ by at most 1. Heights use the cover-page convention (leaf = 0, empty subtree = −1), so a node with a single leaf child has subtree heights 0 and −1, which differ by 1: allowed. A node with a chain of two below it on one side and nothing on the other has heights 1 and −1, which differ by 2: not allowed.

                                          The one habit that prevents most mistakes: write (left, right) heights next to nodes

                                          Before answering anything, redraw the tree and write beside each node the pair (height of left subtree, height of right subtree). Compute them from the leaves up: a node’s own height is 1 + the larger of the two numbers (or 0 for a leaf). Everything in parts (a) to (e) becomes reading this picture, and it makes the AVL checks in (b) and (e) a matter of looking at the differences.

                                          (a) Search path, successor, predecessor, height

                                          Search path. Searching for a key starts at the root and at every node asks “is my key smaller, equal or larger?” to go left, stop, or go right. “The sequence of keys examined” is the list of nodes you compared with, in order, including the last one (where you stop because the key was found). See Minimum, maximum and search.

                                          Search, minimum and maximum, step by step

                                          Successor of a node x (the next key in sorted order): two cases, see Successor and predecessor.

                                          • If x has a right child: the successor is the smallest key in the right subtree (go right once, then left as far as possible).
                                          • If x has no right child: climb up until you arrive at a parent from its left side; that parent is the successor. (If you never do, x was the largest key and has no successor.)

                                          Predecessor is the mirror image: with a left child, the largest key in the left subtree; without one, climb until you come from a right side.

                                          Successor (and predecessor) of a node

                                          Height of the tree is the height of the root (edges on the longest root-to-leaf path). With the (left, right) pairs written down this is read off at the root.

                                          Hint 1 · search path

                                          List the keys in the order you visit them, starting with 40. At each step write “25 < node, go left” or “25 > node, go right” so that the justification is visible. The list ends when you reach 25.

                                          Hint 2 · successor and predecessor

                                          For each of the two nodes decide first which case applies: does the node have a right child (for the successor), a left child (for the predecessor)? The case tells you whether to go down or up. It is easy to get the answer right by guessing the sorted order; the question wants the rule, so write which case you used.

                                          Hint 3 · how to check yourself

                                          List all eight keys in sorted order. The successor of a key is the one right after it in that list, the predecessor the one right before it. Your tree-walking answer must agree with the sorted list (the sorted list is a check, not the method).

                                          (b) Deleting a key that has two children

                                          The chapter’s deletion procedure has three cases (see Deletion): the node is a leaf (just remove it), has one child (the child takes its place), or has two children. The question uses the last case with the rule “replace its key by its immediate in-order successor”. In words:

                                          1. Find the node z that holds the key to delete. It has two children.
                                          2. Find the successor node y: the minimum of z’s right subtree.
                                          3. Copy y’s key into z. The node z stays where it is, now holding a different key.
                                          4. Remove node y from its old position. Since y is a minimum it has no left child, so removal is easy: its right child (if any) takes its place.

                                          The question “which node is physically spliced out”

                                          The node that is physically removed from the tree is the successor node y, not the node that originally held the deleted key. The node z survives (with a new key). Part (i) asks for the key of the node that disappears; do not give the key you were asked to delete unless that really is the node that goes.

                                          Delete a node, case by case

                                          Is the result still an AVL tree? Only nodes on the path from the removed position up to the root can have a changed height, but do not rely on that shortcut when you are unsure: recompute the (left, right) pairs for every node of the new tree and look at the differences. If every difference is 0, 1 or −1 the answer is yes; one bad node is enough for no. Either way write the pair for at least the nodes on that path in your answer.

                                          Hint 1 · which node goes

                                          The key to delete has two children. Starting at its right child, how far down-left can you go? The node where you stop is the one removed. Write the walk: “right child is …, its left child is …, which has no left child, so the successor is …”

                                          Hint 2 · drawing the result

                                          Draw the original tree once more, change the key stored in the node you identified as z, and erase the successor node. Draw the new tree in full, do not rely on “same as before except…”. Check the BST property at the changed node: its new key must sit between the largest key on its left and the smallest on its right.

                                          Hint 3 · AVL check

                                          Make a short table: node, height of left subtree, height of right subtree, difference. Do it for all nodes of the new tree. State the conclusion in one sentence, and if the answer is no, name the node that breaks the rule.

                                          (c) Insertion without rebalancing

                                          Ordinary BST insertion (see Insertion): walk down from the root exactly as for a search for the new key. When you fall off the tree (a null pointer), the new key becomes a new leaf at that spot. “The sequence of existing keys examined” is the list of nodes on that walk. Part (c) deliberately says do not rebalance yet: the point is to look at what the new leaf does to the heights.

                                          After the insertion, update the (left, right) pairs for the four nodes the question names (25, 30, 20, 40): remember that the new leaf has height 0, and that every ancestor of the new leaf can have a larger height than before. The heights change from the bottom of the walk up to the root, and each ancestor’s pair must be recomputed from its children’s new heights.

                                          Hint 1 · the walk

                                          Search for the new key as if it were already there. Where does the search end? Which node will become the parent of the new leaf, and is the new leaf its left or right child?

                                          Hint 2 · heights

                                          Fill the pairs bottom-up. Start with the new leaf (height 0), then its parent (its pair has changed on one side), then the next ancestor up, using the previously computed height of the child on the path and the unchanged height of the other child. Do the same for each of the four named nodes. Do not copy the old heights.

                                          Hint 3 · how to check yourself

                                          A node off the walk path keeps its old pair. A node on the path can only have its height unchanged or increased by 1. Along the path, a height that grows by 1 at one node passes the growth to its parent, until some ancestor was already taller on the other side (then the growth stops there). If an ancestor now shows a difference of 2, the AVL rule is broken, which is what (d) asks you to look for.

                                          (d) The lowest unbalanced ancestor, and the rotation(s)

                                          From the new leaf walk up. The lowest unbalanced ancestor is the first node on that upward walk whose two subtree heights differ by more than 1. (More than one node on the path can be out of balance after the insertion; the question wants the lowest one. Fixing it also repairs the ones above, because the rotation restores the subtree to its pre-insertion height. Read Insertion, the whole algorithm for why.)

                                          Then decide the case by asking two questions about the unbalanced node u:

                                          1. Which side of u is too tall: left or right?
                                          2. Inside that tall child c, which subtree is the tall one: c’s left or c’s right? (This is where the new leaf went.)
                                          Tall side of uTall side of cNameWhat you do
                                          leftleftleft-leftone right rotation at u
                                          rightrightright-rightone left rotation at u
                                          leftrightleft-righta left rotation at c, then a right rotation at u
                                          rightleftright-lefta right rotation at c, then a left rotation at u

                                          The question asks “exactly which rotation(s), at which node(s), and in what order”, so write the case name, then the rotation(s) as a numbered list: “1. left rotation at node …; 2. right rotation at node …”. See Rotations and simple / double cases. The two demos show a rotation and a double rotation on small trees.

                                          Rotate a node

                                          Single rotation versus double rotation

                                          Hint 1 · find the node

                                          Using your pairs from (c), go up from the new leaf and stop at the first node whose two numbers differ by 2 (or more). That is u.

                                          Hint 2 · find the case

                                          Which child of u is on the tall side? Call it c. Now look at c’s two subtrees: which one contains the new leaf? Read the answer off the table above.

                                          Hint 3 · how to check yourself

                                          If your answer is a single rotation, then c’s tall side and u’s tall side point the same way. If they point in different directions you need a double rotation. A mismatch here is the commonest way to lose these marks, so test it on a three-key example: inserting 3, 1, 2 into an empty AVL tree (zig-zag) needs a double rotation, while 3, 2, 1 (straight line) needs one.

                                          (e) Apply the rotation(s), draw the result, verify

                                          A rotation only re-hangs a few subtrees. Draw the tree before, name the nodes involved (u, c and, for a double rotation, c’s inner child), then draw the tree after each step. The BST order is unchanged by a rotation, so the in-order list of keys must be identical before and after: a cheap, reliable check.

                                          For the verification the question asks for the pairs at three named nodes, plus the height of the new tree. Recompute them from the drawn result, not from memory.

                                          AVL insertion, step by step

                                          Hint 1 · what moves in a rotation

                                          In a right rotation at u with left child c: c goes up, u becomes c’s right child, and c’s old right subtree becomes u’s new left subtree. A left rotation is the mirror image. A double rotation is two such steps.

                                          Hint 2 · the checks

                                          After the last rotation: (i) the in-order list of all keys is unchanged; (ii) the subtree that was too tall is now back to the height it had before the insertion; (iii) for each of the three nodes the question names, the two subtree heights differ by at most 1. Then give the height of the whole tree.

                                          Hint 3 · what to hand in

                                          Two or three drawings (before, after each rotation) with the rotated nodes named, the final tree with its height, and a small table of the three required pairs with the difference. Say “AVL” in a closing sentence.

                                          A complete worked example on a different tree

                                          Here is every kind of step on another AVL tree, so you can see what a finished answer looks like. The tree has nine keys: 50 at the root, with 25 and 75 below it; 25 has children 15 and 40; 75 has children 65 and 90; 15 has a left child 10; and 40 has a left child 30.

                                          (a) on the example

                                          • Search path for 30: 50 (30 < 50, left), 25 (30 > 25, right), 40 (30 < 40, left), 30 (found). The keys examined: 50, 25, 40, 30.
                                          • Successor of 30: 30 has no right child, so climb: 30 is the left child of 40, so the climb stops at once and the successor is 40.
                                          • Predecessor of 75: 75 has a left child, so take the largest key in the left subtree. The left child 65 has no right child, so the predecessor is 65.
                                          • Height: the longest path is 50–25–15–10, three edges: height 3.

                                          (b) on the example: delete 25 (two children)

                                          The successor of 25 is the minimum of its right subtree: go right to 40, then left to 30; 30 has no left child, so the successor node is 30, a leaf. Copy 30 into the node that held 25, then splice the old 30 node out. The node physically removed holds key 30 (not 25).

                                          Is it still AVL? Pairs (left, right): node 30: (1, 0); node 15: (0, −1); node 40: (−1, −1); node 75: (0, 0); node 50: left subtree height 2, right subtree height 1, so (2, 1). All differences are at most 1, so yes, it is still an AVL tree. (In other trees the answer is no. That is why the question asks you to check, and why the pairs should be written out rather than assumed.)

                                          (c) on the example: insert 5 without rebalancing (starting again from the original tree)

                                          Walk: 50 (5 < 50, left), 25 (left), 15 (left), 10 (left), then the left pointer of 10 is null: 5 becomes the left child of 10. Keys examined: 50, 25, 15, 10. Heights after the insertion, as (left, right): node 10: (0, −1); node 15: (1, −1) (difference 2); node 25: (2, 1); node 50: (3, 1) (difference 2).

                                          (d) on the example

                                          Going up from the new leaf: 10 is fine, 15 is the first node with a difference of 2. So 15 is the lowest unbalanced ancestor (50 is also unbalanced, but it is higher up). The tall side of 15 is its left, via the child 10, and the tall side of 10 is its left, where 5 went: left-left. The fix is a single right rotation at 15.

                                          (e) on the example

                                          In-order list of keys: 5, 10, 15, 25, 30, 40, 50, 65, 75, 90, the same as before the rotation with 5 added. Pairs: node 10: (0, 0); node 25: left height 1, right height 1, so (1, 1); node 50: (2, 1). All within 1, and the tree height is 3, the same as before the insertion (which is what a correct fix does).

                                          You can replay this example in the AVL insertion demo above: choose “An empty tree” and type the keys 50 25 75 15 40 65 90 10 30 5; the last key triggers the rotation.

                                          Slips that lose marks in Q2

                                          • Giving the successor’s key as the “spliced-out node” but drawing the wrong tree (or the other way around). Draw the tree, then name the node that is gone.
                                          • Using the height of a node where the question asks for the heights of its subtrees. Ask “height of what?”: left subtree and right subtree are two separate numbers.
                                          • Counting an empty subtree as height 0. It is −1 on this cover page.
                                          • Starting (b) or (c) from the output of an earlier part. All of (a), (b), (c) start from the original tree.
                                          • Rotating at the wrong node: the rotation goes at the unbalanced node (and for double rotations first at its tall child), not at the new leaf and not at the root by habit.
                                          • Forgetting to show the check that the final tree is AVL (the three required pairs).

                                          When you have your own answer

                                          Compare with my worked solution in Part 7 (unofficial; the official one will follow). Check the method first, then the numbers.

                                          Part 4 · Question 3 (25 marks)

                                          Question 3: searching a bitonic array

                                          A bitonic array climbs strictly to one peak and then falls strictly: A[1] < … < A[p] > … > A[n], with 1 < p < n, all values distinct. It is not sorted, so ordinary binary search for a value does not work on it directly. The question builds up in three steps: (a) find the peak in O(log n), (b) use that to search for any value in O(log n), (c) analyse time and extra space. The tool for this question is a game; the pseudocode and the explanations are yours to write.

                                          Why a logarithmic time is even possible

                                          Binary search works whenever one cheap test can throw away half of the candidates. For a sorted array the test is “is A[mid] smaller than the target?”. For a bitonic array, ask yourself: what local test can you do at a cell that tells you something about the whole side of the array on its left or right? Look at the shape: up, up, up, peak, down, down. A cell has only two neighbours; what do they say about which side the peak is on?

                                          Picture it

                                          Imagine walking along a hill in thick fog. You can only feel whether the ground at your feet slopes up or down towards the next step. One feeling is enough to know whether the summit is ahead of you or behind you, no matter how far away it is. Binary search is that idea repeated: you jump to the middle of what is left, feel the slope, and discard the half that cannot contain the summit.

                                          Play: find the peak with as few probes as you can

                                          All the numbers are hidden. Press a cell i to learn how A[i] compares with its right-hand neighbour A[i + 1]. The grey hatched cells are the ones the peak can no longer be in. Try a few games with different lengths n. First click anywhere to get a feel, then play again aiming to finish in a fixed small number of probes, even when n doubles. The tool tells you how many probes a “halve the candidates each time” strategy needs at most.

                                          Find the peak: probe a cell to compare it with its right-hand neighbour

                                          What binary search looks like on paper

                                          If binary search itself is not yet automatic, run the chapter’s demo first (Binary search). Its three ingredients are the template for everything in this question:

                                          1. A range of positions that is guaranteed to contain what you are looking for (here: the peak, or the target).
                                          2. A probe at the middle of the range, and a rule for what to keep after each possible outcome.
                                          3. A stopping condition and a promise that every pass shrinks the range (otherwise the loop never ends).

                                          Binary search, step by step

                                          (a) FindPeak(A, n)

                                          You must give pseudocode and explain briefly why it works. A good explanation names the thing that stays true throughout the loop (“the peak is always inside positions lo to hi”), says what each outcome of the comparison lets you discard, and says why the loop stops.

                                          Hint 1 · the probe

                                          Pick a position mid in the range. Compare A[mid] with one neighbour. Play the game again and write down, for the two possible answers (“smaller than the next cell” and “larger than the next cell”), where the peak must be. Which cells can be removed in each case, and does mid itself stay or go?

                                          Hint 2 · the invariant and the update

                                          Write the invariant as one sentence: “the peak index p is in the range [lo, hi]”. For each outcome, say which of lo and hi moves and to what. In exactly one outcome the middle cell must stay inside the range (it could be the peak). In the other it can be discarded. If you discard it in the wrong place you will lose the peak; if you keep it in the wrong place, see the next hint.

                                          Hint 3 · stopping, and why it terminates

                                          Decide what “done” looks like (one candidate left), and what you return. Check two things on paper: (1) while the range has at least two cells, mid + 1 is still inside the range, so the neighbour you compare with exists; (2) in both outcomes the new range is strictly smaller than the old one. If you find a case where it does not shrink (for example lo and hi adjacent), fix how you compute mid or how you update. This is the usual place for an infinite loop.

                                          Hint 4 · test it

                                          Trace your pseudocode by hand on the example in the question, [3, 7, 12, 19, 24, 18, 11, 5, 1], and on the smallest legal arrays, such as one of length 3 (the peak must be the middle cell, because 1 < p < n). The number of passes of your loop should grow like log n: the game’s budget line is a good reference.

                                          (b) BitonicSearch(A, n, x)

                                          Now the target x may be anywhere, or absent, and you must return an index i with A[i] = x or −1. You may call FindPeak and write helper procedures. Think about what the peak does to the array: it cuts it into two pieces, each of which is sorted (one in increasing order, one in decreasing order).

                                          Hint 1 · what the peak gives you

                                          After FindPeak you know p. Describe each side in one phrase: is A[1..p] increasing or decreasing? And A[p..n]? Which kind of search works on a sorted array?

                                          Hint 2 · helpers

                                          You can write one helper, BinarySearchUp (increasing order), exactly like the chapter’s binary search. For the decreasing side either write a second helper with the comparison turned around, or write one helper that takes an extra input saying which direction to use. Both are fine as pseudocode as long as the helper’s inputs (array, left end, right end, target) are clear.

                                          Hint 3 · combining the two

                                          Plan the order: a cheap check against the peak itself (what does x = A[p] mean? what does x > A[p] mean?), then search the rising side, then (only if not found) the falling side. Say precisely which cell ranges each helper receives so that the peak is not searched twice or skipped.

                                          Hint 4 · the traps

                                          (1) The helper returns an index in the original array, not an offset inside the slice. (2) In the decreasing helper, “target smaller than A[mid]” means go right, not left. (3) Return −1 only after both sides failed. (4) Test with three targets: one on the rising side, one on the falling side, and one that is absent (below the smallest, above the largest, and one in a gap).

                                          (c) Time and extra space

                                          You must state the worst-case time and the extra space of your algorithm from (b), assuming iterative (loop) implementations. Your answer should name each phase, give each phase’s cost, and combine them.

                                          Hint 1 · time

                                          List the phases that run one after another. For each one, how many times can its loop run in the worst case, as a function of n, and what does one pass cost? How do costs of phases that run in sequence combine?

                                          Hint 2 · space

                                          “Extra space” is memory beyond the input array. Write down every variable your pseudocode creates (indices, a result, the peak index). Does the count of those variables depend on n? What would change if you used recursion instead (the question rules it out, but think about why it was mentioned)?

                                          Common slips in Q3

                                          • Comparing A[mid] with A[mid − 1] when mid = 1, or with A[mid + 1] when mid = n: an index that does not exist. Decide the range so that the neighbour is always inside it.
                                          • Setting lo = mid when lo and hi are adjacent and mid is rounded down: the range never shrinks. Check every update against a range of two cells.
                                          • Returning the peak value instead of its index in (a).
                                          • Writing a linear scan and calling it logarithmic. A loop that visits cells one by one is O(n) however clever the stopping rule.
                                          • Code instead of pseudocode (the cover page deducts marks). Use words and simple statements.

                                          When you have your own answer

                                          Compare with my worked solution in Part 8 (unofficial; the official one will follow). Check the method first, then the numbers.

                                          Part 5 · Question 4 (30 marks)

                                          Question 4: a robust version of QuickSort

                                          Question 4 is worth the most, but it is one idea used four times: the running time of QuickSort is (the number of levels of recursion) × (the work per level). The first three parts ask how many levels there are under different assumptions about the partitions; the fourth asks you to write a QuickSort that forces a good number of levels. Read PARTITION, how fast is QuickSort? and picking the pivot first if any of that is new.

                                          The idea that makes all four parts short

                                          Draw the recursion as a tree: the whole array at the top; each partition splits a piece into two smaller pieces underneath. Two facts do almost all the work:

                                          1. Pieces on the same level never overlap. They are different parts of the same array. So the total size of all the pieces on one level is at most n, and since partitioning a piece of size m costs Θ(m), the partitioning on one whole level costs at most Θ(n).
                                          2. So the total time is at most (number of levels) × n up to a constant. Everything depends on how many levels there can be, which depends on how fast the pieces shrink.

                                          Tool 1: is this partition “good”?

                                          For this question only, a partition of a piece of size m is good when both parts have at most 3m/4 elements. Slide the two controls and watch the dashed lines at m/4 and 3m/4 on the bar: a split is good exactly when the cut falls between them. The test the tool uses is 4 × size ≤ 3m for both parts; it avoids fractions, so you can write it in pseudocode without worrying about rounding.

                                          Cut a piece of m elements into two parts and test the 3m/4 rule

                                          Tool 2: the levels of the recursion, level by level

                                          This table follows a QuickSort recursion level by level, for the split pattern you choose. For each depth it shows how many partition calls there are, the size of the largest piece, how many elements are partitioned in total at that depth, and how many of the partitions are good. The last rows of a long table are shown so that you can see the end. Try every pattern and keep an eye on how many levels and how much work per level.

                                          The recursion of QuickSort, level by level

                                          (a) Sorted input, first element as pivot

                                          The question has already told you what a call does on a piece of size m: it makes one piece of size 1 and one of size m − 1. You must (i) write the recurrence for the running time and (ii) determine its asymptotic order. The first model in tool 2 (“1 and m−1”) is exactly this situation. The chapter’s own example is in how fast is QuickSort?; its demo below lists every PARTITION call of a real run.

                                          Every PARTITION call of one run, in a table

                                          Hint 1 · the pieces of the recurrence

                                          A recurrence says “the time for size m = the time of the recursive calls + the time of the work done in this call”. Which two subproblem sizes does the question give? What does the partition itself cost (the question tells you)? What does a call on a piece of size 1 cost?

                                          Hint 2 · solving it

                                          Unroll: write the cost of the top call, then of the call it makes on n − 1 elements, then n − 2, and so on down to 1. You get a list of costs. What kind of sum is it? (You have summed it before: Chapter 1’s first example.) Also say whether you claim Θ, O or Ω: the question says “determine the asymptotic running time”, so both a lower and an upper bound are wanted.

                                          Hint 3 · how to check yourself

                                          Compare with tool 2: with the model “1 and m−1” and n = 4096 the table reports the total number of elements partitioned and the number of levels. Does your formula produce the same total for that n? A formula that is off by a constant factor is fine for the asymptotic answer; one that is off by a factor of about n is not.

                                          (b) Every partition is good

                                          You must give the worst-case running time and state (i) the maximum recursion depth asymptotically and (ii) the total partitioning work at each depth. The two numbers multiply. Try tool 2 with the model “larger part = αm” and α = 0.75, then with α = 0.90 (not good!) and compare how the number of levels and the size of the largest piece change.

                                          Hint 1 · how big is the biggest piece after k levels?

                                          On a good partition each part has at most 3/4 of the elements of its parent piece. After one level the largest piece has at most 3n/4 elements. After two levels? After k levels? Write the bound as a formula in k and n.

                                          Hint 2 · when do the pieces stop?

                                          A piece of size 1 (or 0) needs no partition. So the recursion stops by the level k at which your formula is at most 1. Solve that inequality for k (take logarithms). You will get a logarithm to a base that is not 2; convert it to base 2: the two differ by a constant factor, which asymptotics ignore. State the depth with O (or Θ) and explain why this is the maximum.

                                          Hint 3 · the work at one depth, and the product

                                          For (ii): the pieces at the same depth are disjoint parts of the array. What is the largest the sum of their sizes can be? What does partitioning a piece of size m cost? Combine those to bound the work at one depth, then multiply by the number of depths to reach the total. Tool 2 shows the per-depth totals; they never exceed n.

                                          (c) A weaker guarantee: among any two consecutive partition steps, at least one is good

                                          Now partitions may be terrible half of the time. The question is: does O(n log n) still hold? Answer Yes or No and justify. Tool 2’s fourth pattern (“alternating bad / good”) is an example that meets the condition: look at its number of levels and its work per level and compare with the previous pattern.

                                          Hint 1 · group steps in pairs

                                          Take any root-to-leaf path and cut it into pairs of consecutive partition steps. By the condition, at least one step in each pair is good. What does a good step guarantee about the size of the pieces? What does any partition step (good or not) guarantee, at the very least, about the size of the pieces compared with the piece it came from?

                                          Hint 2 · both orders

                                          In a pair, the good step may come first or second. Take the two orders one at a time. Start from a piece of size m; bound its size after the pair in each case. Do both orders end up with the same fraction of m?

                                          Hint 3 · from the pair to the depth

                                          If a pair of steps shrinks the piece by a fixed fraction, how many pairs can a path have? How many partition steps is that? And how much partitioning work can sit on one level, as in (b)? State the conclusion, and say what it does and does not rely on (the condition is only about pairs of consecutive steps on each path).

                                          (d) Writing RobustQuickSort

                                          The idea of the robust algorithm: keep QuickSort’s partitioning, but count how many non-good partitions in a row we have just made (bad). If the counter reaches 2, stop partitioning that piece and sort it with HeapSort, which is slow in constants but always O(m log m). The question lists the rules exactly; your job is to turn them into pseudocode and explain it.

                                          Think of the procedure as answering these questions in this order. They are not the pseudocode; they are the checklist the pseudocode has to answer.

                                          1. When does the call do nothing? (The question tells you the condition.)
                                          2. When does the call hand the whole piece to HeapSort, and what does it do afterwards?
                                          3. Otherwise: call Partition. What does it return, and which two index ranges are the two parts? What are their sizes in terms of p, q, r?
                                          4. Is this partition good? (Tool 1: compare 4 × each part with 3 × the size of the piece. Both parts must pass.)
                                          5. What value of bad goes to the two recursive calls after a good partition? After a non-good one? (The question gives both.)
                                          6. Make the two recursive calls, one for each part.

                                          Concentrate on indexes: the two parts are A[p..q] and A[q + 1..r], so the size of the first is q − p + 1 and the size of the whole is r − p + 1.

                                          Hint 1 · (i) pseudocode, detail

                                          Order matters: the “p ≥ r” check comes before the “bad = 2” check (a piece of size 1 must return immediately, not be heap-sorted), and the “bad = 2” check comes before the call to Partition (the question says no further partitioning when it is 2). Name the sizes with variables so that the goodness test is a single readable line.

                                          Hint 2 · (i) a trace to test it

                                          Trace your pseudocode on a small array of size 8 with a partition you choose to be bad, then bad again: your trace must show the third call sorting the piece with HeapSort. Then trace a case where a bad partition is followed by a good one: the counter must go back to 0 for the next calls.

                                          (ii) Correctness and running time

                                          Two separate claims, each with its own argument. Say them separately.

                                          Hint 3 · correctness

                                          There are only three kinds of call. For each, why does it leave the piece sorted? For the recursive kind, you need two facts: (1) the Partition postcondition (given in the question) says every element of the first part is smaller than every element of the second part; (2) the two recursive calls work on pieces that are smaller than the current one. Why is that so (look at the range of q)? That is a proof by strong induction on the size of the piece, the same pattern as Chapter 1.

                                          Hint 4 · running time: three ingredients

                                          Separate the cost into (1) partitioning work, (2) HeapSort work, (3) everything else (constant work per call). For (1): what does the counter promise about how many non-good partitions can follow each other on one path before partitioning stops? Take the largest window of consecutive partition steps that must contain a good step, and repeat the argument you used for (c), with that window instead of 2. For (2): when a call heap-sorts its piece, does it make any recursive calls afterwards? What does that tell you about whether two heap-sorted pieces can overlap, and so about the sum of their sizes?

                                          Hint 5 · putting the time bound together

                                          Total = partitioning work + HeapSort work + (number of calls) × constant. Use the depth bound from the previous hint for (1) and a bound of the form “each piece costs at most m log m ≤ m log n, and the sizes add up to at most n” for (2). Note that the answer is a bound that holds for every input, not only on average: that is the point of calling the algorithm robust.

                                          Common slips in Q4

                                          • Testing “good” on only one of the two parts. Both must have at most 3m/4 elements.
                                          • Saying the depth is n in (b) or (c). Good steps shrink pieces geometrically; the depth is a logarithm.
                                          • Forgetting that the total work per level is over all pieces on that level, not over one piece.
                                          • Answering (c) with only an example (“e.g. alternating bad/good is O(n log n)”). The condition covers every path and every pattern; the argument must be general.
                                          • In (d), letting bad go on increasing after a good partition. It resets to 0 for both recursive calls.
                                          • Giving the running time of HeapSort as O(n log n) for each piece: it is O(m log m) for a piece of size m, and the sum over disjoint pieces is what you bound.
                                          • Program code instead of pseudocode.

                                          When you have your own answer

                                          Compare with my worked solution in Part 9 (unofficial; the official one will follow). Check the method first, then the numbers.

                                          Part 6 · Solution to Question 1 · 20 marks

                                          Worked solution: Question 1 (trees)

                                          About these solutions

                                          These are my own worked solutions, written in the style of the lectures and the practice sets; they are not the official ones (those are not out yet; they will replace or sit next to these when they are). Every number below was also checked by a program. The hints in Parts 2 to 5 are still there if you would like to try a question first. Remember the cover page: answers you hand in must be written in your own words, so use these to understand the method and to check your work.

                                          The question: the preorder of an ordered tree is A B C D E F G H I, the numbers of children in the same order are 3, 0, 2, 0, 1, 0, ?, 0, 0.

                                          (a) The missing value [3 marks]

                                          The tree has n = 9 nodes, and a tree with n nodes has exactly n − 1 = 8 parent–child links (every node except the root has exactly one parent: Chapter 5). Each link is counted once, in the child count of the parent. So the child counts add up to 8:

                                          3 + 0 + 2 + 0 + 1 + 0 + ? + 0 + 0 = 6 + ? = 8 so ? = 2

                                          Model answer

                                          A tree on 9 nodes has 8 parent–child edges, and the child counts add up to the number of edges. The known counts add up to 6, so G has 2 children. Check with preorder: after G the list has exactly two nodes left (H and I), and they become the two children of G, with nobody left waiting.

                                          Checking it with the “pile of waiting parents”

                                          Read the list from left to right. Every new node is the next child of the parent on top of the pile; a node that promises children is put on the pile; a parent leaves the pile when all its children have arrived (Part 2).

                                          ReadIts childrenBecomes a child ofPile after this step (top on the right; “needs” = children still to come)
                                          A3(the root)A needs 3
                                          B0AA needs 2
                                          C2AA needs 1, C needs 2
                                          D0CA needs 1, C needs 1
                                          E1CC is full and leaves: A needs 1, E needs 1
                                          F0EE is full and leaves: A needs 1
                                          G?AA is full and leaves: the pile is empty, and G must be able to take the two nodes still to come: G needs 2
                                          H0GG needs 1
                                          I0GG is full: the pile is empty and the list has ended ✓

                                          Any other value fails: with ? = 0 or 1, node H or I would arrive when nobody is waiting; with ? = 3 or more, the list ends while G is still waiting for children.

                                          (b) The tree [5 marks]

                                          From the pile table, the parent of every node is:

                                          NodeABCDEFGHI
                                          Parent—AACCEAGG

                                          Model answer

                                          Root A with three children B, C, G (in this order). C has two children D, E. E has one child F. G has two children H, I. B, D, F, H, I are leaves. Reading this tree in preorder gives A B C D E F G H I with child counts 3 0 2 0 1 0 2 0 0, as required.

                                          (c) Postorder and height [4 marks]

                                          Postorder visits the subtrees first, left to right, and the node last (traversals). Do it from the picture: under A the subtrees are B, then the C-family, then the G-family.

                                          • B: just B.
                                          • C-family: D, then the E-family (F, then E), then C: D F E C.
                                          • G-family: H, I, then G: H I G.
                                          • Then A.
                                          postorder: B D F E C H I G A

                                          The height is the number of edges on the longest path from the root to a leaf: A → C → E → F has 3 edges (A → G → H has only 2), so the height of T is 3. (Heights count edges, so the lone root of a one-node tree would have height 0.)

                                          Model answer

                                          Postorder: B, D, F, E, C, H, I, G, A. Height: 3 (longest path A–C–E–F).

                                          (d) The leftmost-child / right-sibling form, and its inorder [8 marks]

                                          In this representation (storing a tree) every node keeps two pointers: lc to its leftmost (first) child and rs to its next sibling on the right. Read the two pointers of each node off the tree:

                                          NodeABCDEFGHI
                                          lc (first child)BNULLDNULLFNULLHNULLNULL
                                          rs (next sibling)NULLCGENULLNULLNULLINULL

                                          Now draw it as a binary tree: for every node, its lc is the left child and its rs is the right child. The root is A (it has no sibling).

                                          Inorder of a binary tree: the left subtree, then the node, then the right subtree (Chapter 5). Work from the bottom:

                                          • Node E: left subtree F, then E: F E. Node D: no left; D; then the right subtree of D, which is E's tree: D F E.
                                          • Node H: no left; H; right subtree I: H I. Node G: left subtree H I, then G: H I G.
                                          • Node C: left subtree D F E, then C, then right subtree H I G: D F E C H I G.
                                          • Node B: no left; B; right subtree C: B D F E C H I G.
                                          • Node A: left subtree B…, then A, no right subtree: B D F E C H I G A.

                                          Model answer

                                          lc/rs table as above. Inorder of the binary tree: B, D, F, E, C, H, I, G, A.

                                          A free check

                                          The inorder of the lc/rs binary tree is the same list as the postorder of the original tree. It must be: the left subtree of a node x in the binary tree contains all the families below x (its first child and, through the rs chain, all the other children, each with its descendants), and these are visited before x itself; the right subtree holds the siblings after x, visited after. That is exactly “subtrees first, then the node”. If your two lists differ, one of them has an error.

                                          Try other trees

                                          Type A B C D E F G H I and 3 0 2 0 1 0 2 0 0 into the tool to watch the pile work on this very tree, or use your own lists.

                                          Rebuild a tree from its preorder and child counts

                                          Where marks are lost in Q1

                                          • Writing ? = 2 without a reason. One sentence (“the counts add up to n − 1”) earns the marks.
                                          • Drawing the children of a node in the wrong order, or giving C’s children to A.
                                          • A height of 4 (counting nodes instead of edges). The cover page says a leaf has height 0.
                                          • In (d): drawing the first child on the right and the sibling on the left. lc is always the left pointer, rs the right one.

                                          Part 7 · Solution to Question 2 · 25 marks · unofficial

                                          Worked solution: Question 2 (BST and AVL tree)

                                          The tree: 40 at the root; 20 and 60 below it; 10 and 30 under 20, with 25 under 30 (on its left); 50 and 70 under 60. As the question says, (a), (b) and (c) each start from this tree; (d) and (e) continue from the tree of (c).

                                          First the habit from Part 3: write (left height, right height) beside every node. A leaf is (−1, −1), because both of its subtrees are empty; a node’s own height is 1 + the larger of its two numbers.

                                          (a) Search path, successor, predecessor, height [4 marks]

                                          1. (i) The keys examined when searching for 25. Start at the root and compare: 25 < 40, go left; 25 > 20, go right; 25 < 30, go left; 25 = 25, found.

                                          Model answer (a)

                                          • (i) 40, 20, 30, 25.
                                          • (ii) The in-order successor of 25 is 30. Node 25 has no right child, so climb: 25 is the left child of 30, and the first parent we arrive at from its left side is the successor (successor). In sorted order 25 is followed by 30.
                                          • (iii) The in-order predecessor of 50 is 40. Node 50 has no left child, so climb until we arrive from a right side: 50 is the left child of 60 (no good), and 60 is the right child of 40 (we arrive at 40 from its right): so 40 is the predecessor. In sorted order 40 comes directly before 50.
                                          • (iv) The height of the tree is 3 (the longest path 40 → 20 → 30 → 25 has 3 edges).

                                          As a check, the in-order list of the eight keys is 10, 20, 25, 30, 40, 50, 60, 70, and in it 30 follows 25 and 40 precedes 50.

                                          (b) Delete 20 [6 marks]

                                          Node 20 has two children (10 and 30), so we use the rule from Chapter 7: find the successor of 20, the minimum of its right subtree; copy the successor’s key into the node; then physically cut out the successor’s old node, which has at most one child. The successor of 20: go right to 30, then left as far as possible: 30 → 25 (no left child), so it is 25.

                                          • (i) The node that is physically spliced out is the node holding 25 (a leaf, the left child of 30). Node 20 itself stays in the tree: it just gets the key 25.
                                          • (ii) The resulting tree:
                                          • (iii) Yes, it is still an AVL tree. Every node’s two subtree heights are equal (the pair is (0, 0) at 25 and 60, (1, 1) at the root, (−1, −1) at the leaves). In fact it is a perfect tree with seven keys and height 2.

                                          Model answer (b)

                                          (i) The node containing 25 (the successor of 20, a leaf) is spliced out; its key replaces 20. (ii) Tree: root 40; left child 25 with children 10 and 30; right child 60 with children 50 and 70. (iii) Yes: all heights differ by 0, so it is an AVL tree.

                                          (c) Insert 27, no rebalancing [6 marks]

                                          Start again from the original tree. Insert by searching for the key until you fall off the tree: 27 < 40 → left; 27 > 20 → right; 27 < 30 → left; 27 > 25 → right, and 25 has no right child: this is the place. The new leaf 27 becomes the right child of 25.

                                          Model answer (c)

                                          (i) The keys examined: 40, 20, 30, 25, and then 27 is attached as the right child of 25. (ii) Heights (left, right) after the insertion: node 25: (−1, 0); node 30: (1, −1); node 20: (0, 2); node 40: (3, 1).

                                          How the pairs come out: 25 now has an empty left subtree (−1) and the leaf 27 on the right (0). The left subtree of 30 is the tree at 25, whose height is 1 + max(−1, 0) = 1, and its right subtree is empty, so 30 has (1, −1). Node 30 has height 2, so the right subtree of 20 has height 2 while its left subtree (the leaf 10) has height 0: (0, 2). Node 20 has height 3, against 60’s height 1: the root has (3, 1).

                                          (d) Which node is broken, and which rotations? [4 marks]

                                          Walk up from the new leaf and test each ancestor: 25 has (−1, 0), which differs by 1: fine. 30 has (1, −1), which differs by 2: broken. So 30 is the lowest ancestor with a difference of more than 1 (20 and 40 are broken too, but higher up).

                                          Which shape? The extra height under 30 is on its left side (the tree at 25), and inside that tree it is on the right (27 hangs to the right of 25): a zig-zag, the left–right (inside-heavy) case. A single rotation cannot fix an inside case (why one rotation is not enough), so we need a double rotation:
