                                          1. First, a left rotation at node 25 (the left child of 30). Node 27 moves up above 25: 27 becomes the left child of 30 and 25 becomes the left child of 27.
                                          2. Second, a right rotation at node 30. Node 27 moves up above 30: 27 takes 30’s place as the right child of 20, with 25 on its left and 30 on its right.

                                          Model answer (d)

                                          The lowest unbalanced ancestor of 27 is node 30 (left height 1, right height −1). The new key went into the right subtree of 30’s left child, a left–right case, so perform a double rotation: (1) a left rotation at 25, then (2) a right rotation at 30.

                                          (e) The result [5 marks]

                                          Model answer (e)

                                          Root 40; left child 20 with children 10 and 27; right child 60 with children 50 and 70; node 27 has children 25 (left) and 30 (right). The height of the tree is 3. Heights (left, right): node 20: (0, 1); node 27: (0, 0); node 40: (2, 1). The differences are 1, 0 and 1, all at most 1, and every other node is (0, 0) or a leaf, so the tree is an AVL tree.

                                          Where the numbers come from: node 27 now has the leaves 25 and 30 under it, so both subtree heights are 0 and its own height is 1. Node 20 has the leaf 10 on the left (0) and the tree at 27 (height 1) on the right: (0, 1), height 2. Node 40 has 20 (height 2) on the left and 60 (height 1) on the right: (2, 1). The whole tree has height 1 + 2 = 3.

                                          Why one repair was enough

                                          Before the insertion the subtree under 20’s right pointer (the tree at 30) had height 1. After the double rotation, the subtree under that same pointer (the tree at 27) again has height 1. So nothing above it changed, and 20 and 40 are balanced again without any further rotation. This is the lecture fact that an insertion needs at most one rebalancing (single or double) (AVL insertion). Also check that the in-order list is still 10, 20, 25, 27, 30, 40, 50, 60, 70: rotations never change it.

                                          Where marks are lost in Q2

                                          • Carrying the deletion of (b) into (c). Parts (a), (b) and (c) all start from the original tree.
                                          • In (b)(i) saying that node 20 is removed. The node cut out is the successor’s old node; the node of 20 stays and receives the key 25.
                                          • In (c)(ii) giving heights after the rotation, or counting nodes instead of edges (a leaf has height 0, an empty subtree −1).
                                          • In (d) naming 20 or 40 as the node to rotate. The rotation is done at the lowest unbalanced ancestor, 30, and the double rotation starts at its child 25.
                                          • Rotating the wrong way: for the left–right case the first rotation is a left rotation (at the child), the second a right rotation (at the broken node).

                                          Part 8 · Solution to Question 3 · 25 marks · unofficial

                                          Worked solution: Question 3 (bitonic array)

                                          The array A[1..n] has distinct numbers, climbs strictly to one peak A[p] with 1 < p < n, and then falls strictly. Example: [3, 7, 12, 19, 24, 18, 11, 5, 1], peak 24 at index 5. Everything must be O(log n), so we need binary search (Chapter 6): one test per round that throws away half of what is left.

                                          (a) FindPeak [9 marks]

                                          The test at a cell mid: compare it with its right neighbour. Because the array rises up to p and falls after it:

                                          • if A[mid] < A[mid+1], we are still on the way up, so mid < p: the peak is to the right of mid;
                                          • if A[mid] > A[mid+1] (they are never equal, the numbers are distinct), we are already on the way down or at the top, so mid ≥ p: the peak is at mid or to its left.
                                          function FindPeak(A, n): low = 1 high = n while low < high: mid = floor((low + high) / 2) if A[mid] < A[mid + 1]: low = mid + 1 # the peak is to the right of mid else: high = mid # the peak is at mid or to its left return low
                                          low = 1, high = n

                                          the peak is somewhere in A[low..high]; at the start that is the whole array.

                                          while low < high

                                          keep going while at least two cells are still possible. When low = high only one cell is left.

                                          mid = floor((low + high) / 2)

                                          the middle cell of the range, rounded down. Because low < high, mid < high, so mid + 1 ≤ high ≤ n exists.

                                          if A[mid] < A[mid + 1]

                                          the slope goes up at mid, so the peak is further right.

                                          low = mid + 1

                                          mid itself cannot be the peak (its right neighbour is larger), so it can be thrown out.

                                          high = mid

                                          the slope goes down at mid: mid might be the peak, so it must stay; only the cells to its right are thrown out.

                                          return low

                                          the loop ended with low = high: the one cell left is the peak.

                                          Model answer: how it works

                                          FindPeak keeps a range low..high that always contains the peak. In each round it compares A[mid] with A[mid+1]. If A[mid] < A[mid+1] the array is still increasing at mid, so the peak lies to the right and we set low = mid + 1; otherwise the array is decreasing at mid, so the peak is at mid or to its left and we set high = mid. The range shrinks by about half each round, so after at most ⌈log n⌉ rounds only one cell is left, and it is the peak. Worst-case time O(log n).

                                          Why it is correct (the invariant)

                                          • Invariant: before every round, the peak index p satisfies low ≤ p ≤ high. At the start this is true (1 ≤ p ≤ n). If A[mid] < A[mid+1] then mid < p (every cell from p on is larger than its right neighbour), so p ≥ mid + 1 = the new low. Otherwise mid ≥ p, so p ≤ mid = the new high. Either way the invariant stays true.
                                          • Progress: low becomes mid + 1 > low, or high becomes mid < high, so the range strictly shrinks and the loop stops. At the end low = high and the invariant says that this cell is p.

                                          Trace on the example [3, 7, 12, 19, 24, 18, 11, 5, 1]: (low, high) = (1, 9): mid = 5, 24 > 18, so high = 5. (1, 5): mid = 3, 12 < 19, so low = 4. (4, 5): mid = 4, 19 < 24, so low = 5. Now low = high = 5: the peak is at index 5, the value 24. Three rounds for 9 cells.

                                          (b) BitonicSearch [12 marks]

                                          The peak splits the array into two sorted pieces: A[1..p−1] is increasing and A[p+1..n] is decreasing. Binary search works on each of them: the first is an ordinary binary search; on the second we mirror the comparisons, because bigger values are on the left. The numbers are distinct, so x is at most once in the array. We use helper procedures, as the question allows.

                                          function BinarySearchUp(A, low, high, x): # A[low..high] is increasing while low <= high: mid = floor((low + high) / 2) if A[mid] == x: return mid else if A[mid] < x: low = mid + 1 # x can only be to the right else: high = mid - 1 # x can only be to the left return -1 function BinarySearchDown(A, low, high, x): # A[low..high] is decreasing while low <= high: mid = floor((low + high) / 2) if A[mid] == x: return mid else if A[mid] > x: low = mid + 1 # bigger values are on the left, so x is to the right else: high = mid - 1 # x can only be to the left return -1 function BitonicSearch(A, n, x): p = FindPeak(A, n) if A[p] == x: return p i = BinarySearchUp(A, 1, p - 1, x) if i != -1: return i return BinarySearchDown(A, p + 1, n, x)
                                          p = FindPeak(A, n)

                                          one call of part (a): O(log n).

                                          if A[p] == x: return p

                                          the peak belongs to neither side, so test it on its own.

                                          BinarySearchUp(A, 1, p - 1, x)

                                          the climbing side. This is the lecture’s binary search: a smaller middle element means x is to the right.

                                          if i != -1: return i

                                          found on the left side: done.

                                          BinarySearchDown(A, p + 1, n, x)

                                          the falling side. The only change is the direction: a larger middle element means x is to the right, because the numbers get smaller as the index grows.

                                          return -1 (inside the helpers)

                                          the range became empty (low > high), so x is not on that side.

                                          Model answer: how it works

                                          First find the peak index p with FindPeak. The peak itself is checked directly. The elements to its left are increasing and those to its right are decreasing, so each side is sorted and ordinary binary search applies: in BinarySearchUp we compare A[mid] with x as usual; in BinarySearchDown the comparison is reversed. If neither side contains x, return −1. Every call is a binary search or a FindPeak, so the total is O(log n).

                                          Trace on the example (x = 11): p = 5, and 24 ≠ 11. BinarySearchUp on indices 1..4 (3, 7, 12, 19): mid = 2, 7 < 11, so low = 3; mid = 3, 12 > 11, so high = 2; now low > high: −1. BinarySearchDown on indices 6..9 (18, 11, 5, 1): mid = 7, A[7] = 11: found, return 7. For x = 4: both sides run out and the answer is −1.

                                          BitonicSearch step by step on your own array

                                          (c) Time and extra space [4 marks]

                                          • FindPeak. Each round does O(1) work and replaces a range of size s by one of size at most ⌈s/2⌉. Starting from n cells, after k rounds at most ⌈n/2k⌉ remain, so the loop stops after at most ⌈log n⌉ rounds: O(log n).
                                          • Each binary search. The range has at most n − 1 cells and is halved every round, so at most ⌊log n⌋ + 1 rounds of O(1) work (the same count as in Chapter 6): O(log n).
                                          • Total. One FindPeak plus at most two binary searches in a row: O(log n) + O(log n) + O(log n) = O(log n) in the worst case.
                                          • Extra space. Only a constant number of integer variables (low, high, mid, p, i), no copy of the array and, because everything is iterative, no recursion stack: O(1).

                                          Model answer (c)

                                          Worst-case time O(log n): FindPeak takes at most ⌈log n⌉ rounds and each of the (at most two) binary searches at most ⌊log n⌋ + 1 rounds, each round costing O(1). Extra space O(1): a few integer variables only, because the procedures are iterative.

                                          Where marks are lost in Q3

                                          • Comparing A[mid] with A[mid-1] and A[mid+1] without checking the ends (index 0 or n + 1). With while low < high and mid < high the access A[mid+1] is always legal.
                                          • Setting high = mid - 1 in FindPeak: mid might be the peak. And low = mid instead of mid + 1 can loop forever (when high = low + 1, mid = low).
                                          • Running binary search on the decreasing side with the increasing comparisons.
                                          • Finding the peak by scanning (O(n)), or copying the two halves into new arrays (O(n) time and space).
                                          • In (c): saying the space is O(log n); that would be the recursion stack of a recursive version, and the question asks for the iterative one.

                                          Part 9 · Solution to Question 4 · 30 marks · unofficial

                                          Worked solution: Question 4 (robust QuickSort)

                                          QuickSort’s cost is decided by the shape of its recursion (Chapter 10): every call pays Θ(size) to partition, so the total is (work per level) × (number of levels). A good partition makes the levels few; this question asks what the levels look like in four situations. Notation: a call on a piece of size m does Θ(m) work, say c·m for a constant c.

                                          (a) The sorted input [5 marks]

                                          On a sorted array with the first element as pivot, a piece of size m splits into a piece of size 1 and a piece of size m − 1 (the question says so). Partitioning costs Θ(m), and the piece of size 1 costs Θ(1). So

                                          T(m) = T(m − 1) + T(1) + c m for m ≥ 2, T(1) = c'

                                          Unroll it (or draw the recursion tree: one long left-leaning chain with a leaf hanging off each node):

                                          T(n) = c n + c (n−1) + … + c 2 + (n − 1) c' + c' = c (n (n+1)/2 − 1) + n c' = Θ(n²)

                                          Model answer (a)

                                          T(m) = T(m − 1) + T(1) + Θ(m). The recursion is n levels deep and level k partitions a piece of size n − k + 1, so the total is about c(n + (n − 1) + … + 2) = c(n(n + 1)/2 − 1), which is Θ(n²). QuickSort is quadratic on an already sorted input if the first element is the pivot.

                                          (b) Every partition is good [6 marks]

                                          Good means: both parts have at most 3m/4 elements. Then a piece of size m splits into pieces of size at most (3/4)m.

                                          (i) Maximum recursion depth. A piece at depth d has at most (3/4)dn elements. The recursion stops at pieces of size at most 1, which is certainly the case when (3/4)dn ≤ 1, that is when d ≥ log4/3 n. So the depth is at most ⌈log4/3 n⌉ + 1 = O(log n) (log4/3 n = log n / log(4/3), a constant times log n).

                                          (ii) Partitioning work at each depth. The pieces at one depth are separate, non-overlapping parts of the array, so their sizes add up to at most n. Partitioning costs c times the size, so the work at one depth is at most c n = O(n).

                                          total ≤ (number of depths) × (work per depth) = O(log n) × O(n) = O(n log n)

                                          Model answer (b)

                                          With good partitions the size at depth d is at most (3/4)dn, so the maximum recursion depth is at most log4/3 n + 1 = O(log n). The pieces at one depth are disjoint, so the total partitioning work at each depth is O(n). Hence the worst-case running time is O(n log n). (It is also Ω(n log n): a good part has at least m/4 elements, so no piece of size above 1 disappears before depth log4 n, and each of those depths costs about n; so the bound is tight.)

                                          Same recurrence as the lecture

                                          This is the recurrence T(n) ≤ T(3n/4) + T(n/4) + cn from the Chapter 10 discussion of a 3-to-1 split (any split in a fixed proportion gives n log n). If you prefer the recursion-tree style of the lecture, draw the tree and write “each level costs at most cn, the longest path has log4/3 n levels”.

                                          (c) Only “one of every two is good” [7 marks]

                                          Answer: Yes, O(n log n) is still guaranteed.

                                          Justification. A partition never makes the piece bigger: both parts have at most m − 1 elements (as p ≤ q < r). A good partition makes it at most 3/4 as big. Take any root-to-leaf path and cut it into consecutive pairs of partition steps. Each pair contains at least one good partition by the guarantee, so each pair shrinks the size by a factor of at least 3/4 (the other step does not increase it). After 2k steps the size is at most (3/4)kn, which is at most 1 once k ≥ log4/3 n. So the depth is at most 2 log4/3 n + 2 = O(log n): only a constant factor (2) more than in (b). As before the pieces at one depth are disjoint, so each depth costs O(n) and the total is O(log n) × O(n) = O(n log n).

                                          Model answer (c)

                                          Yes. Because every partition step reduces the size and at least one in every two consecutive steps reduces it to at most 3/4, the size after 2k steps is at most (3/4)kn. The recursion depth is therefore at most 2 log4/3 n + 2 = O(log n), each depth costs O(n) in total, so the running time is O(n log n).

                                          (d) RobustQuickSort [12 marks]

                                          (i) Pseudocode [6 marks]

                                          It is the lecture’s QuickSort with three additions: a counter bad, a test for a good partition and an escape to HeapSort. A part of size L is at most 3m/4 exactly when 4L ≤ 3m, which avoids fractions.

                                          RobustQuickSort (A, p, r, bad) { if (p >= r) return; // zero or one element: already sorted if (bad == 2) { // two non-good partitions in a row HeapSort(A, p, r); // sort this piece for sure in O(m log m) return; } q = Partition(A, p, r); // p <= q < r m = r - p + 1; // size of the piece if (4 * (q - p + 1) <= 3 * m and 4 * (r - q) <= 3 * m) newbad = 0; // good partition: start counting again else newbad = bad + 1; // one more non-good partition in a row RobustQuickSort(A, p, q, newbad); RobustQuickSort(A, q + 1, r, newbad);}
                                          if (p >= r) return

                                          the first rule: a piece with at most one element needs nothing.

                                          if (bad == 2) { HeapSort(A, p, r); return; }

                                          the second rule: the whole piece is sorted by the black box and no further partition is made on this piece.

                                          q = Partition(A, p, r)

                                          the black box from the lectures; it gives the two parts A[p..q] and A[q+1..r].

                                          m = r - p + 1

                                          the size of the piece, needed for the 3m/4 test.

                                          4*(q-p+1) <= 3*m and 4*(r-q) <= 3*m

                                          both parts have at most 3m/4 elements: the definition of a good partition. The left part has q-p+1 elements and the right part r-q.

                                          newbad = 0

                                          after a good partition the counter is reset to 0 for both recursive calls.

                                          newbad = bad + 1

                                          after a non-good partition the counter grows by 1, again for both recursive calls.

                                          RobustQuickSort(A, p, q, newbad)

                                          left part, with the counter just computed. The right part follows with the same newbad.

                                          The first call is RobustQuickSort(A, 1, n, 0).

                                          RobustQuickSort: watch the bad counter and the HeapSort escape

                                          On a sorted array of 16 numbers: the first partition splits 1 | 15 (15 is more than 12 = 3·16/4: not good), the second splits 1 | 14 (more than 11.25: not good), so the third call has bad = 2 and HeapSorts its 14 elements. Only two partitions are made instead of fifteen. (Compare with part (a): that is exactly the case where plain QuickSort goes quadratic.)

                                          (ii) Why it is correct, and why O(n log n) [6 marks]

                                          Correctness. By strong induction on the size of the piece, RobustQuickSort(A, p, r, bad) sorts A[p..r] whatever bad is. If p ≥ r there is at most one element: sorted. If bad = 2, HeapSort sorts the piece. Otherwise Partition gives A[p..q] and A[q+1..r] with every element of the first smaller than every element of the second, and p ≤ q < r, so both parts are non-empty and strictly smaller than the piece (so the recursion ends and the induction applies). Each part is sorted by its recursive call, and since nothing in the left part is bigger than anything in the right part, the whole piece A[p..r] is sorted. The counter bad only decides which sorting method is used, never what the result is.

                                          Running time.

                                          • Depth of the partitions. A call with bad = 2 does not partition. So on any root-to-leaf path there are never three non-good partitions in a row: after two of them, the next call is the HeapSort and the path ends. Hence among any three consecutive partition steps on a path, at least one is good, and it cuts the size to at most 3/4. After 3k partitions the size is at most (3/4)kn, so no path has more than 3 log4/3 n + 3 = O(log n) partition steps. (Same argument as part (c), with three instead of two.)
                                          • Partitioning work. The pieces at one depth are disjoint, so their sizes add up to at most n and the partitions at this depth cost O(n) together. With O(log n) depths: O(n log n).
                                          • HeapSort work. A HeapSort call ends its path, so no HeapSort piece lies inside another one: the pieces are disjoint and their sizes m1, m2, … add up to at most n. The total HeapSort time is ∑O(mi log mi) ≤ ∑O(mi log n) = O(n log n).
                                          • Everything else (the tests, the counter, the calls that return at once) is O(1) per call, and there are at most 2n − 1 calls, so O(n).
                                          T(n) = O(n log n) [partitions] + O(n log n) [HeapSorts] + O(n) [other] = O(n log n)

                                          Model answer (d)(ii)

                                          Correctness: by induction on the size, each call sorts its piece: trivially if it has at most one element, by HeapSort if bad = 2, and otherwise because Partition puts everything in the left part before everything in the right part and both parts are smaller and are sorted recursively. Time: a path can never contain three non-good partitions in a row, because the call with bad = 2 stops partitioning. So at least one in every three partitions on a path shrinks the size by a factor 3/4, giving depth O(log n); each depth costs O(n) to partition, so partitioning costs O(n log n). The HeapSort calls work on disjoint pieces of total size at most n and cost O(m log m) = O(m log n) each, in total O(n log n). The worst case is O(n log n).

                                          Where marks are lost in Q4

                                          • (a): writing T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n (that is the balanced case). The pieces here are 1 and m − 1.
                                          • (b): giving the depth as log2 n without a reason. The depth is log4/3 n, which is still O(log n); and forgetting to say why the work at a depth is only O(n) (disjoint pieces).
                                          • (c): answering “No” because “a bad partition can be very unbalanced”. A bad partition can be as bad as 1 | m − 1, but it cannot happen twice in a row.
                                          • (d): passing the new counter to only one of the two recursive calls; not resetting bad to 0 after a good partition; recursing on (p, q − 1) and (q + 1, r) (that is for a Partition that puts the pivot at q; here Partition gives A[p..q] and A[q+1..r]); and partitioning again after calling HeapSort instead of returning.
                                          • (d)(ii): saying “HeapSort is O(n log n) so the total is O(n log n)” without noticing that HeapSort is called on many pieces; the fix is that the pieces are disjoint.

                                          Part 10 · The assignment's ideas on one page

                                          Summary and practice questions on fresh examples

                                          The four questions, reduced to one idea each

                                          QuestionThe idea to hold on toThe check that catches mistakes
                                          Q1 TreesPreorder lists a node, then each of its subtrees in turn; the child counts say how many subtrees follow, and a pile of “parents still waiting for children” tells you where each subtree ends. Postorder, height and the lc/rs picture are read from the drawing.Number of parent–child links = number of nodes − 1; the picture read back in preorder reproduces the list.
                                          Q2 BST and AVLKeep the (left, right) subtree heights beside every node. Successor/predecessor have a “go down” case and a “climb up” case. Deleting a node with two children physically removes its successor. After an insertion, fix the lowest unbalanced ancestor with the rotation that matches the zig-zag or straight shape.The in-order list of keys is unchanged by rotations; after the fix every node’s two heights differ by at most 1.
                                          Q3 Bitonic arrayA comparison with a neighbour says which side of the middle the peak is on, so binary search works; after the peak is known the two sides are each sorted (in opposite orders) and can be binary-searched.The range strictly shrinks on every pass; trace the tiny cases (length 3, absent target).
                                          Q4 QuickSortTime = (levels) × (work per level), with at most n elements partitioned per level. Pieces that keep shrinking by a fixed fraction give logarithmically many levels. A counter on each path lets you fall back to HeapSort when partitions keep being bad.Test “good” on both parts with whole numbers (4 × size ≤ 3m); HeapSort pieces never overlap.

                                          What the marks usually look for

                                          • A picture at every step for Q1 and Q2: trees drawn clearly, with nodes and heights labelled, one picture per stage.
                                          • Named facts with your numbers in them for every “justify”: the definition used, then the actual heights or counts.
                                          • Pseudocode that is checkable in Q3 and Q4(d): clear loop conditions, updates that provably shrink the range, a return value in every case, and a one-line explanation of what stays true on every pass.
                                          • Cover-page conventions: leaf height 0, empty tree height −1, logs to base 2, no program code.

                                          Practice questions (new examples, answers included)

                                          These are not the assignment’s questions; they use the same methods on different data so that you can test your technique, then compare with the folded answers.

                                          1. (Trees) The preorder of an ordered tree is K, L, M, N, O, P and the child counts in the same order are 2, 1, 0, 2, 0, 0. Draw the tree, give its postorder and its height.

                                            Show the answer

                                            Pile method: K is the root (2 children, waiting). L is K’s first child (1 child, waits on top). M is L’s child (leaf); L is full and leaves the pile. N is K’s second child (2 children). O and P are N’s children. So K has children L, N; L has child M; N has children O, P. Postorder: M, L, O, P, N, K. Height: the longest root-to-leaf path has 2 edges (K–L–M or K–N–O): 2.

                                          2. (A missing count) A tree has 7 nodes. In preorder the child counts are 2, 0, 3, 0, ?, 0, 0. What must the question mark be? Which tree results?

                                            Show the answer

                                            7 nodes have 6 parent–child links, so the counts add up to 6. The known ones give 2 + 0 + 3 + 0 + 0 + 0 = 5, so ? = 1. The tree: the root has 2 children (the 2nd node, a leaf, and the 3rd node); the 3rd node has 3 children: the 4th (leaf), the 5th (which has 1 child, the 6th, a leaf) and the 7th (leaf).

                                          3. (lc / rs) For the tree in question 1, give lc and rs of every node, draw the binary tree and write its inorder. What do you notice?

                                            Show the answer

                                            lc: K→L, L→M, N→O, the rest null. rs: L→N, O→P, the rest null. Binary tree: K with left child L; L with left child M and right child N; N with left child O; O with right child P. Inorder: M, L, O, P, N, K. This is exactly the postorder of the original tree from question 1: with lc = children and rs = later siblings, “left subtree, node, right subtree” visits a node’s children (and their later siblings) before the node itself.

                                          4. (BST) Insert 8, 3, 10, 1, 6, 14, 4, 7, 13 into an empty BST in that order. Find the successor of 7, the successor of 14, the predecessor of 8. Then delete 3 using the successor rule: which node is physically removed and what is the new tree?

                                            Show the answer

                                            Successor of 7: 7 has no right child and is the right child of 6, which is the right child of 3, which is the left child of 8: so 8. Successor of 14: 14 has no right child, and climbing from 14 we reach 10 and then 8 always from their right side, so there is none (14 is the largest key). Predecessor of 8: largest key in the left subtree: 3 → 6 → 7, so 7. Delete 3 (children 1 and 6): the successor is the minimum of the right subtree: 6 → its left child 4, which has no left child, so the node with key 4 is physically removed; the node that held 3 now holds 4. New tree: root 8; left child 4 (with children 1 and 6, where 6 has right child 7); right child 10 (with right child 14, which has left child 13).

                                          5. (AVL) Insert 30, 10, 20 (in that order) into an empty AVL tree. Which node becomes unbalanced, which case is it, and what rotations are applied? Then insert 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7 in order into another empty AVL tree: how many rotations happen, what is the root and the height?

                                            Show the answer

                                            After 30, 10, 20 the node 30 has left height 1 (its child 10 has a right child 20) and right height −1. The tall child 10 is tall on its right: left-right case. Rotations: a left rotation at 10, then a right rotation at 30. The result has root 20 with children 10 and 30. For 1 to 7: left rotations at 1 (when 3 arrives), at 3 (when 5 arrives), at 2 (when 6 arrives) and at 5 (when 7 arrives): 4 rotations, all single. Final tree: root 4, children 2 and 6, leaves 1, 3, 5, 7: a perfect tree of height 2.

                                          6. (Bitonic) For the array [2, 9, 15, 21, 17, 8, 3] (positions 1 to 7), run the halving strategy with mid = ⌊(lo + hi)/2⌋ starting from lo = 1, hi = 7. Which cells are compared with their right neighbour and where does the range end up? Roughly how many probes does the strategy need for an array of 1000 cells?

                                            Show the answer

                                            mid = 4: 21 > 17, so the peak is at 4 or to the left: hi = 4. mid = 2: 9 < 15, so the peak is to the right of 2: lo = 3. mid = 3: 15 < 21, so lo = 4. Now lo = hi = 4: the peak is at position 4 (value 21) after 3 probes. For 1000 cells there are 998 candidate positions (not the first or last), and 210 = 1024 ≥ 998, so about 10 probes.

                                          7. (Good partitions) A piece of size 20 is split into 15 and 5. A piece of size 20 is split into 16 and 4. A piece of size 9 is split into 7 and 2. Which of these three partitions are good?

                                            Show the answer

                                            Size 20: 3m = 60. 15 and 5: 4 × 15 = 60 ≤ 60 and 4 × 5 = 20 ≤ 60: good. 16 and 4: 4 × 16 = 64 > 60: not good. Size 9: 3m = 27; 7 and 2: 4 × 7 = 28 > 27: not good (7 is more than 3 × 9/4 = 6.75).

                                          8. (Fractions) Suppose every partition puts at most 9/10 of the piece in the larger part. How many levels can the recursion have, and what is the running time? Does it matter that 9/10 is not 3/4?

                                            Show the answer

                                            The largest piece after k levels is at most n(9/10)k, which falls to 1 when k = log10/9 n = (log n)/(log(10/9)), a constant times log n. Each level partitions at most n elements. Total: O(n log n). The constant is bigger (about 6.6 log n levels against about 2.4 log n for 3/4), but any fixed fraction below 1 gives the same order.

                                          9. (The counter) In RobustQuickSort, why do both recursive calls receive the same new value of bad? And if the threshold 2 were replaced by 5, would the running time still be O(n log n)?

                                            Show the answer

                                            The counter describes the path from the root to the current call. Both children continue that path (the partition just made is the latest step on both of their paths), so both are told the same count. With threshold 5 a path can have at most five non-good partitions in a row, so among any six consecutive partition steps one is good; each such window shrinks pieces by a fixed fraction, giving O(log n) levels. The HeapSort pieces still do not overlap. So yes, still O(n log n), with a bigger constant.

                                          What to remember

                                          For trees, draw first, then read. For AVL questions, write the heights down, then decide. For logarithmic algorithms, name what stays true on every pass and show that the range shrinks. For QuickSort, count levels, then multiply by the work per level. The assignment is four applications of these four sentences.

                                          In-class quiz · 27 Oct 2026 · 20% of the course · Chapters 1–7 · worked solutions (not official)

                                          The Quiz Explained

                                          All five questions, every blank and every bound, with the reasoning a marker wants to see. The quiz is also the best preview you have of the final exam (60%): same conventions on the cover, same kinds of blanks, the same “faulty version” traps. The last part turns what it teaches into a checklist for the final.

                                          In this chapter

                                            Part 1 · Cover page

                                            The cover page is part of the question

                                            The quiz printed a block of general conventions. Each one closes a loophole, and each one costs marks if you ignore it. Expect the same block on the final.

                                            ConventionWhat it means for your answer
                                            All logarithms have base 2Write log n; inside Θ the base does not matter, but in exact counts (like the number of calls) it does.
                                            Integer arithmetic, comparisons, array access, pointer operations, one stack/queue operation: constant timeCount operations, not the size of the numbers. Score(n) adding big numbers is still Θ(1) per add.
                                            Running time includes all recursive callsTwo recursive calls on n/2 is T(n) = 2T(n/2) + Θ(1), not T(n/2).
                                            Auxiliary space excludes the input but includes the recursion stackA recursive procedure with depth log n uses Θ(log n) space even with no arrays. An iterative loop with a few variables uses Θ(1).
                                            Express a tight bound with Θ“O(n²)” for something that is Θ(n) is true but scores zero. Give Θ.
                                            Code completions: fill only the blanks; no new statements or variables; no side effects; a statement blank is one assignmentNo i++ inside an expression, no extra if. If you need something the code does not have, your idea is not the intended one.

                                            Part 2 · Question 1 · 25 marks

                                            Q1: Score(n), two identical calls

                                            Score(n): // n = 2^r if n == 1: return 1 a = Score(n / 2) b = Score(n / 2) return a + b + n

                                            (a) Run it by hand on n = 4

                                            Work bottom-up. Score(1) = 1. Score(2) = 1 + 1 + 2 = 4. Score(4) = 4 + 4 + 4 = 12.

                                            Calls: Score(4) makes two calls to Score(2); each makes two calls to Score(1). Total = 1 + 2 + 4 = 7.

                                            Try it yourself: Score against FastScore

                                            r = 2

                                            (b) Count the calls with a recurrence

                                            Answer

                                            (i) C(1) = 1 and C(n) = 2C(n/2) + 1 for n > 1 (this call, plus everything inside the two calls). (ii) C(n) = 2n − 1. (iii) Θ(n): each call does constant work besides its calls, so the time is Θ(C(n)). (iv) Yes: n = o(n log n) because n / (n log n) = 1/log n → 0.

                                            Why 2n − 1? (two ways to see it)

                                            Unwrap: C(n) = 1 + 2 + 4 + … + 2r (one term per level of the call tree), a geometric series = 2r+1 − 1 = 2n − 1.

                                            Check: C(1) = 1 ✓, C(2) = 3 ✓, C(4) = 7 ✓ (part (a)). The call tree is a full binary tree with n leaves, and such a tree has n − 1 internal nodes.

                                            (c) Prove Score(2r) = 2r(1 + r) by induction on r

                                            Show the model proof (the four labelled pieces)

                                            Claim P(r): Score(2r) = 2r(1 + r).

                                            Base case r = 0: Score(1) returns 1, and 20(1 + 0) = 1. ✓

                                            Inductive hypothesis: assume P(k) holds for some k ≥ 0: Score(2k) = 2k(1 + k).

                                            Inductive step: for n = 2k+1 > 1 both calls are Score(2k), so by the hypothesis Score(2k+1) = 2 · 2k(1 + k) + 2k+1 = 2k+1(1 + k) + 2k+1 = 2k+1(2 + k) = 2k+1(1 + (k + 1)). That is P(k + 1). By induction P(r) holds for all r ≥ 0. ∎

                                            Where marks go

                                            The question says “state the base case, inductive hypothesis and inductive step”. Label all three. Say where you use the hypothesis (“by the IH, each call returns …”), and why the step applies (n > 1, so the code takes the recursive branch).

                                            (d) FastScore: one call instead of two

                                            Answer

                                            (i) 2 * a + n. (ii) The two calls in Score have the same argument and Score has no side effects, so they return the same value: a + b = 2a. (iii) T(n) = T(n/2) + Θ(1) → Θ(log n): log n + 1 calls, constant work each. (iv) Θ(log n) auxiliary space: the recursion is log n deep and each frame is constant size (the convention counts the stack).

                                            Trap

                                            Saying “Θ(1) space, it has no arrays” for (iv) loses the marks. The cover says auxiliary space includes the recursion stack. Also, original Score has the same depth, so it also uses Θ(log n) space, even though it takes Θ(n) time.

                                            Part 3 · Question 2 · 15 marks

                                            Q2: split one list into urgent and ordinary

                                            (a) Input A(f) → B(t) → C(t) → D(f) → E(t). Keep the order inside each output: urgent list B → C → E; ordinary list A → D.

                                            Split(head): urgentHead = urgentTail = null ordinaryHead = ordinaryTail = null p = head while p != null: nextNode = p.next // (i) save the rest first p.next = null // (ii) p will be the new tail if p.urgent: if urgentHead == null: urgentHead = p else: urgentTail.next = p // (iii) urgentTail = p else: if ordinaryHead == null: ordinaryHead = p else: ordinaryTail.next = p // (iv) ordinaryTail = p p = nextNode return (urgentHead, ordinaryHead)

                                            Why (ii) is null: each node becomes the last node of its output list at the moment it is appended. Cutting its old next makes sure the two output lists end properly (otherwise E’s list could still point into the other list). Empty input: the loop never runs and both heads stay null; one category only: the other head stays null. Both are handled.

                                            Try it yourself

                                            Answer (c)

                                            (i) Θ(n): one pass, constant work per node. (ii) Θ(1): a fixed number of pointers, no recursion, no new nodes. Faulty order p.next = null; nextNode = p.next: (iii) nextNode is null in the first iteration (we read the pointer we just erased). (iv) 1 iteration: p = nextNode = null ends the loop, so only A is placed and B…E are lost.

                                            The lesson for the final

                                            “Faulty version” questions are answered by running the faulty code on the given input, line by line, not by describing it in general. The order of two pointer statements is a classic: save before you overwrite.

                                            Part 4 · Question 3 · 15 marks

                                            Q3: queue traversal, then the same with a stack

                                            Adjacency lists: A: B, D · B: A, C, E · C: B, D, F · D: A, C, E · E: B, D, F · F: C, E · G: none. Mark a vertex when it is enqueued (so nothing enters the queue twice).

                                            Try it yourself

                                            Answer (a)

                                            (i) Removal order: A, B, D, C, E, F. G is never reached (no edges). (ii) After D’s neighbours are examined the queue is [C, E] (front to back): A’s turn added B, D; B’s turn added C, E; D’s neighbours A, C, E were all already marked.

                                            Answer (b)

                                            for each v in V: if not visited[v]: BFSFrom(v). (iii) Θ(|V| + |E|): every vertex is enqueued once and every adjacency list is scanned once (each undirected edge appears twice), plus the outer loop over all vertices.

                                            Answer (c)

                                            (i) Pops: A, D, E. Pop A, push B then D; pop D (top), push C then E; pop E. (ii) No. (iii) After E is popped, B is still in the stack: dist(A, B) = 1, but the third vertex popped, E, has dist(A, E) = 2. A stack does not process vertices in order of distance, which is why only BFS gives shortest paths in unweighted graphs.

                                            Part 5 · Question 4 · 20 marks

                                            Q4: a set stored with linear probing

                                            Table size 11, h(k, i) = (k + i) mod 11. Search stops at the key, at EMPTY, or after 11 probes; it does not stop at DELETED.

                                            Try it yourself

                                            Answer (a)

                                            30 mod 11 = 8. (i) Slots 8, 9, 10, 0: found at 0, present (9 is DELETED, so search goes on). (ii) 52 mod 11 = 8. Slots 8, 9, 10, 0, 1, 2: slot 2 is EMPTY, so absent.

                                            Answer (b)

                                            (i) Slots 8, 9. (ii) Slot 9 is overwritten with 30 and it returns INSERTED. (iii) No. 30 was already stored in slot 0, further along the probe sequence. A DELETED slot only means “something used to be here”; it says nothing about whether k is stored later. Now 30 appears twice, which breaks the set requirement.

                                            InsertIfAbsent(T, m, k): firstDeleted = NONE for i = 0 to m - 1: j = (k + i) mod m if T[j] == k: return PRESENT if T[j] == DELETED and firstDeleted == NONE: // (i) firstDeleted = j if T[j] == EMPTY: if firstDeleted != NONE: j = firstDeleted // (ii) T[j] = k return INSERTED if firstDeleted != NONE: // (iii) T[firstDeleted] = k // (iv) return INSERTED return FULL

                                            Answer (c)

                                            (i)–(iv) as shown. The “and firstDeleted == NONE” is what makes it the first deleted slot “without replacement by a later one”. Reaching EMPTY proves k is absent (the table is valid for search), so it is safe to reuse the first DELETED slot. (v) Θ(m) worst case (all m slots probed). (vi) With no EMPTY slot it returns INSERTED exactly when k is not stored and at least one slot is DELETED: the loop then checks all m slots (so k is really absent) and uses the first DELETED one.

                                            Part 6 · Question 5 · 25 marks

                                            Q5: R(x), the number of stored keys smaller than x

                                            The BST: root 24; 11 (children 5, 17) and 38 (children 31, 46); 35 is the right child of 31.

                                            Answer (a)

                                            (i) Inorder: 5, 11, 17, 24, 31, 35, 38, 46 (always sorted for a BST). (ii) R(35) = |{5, 11, 17, 24, 31}| = 5 (strictly smaller, so 35 itself is not counted).

                                            ArrayRank(A, n, x): lo = 0; hi = n // answer always lies in [lo, hi] while lo < hi: mid = floor((lo + hi) / 2) if A[mid] < x: lo = mid + 1 // A[0..mid] all count else: hi = mid // A[mid..] count for nothing return lo

                                            Why these blanks: the invariant is “every index below lo holds a key < x, every index from hi on holds a key ≥ x”. If A[mid] < x, mid itself counts, so lo = mid + 1; otherwise mid might be the first key ≥ x, so keep it: hi = mid (not mid − 1). It returns 0 for n = 0 and works for x outside the range.

                                            Try it yourself: TreeRank on the quiz tree

                                            Answer (c)

                                            if x <= u.key: return TreeRank(u.left, x) · else: return Size(u.left) + 1 + TreeRank(u.right, x). (iv) u.key ≥ x, so u is not smaller than x, and every key in the right subtree is larger than u.key ≥ x. (v) u.key < x, so u counts one; every left-subtree key is smaller than u.key < x, so the whole left subtree counts, and its stored size gives that number in constant time.

                                            Answer (d)

                                            (i) Sorted array: Θ(log n). (ii) BST of height h: Θ(h) (one root-to-leaf path, constant work per node). (iii) Arbitrary shape with n keys: Θ(n) (a chain has h = n − 1). Without size fields, perfect tree, query n + 1: (iv) the root goes right and calls Size on its left subtree, (n − 1)/2 nodes. (v) Θ(n). (vi) Yes: h = log(n + 1) − 1, so O(h) = O(log n), but this single helper call already takes Θ(n) time.

                                            Trap

                                            “Θ(log n)” for (ii) is wrong: the question asks in terms of h, and a BST is not necessarily balanced. Save “log n” for AVL trees and sorted arrays.

                                            Part 7 · Lessons

                                            Six question types, and how to score on each

                                            TypeQuiz exampleRecipe
                                            TraceScore(4); BFS order; probe sequences; inorderWrite every intermediate state (queue contents, slot by slot). Partial traces earn partial marks.
                                            Recurrence and closed formC(n) = 2C(n/2) + 1 = 2n − 1Base value + “this call + the calls inside”. Check the closed form on the values you traced.
                                            Induction proofScore(2r) = 2r(1 + r)Label base, IH, step; show where the IH is used.
                                            Fill the blanksSplit, BFS-all, InsertIfAbsent, ArrayRank, TreeRankState the invariant in words first (“lo: everything below counts”), then each blank follows. Test on empty input and on one element.
                                            Tight boundsΘ(n), Θ(log n), Θ(|V|+|E|), Θ(m), Θ(h)Θ, in the variables asked (h vs n); count the recursion stack in space.
                                            Faulty version / does it violate the claimswapped pointer lines; DELETED reuse; Size without fieldsRun it on the given input and point to the exact step that breaks; answer Yes/No first, then one sentence of evidence.

                                            Three C++ programs on a network of courses where some courses are prerequisites of others: the cheapest way to become eligible for a course, the courses that depend completely on one course, and a tidy ordering of all courses. Parts 2 to 6 explain what each task is really asking, show the statement’s own samples as pictures, list the traps in the wording and give a ladder of hints for every task. Parts 7 to 9 are my own worked solutions: a C++14 program for each task, with the reasoning, the running time, a trace of the sample and a step-by-step demo. They are unofficial; the official solutions will follow when they are released.
