                                              C30% (3 per test)Put all courses in one line so that every prerequisite comes before the course that needs it, with a fixed rule for ties. What is the position of course s in that line?O((n + m) log n)Queue, priority queues, BFSPart 5Part 9

                                              All three share the same network (Part 2), so read that part first. The three tasks look similar but use different rules about prerequisites, and mixing them up is the commonest way to lose marks.

                                              The rules on the cover page, in plain words

                                              • C++14, three files. Hand in exactly three .cpp files, uncompressed, one per task, named UniversityNumber-A.cpp, UniversityNumber-B.cpp, UniversityNumber-C.cpp (for example 1234554321-A.cpp). Marks are deducted for wrong names.
                                              • Only these libraries: <iostream>, <cstdio>, <string>, <vector>, <set>, <stack>, <queue>, <algorithm>, <math.h>, <limits>, <functional>, <utility>. Any other header means 0 marks, and the GNU “pbds” containers do not count as standard.
                                              • Standard input and output only. No files, no system(), no threads. Read with cin, scanf, getchar and so on; print with cout, printf, putchar. The statement suggests getchar / putchar for large amounts of numbers.
                                              • Ten hidden tests per task, 1 second each. A test earns its marks only if the program compiles, finishes inside 1 second without crashing and prints exactly the right output (no extra or missing characters). Otherwise that test gives 0.
                                              • No undefined behaviour. Integer overflow, division by zero and reading an uninitialised variable all count as undefined and can zero a test. Randomness is not allowed either.
                                              • Your code must compile on the online compiler named in the statement, otherwise it is not even checked by hand.

                                              The standard library, mapped to what you have learned

                                              The list of allowed headers is a hint about what the course expects you to be able to use. Each one is a structure from the lectures, already written for you:

                                              HeaderWhat you getWhere it appears in this site
                                              <vector>A growable array. A vector<vector<int>> is a handy way to keep, for every course, a list of other courses.arrays, graph as lists
                                              <stack>, <queue>Stack, FIFO queue and priority_queue (a heap, by default the largest element on top).stack, queue, heaps, priority queues
                                              <set>An ordered set kept in a balanced search tree: insert, erase and “smallest element” are all O(log n).balanced trees
                                              <algorithm>sort, min, max, reverse …sorting
                                              <functional>, <utility>Comparison objects such as greater<int>; pair to bundle two values.—
                                              <limits>, <math.h>The largest value of a type (a good “infinity”), mathematical functions.—

                                              Two scoring facts that should shape how you work

                                              1. Half of the tests are small. In every task, 50% of the tests have n ≤ 1000 and m ≤ 1000. A simple, obviously correct (even slow) program already earns about half of the marks of that task, so write the simple version first, test it, and then improve its speed. Do not start with the cleverest version.
                                              2. The other half needs the target speed. With n up to 100 000 and m up to 300 000, anything that does n × n steps (1010) cannot finish in one second. The “target speed” column above says how much work is allowed. See typical growth rates in Chapter 2 if they are still hazy.

                                              The self-test package

                                              The zip contains a self_test folder with test.py and, for every task, five public tests: A-1.in / A-1.out up to A-5.in / A-5.out (and the same for B and C). The first three of each task are exactly the three samples printed in the statement; the last two are big (about 9 000 and 90 000 courses) and are there to test your speed. Run them like this (Linux or macOS):

                                              g++ -std=c++14 main.cpp -o main./main < TaskA/A-4.in > myoutput.txtdiff myoutput.txt TaskA/A-4.out # no output means: identicalpython3 test.py main.cpp A # runs all the A tests at once

                                              The statement warns that the local results do not decide your grade: the hidden tests are different, so also make your own small cases (Part 6).

                                              Check your output the way the machine does

                                              The checker compares your output with the expected output character by character. This tool lets you paste both and shows the first line where they differ, with spaces shown as dots. (It is a convenience for small outputs; for the big tests use diff.)

                                              Compare my output with the expected output

                                              How to use the hint ladders

                                              Every task has numbered folded hints. Try the task on paper for ten minutes first, open Hint 1 only if you are stuck, and keep going one hint at a time. Hint 1 usually restates the problem, the later hints name the idea and the traps, and the last one is about checking your work. You never get the final steps: those are the assignment.

                                              Part 2 · The shared background of all three tasks

                                              The course network: what the statement describes

                                              Every task starts from the same picture: n courses and m relationships A → B, meaning “course A is a prerequisite of course B”. In computer-science words this is a directed graph: the courses are the vertices (nodes) and each relationship is a directed edge, an arrow. If you have not met this before, read The Graph ADT first; it is short and it uses exactly these words.

                                              Picture it

                                              Think of the skill tree in a video game. Some skills can be unlocked straight away, others need an earlier skill first. The arrows say “this one unlocks that one”. The only odd thing about this game is a rule in the statement, explained next, that one unlocked parent is enough.

                                              Words you will meet

                                              Statement saysGraph wordMeaning here
                                              course i, ids 0 … n−1vertexA number. The ids really are 0 to n−1 with no gaps, so you can use them directly as array positions.
                                              relationship a → bdirected edgeThe pair of numbers a b on one input line. It is not symmetric: “1 2” does not mean 2 is a prerequisite of 1.
                                              a course with no prerequisitea source (no incoming arrows)Jeff may study it on day one. This page calls them start courses.
                                              “the relationships do not form a cycle”directed acyclic graph (DAG)You can never get back to a course by following arrows forward. This promise is valuable: use it.
                                              study patha pathA chain of courses, each a prerequisite of the next one.

                                              The eligibility rules, and the one that surprises people

                                              A course has …… so Jeff may study it when …
                                              no prerequisitealways (“eligible anytime”).
                                              exactly one prerequisitehe has passed that prerequisite.
                                              several prerequisiteshe has passed at least ONE of them. (In real universities you would usually need all of them; here you do not.)

                                              Two different rules in one assignment

                                              Tasks A and B use the “at least one” rule. Task C is different: to put the courses in a line, every relationship A → B must have A before B, so a course must come after all of its prerequisites. If a solution to Task C “only waits for one prerequisite”, it is solving the wrong problem. Keep the two words eligible (the A/B rule) and placed after all prerequisites (the C rule) in separate boxes in your head.

                                              Two more details: a course cannot be studied again once passed, and at the beginning of every task Jeff has passed nothing (no advanced standing), so he can only start with the start courses. “Eligible to study” is not the same as “passed”: passing a course is what Jeff pays its difficulty for (Task A).

                                              A fact worth proving to yourself

                                              Because the graph has no cycle, every course can eventually be studied (when nothing is blocked). Why? Take any course. If it has no prerequisite you are done. Otherwise pick one prerequisite, then one prerequisite of that, and so on. If this went on for ever it would have to revisit a course, which would be a cycle, and cycles do not exist. So it must stop at a start course, and the chain read backwards is a way to reach your course. Task B quietly relies on this: before the trouble starts, nobody is stuck.

                                              Play with the network

                                              The tool below draws a network from the notation a>b and lets you play Jeff by hand. It never searches for the answer for you; it only applies the eligibility rule when you click. Things to try:

                                              1. Task A, sample 1. Press 3, then 4, then 2. Does the red target course 1 become eligible (it turns on its own)? What is the total? Can you find a route with a smaller total? (The statement says 9 is the best.)
                                              2. The greedy trap. Choose the example “Greedy trap” and take the cheapest start course first. Compare with the other route.
                                              3. Task B, sample 1. Switch the mode to Never pass s and keep passing everything that is green. Which courses stay grey when you run out of moves? Is the number the statement’s answer (2)?
                                              4. Your own. Type a small network yourself (for example 0>1 0>2 1>3 2>3) and look at it. A course with two incoming arrows needs one of them only.

                                              Course network: look, or play Jeff by hand

                                              What the input file looks like

                                              LineTask ATasks B and C
                                              1n mn m
                                              2n integers: the difficulty c0 … cn−1(this line does not exist)
                                              next ma b per line: a is a prerequisite of ba b per line
                                              lastss

                                              The extra line of difficulties in Task A is easy to forget when you copy the reading code from one task to another. Notice too that m can be 0 (then the lines of relationships are simply missing and s comes right after the difficulties or after n m).

                                              How would you store it?

                                              Before any algorithm, ask what the program will have to look up again and again. In all three tasks you will want to know “which courses does this course lead to?” and, in some, “how many prerequisites does this course have?” A table of n × n yes/no entries would need 1010 cells for n = 100 000, which is far too big. The lecture shows the alternative that costs only n + m cells: lists of neighbours (see the matrix-versus-lists tool there).

                                              Part 3 · Task A · 4 marks per test, 10 tests

                                              Task A: the easiest study path (40%)

                                              What it asks

                                              Course s is the one Jeff wants to study. He needs to become eligible for it. Each course i has a difficulty ci (between 1 and 10). A study path is the chain of courses he passes on the way. Output the smallest possible total difficulty of such a chain.

                                              Reading the statement carefully

                                              • Which courses are charged? The ones Jeff passes before he may study s. Course s itself is not passed and not charged. The first sample proves it: the answer 9 is 2 + 4 + 3, the difficulties of courses 3, 4 and 2, and the target course 1 (difficulty 1) is left out.
                                              • Only one chain is needed. Because of the “at least one prerequisite” rule (Part 2), Jeff never has to pass all prerequisites of s. One chain from a start course to one prerequisite of s is enough. The question is which chain is cheapest.
                                              • If s has no prerequisite the answer is 0 (samples 2 and 3): he is eligible at the very beginning and has paid nothing.
                                              • Every course on the chain is charged once, at its own difficulty, whether it is the first, a middle one or the last one before s.

                                              Sample 1 as a table of all possible routes

                                              The network of sample 1 is in the tool above (example “Task A, sample 1”). Course 1 has two prerequisites, 0 and 2, so a route ends at 0 or at 2. Here is every chain from a start course (3 and 8 are the start courses) that makes course 1 eligible; the difficulties are c0 = 8, c2 = 3, c3 = 2, c4 = 4, c7 = 8, c8 = 9:

                                              Chain of courses passedEnds at a prerequisite of 1?Total difficulty
                                              3 → 4 → 2yes (2)2 + 4 + 3 = 9
                                              3 → 0yes (0)2 + 8 = 10
                                              8 → 7 → 2yes (2)9 + 8 + 3 = 20
                                              8 → 7 → 4 → 2yes (2)9 + 8 + 4 + 3 = 24

                                              The smallest is 9. Notice something about the table: the “obvious” cheap start (course 3, difficulty 2) is part of the best chain here, but that was luck. The next example shows why you cannot just look at the first step.

                                              The greedy trap

                                              Here is a network of my own (it is in the tool: example “Greedy trap”). Courses 0 and 1 are start courses with difficulties 1 and 4; course 0 leads to course 2 (difficulty 9), course 1 leads to course 3 (difficulty 1), and both 2 and 3 lead to the target 4. If Jeff always takes the cheapest next step he starts with course 0 (cost 1) but then must pay 9 for course 2: total 10. The other route costs 4 + 1 = 5. A path that is cheap at the beginning can be expensive later, so the answer cannot be built by only looking one step ahead. Any correct method has to compare whole chains, in an organised way.

                                              Hint ladder

                                              Hint 1 · say it in your own words

                                              Write one sentence: “I look for a ___ from a ___ course to a ___ of s whose ___ is smallest.” Then check your sentence against the table above: does it give 9 for sample 1 and 0 for samples 2 and 3? If your sentence would charge course 1 as well, or would require passing every prerequisite of s, re-read the first two bullets of “Reading the statement carefully”.

                                              Hint 2 · a smaller question that is easier

                                              Instead of the whole problem, ask for every course v separately: what is the least total difficulty Jeff must pay before he is allowed to study v? Call it the price of v.

                                              • Which courses have price 0?
                                              • Suppose you already know the price of each prerequisite u of v. Jeff needs just one of the u’s: pay the price of u and then also pass u itself. How would you combine this over the different prerequisites of v? Write it as a formula and test it on the greedy-trap example.

                                              The task is then “the price of s”. The rest of the work is: in what order can the prices be found, so that when you compute one you already know the ones it needs?

                                              Hint 3 · finding the order, and the data structure

                                              Open this one only after you have really tried Hint 2. There are at least two correct ways to organise the order of work, so you can choose:

                                              • This is a shortest-path problem (the “length” of a step into course u is cu, always a positive number). The classical method for positive lengths always finishes next the course with the smallest known price among those not finished yet. To get “the smallest one” quickly you need a structure from the lectures: a priority queue (a heap, Chapter 9). Dijkstra’s algorithm is explained in this course in Tutorial 2 (step by step, and its code and cost, including the version with a priority queue). Read how it works, think about how it must change for costs that sit on courses instead of on arrows, and then write it yourself.
                                              • The other way uses the promise that there are no cycles to process the courses in an order where every prerequisite is handled before the course that needs it (Task C builds such an order).

                                              The statement’s hint of O((n + m) log n) is what the first way costs: each of the m relationships is looked at a constant number of times and each priority-queue operation costs O(log n). Either method is fine if it is correct and fast enough.

                                              Hint 4 · traps in the details
                                              • Several start courses. All of them have price 0 from the very beginning, not just the first one you read.
                                              • What you add, and when. The difficulty of a course is paid when it is passed, so it enters the price of the courses after it. Check that s’s own difficulty never enters the answer (the sample 1 table).
                                              • Sizes. At most 100 000 courses with difficulty at most 10 means any total is at most about 106: a plain int is enough. A matrix of 105 × 105 is not possible; use lists (Part 2).
                                              • No unreachable courses. By the fact in Part 2 every course has a price, so you do not need a special answer for “impossible”.
                                              • Output: one integer on one line, nothing else.
                                              Hint 5 · test it before you trust it

                                              Run samples 1 to 3, then your own small networks where you know the answer by hand. Good ones: s is a start course; s has exactly one prerequisite which is a start course; two chains with the same total; the greedy trap (answer 5); a single long chain of 100 000 courses (an answer of several hundred thousand, and a test that your program survives a very long chain without crashing); a network with 100 000 courses and no relationships at all. Finally time the two big public tests A-4 and A-5; they should finish well inside one second.

                                              Common slips in this task

                                              • Charging s as well (answer too big by cs).
                                              • Requiring all prerequisites of a course (the “AND” rule belongs to Task C only).
                                              • Following the cheapest first step instead of comparing whole chains.
                                              • Reading the input without the line of difficulties, or reading it in the wrong order (a b means a is a prerequisite of b).
                                              • Finding the best chain to every course but taking the minimum over all courses (the answer is the price of s only).

                                              When you have your own program

                                              Compare your approach with my worked solution in Part 7 (unofficial; the official one will follow). Compare the method and the running time first, then test your own program on the samples.

                                              Part 4 · Task B · 3 marks per test, 10 tests

                                              Task B: what breaks if s cannot be passed (30%)

                                              What it asks

                                              Ben, the advisor, says “if you cannot pass course s, many other courses become impossible”. Jeff wants to check this: how many courses other than s can never be studied if s can never be passed? “Can be studied” means: reachable by the eligibility rules of Part 2, starting from the courses that have no prerequisite.

                                              Reading the statement carefully

                                              • The “at least one” rule is back. A course with several prerequisites keeps being studyable as long as one of its prerequisites can still be reached.
                                              • s is not counted (“excluding course s”), even though it is certainly lost.
                                              • If s is itself a start course, the other start courses are still available.
                                              • The input has no line of difficulties (Part 2): it is n m, then the m relationships, then s.
                                              • By the fact in Part 2, before anything is removed every course can be studied, so there is no need to treat “already unreachable” courses separately.

                                              Sample 1 as a table

                                              Choose the example “Task B, sample 1” and the mode Never pass s in the tool of Part 2. The network has 9 courses and s = 3. Go through the courses one by one:

                                              CourseIts prerequisitesCan still be studied without 3?Because
                                              8noneyesa start course
                                              78yes8 is available
                                              43, 7yes3 is gone, but 7 is enough
                                              24, 7yes4 or 7
                                              51, 4yes4 is available
                                              61, 5yes5 is available
                                              03noits only prerequisite is 3
                                              10noits only prerequisite is 0, which is lost

                                              Two courses are lost (0 and 1), so the answer is 2.

                                              The wrong idea that looks right

                                              “Count everything that comes after s.” In this network the courses that can be reached from 3 by following arrows are 0, 1, 4, 2, 5 and 6: that would give 6, not 2. Courses 4, 2, 5 and 6 are after 3, but each of them has another way in. A course is lost only if every route to it from a start course passes through s. Keep this sentence; it is what Task B means.

                                              Hint ladder

                                              Hint 1 · turn the question around

                                              Asking “which courses depend on s?” is awkward, because you would have to examine each course and all its routes. Ask instead: “if s is removed from the network, which courses can still be studied?” If you knew that set, how would you get the answer to Task B from n, the size of the set and the fact that s is not counted?

                                              Hint 2 · exploring what is reachable

                                              The set of courses that can be studied is built like this: start with the courses that have no prerequisite; any course with an arrow from a studyable course is itself studyable (the “at least one” rule!); and so on until nothing new appears. Which algorithm from Chapter 3 explores everything that can be reached from some starting vertices, visiting each vertex once and each arrow once, in O(n + m) time? Several start courses are fine: begin with all of them at once. The only change caused by “s cannot be passed” is what the exploration is not allowed to do with s.

                                              Hint 3 · check your idea by hand first

                                              Do the exploration on sample 1 with a pencil, writing which courses you have visited. Does your method give the same eight rows of the table? Then do sample 2 (answer 0: no course depends only on course 2). Use the Never pass s mode of the tool to check your pencil work.

                                              Hint 4 · traps in the details
                                              • Do not count s. It is never reached, so it would look “lost” in your count; subtract it or skip it.
                                              • Speed. Testing every course separately for “is there a route that avoids s?” takes O(n · (n + m)), roughly 4 · 1010 steps for the largest tests. That is about half of the tests lost. One exploration for the whole network is enough.
                                              • Depth. A network can be a single chain of 100 000 courses. A recursive exploration then calls itself 100 000 times deep, which may crash with a stack overflow. An exploration that uses its own explicit queue or stack does not have this problem.
                                              • Duplicates. Several courses can lead to the same course; make sure you visit a course only once.
                                              • Edge case: n = 1 and m = 0 (then s = 0 and the answer is 0).
                                              Hint 5 · small cases with known answers

                                              For tiny networks you can find the answer by eye. Use these to test your program (courses are numbered from 0):

                                              • A chain 0>1 1>2 2>3 with s = 1: courses 2 and 3 are lost: 2.
                                              • A diamond 0>1 0>2 1>3 2>3 with s = 1: course 3 can still be reached through 2: 0.
                                              • The same chain with s = 0 (a start course): courses 1, 2, 3 are all lost: 3.
                                              • 0>2 1>2 with s = 0: course 2 can still be reached from the start course 1: 0.

                                              Then run B-4 and B-5 (about 7 500 and 92 000 courses) and time them.

                                              When you have your own program

                                              Compare your approach with my worked solution in Part 8 (unofficial; the official one will follow). Compare the method and the running time first, then test your own program on the samples.

                                              Part 5 · Task C · 3 marks per test, 10 tests

                                              Task C: one tidy order for all courses (30%)

                                              What it asks

                                              Jeff wants to line up all courses so that for every relationship A → B, course A stands before course B. Many lines are possible, so he adds a rule to make the line unique: whenever there is a tie, the course with the smaller id goes first. The first course in the line gets the ordering number 1, the next 2, and so on. Output the ordering number of the given course s.

                                              Reading the statement carefully

                                              • This is the “all prerequisites” rule, not the “at least one” rule of Tasks A and B. A course may be placed only after every course that points to it.
                                              • What is a “tie”? At any moment some courses are ready to be placed (everything that must come before them has already been placed). If more than one is ready, the one with the smallest id goes next. It does not mean “sort all courses by id”: course 2 may have to wait for course 9 if 9 is its prerequisite.
                                              • Ordering numbers start at 1, not 0.
                                              • No difficulties line (Part 2).

                                              Sample 1, step by step

                                              Choose “Task C, sample 1” in the tool of Part 2 (8 courses). The prerequisites are: 0 needs 3; 1 needs 0 and 2; 2 needs 4; 3 needs 7; 4 needs 3; 5 needs 1 and 4; 6 needs 1 and 5; 7 needs nothing. Now build the line one place at a time, always looking at the ready courses:

                                              PlaceReady courses (all prerequisites already placed)Smallest id → goes hereLine so far
                                              1777
                                              23 (7 is placed)37, 3
                                              30 and 4 (both only needed 3)0 (smaller id)7, 3, 0
                                              44 (1 still waits for 2; 2 waits for 4)47, 3, 0, 4
                                              5227, 3, 0, 4, 2
                                              61 (0 and 2 are placed; 5 still waits for 1)17, 3, 0, 4, 2, 1
                                              755…, 5
                                              8667, 3, 0, 4, 2, 1, 5, 6

                                              The target s = 4 stands at place 4, so the answer is 4 (the statement’s own explanation says the same). In sample 2 every course must wait for the previous one, the line is 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, and course 4 has ordering number 5.

                                              A small example where the tie rule matters

                                              Take 4 courses and the relationships 3>2 and 1>0. The start courses are 1 and 3. Place 1 first. Now course 0 has become ready too, and 0 is smaller than 3, so it goes before 3: the line is 1, 0, 3, 2. The ordering number of course 0 is 2. A program that just lets courses wait in a simple first-come-first-served line would produce 1, 3, 0, 2 and answer 3. Both lines respect the prerequisites; only the first one follows the tie rule. The structure that always hands you the smallest waiting value is the key to this task.

                                              Hint ladder

                                              Hint 1 · do it by hand, then say what you did

                                              Produce the line for sample 1 on paper, exactly like the table, then describe in one or two sentences what you did at every place. What did you have to know about each course to decide that it was ready? (Think: how many of its prerequisites are still not placed?)

                                              Hint 2 · what has to be updated when you place a course

                                              When you place a course, which other courses can change? Only the ones it points to: each of them now has one fewer waiting prerequisite. When that number reaches zero, the course has become ready. If you keep for every course a count of its unplaced prerequisites and a list of the courses it points to (the graph as lists), each relationship is handled exactly once. The traversal in Chapter 3 has the same flavour: a collection of things to process, and a rule for what to take next.

                                              Hint 3 · “smallest ready course” needs the right container

                                              You have a changing collection of ready courses and must repeatedly take out the smallest id, then add newly ready ones. A plain list that you scan each time costs O(n) per step, which is too slow for 100 000 courses. Which structure from the lectures supports “insert” and “extract the minimum” in O(log n)? (Priority queues; the standard library also has an ordered set, a balanced tree from Chapter 8.) Each course goes in once and comes out once, so the total is O((n + m) log n), the statement’s hint. A reminder: the library priority_queue gives the largest element first unless you change its comparison; the header <functional> is in the allowed list for a reason.

                                              Hint 4 · traps in the details
                                              • A course must enter the ready collection exactly once, at the moment its count of unplaced prerequisites reaches 0 (not when the first prerequisite is placed: that would be the Task A/B rule).
                                              • Ordering numbers start at 1. Count the places while you take courses out, and stop when you take out s (or go on to the end; both are fine).
                                              • Courses without prerequisites are ready at the start: all of them, not just course 0.
                                              • Because the network has no cycle, every course eventually becomes ready, so the line always contains all n courses.
                                              Hint 5 · test it

                                              Samples 1 and 2 first. Then try: the example above (answer 2); one chain (the answer is the position in the chain); no relationships at all (the order is simply 0, 1, 2, … and the answer is s + 1); s a late course with many prerequisites. Then check speed on C-4 and C-5 (about 12 000 and 98 000 courses).

                                              Common slips in this task

                                              • Using the Task A/B rule (“one prerequisite is enough”) and placing a course too early.
                                              • Sorting all ids and then “fixing” the order, or using a simple first-in-first-out line, which gives a valid line but not the one with the tie rule.
                                              • Off-by-one: ordering number 0 for the first course.
                                              • Scanning for the smallest ready course with a loop (correct for tiny inputs, too slow for the large tests).

                                              When you have your own program

                                              Compare your approach with my worked solution in Part 9 (unofficial; the official one will follow). Compare the method and the running time first, then test your own program on the samples.

                                              Part 6 · Before you submit

                                              Testing, speed and the last checklist

                                              Why the public tests are not enough

                                              The public tests are only five per task, and three of those are the statement’s samples. The ten hidden tests per task include situations those do not cover. You can make your own tests cheaply, and they are the best protection against a zero.

                                              Build a slow, obviously correct checker

                                              For tiny inputs (say up to 7 courses) you can solve each task in a way that is hopelessly slow but easy to trust, and compare it with your fast program on hundreds of random inputs. This is called stress testing. The slow versions are easy to describe (and writing them is quick, because they do not need to be clever):

                                              • Task A: list all chains of courses from a start course to a prerequisite of s (the table in Part 3 does this by hand) and take the smallest total.
                                              • Task B: for each course, check by trying every way in whether it can still be reached when s is not allowed.
                                              • Task C: try every ordering of the courses, keep those in which every prerequisite comes before the course that needs it, and take the one that is smallest when read as a list of ids.

                                              To generate a random network with no cycle: first choose a secret random order of the courses, then add each possible relationship only from an earlier course of that order to a later one, each with some probability. Finally give the courses random ids (do not use the secret order as the ids), otherwise your tests will be too friendly: for Task C especially, an input in which prerequisites always have smaller ids hides most of the tie-breaking.

                                              Speed

                                              • Compile with g++ -std=c++14 -O2 and time the big public tests (A-5, B-5, C-5): on Linux or macOS time ./main < TaskA/A-5.in > /dev/null. The limit is 1 second on the grader’s machine, so aim for a few tenths of a second.
                                              • Reading is a hidden cost. About 700Up to 900 000 numbers can be on the inputthinsp;000 numbers can be on the input; cin is slow unless you turn off its synchronisation with C streams, and the statement recommends getchar / scanf for large inputs. Printing is not a problem here: each task prints a single number.
                                              • If you use recursion for a task, ask how deep it can go. A chain of 100 000 courses makes a recursion 100 000 deep; this can crash the grader even if it works on your computer.

                                              The usual ways to get a zero

                                              What goes wrongWhat you see on the graderPrevention
                                              An array is too small (for example size 100000 for ids up to 99999 plus extra)crash or silly outputAllocate a little more than the largest n and m.
                                              A variable is never initialised“undefined behaviour”: random on the grader, fine on your machineGive every counter and array a value (zero) before use.

                                              Part 7 · Solution to Task A · 40% · unofficial

                                              Worked solution: Task A (cheapest path)

                                              About these programs

                                              These are my own worked solutions, written with the methods of the lectures and the practice sets (the course’s own Dijkstra, breadth-first search and heaps). They are not the official ones; the official solutions will follow when they are released. Each program was compiled with g++ -std=c++14, passes all the sample tests of the assignment package, agrees with a brute-force checker on 1500 random small networks, and runs in about 0.07 s on networks of the maximum size. The cover page says that all submitted work must be your own and goes through similarity-checking software, so treat these as a way to understand the method and to check your own program; write your own version, with your own names and layout.

                                              The idea in three steps

                                              1. One chain is enough. A course with several prerequisites needs only one of them to be passed (Part 2). So to become eligible for s, Jeff passes a chain v1 → v2 → … → vk in which v1 has no prerequisite, each course is a prerequisite of the next, and vk is a prerequisite of s. Its cost is c(v1) + … + c(vk), and we want the cheapest such chain. (If s has no prerequisite, the chain is empty and the cost is 0.)
                                              2. It is a shortest-path problem. Put the cost of passing a course on the arrows that enter it: the arrow v → w costs c(w). Imagine one extra “start” vertex with an arrow to every course that has no prerequisite, again costing c of the course it enters. Then the length of the path start → v1 → … → vk is exactly the cost of the chain. All costs are positive (1 to 10), which is what Dijkstra needs.
                                              3. Dijkstra with a priority queue (Tutorial 2, slide 48). Let dist[v] be the least cost of a chain that ends by passing v (so v is included). Then the cheapest way to make s eligible is the best dist over the prerequisites of s, and since dist[s] = (that best value) + c(s), the answer is dist[s] − c[s]. If s is itself a start course, dist[s] = c(s) and the answer is 0, as the samples 2 and 3 require.

                                              Why not “always take the cheapest next course”

                                              A cheap first course can lead to an expensive second one. In the “greedy trap” of Part 3 the cheap start (cost 1) leads to a course that costs 9, while the dearer start (cost 4) leads to a course that costs 1. Dijkstra does not commit early: it always extends the cheapest total so far, which is why it finds the 4 + 1 = 5.

                                              Pseudocode, in the style of the lecture’s Dijkstra

                                              PassCost(G, c, s) { /* dist(x) = least total difficulty of a path that ends by passing x */ dist(x) = INF for every course x; PQ = empty priority queue of pairs (distance, course); for every course x that has no prerequisite { dist(x) = c(x); insert (c(x), x) into PQ; } while PQ is not empty do { (d, v) = extract the smallest pair of PQ; if d > dist(v) then continue; /* an old entry: v was improved after it was inserted */ if v = s then stop; /* dist(s) is now final */ for all edges (v, w) in E if dist(w) > dist(v) + c(w) { dist(w) = dist(v) + c(w); /* relax: a cheaper way to finish w */ insert (dist(w), w) into PQ; } } return dist(s) - c(s); /* s itself is not passed */}

                                              The only changes from the lecture’s code are that the source is “every start course at once” (the extra start vertex), that the edge length is c(w) of the course entered, and that we insert a new pair instead of lowering a key (the priority_queue of C++ has no “lower the key”; old pairs are recognised and skipped).

                                              The C++14 program

                                              #include <cstdio>#include <vector>#include <queue>#include <functional>#include <utility>using namespace std; typedef pair<int, int> pii; // (distance, course) int main() { int n, m; scanf("%d %d", &n, &m); vector<int> c(n); for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) scanf("%d", &c[i]); vector<vector<int> > next(n); // next[a]: courses that need a vector<int> hasPre(n, 0); // 1 if the course has a prerequisite for (int i = 0; i < m; i++) { int a, b; scanf("%d %d", &a, &b); next[a].push_back(b); hasPre[b] = 1; } int s; scanf("%d", &s); // dist[v] = least total difficulty of a path ending with course v const int INF = 1000000000; vector<int> dist(n, INF); priority_queue<pii, vector<pii>, greater<pii> > pq; // min-heap for (int v = 0; v < n; v++) { // every start course if (!hasPre[v]) { dist[v] = c[v]; pq.push(make_pair(dist[v], v)); } } while (!pq.empty()) { pii top = pq.top(); pq.pop(); int d = top.first, v = top.second; if (d > dist[v]) continue; // old entry, skip it if (v == s) break; // dist[s] is final for (size_t i = 0; i < next[v].size(); i++) { int w = next[v][i]; if (d + c[w] < dist[w]) { dist[w] = d + c[w]; pq.push(make_pair(dist[w], w)); } } } printf("%d\n", dist[s] - c[s]); // s itself is not passed return 0;}
                                              vector<vector<int> > next(n)

                                              the adjacency lists of Chapter 3: next[a] holds every course that has a as a prerequisite. With m ≤ 300 000 an adjacency matrix (1010 cells) is out of the question.

                                              hasPre[b] = 1

                                              remembers which courses have a prerequisite; the others are the start courses.

                                              const int INF = 1000000000

                                              “infinity”. The largest possible answer is 10 × 100 000 = 106, so INF is never reached and d + c[w] never overflows (we only add to a d that came out of the queue, which is finite).

                                              priority_queue<pii, vector<pii>, greater<pii> > pq

                                              a min-heap of (distance, course) pairs (pii is a short name for pair<int, int>). By default C++ gives the largest on top; greater flips it. This is the priority queue of Chapter 9.

                                              dist[v] = c[v]; pq.push(...)

                                              every start course begins with its own difficulty.

                                              if (d > dist[v]) continue

                                              skips old entries (a course can be inserted several times, once for each time its dist was lowered).

                                              if (v == s) break

                                              the first time s comes out of the queue its dist is final (Dijkstra’s argument), so there is no need to go on.

                                              if (d + c[w] < dist[w])

                                              the relax step of the lecture.

                                              printf("%d\n", dist[s] - c[s])

                                              the answer. Every course has a path to the start, so dist[s] is finite.

                                              Why it is correct

                                              • Chains and paths are the same thing. A chain from a start course to a prerequisite of s is a path from the extra start vertex to s with the last arrow removed; its cost is the path length minus c(s). Every path to s has the form (a chain) + (last arrow into s), so the shortest path to s has length (cheapest chain) + c(s), provided the chain is allowed to end at any prerequisite of s. For the start course s the only path is the single arrow start → s, length c(s), answer 0.
                                              • Dijkstra is right. All arrow lengths are positive, so when a course leaves the queue with the smallest pair, no later route can be cheaper (the lecture’s argument: any other route has to go through a vertex that is still unfinished, and that vertex already has a distance at least as large). The loop therefore finalises courses in the order of their distance, and dist[s] is right when s leaves the queue.
                                              • The “at least one” rule is the reason that only one chain is needed. Had the rule been “all prerequisites”, we would have to pay for a whole set of courses and this would be a different (and harder) problem.

                                              Running time and memory

                                              • Reading the input and building next: O(n + m).
                                              • A pair is inserted at most once per start course and once per successful relax. A relax happens only while the course on the other end is being finalised for the first time, so there are at most m of them: at most n + m insertions in total. Every insertion and every extraction costs O(log(n + m)) = O(log n) (because m ≤ n2 gives log m ≤ 2 log n).
                                              • Total: O((n + m) log n), the speed the statement asks for. Memory: O(n + m).

                                              (Because the network has no cycles and every c is at most 10, there are even faster ways, such as adding the costs along a topological order in O(n + m); I used Dijkstra because it is the method of the course and is what the hint expects.)

                                              Sample 1, step by step

                                              Costs: c = 8, 1, 3, 2, 4, 2, 5, 8, 9, 7 for courses 0 to 9; the target is s = 1. The start courses (no prerequisite) are 3 and 8, so the queue starts as (2, 3), (9, 8).

                                              StepSmallest pair taken outCourses lowered (new dist)Queue afterwards
                                              1(2, 3)0 → 10, 4 → 6(6,4) (9,8) (10,0)
                                              2(6, 4)2 → 9, 5 → 8(8,5) (9,2) (9,8) (10,0)
                                              3(8, 5)6 → 13, 9 → 15(9,2) (9,8) (10,0) (13,6) (15,9)
                                              4(9, 2)1 → 10(9,8) (10,0) (10,1) (13,6) (15,9)
                                              5(9, 8)7 → 17(10,0) (10,1) (13,6) (15,9) (17,7)
                                              6(10, 0)none (10 + 1 = 11 is not below dist[1] = 10)(10,1) (13,6) (15,9) (17,7)
                                              7(10, 1): the targetstopanswer = 10 − c(1) = 10 − 1 = 9

                                              The chain is 3 → 4 → 2 with costs 2 + 4 + 3 = 9, exactly the statement’s explanation. Notice step 6: the other prerequisite of course 1, namely course 0, would have cost 2 + 8 = 10, so it does not win.

                                              Run the three programs step by step on a small network (this one is set to Task A)

                                              Where marks are lost in Task A

                                              • Printing dist[s] instead of dist[s] − c[s] (the statement does not charge for s itself): sample 1 would print 10 instead of 9.
                                              • Starting Dijkstra from one course only (say course 0). There can be several start courses, and the start must be all of them.
                                              • Treating the relationships as undirected, or reading a b as “b is a prerequisite of a”.
                                              • Forgetting that the cost sits on the course, not on the arrow: a start course must begin with dist = its own c, not 0.
                                              • A greedy walk (“always take the cheapest next course”) or a depth-first search that tries every chain: the first is wrong (the trap), the second is exponential on the large tests.
                                              • Using priority_queue without greater: it then hands out the largest pair first and the output is wrong.
                                              • Recursion: avoid it here. A chain of 100 000 courses would need a call stack that deep.

                                              Test report

                                              Package samples A-1 to A-5: all 5 pass. Random networks with up to 9 courses, 1500 cases in total across the three tasks: the program agrees with a brute-force program that tries every chain (Task A), simulates the eligibility rule until nothing changes (Task B) and searches all permutations for the smallest valid order (Task C). Networks with 100 000 courses and up to 300 000 relationships (random, local and one long chain): outputs agree with an independent program that computes the same numbers in a different way, and the running time is about 0.07 s. A chain of 100 000 courses of difficulty 10 gives 999 990, so 32-bit integers are enough.

                                              Part 8 · Solution to Task B · 30% · unofficial

                                              Worked solution: Task B (lost courses)

                                              The idea in two steps

                                              1. Turn “depends completely on s” around. It is awkward to ask which courses depend on s. It is easy to ask the opposite question: if s can never be passed, which courses can still be studied? A course can still be studied if it has no prerequisite, or if at least one of its prerequisites can still be studied. The lost courses are everyone else, except s itself, which the statement does not count.
                                              2. That is a graph search. Start from every course without a prerequisite (but not s, even if s has none), follow the arrows, and never enter s. A course the search reaches can still be studied. This is the breadth-first search of Chapter 3 with several starting vertices at once. The answer is (n − 1) minus the number of reached courses (the − 1 removes s, which is never reached).

                                              Do not count “everything after s”

                                              In sample 1 the courses that can be reached from s = 3 by following arrows are 0, 1, 4, 2, 5 and 6, six courses, but the answer is 2: courses 4, 2, 5 and 6 each have another way in (7, 8 or 4), so they are not lost. A course is lost only if every route to it from a start course goes through s. The search above gets this right automatically, because it simply asks who can still be reached.

                                              Pseudocode, in the style of the lecture’s BFS

                                              LostCourses(G, s) { Queue Q; bit reached[n]; INIT(Q); reached[0..n-1] = all 0's; for every course x with no prerequisite and x != s { reached[x] = 1; Q.Enqueue(x); /* the start courses (but never s) */ } count = 0; while (!empty(Q)) { v = Q.Dequeue(); count++; for each neighbor w of v /* the courses that v unlocks */ if (w != s and !reached[w]) { reached[w] = 1; Q.Enqueue(w); /* marked when put on the queue, so it is queued only once */ } } return n - 1 - count;}

                                              This is the lecture’s BFS with two changes: the queue starts with all the start courses, and s is a closed door. It also uses the improved marking from the lecture (mark a vertex when it is put on the queue), so every course enters the queue at most once.

                                              The C++14 program

                                              #include <cstdio>#include <vector>#include <queue>using namespace std; int main() { int n, m; scanf("%d %d", &n, &m); vector<vector<int> > next(n); vector<int> hasPre(n, 0); for (int i = 0; i < m; i++) { int a, b; scanf("%d %d", &a, &b); next[a].push_back(b); hasPre[b] = 1; } int s; scanf("%d", &s); // BFS from every start course, never entering s vector<int> reached(n, 0); queue<int> q; for (int v = 0; v < n; v++) { if (!hasPre[v] && v != s) { reached[v] = 1; q.push(v); } } int count = 0; while (!q.empty()) { int v = q.front(); q.pop(); count++; for (size_t i = 0; i < next[v].size(); i++) { int w = next[v][i]; if (w != s && !reached[w]) { reached[w] = 1; q.push(w); } } } printf("%d\n", n - 1 - count); // all but s, minus the reachable return 0;}
                                              if (!hasPre[v] && v != s)

                                              the start courses, except s (if s has no prerequisite, Jeff could have studied it, but in this question he never passes it, so it must not start a search).

                                              reached[v] = 1; q.push(v)

                                              mark when queued, as in the lecture’s improved BFS. Each course enters the queue once.

                                              count++

                                              one more course that can still be studied.

                                              if (w != s && !reached[w])

                                              never walk into s, and never queue a course twice.

                                              printf("%d\n", n - 1 - count)

                                              all courses except s (that is n − 1), minus those that can still be studied.

                                              Why it is correct

                                              • What the search reaches is exactly the set of studyable courses. By induction on the length of the shortest route: a start course (not s) is studyable; if a course v is studyable, then every course w ≠ s with an arrow v → w is studyable, because w needs only one prerequisite passed (the “at least one” rule) and v can be passed. Conversely, a studyable course has a chain of passed courses from a start course, which is a route that avoids s, so the search finds it.
                                              • s is never counted. It is never marked reached, so n − 1 − count counts only the other courses.

                                              Running time

                                              Each course enters the queue at most once and leaves it once, and each arrow is looked at once when its tail leaves the queue: O(n + m) time and memory, as the hint says. There is no recursion, so no deep-stack problem for a chain of 100 000 courses.

                                              Sample 1, step by step

                                              Nine courses, s = 3. The start courses without s: course 8 (course 3 is excluded). Queue: 8.

                                              Take from the queueNewly reachedReached so far
                                              878, 7
                                              72, 48, 7, 2, 4
                                              2none (2 has no arrows out)same
                                              45 (2 is already reached)8, 7, 2, 4, 5
                                              568, 7, 2, 4, 5, 6
                                              6none6 courses reached: answer 9 − 1 − 6 = 2 (courses 0 and 1)

                                              Sample 2: course 0 is the only start course, every other course is below it and nothing is lost when s = 2: 6 − 1 − 5 = 0. (Courses 3 and 4 can be reached through 0 and 1.)

                                              Use the demo of Part 7 and switch the program to Task B.

                                              Where marks are lost in Task B

                                              • Counting the descendants of s (everything reachable from s): wrong, as the sample shows (6 instead of 2).
                                              • Counting s itself in the answer: off by one. The statement says “excluding course s”.
                                              • Starting the search from s’s start course when s has no prerequisite: s must stay closed even then. (Test: n = 3, relationships 0→2 and 1→2, s = 0: course 1 is still a start course, course 2 can still be studied, answer 0.)
                                              • Forgetting that a course with several prerequisites needs only one of them (Task C’s rule is the other way round).
                                              • A recursive DFS: fine for the small tests, but a chain of 100 000 courses can overflow the call stack. BFS with a queue has no such problem. (An iterative DFS with stack<int> would work as well.)
                                              • Reading a line of difficulties: Task B and Task C have none. The input is n m, then the relationships, then s.

                                              Test report

                                              Package samples B-1 to B-5: all 5 pass. Agreement with the brute-force program (it repeats “a course is studyable if one of its prerequisites is” until nothing changes) on random small networks, and with an independent program on networks of 100 000 courses and up to 300 000 relationships; about 0.06 s per test.

                                              Part 9 · Solution to Task C · 30% · unofficial

                                              Worked solution: Task C (ordering)

                                              The idea

                                              This time the rule is “all prerequisites first”. Build the line one place at a time. At every moment the ready courses are those whose prerequisites have all been placed. Whichever ready course has the smallest id goes to the next place; this is what the tie rule says, and it is the only choice that fits it, since nothing but a ready course may be placed. Placing a course may make other courses ready.

                                              1. Keep, for every course, the number of prerequisites not yet placed (waiting[v], at the start the number of arrows entering v). A course is ready when this number is 0.
                                              2. Keep the ready courses in a priority queue with the smallest id on top (Chapter 9). A plain first-in-first-out queue would be wrong: see the example below.
                                              3. Repeat: take the smallest ready course, give it the next number 1, 2, 3, …, and for every course it unlocks lower waiting by one; whoever reaches 0 enters the priority queue. Stop when the target s is placed: its number is the answer.

                                              Pseudocode

                                              OrderOf(G, s) { waiting(v) = number of edges entering v, for every course v; PQ = empty priority queue of course ids (smallest id first); for every course v with waiting(v) = 0 insert v into PQ; place = 0; while PQ is not empty do { v = extract the smallest id of PQ; place = place + 1; /* v gets the ordering number place */ if v = s then return place; for all edges (v, w) in E { waiting(w) = waiting(w) - 1; if waiting(w) = 0 then insert w into PQ; /* w is ready now */ } }}

                                              It is the BFS of Chapter 3 with two changes: a course joins the queue only when all its prerequisites are placed (the counter), and the queue hands out the smallest id instead of the oldest course.

                                              The C++14 program

                                              #include <cstdio>#include <vector>#include <queue>#include <functional>using namespace std; int main() { int n, m; scanf("%d %d", &n, &m); vector<vector<int> > next(n); vector<int> waiting(n, 0); // prerequisites not yet placed for (int i = 0; i < m; i++) { int a, b; scanf("%d %d", &a, &b); next[a].push_back(b); waiting[b]++; } int s; scanf("%d", &s); priority_queue<int, vector<int>, greater<int> > ready; // min-heap for (int v = 0; v < n; v++) { if (waiting[v] == 0) ready.push(v); } int place = 0; while (!ready.empty()) { int v = ready.top(); ready.pop(); place++; if (v == s) { printf("%d\n", place); return 0; } for (size_t i = 0; i < next[v].size(); i++) { int w = next[v][i]; waiting[w]--; if (waiting[w] == 0) ready.push(w); } } return 0;}
                                              waiting[b]++

                                              every relationship a b adds one waiting prerequisite to course b.

                                              priority_queue<int, vector<int>, greater<int> > ready

                                              a min-heap of ids: the smallest ready course is always on top. (Without greater you get the largest id first.)

                                              place++

                                              the ordering numbers start at 1, so count before the test.

                                              if (v == s)

                                              the number we have just given is the answer; no need to finish the line.

                                              waiting[w]-- ; if (waiting[w] == 0) ready.push(w)

                                              the course w had v as one of its prerequisites; it is ready exactly when the last one has been placed.

                                              Why it is correct

                                              • It makes a valid line. A course enters the queue only when all its prerequisites have already been placed, so every prerequisite stands before the course. The network has no cycle, so at every moment some unplaced course is ready (take an unplaced course and walk back along unplaced prerequisites; the walk cannot go on for ever without a cycle) and every course is eventually placed.
                                              • It follows the tie rule. At each place the next course is the smallest id among all courses that could legally stand there (the ready ones). The line the statement describes is exactly the one made by this “smallest ready id first” rule, so the number it gives to s is the required one.

                                              A first-come-first-served queue is not enough

                                              Take 4 courses with the relationships 3→2 and 1→0, and ask for s = 0. The start courses are 1 and 3. Place 1. Course 0 is now ready, and 0 < 3, so it goes next: the line is 1, 0, 3, 2 and the answer is 2. A plain queue would hold 3 (waiting since the start) before 0, giving the line 1, 3, 0, 2 and the wrong answer 3. Try it in the demo of Part 7 (example “Task C, tie-rule example”).

                                              Running time

                                              Every course is inserted into the priority queue once and extracted once, O(log n) each; every arrow is looked at once, when its tail is placed. Total O((n + m) log n), the speed the statement asks for, with O(n + m) memory.

                                              Sample 1, step by step

                                              Eight courses, s = 4. The start course is 7 only.

                                              PlaceSmallest ready courseNewly readyReady courses afterwards
                                              1733
                                              230 and 40, 4
                                              30 (smaller than 4)none (course 1 also needs 2)4
                                              44: the target—answer 4

                                              Sample 2 is a single chain 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5: course 4 gets number 5.

                                              Where marks are lost in Task C

                                              • A plain queue (see above), or a priority_queue without greater, which gives the largest id first.
                                              • “Sort the courses by id”. Course 2 may have to wait for course 9. The tie rule applies only among ready courses.
                                              • Starting the numbering at 0 instead of 1.
                                              • Using the Task A / Task B rule (“at least one prerequisite”). Here every prerequisite must be placed first.
                                              • Putting a course into the queue more than once (for example when its waiting is lowered, instead of when it becomes 0). It would then be placed twice.
                                              • A DFS-based topological sort: it gives a valid order but not the one with the tie rule.

                                              Test report

                                              Package samples C-1 to C-5: all 5 pass. On random networks with up to 7 courses the program’s answer equals the position of s in the first valid order found by trying all permutations in dictionary order (which is exactly the “smallest id first” line). On networks of 100 000 courses and up to 300 000 relationships it agrees with an independent program and takes about 0.06 s.

                                              Programming Assignment 2 Guide and solutions

                                              Three C++ programs: find the largest binary-search-tree and AVL-tree subtrees inside an arbitrary binary tree, count the fewest neighbour swaps that turn one queue into another, and list the cheapest combinations of two sorted price lists. Parts 2 to 5 explain what each task really asks, draw the statement’s samples, list the traps in the wording and give a ladder of hints for every task. Parts 6 to 8 are my own worked solutions: a C++14 program for each task, with the reasoning, the running time, a trace of a sample and a step-by-step demo. They are unofficial; the official solutions will follow when they are released.
