                                                C Cheapest Combinations30% (3 per test)Two price lists, each sorted. List the k cheapest pairs (one price from each), in a fixed order, without generating all n · m pairs.O((n + m + k) log(n + m + k))priority queues, merging sorted listsPart 4Part 8

                                                Task B has the most marks. All three tasks are about the same size of reading, so start each one with the samples drawn in this guide.

                                                The rules on the cover page, in plain words

                                                • C++14, three files. Three .cpp files, uncompressed, named UniversityNumber-A.cpp, -B.cpp, -C.cpp (for example 1234554321-A.cpp). Wrong names lose marks.
                                                • Only these libraries: <iostream>, <cstdio>, <string>, <vector>, <set>, <stack>, <queue>, <algorithm>, <math.h>, <limits>, <functional>, <utility>. Any other header gives 0 marks; the GNU “pbds” containers are not standard and are not allowed.
                                                • Standard input and output only (no files, no system(), no parallel code). For many numbers the statement suggests getchar to read and putchar to write.
                                                • One input file is one test case. Ten hidden tests per task, 1 second each. A test gives its marks only if the program compiles, finishes in time without crashing and prints exactly the right output. Otherwise that test gives 0. (The statement stresses that the target speeds guide the design but only correct output within the time counts.)
                                                • No undefined behaviour: integer overflow, division by zero, uninitialised variables, randomness. These can turn a test into 0.
                                                • The program must compile on the online compiler named in the statement, otherwise it is not checked by hand.

                                                Half of the tests are small

                                                In every task, five of the ten hidden tests are small (Tasks A and B: n ≤ 2000; Task C: n, m ≤ 100) and five use the full limits (up to 200 000). So a simple, obviously correct program, even a slow one, already earns about half of the marks. Write that first, test it, and only then work on the fast version, which you can compare against the simple one. The slow version is also your best self-made checker (Part 5).

                                                The self-test package

                                                The zip contains a self_test folder with test.py and, for every task, twelve public tests (A-1.in / A-1.out up to A-12.in / A-12.out, and the same for B and C). The first few are the statement’s samples; some of the later ones are the big, nasty cases (Part 5 says what to expect). The script’s own safety timeout is 5 seconds, but the real limit is 1 second. On Linux or macOS:

                                                cd self_testg++ -std=c++14 -O2 main.cpp -o main./main < TaskA/A-1.in > myoutput.txtdiff myoutput.txt TaskA/A-1.out # no output means: identicalpython3 test.py main.cpp A # all the public tests of Task A

                                                The script ignores spaces at the end of lines and the Windows-style line endings but not spaces inside a line. The cover page repeats that local results do not decide your grade.

                                                Check your output the way the machine does

                                                Compare my output with the expected output

                                                How to use the hint ladders

                                                Each task has numbered folded hints. Try the task on paper for ten minutes, open Hint 1 only if you are stuck, and go one hint at a time. Early hints restate the problem or ask a question; the later ones name the idea and the traps, and the last one is about checking your work. The final steps are the assignment and are not given.

                                                Part 2 · Task A · 3 marks per test, 10 tests

                                                Task A: Search Subtrees (30%)

                                                What it asks

                                                Bob has drawn a binary tree with an integer key at every node. It is not necessarily a search tree. Somewhere inside it there are subtrees (a node together with everything below it) that happen to be binary search trees, and some of those are even AVL trees. Report, for each of the two kinds, the size (number of nodes) of the largest such subtree and the id of its root. Two lines of output.

                                                Reading the statement carefully

                                                • A subtree is all or nothing. It contains the chosen node and all of its descendants, with their original keys and pointers. You may not cut some descendants away, change keys or rotate. So a node whose subtree has one bad key deep down is not a BST subtree, even if its top part looks fine.
                                                • BST, strictly. At every node, all keys in the left subtree are strictly smaller than its key and all keys in the right subtree are strictly larger. Equal keys are therefore not allowed (sample 2 is built on this). Remember how a BST is defined in Chapter 7: the condition is about the whole subtrees, not just the two children.
                                                • AVL = a BST in which, at every node, the heights of the left and right subtrees differ by at most 1 (the AVL rule). An empty subtree has height −1, a leaf has height 0. A single node is both a BST and an AVL tree, so the answer is never smaller than 1.
                                                • Ties. If several subtrees have the same largest size, output the one whose root has the smallest node id. The two categories (BST, AVL) are decided independently; the AVL winner can be a different node from the BST winner.
                                                • Ids and keys are different things. Node ids are 1 to n (the line number of the input); keys are the values vi in the first column. The output uses ids.

                                                The input format, drawn

                                                First line: n r (the number of nodes and the id of the root). Then n lines in id order; line i is key left right for node i, where a child id of 0 means “no child”. The ids do not tell you any order of the keys: node 2 is not “the second smallest”. The root is not necessarily node 1. Use the tool to see how the lines turn into a tree (the two presets are the statement’s samples) and to inspect any subtree. The tool only reports facts about the subtree you choose; it does not say whether it is a BST.

                                                From input lines to a tree: inspect any subtree

                                                Sample 1, node by node

                                                This is the statement’s first sample (8 nodes, root 1) worked out for every node. Check each row against the picture above.

                                                Node id (key)Size of its subtreeHeightA BST?An AVL tree?Why
                                                4 (key 2)10yesyesa single node
                                                5 (key 12)10yesyesa single node
                                                2 (key 5)31yesyes2 < 5 < 12, both subtrees have height 0
                                                8 (key 30)10yesyesa single node
                                                7 (key 25)21yesyes25 < 30; heights −1 and 0 differ by 1
                                                6 (key 20)32yesnoa chain 20, 25, 30: heights −1 and 1 differ by 2
                                                3 (key 15)43yesnoa chain 15, 20, 25, 30 (a BST, but far out of balance)
                                                1 (key 10)84nonothe key 12 is in its left subtree but is larger than 10

                                                So the biggest BST subtree has size 4 with root 3, and the biggest AVL subtree has size 3 with root 2: output 4 3 and 3 2. Look at the last row: the whole tree fails the BST test only because of key 12, which lies two levels below node 1 and agrees perfectly with its own parent (5). A check that compares each node with its two children never notices this. Every subtree, including the small ones, has to be judged as a whole.

                                                Sample 2 has keys 4, 4, 8, 10 with node 3 (key 8) as root: node 2 (key 4) has a left child with the same key 4, so the subtrees at nodes 2 and 3 are not BSTs. Nodes 1 and 4 are leaves, so both answers have size 1; node 1 wins the tie by id: 1 1 twice.

                                                Hint ladder

                                                Hint 1 · do the sample by hand

                                                Without any program, decide for each node of sample 1 whether its subtree is a BST and whether it is an AVL tree (the table above is the answer; cover it first). For every “no” write down which fact made it fail. You will find that there are exactly two kinds of reasons: one about the keys and one about the heights.

                                                Hint 2 · what does a parent need to know about its children?

                                                The statement asks: “what information from each child subtree would help you decide whether the entire subtree rooted at the parent is a BST or an AVL tree?” Try it with the tool: choose a node, look at the facts it lists, and ask which of them would let you decide without looking inside the child subtrees again.

                                                • For the key rule: you must compare the parent’s key with all keys of the left subtree and all keys of the right subtree. Is there a single number per subtree that is enough for each comparison?
                                                • For the height rule: what do you need from the two children?
                                                • Whether a child subtree is itself a BST or an AVL tree: does it matter for the parent? Why?
                                                • Which facts must the parent pass on to its own parent, so that the information keeps flowing upwards?
                                                Hint 3 · an order that works: children before parents

                                                If the answer for a node depends on its two children, the children have to be handled first. Which traversal order from Chapter 5 visits both children before their parent? Each node is then visited once and does a constant amount of work: O(n) in total, the statement’s target. Two other points: you need to start from the root r, and every node id from 1 to n must be visited exactly once.

                                                Hint 4 · the depth trap

                                                The statement warns: “a long chain may exceed the language’s recursion stack”. A tree that is a single chain of 200 000 nodes makes a recursive function call itself 200 000 times deep, and the program may crash with a stack overflow on the grader even though it works on small tests. The public test A-4 is exactly such a chain. Two ways out: use your own stack (<stack> or a vector) to drive the traversal, or find an order in which the nodes can be processed one after another in a simple loop (for example: first list the nodes in some order that puts every parent before its children, then run through that list backwards; why does this give you children before parents?).

                                                Hint 5 · the answer: ties and bookkeeping
                                                • Every node is a candidate; the best BST and the best AVL are kept separately.
                                                • If you visit nodes in an arbitrary order you cannot rely on “the first one wins”; compare sizes, and for equal sizes compare ids, explicitly.
                                                • The output is two lines, each with two integers separated by one space: size id.
                                                • An AVL subtree is a BST; so the best AVL is never larger than the best BST.
                                                Hint 6 · numbers and edge cases
                                                • Keys lie between −109 and 109 and repeat: they fit an int. If you store a “smallest key” and a “largest key” for each subtree, think about what to store for an empty subtree so that the comparisons still work (a value outside the key range, or a flag), and be careful that a sentinel never equals a real key.
                                                • n = 1: one node, answers 1 1 and 1 1 (if the root is node 1).
                                                • Equal keys: a node and its child with equal keys is not a BST. Strictness matters at both sides.
                                                • The root is given by r; do not assume it is node 1.
                                                Hint 7 · make your own tests

                                                Public test A-4 is the long chain (and its root is node 200 000, not node 1); A-12 is a big tree of 131 071 nodes in which every key is the same, so no subtree with more than one node is a BST. Run both. In addition make small trees (3 to 7 nodes) by hand where you can see the answer: a perfect BST (the whole tree is the answer); a BST with one wrong key near a leaf; a BST where one key at the bottom of the left side is larger than the root (the sample 1 trap); a chain that goes left only; a tree where all keys are equal; a tree in which the largest BST is not the largest AVL.

                                                Common slips in this task

                                                • Comparing a node only with its two children instead of with all keys of each side.
                                                • Allowing equal keys.
                                                • Judging a node’s subtree “good” while a bad node sits further down it (a good top over a bad bottom).
                                                • Counting a subtree that has been trimmed (“the largest BST I can find after removing nodes”) instead of a complete subtree.
                                                • Forgetting that a leaf is height 0 and an empty subtree is −1 in the height rule.
                                                • A recursive solution that crashes on the long chain.

                                                When you have your own program

                                                Compare your approach with my worked solution in Part 6 (unofficial; the official one will follow). Compare the method and the running time first, then test your own program on the samples.

                                                Part 3 · Task B · 4 marks per test, 10 tests

                                                Task B: Restore the Queue (40%)

                                                What it asks

                                                Bob has a queue of n packages with integer labels (labels may repeat). The labels now read A1, …, An from the front. He needs them to read B1, …, Bn. In one move he may swap two neighbouring packages. What is the fewest moves needed? Only the number is asked, not the moves.

                                                Reading the statement carefully

                                                • Only neighbours. A package cannot jump; moving a package five places costs five swaps.
                                                • Equal labels are interchangeable. If the queue has three packages labelled 7, any of them may end up at any target position that wants a 7. The target is a row of labels, not of individual packages. The two rows contain every label the same number of times.
                                                • The target is not necessarily sorted (sample 3: the queue 3 1 3 2 is already the target, answer 0).
                                                • The answer can be big. It “may exceed the signed 32-bit integer range, but fits in a signed 64-bit integer”. The public test B-4 has n = 200 000 and the answer 19 999 900 000, which is nearly ten times the largest 32-bit integer.
                                                • Sizes: n up to 200 000, labels from 1 to n.

                                                The samples

                                                • Sample 1: 2 1 2 3 → 2 2 3 1. Move the 1 two steps to the right: two swaps. The statement’s argument that fewer is impossible is worth remembering: the package labelled 1 must travel two positions, and one swap moves it by one.
                                                • Sample 2: 1 2 1 3 2 1 → 1 1 1 2 2 3. Five swaps (the statement lists the five intermediate rows).
                                                • Sample 3: already equal: 0.

                                                Play with the swap puzzle: each swap of two neighbours is one button press. The tool does not know the best answer for your own example (and does not search for it); for the three samples it shows the number from the statement. Try to find a strategy that reaches the target in that many moves, and ask yourself why you cannot do better.

                                                Swap puzzle: turn the queue into the target, neighbours only

                                                Hint ladder

                                                Hint 1 · the easiest version of the problem

                                                Ignore repeats and the odd target for a moment: suppose all labels are different and the target is the sorted order 1, 2, …, n. How many neighbour swaps are needed to sort a row? Revisit “Bubble sort: counting” in Chapter 9: bubble sort only ever swaps neighbours, and it swaps exactly the pairs that are in the wrong order. Which number counts those pairs? And why can no method that swaps only neighbours do better? (Hint: what does one neighbour swap do to the number of wrongly-ordered pairs?)

                                                Hint 2 · a target that is not sorted

                                                Back to different labels, but the target B is an arbitrary arrangement. You can rename every package so that the target becomes 1, 2, 3, …, n in order: give each label the position it has in B. After that the question is the one from Hint 1, applied to the renamed row. Try it on sample 1 with the two 2s kept apart in your mind: which renaming do you get, and what is the count?

                                                Hint 3 · now with repeated labels: who goes where?

                                                The renaming in Hint 2 is no longer unique when a label occurs several times in B. The statement’s hint asks: in a shortest sequence of moves, is it ever necessary to change the relative order of equal labels? Think about two packages with the same label that swap with each other. Did that swap change anything visible? Then: if you may assume equal labels never cross, which position of B must the first 2 of A go to, which one the second 2, and so on? Once every package of A has been given a target position, you are back at the situation of Hint 2.

                                                Hint 4 · counting the wrongly-ordered pairs fast

                                                Checking every pair costs about n2/2 = 2 · 1010 steps for n = 200 000, far too slow for the big tests (but fine for the small ones, n ≤ 2000). The target is O(n log n). Chapter 10 has the idea: merge sort splits the row, sorts both halves and merges. When you merge two sorted halves and have to take an element from the right half before some elements of the left half, what have you learned about the pairs involving it? Can you count those pairs without looking at them one by one? (Some people use a different structure for the same job; the one from the lectures is enough.)

                                                Hint 5 · details that cost marks
                                                • 64-bit. Use long long for the count and for any sum that goes with it. A 32-bit counter wraps around silently on the big tests, which is undefined behaviour in C++.
                                                • Matching equal labels: keep, for each label, the positions where it occurs in B in order, and use them up in order while you go through A. Labels are from 1 to n, so plain arrays indexed by label are possible.
                                                • Reading: there are 400 000 numbers to read; use fast input.
                                                • Already equal: output 0 (public tests B-3, B-6, B-7 and B-11 have answer 0).
                                                Hint 6 · test it

                                                Small cases with answers you can check by hand: 1 2 → 2 1 needs 1; 1 1 2 → 2 1 1 needs 2; 1 1 2 2 → 2 2 1 1 needs 4 (every 1 must pass every 2); the three samples. A slow checker that is easy to trust: a breadth-first search over all rearrangements for n ≤ 7 (each swap of neighbours is one step; the first time you reach the target, the number of steps is the answer). Compare your fast program with it on many random small cases. Then run B-4 (answer 19 999 900 000) and B-12 (answer 10 000 000 000) and time them.

                                                Common slips in this task

                                                • Matching equal labels the wrong way (for example the first 2 of A to the last 2 of B), which makes the count too large.
                                                • A 32-bit counter.
                                                • Counting only the distance each package has to move (it is not the same: moving one package can help another).
                                                • An O(n2) double loop (correct, but the large tests time out).
                                                • Printing the swaps instead of their number.

                                                When you have your own program

                                                Compare your approach with my worked solution in Part 7 (unofficial; the official one will follow). Compare the method and the running time first, then test your own program on the samples.

                                                Part 4 · Task C · 3 marks per test, 10 tests

                                                Task C: Cheapest Combinations (30%)

                                                What it asks

                                                Two catalogues list prices: catalogue A has n prices a1 ≤ … ≤ an, catalogue B has m prices b1 ≤ … ≤ bm (both already sorted, repeats allowed). A combination (i, j) takes item i from A and item j from B and costs ai + bj. There are n · m combinations. Print the first k of them, one per line as i j total, in this order:

                                                1. smaller total price first;
                                                2. if the totals tie, smaller i first;
                                                3. if both tie, smaller j first.

                                                Reading the statement carefully

                                                • Every pair of ids is a different combination, even when the prices are equal (sample 2: four different combinations all cost 3). Each pair appears at most once.
                                                • An item can appear in many combinations. This is not a shopping list where each item is bought once.
                                                • The number n · m can be 4 · 1010, far beyond a 32-bit integer, and you must never build all of them. But k is at most 200 000, so the output is small.
                                                • Ids start at 1 in each catalogue, and the third number on each line is the total price.
                                                • Prices go up to 109, so a total can reach 2 · 109. That still fits in a signed 32-bit integer (the limit is about 2.147 · 109), but only just; a 64-bit type removes the worry.

                                                The slow reference, as a table

                                                The tool lists all pairs for small catalogues, writes each total with its rank in the official order (the number after #), shades the first k and prints the expected output. It does this by sorting everything, which is exactly what you must not do for n = m = 200 000, but it is a precise picture of what the answer is. Try the three samples; then your own lists. Look along a row and down a column.

                                                All combinations with their rank: what the output should be

                                                The samples

                                                • Sample 1 (k = 5): the printed combinations are (1,1), (2,1), (1,2), (1,3), (2,2) with totals 2, 3, 4, 5, 5. The last two both cost 5; (1,3) comes first because its A-id 1 is smaller than 2.
                                                • Sample 2 (k = 5): catalogue A is 2, 2 and B is 1, 1, 4. Four combinations cost 3; they are ordered by i and then j. The fifth printed one costs 6 (combination (1,3)).
                                                • Sample 3: only two combinations exist and both are printed.

                                                Hint ladder

                                                Hint 1 · understand the shape of the answer

                                                Fill the grid for sample 1 by hand and number the cells in the official order, then compare with the tool. Questions: which cell is always first? When the first k cells are shaded, what shape do they make (could a cell be shaded without the cells to its left and above it being shaded as well)? Why does the order of the ties (i, then j) not change which cells are in the list, but only the order inside equal totals?

                                                Hint 2 · the statement’s own hint: fix one item of catalogue A

                                                Take a single item i of A. Its combinations with all items of B form a row of totals ai + b1, ai + b2, …. What do you know about the order of these totals, because B is sorted? So the problem can be seen as n sorted lists (one per item of A) from which you want the first k items of their combined sorted order. You have seen how to combine two sorted lists in merge sort; here there are many lists.

                                                Hint 3 · who can be next?

                                                When you have already printed some combinations, the next one to print must be, in every row, the first row entry that has not been printed yet (why? because a row is sorted, you cannot print a later entry of a row before an earlier one with a smaller or equal total and a smaller j). So the candidates for the next line are at most n cells, one per row. Which structure from the lectures finds “the smallest of a changing collection” and lets you add a new one after you remove one? (Priority queues.) After you print a combination, what new candidate does it create, and in which row?

                                                Hint 4 · the tie rule belongs inside the comparison

                                                “Smaller total, then smaller i, then smaller j” is a comparison between whole combinations. Whatever you keep in the priority queue must carry all three numbers and must be compared in exactly this order. (In C++ a pair of a pair compares lexicographically, and the default priority_queue hands out the largest element, so look at greater<> from <functional>.) If the tie rule is not in the comparison, your output has the right totals in the wrong order and the test fails.

                                                Hint 5 · how big can things get?

                                                The statement’s target is O((n + m + k) log(n + m + k)): reading the input, then k removals and a few insertions, each O(log size). Check that the number of candidates in your queue never exceeds about n + k. Do you really need all n rows in the queue at the start? (Either way is fast enough here; thinking about it is good practice.)

                                                Hint 6 · output and arithmetic
                                                • Up to 200 000 lines of output. Slow output is a real danger: cout with endl flushes after every line. Use "\n" or printf / putchar.
                                                • Do not compute n · m as an int; it overflows (undefined behaviour). You do not need the product: k is already guaranteed to be at most n · m.
                                                • Totals: use long long to be safe.
                                                • The first number is the A-id, the second the B-id, the third the total; ids start at 1.
                                                Hint 7 · test it

                                                First the three samples, then compare with the slow table method on many small random catalogues, especially with many equal prices (all prices equal; two values only) because that is where the tie rule shows. Edge cases: n = 1 or m = 1 (public tests C-7 and C-8); k = 1 (C-11); k = n · m (C-9 has 4 × 4 and k = 16; C-10 has 100 × 100 and k = 10 000); and the huge ones C-4, C-5 (n = m = k = 200 000).

                                                Common slips in this task

                                                • Generating all n · m pairs and sorting them: correct for the small tests only (about half of the marks).
                                                • Leaving the third tie-break (j) out of the comparison.
                                                • Printing with endl or reading with slow cin on the big tests.
                                                • Item ids starting at 0 instead of 1.
                                                • Pushing a new candidate into the queue twice (the same combination printed twice) or not at all (a combination missing).

                                                When you have your own program

                                                Compare your approach with my worked solution in Part 8 (unofficial; the official one will follow). Compare the method and the running time first, then test your own program on the samples.

                                                Part 5 · Before you submit

                                                Testing, speed and the last checklist

                                                What the twelve public tests of each task contain

                                                The public tests are not random: looking at them tells you which situations the hidden tests are likely to contain as well. This is what is in the files you were given:

                                                TaskSmall public testsBig public testsWhat to watch for
                                                Athe two statement samples, a single node, trees of 4 to 8 nodes, one with 80 nodes, one with 2000 nodes, equal keys in several of themA-4: a chain of 200 000 nodes; A-5: a balanced tree of 200 000 nodes (height 17); A-12: 131 071 nodes, all keys equalrecursion that is 200 000 levels deep; equal keys; the root is not node 1
                                                Bthe three samples, n = 1, n = 8, an n = 2000 caseB-4, B-5, B-11, B-12: n = 200 000 with answers 19 999 900 000, 876 434 031, 0 and 10 000 000 00064-bit answers; speed of the counting; answer 0
                                                Cthe three samples, 1 × 1, 1 × 7, 7 × 1, 4 × 4 with k = 16, 100 × 100 with k = 10 000C-4, C-5: n = m = k = 200 000; C-11: the same size but k = 1; C-12: n = 200 000, m = 1output of 200 000 lines; ties; very unbalanced shapes

                                                Build a slow, obviously correct checker

                                                For tiny inputs you can solve every task in a way that is slow but easy to trust. Then you generate hundreds of random tiny inputs and compare the two programs (stress testing); any difference gives you a small input that shows the bug.

                                                • Task A: for every node, collect all keys in its subtree in a list, check the BST condition against that list and check the heights directly (a slow but simple function that works for a tree of up to 15 nodes). Random trees: choose a random shape, then give keys from a very small range such as 1 to 5, so that equal keys and violations are frequent; also trees that are valid BSTs with one key changed.
                                                • Task B: breadth-first search over all rearrangements of the row (each neighbour swap is one step), for n ≤ 7. Random inputs: random row A, then B as a random shuffle of A, with few distinct labels so repeats are common.
                                                • Task C: generate all n · m pairs, sort by (total, i, j), print the first k: exactly the table of Part 4. Random inputs: sorted prices from a tiny range so that ties are frequent; sometimes k = n · m.

                                                Your two programs must give the same output on every case; the output comparer in Part 1 helps if a space is in doubt.

                                                Speed

                                                • Compile with -O2 and time the largest public tests: time ./main < TaskB/B-4.in > /dev/null. The limit is 1 second on the grader; aim for a few tenths of a second.
                                                • Reading. Task A has 600 000 numbers, Task B 400 000, Task C 400 000. cin is slow unless its synchronisation with C streams is turned off; scanf or getchar is faster, and the statement recommends them.
                                                • Writing. Task C prints up to 200 000 lines. endl flushes the output every time and is very slow; use "\n" or printf / putchar.
                                                • Depth. Task A on a chain.

                                                The usual ways to get a zero

                                                What goes wrongWhere it shows upPrevention
                                                Stack overflow in a recursive traversalTask A on the chain (A-4)Use an explicit stack or an order that goes through the nodes in a loop (Part 2, Hint 4).
                                                32-bit overflowTask B answers up to 2 · 1010; Task C if you compute n · mlong long wherever a count or a sum can grow.
                                                Uninitialised variables or arrayseverywhere; random on the grader, fine on your computerGive every counter, flag and array a value before it is read.
                                                Array too small by oneids from 1 to n (Task A), labels 1 to n (Task B)Allocate n + a few extra; remember Task A’s ids start at 1.
                                                A header not on the list; wrong file nameevery taskCheck #include lines and UniversityNumber-X.cpp.
                                                Extra output (debug prints)every taskPrint only what the output format says, nothing else.
                                                Does not compile in the online compilerevery taskLast step: paste each file into it.

                                                Last checklist

                                                1. Three files with exactly the right names, uncompressed.
                                                2. Each compiles with -std=c++14 and in the online compiler without errors.
                                                3. All public tests of each task pass: python3 test.py main.cpp A (then B, C), or one by one with diff.
                                                4. The big tests finish in well under a second (A-4, A-5, B-4, B-12, C-4, C-5).
                                                5. Your stress test of fast against slow found no difference on a few hundred random small inputs.
                                                6. You can explain every line of every program in your own words. The programs are your own work; the similarity checker compares them with everyone else’s.

                                                My own worked solutions are in Part 6 (Task A), Part 7 (Task B) and Part 8 (Task C). Next: the contents (and the revision notes).

                                                Part 6 · Solution to Task A · 30% · unofficial

                                                Worked solution: Task A (search subtrees)

                                                About these programs

                                                These are my own worked solutions, written with the methods of the lectures and the practice sets (tree traversals, BST and AVL definitions, inversions and merge sort, heaps and priority queues). They are not the official ones; the official solutions will follow when they are released. Each program was compiled with g++ -std=c++14, passes all 12 public tests of its task, agrees with a brute-force checker on 1500 random small inputs, and runs in well under 0.1 s on inputs of the maximum size. The cover page says that all submitted work must be your own and is compared by similarity-checking software, so use these to understand the method and to check your own program, and write your own version.

                                                The idea

                                                For every node we want to know two yes/no facts about the subtree that hangs below it: is it a BST, is it an AVL tree? Then we pick the largest. The trap (see Part 2) is that a node can look fine next to its two children while a key deep below breaks the rule (in sample 1, key 12 sits in the left subtree of key 10). So we need summaries of the child subtrees, and that makes the plan:

                                                1. Decide what each subtree must report to its parent: its size, its height (empty: −1), its smallest and largest key, and the two facts isBST and isAVL.
                                                2. Combine two children into the parent in O(1):
                                                  • size = size(left) + size(right) + 1; height = max(height(left), height(right)) + 1;
                                                  • isBST(v) = isBST(left) and isBST(right) and (the left subtree is empty or its largest key < key(v)) and (the right subtree is empty or key(v) < its smallest key). The inequalities are strict, as the statement demands, so equal keys fail. Because the left subtree is itself a BST, comparing with its single largest key is enough to compare with all of them (that is the idea of Chapter 7: a BST is the root plus two BSTs with the keys on the correct sides).
                                                  • isAVL(v) = isBST(v) and isAVL(left) and isAVL(right) and |height(left) − height(right)| ≤ 1. Both subtrees must be AVL too, since the AVL rule holds at every node (Chapter 8).
                                                3. Handle every node after both its children (the postorder idea). Then each node is processed once, in O(1): O(n) in total, the statement’s target.

                                                Why not a recursive postorder

                                                The statement warns that the tree may be a single chain of 200 000 nodes. A recursive function would then be 200 000 calls deep, which can overflow the call stack. So the program builds the order itself with an explicit stack: it lists every node before its descendants (root first, like preorder), and then simply reads that list backwards, which lists every node before its parent. That is all that “children before parents” needs.

                                                Pseudocode

                                                Subtrees(T, r) { /* 1. an order in which every node comes before its descendants */ Stack S; order = empty list; S.Push(r); while (!empty(S)) { v = S.Pop(); append v to order; if (left(v) != 0) S.Push(left(v)); if (right(v) != 0) S.Push(right(v)); } /* 2. go through it backwards: both children of v are finished before v */ size(0) = 0; height(0) = -1; isBST(0) = isAVL(0) = true; /* the empty subtree */ for v in order, from the last to the first { l = left(v); rt = right(v); size(v) = size(l) + size(rt) + 1; height(v) = max(height(l), height(rt)) + 1; min(v) = smallest of key(v) and the min of the non-empty children; max(v) = largest of key(v) and the max of the non-empty children; isBST(v) = isBST(l) and isBST(rt) and (l = 0 or max(l) < key(v)) and (rt = 0 or key(v) < min(rt)); isAVL(v) = isBST(v) and isAVL(l) and isAVL(rt) and |height(l) - height(rt)| <= 1; } /* 3. the largest of each kind; the smallest id wins a tie */ for v = 1 to n: keep the first v with the largest size among those with isBST(v), and again for isAVL(v)}

                                                The C++14 program

                                                #include <cstdio>#include <vector>#include <algorithm>using namespace std; int main() { int n, r; scanf("%d %d", &n, &r); vector<int> key(n + 1), L(n + 1), R(n + 1); for (int i = 1; i <= n; i++) scanf("%d %d %d", &key[i], &L[i], &R[i]); // 1. an order where every node comes before its descendants (explicit stack) vector<int> order, st; st.push_back(r); while (!st.empty()) { int v = st.back(); st.pop_back(); order.push_back(v); if (L[v]) st.push_back(L[v]); if (R[v]) st.push_back(R[v]); } // 2. facts about the subtree of every node; node 0 is the empty subtree vector<int> sz(n + 1, 0), ht(n + 1, 0), mn(n + 1, 0), mx(n + 1, 0); vector<char> isBST(n + 1, 1), isAVL(n + 1, 1); ht[0] = -1; // empty: size 0, height -1 for (int t = n - 1; t >= 0; t--) { // children before their parent int v = order[t], l = L[v], rr = R[v]; sz[v] = sz[l] + sz[rr] + 1; ht[v] = max(ht[l], ht[rr]) + 1; mn[v] = key[v]; mx[v] = key[v]; if (l) { mn[v] = min(mn[v], mn[l]); mx[v] = max(mx[v], mx[l]); } if (rr) { mn[v] = min(mn[v], mn[rr]); mx[v] = max(mx[v], mx[rr]); } isBST[v] = isBST[l] && isBST[rr] && (!l || mx[l] < key[v]) && (!rr || key[v] < mn[rr]); isAVL[v] = isBST[v] && isAVL[l] && isAVL[rr] && ht[l] - ht[rr] <= 1 && ht[rr] - ht[l] <= 1; } // 3. the largest of each kind; going upwards through the ids, the first one wins a tie int bestBST = 0, idBST = 0, bestAVL = 0, idAVL = 0; for (int v = 1; v <= n; v++) { if (isBST[v] && sz[v] > bestBST) { bestBST = sz[v]; idBST = v; } if (isAVL[v] && sz[v] > bestAVL) { bestAVL = sz[v]; idAVL = v; } } printf("%d %d\n%d %d\n", bestBST, idBST, bestAVL, idAVL); return 0;}
                                                node 0 as the empty subtree

                                                ids start at 1, so index 0 is free: sz[0] = 0, ht[0] = -1, and isBST[0] = isAVL[0] = 1 (the vectors are initialised to 1). The code then needs no special case for a missing child except in the two key tests.

                                                st.push_back(r) ... order.push_back(v)

                                                the explicit stack of Chapter 3: take a node, record it, push its children. A node is recorded before its children, so every node comes after its parent in order.

                                                for (int t = n - 1; t >= 0; t--)

                                                the list read backwards: when v is reached, both children have been finished already.

                                                mn[v] = key[v]; ... min(mn[v], mn[l])

                                                the smallest and largest key of the whole subtree, built from the children’s.

                                                isBST[v] = isBST[l] && isBST[rr] && (!l || mx[l] < key[v]) && (!rr || key[v] < mn[rr])

                                                the BST test, with strict inequalities and only for children that exist.

                                                isAVL[v] = isBST[v] && isAVL[l] && isAVL[rr] && ht[l] - ht[rr] <= 1 && ht[rr] - ht[l] <= 1

                                                the AVL test. The two subtractions replace abs, so that no header beyond the allowed list is needed.

                                                if (isBST[v] && sz[v] > bestBST)

                                                going through the ids upwards and replacing only for a strictly larger size keeps the smallest id on a tie, as the statement requires.

                                                Why it is correct

                                                • The order is right. A node enters order only after its parent was taken from the stack, so each node appears after its parent, hence (read backwards) before it. All n nodes appear because every node is reachable from r.
                                                • The BST rule. The subtree of v is a BST exactly when both child subtrees are BSTs, all keys on the left are smaller than key(v), and all keys on the right are larger. For a valid left BST, “all keys are smaller” is the same as “the largest key is smaller”. If a child subtree is not a BST, then the parent cannot be one: any subtree of a BST is a BST. So isBST[l] and isBST[rr] are needed, and enough.
                                                • The AVL rule. An AVL tree is a BST in which every node is balanced. The root of the subtree is balanced when the two heights differ by at most 1; every other node of the subtree lies in a child subtree, which has to be AVL itself.
                                                • The tie rule and independence. The two categories are searched separately (a different winner is possible); in each, the first id with the largest size wins.

                                                Running time and memory

                                                Every node is pushed once and popped once (O(n)), then handled once in O(1) (O(n)), then looked at once more to pick the winners (O(n)): O(n) time and O(n) memory, with no recursion. (Computing “is this subtree a BST?” from scratch for each node would be O(n2) on a chain.)

                                                Sample 1, node by node

                                                The order in which the program lists the nodes is 1, 3, 6, 7, 8, 2, 5, 4 (it takes the right child first, because the stack hands out the last node pushed). Read backwards it is 4, 5, 2, 8, 7, 6, 3, 1:

                                                Node (key)sizeheightkeysBST?AVL?
                                                4 (2)102 .. 2yesyes
                                                5 (12)1012 .. 12yesyes
                                                2 (5)312 .. 12yes: 2 < 5 < 12yes: heights 0 and 0
                                                8 (30)1030 .. 30yesyes
                                                7 (25)2125 .. 30yesyes: heights −1 and 0
                                                6 (20)3220 .. 30yesno: heights −1 and 1
                                                3 (15)4315 .. 30yesno
                                                1 (10)842 .. 30no: the left subtree has the key 12, not smaller than 10no

                                                Largest BST: size 4 at node 3. Largest AVL tree: size 3 at node 2. Output 4 3 and 3 2. Sample 2: keys 4, 4, 8, 10, root 3: node 2 (key 4) has a left child with key 4, and 4 is not smaller than 4, so the subtrees of nodes 2 and 3 fail; nodes 1 and 4 are single nodes, so both answers are size 1, and node 1 wins the tie: 1 1 twice.

                                                Run the three programs step by step on a small input (this one is set to Task A)

                                                Where marks are lost in Task A

                                                • Comparing a node only with its two children. That accepts the whole tree of sample 1 as a BST. The comparison must be with the largest key on the left and the smallest key on the right.
                                                • Non-strict comparisons (<=). Equal keys must fail; sample 2 is built to catch this.
                                                • Mixing up ids and keys. The output uses node ids (line numbers), not keys. And the root is node r, not necessarily node 1.
                                                • Height of the empty subtree. It is −1 and a leaf is 0, so a node with one child has heights −1 and 0 and is balanced. Using 0 for the empty subtree gives the same differences here but breaks as soon as you compare with a leaf in the wrong convention; keep to the statement.
                                                • Forgetting that an AVL tree must be a BST: a balanced shape alone is not enough.
                                                • Recursion on a chain (stack overflow at n = 200 000), and an O(n2) re-check of every subtree.
                                                • Reporting the largest id on a tie instead of the smallest, or choosing one winner for both categories.

                                                Test report

                                                Public tests A-1 to A-12: all 12 pass. 1500 random trees with up to 11 nodes (random shapes, chains, many equal keys, near-BSTs with a few spoiled keys) agree with a brute-force program that checks the BST and AVL definitions on every subtree by looking at all its keys. Trees with 200 000 nodes (a left chain, a right chain, a nearly perfect tree, random trees): about 0.03 to 0.05 s.

                                                Part 7 · Solution to Task B · 40% · unofficial

                                                Worked solution: Task B (restore the queue)

                                                The idea in three steps

                                                1. If all packages were different, the answer would be the number of inversions. Give package i the number p[i] = its target position. The lectures already say how many neighbour swaps it takes to sort such a list (Chapter 9): an inversion is a pair i < j with p[i] > p[j]; a swap of two neighbours changes the number of inversions by exactly one; and bubble sort, which only swaps neighbours that are out of order, uses exactly as many swaps as there are inversions. So at least that many swaps are needed (each removes at most one inversion, and we must reach zero) and that many are enough (bubble sort).
                                                2. Equal labels: match them in order. Packages with the same label are interchangeable, so we may choose which one goes where. The best choice is: the first package with label x goes to the first target position that wants an x, the second to the second, and so on. (Reason below.)
                                                3. Count the inversions of p in O(n log n) by adding a counter to the merge sort of Chapter 10. A double loop over all pairs would be 2 · 1010 steps.

                                                Why matching in order is best

                                                Suppose that two packages i < j with the same label are matched “crossed”: p[i] = y > x = p[j]. Exchange their targets (the label at both places is the same, so this is allowed). The pair (i, j) was an inversion and is not any more. For a package k with i < k < j and target q, the number of inversions that k forms with i and j was [y > q] + [q > x] and becomes [x > q] + [q > y]: it is 1 and 1 if q < x or q > y, and it drops from 2 to 0 if x < q < y. For a package k outside the range i..j, the two targets are the same two numbers, only swapped, so nothing changes. Hence the exchange never increases the inversion count, and it lowers it by at least one. So a best matching has no crossed pair of equal labels, which is exactly “match in order”. (In the other direction, any matching without crossed equal labels is the in-order matching, so it is unique.)

                                                Pseudocode

                                                RestoreQueue(A, B, n) { /* where[x] = the target positions of label x, from left to right */ for i = 1 to n: append i to where[B[i]]; /* match equal labels in order: the t-th package with label x goes to the t-th position of where[x] */ for i = 1 to n: p[i] = next unused position of where[A[i]]; inversions = 0; MergeSort(p, 1, n); /* sorts p and counts the inversions */ return inversions;} MergeSort(p, low, high) { if (low < high) { mid = floor((low + high) / 2); MergeSort(p, low, mid); MergeSort(p, mid + 1, high); merge p[low..mid] and p[mid+1..high]: whenever the next element comes from the RIGHT half, inversions = inversions + (number of elements still waiting in the LEFT half); }}

                                                While merging, an element taken from the right half is smaller than every element still waiting in the left half (the left half is sorted and its front is bigger than it), and it stands to the right of all of them in the original order: that is one inversion per waiting element. Each inversion (i < j, p[i] > p[j]) is counted exactly once, at the merge where i and j first lie in different halves.

                                                The C++14 program

                                                #include <cstdio>#include <vector>using namespace std; long long inversions = 0; // MergeSort of the lecture, with counting: sorts p[low..high]void mergeSort(vector<int> &p, vector<int> &tmp, int low, int high) { if (low >= high) return; int mid = (low + high) / 2; mergeSort(p, tmp, low, mid); mergeSort(p, tmp, mid + 1, high); int i = low, j = mid + 1, k = low; while (i <= mid && j <= high) { if (p[i] <= p[j]) { tmp[k++] = p[i++]; } else { tmp[k++] = p[j++]; inversions += mid - i + 1; // p[j] is smaller than all of p[i..mid] } } while (i <= mid) tmp[k++] = p[i++]; while (j <= high) tmp[k++] = p[j++]; for (k = low; k <= high; k++) p[k] = tmp[k];} int main() { int n; scanf("%d", &n); vector<int> A(n), B(n); for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) scanf("%d", &A[i]); for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) scanf("%d", &B[i]); // the positions of every label in the target, from left to right vector<vector<int> > where(n + 1); for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) where[B[i]].push_back(i); // the t-th package with label x goes to the t-th position that wants x vector<int> used(n + 1, 0), p(n), tmp(n); for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) p[i] = where[A[i]][used[A[i]]++]; mergeSort(p, tmp, 0, n - 1); // the answer is the number of inversions of p printf("%lld\n", inversions); return 0;}
                                                long long inversions

                                                it can reach n(n − 1)/2, about 2 · 1010 for n = 200 000: far beyond 32 bits. The statement says so. The public test B-4 has the answer 19 999 900 000.

                                                where[B[i]].push_back(i)

                                                for every label, the positions where the target wants it, in increasing order.

                                                p[i] = where[A[i]][used[A[i]]++]

                                                the next unused position of that label: the in-order matching.

                                                if (p[i] <= p[j])

                                                the left element goes first (take it when equal; here all values are distinct anyway).

                                                inversions += mid - i + 1

                                                p[j] (from the right half) goes out while p[i..mid] are still waiting: that many inversions.

                                                mergeSort(p, tmp, 0, n - 1)

                                                recursion is only about log2 n = 18 levels deep, so there is no stack problem here.

                                                Running time and memory

                                                Building where and p: O(n). Merge sort: O(n log n) (the recurrence T(n) = 2T(n/2) + cn of Chapter 10; the counter adds O(1) to every step of the merge). Total O(n log n) time, O(n) memory.

                                                Sample 2, step by step

                                                A = 1 2 1 3 2 1 and B = 1 1 1 2 2 3. The label 1 is wanted at positions 1, 2, 3, the label 2 at 4, 5, and the label 3 at 6. Matching in order gives p = (1, 4, 2, 6, 5, 3). The merge sort:

                                                Merge of positionsLeft halfRight halfAddedTotal
                                                1–21400
                                                1–31, 421 (2 goes out before the 4)1
                                                4–56512
                                                4–65, 632 (3 goes out before 5 and 6)4
                                                1–61, 2, 43, 5, 61 (3 goes out before the 4)5

                                                The answer is 5, as in the statement. Sample 1: A = 2 1 2 3, B = 2 2 3 1 gives p = (1, 4, 2, 3) with the two inversions (4, 2) and (4, 3): answer 2. Sample 3: A = B gives p = (1, 2, 3, 4): no inversion, answer 0.

                                                Run the three programs step by step on a small input (switch the program to Task B)

                                                Where marks are lost in Task B

                                                • int for the answer. The sum overflows for n near 200 000 (and signed overflow is undefined behaviour). Use long long and %lld.
                                                • Matching equal labels in any other way (for instance first with last, or the same position always): the answer is then too big. In order is the only right choice.
                                                • Counting the pairs of positions that differ (A[i] ≠ B[i]), or the sum of distances: neither equals the number of swaps.
                                                • A double loop for the inversions: O(n2), far too slow at n = 200 000 (it solves only the five small tests).
                                                • Counting inversions by mid - low + 1 instead of mid - i + 1 (the elements still waiting, not all of the left half).
                                                • Using < instead of <= in the merge: harmless here, since the p[i] are all different, but it matters if you ever count inversions of a list with repeats.

                                                Test report

                                                Public tests B-1 to B-12: all 12 pass. 1500 random queues with up to 7 packages (labels 1 to 3) agree with a breadth-first search that tries every sequence of adjacent swaps. For n = 200 000 (reversed, all equal, two alternating labels, random labels) the answers agree with an independent program that counts inversions in a different way, and the run takes at most 0.06 s. The answer for the reversed queue is 19 999 900 000, which does not fit in 32 bits.

                                                Part 8 · Solution to Task C · 30% · unofficial

                                                Worked solution: Task C (cheapest combinations)

                                                The idea

                                                Write the n · m totals as a table: row i holds ai + b1, ai + b2, …, ai + bm. Because the catalogue B is sorted, every row is already sorted: the totals never decrease from left to right (and when two totals in a row are equal, the one with the larger j comes later, as the tie rule says). So we have n sorted lists and want the first k items of their merge. That is the picture of merging in Chapter 10, except that there are many lists, and the “smallest front element” is found with the priority queue of Chapter 9:

                                                1. Keep one entry per row in a min-heap: the smallest pair of that row that has not been printed yet, stored as (total, i, j). At the start this is the first pair (i, 1) of each row.
                                                2. Repeat k times: take the smallest entry out, print it, and put the next pair of the same row, (i, j + 1), into the heap (if there is one).
                                                3. The heap compares (total, i, j) in that order, which is exactly the order of the statement: smaller total first, then smaller i, then smaller j. So the smallest entry of the heap is always the next line of output.

                                                Only the first k rows matter

                                                If n > k, a row i > k never needs to be put in the heap: the pairs (1,1), (2,1), …, (i − 1, 1) all come before (i, 1) in the official order (their totals are no larger and their i is smaller), and there are at least k of them. So the heap starts with min(n, k) entries, and never holds more, because every step removes one entry and adds at most one.

                                                Pseudocode

                                                Cheapest(a, b, n, m, k) { PQ = empty min-priority queue of triples (total, i, j); /* compared in this order */ for i = 1 to min(n, k) insert (a[i] + b[1], i, 1) into PQ; for t = 1 to k { (total, i, j) = extract the smallest triple of PQ; print i, j, total; if (j < m) insert (a[i] + b[j+1], i, j+1) into PQ; }}

                                                The C++14 program

                                                #include <cstdio>#include <vector>#include <queue>#include <functional>#include <utility>using namespace std; typedef pair<long long, pair<int, int> > entry; // (total price, (i, j)) int main() { int n, m, k; scanf("%d %d %d", &n, &m, &k); vector<long long> a(n), b(m); for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) scanf("%lld", &a[i]); for (int j = 0; j < m; j++) scanf("%lld", &b[j]); // row i of the table is the list a[i] + b[0], a[i] + b[1], ...: already sorted priority_queue<entry, vector<entry>, greater<entry> > pq; for (int i = 0; i < n && i < k; i++) // a row below the k-th cannot be needed pq.push(make_pair(a[i] + b[0], make_pair(i, 0))); for (int t = 0; t < k; t++) { entry top = pq.top(); pq.pop(); int i = top.second.first, j = top.second.second; printf("%d %d %lld\n", i + 1, j + 1, top.first); if (j + 1 < m) pq.push(make_pair(a[i] + b[j + 1], make_pair(i, j + 1))); } return 0;}
                                                typedef pair<long long, pair<int, int> > entry

                                                a triple (total, i, j) as a nested pair. C++ compares pairs first by the first member, then by the second: that is, by total, then by i, then by j, exactly the order of the statement.

                                                priority_queue<entry, vector<entry>, greater<entry> > pq

                                                a min-heap (by default the largest would be on top).

                                                for (int i = 0; i < n && i < k; i++)

                                                one front entry per row, for the first min(n, k) rows.

                                                printf("%d %d %lld\n", i + 1, j + 1, top.first)

                                                ids start from 1 in the output; the total is a long long (at most 2 · 109, which still fits in 32 bits, but with long long there is no question).

                                                if (j + 1 < m) pq.push(...)

                                                the next pair of the same row takes the place of the one just printed.

                                                Why it is correct

                                                • Invariant: before each output step, the heap holds, for each of the first min(n, k) rows, the first pair of that row that has not been printed yet (if the row has one).
                                                • The smallest entry is the next line. Every pair of a row comes after the front of its row in the official order (totals along a row never decrease, and for equal totals the larger j comes later). So the next pair overall, in the official order, is the smallest of the fronts. It is either in one of the rows we track, or it belongs to a row below the k-th, which can only be needed after more than k other pairs (the information note above).
                                                • Each pair is printed once: it enters the heap once (when its predecessor in the row leaves) and leaves once.

                                                Running time and memory

                                                Reading the input: O(n + m). The heap never has more than min(n, k) entries, so every insertion and extraction costs O(log(n + m + k)) at most. There are at most min(n, k) + k insertions and k extractions, and k lines to print: O((n + m + k) log(n + m + k)), the statement’s target. Memory O(n + m + k). Never build the n · m table: that has up to 4 · 1010 cells.

                                                Sample 1, step by step

                                                a = 1, 2, 5; b = 1, 3, 4; k = 5. The heap starts with the fronts (2, 1, 1), (3, 2, 1), (6, 3, 1).

                                                StepSmallest entry: printedPut into the heapHeap afterwards
                                                1(2, 1, 1): 1 1 2(4, 1, 2)(3,2,1) (4,1,2) (6,3,1)
                                                2(3, 2, 1): 2 1 3(5, 2, 2)(4,1,2) (5,2,2) (6,3,1)
                                                3(4, 1, 2): 1 2 4(5, 1, 3)(5,1,3) (5,2,2) (6,3,1)
                                                4(5, 1, 3): 1 3 5 (tie with (5,2,2): the smaller i goes first)nothing (row 1 is used up)(5,2,2) (6,3,1)
                                                5(5, 2, 2): 2 2 5(not needed: k lines are done)

                                                The five lines are exactly the expected output of sample 1. Item 1 of catalogue A appears in three combinations, as the statement notes.

                                                Run the three programs step by step on a small input (switch the program to Task C)

                                                Where marks are lost in Task C

                                                • Generating all n · m pairs and sorting them (it solves only the five small tests), or putting all n · m pairs in the heap.
                                                • Forgetting the tie rule. A heap that compares only the total gives some valid-looking order but not the required one; sample 1 has a tie at 5. The comparison must be (total, i, j).
                                                • A heap without greater: it gives the most expensive combination first.
                                                • Putting a whole row in the heap at once, or pushing both (i + 1, j) and (i, j + 1) after each pop: then a pair can be put in twice (once from each side) and printed twice.
                                                • Slow output. 200 000 lines are fine with printf; with cout and endl (a flush after every line) it can be too slow.
                                                • Printing the ids starting from 0 instead of 1, or the individual prices instead of the total.

                                                Test report

                                                Public tests C-1 to C-12: all 12 pass. 1500 random catalogues (up to 9 × 9, many equal prices, prices up to 109, any k) agree with a brute-force program that sorts all pairs. For n = m = k = 200 000 (random prices, all prices equal), one catalogue of size 1, and 450 × 450 with k = 200 000, the output agrees with an independent program that uses a different heap, and the run takes about 0.04 to 0.07 s.

                                                  Four habits that earn marks in every chapter

                                                  1. Say what “size” is. Every cost is a function of something (n items, h height, V + E). Write the size before the cost.
                                                  2. Say the worst case separately from the average. Quick sort, hashing, interpolation search and plain search trees all have a good average and a bad worst case; mixing them up loses marks.
                                                  3. Draw a small example. Almost every question (rotations, deletion, heap, probing, a recurrence) becomes mechanical on 5 to 7 items drawn one step at a time.
                                                  4. Justify in three pieces: the claim, the fact you use (a definition or a property from the lectures), and the step connecting them with your actual numbers.

                                                  Part 2 · Chapters 1 and 2

                                                  Recursion and analysing algorithms

                                                  The recipe for anything recursive full cheat sheet

                                                  1. Size. Pick one number that says how big the problem is.
                                                  2. Base case. The smallest sizes, where the answer is obvious (there can be several).
                                                  3. Step. Assume the smaller problem is solved (“leap of faith”), then build your answer from it.
                                                  4. Progress. Every call goes strictly closer to a base case. No base case or no progress means the calls never stop.

                                                  Tutorial 1 adds the design step: choose how to cut the problem (n − k, one part of n/k, or all n/k parts) and let the time limit hint which cut is allowed (cuts, time limit).

                                                  Recurrences: from code to a formula unwrapping · tutorial 1

                                                  RecurrenceSolutionTypical algorithm
                                                  T(n) = T(n − 1) + cO(n)factorial, walk down a list
                                                  T(n) = T(n/2) + cO(log n)binary search, fast power xn
                                                  T(n) = 2T(n/2) + cnO(n log n)merge sort, maximum subarray
                                                  T(n) = 2T(n − 1) + 12n − 1Towers of Hanoi (also the lower bound, so optimal)
                                                  T(n) = T(n − 1) + T(n − 2) + 1exponential, Θ(φn)naive Fibonacci (it recomputes; the loop is Θ(n))

                                                  Two ways to get the formula: unwrap (replace T(n) by its rule again and again until the base case, then add up the pattern) or count work per level times the number of levels. Always prove the guess by induction; a table of matching values is evidence, not proof.

                                                  Induction in four lines chapter 1 · tutorial 1

                                                  1. Claim P(n) for all n ≥ n0.
                                                  2. Base: check exactly the base cases you state (checking n = 0 and concluding P(1) is a classic slip).
                                                  3. Hypothesis: assume P for all smaller sizes the recursion uses (strong induction when it calls T(n−1) and T(n−2)).
                                                  4. Step: go through every line of the combine step; use the hypothesis where the recursive calls are.

                                                  The asymptotic symbols chapter 2

                                                  SymbolMeaningDefinition (for large n)
                                                  f = Θ(g)same growthc1g ≤ f ≤ c2g for all n ≥ n0
                                                  f = O(g)grows no fasterf ≤ c g
                                                  f = Ω(g)grows no slowerf ≥ c g
                                                  f = o(g), f = ω(g)strictly slower, strictly fasterfor every c; the limit of f/g is 0, respectively ∞

                                                  To prove a bound by definition, name the constants: “n² + 10n ≤ 2n² for n ≥ 10, so c2 = 2, n0 = 10” (WA1 Q1(b)). To disprove, show that no constants work (the ratio is unbounded).

                                                  Reading cost off code chapter 2

                                                  • Loops multiply (a loop of n inside a loop of n is n²; an inner loop that always runs 5 times just contributes the constant 5).
                                                  • Things in a row: the largest one wins. if/else: the worse branch. A function call: analyse the function first.
                                                  • Throw away lower-order terms and constant factors: 3n² + 100n + 7 = Θ(n²).
                                                  • Ranking, slowest growth first: log n, n, n log n, n², n³, 2n (typical growth rates).
                                                  • Space: overall space = input + extra; extra counts only the temporaries (and, in practice, the recursion stack: tutorial 1).
                                                  • Upper bound = an algorithm proves it; lower bound = no algorithm can do better; when they meet the problem is solved optimally.

                                                  Mistakes to avoid chapter 1

                                                  • No base case, or no progress.
                                                  • Borrowing an array by swapping and not swapping back (the second swap in the permutations code).
                                                  • Testing p == q where p = q or p ≥ q is meant (the pointers can jump past each other).
                                                  • Following every call in your head. Trust the smaller call and check one level.

                                                  Practice: Practice Problems 1 (all 16 solutions) and Written Assignment 1 (the official solution explained).

                                                  Part 3 · Chapters 3 and 4

                                                  Lists, stacks, queues, graphs and hashing

                                                  What each structure costs chapter 3

                                                  StructureWhat it isCosts to remember
                                                  Array listboxes side by side plus a lengthfind the i-th Θ(1); search, insert, delete Θ(n) (shifting)
                                                  Linked listnodes joined by next; a filler head nodesearch O(n); insert/delete O(1) given the pointer
                                                  Doubly linkedadds prevdelete a given node in O(1); watch the NULL ends
                                                  StackLIFO; array with tospush, pop, top Θ(1)
                                                  QueueFIFO; circular array with head, tail, lengthenqueue, dequeue Θ(1)
