                                                  Graph, listsa list of neighbours per vertexspace O(V + E); all edges in O(V + E)

                                                  There is no best data structure: list the operations your problem needs most, then choose (choosing). Tutorial 3 builds them from each other: a queue from two stacks (ENQUEUE pushes on IN; DEQUEUE pops OUT and refills it from IN only when empty: worst case O(n), amortised O(1)) and a stack from two queues (one of PUSH/POP must move n items). The monotone stack answers “next lower item” in O(n) because each index is pushed and popped once (T3, T3, WA2 Q2).

                                                  Graph searches tutorial 2

                                                  DFSBFSDijkstra
                                                  Findseverything reachable; a patheverything reachable; a path with the fewest edgesshortest total weight from one source to all vertices
                                                  Edgesunweightedunweightedweighted, non-negative
                                                  Toolstack (newest first)queue (oldest first, level order)array of guesses, or a priority queue
                                                  TimeO(V + E) with lists, O(V²) with a matrixsameO(V²) with an array; O((E + V) log V) with a priority queue

                                                  BFS and DFS are one loop that differs in one line (which end of the waiting collection you take from). Dijkstra finalises the closest vertex not yet done; a negative edge breaks it (why). BFS · DFS · Dijkstra.

                                                  Lists: four forms tutorial 3

                                                  • Doubly linked makes DELETE(x) and PREDECESSOR cheap; sorted makes SUCCESSOR, MINIMUM, MAXIMUM cheap and INSERT slow; SEARCH is O(n) in all four.
                                                  • Stack on a list: at the head. Queue: remove at HEAD, add at TAIL (set TAIL to NIL when it empties). All O(1).
                                                  • UNION of disjoint lists with HEAD and TAIL splices in O(1); overlapping sets need duplicates removed: much more work. Two pointers meeting where two lists join: WA2 Q1.

                                                  Hashing: the three conditions chapter 4

                                                  Dictionary operations take constant time on average if (1) the hash function spreads the keys, (2) the table is not too full, (3) there is a sensible collision plan. Break any one and it can fall back to O(n). Load factor α = n/m (items over slots).

                                                  ChainingOpen addressing
                                                  Elements livein lists hanging off the slotsin the table itself
                                                  Load factorcan exceed 1must be below 1; keep it below about 0.5
                                                  Search costO(1 + α) (simple uniform hashing)grows quickly as α → 1
                                                  Deleteunlink the nodeneeds a DELETED marker
                                                  When fullchains get longerrehash into a bigger table
                                                  Probingh(k, i)ClusteringNeeds
                                                  Linear(h1 + i) mod mprimarynothing: visits every slot
                                                  Quadratic(h1 + i²) mod msecondarym prime and m prime and α < ½ to be safealpha; m prime and α < ½ to be safelt; m prime and α < ½ to be safefrac12; to be safe
                                                  Double hashing(h1 + i · h2) mod mlittleh2 never 0 and coprime to m (e.g. m prime)

                                                  Hand-filling tables (WA2 Q4): write the probe sequence for each key in order and note the first free slot; with double hashing check that h2 can never be 0 (worked). See also PP2 hash tables and hash functions in algorithm design.

                                                  Part 4 · Chapters 5 to 8

                                                  Trees, searching, search trees and AVL trees

                                                  Tree words and traversals chapter 5 on one page

                                                  IdeaRemember
                                                  Treen nodes, one root, every other node has exactly one parent, so n − 1 edges. Recursive definition: a node on top of some smaller trees (tree words).
                                                  Depth, heightDepth = links from the root (root 0). Height of the tree = largest depth; a one-node tree has height 0 and the empty tree −1.
                                                  DegreeCounts all neighbours, parent included (the slides’ definition).
                                                  Storing itLeftmost child lc + right sibling rs: two pointers per node, n + 1 of them NULL (storing a tree).
                                                  Preorder / postorder / inorderNode first / node last / left, node, right (binary trees only). All O(n) (traversals).
                                                  Binary treeAt most 2 children. Full: 0 or 2 each. A perfect (complete) tree of height h has 2h+1 − 1 nodes (binary trees).

                                                  The tree habit: “what do I do with the root, and what do I let the same procedure do on each subtree?”

                                                  Searching: what one comparison can rule out chapter 6 on one page

                                                  MethodNeedsWorst case (comparisons)
                                                  Linear searchnothingn, and no method can do better on unsorted data (the adversary hides X in an unopened box: adversary)
                                                  Jump search, jump ksorted⌊n/k⌋ + k − 1; best k ≈ √n gives about 2√n − 1 (jump, square root)
                                                  Binary searchsorted array⌊lg n⌋ + 1 (1000 numbers: 10). Doubling the list adds one comparison (binary search)
                                                  Interpolation searchsorted and evenly spreadaverage O(lg lg n) on even data, can be worse than binary search on uneven data (interpolation)
                                                  Hashingexact lookups onlyO(1) on average; no range queries (which to use)

                                                  Unwrapping binary search uses ⌊⌊n/2⌋/2⌋ = ⌊n/4⌋ (write n = 4q + r). The egg puzzle (egg problem) is a search where a wrong toss also costs an egg.

                                                  Binary search trees chapter 7 on one page

                                                  The rule at every node: all keys in the left subtree are smaller and all keys in the right subtree are bigger. It is about whole subtrees, never only about the two children (what a BST is). An inorder walk prints the keys in increasing order.

                                                  OperationHowCost
                                                  Searchcompare with the key, go left or rightO(h)
                                                  Minimum / maximumkeep going left / keep going right (min, max, search)O(h)
                                                  Successorright subtree non-empty: its minimum. Else climb until you come up from a left child: that parent (successor)O(h)
                                                  Insertsearch; the NULL where the search ends is where the new leaf hangs (insertion)O(h)
                                                  Delete0 children: remove. 1 child: splice it out. 2 children: copy the successor’s key into the node and physically remove the successor (deletion)O(h)
                                                  Is this tree a BST?pass a (low, high) range down, or check that the inorder keys increaseO(n)
                                                  Sorted data → treemiddle element is the root, recurse on each halfO(n)

                                                  Height: best ⌊lg n⌋, worst n − 1 (sorted insertion makes a list). Random insertion orders give average height O(lg n), but always deleting with the successor makes the tree lean (how tall, random trees, leaning). Everything depends on the height; a plain BST cannot guarantee it. Practice: PP3 statements and average cost, four algorithms on a search tree, where a new key hangs.

                                                  AVL trees: enforce the height chapter 8 on one page

                                                  • The AVL rule: at every node the heights of the left and right subtrees differ by at most 1 (empty = −1, leaf = 0). Keep the pair of heights beside every node (the rule).
                                                  • Thinnest AVL tree of height h: F(h) = 1 + F(h−1) + F(h−2): 1, 2, 4, 7, 12, 20, 33, 54, 88, 143, … so h ≤ 1.44 lg n, i.e. O(lg n). With 100 nodes the tallest AVL tree has height 8 (how tall, PP3 thinnest trees).
                                                  • A rotation swaps a parent with a child, keeps the inorder list, costs O(1) (rotations).
                                                  Where the extra height sitsNameFix at the lowest broken node
                                                  left child’s left side (outside)left-leftone right rotation (simple cases)
                                                  right child’s right side (outside)right-rightone left rotation
                                                  left child’s right side (inside, zig-zag)left-rightdouble: left rotation at the child, then right rotation at the broken node (why one is not enough)
                                                  right child’s left side (inside, zig-zag)right-leftdouble: right rotation at the child, then left rotation at the broken node
                                                  • Insertion: ordinary insert, climb up updating heights, repair the first broken ancestor. At most one repair is needed. O(lg n) (whole algorithm).
                                                  • Deletion: ordinary delete, climb up from the parent of the node that was cut out, repair every broken node on the way (up to lg n rotations). O(lg n) (deletion).
                                                  • Inserting 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7 gives four left rotations and the perfect tree rooted at 4 (a plain BST would have height 6).

                                                  Practice: PP3 insertion and deletion sequences, AVL facts, pruning leaves, splaying and range queries. Written Assignment 3 (worked solutions included) uses these ideas in trees from a preorder list, BST and AVL, a bitonic array (searching) and a robust QuickSort (next part).

                                                  Part 5 · Chapters 9 to 11

                                                  Sorting and Huffman coding

                                                  The simple sorts and the heap chapter 9 on one page

                                                  • Model: we learn about the order only by comparing two elements; we count comparisons and swaps.
                                                  • Inversion: a pair that is out of order. Sorted: 0. Reversed: n(n−1)/2. Average list: n(n−1)/4 (pair every list with its reverse). A swap of two neighbours removes exactly one inversion, so every neighbour-swapping sort needs Ω(n²) on average (counting).
                                                  • Bubble sort makes n(n−1)/2 comparisons always (8 numbers: 28) and as many swaps as there are inversions (bubble). Insertion sort: swaps = inversions; Θ(n) on a sorted list (insertion). Selection sort: n(n−1)/2 comparisons always but at most n − 1 swaps (selection).
                                                  • Heap: a left-complete binary tree stored in an array; parent ≥ children; node i has children 2i and 2i+1 and parent ⌊i/2⌋ (1-based); the maximum is A[1] (heaps).
                                                  • Heapify (push a number down, swapping with the larger child): O(lg n). BuildHeap (Heapify for i = ⌊n/2⌋ down to 1): O(n) in total, not n lg n, because most nodes are near the leaves (BuildHeap). HeapSort: BuildHeap, then repeat swap root with last, shrink, Heapify the root: O(n lg n), in place (HeapSort).
                                                  • Priority queue: MAXIMUM O(1), INSERT (push up) and DELETE_MAX (swap, Heapify) O(lg n) (priority queues).

                                                  Divide and conquer, and the limit chapter 10 on one page

                                                  • Merge sort: cut in half, sort each half, merge by comparing the two fronts. T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n) = O(n lg n) always; needs an extra array (merge sort). Merging 2 5 9 with 1 3 4 10 takes 6 comparisons (the last 10 is copied for free).
                                                  • PARTITION: pivot v = A[p]; the left finger stops at a number ≥ v, the right finger at a number ≤ v; swap; stop when they meet. About n comparisons (partition). Quick sort: partition, then sort both parts; no merge, no extra array; best and average O(n lg n), worst O(n²) (already sorted with the first element as pivot) (recursion, how fast). Pivot choice: first (risky), random, median of three; the true median is too expensive (pivots).
                                                  • The lower bound: a comparison sort is a binary decision tree (node = comparison, leaf = a possible order). It needs at least n! leaves, a tree of height h has at most 2h, so h ≥ lg(n!) ≥ (n/2) lg n: Ω(n lg n) (detective game, decision tree, the bound).
                                                  • Counting sort: keys 1…k: count, running totals, place from the back (stable); O(n + k) (counting). Radix sort: d digits in base k, rightmost digit first, each pass stable: O((n + k) d) (radix). They beat the bound because they do not compare.

                                                  The “stable?” column is not printed on the slides except for counting and radix sort; it is true for the versions of the code in these chapters.

                                                  • Which one? General and fast in practice: quick sort with a random or median-of-three pivot. A guarantee whatever the input: merge sort (extra array, stable) or heap sort (no extra memory). Small, almost sorted or arriving one by one: insertion sort. Small whole numbers: counting sort. Fixed number of digits: radix sort. Only “the biggest, now” with new items arriving: not a sort, a priority queue.
                                                  • Check the big-O of any written sorting variant by (levels) × (work per level): pieces that shrink by a fixed fraction give logarithmically many levels with at most n elements partitioned per level.

                                                  Huffman coding chapter 11 on one page

                                                  • Fixed vs variable length: variable lengths save space (frequent symbols get short codewords) but the code must stay readable (codes).
                                                  • Prefix code: no codeword is the beginning of another, so decoding is never ambiguous: read bits until they spell a codeword, then start again (prefix codes). Example (slide 3): E = 0, T = 11, N = 100, I = 1010, S = 1011.
                                                  • As a tree: 0 = left, 1 = right; a code is a prefix code exactly when every symbol sits at a leaf; codeword length = leaf depth (code trees).
                                                  • Cost C(T) = Σ wi · di (weight times depth): the total number of bits. Shortcut: the sum of the weights of all inner nodes (cost).
                                                  • Algorithm: put one-leaf trees in a heap; repeat: take the two lightest, join them under a new node whose weight is the sum, put it back. O(n log n) (Huffman’s algorithm).
                                                  • Worked example (weights 3, 5, 9, 14, 16, 35): merge 3+5 = 8; 8+9 = 17; 14+16 = 30; 17+30 = 47; 47+35 = 82. Inner weights add to 8 + 17 + 30 + 47 + 82 = 184, the total cost. Left and right may be mirrored; the cost is the same.
                                                  • Why it is optimal: the two lightest leaves can be made siblings at the bottom (exchange argument), then merge them and use induction on the smaller problem (why it works). Careful: “the two rarest get the longest codewords” is true for some best code, not for every best code, if weights tie.

                                                  The standard moves in a written answer

                                                  1. “Prove by induction.” Claim, base cases (exactly those the recursion has), hypothesis (strong if the recursion calls several smaller sizes), step. Finish with a sentence that says what has been shown (induction).
                                                  2. “Show f = O(g).” Name c and n0 and check the inequality for all n ≥ n0. To disprove, show that no constants can work (symbols, worked).
                                                  3. “Solve the recurrence.” Unwrap two or three times, spot the pattern after i steps, set i so the base case is reached, then prove the guess by induction (unwrapping, worked).
                                                  4. “Give an algorithm.” (1) one sentence for the idea; (2) pseudocode, not C++ (when told so), with indentation; (3) why it is correct (an invariant, or induction); (4) running time; (5) extra space (recipe).
                                                  5. “Running time of this code.” Loops multiply, things in a row add (the biggest wins), recursion becomes a recurrence. State the size you measure in (from the code).
                                                  6. “Show the data structure after each step.” Draw it after every operation, with heights next to tree nodes, probe sequences next to hash keys. Marks are given for the intermediate pictures.
                                                  7. Conventions. Logarithms to base 2 unless told otherwise. Leaf height 0, empty tree −1. Ids and positions may start at 0 or 1: say which, and keep it consistent.

                                                  Final Exam Preparation

                                                  The quiz showed the examiner’s style: small traces, a recurrence, a proof, code with blanks, tight Θ bounds and a “faulty version”. It covered Chapters 1–7. This page drills the same style on the chapters the quiz did not reach (AVL trees, heaps, sorting, Huffman), then gives you one table of tight bounds and a checklist for the exam room.

                                                  In this chapter

                                                    Part 1 · Plan

                                                    How to use this page

                                                    1. Redo the quiz on paper without looking, then mark it with the explanations. Note every lost mark by type (trace, blank, bound, proof, faulty version).
                                                    2. Do the six practice questions below on paper, one sitting each, before opening the answers. They use the course’s own code conventions: Hoare-style PARTITION with pivot A[p], 1-based array heaps, heights counted in edges (empty tree −1).
                                                    3. Learn the bounds table in Part 8 until you can write it from memory, with auxiliary space.
                                                    4. Then go back to the practice problems (PP1, PP2, PP3) and the written assignments for volume.

                                                    Part 2 · Practice 1 · Chapter 7

                                                    P1: deleting from the quiz’s BST

                                                    Use the BST of quiz Q5: root 24; 11 (5, 17); 38 (31, 46); 35 is the right child of 31.

                                                    (a) Give the inorder successor of 24 and of 17. [4] (b) Delete 24 using the successor rule. Draw the result. [4] (c) Complete the blank: the successor of a node u with a right child is Min( (i) ), where Min(v) follows (ii) pointers until null. [4] (d) Give the tight worst-case time of Delete on a BST of height h, and on any BST with n keys. [2]

                                                    Show the worked solution

                                                    (a) Successor = next key in the inorder list 5, 11, 17, 24, 31, 35, 38, 46. Successor of 24 is 31 (the minimum of its right subtree). Successor of 17 is 24: 17 has no right child, so go up until you arrive from a left child (17 is in 11’s right subtree, 11 is 24’s left child).

                                                    (b) 24 has two children. Replace its key by its successor 31, then delete 31 from the right subtree. 31 has only a right child (35), so 35 takes its place. Result: root 31; left 11 (5, 17); right 38 with children 35 and 46. Check: inorder is still sorted.

                                                    (c) (i) u.right; (ii) left.

                                                    (d) Θ(h); over arbitrary shapes Θ(n) (a chain). Only a balanced tree (Chapter 8) makes it Θ(log n).

                                                    Part 3 · Practice 2 · Chapter 8

                                                    P2: insert 10, 20, 30, 25, 28, 27 into an empty AVL tree

                                                    (a) After each insertion that unbalances the tree, name the lowest unbalanced node, the case (LL, LR, RR, RL) and draw the tree after the rotation. [12] (b) What is the height of the final tree (edges)? Is that the smallest possible for 6 keys? [3] (c) Explain in one sentence why at most one (single or double) rotation is needed per insertion. [3]

                                                    Show the worked solution (checked by running AVL insert)
                                                    1. Insert 10, then 20: 10 (right child 20). Balanced.
                                                    2. Insert 30: node 10 has balance −2 (left −1, right 1), and 30 went right-right: RR at 10, single left rotation. Tree: 20 (10, 30).
                                                    3. Insert 25: goes 20 → 30 → left. Tree: 20 (10, 30 (25, ·)). Balanced (20: left 0, right 1).
                                                    4. Insert 28: goes 20 → 30 → 25 → right. Node 30: left height 1, right −1: unbalanced, and 28 went left-right: LR at 30 (rotate left at 25, then right at 30). Tree: 20 (10, 28 (25, 30)).
                                                    5. Insert 27: goes 20 → 28 → 25 → right. Node 20: left 0, right 2: unbalanced, 27 went right-left: RL at 20 (rotate right at 28, then left at 20). Tree: 25 (20 (10, ·), 28 (27, 30)).

                                                    (b) Height 2. A binary tree of height 1 holds at most 3 keys, so 6 keys need height ≥ 2: it is the smallest possible.

                                                    (c) The rotation brings the unbalanced subtree back to the height it had before the insertion, so no ancestor’s balance changes and nothing above needs fixing.

                                                    Trap

                                                    Fix the lowest unbalanced node on the path from the new key, and read the case from the first two steps of the path from that node toward the new key (not from the root).

                                                    Part 4 · Practice 3 · Chapter 9

                                                    P3: a max-heap in A[1..n]

                                                    Heapify(A, i, n): // push A[i] down; subtrees of i are heaps r = i while r <= floor(n / 2): if 2r == n: if A[r] < A[2r]: swap(A[r], A[2r]) break if A[2r] > A[2r+1]: c = 2r else: c = ___(i)___ if A[r] < A[c]: swap(A[r], A[c]); r = ___(ii)___ else: breakBuildHeap(A, n): for i = ___(iii)___ downto 1: Heapify(A, i, n)

                                                    (a) Fill (i)–(iii). [6] (b) Run BuildHeap on A = [4, 1, 3, 2, 16, 9, 10, 14, 8, 7]. [5] (c) Tight bounds: Heapify, BuildHeap, HeapSort; auxiliary space of this Heapify. [4] (d) A student runs the loop of BuildHeap upward, i = 1 to floor(n/2). Does it always build a heap? Use A = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7]. [5]

                                                    Show the worked solution (checked by running the code)

                                                    (a) (i) 2r + 1; (ii) c; (iii) floor(n / 2) (positions after it are leaves, already heaps).

                                                    (b) Result: [16, 14, 10, 8, 7, 9, 3, 2, 4, 1]. Order of work: i = 5 (16 vs child 7: fine), i = 4 (2 sinks below 14), i = 3 (3 swaps with 10), i = 2 (1 sinks: swap with 16, then with 7), i = 1 (4 sinks: swap with 16, 14, 8).

                                                    (c) Heapify Θ(log n) worst case (one root-to-leaf path). BuildHeap Θ(n), not Θ(n log n): most nodes are near the bottom and sink only a little (sum of heights = O(n)). HeapSort Θ(n log n). Space Θ(1): this Heapify is a loop, no recursion.

                                                    (d) No. Upward: i = 1 swaps 1 with 3 and then sinks it below 7 → [3, 2, 7, 4, 5, 6, 1]; i = 2 swaps 2 with 5 → [3, 5, 7, 4, 2, 6, 1]; i = 3: 7 is fine. Final [3, 5, 7, 4, 2, 6, 1]: root 3 < its child 7, not a heap. Heapify assumes both subtrees are already heaps, which only the downward order guarantees. (Correct downward order gives [7, 5, 6, 4, 2, 1, 3].)

                                                    Part 5 · Practice 4 · Chapter 10

                                                    P4: the two-finger PARTITION

                                                    PARTITION(A, p, r): v = A[p]; i = p - 1; j = r + 1 while TRUE: do j-- while ( ___(i)___ ) do i++ while ( ___(ii)___ ) if ( ___(iii)___ ) swap(A[i], A[j]) else return ___(iv)___QuickSort(A, p, r): if p < r: q = PARTITION(A, p, r) QuickSort(A, p, ___(v)___); QuickSort(A, ___(vi)___, r)

                                                    (a) Fill (i)–(vi). [6] (b) Trace PARTITION on A[1..7] = [5, 3, 8, 1, 9, 2, 7]: give every swap and the returned q. [6] (c) A student writes QuickSort(A, p, q − 1); QuickSort(A, q + 1, r). Does it sort the array above? [4] (d) Tight worst-case time and auxiliary space; which input causes it? [4]

                                                    Show the worked solution (checked by running the code)

                                                    (a) (i) A[j] > v; (ii) A[i] < v; (iii) i < j; (iv) j; (v) q; (vi) q + 1.

                                                    (b) v = 5. j stops at 6 (A = 2), i stops at 1 (A = 5): swap → [2, 3, 8, 1, 9, 5, 7]. j stops at 4 (A = 1), i stops at 3 (A = 8): swap → [2, 3, 1, 8, 9, 5, 7]. j stops at 3 (A = 1), i stops at 4 (A = 8): i ≥ j, return q = 3. Left part [2, 3, 1] ≤ 5 ≤ right part [8, 9, 5, 7].

                                                    (c) No. With this PARTITION, A[q] is not the pivot in its final place (A[3] = 1 here). Skipping index q leaves it unsorted: the result is [2, 3, 1, 7, 5, 8, 9]. The q − 1 / q + 1 form belongs to a different partition scheme that puts the pivot at q.

                                                    (d) Θ(n²) time when every split is 1 against n − 1, e.g. an already sorted array (pivot A[p] is the minimum; PARTITION returns q = p). The recursion is then n deep, so auxiliary space is Θ(n) in the worst case. Average and best case Θ(n log n).

                                                    Part 6 · Practice 5 · Chapter 10

                                                    P5: counting sort, keys in 0..k

                                                    CountingSort(A, B, n, k): for i = 0 to k: C[i] = 0 for j = 1 to n: C[A[j]] = C[A[j]] + 1 for i = 1 to k: C[i] = ___(i)___ for j = n downto 1: B[ ___(ii)___ ] = A[j] C[A[j]] = C[A[j]] - 1

                                                    (a) Fill (i) and (ii). [4] (b) Sort the records 2a, 0b, 2c, 1d, 0e (key then label) and give C after the third loop. [4] (c) If the last loop ran j = 1 to n, would B still be sorted? Would it be stable? Why does radix sort care? [5] (d) Time and auxiliary space. [2]

                                                    Show the worked solution (checked by running the code)

                                                    (a) (i) C[i] + C[i - 1] (now C[i] = number of keys ≤ i); (ii) C[A[j]] (the last free position for that key).

                                                    (b) Counts [2, 1, 2] → cumulative C = [2, 3, 5]. Result 0b, 0e, 1d, 2a, 2c: equal keys keep their input order.

                                                    (c) Still sorted, but not stable: it gives 0e, 0b, 1d, 2c, 2a (equal keys reversed). Radix sort sorts by the least significant digit first and relies on each pass being stable, so that the order from earlier digits survives among equal later digits. An unstable pass destroys it.

                                                    (d) Θ(n + k) time and Θ(n + k) auxiliary space (B and C). It beats the Ω(n log n) bound because it never compares keys.

                                                    Part 7 · Practice 6 · Chapter 11

                                                    P6: frequencies a 2, b 3, c 7, d 8, e 10

                                                    (a) Run Huffman’s algorithm: list each merge. [5] (b) Give a codeword length for each letter and the total cost in bits. [4] (c) How many bits would a fixed-length code need? [2] (d) Complete: in each of the (i) iterations, extract the two smallest x and y and insert z with z.freq = (ii). Tight running time with a binary heap? [4]

                                                    Show the worked solution (checked by running Huffman)

                                                    (a) a + b = 5; 5 + c = 12; d + e = 18; 12 + 18 = 30 (root).

                                                    (b) Lengths: a 3, b 3, c 2, d 2, e 2. Cost = 2·3 + 3·3 + 7·2 + 8·2 + 10·2 = 65 bits. Check: the cost also equals the sum of the internal node weights, 5 + 12 + 18 + 30 = 65 ✓ (a quick way to catch arithmetic slips).

                                                    (c) 5 letters need 3 bits each: 30 × 3 = 90 bits.

                                                    (d) (i) n − 1; (ii) x.freq + y.freq. Θ(n log n): BuildHeap Θ(n), then n − 1 rounds of a constant number of Θ(log n) heap operations.

                                                    Part 8 · Reference

                                                    Tight bounds, with auxiliary space

                                                    Auxiliary space follows the quiz convention: input excluded, recursion stack included.

                                                    OperationTime (tight)Aux. spaceRemember
                                                    Binary search (iterative / recursive)Θ(log n) worstΘ(1) / Θ(log n)needs a sorted array
                                                    BFS, DFS (adjacency lists)Θ(|V| + |E|)Θ(|V|)adjacency matrix: Θ(|V|²)
                                                    Hashing with chainingΘ(1 + α) average; Θ(n) worstΘ(1)α = n/m
                                                    Open addressing (linear probing)Θ(m) worstΘ(1)DELETED: search goes on, insert may reuse
                                                    BST search / insert / deleteΘ(h); Θ(n) worst shapeΘ(1) iterative, Θ(h) recursiveh = n − 1 for a chain
                                                    AVL search / insert / deleteΘ(log n)Θ(log n) if recursiveinsert: ≤ 1 (double) rotation; delete: maybe one per level
                                                    Bubble / selection / insertion sortΘ(n²) worst; insertion Θ(n) bestΘ(1)insertion sort = Θ(n + inversions)
                                                    Heapify / BuildHeap / HeapSortΘ(log n) / Θ(n) / Θ(n log n)Θ(1) (loop version)not stable
                                                    Merge sortΘ(n log n) alwaysΘ(n)stable; T(n) = 2T(n/2) + Θ(n)
                                                    QuicksortΘ(n²) worst; Θ(n log n) averageΘ(n) worst stacksorted input with pivot A[p] is the worst case
                                                    Any comparison sortΩ(n log n) worstn/adecision tree has ≥ n! leaves: height ≥ log(n!) = Θ(n log n)
                                                    Counting sort / radix sort (d digits)Θ(n + k) / Θ(d(n + k))Θ(n + k)stable passes are essential for radix
                                                    Huffman with a heapΘ(n log n)Θ(n)cost = sum of internal node weights
                                                    Linked-list one pass (e.g. quiz Split)Θ(n)Θ(1)save next before you overwrite it

                                                    Part 9 · Checklist

                                                    In the exam room

                                                    • Read the conventions box first. Logs base 2; Θ for tight bounds; aux space includes the recursion stack.
                                                    • For each blank, write the invariant in words in the margin, then the expression. Check the blank on an empty input and on one element.
                                                    • Never add statements, variables or side effects to a code completion.
                                                    • For a trace, write the state after every step (queue, stack, table, array). Partial work earns partial marks.
                                                    • For a closed form, check it against the small cases you traced.
                                                    • For induction, label base case, hypothesis and step, and point to where the hypothesis is used.
                                                    • For “faulty version” or “does this violate the claim”: answer Yes/No, then run the given input and point at the exact failing step.
                                                    • Give bounds in the variables asked (h, m, |V| + |E|), not automatically in n.
